It says that at sixteen he was kidnapped by Irish raiders and taken as a slave to Ireland, where he worked six years as a shepherd. Tradition holds that he died on 17 March and was buried at Downpatrick, and many legends grew up around him over the following centuries.

His feast day was already observed by the Irish in Europe in the ninth and tenth centuries as a kind of national day. It was placed on the liturgical calendar of the Catholic Church in the early 1600s, through the influence of the Waterford-born Franciscan scholar Luke Wadding. In the Irish calendar it was seen as the middle day of spring: weather was expected to improve and farmers began to plant potatoes.

Observances generally involve parades and festivals, Irish traditional music sessions and the wearing of green clothing or shamrocks. Saint Patrick is said to have used the shamrock to explain the Holy Trinity to the pagan Irish, a story that first appears in writing in 1726, though it may be older; Patricia Monaghan says there is no evidence the shamrock was sacred to the pagan Irish. The first link between green and Ireland comes from a legend in the 11th-century Lebor Gabála Érenn about Goídel Glas, ancestor of the Gaels.

Parades began in North America in the 18th century but did not reach Ireland until the 20th, and until the late 20th century the day was often a bigger celebration among the diaspora than in Ireland. Irish soldiers in the Montreal Garrison observed it as early as 1759, and Montreal's parade has been held yearly since 1824.

In 1903 the day became an official public holiday in Ireland under the Bank Holiday (Ireland) Act 1903, introduced by the MP James O'Mara. The first parade in Ireland was held in Waterford that year. On the day in 1916 the Irish Volunteers held parades throughout Ireland, and the authorities recorded 38 of them with 6,000 marchers; the Easter Rising began the following month. The day is also a public holiday in Northern Ireland, in Newfoundland and Labrador for provincial government employees, and in Montserrat. Its celebrations have been criticised as commercialised, as linked to heavy drinking and as encouraging stereotypes of the Irish.
saint-petersburg: Saint Petersburg lies in the middle taiga lowlands along the shores of the Neva Bay of the Gulf of Finland, at the head of the Baltic Sea, and on the islands of the Neva delta. The largest of these are Vasilyevsky Island and Petrogradsky Island. In the south the city crosses the Baltic-Ladoga Klint and meets the Izhora Plateau. Before the 17th century the area was inhabited by the Finnic Izhorians and Votians, and Ingrian Finns moved there from Karelia and Savonia under Swedish rule.

Swedish colonists built the fortress of Nyenskans at the mouth of the Neva in 1611, and the small town of Nyen grew up around it. At the end of the 17th century Peter the Great wanted a seaport to trade with the rest of Europe, since the main one, Arkhangelsk on the White Sea, was closed to shipping in winter. On 12 May 1703 (1 May, old style), during the Great Northern War, he captured Nyenskans. On 27 May 1703 (16 May, old style), he laid down the Peter and Paul Fortress on Zayachy Island, the first brick and stone building of the new city. It was named after the apostle Saint Peter.

The city served as the capital of the Tsardom of Russia and of the Russian Empire from 1712 to 1918, except around 1728 to 1730, when Moscow replaced it. After the October Revolution in 1917 the Bolsheviks moved their government to Moscow. The city was renamed Petrograd and then Leningrad after Lenin's death in 1924. It was the site of the siege of Leningrad in World War II, the most lethal siege in history. In June 1991 voters supported restoring the original name, which took effect on 1 October 1991.

The first Russian railway was built there in 1837. The Kunstkamera, whose collection Peter the Great established in 1714 to gather curiosities from around the world, is sometimes considered the first museum in Russia. In 1914 an international chess tournament, partly funded by Tsar Nicholas II, was the first at which the title Grandmaster was formally conferred, on Lasker, Capablanca, Alekhine, Tarrasch and Marshall.

Saint Petersburg is the second-largest city in Russia, with 5,601,911 residents in the 2021 census, and is governed as a federal city. Its historic centre, mostly Baroque and Neoclassical buildings of the 18th and 19th centuries, has been largely preserved. The Historic Centre of Saint Petersburg and Related Groups of Monuments have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The city has more than two hundred museums, the largest being the Hermitage, which occupies the former imperial residence.
saint-pierre-martinique: Saint-Pierre was founded in 1635 by Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc, a French trader and adventurer, as part of the early colonial establishment of Martinique by the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique. Its sheltered bay and position on Caribbean trade routes made it an important port. In the 18th century it became the principal town and de facto capital, with a port economy based on sugar and coffee exports from the surrounding plantations. The Great Hurricane of 1780 sent a storm surge of about 8 metres over the city and destroyed much of its infrastructure; it is estimated to have caused 9,000 deaths on Martinique. The city was rebuilt.

In the 19th century Saint-Pierre had theatres, cafés and newspapers, and a busy port handling much of the island's trade. Wealth was concentrated among plantation owners and merchants. By the late 19th century Fort-de-France was growing in administrative importance because of its harbour and military significance, though Saint-Pierre remained the largest commercial centre.

In the weeks before 1902, Mount Pelée showed ash emissions and seismic disturbances. Pyroclastic flows, called nuées ardentes in French, were not yet understood, and fears centred on lava flows, which were thought unlikely to reach the city because of the surrounding terrain. When the volcano erupted, a fast-moving pyroclastic flow swept through Saint-Pierre and killed about 28,000 people, including refugees from nearby settlements. Accounts name a few survivors, among them the prisoner Louis-Auguste Cyparis and the shoemaker Léon Compère-Léandre.

After the eruption the capital was moved to Fort-de-France, which had not been destroyed, and Saint-Pierre was never rebuilt as a major commercial or administrative centre. It was partly reoccupied but did not regain its former population. It is now a small town, the seat of the Arrondissement of Saint-Pierre, and is designated a City of Art and History. Its historic remains and the Volcanological Museum (Musée Frank-A.-Perret) draw visitors, as do the wrecks of ships sunk in the harbour by the eruption, which divers visit.
saint-pol-de-leon: Saint-Pol-de-Léon, in Breton Kastell-Paol, is a commune in the Finistère department of Brittany, on the coast of north-western France. It lies on a stretch of about 13 kilometres of coastline, with beaches and creeks, and is linked to the Sainte-Anne islet by a strand of sediment called the Groue, which forms the bay of Pempoul with its harbour. Its inhabitants are called Saintpolitains. The Latin name of the region is Léon, in French Pays Léonard.

A well-preserved double stone alley is the last remnant of prehistoric occupation on the site, and several vestiges show a Roman military presence in the 3rd century. From the 6th century the monastery site became an episcopate, called Kastell Paol, and the city grew beyond its walls. It was long the seat of a bishop and became a sort of religious capital. In the 15th century it was a noted spiritual and cultural centre, the Pempoul harbour was rising, and fortified gates protected its 2,000 inhabitants until the 18th century.

A battle of the Breton War of Succession was fought there in the 14th century, in which the Montfortists and their English allies defeated an army led by Charles of Blois. In the 18th century the bishops of Léon strongly influenced the city's architecture: a new episcopal house was built in 1706 and extended in 1750, the seminary dates from 1708 and the Catholic college from 1788.

The French Revolution took away the episcopate, a rich chapter, a college and many religious houses, and a hundred years of economic decline began; Flaubert judged in 1847 that the town was a dead city. The railway of 1883 expanded agricultural production, and in 1890 the town became the main commercial centre in France for the export of vegetables.

The former cathedral, of the 13th century, stands on the site of the original founded by Paul Aurelian in the 6th century and shows the influence of Norman art on Breton architecture. The Kreisker chapel, of the 14th and 15th centuries, has the highest steeple in Brittany at 80 metres. The old episcopal palace is now the town hall, with a monumental staircase, and the town keeps a 16th-century prebendal house in Breton Renaissance style and the Kéroulas manor, built for a noble canon around 1520. The region remains a strong centre of horticultural production.
saint-remigius: Tradition places Remigius's birth at Cerny-en-Laonnois, near Laon, in the highest levels of Gallo-Roman society. He is said to have been the son of Emilius, count of Laon, who is not otherwise attested, and of Saint Celine, and the brother of the Bishop of Soissons, a city Clovis conquered in 487. He studied at Reims and became so noted for learning and sanctity that he was elected Bishop of Reims at 21, though still a layman.

The story of the Vase of Soissons, sacred vessels stolen from the church of Soissons and returned, testifies to friendly relations between Remigius and Clovis. Even before his conversion the king had showered benefits on Remigius and the Christians of Reims. Remigius converted him with the help of Vedast and of Clotilde, the Burgundian princess who was Clovis's wife, and baptised him at Reims in the presence of a large company of Franks and Alamanni. According to Gregory of Tours, 3,000 Franks were baptised with the king. The event was important in the Christianization of the Franks and brought a Nicene Christianity to Germanic lands where most had been converted to Arian Christianity.

Clovis granted Remigius stretches of territory, where he founded and endowed churches. He set up bishoprics at Tournai, Cambrai, Thérouanne, where he personally ordained the first bishop in 499, Arras, where he installed Saint Vedast, and Laon, which he gave to his niece's husband Gunband. In 530 he consecrated Medardus as Bishop of Noyon. Although he never attended a church council, he held a synod at Reims in 517 and converted a bishop of Arian views after a heated discussion.

Few authentic works survive. Four letters are preserved in the Epistulae Austrasicae: his defence in the matter of the priest Claudius, two to Clovis and one to Bishop Falco of Tongres. His Declamations, which Sidonius Apollinaris admired, are lost, and his Testament is apocryphal. His relics were kept in Reims Cathedral, translated by Hincmar to Épernay during the Viking invasions and taken in 1099 to the Abbey of Saint-Rémy. A commissioner of the Convention deliberately desecrated his tomb on 7 October 1793, during the French Revolution, because of its link with royal patronage. His feast day is traditionally 1 October, and the Church of England and the Episcopal Church also honour him then.
saint-sava: Rastko Nemanjić was born in the village of Miščiće in the Deževa Valley, in the area of present-day Novi Pazar, the youngest son of Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja and his wife Ana. With his brothers Vukan and Stefan he belonged to the first generation of the Nemanjić dynasty and received an education in the Byzantine tradition at court. His biographers say he was born after a pause in the couple's childbearing and was especially dear. Made prince of Hum, between the Neretva and Dubrovnik, at an early age, he gained a practical schooling in administration. Teodosije the Hilandarian described him as mild and gentle, loving the poor and respectful of monastic life, with no interest in fame, wealth or the throne.

At Mount Athos Rastko entered the Russian monastery of Saint Panteleimon and took the monastic name Sava. He then spent seven years at the Greek monastery of Vatopedi, learning Greek theological and church literature. When his father tried to persuade him to return, Sava answered that Nemanja had done all that a Christian sovereign should and should join him in the true Christian life. After 14 years on Athos he returned to Serbia in 1206 as hegumen of Studenica, and gave the monastery an independent status in the Studenica Typikon, taking advantage of the chaos that followed the fall of Constantinople to the crusaders in 1204.

In 1219 the patriarchate in exile at Nicaea recognised him as the first Serbian archbishop. It mattered to him that the head of the Serbian Church was appointed by Constantinople and not by Rome. After the crowning of his nephew Radoslav he went on a pilgrimage to Palestine in 1229 and bought two monasteries there for Serbian monks. After the throne passed to Vladislav in 1234 he began a second journey, having named his pupil Arsenije Sremac as successor.

Sava's earliest works were rules for monastic life: the Karyes Typikon, a translation of a standard Greek ascetic typikon, and the Hilandar Typikon, adapted from the Theotokos Euergetis typikon of Constantinople with regulations of his own, both written in 1199. The Hilandar rule became the general order for other Serbian monasteries, and he wrote the Studenica Typikon in 1208. He also founded or reconstructed churches wherever he stayed, and with his father became the great second founder of Hilandar in 1198.

He is venerated as the protector of the Serbs, and his feast day is Savindan. In 1594, when Serbs in Banat rose against the Ottomans carrying his portrait on their war flags, the Ottoman commander Koca Sinan Pasha had his relics brought from Mileševa to Belgrade and burned on 27 April. The Church of Saint Sava in Belgrade stands on the site.
saint-sophia-cathedral-kyiv: Saint Sophia was built as the metropolitan cathedral of Kyiv during the reign of Yaroslav the Wise, and an earlier wooden church of the same name may have existed. It was designed as a burial place for Yaroslav and his descendants, and he was interred in a marble sarcophagus that now stands in the northern inner gallery. The metropolitan bishops of Kyiv were probably buried there too, the earliest known case being Cyril II in the 1280s.

The architects faced a task not previously met, a huge church with spacious choirs, and they departed from the standard Byzantine model. To reduce costs they used local materials: brick cross-shaped pillars instead of marble columns, and slabs of pink Ovruch pyrophyllite slate and ceramic tiles instead of marble. It is one of the largest churches built in Europe in the 11th century.

The interior walls keep early 11th-century mosaics and frescoes. The mosaics cover 260 square metres and the frescoes 3,000. Among the masterpieces are the Pantocrator, the Communion of the Apostles, the Deisis, the Annunciation and the Virgin Orans, which is 6 metres high and dominates the vault of the central apse. Eight craftsmen probably worked on the mosaics, each of which carries an explanatory inscription in Medieval Greek.

Priests and visitors also scratched graffiti into the walls. More than 7,000 drawings and texts from the 11th to the 18th century have been found, some in Glagolitic script. They include a record of the death of Yaroslav the Wise, the autograph of Grand Prince Volodymyr Monomakh and a record of a peace treaty between princes at the end of the 11th century.

From 1497 until 1577 the cathedral stood abandoned, until Bogusz Gulkevych-Glibovsky renovated it at his own expense. After the Union of Brest in 1596 it passed to the Ruthenian Uniate Church, and in the 17th century Mohyla regained it for the Orthodox Metropolis and founded a monastery. The mosaics and frescoes had been whitewashed by 1701, and the art historian Adrian Prakhov rediscovered the mosaics in 1884.

In the 1920s the Soviet government called for the cathedral to be demolished and the grounds made into a park, but it was saved. The National Reserve Sophia of Kyiv was established in 1934, services were banned that year, and the reserve opened to visitors in 1935. Reconstruction work won the European Gold Medal for the Protection of Historic Monuments in 1987, and in 1990 the cathedral was included on the World Heritage List.
saint-thomas-christians: The Saint Thomas Christians are an ethno-religious community of Kerala, on the Malabar coast, who speak Malayalam and use Syriac in worship. According to tradition, Thomas the Apostle came to Muziris, in present-day Pattanam near Kodungallur, in 52 CE, though historians dispute the visit. The earliest known source linking the apostle with India is the Acts of Thomas, probably written in the early 3rd century, perhaps in Edessa. Roman writers of the 3rd and 4th centuries, including Ambrose of Milan, Jerome and Ephrem the Syrian, also mention his journey. Cochin Jews lived in Kerala in the 1st century, so an Aramaic-speaking Jew from Galilee could have made the trip.

As East Syriac Christians immigrated, the community's ties with the Church of the East, centred at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in Persia, strengthened. From the early 4th century the Patriarch supplied India with clergy and holy texts, and about 650 Patriarch Ishoyahb III confirmed his jurisdiction. In the 8th century Patriarch Timothy I organised the Ecclesiastical Province of India under a metropolitan sent from Persia, with a native Archdeacon who held authority over the clergy and considerable secular power.

The community first met the Portuguese in 1498, during Vasco da Gama's expedition. Thriving in the spice trade and protected by its own militia, it quickly allied with the newcomers. The Portuguese set up a Latin hierarchy at Goa and worked to bring the Saint Thomas Christians under its Archbishop. The Synod of Diamper in 1599 imposed the Roman Rite. The Coonan Cross Oath protest of 1653 led to a permanent schism between the Puthankoor, or New Allegiance, who took the West Syriac Rite in communion with the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, and the Old Allegiance. In 1815 the British Resident John Munro founded a seminary at Kottayam and invited Anglican missionaries to teach there.

Today the community is divided among Eastern Catholic, Oriental Orthodox, Protestant and independent churches, each with its own liturgy. It is also divided into the Vadakkumbhagar and the Tekkumbhagar, also called Knanaya, who trace their descent from the merchant Knai Thoma. Their saying runs that they are Indian in culture, Christian in faith and Syrian in liturgy. Church buildings often followed the model of Hindu temples, with a large granite cross in the yard, while the interior follows East Syriac design. The Quilon Syrian copper plates record the building of the church of Tharisapally. Holy Thursday is called Pesaha, from the word for Passover, and the community shares Pesaha Appam after the service.
saint-thomas-u-s-virgin-islands: Saint Thomas is the second largest of the three main islands of the U.S. Virgin Islands, between Saint Croix, the largest, and Saint John, the smallest. It has a land area of 32 square miles (83 km2). Crown Mountain is its highest point and the highest in the whole territory. The coast holds a number of natural bays and harbours, among them Magens Bay, Great Bay and Long Bay, and the climate is tropical savanna, with a drier and a wetter season.

The island was first settled around 1500 BCE by the Ciboney, and later inhabited by the Arawaks and then the Caribs. Christopher Columbus sighted the island in 1493 on his second voyage and named the group after the legend of Saint Ursula and her 11,000 virgins. The Dutch West India Company established a post on Saint Thomas in 1657. A first Danish attempt at settlement in 1665 failed.

The Danes resettled the island in 1672 under the Glueckstadt Company, later the Danish West India Company. The first slave ships arrived in 1673, and Saint Thomas became a slave market. In 1685 the Danes leased part of the island to the Brandenburger Company, which was resold to them in 1754, and the island was granted free port status in 1764. The land was divided into plantations and sugarcane became the main economic activity, so that the economies of Saint Thomas, Saint John and Saint Croix depended on enslaved African labour and the slave trade.

In 1915 David Hamilton Jackson persuaded the king of Denmark to allow freedom of the press in the islands and began their first newspaper, The Herald. In 1917 the United States bought Saint Thomas, with Saint Croix and Saint John, for $25 million in gold, as part of a strategy to hold the Caribbean and the Panama Canal during the First World War; the transfer took place on 31 March 1917. Residents received United States citizenship in 1927, the Organic Act of 1954 gave the islands territorial status and a local senate, and full home rule came in 1970.

Charlotte Amalie, on Saint Thomas, is the territorial capital and port of the United States Virgin Islands. The census of 2020 counted 42,261 people on the island. A Jewish community that developed in Charlotte Amalie from 1796 established the synagogue Beracha Veshalom Vegmiluth Hasadim, the second oldest in the United States.
saint-valery-sur-somme: Saint-Valery-sur-Somme is a commune in the Somme department, a seaport and resort on the south bank of the estuary of the River Somme. It lies on the Hauts-de-France coast by the Baie de la Somme, 30 kilometres north-west of Abbeville and west of the battlefields of the Somme. The river is canalised, with sea locks at the eastern end of the town, and the Canal de la Somme runs straightened from here to Abbeville. A narrow-gauge tourist railway, the Chemin de Fer de la Baie de Somme, has a station in the town.

The settlement dates from before the Roman invasion, when it was a small settlement inhabited by Gauls; after the Romans left it came under the power of the Franks. In 611 the monk Gualaric, also known as Valery, arrived and settled as a hermit on the headland of Leuconaus, now Cap Hornu. His virtue and miracles attracted disciples, who formed a primitive abbey. He was buried there in 622, Clotaire II, King of Neustrie, provided the foundations of the new abbey in 627, and the sailors' chapel was built over his tomb in 628. His relics drew many pilgrims, and the abbey and village were plundered by the Vikings several times in the 8th and 9th centuries.

The village grew in the 10th and 11th centuries and was historically significant as the place where William the Conqueror assembled his fleet before sailing to invade England in 1066. During the Hundred Years' War it passed between French, English and Burgundian control, and the English demolished the abbey and cloister to strengthen the nearby castle. In 1431 Joan of Arc was held prisoner in the local prison before being taken to Rouen, and a stone tower where tradition says she was detained survives.

The 15th, 16th and 17th centuries brought peace and prosperity. The abbey was rebuilt, and the port flourished through the export of wine and a growing herring industry; it lay near enough to Paris to be an early supplier of the chasse-marée merchants. The town was also a site of conflict between Protestants and Catholics and, later, during the French Revolution. In the 19th century Victor Hugo, Jules Verne, Alfred Sisley and Edgar Degas all had villas there at one time or another, and Anatole France lived in a house that can still be seen.

Fishing is in marked decline because of the silting of the bay, and tourism now dominates the economy. The medieval character of the town, its ramparts, its Gothic church and its long waterside boardwalk draw visitors. Each July a festival commemorates the departure of William the Conqueror, and the town is twinned with Battle in the United Kingdom and Ronse in Belgium.
saint-vitus: Vitus, sometimes rendered Guy or Guido, was a Christian martyr from Sicily, and the dates of his actual life are unknown. The earliest testimony to his veneration is a note in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, found in its three most important manuscripts and so probably in their common exemplar of the fifth century. J. P. Kirsch held that this public veneration shows he was a historical martyr, though no historical accounts of him survive. Modestus and Crescentia were originally separate traditions that later became combined with his, and they are probably fictitious.

A purely fanciful account appeared in the sixth and seventh centuries. It makes Vitus the seven-year-old son of a senator of Lucania, who resisted his father's attempts to turn him from his faith and fled with his tutor Modestus and Modestus's wife Crescentia, his nanny. In Rome he drove a demon from a son of Emperor Diocletian, but because he stayed Christian he and his tutors were tortured, and they died in Lucania.

According to the hagiography Vitus died in the Diocletianic Persecution in 303. His veneration spread rapidly in southern Italy and Sicily. In 756 Abbot Fulrad is said to have brought his relics to the monastery of St-Denis, and in 836 Abbot Warin of Corvey in Germany transferred some to his abbey, from which the cult spread through Westphalia and eastern and northern Germany. In 925 King Henry I of Germany gave the bones of one hand to Wenceslaus, Duke of Bohemia, and this relic remains in the Saint Vitus Cathedral in Prague.

In the Middle Ages he was counted among the Fourteen Holy Helpers, and in Germany his feast on 15 June was marked with dancing before his statue. The dancing gave its name to Saint Vitus' Dance, the neurological disorder Sydenham's chorea, and made him patron of dancers and entertainers. In Slavic lands his name, Sveti Vid, may have replaced the older worship of the god Svetovid, and in Serbia his feast, Vidovdan, is tied to the Battle of Kosovo. He is shown as a young man with a palm leaf, in a cauldron of boiling tar and molten lead from which, according to the legend, he escaped unharmed.
sainte-marie-aux-mines: Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines (German: Markirch) is a commune in the Haut-Rhin department and Grand Est region of France. It lies in the Vosges, where it occupies the V-shaped valley of the Lièpvrette River, which separates the town into two parts and formerly into two parishes. Lorraine can be reached by road over the Col de Sainte-Marie (772 metres) or the Tunnel Maurice-Lemaire, and Sélestat lies 26 km to the east. The valley is sometimes called the Val d'Argent, the Silver Valley. Early Latin documents call the town Fanum S. Mariae or S. Maria ad Fodinas, and in year II of the Republic it was named Val-aux-Mines.

The town owes its fame to its mines, and its whole development was shaped by their working. A hypothesis that Gallo-Romans began mining there in the 2nd or 3rd century was suggested but quickly abandoned for lack of documents; Robert Forrer revived it in 1927 from antimony found in coins. According to a monk of the 13th century, a monk named Blidulphe founded the convent of Échéry in the 10th century, and the monks soon found that the valley was rich in ore. They were then threatened in their possessions by the family of Échéry, who built the castle of Hoh-Eckerich in the 13th century and eventually monopolised the mines.

The first mention of the place dates from 1078, when Theodoric II, Duke of Lorraine, returned the tithes to the convent of Lièpvre, of which his father Gérard of Alsace had deprived it in 1052. The silver mines of the valley are mentioned as early as 963. The town itself, in Latin Sancte Maria ad Fodinas, owes its name and its origin to the working of the mines and to a church of Saint Mary, and it is mentioned for the first time in 1317. Between 1795 and 1802 the valley was temporarily divided in two, with Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines in one part and four other municipalities centred on Sainte-Croix-aux-Mines in the other.

The coat of arms granted on 28 July 1892 shows the arms of Ribeaupierre and of Lorraine with a shield of crossed mining hammers, recalling both the divided political position of the town before the Revolution and its mining industry. On 31 January 1945 Eddie Slovik, the only U.S. soldier of World War II executed for desertion, was shot by firing squad near the town.

The Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines Mineral Show is an international fair on mining products and nature-related arts. It goes back to the early 1960s, when François Lehmann organised a small mineral exhibition, and it took its present form in 1966. It now hosts more than 900 exhibitors from 60 countries in the streets of the old town, with visits to mines of the Val d'Argent.
saipan: Saipan lies about 190 kilometres north of Guam and 9.3 kilometres north-east of Tinian, from which the Saipan Channel separates it. It is about 19 kilometres long and 9 kilometres wide, with a land area of 115.38 square kilometres. The western side is lined with sandy beaches and an offshore coral reef that creates a large lagoon, while the eastern shore is mostly rugged rocky cliffs. Archaeologists have found traces of human settlement over 4,000 years old, including petroglyphs and latte stones. Saipan is one of the main homes of the Chamorro and the Carolinians, the indigenous people of the Mariana Islands.

Spanish rule began in the 17th century, and the island was possibly first sighted by Europeans during Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, which landed in the southern Marianas on 6 March 1521. After the Spanish–American War of 1898 the United States occupied Saipan, but Spain sold it to the German Empire under the German–Spanish Treaty of 1899. Germany administered it as part of German New Guinea and made no attempt to develop or settle it.

Japan captured the island in 1914 and was awarded formal control in 1919 by the League of Nations as part of the South Seas Mandate. From the 1920s settlers from Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Okinawa developed large sugar plantations, and the South Seas Development Company built refineries, ports, roads and schools. By October 1943 there were 29,348 Japanese settlers and 3,926 Chamorro and Carolinian islanders.

Japan treated Saipan as part of the last line of defence of the homeland and garrisoned it heavily, with nearly 30,000 troops by mid-1944. The Battle of Saipan lasted from 15 June to 9 July 1944; American forces landed on the south-western beaches and took the island after more than three weeks of heavy fighting, at a cost of 3,426 killed and 10,364 wounded. After the war Saipan became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States. The Northern Mariana islanders voted to join the United States in 1975, and the island became a municipality of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands in 1978. Islanders became United States citizens on 4 November 1986.

About 90 per cent of the population of the Northern Mariana Islands lives on Saipan, and since the whole island is one municipality most publications call it the Commonwealth's capital. The legislative and executive branches of government are in the village of Capitol Hill and the judicial branch in Susupe. Most of the native Chamorro and Carolinian population is Roman Catholic. Sites from the past include latte stones, the Last Command Post of the Battle of Saipan and a Japanese lighthouse built in 1934.
saito-makoto: Saito Makoto was born on 27 October 1858 in Mizusawa Domain, Mutsu Province, now part of Oshu in Iwate Prefecture, the son of a samurai of the Mizusawa clan. In 1879 he graduated from the 6th class of the Imperial Japanese Naval Academy, ranking third of 17 cadets, and in 1882 he was commissioned an ensign. From 1884 he spent four years in the United States as a military attache, and after his return in 1888 he served on the Imperial Japanese Navy General Staff.

During the First Sino-Japanese War he captained the cruisers Akitsushima and Itsukushima. He became Vice Minister of the Navy in 1898, rear admiral in 1900 and, in the Russo-Japanese War, vice admiral on 6 June 1904. He served as Navy Minister from 1906 to 1914, continually striving to expand the navy, was made a baron in 1907 and became a full admiral in 1912. He was forced to resign in April 1914 over implications of involvement in the Siemens scandal.

In September 1919 Saito was appointed third Japanese Governor-General of Korea, right after the culmination of the Korean independence movement, and was immediately the target of an assassination attempt by the radical Korean nationalist Kang Woo-kyu. He served in 1919-1927 and again in 1929-1931, implementing measures to moderate Japan's policies on Koreans, and was raised to viscount in 1925. In 1927 he was a member of the Japanese delegation to the Geneva Naval Conference on disarmament.

After fanatical navy officers assassinated Prime Minister Inukai Tsuyoshi on 15 May 1932, the May 15 Incident, Prince Saionji Kinmochi, trying to stop the slide towards a military take-over, chose Saito as a compromise. Sadao Araki remained War Minister and made demands on the new government. During Saito's tenure Japan recognised the independence of Manchukuo and withdrew from the League of Nations. His cabinet resigned en masse on 8 July 1934 because of the Teijin Incident bribery scandal, and Keisuke Okada succeeded him.

Saito became Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal in December 1935. He was assassinated at his home in Yotsuya, Tokyo, during the February 26 Incident of 1936, the same day as his predecessor as prime minister Takahashi Korekiyo, and was posthumously awarded the Supreme Order of the Chrysanthemum.
sajid-dynasty: The Sajids were a Muslim dynasty of Iranian origin, also known as the Banu Saj. They came from the Central Asian province of Ushrusana and were of Sogdian descent, culturally Arabised. Abu'l-Saj Devdad had fought under the Ushrusanan prince Afshin Khaydar in his final campaign against the rebel Babak Khorramdin in Azerbaijan, and later served the caliphs.

His son Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj was appointed ruler of Azerbaijan in 889 or 890. As the authority of the Abbasid Caliphate weakened, Muhammad was able to form a virtually independent state. Coins in his name were minted in 898-900, and he incorporated much of the South Caucasus into the Sajid state. The first capital was Maragha, though the Sajids usually resided at Barda. Much of their energy went into attempts to take control of neighbouring Armenia.

Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj came to power in 901, demolished the walls of Maragha and moved the capital to Ardabil. His state reached the Caspian Sea in the east and the cities of Ani and Dabil (Dvin) in the west. Relations with the caliph were poor. A large army sent by Caliph al-Muqtadir forced Yusuf to pay a tribute of 120 thousand dinars a year, and the vizier Abu'l-Hasan Ali ibn al-Furat helped to make peace. Yusuf then received investiture as governor of Azerbaijan from the caliph in 909. After ibn al-Furat's dismissal in 912 he stopped paying the annual tax.

According to the historian Abbasgulu aga Bakikhanov, the Sajids made the Shirvanshah Mazyadids dependent on them between 908-909 and 919. Raiders described as Russian attacked Sajid territory down the Volga in 913-914, and Yusuf repaired the wall of Derbent. In 914 he campaigned in Georgia from Tbilisi, occupying Kakheti and capturing the fortresses of Ujarma and Bochorma.

The dynasty's chronology lists Muhammad (889-901), Devdad (901), Yusuf (901-919), Subuk, a servant of the Sajids who acted as caretaker (919-922), Yusuf again (922-928) and Fath ibn Muhammad (928-929). Fath, the last ruler, was poisoned in Ardabil by one of his slaves. This ended the dynasty and later allowed the Sallarid dynasty to expand into Azerbaijan in 941.
sajudis: In the mid-1980s the leadership of the Communist Party of Lithuania hesitated to embrace Mikhail Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost. The death in 1987 of Petras Griškevičius, first secretary of the party, was followed only by the appointment of another rigid communist, Ringaudas Songaila. Encouraged by Gorbachev's rhetoric, by the strengthening of Solidarity in Poland and by the Pope and the U.S. Government, Baltic independence activists began to hold public demonstrations in Riga, Tallinn and Vilnius.

On 3 June 1988, at a meeting at the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences, communist and non-communist intellectuals formed the Sąjūdis Initiative Group to organise a movement supporting glasnost, democratisation and perestroika. It had 35 members, mostly artists, and 17 of them were party members. In October 1988 a founding conference in Vilnius elected a 35-member council, chaired by Vytautas Landsbergis, a professor of musicology who was not a party member.

Sąjūdis used mass meetings. A gathering on 21 June 1988 was followed by others, one in Vingis Park in July with about 100,000 people and one on 23 August 1988 with about 250,000, protesting against the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and its secret protocol. A samizdat paper, Sąjūdis News, appeared on 19 June 1988, and about 150 newspapers in all supported the movement. Its demands included the Lithuanian language as the official language, the truth about the Stalinist years, protection of the environment and a halt to a third reactor at the Ignalina nuclear power plant. Its candidates won 36 of the 40 districts they contested in elections to the Congress of People's Deputies.

In February 1989 Sąjūdis declared that Lithuania had been forcibly annexed and that its goal was restoring independence. Lithuanian sovereignty was proclaimed in May 1989. On 23 August 1989 a human chain of two million people, 600 kilometres long, linked Tallinn and Vilnius, which became known as the Baltic Way. In December the Communist Party of Lithuania seceded from the Soviet party and gave up its monopoly on power. In February 1990 Sąjūdis and its supporters won 101 of 141 seats in the Supreme Council, which elected Landsbergis its chairman and declared the restoration of independence on 11 March 1990.

About a month after independence, reform communists and Vilnius liberal intellectuals left Sąjūdis, partly over growing nationalist rhetoric. Some formed the Independence Party, and liberal members helped found the Liberal Union of Lithuania. The movement lost support in rural areas over its agricultural reforms, and in 1992 its coalition lost the Seimas elections to the Democratic Labour Party, the former Communist Party. Many members, including Landsbergis, formed the core of the Homeland Union.
saka-era: The Shaka era, also called the Shalivahana era, is a historical Hindu calendar era whose epoch, its year zero, corresponds to 78 CE. It counts elapsed years, as a person's age is counted. Its origin is highly controversial. Scholars distinguish an Old Shaka era, whose epoch is uncertain and which ancient Buddhist and Jaina inscriptions and texts are thought to use, from the Shaka era of 78 CE, common in the inscriptions of southern India.

The beginning of the era of 78 CE is now widely equated with the accession of the Indo-Scythian king Chashtana. His inscriptions at Andhau in Kutch, dated to the years 11 and 52, are read as Shaka years 11 (89 CE) and 52 (130 CE). An older view tied it to the accession of Kanishka I, but Henry Falk's research placed Kanishka's accession in 127 CE, and Kanishka was a Kushana, not a Shaka.

The name Shalivahana rests on a legend, reported by Brahmagupta in the 7th century CE, by al-Biruni and by others, that a grandson of the emperor Vikramaditya of tradition defeated the Shakas in 78 CE. The historian Dineshchandra Sircar called this notion historically inaccurate. He thought it drew on the victory of the Satavahana ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni over Shaka (Western Kshatrapa) kings, and perhaps on the Vikrama legend. In time the word Shaka became generic and came to mean an era.

The earliest known users of the era were the Western Satraps, the Shaka rulers of Ujjain. From the reign of Rudrasimha I (178-197) they recorded the minting date on their coins in the Shaka era, in Brahmi numerals. Its use survived into the Gupta period and became part of Hindu tradition after the decline of Buddhism in the Indian subcontinent. It was in widespread use by the 6th to 7th centuries, for instance in the works of Varahamihira and Brahmagupta, and by the 7th century it also appears in inscriptions in Hindu Southeast Asia.

It remained in use in India and Southeast Asia through the medieval period, with the Vikram Samvat era (56 BCE) as the main alternative in traditional Hindu timekeeping. It is still used in the Balinese saka calendar, and it was adopted as the era of the Indian national calendar in 1957. The official year is tied to 22 March in the Gregorian calendar, or 21 March in a leap year. The lunisolar Shalivahana Shaka remains in wide use in southern and western India for religious purposes and for some secular ones, such as sowing.
sakamoto-ryoma: Sakamoto Ryoma was born on 3 January 1836 in Kochi, in the Tosa Domain on Shikoku. His family held the rank of country samurai, the lowest in the samurai hierarchy, which earlier generations had bought with wealth gained as sake brewers. Tosa strictly separated high-ranking from low-ranking samurai, and the two groups lived in segregated areas. Unwilling to study, he took up fencing at fourteen and became a master swordsman. In 1853 his domain allowed him to go to Edo, where he trained at the Chiba Dojo and became a teacher there.

The arrival of Commodore Matthew C. Perry in 1853 and the Convention of Kanagawa of 1854 damaged the prestige of the shogun, and Sakamoto came to support returning power to the Imperial Court in Kyoto. In 1862 he left Tosa without permission, a step that carried the death penalty, and worked against the shogunate under the alias Saitani Umetaro. He set out to kill Katsu Kaishu, a Tokugawa official who favoured modernisation, but Katsu persuaded him of the need for a long-term plan to strengthen Japan, and Sakamoto became his assistant.

In 1866 Sakamoto took part in negotiating the secret Satcho Alliance between the Satsuma and Choshu domains, long enemies. His role as a neutral outsider is often said to have been decisive, but the critical part was played by Komatsu Tatewaki. With Satsuma's help he founded the private navy and trading company Kameyama Shachu in Nagasaki, which later became the Kaientai. In March 1866 shogunate agents ambushed him at the Teradaya inn in Kyoto; his future wife, Narasaki Ryo, warned him, and he fought them off with a revolver.

In 1867 he drafted the Eight Proposals While Shipboard with Goto Shojiro, calling for an elected two-chamber legislature, a constitution, a national army and navy and regulated exchange rates for gold and silver. His negotiations for Tosa helped bring about the voluntary resignation of the shogun Tokugawa Yoshinobu.

On 10 December 1867 assassins attacked Sakamoto and his associate Nakaoka Shintaro at the Omiya Inn in Kyoto. Sakamoto died that night, at 31, and Nakaoka two days later. Early reports blamed the Shinsengumi, and its leader Kondo Isami was executed on that charge, but members of the Mimawarigumi, another pro-shogunate group, confessed in 1870. The true assassin has never been proved. His proposals are thought to form the basis of the parliamentary system Japan adopted afterwards, and he has been heavily romanticised in Japanese popular culture.
sakarya-river: The Sakarya runs through the region known in ancient times as Phrygia. The source of the river is the Bayat Plateau, north-east of Afyon. It is joined by the Porsuk Creek close to the town of Polatlı and runs through the Adapazarı Plains before it reaches the Black Sea. Four dams stand on it, which from downstream to upstream are Akçay, Yenice, Gökçekaya and Sarıyar.

In Greek classical antiquity the river was considered one of the principal rivers of Asia Minor and is mentioned in the Iliad and in Theogony. Its name appears as Sagraphos, Sangaris or Sagaris. Strabo wrote that it had its sources on Mount Adoreus, near the town of Sangia in Phrygia, not far from the border with Galatia, and flowed in a very tortuous course: east, then north, then north-west and finally north through Bithynia into the Euxine, the Black Sea. Part of its course formed the boundary between Phrygia and Bithynia. Its Bithynian part was navigable and noted for the abundance of fish. Its principal tributaries were the Alander, the Bathys, the Thymbres and the Gallus.

Pseudo-Plutarch told that a man named Sagaris, who often derided the priests of the Mother of the Gods, was struck with madness by her and threw himself into the river Xerobates, which from then on was called Sagaris. The Sangarius Bridge was built by the Eastern Roman Emperor Justinian I, who reigned from 527 to 565. In the 13th century the valley formed part of the border between the Eastern Roman Empire and the home of the Söğüt tribe. By 1280 Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos had built a series of fortifications along the river, but a flood in 1302 changed its course and made them useless. The Söğüt tribe migrated across the river and later established the Ottoman Empire.
sakhalin: Sakhalin is 948 km long and 25 to 170 km wide, with an area of 72,492 square kilometres, and separates the Sea of Okhotsk from the Sea of Japan. Its north coast lies 6.5 km from the Russian mainland across the narrow Strait of Tartary, and its southern tip lies 40 km north of Hokkaido across the La Pérouse Strait. Nearly two thirds of the island is mountainous. The name comes from the Manchu Sahaliyan, meaning black, which is also the Manchu name of the Amur River.

Humans lived on Sakhalin in the Neolithic. The Ainu live in the southern half, the Oroks in the centre and the Nivkhs in the north. The Ainu later paid tribute to the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties, which called the island Kuyedao, the island of the Ainu; control from China was mostly loose and there was no fixed border. Japan proclaimed sovereignty over the whole island in 1845, holding it to be an extension of Hokkaido, against competing Russian claims, and Russian settlers began to establish coal mines, schools and churches.

The Treaty of Shimoda of 1855 allowed nationals of both countries to live on the island, Russians in the north and Japanese in the south, with no clear boundary. Japan surrendered its claims in the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1875 in exchange for the northern Kuril Islands. Under the Treaty of Portsmouth of 1905 Japan received the part south of the 50th parallel, which it governed as Karafuto Prefecture, with its capital at Toyohara, now Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The Soviet Union invaded southern Sakhalin on 11 August 1945 and completed the conquest on 25 August.

Sakhalin is the largest island of Russia and is administered as part of Sakhalin Oblast. Its population is roughly 500,000, most of them Russians, and the indigenous Ainu, Oroks and Nivkhs are present in very small numbers. Most Ainu on Sakhalin moved to Hokkaido in 1949, when Japanese civilians were displaced from the island.
sakhalin-oblast: Sakhalin Oblast, in the Russian Far East, has an area of 87,100 square kilometres. It borders by sea Khabarovsk Krai to the west and Kamchatka Krai to the north, and Hokkaido in Japan to the south. The name Sakhalin goes back to the Manchu hydronym Sahaliyan Ula, meaning Black River, the Amur. The indigenous peoples of Sakhalin are the Nivkh, Orok and Ainu, the Ainu historically living in the southern part of the island and the Nivkh mainly in the north.

Mamiya Rinzō, who explored and mapped the island in 1809, showed that it is not attached to the Asian continent, and the Russian navigator Gennady Nevelskoy recorded this definitively in 1849. Japan proclaimed sovereignty over the whole island in 1845, but Russian settlers ignored the claim and from the 1850s set up coal mines, prisons and churches. In 1875 the Treaty of Saint Petersburg gave all of it to Russia in exchange for the Kuril Islands, and in 1905 the Treaty of Portsmouth passed the part below 50° N to Japan, which administered it as Karafuto.

In August 1945 the Soviet Union took over the whole of Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands, and by 2 January 1947 the present boundaries of the oblast were set. Most Japanese residents were repatriated, but at least a third of the Koreans who had arrived in the late 1930s and early 1940s were refused permission to leave, and they and their descendants became known as the Sakhalin Koreans. Japan does not count the southern Kuril Islands, which it calls the Northern Territories, as included in its renunciation under the Treaty of San Francisco of 1952.

The administrative centre and largest city is Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk. The population was 466,609 at the 2021 census, and most inhabitants descend from Russian and other Slavic settlers. Oil and natural gas are drilled on and around the island, and coal and some manganese have been mined there since the 1920s. The 1995 Neftegorsk earthquake killed 1,989 people, and the settlement was not rebuilt.
sakoku: The word sakoku comes from the Sakoku-ron, a manuscript written in 1801 by the astronomer and translator Shizuki Tadao while translating a work by the seventeenth-century German traveller Engelbert Kaempfer. Scholars now often prefer kaikin, "maritime prohibitions", the term used at the time, since trade prospered and the country was far from closed.

Conventionally the shogunate is held to have imposed the policy to remove Spanish and Portuguese colonial and religious influence, seen as a threat to stability, with the rising number of Catholic converts in Kyūshū a main concern. Some historians since the 1970s call this only a partial explanation. They point to the shogunate's wish to control foreign policy and to keep the tozama daimyō, who had profited from East Asian trade, from growing strong, and to direct trade through Nagasaki to raise revenue. The direct trigger is said to have been the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637-38, an uprising of 40,000 mostly Christian peasants.

Under Tokugawa Iemitsu a series of edicts from 1633 to 1639 banned almost all foreign nationals from entering Japan and kept Japanese people from leaving. After the rebellion missionaries were expelled and Christianity was banned on penalty of death; the remaining Christians, mostly around Nagasaki, formed underground communities called Kakure Kirishitan.

Japan traded with five entities through four gateways. Chinese merchants and the Dutch East India Company traded at Nagasaki, the Dutch confined to the island of Dejima, where conditions were humiliating. The Sō clan of Tsushima dealt with Joseon Korea, the Matsumae domain traded with the Ainu, and Satsuma controlled the Ryūkyū Kingdom. Western learning entered through Rangaku, Dutch studies.

Foreign attempts to open Japan were mostly rejected. In 1640 the Portuguese Macau embassy was captured, its ship burnt and 61 members executed. Russian, British and American visitors followed in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, and in 1825 the shogunate ordered coastal authorities to drive away foreign ships. It relaxed this in 1842 after news of China's defeat in the Opium War.

On 8 July 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry arrived in Edo Bay with four ships. He returned with eight, and the Convention of Kanagawa of 31 March 1854 established relations with the United States. The Anglo-Japanese Friendship Treaty followed that year, the Treaty of Shimoda with Russia in 1855 and the Harris Treaty in 1858. Japanese intellectuals widely regarded these Ansei Treaties as unequal.
saladin: Saladin was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq. His personal name was Yusuf; Salah ad-Din is an honorific meaning Righteousness of the Faith. His parents were of Kurdish Rawadiya ancestry, a tribe originally of Arab descent that had become Kurdicized, and his father Najm al-Din Ayyub was a Kurdish mercenary. His military career began under his paternal uncle Shirkuh, a commander in the service of Nur al-Din. In 1164, aged 26, Saladin went with Shirkuh to Egypt to help restore the vizier Shawar, though his role in that expedition was minor.

Shirkuh and Saladin returned in 1169, when Amalric I of Jerusalem besieged Cairo; Shirkuh became vizier and died the same year, and the Fatimid caliph al-Adid appointed Saladin. In 1171, after al-Adid's death, the Abbasid khutba was pronounced in Cairo, ending the Isma'ili Fatimid Caliphate and returning Egypt to the Sunni Abbasid caliph. After Nur al-Din died in 1174, Saladin peacefully entered Damascus, took Hama and Homs, defeated the Zengids at the Battle of the Horns of Hama in 1175 and was proclaimed Sultan of Egypt and Syria by the Abbasid caliph. By 1182 he had taken Aleppo, though he failed to take Mosul, and he escaped two attempts on his life by the Order of Assassins.

On 25 November, at Montgisard near Ramla, a small Templar force surprised his army and he fled to Egypt. His army defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187, and Jerusalem capitulated on 2 October 1187. Balian of Ibelin threatened to kill the Muslim hostages and destroy the Dome of the Rock if quarter were refused, and Saladin accepted terms allowing ransom. About 18,000 poorer citizens were ransomed through a collection, while another 15,000 were enslaved.

Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem prompted the Third Crusade (1189 to 1192), partly financed by a special Saladin tithe in 1188. Saladin died of a fever at Damascus on 4 March 1193, having given away most of his wealth; he was buried in a mausoleum beside the Umayyad Mosque. Medieval Europeans held him up as a model of kingship, and Dante placed him among the virtuous non-Christians in limbo. His reputation had been largely forgotten in the Muslim world, eclipsed by figures such as Baybars, until the 19th century, when Walter Scott's romantic portrayal and Wilhelm II's visit to his tomb in 1898 helped to make him a hero of the struggle against the West in the Arab world.
salamanca: Salamanca lies on the northern half of the Meseta Central, in the west-central part of the Iberian Peninsula, straddling the Tormes river, in the comarca of Campo Charro. It is the capital of the Province of Salamanca and stands 64 kilometres from Zamora, 121 kilometres from Valladolid and 123 kilometres from Portugal. The three small hills on which settlements grew, formed by the erosion of two streams, and the nearness of the river suited the early functions of defence and control of the surrounding land.

The Iron Age hilltop site of Cerro de San Vicente, on the right bank of the Tormes, is the first stable settlement, dating to the 7th century BCE. By the 3rd century BCE a settlement at the Teso de las Catedrales had consolidated under the influence of the Vaccaei and Vettones, Celtic tribes. After Roman conquest it became the civitas of Salmantica. After the Roman period the Alans, then the Visigoths, held it, and in 589 it was an episcopal seat that sent bishops to the councils of Toledo. Christian resettlement under the Kingdom of León, led by Raymond of Burgundy, took hold in the 11th century.

Salamanca joined the revolt of the Communities of Castile in 1520 against the taxes of Charles V, and afterwards the king had the upper parts of the towers of the rebels' palaces removed. During the Peninsular War the city was occupied by the troops of Marshal Soult in 1809 and stayed in French hands until the Battle of Arapiles in 1812, when an Anglo-Portuguese army under Wellington defeated Marmont's French army. The French destroyed much of the city for building materials, including the university's colegios mayores.

The University of Salamanca received its royal charter as an Estudio General from Alfonso IX of León in 1218. It was the first institution to receive the title of university, in 1254, and under Alfonso X its schools of canon and civil law drew students even from Paris and Bologna. Antonio de Nebrija's grammar of Spanish appeared here in 1492, and Hernán Cortés studied here briefly before leaving in 1501.

The Old City was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. It holds the Baroque Plaza Mayor, designed by Alberto and Nicolás Churriguera, the Casa de las Conchas, whose facade carries about 350 scallop shells, and two cathedrals, the Romanesque Old Cathedral of the 12th century and the much larger Gothic New Cathedral, begun in the 16th century and completed in the 18th. The city had 144,458 inhabitants in 2024 and its Holy Week processions are of international tourist interest.
salamis-cyprus: Salamis lay on the east coast of Cyprus at the mouth of the river Pedieos, 6 km (3.7 mi) north of modern Famagusta. According to tradition its founder was Teucer, son of Telamon, king of the Greek island of Salamis, who could not return home after the Trojan War because he had failed to avenge his brother Ajax. There is little direct evidence for this myth, and some evidence that the area was occupied long before, with the town developing as a replacement when Enkomi was cut off from the sea.

Children's burials in Canaanite jars indicate a Phoenician presence, and Assyrian inscriptions name the town among the kingdoms of Iadnana, as Cyprus was called. In 708 BCE the city-kings of Cyprus paid homage to Sargon II of Assyria, but they kept relative independence as long as they paid tribute, which let them gather wealth and power. The royal tombs of Salamis hold chariots and rich grave goods, much of it from the Levant or Egypt, and burial customs such as the sacrifice of horses echo Homeric rites. The first coins were minted in the 6th century BCE.

In 450 BCE Salamis was the site of a simultaneous land and sea battle between the Delian League and the Persian Empire. It was later besieged and conquered by Artaxerxes III. Under King Evagoras I (411–374 BCE) Greek culture and art flourished. In 306 BCE Demetrius I of Macedon defeated the fleet of Ptolemy I of Egypt off Salamis and captured the island. Rome annexed Cyprus in 58 BCE, and the governor's seat moved to Nea Paphos, though Salamis kept its wealth and the Emperors Trajan and Hadrian restored its public buildings.

Paul the Apostle and Barnabas landed at Salamis on their first journey, and tradition holds that Barnabas was stoned to death there around 61 CE. Earthquakes destroyed the town early in the 4th century. Constantius II rebuilt it as Constantia, and it became an episcopal seat, its best-known occupant being Saint Epiphanius. The silting of the harbour led to a gradual decline, and the city was finally abandoned during the Arab invasions of the 7th century.

The ruins are very extensive, with a gymnasium, theatre, amphitheatre, stadium and public baths; the theatre could seat up to 15,000. The necropolis covers around 7 km2 to the west of the town. Excavations began in the late nineteenth century under the Cyprus Exploration Fund, and finds from them are in the British Museum in London.
salamis-island: Salamis lies about two kilometres from the coast of Piraeus, Athens' port, and about 16 km west of the centre of Athens. It has an area of 93 square kilometres, and a significant part of it is rocky and mountainous; the highest point is Mavrovouni at 404 metres. The chief city, Salamina, stands on Salamis Bay, and the main port, Paloukia, on the eastern side connects the island with Perama by ferry.

The traditional etymology derives the name from the nymph Salamis, mother of Cychreus, the first king of the island in tradition. A more modern theory connects it with a root meaning salt and a suffix meaning middle, so that Salamis would be the place amid salt water. From at least the 13th century until the 19th the island was called Koulouri, after its round shape, and the ancient name was then revived.

Salamis was probably first colonised by Aegina and later occupied by Megara, and it became an Athenian possession after a war between Athens and Megara. According to Homer's Iliad it sent twelve ships to the Trojan War under Ajax, who is said to have been born on the island, as was the playwright Euripides, whose birth is popularly placed on the day of the battle. In 480 BCE the allied Greek fleet led by Athens and by Themistocles won its decisive naval victory over the Persian Empire off the island. In the north of the Kynosoura peninsula lie the remains of an ancient tumulus thought to be the burial site of Greek warriors of that battle.

The ancient capital lay in the south according to Strabo, in classical times on the Kamatero Peninsula overlooking the strait, and in modern times lies in the west. The oldest known counting board, of marble and about 150 by 75 centimetres, was found on the island in 1899 and is thought to have been used by Babylonians about 300 BCE. Arvanites were recorded among the inhabitants in 1688. On 23 April 1941, during the German invasion of Greece, the Luftwaffe bombed the harbour and sank the Greek battleships Kilkis and Lemnos.

Since the local government reform of 2011 the island has been administered as one municipality in the Islands regional unit of Attica. About 31,000 people live there permanently, many working in fishing, ferries and shipyards or commuting to Athens, and the number rises sharply in the holiday season. Salamis Naval Base, a major base of the Hellenic Navy, stands beside Paloukia. A festival called Salaminia commemorates the naval battle each year, and the island has a Museum of Folklore Art and History.
salamiyah: Salamiyah lies in a fertile plain on the edge of the Syrian steppe, 33 kilometres south-east of Hama and 45 kilometres north-east of Homs, at an average elevation of about 460 metres. It is administratively part of the Hama Governorate. In the Byzantine period it was a flourishing town called Salaminias or Salamias, linked by roads to Emesa (Homs), Chalcis and Resafa. Its bishop Julian attended the consecration of Patriarch Severus of Antioch in 512, and one dated inscription records the building of a church of the Theotokos in 604.

Muslim Arabs conquered Salamiyah in 636. Not long after the Abbasids came to power in 750, the dynast Salih ibn Ali and his descendants settled it, and his son Abdallah built its irrigation networks. In the early 9th century the great-grandson of Ja'far al-Sadiq, also named Abdallah, settled there concealing his identity as a merchant, and his palace became the seat of the Ismaili da'wa.

Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah was born in Salamiyah in 873 or 874, and his reforms led to a break with Hamdan Qarmat. The Qarmatians razed the town in 903 and massacred its inhabitants; al-Mahdi had left the year before and went on to found the Fatimid Caliphate.

Salamiyah then declined. It was captured by a Fatimid general in 1009, passed in 1092 to Tutush, brother of the Seljuk sultan Malikshah, and to Saladin in 1174–1175, and was incorporated into the Mamluk empire after 1263. The Mamluk army was defeated by the Mongols under Ghazan there in 1299.

Under early Ottoman rule, from 1517, it was a large ruin held by Bedouin emirs, and in the 1830s it was still uninhabited. In July 1849 Isma'il ibn Muhammad, the Ismaili emir of Qadmus, obtained a firman from Sultan Abdülmecid I to settle the site with his followers, who called it Mecidabad. Many Ismailis followed from the Jabal Ansariya, and by the end of the 19th century about 6,000 people lived there.

Salamiyah had 66,724 inhabitants at the 2004 census, and a little more than half of its residents are Ismaili. It is the largest population centre of Ismailis in the Arab world and holds the headquarters of the Ismaili Higher Council of Syria. The mausoleum of the Ismaili imam Abdallah, rebuilt in 1088 according to an inscription, still stands, and the poet Muhammad al-Maghut was born there in 1934. The city is an agricultural centre.
salammbo: After the legal troubles that followed Madame Bovary, for which he was tried and acquitted on a charge of immorality, Flaubert looked for a less controversial subject. His principal source was Book I of the Histories of the Greek historian Polybius. In 1857 he wrote to the archaeologist Félicien de Saulcy about his plans, and from 12 April to 5 June 1858 he travelled in Tunisia to see the places of the novel, though little survived from ancient times. He changed the name of the Carthaginian general Hannibal, whom the mercenaries executed, to Hanno, so as not to confuse him with the Hannibal of the Second Punic War.

After the First Punic War, Carthage cannot pay its army of mercenaries and comes under attack. The fictional title character, a priestess of the goddess Tanit and the daughter of the general Hamilcar Barca, is the object of the obsessive desire of Matho, a Libyan leader of the mercenaries. With the help of the freed slave Spendius, Matho steals the Zaïmph, the sacred veil of Carthage, which kills anyone who touches it. Salammbô goes into the mercenaries' camp to retrieve it, and Matho and she make love in his tent.

Hamilcar then defeats the mercenaries, many of whom starve in a defile. The novel's fifteen chapters include the sacrifice of Carthaginian children to Moloch, and it ends with Matho's torture and execution, at the sight of which Salammbô dies.

The novel was a bestseller on publication in 1862, though its violence and sensuality bore little resemblance to Madame Bovary. Readers praised its style and story, its descriptions of Carthaginian dress influenced fashion, and its picture of Roman North Africa stirred interest in archaeological exploration there. Eleanor Marx made the first English translation in 1886. The book renewed interest in the conflict between Rome and Carthage and inspired operas by Ernest Reyer in 1890 and Josef Matthias Hauer in 1929, as well as silent films, among them Pierre Marodon's of 1925.
sale: Salé lies in northwestern Morocco on the right bank of the Bou Regreg river, opposite the national capital Rabat, which it serves as a commuter town. Rabat and Salé together form a single metropolitan area. The Phoenicians established a settlement called Sala on the south side of the estuary, later the site of a Roman colony, Sala Colonia. The town of Salé proper was probably founded in the 11th century by families from al-Andalus, most importantly the Banu 'Ashara, who included learned jurists and judges and became the city's de facto rulers.

The Banu 'Ashara reportedly hosted Ibn Tumart, the founder of the Almohad movement, in 1121. They resisted his successor 'Abd al-Mu'min, who destroyed the city walls, eliminated the family and seized their palace. In the 12th century the Almohad caliph Yaqub al-Mansur founded Ribat al-Fath, present-day Rabat, across the river, and Salé remained important as a residence of the Almohad caliphs.

He ordered the Great Mosque built in 1196. In September 1260 warriors sent by Alfonso X of Castile raided and occupied Salé, and the Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub reconquered it and helped rebuild the walls, including the gate of Bab el-Mrisa. The Marinids also built a protected harbour and the Madrasa of Abu al-Hasan.

In the 17th century Salé became a haven for Barbary pirates, among them Moriscos expelled from Spain after Philip III's decree of 1609. About 2,000 refugees from Hornachos settled around Salé and occupied the kasbah, and thousands more joined them. Rabat and Salé united to form the Republic of Bou Regreg in 1627.

The corsairs captured ships and sold their crews and sometimes passengers into slavery, although their ships were based across the river in Rabat. Spain bombarded Salé in May 1628, and the French admiral Isaac de Razilly did so on 20 July 1629, destroying three corsair ships. Salé was later incorporated into Alawi Morocco.

Salé's historic medina occupies a large area near the mouth of the Bou Regreg and is enclosed by walls, of which Bab el-Mrisa, dating to the 1270s, is the most notable gate. The Great Mosque is the religious centre, beside the Madrasa of Abu al-Hasan, dating to 1342. The Sufi Ibn 'Ashir, who moved to Salé in the 14th century, became the city's patron saint, and his mausoleum dominates the seaside cemetery. Salé was a stronghold of the Moroccan national movement before independence, and many of its activists signed the Manifesto of Independence of Morocco on 11 January 1944.
salem-baden-wurttemberg: Salem lies in the Linzgau, about 9 km north of Lake Constance, mainly in the valley of the Linzer Aach. It is about nine kilometres east of Überlingen and ten kilometres north-east of Meersburg, and has a population of 11,100. The municipality consists of eleven member locations, of which Salem Stefansfeld is the chief town, and covers about 6,270 hectares. The district of Oberstenweiler lies on a side peak of the Gehrenberg, rising to about 600 metres.

The area has been settled since at least the Bronze Age. From the 3rd century the Alemanni and later the Franks established several villages, among them the small settlement of Salemanneswilare, later Salmannsweiler. Salem Abbey was founded here in 1134, when the knight Guntram von Adelsreute donated land to the Cistercians, and it quickly attained the rank of an imperial abbey. It had its own scriptorium in the 12th century and held one of the most important monastery libraries in Europe.

The High Gothic minster was built from about 1285 to 1425. In the 17th century the monastery suffered serious setbacks, including the Thirty Years' War. In 1697 a fire destroyed most of the buildings and many art treasures, and the Baroque buildings now on the site were then raised under the master builder Franz Beer of Vorarlberg. In 1749 Abbot Anselm II Schwab founded an Orphans' Fund, considered the first savings bank in Germany, and he also had the pilgrimage church of Birnau built on the shore of Lake Constance. The abbey's heyday ended with the German mediatization of 1803, when it was secularized and its territory fell to the Margraviate of Baden.

The abbey complex covers 17 hectares. Its grounds house the middle school campus of Schule Schloss Salem, a boarding school founded in 1920 by Kurt Hahn and Prince Max of Baden. The Gothic minster, the former abbey church, and a Baroque chapel remain among the main sights. The Rococo plasterer and sculptor Joseph Anton Feuchtmayer (1696–1770) is among the notable people associated with the town, as is Johann Baptist von Keller (1774–1845), Bishop of Rottenburg.
salem-massachusetts: Salem lies on Massachusetts Bay, between Salem Harbor, which divides it from Marblehead, and Beverly Harbor. Between the two harbors lie Salem Neck and Winter Island. The city has a total area of 18.1 square miles, of which 8.1 square miles is land and the rest water. The peninsula was known as Naumkeag to the Native people who lived there in the early 1600s, the Naumkeag people, whose settlement controlled territory from the Merrimack to the Mystic rivers.

Colonists settled in Naumkeag in 1626, when a company of fishermen from Cape Ann arrived under Roger Conant. The Massachusetts Bay Company replaced him with John Endecott, and Conant received 200 acres in compensation. To mark this peaceful change of government the settlement was renamed Salem, a form of Shalem, the royal city of Melchizedek, which is identified with Jerusalem. Early musters of militia on Salem Common laid a foundation for what became the Army National Guard. On 26 February 1775 patriots raised the drawbridge at the North River and stopped Colonel Alexander Leslie and 300 troops of the 64th Regiment of Foot from seizing stores hidden in North Salem; an agreement ended the standoff without bloodshed.

The Salem witch trials began in 1692 after girls including Abigail Williams and Betty Parris played with an egg and a glass to learn their future husbands' trades. Nineteen people were hanged, and Giles Corey was pressed to death for refusing to plead. After the American Revolution, Salem's owners of large privateers turned to distant trade. In 1795 Captain Jonathan Carnes brought home a bulk cargo of pepper from Sumatra, the first imported into the country, sold at a profit of seven hundred per cent. Elias Hasket Derby owned the Grand Turk, the first New England vessel to trade with China.

Salem is a residential and tourist city of 44,480 people at the 2020 census. It was one of two county seats of Essex County until county governments in Massachusetts were dissolved in 1999. The Salem Maritime National Historic Site, the House of the Seven Gables (1668), the Peabody Essex Museum and the Chestnut Street District preserve its maritime and colonial past. The site of the 1692 executions was identified in 2016 as Proctor's Ledge, now a memorial. Salem State University, founded in 1854 as the Salem Normal School, is in the city.
salem-new-jersey: Salem is the county seat of Salem County, the most rural county in New Jersey, and lies along the Salem River. It is part of the Philadelphia metropolitan area. The name of both city and county is derived from the Hebrew word shalom, meaning peace. The Port of Salem was designated by the British Crown in 1682 as a port of entry on the Salem River, reached from the Delaware River.

The town and colony were laid out in 1675 by John Fenwick, a Quaker. Fenwick had a financial dispute with another Quaker, Edward Byllynge, who had bought a share of New Jersey from Lord John Berkeley, then went bankrupt and had the property transferred to Fenwick to hold in trust. William Penn was asked to adjudicate and awarded 90 per cent of the claim to Byllynge and 10 per cent to Fenwick, but Fenwick refused the decision. He sailed to Delaware Bay with settlers and governed the Fifth Tenth near the abandoned Swedish settlement of Fort Nya Elfsborg, issuing land patents in defiance of Byllynge and Penn. The court of Dominion Governor Andros upheld his claim, and he governed the Salem tenth by 1689.

In October 1693 the community was given permission to choose its own officers. On 18 March 1778, during the American Revolutionary War, British forces under Lieutenant-Colonel Charles Mawhood raided Salem and defeated American militia at a nearby bridge. Three days later Major John Graves Simcoe led a surprise attack on Hancock House, where between 20 and 30 militiamen were killed, some reportedly while trying to surrender; the Loyalist judge William Hancock Jr. was fatally injured. After the war, treason trials were held at the county courthouse, and four men sentenced to death were pardoned by Governor William Livingston and exiled. Salem was incorporated as a township on 21 February 1798 and reincorporated as Salem City on 25 February 1858.

The Old Salem County Courthouse, built in 1735 of locally made bricks, is the oldest courthouse in New Jersey still in active use and the second-oldest in continuous use in the United States. A legend holds that Colonel Robert Gibbon Johnson proved the tomato safe to eat on its steps in 1820; it did not appear in print until 1948, and modern scholars question it. At the 2020 census the city had 5,296 inhabitants.
salem-witch-trials: Witch trials were fading across much of Europe by the middle of the seventeenth century but continued on its fringes and in the American colonies. Witchcraft had been a capital offence in the Massachusetts Body of Liberties since 1641, although the provision was repealed in 1684. The Puritans who settled New England would have been familiar with witch trials in England. The 1629 royal charter of the Massachusetts Bay Colony was vacated in 1684, and the colony passed through constitutional turmoil. Salem Village, now Danvers, was known for a fractious population that quarrelled over property lines, grazing rights and church privileges.

In February 1692 Betty Parris, aged nine, and her cousin Abigail Williams, aged eleven, the daughter and niece of the Reverend Samuel Parris, began to have fits. Local women were accused of causing the girls harm by witchcraft, and when Sarah Cloyce and Elizabeth Proctor were arrested in April they were examined by the magistrates John Hathorne and Jonathan Corwin. A Court of Oyer and Terminer convened in Salem Town on 2 June 1692 under William Stoughton, and Bridget Bishop was the first case brought to the grand jury.

Much of the evidence was spectral evidence, the testimony of the afflicted that they saw the apparition of the accused. The court held that the Devil could not use a person's shape without that person's permission, so such testimony was taken as proof of complicity. On 19 September 1692 Giles Corey refused to plead and was killed by peine forte et dure, a form of torture in which the subject is pressed beneath stones. A new Superior Court of Judicature convened in January 1693 and did not allow spectral evidence; of the cases it heard, three people were found guilty, one of them Elizabeth Johnson Jr.

In 1702 the General Court of Massachusetts declared the trials unlawful, and in 1711 the colonial legislature annulled the convictions. Several accusers, mostly teenage girls, later admitted that they had fabricated their charges. The historian George Lincoln Burr wrote that the Salem witchcraft was the rock on which the New England theocracy shattered.

Acts of 1957 and 2001 absolved victims. The executions took place at Proctor's Ledge, at the foot of Gallows Hill. Researchers have proposed medical explanations for the fits, among them convulsive ergotism from infected rye, while some historians prefer motives such as jealousy and a need for attention.
salento: Salento is a cultural, historical and geographic region at the southern end of Apulia, a sub-peninsula of the Italian Peninsula. It encompasses the entire Province of Lecce, most of the Province of Brindisi and the south-eastern part of the Province of Taranto, though not Taranto itself. The peninsula is composed of limestone and divides the Gulf of Taranto in the west from the Strait of Otranto in the east, with the Adriatic Sea to the north and the Ionian Sea to the south. A depression called the Messapic threshold, running along the Taranto-Ostuni line, separates it from the Murge. The climate is Mediterranean, suited to olives, citrus fruits and palm trees.

In ancient times the peninsula was called Sallentina or Messapia, and the Iapygians are said to have migrated to it from the Illyrian coast in the eleventh century BCE. The Romans took control in 272 BCE. Under Roman rule it was known as Calabria and had a flourishing agricultural economy of wheat and olive oil. The name Calabria later moved to the region now called by it: from 580 the Calabrian province was gradually expanded westward, and by the 10th century the term had shifted.

Justinian I's reconquest of Italy, the Gothic War of 535 to 554, brought Byzantine rule, which strengthened Greek influence, shown in the use of the Greek language and the Byzantine rite. The Lombards tried to conquer the region from 569 and were pushed back.

The Saracens occupied Taranto and other places in 847 and destroyed Ugento in 870, deporting its inhabitants to Africa. The Normans arrived in southern Italy in 1016, and Robert Guiscard governed Apulia from 1059, beginning a period of prosperity. In 1480 the Ottomans under Gedik Ahmed Pasha besieged and sacked Otranto; they killed hundreds of men who refused to convert to Islam, and neighbouring towns were fortified. The Venetians briefly controlled Salento between 1482 and 1484, and in 1534 Charles V restored several castles, among them that of Lecce.
