Sven Aggesen, a Danish nobleman who wrote a slightly earlier history of Denmark, describes him as his contubernalis, or tent-comrade, which suggests that both may have served in the royal guard, the Hird. Saxo writes that he comes from a warrior family: he follows the ancient right of hereditary service, and his father and grandfather frequented the war camp of Valdemar I. Whether he was a layman or a cleric is uncertain, but either way he was well educated.

Saxo was in the retinue of Absalon, Archbishop of Lund and the foremost adviser to Valdemar I, and received his patronage. In his will Absalon forgives his clerk Saxo a small debt of two and a half marks of silver and tells him to return two borrowed books to the monastery of Sorø. In the preface to his history Saxo writes that Absalon had encouraged him to write a heroic history of the Danes, to glorify the fatherland on the model of Virgil's Aeneid. The work is thought to have been begun about 1185. Saxo wrote the preface last, under Anders Sunesen, who replaced Absalon as archbishop, and in it he warmly praised both archbishops and the reigning king, Valdemar II.

The Gesta Danorum begins with the founders of the Danish people, Dan I of Denmark and Angul, and extends to about the year 1187. The first four books treat the Danes before Christ, the next four their history after Christ, books 9 to 12 Christian Denmark, and books 13 to 16 promote Lund and exploits before and during Saxo's own lifetime. His sources were of questionable historical value: oral tales of the Icelanders, ancient volumes, letters carved on rocks and stone, and the statements of Absalon.

Saxo's world has very warlike values, and he glorifies heroes who made their names in battle far more than those who made peace. His gods are not always good characters. Odin teaches Harald, in Saxo's tale a king of the Danes, the ways of war and then betrays and kills him. Erasmus praised Saxo's Latin, and early in the sixteenth century Christiern Pedersen of Lund printed the work with Jodocus Badius Ascensius.
saxons: The earliest possible record of the Saxons is a reference in Ptolemy's Geographia to a tribe north of the lower Elbe, but the manuscripts differ, some reading Saxones and others Axones, and its interpretation is disputed. The first undoubted use of the name comes from the third to fifth centuries, when it described coastal raiders who attacked the Roman Empire by boat from north of the Rhine. Scholars believe the term was then used something like the much later word Viking and was probably not the name of any specific tribe. The raiders included Frisians, Angles and Jutes, as well as the Anglo-Saxons who became established in Britain. The name has traditionally been derived from the seax, a kind of knife.

The continental Saxons appear as inland opponents of the Franks in the sixth century, after the Franks conquered Thuringia, about 531. They do not seem to have been politically united until the generations of conflict that led to their defeat by Charlemagne. Frankish rulers of Austrasia, Merovingian and Carolingian, fought many campaigns against them. Charlemagne conquered them in the Saxon Wars of 772–804 and forced them to convert to Christianity. He deported 10,000 Nordalbingian Saxons to Neustria. In 804 Saxony became a Carolingian stem duchy.

The dukes of Saxony expanded eastwards at the expense of the Slavic-speaking Wends. They became kings of Germany with Henry I the Fowler in 919 and then emperors, beginning with his son Otto I, in the tenth century, but lost this position in 1024. The duchy was divided in 1180 when Duke Henry the Lion refused to follow Emperor Frederick Barbarossa into war in Lombardy.

Bede, writing about 730, remarks that the continental Saxons had no king but were governed by several satraps, who cast lots for leadership in war and were equal in peacetime. Their territory was divided into Westphalia, Eastphalia and Angria, comprising about one hundred districts called Gaue. Sources on Saxon paganism come only from after their conversion and were written by Christians. The Old Saxon Baptismal Vow required converts to renounce the worship of Thunaer, Wodan and Saxnot, and Charlemagne's capitulary prohibited cremation burial, punishable by death.

The Saxons of Germany no longer form a distinct people, but their name survives in Lower Saxony, which includes most of the original duchy. Old Saxon evolved into Middle Low German and then Low German, the lingua franca of the Hanseatic League.
saxony: The Free State of Saxony is a landlocked state of Germany. It borders Brandenburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Bavaria, and its southern and eastern boundaries form part of Germany's frontiers with the Czech Republic and Poland. The land rises from the lowlands of the North German Plain in the north, which include the Leipzig Bay and much of Lusatia, to uplands along the Czech border.

Some of the largest ancient monumental temples of central Europe stood here, dating from the fifth millennium BCE. Since the late 6th century the area was populated by Polabian Slavs, most prominently the Sorbs, and it was conquered by Francia and organized as the Sorbian March. The territory became part of the Holy Roman Empire by the 10th century, and the Margravate of Meissen was founded in 985 as a frontier march. In 1423 Saxe-Wittenberg became subject to the margravate, ruled by the Wettin dynasty, creating a new and powerful state. Although its centre lay far to the southeast of the old Saxony, it came to be called Upper Saxony and then simply Saxony, while the northern Saxon lands became Lower Saxony.

In 1806 Napoleon made the Electorate of Saxony a kingdom, in exchange for military support. At the Congress of Vienna the king was restored but forced to cede the northern part of the kingdom to Prussia, a loss of nearly 60 percent of the territory and 40 percent of the population. Frederick Augustus III abdicated on 13 November 1918, and Saxony became the Free State of Saxony. It was broken up under communist rule and re-established on 3 October 1990, on German reunification.

Dresden is the capital of Saxony and Leipzig its largest city. Dresden's Baroque cityscape and art collections, Leipzig's musical traditions and the mining heritage of the Ore Mountains are among its best-known cultural features.
saxony-anhalt: Saxony-Anhalt is a landlocked state of Germany of 20,555 square kilometres, bordering Brandenburg, Saxony, Thuringia and Lower Saxony. In the north the North German Plain dominates, with the old Hanseatic towns of Salzwedel, Gardelegen, Stendal and Tangermünde in the sparsely populated Altmark, and the fertile Magdeburg Börde beyond it. The Harz mountains lie in the south-west; their highest peak, the Brocken at 1,141 metres, is the highest in northern Germany. The wine-growing area of Saale-Unstrut lies in the south, and the Halle area forms an agglomeration with Leipzig, known for its chemical industry at Leuna, Schkopau and Bitterfeld.

Saxony-Anhalt has a short history as a state and consists mainly of three historical regions: the area around Magdeburg, the formerly independent Anhalt, and a southern part that had once belonged to Saxony and was annexed by Prussia in the nineteenth century. Anhalt takes its name from Anhalt Castle near Harzgerode. In April 1945 the US Army took control of most of the western and northern area; it withdrew to make way for the Red Army, as the London Protocol of 1944 had agreed. The Soviet administration then merged the Free State of Anhalt, Halle-Merseburg, the governorate of Magdeburg and some further territories with the Province of Saxony, and appointed Erhard Hübener to head the new provincial administration at Halle.

The Province of Saxony was renamed the Province of Saxony-Anhalt on 20 October 1946, and after the Allied decision to dissolve the Free State of Prussia it became the State of Saxony-Anhalt on 6 October 1947. Hübener, elected minister-president in December 1946, was the only governor in the Soviet zone who did not belong to the Socialist Unity Party. The state joined the German Democratic Republic in 1949. In 1952 the East German states were dissolved and its territory divided into the districts of Halle and Magdeburg, apart from the area around Torgau, which went to Leipzig. In 1990, during German reunification, the districts were reintegrated as a state, though Torgau did not return and joined Saxony.

Magdeburg is the capital and largest city, and Halle (Saale) the second-largest. The state's constitution was adopted by its Landtag in 1992. Six UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Germany lie in Saxony-Anhalt, among them the Bauhaus sites in Dessau and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm, and the Nebra Sky Disc is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Many sites tied to Martin Luther's life stand there, including Lutherstadt Eisleben and Lutherstadt Wittenberg.
sayyid-dynasty: The Sayyid dynasty was the fourth dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, with four rulers between 1414 and 1451. Its founder, Khizr Khan, was the son of Malik Sulaiman, an adopted son of Malik Mardan Daulat, governor of Multan under the Tughlaq dynasty. The epithet sayyid came from a claimed descent from Muhammad. According to Yahya Sirhindi, a contemporary writer, the Sufi saint Syed Jalaluddin Bukhari established Malik Sulaiman's Syed identity during a visit to Mardan Daulat.

Modern historians doubt the claimed descent. Several scholars suggest that Khizr Khan came from an Arab family long settled at Multan, while others suggest that he was a Punjabi chieftain of the Khokhar clan who rose through contacts in the Timurid Empire.

Khizr Khan was a noble and governor of Multan under Sultan Firuz Shah, in a period of civil war among the nobles. Sarang Khan, governor of Dipalpur, expelled him from Multan. After Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 Timur appointed him deputy of Multan in Punjab, with charge of Lahore, Dipalpur and upper Sindh. He defeated and killed Mallu Iqbal Khan in 1405 and captured Delhi on 28 May 1414. He never took the title of sultan but kept up the fiction of allegiance to the Timurids as Rayat-i-Ala, or vassal. The name of Shah Rukh was recited in the khutba with his own, but the coins kept the name of the old Tughlaq sultan, and none are known in Khizr Khan's name.

His son Mubarak Shah succeeded him on 20 May 1421 and dropped the nominal allegiance to the Timurids, using the title shah and professing allegiance to the caliph alone. He defeated Hoshang Shah of Malwa and forced him to pay heavy tribute. His nephew Muhammad Shah, who ruled from 1434, faced many rebellions and conspiracies, and Multan became independent under the Langahs. Muhammad Shah's son Ala-ud-Din Alam Shah was an ineffective ruler who left his duties to his minister Hamid Khan. He appointed Bahlol Lodi governor of Sirhind, and Bahlol gathered enough strength to attack Delhi. On 19 April 1451 Alam Shah abdicated in his favour and left for Badaun, where he died in 1478.
sayyid-qutb: Sayyid Qutb was born on 9 October 1906 and raised in the village of Musha in Asyut Province, Upper Egypt. His father, a landowner and the administrator of the family estate, was known for his political activism and held weekly meetings to discuss political events and Quranic recitation. Qutb learned melodic recitation there and had memorised the whole Quran by the age of ten. In the United States he worked and studied at Wilson Teachers' College in Washington, D.C., at Colorado State College for Education in Greeley and at Stanford University, and he spent time in Europe on his way home.

Before he left the United States he was still Western in many ways, in his dress and his love of classical music and Hollywood films, and he had read Charles Darwin, Albert Einstein, Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley in translation. Yet he concluded that major aspects of American life were primitive and shocking, and he saw Americans as numb to faith in religion, art and spiritual values. This experience formed in part the impetus for his rejection of Western values.

Qutb wrote 24 published books and at least 581 articles, including novels, literary criticism and works on education. From 1948 his outlook turned Islamist, beginning with the treatise al-ʿAdāla, and he later denounced his literary works of the 1940s as un-Islamic. His 30-volume Quran commentary, Fi Zilal al-Qur'an (In the Shade of the Qur'an), began to appear in 1954. In Milestones (Ma'alim fi-l-Tariq) he held that there are only two kinds of societies, Islamic and jahili, and that existing Muslim societies are jahili because they gave the legislative attribute of God to others.

He called for a revolutionary vanguard, which scholars have compared with Lenin's, although he rejected all Western ideologies, socialism included. His view of jihad changed from defensive to offensive. In 1950 he published Our Struggle against the Jews, which embraced antisemitic conspiracy theories.

Qutb joined the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1950s and edited its weekly. He and the Brotherhood welcomed the July 1952 coup led by Gamal Abdel Nasser, but their cooperation soured as the secular nationalism of Nasserism proved incompatible with the Brotherhood's Islamism. He was in prison from 1954 to 1964, and one common explanation for his turn to sharia is the torture and killing of Brotherhood members that he saw there. He was convicted of plotting Nasser's assassination and hanged on 29 August 1966.

Followers describe him as a great thinker and a martyr for Islam, while Western observers and some Muslims see him as a key originator of Islamist ideology. The ulama of Al-Azhar University placed him on their index of heresy as a deviant. His ideas on jahiliyya have influenced Islamist and jihadist movements.
sayyida-al-hurra: Lalla ʿĀʾisha bint ʿAlī ibn Rāshid al-ʿAlamī, known as Sayyida al-Hurra, the Free lady, was born in Chefchaouen, though the year of her birth is uncertain. Her family were Andalusian nobles expelled to Morocco after the fall of Granada. Her father, Ali ibn Rashid al-Alami, was the founder and emir of Chefchaouen, and her mother, Lalla Zohra Fernandez, came from Vejer de la Frontera near Cadiz. She was a Sharifian, a descendant of the Moroccan Sufi saint Abd al-Salam ibn Mashish al-Alami. At sixteen she was married to Sidi al-Mandri II, thirty years older than she, the re-founder and governor of Tétouan, himself an Andalusian refugee.

She assisted her husband in his business affairs and acted as a de facto vice-governor whenever he travelled. When he died in 1515 the people of Tétouan, accustomed to seeing her exercise power, accepted her as governor and gave her the title al-Hurra. Under her the city became a privateering hub and a refuge for Moorish refugees. Spanish and Portuguese sources describe her as their partner in the diplomatic game. She allied with the Ottoman admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa of Algiers, and she was respected by her Christian enemies as a queen who controlled the western Mediterranean and the release of Portuguese and Spanish captives.

In 1541 she accepted a proposal from Ahmad al-Wattasi, the Wattasid sultan, who travelled from Fez to Tétouan to marry her, because she would not give up her rule or leave the city. It is the only recorded case of a Moroccan king marrying outside his capital. She made her brother Moulay Ibrahim vizier to the sultan. In October 1542 her son-in-law Muhammad al-Hassan al-Mandri, governor of Fnideq, overthrew her. She retired to Chefchaouen and devoted herself to religious work.

The Moroccan historian Muhammad Ibn Azzuz Hakim called her the only woman to have held sovereign power in Morocco. The year of her death is disputed, with some sources giving 1552 and others 1561 or 1562. Local Moroccan historians note that Arab historians of her own time did not write about her, although she has stayed known in her home city. One place where she is remembered is the Qasbah of Chefchaouen, a fortress built against the Portuguese that belonged to her father.
sbeitla: Sbeitla, known in antiquity as Sufetula, is a town in west-central Tunisia, in the Kasserine Governorate, in the semi-arid High Steppes. By road it lies 33 km north-east of Kasserine and 246 km south-west of Tunis. The Roman town stood on a plateau in a bend of the Sbeitla wadi, below an abundant perennial spring whose water was carried into the town by a bridge-aqueduct.

Little is known of the area before the Roman period. The Roman town of Sufetula Musuniorum was founded in the third quarter of the 1st century CE, under the Flavians. According to the Tunisian nomination file it is the only known example in the Roman Empire of a town founded on the colonial model not to settle Roman citizens but to settle an indigenous, largely nomadic tribe, the Musunii. The town prospered in the 2nd century through olive oil, as the olive presses in the ruins show, and this wealth financed its forum and public buildings. Under Christianity it became a bishopric of the province of Byzacena.

After the Byzantine reconquest of 533 it became an important stronghold, refortified piecemeal with small forts and fortified houses along the main street. In the 640s the exarch Gregory the Patrician broke with Constantinople, proclaimed himself emperor and made Sufetula his residence. In 647, under Caliph Uthman ibn Affan, an Arab army led by Abdallah ibn Sa'd met Gregory's Byzantine and Berber forces before the town. Gregory was killed, and the town was taken and sacked, though Syriac sources claim he fled. The defeat undermined Byzantine rule in Africa and opened the way to the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb, but urban life continued: eight churches were in use in the 7th century, and some quarters were still inhabited in the 11th.

A European settlement grew up beside the ruins under the French protectorate, and the railway arrived in 1908. In February 1943 the town was fought over in the Tunisian campaign: German panzer divisions attacked it on 16 February, and the US 1st Armored Division withdrew on 17 February. It then served as a staging point for the Axis offensive towards the Kasserine Pass.

Next to the town lie the ruins of Sufetula, whose three Capitoline temples are among the best-preserved Roman forum temples in North Africa, together with baths, a theatre and Byzantine churches. Tunisia added the site to its UNESCO tentative list on 15 April 2021. The municipality, created in 1927, had 42,359 inhabitants at the census of 2024.
scandinavia: The geography of Scandinavia is varied. It includes the Norwegian fjords, the Scandinavian Mountains that cover much of Norway and parts of Sweden, the flat, low land of Denmark, and the archipelagos and lakes of the east. Finland and Sweden have many lakes and moraines, left by the ice age that ended about ten millennia ago. The region extends north of the Arctic Circle but has relatively mild weather for its latitude because of the Gulf Stream.

The name goes back to the Proto-Germanic compound *Skaðin-awjō, which is also the source of Scania, the southernmost province of Sweden. The earliest identified source for Scandinavia is Pliny the Elder's Natural History of the 1st century CE, which describes Scatinavia as an island.

The Viking Age lasted from about 793 to 1066 CE. Scandinavians raided, conquered, colonised and traded across Europe, and their longships took them to North America, where they were the first Europeans to arrive. Those known as Varangians, mostly from what is now Sweden, travelled east along the river routes into Russia. The expansion produced settlements and realms such as the Danelaw, the Kingdom of Dublin, the Duchy of Normandy and the Kievan Rus', and the Faroe Islands, Iceland and Greenland were settled. The North Sea Empire briefly joined large parts of Scandinavia and Great Britain.

Between the 10th and 13th centuries, as the region became Christian and its states formed, petty kingdoms and chiefdoms were unified into Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The historian Sverre Bagge notes that this division suits the geography, since forests, mountains and empty land separated the three.

Later unions followed, notably the Kalmar Union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, which lasted over a century until King Gustav I led Sweden out of it. Denmark and Norway then stayed united until 1814. The Treaty of Kiel of 14 January 1814 dissolved that union and ceded Norway to the King of Sweden, but Norwegian resistance led to a constitution drawn up at Eidsvoll and a personal union with Sweden, which ended in 1905. The Scandinavist movement, which stressed a common heritage, peaked in the middle of the 19th century.

In its narrow, local sense Scandinavia comprises Denmark, Norway and Sweden, a subset of the Nordic countries, which also include Finland and Iceland. In English the word is sometimes used for all of them. Danish, Norwegian and Swedish form a dialect continuum and are considered mutually intelligible. Sámi and Finnish, of the unrelated Uralic family, have also been spoken in the region since prehistory.
scania: Scania, called Skåne in Swedish, lies at the south tip of the geographical region of Götaland. To the north it borders the historical provinces of Halland and Småland, to the north-east Blekinge, to the east and south the Baltic Sea, and to the west the Öresund. It extends about 130 kilometres from north to south and covers less than 3 per cent of Sweden's area. Unlike much of Sweden its landscape is generally not mountainous: a large part consists of plains, with lake-rich and densely forested country in the north (Göinge) and rolling hills on the Bjäre and Kulla peninsulas. It has the mildest climate in Sweden.

The names Scania and Scandinavia are considered to have the same etymology. The Romans called the southern tip of what is now Sweden Scania and thought it an island. The origin of the word is uncertain and long debated, though it may derive from a Germanic root related to Old Norse Skáney.

Scania was first mentioned in written texts in the 9th century and came under the Danish king Harald Bluetooth in the middle of the 10th century. As the eastern part of the kingdom of Denmark, it was the focal point of the frequent Dano-Swedish wars for hundreds of years. Lund has held town rights since about 990 and Helsingborg since 1085, and by 1658 ten places in Scania were chartered towns.

By the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658 all Danish lands east of the Öresund were ceded to Sweden. The province was first placed under a Governor-General and was eventually integrated into the Swedish kingdom. Denmark occupied parts of it during the Scanian War of 1676–1679 and again briefly in 1710 during the Great Northern War. The last Danish attempt to regain the lost provinces failed after the Battle of Helsingborg in 1710. Because Scania had had no coat of arms in the Danish era, new provincial arms were created in 1660 for the funeral of Charles X Gustav, based on the arms of Malmö.

Scania is the southernmost of the historical provinces of Sweden and corresponds roughly to Skåne County, created in 1997, with 33 municipalities. Its largest city is Malmö. Since 2000 a road and railway bridge, the Öresund Bridge, has connected it with Denmark. Its trade with other communities along the continental coast has made its culture distinct from other regions of Sweden, and artists and authors have compared its open fields of wheat and rapeseed with Provence and Zeeland.
scanian-war: Sweden had suffered a financial crisis in the 1660s and early 1670s. In April 1672 it allied with France, which promised subsidies for a Swedish army in its German dominions and later raised them to 900,000 riksdaler, threatening to withdraw them if the army was not used. In December 1674 Louis XIV called on Sweden to invade Brandenburg. The Swedish army was defeated at the Battle of Fehrbellin on 28 June 1675, the first such defeat of Swedish forces since the Thirty Years' War. Christian V of Denmark-Norway, who had hesitated to join the Dutch against France, now saw his chance and, overcoming the opposition of his adviser Peder Griffenfeld, attacked.

The Danish aim was to recover Scania and the other provinces ceded to Sweden after the Northern Wars. Christian V took Helsingborg on 29 June 1676 with 15,000 troops against about 5,000 Swedes, and much of the peasantry sided with Denmark, so that within a month only Malmö remained Swedish. On the Norwegian front, in the Gyldenløve War, Ulrik Frederick Gyldenløve took Uddevalla and Vänersborg and later Marstrand and regained Bohuslän, and Norwegian forces retook Jämtland in 1677.

In October 1676 the 19-year-old Charles XI marched into Scania with 12,000 men, and the Danish army was beaten at the Battle of Lund on 4 December. In July 1678 Christian V chose not to give battle at Kristianstad and evacuated his troops from Scania.

At sea the Danish and Dutch fleet won at Öland on 1 June 1676, sinking the Swedish ship Kronan, and Niels Juel won at Fehmarn on 31 May 1677 and again at Køge Bay, where the Swedes lost over 3,000 men to about 375 on the Danish-Norwegian side. In Germany, Brandenburg and its allies took Bremen-Verden and Swedish Pomerania, with Stettin falling in December 1677, Stralsund on 11 October 1678 and Greifswald on 5 November.

France negotiated peace for Sweden in the Treaty of Fontainebleau of 23 August 1679, which required that all territory Sweden had lost be returned. The Treaty of Lund confirmed it between Denmark-Norway and Sweden, and Denmark received minor reparations while returning Rügen. Brandenburg returned most of its gains in the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye. In Scania the war raised the hopes of the pro-Danish guerrillas known as Snapphane and their sympathisers, who then suffered harsh repression from the restored Swedish authorities. Scholars disagree about the result: some see a Swedish defeat, others an inconclusive war.
schaan: Schaan is the northernmost municipality in the Liechtenstein Oberland and covers 26.92 square kilometres, including mountains and forest. It is bordered to the south by Vaduz, to the east by Planken and Triesenberg, and to the north by Eschen and Gamprin. In the west the Rhine forms the natural border with Switzerland, and in the east the town is dominated by the Drei Schwestern mountain range. Schaan has four exclaves within other municipalities, and two enclaves within its main territory, so that it borders Austria in three separate places.

Recent archaeological finds show that Schaan has been inhabited for over 6,000 years. In 15 BCE the Romans under Augustus conquered the territory of present-day Liechtenstein and established the province of Raetia. In the 1st century CE a military road was built from Milan to Bregenz, and settlements arose in what is now Schaan. In 1887 two Roman legionaries' helmets, engraved with the names of Publius Cavidius Felix and Numerius Pomponius, were found buried above Dux.

The most important Roman building in the municipality is Fort Schaan, built in the valley to protect against the ever more frequent Alemannic invasions. Part of its foundations and the gate tower can be seen from St Peter's Church, where excavation found a 5th-century baptistery that suggests early Christianization, and traces of a prehistoric settlement. Alemannic settlement is shown by numerous graves. At that time Schaan consisted of two parts: the Romanized Räter-people had their centre at St Peter, while the Alemannic population settled around Specki. This division survives in two alpine cooperatives, the Alemannic Gritsch and the Rhaeto-Roman Guschg.

Schaan is an important traffic hub and industrial location, and the Hilti Corporation has its headquarters on its outskirts. It lies on the Feldkirch–Buchs railway line between Switzerland and Austria and is served by the Schaan-Vaduz station. The municipality is administered by a mayor and a council of 13, elected every four years since 1975.
scheldt: The Scheldt has its headwaters at Gouy in the Aisne department of northern France. It flows north through Cambrai and Valenciennes and enters Belgium near Tournai. Ghent developed at the confluence of the Scheldt and the Lys, one of its main tributaries, after which the river turns east. Near Antwerp, the largest city on its banks, it flows west into the Netherlands towards the North Sea. Its name derives from an adjective corresponding to Old English sceald, meaning shallow.

Originally two branches left the river there, the Oosterschelde and the Westerschelde. In the 19th century the Dutch built a dyke that cut the river off from the eastern branch and joined Zuid-Beveland to the mainland. The river now continues only into the Westerschelde estuary, passing Terneuzen and reaching the sea between Breskens and Vlissingen.

The estuary has always had commercial and strategic importance. Called Scaldis in Roman times, it was important for the shipping lanes to Roman Britain, and the goddess Nehalennia was venerated at its mouth. The Franks took control of the region about 260 and at first raided the Roman supply routes as pirates, but later became allies of the Romans. With the divisions of the Frankish Empire in the 9th century the Scheldt became the border between its western and eastern parts, which later became France and the Holy Roman Empire. This status held, at least on paper, until 1528.

After Antwerp, then the most prominent harbour in Western Europe, fell back under Spanish control in 1585, the Dutch Republic took Zeelandic Flanders on the left bank and closed the Scheldt to shipping. Trade shifted to Amsterdam and Middelburg and Antwerp was seriously crippled, an important and traumatic element in later relations between the Netherlands and what became Belgium. The Kettle War of 1784 was fought over access, and the river was reopened in 1792.

After Belgium became independent in 1830 the river was to remain open to ships bound for Belgian ports, though the Dutch government demanded a toll until 16 July 1863. In the Second World War the Canadian First Army cleared the German positions in the estuary in the Battle of the Scheldt, and supply convoys could reach Antwerp by November 1944.

The Scheldt is an important waterway, navigable from its mouth up to Cambrai, and the port of Antwerp developed on its banks. Canals, among them the Scheldt-Rhine Canal and the Albert Canal, connect it to the basins of the Rhine, Meuse and Seine and to industrial areas around Brussels, Liège, Lille and Mons.
schenectady-new-york: Schenectady is the county seat of Schenectady County, in eastern New York near the confluence of the Mohawk and Hudson rivers. Albany, the state capital, lies about 24 km to the southeast, and with Albany and Troy the city is one of the three principal population and industrial centres of the Capital District. The name comes from the Mohawk word skahnéhtati, meaning beyond the pines, which was used for the area around Albany.

When Europeans first arrived, the Mohawk Valley was the territory of the Mohawk nation, one of the Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, who had held land in the region since at least 1100 CE. In the early 1600s the Mohawks moved their settlements closer to the river, and by 1629 they had taken over territory on the west bank of the Hudson that had belonged to the Algonquian-speaking Mahican. Dutch colonists, many of them from the Albany area, founded Schenectady on the south side of the Mohawk River in the 17th century and laid out farms on strip plots along the river.

After the Revolutionary War the villagers reduced the power of the descendants of the early trustees and gained representative government. Members of the three oldest churches, the Dutch First Reformed Church, St. George's Episcopal Church and First Presbyterian Church, formed a union and founded Union College in 1795; it was the first private nondenominational institution of higher education in the United States. The Mohawk River and the Erie Canal then tied Schenectady to the trade, manufacturing and transport corridor of the Mohawk Valley, and by 1824 more people worked in manufacturing than in agriculture or trade.

General Electric and the American Locomotive Company made the city a manufacturing centre known as the City that Lights and Hauls the World. In the early 20th century it drew immigrants from Eastern and Southern Europe and African Americans leaving the rural South. General Electric's radio station WGY was the second commercial radio station in the United States, and in 1928 its experimental station W2XB began the first regular television broadcasts in the country. The locomotive company's Schenectady plant closed in 1969.

The Stockade Historic District, named after the stockade that once surrounded the colonial settlement, has dozens of Dutch and English colonial houses of the 18th and 19th centuries. It was designated in 1965 as the first historic district in New York State. St. George's Episcopal Church dates from 1735, and the First Reformed Church was formed in the 17th century. Proctors Theatre, built in 1926 as a vaudeville and movie theatre, was the site of one of the first public demonstrations of television.
schengen-agreement: Free movement of people was a core part of the original Treaty of Rome, and from the early days of the European Economic Community nationals of member states could travel from one to another on production of a passport or national identity card. Systematic identity controls nevertheless remained at the border between most member states. Disagreement among them led to an impasse on abolishing border controls within the Community. Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands had already abolished common border controls in 1970 as part of the Benelux Economic Union.

Five of the then ten member states, Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, signed the agreement on 14 June 1985 aboard the MS Princesse Marie-Astrid on the Moselle near the town of Schengen, at the tripoint between France, Germany and Luxembourg. It was signed independently of the European Union, in part because member states did not agree whether the Union had the authority to abolish border controls, and in part because those ready to act did not wish to wait for others. It provided for the harmonisation of visa policies, for residents of border areas to cross away from fixed checkpoints, and for passport checks to be replaced by visual surveillance of vehicles at reduced speed, so that vehicles could cross without stopping.

In 1990 the agreement was supplemented by the Schengen Convention, which created the Schengen Area through the abolition of border controls between members, common rules on visas, and police and judicial cooperation. The agreement and convention were enacted in 1995 for only some signatories. At the Amsterdam Intergovernmental Conference, just over two years later, all member states of the Union except the United Kingdom and Ireland had signed. The Amsterdam Treaty incorporated the Schengen rules into European Union law in 1999, with opt-outs for those two states.

Norway and Iceland signed an association agreement in December 1996 and became part of the area through similar agreements with the Union. Switzerland finalised entry in 2009, after a popular referendum accepted an association agreement in 2005. Border controls have been reintroduced temporarily at various times, for example in several countries in 2016.
schengen-area: Before the First World War most countries of the world, including those in Europe, had lax border policies, which made such educational trips as the Grand Tour possible among the wealthy. The first move towards abolishing border controls between members of the European Communities came on 14 June 1985, when five of the then ten EEC members signed the Schengen Agreement: the Benelux countries, France and West Germany. They did so separately from the European Communities, because consensus could not be reached among all member states.

The agreement, on the gradual abolition of checks at the signatories' common borders, was supplemented by the 1990 Schengen Convention. The area originally had its legal basis outside the European Economic Community, in these two international agreements made by a subset of its members.

The Treaty of Amsterdam incorporated the Schengen rules, known as the Schengen acquis, into European Union law, and the change took effect on 1 May 1999. When the treaty was negotiated, only Ireland and the United Kingdom had not signed the agreement. The United Kingdom chose not to join, and Ireland, which wished to keep its Common Travel Area with the United Kingdom, also declined; both negotiated an opt-out. In 1999 the United Kingdom asked to take part in provisions on police and judicial cooperation, which the Council approved on 29 May 2000.

Denmark adopted the Schengen rules on an intergovernmental basis under a specific opt-out. Iceland and Norway, members of the Nordic Passport Union, became associated with the Schengen activities of the Union, and Switzerland was allowed to take part in the same manner in 2008 and Liechtenstein in 2011.

A state that wishes to join is assessed by the European Commission on border control legislation, infrastructure and organisation, personal data protection, visas, deportations and police cooperation. It must take responsibility for controlling the Union's external borders, apply common rules for land, sea and air frontiers, issue uniform Schengen visas, cooperate with the law enforcement agencies of other members and connect to the Schengen Information System. Admission then requires a unanimous decision of the Council of the European Union after consulting the European Parliament.

Some territories have special arrangements: Ceuta, Melilla and Mount Athos are fully inside the area with specific border control arrangements, while the Faroe Islands and Svalbard are excluded. Monaco is administered as part of the area through its open border with France under a 1963 convention. Andorra, San Marino and Vatican City have open or semi-open borders with their neighbours without being formal members.
scheveningen: Scheveningen is one of the eight districts of The Hague and also a subdistrict of that city. It has a long sandy beach, an esplanade, a pier and a lighthouse, and its harbour serves both fishing and tourism. It was never an independent municipality, but it has its own coat of arms, officially recognised by the Hague council in 1984, and it has always kept a strong identity of its own. It once had its own football club in the top Dutch division, Scheveningen Holland Sport, which was forced to merge with ADO Den Haag in the later twentieth century.

The name Sceveninghe first appears around 1280. The first inhabitants may have been Anglo-Saxons, though other historians favour a Scandinavian origin, and fishing was the main source of food and income. On 10 August 1653 English and Dutch fleets fought the Battle of Scheveningen off the coast while thousands watched from the shore. In 1660 Montagu's flagship picked up the English king at Scheveningen to accomplish the Restoration. A road to The Hague was built in 1663.

Storms destroyed the church and half the houses in 1470 and struck again in 1570, 1775, 1825, 1860, 1881 and 1894. After the last, the villagers decided to build a harbour, finished in 1904, since fishing boats with flat bottoms, the bomschuiten, had until then been pulled up the beach. By about 1870 over 150 of them were in use. In 1818 Jacob Pronk built a wooden bathing house on a dune, the start of the resort, and the Kurhaus hotel opened in 1886. Painters including Adriaen van de Velde, Simon de Vlieger and Hendrik Willem Mesdag recorded the village; Mesdag's panorama, 14 m high and 120 m wide, preserved the view of 1881.

The International Skating Union was founded here in 1892. A chess tournament held in the district in 1923 gave its name to the Scheveningen Variation of the Sicilian Defense, played there by several players including Max Euwe.

From 21 April 1960 the pirate station Radio Veronica broadcast from a ship anchored about four miles off the coast, joined later by Radio Noordzee Internationaal and Radio Caroline, until the Netherlands ratified the Treaty of Strasbourg on 1 September 1974. Since the 1970s the fishing industry has declined, most fishermen's houses have been demolished, and some, including original hofjes, have been protected. The old local dress and dialect have largely gone, as have the family nicknames once used to tell apart the many people who shared surnames such as Pronk. Annual events include the New Year's Day winter swim and a competition between Duindorp and Scheveningen dorp to build the largest bonfire tower.
schleswig: Schleswig, or Southern Jutland, covers the area from about 60 kilometres north to 70 kilometres south of the present border between Germany and Denmark. From early medieval times it was a buffer zone between Denmark and the Holy Roman Empire and a transit area for goods between the North Sea and the Baltic. Its early inhabitants were Danes in the north, North Frisians on the coast and islands, and Saxons in the south. Hedeby, Scandinavia's biggest trading centre in the early Viking Age, stood here, with the Danevirke, whose great expansion around 737 has been read as a sign of a unified Danish state.

The Treaty of Heiligen of 811 between King Hemming and Charlemagne set the border at the Eider, and Conrad II and Canute the Great fixed it there again in 1027. In the 1230s Southern Jutland was given as an appanage to Abel Valdemarsen, a younger son of Valdemar II of Denmark, whose descendants pressed claims to the Danish throne for much of the next century. Close ties with the German Duchy of Holstein, a fief of the Empire, followed, while Schleswig remained a Danish fief. This double loyalty later became a root of the dispute between the German states and Denmark.

From about 1830 many inhabitants came to see themselves as German or Danish. Danish National Liberals demanded the duchy under the slogan Denmark to the Eider, and their rise to power in early 1848 provoked a German uprising and the First Schleswig War (1848–51). The London Protocol of 1852 confirmed the king of Denmark as duke but kept the duchies distinct from Denmark. After Denmark's November Constitution of 1863 came the Second Schleswig War of 1864, and Austria and Prussia governed the duchies jointly. Prussia annexed Schleswig and Holstein after the Austro-Prussian War of 1866.

The Treaty of Versailles provided for plebiscites, held in 1920. Northern Schleswig voted by 75 per cent to join Denmark and Central Schleswig by 80 per cent to remain German; Southern Schleswig held no vote. Substantial minorities remained on both sides of the new border. In the Copenhagen-Bonn declaration of 1955 West Germany and Denmark promised to uphold each other's minorities. Southern Schleswig is part of the German state of Schleswig-Holstein, and Northern Schleswig is in Denmark; the two co-operate as the Euroregion Sønderjylland–Schleswig.
schleswig-holstein: Schleswig-Holstein lies at the base of the Jutland Peninsula between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, and covers 15,763 km2. It borders Denmark, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Lower Saxony and Hamburg. The state consists of Holstein, the southern part of the former Duchy of Schleswig, Lauenburg and the formerly independent city of Lübeck. The Kiel Canal connects Brunsbüttel on the North Sea with Kiel on the Baltic Sea.

Saxon Holstein became part of the Holy Roman Empire after Charlemagne's Saxon campaigns in the late 8th century, and from 811 the River Eider was its northern border. Between 500 and 1200 Schleswig was part of Denmark. In the 12th century Duke Abel came into conflict with his brother King Eric IV and won autonomy for Schleswig as a duchy. From 1460 the Danish king ruled both Schleswig and Holstein as their duke, although Holstein belonged to the Holy Roman Empire.

In the 19th century both Danes and Germans claimed the duchies, in a dispute called the Schleswig-Holstein Question. Germans wanted both to join the German Confederation and cited the Treaty of Ribe, by which they were to stay forever undivided, while Danes held that the Eider was Denmark's natural border. Holstein was entirely German-speaking, while Schleswig was predominantly Danish-speaking until a shift to German began in the south in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

In 1848 Denmark tried to annex the area and Prussia invaded, beginning the First Schleswig War, which Denmark won. Prussia and Austria won the Second Schleswig War of 1864, and the territory became the Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein rather than the independent state that German Schleswig-Holsteiners had hoped for.

After the First World War the Allies arranged plebiscites in 1920, and the Danish-speaking north returned to Denmark. After the Second World War the province came under British occupation, and on 23 August 1946 the military government reconstituted it as a separate state.

Schleswig-Holstein is the northernmost of the sixteen German states, with its capital at Kiel and other main cities at Lübeck and Flensburg. German is its official language, and Low German, Danish and North Frisian are recognised minority languages. Its culture combines Danish, Frisian and German elements.
schleusingen: Schleusingen lies in the district of Hildburghausen in Thuringia, 10 kilometres north of Hildburghausen and 12 kilometres southeast of Suhl, in the region known as the Henneberger Land. The town takes its name from the river Schleuse, which passes through two of its outlying districts, but the town itself stands on the Nahe, a tributary of the Schleuse. The river Erle joins the Nahe in the town from the north. Besides the core town it includes seventeen other districts.

Schleusingen was first mentioned in documents in 1232 as Villa Slusungen. Count Poppo VII of Henneberg built the Bertholdsburg as a residence and fortification between 1226 and 1232. When the County of Henneberg was partitioned into three lines in 1274, the castle became the residence of the Schleusingen line. The town suffered a catastrophic fire in 1353, and further fires in 1679, 1765, 1773 and 1876 destroyed whole districts. It received town rights in 1412, but the right to hold a market only in 1533.

In 1502 Count Wilhelm IV founded a Barfüsser friary on the outskirts. During the German Peasants' War of 1525 the people, documents and valuables of the neighbouring monasteries of Veßra and Trostadt were sent to the Bertholdsburg for safety. The Reformation was introduced in 1544, and the Aegidienkapelle of St Johannis Church became the burial place of the counts of Henneberg in 1566. The friary became state property and served as a school from 1560, which was inaugurated as a Gymnasium on 7 June 1577 and still exists as the Hennebergisches Gymnasium Georg Ernst.

Schleusingen was the seat of the counts of Henneberg until 1583. When Count Georg Ernst died and the Henneberg line became extinct, the town passed to the Saxon dukes of the Ernestine and Albertine lines, at first under joint administration. From 1500 to 1806 it belonged to the Franconian Circle of the Holy Roman Empire.

The main sights are Bertholdsburg castle, the town church of St Johannis, the Teutsche Schule and the market place. The Hennebergisches Gymnasium Georg Ernst, inaugurated in 1577, still exists, and the town has grown by incorporating neighbouring villages, among them Fischbach in 1970 and Nahetal-Waldau and Sankt Kilian in 2018.
schlieffen-plan: The name Schlieffen Plan was given after the First World War to German war plans influenced by Field Marshal Alfred von Schlieffen, who was Chief of the General Staff of the German Army from 1891 to 1906. In 1905 and 1906 he devised an army deployment plan for a decisive offensive against France, in which German forces were to invade through the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Belgium rather than across the common border.

German strategic thinking in those decades was shaped by the Wars of Unification, which had been short and decided by great battles. Helmuth von Moltke the Elder, however, had come to doubt that a quick victory over France was possible once it introduced conscription in 1872, and from 1877 he wrote plans that allowed for an incomplete victory settled by diplomats. Schlieffen was appointed in February 1891 as a safe choice, junior and little known outside the General Staff.

Helmuth von Moltke the Younger succeeded Schlieffen on 1 January 1906, beset with doubts about a German victory in a great European war. He kept the idea of a large enveloping manoeuvre, partly because the Japanese victory in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905 had weakened Russia. Records of his thinking are fragmentary, and most pre-war planning was secret.

When war came, the German deployment plan, Aufmarsch II, concentrated the army, less 20 per cent to defend Prussia and the coast, on the Belgian border, to force a decisive battle against the French north of their frontier fortifications. France put into effect Plan XVII, an offensive into Alsace-Lorraine and southern Belgium, in the fighting later named the Battle of the Frontiers. The French attacks suffered worse losses than expected and were repulsed.

After the defeat of 1918, official historians of the Reichsarchiv described the plan as a blueprint for victory, and blamed Moltke for ruining it after the First Battle of the Marne, 5–12 September 1914. In 1956 Gerhard Ritter's Der Schlieffenplan: Kritik eines Mythos began a revision, and from the 1970s Martin van Creveld, John Keegan, Hew Strachan and others judged that railways and roads made it impossible to move enough troops far enough and fast enough for a decisive battle if the French retreated.

Much of the Prussian army archive was destroyed in the bombing of Potsdam in April 1945, but some records resurfaced after the fall of the German Democratic Republic, allowing an outline of German war planning for the first time. Terence Zuber argued that the plan was a myth of the 1920s; later scholarship did not uphold this, though it revealed that Schlieffen had been far less dogmatic than presumed.
schmalkalden: Schmalkalden lies in the district of Schmalkalden-Meiningen, in the south-west of Thuringia. It stands on the southern slope of the Thuringian Forest, on the Schmalkalde river, a tributary of the Werra. It is twinned with Fontaine in the Isère in France and with Recklinghausen in Germany.

The place is first mentioned in a deed of 874 as Smalcalta, in the Frankish duchy of Thuringia, and received town privileges about 1180. When Landgrave Henry Raspe of Thuringia died without issue in 1247, it passed to the House of Henneberg-Schleusingen, while the major part of the landgraviate fell to the House of Wettin in Meissen. To secure their acquisition the counts of Henneberg allied with the Landgraviate of Hesse and concluded an inheritance treaty. In 1360, together with Landgrave Henry II of Hesse, they paid off Frederick V, Burgrave of Nuremberg, a son of Elisabeth of Henneberg.

In 1531 the town hall was the site where Protestant princes under the lead of Landgrave Philip I of Hesse established the Schmalkaldic League, to protect their religious and political interests. In 1537 the Smalcald Articles were drawn up there by Martin Luther, Philipp Melanchthon and other reformers. When the Henneberg line became extinct in 1583, its share was inherited by William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, who made the town a residence and built Wilhelmsburg Castle, finished in 1590.

The Lordship of Schmalkalden remained an exclave of Hesse. From 1868 it was part of the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau, until it was incorporated into the Province of Saxony in 1944; in 1945 it became part of the State of Thuringia. The town was heavily damaged by bombing in the war and from 1949 formed part of East Germany with Thuringia. It has its present political configuration since reunification.
schmalkaldic-league: The League was officially established on 27 February 1531 as a defensive religious alliance: its members pledged to defend each other if Emperor Charles V attacked their territories. At the insistence of the Elector of Saxony, membership was conditional on agreement to the Lutheran Augsburg Confession or the Reformed Tetrapolitan Confession. Unlike earlier alliances such as the League of Torgau it had a substantial military, the members agreeing to provide 10,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry for their mutual protection.

Its formation, together with the advance of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in 1532, led Ferdinand of Austria to grant a religious peace, concluded at Nuremberg on 23 July 1532. Supporters of the Reformation obtained religious liberty until the meeting of a council.

In December 1535 the League opened itself to anyone who subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, and Anhalt, Württemberg, Pomerania and the cities of Augsburg, Frankfurt am Main and Kempten joined. It allied with Denmark-Norway in 1538 and gained the Electoral Palatinate in 1545. The members rarely provoked Charles directly, but they confiscated church land, expelled bishops and Catholic princes and helped spread Lutheranism through northern Germany. Martin Luther attended the meeting of 1537, for which he prepared the Smalcald Articles; they were not formally adopted then but entered the Book of Concord in 1580.

For fifteen years the League met no opposition, because Charles was at war with France and the Ottoman Empire. Francis I of France, though he persecuted Protestants at home, supported the princes from 1535 until the Treaty of Crépy in 1544. Once at peace, Charles turned on the League. In the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–1547 its leaders could not agree on a plan of battle; on 24 April 1547 the imperial forces routed them at the Battle of Mühlberg, and Philip of Hesse surrendered in May. Reformers such as Martin Bucer fled to England.

In 1548 Charles forced the League to accept the Augsburg Interim. A Protestant victory in the Second Schmalkaldic War in 1552 made him flee across the Alps, and Ferdinand signed the Peace of Passau, which granted some freedoms to Protestants. Three years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism official status in the Holy Roman Empire and let princes choose the religion of their domains, by the principle of cuius regio, eius religio.
schmalkaldic-war: Many imperial states adopted Lutheranism despite the opposition of the Catholic House of Habsburg, which saw the conversions as a quest for autonomy at the expense of imperial authority. The Diet of Worms of 1521 placed Martin Luther under the imperial ban. Lutheran states led by Elector John Frederick I of Saxony and Landgrave Philip I of Hesse formed the Schmalkaldic League at Schmalkalden in 1531.

In 1544 Charles V returned to Germany after the Treaty of Crépy and sought allies, among them Pope Paul III and the Lutheran Duke Maurice of Saxony, cousin of John Frederick. On 4 July 1546 the League's leaders met at Ichtershausen and decided on a preventive war. Luther had died in February 1546; he had argued against the legality of such a war.

The war began in Swabia in July 1546, when the League's army occupied Füssen. The League would not give battle against the entrenched imperial troops, and William IV of Bavaria and Archduke Ferdinand I declared themselves neutral. On 20 July Charles placed John Frederick and Philip under the imperial ban. In October Maurice, helped by Ferdinand, invaded his cousin's Ernestine lands, and John Frederick turned back to retake them.

Meanwhile the imperial cities and princes of the south, among them Duke Ulrich of Württemberg, submitted to the emperor. In 1547 Charles went to Bohemia, where he joined his brother Ferdinand, and on 24 April the League's forces were routed at the Battle of Mühlberg, where John Frederick was taken prisoner. Only Bremen and Magdeburg held out.

John Frederick was sentenced to death and, to obtain a pardon, signed the Capitulation of Wittenberg on 19 May 1547. He lost the electoral dignity to Maurice, who was declared elector on 4 June. Philip of Hesse surrendered and was imprisoned at once.

In 1548 Charles issued the Augsburg Interim to prepare the return of Protestants to the Catholic Church. It provoked a revolt in 1552, the Second Schmalkaldic War, led by Maurice with the backing of Henry II of France. Charles fled and cancelled the Interim in the Peace of Passau. The Peace of Augsburg followed three years later, and the next year Charles abdicated in favour of Ferdinand.
schneeberg-saxony: Schneeberg lies on the Silver Road in the upper western Ore Mountains, in Saxony's district of Erzgebirgskreis, 4 km west of Aue and 17 km southeast of Zwickau. The heart of the town stands on the Schneeberg, which reaches 470 metres above sea level and gives the town its name. Among the surrounding peaks are the Gleesberg to the east and the Keilberg to the north, and the church of St. Wolfgang is visible from afar.

Schneeberg's history of more than 500 years has been shaped by mining more than anything else, and mining laid the groundwork for the town's founding. The original silver mining also yielded cobalt and bismuth mining by the middle of the sixteenth century. Uranium mining between 1946 and 1958 caused the population to rise quickly, and from 1952 to 1958 Schneeberg was a district-free town. Between 1952 and 1990 it was part of the Bezirk Karl-Marx-Stadt of East Germany.

The town grew by amalgamation. Bergstadt Neustädtel joined in 1939, the community of Griesbach in 1952 and Lindenau in 1999. A railway spur of 5 km linked it to Niederschlema from 1859 to 1952, and Albert motorcycles with 183cc two-stroke engines were made there by Theodore Albert between 1922 and 1924. Its schools grew from a lyceum into a Gymnasium, and the town also had a lace tatting school, an art school and a teachers' college.

Schneeberg has roughly 16,400 inhabitants and belongs to the Town League of Silberberg. The church of St. Wolfgang is one of the biggest and architecturally most mature Late Gothic churches, an early type of Reformation church, and holds works by Lucas Cranach the Elder and the Crodel family of painters. Other sights include the neo-Gothic Town Hall, newly built in the mid nineteenth century, Baroque buildings and mining memorials.
schola-medica-salernitana: The school was founded in the 9th century at Salerno on the Tyrrhenian Sea, originally in the dispensary of a monastery, though documentation for the first period is poor and it is unclear whether it already had a formal organisation. A legend ascribes its foundation to four masters who met by chance sheltering under the arches of an aqueduct: the Greek Pontus, the Latin Salernus, the Jew Helinus and the Arab Abdela, who agreed to form a partnership to collect and spread their knowledge. Reports from the late 10th century show that Salerno was known as a centre of medicine from 985, and in 988 Adalbero II of Verdun went there to be cured.

The arrival of Constantine the African in 1077 began its classic period. Through the encouragement of Alfano I, Archbishop of Salerno, and Constantine's translations from Arabic, Salerno gained the title of Hippocratica Civitas. Constantine translated works including the Pantegni of Haly Abbas, the Viaticum of al-Jazzār and treatises of Rhazes and Isaac Israel, and his translations became the centre of the school's teaching after the middle of the 12th century. The city's position as a Mediterranean port, near Muslim and Jewish communities, brought a diversity of ideas, and the school joined the Greek-Latin tradition with Arab and Jewish learning, with an approach based on prevention rather than cure.

Women taught and studied there. The best known, Trota, is credited with works on gynaecology and cosmetics known together as The Trotula, and others were known as the mulieres Salernitanae. The curriculum is described as three years of logic, five of medicine, including surgery and anatomy, and a year of practice with an experienced physician. Ruggiero di Fugaldo wrote an early treatise on surgery. The school also produced the Antidotarium Nicolai, a pharmacopeia of the Middle Ages, and the Latin verse Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum, a collection of rules of hygiene whose author gave it a Salernitan origin, in the 12th or 13th century, to advertise it.

With the rise of the University of Naples, and of Montpellier, Padua and Bologna, the school lost importance. Gioacchino Murat abolished it on 29 November 1811 in his reorganisation of public education in the Kingdom of Naples, and its remaining doctors of medicine and law worked in Salerno's Convitto Tasso until 1861, when Francesco De Sanctis closed them. Because it also taught philosophy, theology and law, some consider it the first university.
scholar-officials: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.
scholasticism: The words scholastic and scholasticism come from the Latin scholasticus, the Latin form of the Greek scholastikos, meaning of or pertaining to schools, so that the scholastics were roughly schoolmen. Its foundations were laid by Boethius through his logical and theological essays. The Carolingian Renaissance brought the first significant renewal of learning in the West: Charlemagne drew scholars from England and Ireland and by a decree of 787 established schools at every abbey in his empire. Among them was Johannes Scotus Eriugena (815–877), who knew Greek and translated works into Latin. Lanfranc and Anselm of Canterbury in the 11th century and Peter Abelard in France are counted among its founders.

Scholasticism was a method of learning more than a philosophy or a theology, with a strong emphasis on dialectical reasoning to extend knowledge by inference and to resolve contradictions. A teacher would choose a book by an established authority and read it with the class. Points where sources disagreed were written down as sententiae, and the two sides were then reconciled by philological analysis, which showed that words could have several meanings, or by logical analysis.

Instruction had several parts. In the lectio a teacher read an authoritative text followed by a commentary, with no questions allowed. The meditatio let students reflect on the text, and in the quaestio they could ask the questions that had occurred to them. Disputations were arranged to resolve controversial questions: each side of an either/or question was argued in turn and the arguments against the chosen position were refuted.

The 13th and early 14th centuries are generally seen as the high period of scholasticism. Universities grew in the large cities, and the Franciscans, founded by Francis of Assisi in 1209, and the Dominicans, founded by St Dominic in 1215, competed for control of them. The Franciscan Bonaventure held that reason can discover truth only when it is illuminated by faith. The Dominicans Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas made more use of Aristotle. Aquinas's Summa Theologica (1265–1274) is considered the pinnacle of scholastic philosophy.

Scholastic methods outlasted the Middle Ages. After the Reformation Calvinists largely adopted the scholastic method of theology, while differing about sources of authority and its content. A revival of medieval scholastic philosophy, sometimes called neo-Thomism, began in the second half of the 19th century.
scipio-aemilianus: Scipio Aemilianus was the second son of Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, the victor of the Third Macedonian War, and his first wife, Papiria Masonis. He was adopted by his first cousin Publius Cornelius Scipio, a son of Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, who had defeated Hannibal. At seventeen he took part in his father's campaign in Greece. Plutarch relates that when he was missing after the Battle of Pydna the whole army searched for him, and that he returned late, covered with the blood of the enemies he had slain.

In 151 BCE, when Roman recruitment for the war in Hispania had collapsed, he asked the Senate to send him there as a military tribune or legate, and his example led others to volunteer. In the Third Punic War he was a military tribune who repeatedly saved Roman forces from disaster. In 147 BCE he was elected consul although under the legal age and was assigned to Africa without the usual drawing of lots. After a year of fighting he took Carthage and made about 50,000 survivors prisoner, roughly one tenth of the city's population. On the Senate's orders he had the city burnt and razed. It was formerly believed that he also salted the ground, but modern scholars have found no evidence of that.

Elected consul again in 134 BCE, he took command in the Numantine War, restored discipline in a demoralized army and besieged Numantia with a circuit of fortifications nine kilometres long. The Numantines were starved into surrender, and Scipio sold the survivors into slavery and destroyed the city. He served as censor in 142 BCE. A patron of writers and philosophers, he gathered the Scipionic circle, which included Polybius, Panaetius, Lucilius and Terence.

Scipio disliked the land reforms of his brother-in-law Tiberius Gracchus, and he became unpopular when he took the side of Rome's Italian allies against the commission applying the land law of Gracchus. He died at home in 129 BCE, and rumours of murder circulated, naming Cornelia, Sempronia, Fulvius Flaccus, Gaius Gracchus and Gaius Papirius Carbo. Modern historians see no strong evidence for any cause but natural death. According to Polybius, Scipio wept at the burning of Carthage and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy, saying he feared the same fate for Rome.
scipio-africanus: Publius Cornelius Scipio was born in 236 BCE into the patrician Cornelii Scipiones, one of the major families of Rome. His father, also called Publius, was consul in 218 BCE. He followed his father to the war against Carthage that began that year. Polybius claims that at the river Ticinus the son saved his father's life, though other sources credit an unnamed Ligurian slave. He survived the Roman disaster at Cannae.

In 211 BCE his father and uncle, who commanded Rome's armies in Spain, divided their forces against three Carthaginian armies and fell in separate battles. In 210 BCE Scipio, though he had never held consular office, was elected to command in Hispania. His campaign led to victory at Ilipa in 206 BCE against Hannibal's brother Mago Barca and to the Roman conquest of Carthaginian Iberia. He was elected consul for 205 BCE, at 31 still technically too young, and demanded the province of Africa. Despite the opposition of Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, the senate gave him Sicily with permission to cross into Africa. It assigned him no additional soldiers, so he recruited volunteers.

His invasion of the Carthaginian homeland forced the recall of Hannibal. After failed negotiations Scipio routed Hannibal's army at Zama in 202 BCE, forcing Carthage to sue for peace and ending the Second Punic War. He earned the epithet Africanus. He was censor in 199 BCE and consul again in 194 BCE.

Scipio had many political opponents, among them Cato the Elder. In 187 BCE he and his brother Lucius were tried for bribes they were said to have received from the Seleucid king Antiochus III. He retired to his estate at Liternum on the coast of Campania, where he died. Sources give different dates, but most modern ones, such as the Oxford Classical Dictionary, prefer 183 BCE.

His memoirs, written in Greek, are lost, so accounts of his life rest on Polybius, Livy, Appian and Cassius Dio. He was the first Roman general to expand Roman territory outside Italy and the nearby islands, and his victory at Zama paved the way for the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE. His interest in Greek culture influenced the Roman elite. Petrarch made him the hero of his Latin epic Africa, and the Continence of Scipio, in which he returns a captive woman to her fiancé, was painted by artists from Mantegna to Poussin.
scotland: The mainland of Scotland makes up the northern third of the island of Great Britain, with a total area of 30,977 square miles (80,231 km2). Its only land border, with England, runs for 96 miles (154 km) between the basin of the River Tweed and the Solway Firth. The mainland is divided into the Highlands, a mountainous region in the north and north-west, the Lowlands, a flatter plain across the centre, and the Southern Uplands along the border. Ben Nevis, at 4,413 feet (1,345 m), is the highest peak of the British Isles.

The earliest known evidence of people in Scotland is stone tools of the Hamburgian culture, made by hunter-gatherers who arrived around 14,500 to 14,000 years ago, soon after the ice sheet retreated. Neolithic farmers came about 6000 years ago. Skara Brae on Orkney, the Callanish Stones on Lewis and Maes Howe on Orkney belong to this period, the stone monuments of the third millennium BCE. The Greek sailor Pytheas made the first written reference in 320 BCE, calling the northern tip of Britain Orcas.

The Roman governor Agricola invaded in 79 CE and defeated a Caledonian army at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 83 CE, but within three years the Roman armies had withdrawn to the Southern Uplands. Under Trajan, who reigned from 98 to 117, Roman control had lapsed to the south of a line between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth, where Hadrian later built his wall. The Kingdom of Scotland emerged as a sovereign state in the 9th century and kept its independence from England partly through an alliance with France.

Its extent was largely fixed by the Treaty of York of 1237 with England and the Treaty of Perth of 1266 with Norway. Orkney and Shetland were acquired from Norway in 1472, and Berwick-upon-Tweed was ceded to England in 1482. James VI succeeded to the English and Irish thrones in 1603, and on 1 May 1707 Scotland and England combined as the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom, with Edinburgh as its capital and Glasgow as its largest city. The census of 2022 counted 5,436,600 people. A Scottish Parliament was re-established in 1999 with devolved authority over many areas of domestic policy. Scotland keeps its own legal system, education system and religious history. English and Scots are the most widely spoken languages, while Scottish Gaelic is spoken natively mainly in the Hebrides. Its seven World Heritage Sites include St Kilda, the Old Town and New Town of Edinburgh, New Lanark and the Antonine Wall.
scottish-enlightenment: The Scottish Enlightenment was the period in the 18th and early 19th centuries in Scotland marked by an outpouring of intellectual and scientific work. By the eighteenth century Scotland had a network of parish schools in the Lowlands and five universities: St Andrews, Glasgow, Edinburgh, King's College and Marischal College. The union with England in 1707 ended the Scottish Parliament and drew politicians to London, but Scots law, the Church of Scotland, the universities and the medical establishment stayed in Scotland. Their lawyers, ministers, professors, doctors and architects formed a new middle-class elite that dominated urban Scotland and made the Enlightenment possible. Glasgow's trade with the Americas, especially in tobacco, brought wealth, and banking grew.

Intellectual life centred on books and on clubs, beginning in Edinburgh in the 1710s with the Easy Club. Others included the Select Society, formed by the painter Allan Ramsay the younger with David Hume and Adam Smith, and the Poker Club, formed in 1762 and named by Adam Ferguson. Glasgow had a Political Economy Club to link academics and merchants.

Its thinkers shared the rational outlook of the wider Enlightenment, asserting the importance of reason and rejecting authority that reason could not justify. In Scotland it was marked by a thorough empiricism and practicality, whose chief values were improvement, virtue and practical benefit. Francis Hutcheson, professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow from 1729 to 1746, was its first major philosopher. David Hume's Treatise of Human Nature (1738) helped set out philosophical empiricism and scepticism, while Thomas Reid, in An Inquiry into the Human Mind (1764), formulated Common Sense Realism. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, is the starting point of modern economics.

Its influence reached far beyond Scotland, carried by the Scottish diaspora and by foreign students at its universities. The new Encyclopædia Britannica was designed in Edinburgh and first published in three volumes between 1768 and 1771. The architect Robert Adam influenced building in Britain, Western Europe, North America and Russia. The political ideas had an impact on the Founding Fathers of the United States, and Common Sense Realism was influential in nineteenth-century American thought. The movement was long linked with abolitionism, but the academic John Stewart argues that many of its members supported slavery and scientific racism, a result of Scotland's large part in the Atlantic slave trade.
scottish-highlands: The Highlands are the northernmost mountain ranges of Great Britain, divided by the Great Glen between the Grampian Mountains to the south-east and the Northwest Highlands. The name also covers the area north and west of the Highland Boundary Fault, which runs from Arran to Stonehaven, though the exact boundary is not clearly defined, particularly in the east. The region lies on ancient Cambrian and Precambrian rocks uplifted in the Caledonian Orogeny, with Lewisian gneiss up to 3 billion years old, and includes Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the British Isles. The Highlands are the only area in the British Isles with a boreal forest biome, with remnants of the Caledonian Forest.

The region was home to the Caledonians or Picts and became the mainland stronghold of the Hebridean Gaels, whose Gaelic language succeeded that of their neighbours. The cultural distinction between Highlander and Lowlander was first noted towards the end of the 14th century. The clan was the main social unit, and James VI saw clans as a challenge to royal authority. The Statutes of Iona in 1609 began integrating clan leaders into Scottish society. After the Jacobite rising of 1745 the British government banned the bearing of arms and the wearing of tartan, laws mostly repealed by the end of the 18th century. The Black Watch, raised in 1739, was the first Highland regiment of the British Army.

Between about 1760 and 1850 agricultural improvement brought the Highland clearances, in which many tenants were evicted to make way for large-scale sheep farms; in the west and north they were resettled in crofting communities and worked in kelping and fishing. Famine recurred, and potato blight arrived in 1846. The population, around 300,000 in the 18th and early 19th centuries, then declined through emigration, mostly to Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Crofters, many in the Free Church after 1843, challenged landlords through the Highland Land League in the 1880s, and the Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886 reduced rents and guaranteed fixity of tenure.

Inverness is regarded as the capital of the Highlands, and the Highland Council has its administrative centre there. The area is among the most sparsely populated in Europe. Scottish Gaelic, once the language of the region, is now largely confined to the Hebrides, and a Highland form of Scottish English predominates. Tartan and the kilt were adopted by elites in the 1820s after the Ossian cycle and Walter Scott's staging of George IV's visit in 1822, and tartan became a major symbol of Scottish identity.
scramble-for-africa: By 1841 European businessmen had set up small trading posts along the African coasts, but they seldom moved inland, and large parts of the continent were close to uninhabitable for Europeans because of tropical diseases such as malaria. As late as the 1870s Europeans controlled about 10 per cent of Africa, all of it near the coasts, chiefly Angola and Mozambique, held by Portugal, the Cape Colony, held by the United Kingdom, and Algeria, held by France. Steamships, railways, telegraphs and quinine made the interior far more accessible.

During the Long Depression of 1873–1896 Africa offered European states an open market and raw materials such as ivory, rubber, palm oil, cocoa, diamonds, tea and tin. Britain also wished to secure the route to India and the Suez Canal, completed in 1869, and navies needed coaling stations and bases.

Seven Western European powers took part: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom. In the Congo, Henry Morton Stanley made treaties with chiefs on behalf of Leopold II of Belgium, and by 1882 these gave a base for the Congo Free State. In 1881 Pierre de Brazza raised the French flag over the newly founded Brazzaville. Portugal, which claimed the area under old treaties with the Kingdom of Kongo, made a treaty with Britain on 26 February 1884 to block Leopold's access to the Atlantic.
