He died unexpectedly in 225 BCE after a fall from his horse. He was succeeded by his eldest son, who took the name Seleucus III, and then by a younger son, Antiochus III the Great, in 222 BCE, under whom the empire was restored.
selim-i: Selim was born in Amasya on 10 October 1470, the son of Şehzade Bayezid, later Bayezid II, and Gülbahar Hatun, a Pontic Greek concubine. In 1487 his father sent him to Trabzon as governor. There he faced the Safavids on the eastern frontier. In 1505 a Safavid prince, Ebrahim Mirza, marched on Trabzon with 3,000 men, and Selim repelled him with an expeditionary force of 450 and chased him to Erzincan. In 1507 Selim attacked Erzincan and Bayburt and defeated a Safavid army of 10,000, at a time when his father had not answered Shah Ismail I's violations of Ottoman sovereignty.

Selim's early reign was dominated by tension with Shah Ismail I, who had made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Persia and by 1510 held Iran, Azerbaijan, Mesopotamia and eastern Anatolia. In 1511 Ismail supported the Şahkulu Rebellion in Anatolia, and Selim's mufti issued a fatwa of takfir against him and his followers. Selim had Shiites aged 7 to 70 listed in central Anatolian cities including Tokat, Sivas and Amasya, and his forces executed those they found, most by beheading, in what was the largest massacre in Ottoman history until the end of the 19th century. During the advance of 1514 his troops suffered from Ismail's scorched-earth tactics.

In 1516 Selim attacked the Mamluk Sultanate and defeated it at Marj Dabiq on 24 August 1516 and at Ridaniya on 22 January 1517. He annexed Syria, Palestine, the Hejaz and Egypt, and with them the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He took the title Servant of the Two Holy Cities. The last Abbasid caliph, al-Mutawakkil III, was sent to Istanbul. An account of a formal transfer of the caliphate to Selim emerged in the eighteenth century, but it was a later invention, and Selim himself made no claim to the office. The conquest ended the Portuguese–Mamluk naval war, and the Ottomans took over attempts to check Portuguese expansion in the Indian Ocean.

Selim was planning a campaign westward when he fell ill and died on 22 September 1520, aged 49. The official cause was a mistreated carbuncle, though some historians suggest cancer or poison, and others note that plague was then present in the empire. He was buried in what became known as the Yavuz Selim Mosque, commissioned by his son Suleiman I.

He was bilingual in Turkish and Persian and wrote poetry in both under the pen name Selimi. He had a fiery temper, and a popular Ottoman curse wished that one might be a vizier of Selim's. Many historians hold that he prepared the empire for its height under Suleiman I.
selim-ii: Selim was born on 28 May 1524 in the Topkapı Palace, Constantinople, the second surviving son of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan. In 1542 he became governor of Karaman, with Konya as his seat, and after the death of his brother Şehzade Mehmed in November 1543 he was appointed governor of Saruhan, residing in Manisa. The execution of his elder half-brother Şehzade Mustafa on Suleiman's order in September 1553 left Selim and his brother Bayezid as the main contenders for the throne. Their rivalry ended when Bayezid marched on Konya in 1559 and Selim, with troops sent by Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, won the engagement.

Selim took the throne on 29 September 1566. Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept Suleiman's death secret until Selim reached the army at Belgrade, where the allegiance ceremony was held. The soldiers, refused an accession payment, revolted in Istanbul until Selim's sister Mihrimah Sultan paid the Janissaries from her own fortune. Sokollu, grand vizier from 1565 until his assassination in 1579, persuaded Selim to make peace with the Habsburgs, and the Treaty of Edirne of 1568 had Maximilian II recognise Ottoman conquests in Hungary and keep paying tribute. Sokollu opposed the Cyprus campaign, but Selim ordered it.

Elsewhere the reign met mixed fortunes. In 1567 the Zaydi imam al-Mutahhar ibn Yahya Sharaf al-Din rose in Yemen and took Sana'a and Ta'izz; Ottoman forces recovered Aden, Ta'izz and much of the highlands, and a peace at Kawkaban in May 1570 brought recognition of Ottoman suzerainty. A fleet intended for Aceh, which had asked for help against the Portuguese, was diverted to Yemen, and only two ships with cannon and gunsmiths arrived. An attempt on Astrakhan in 1569 failed, and a canal between the Don and Volga was left unfinished. The Ottomans also pressed for Henry of Valois's election in Poland in 1573. Venice ceded Cyprus in a peace of 7 March 1573 and agreed to pay 300,000 ducats.

Selim died on 15 December 1574. His wife Nurbanu Sultan kept the death hidden for several days so that her son Murad could arrive and claim the throne unopposed. Murad III later had five of Selim's young sons executed. Selim was buried in Hagia Sophia. He wrote poetry under the pen name Selimi, supported poets, and restored the stipend of Mahidevran, mother of Mustafa. The Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, built by Sinan between 1569 and 1575, is the largest of all Ottoman mosques, and Sinan also renovated Hagia Sophia between 1572 and 1574.
selim-iii: Selim III was the son of Sultan Mustafa III and his wife Mihrişah Sultan, who was ethnically Georgian. Mustafa III believed in the necessity of reform and had tried to build a professional army in peacetime, partly from fear of a Russian invasion. He died in 1774, and Selim's uncle Abdul Hamid I took the throne, looked after Selim and emphasised his education. Selim succeeded him on 7 April 1789, aged 27. He was fond of literature, calligraphy and music, and wrote poetry under the pen name İlhami.

Contemporaries saw Selim as capable and energetic, and his accession raised expectations of reform. Austria and Russia left him little room for anything but defence until the Peace of Iaşi in 1792. He then abolished the military tenure of fiefs, changed the fiscal administration, and in 1797 formed the Nizam-i Cedid, or New Order, from Turkish peasant youths of Anatolia, trained by foreign officers and equipped with modern weapons. By 1806 it numbered around 23,000 troops, but Selim never integrated it with the regular army. He also pushed for permanent embassies in European courts, and resident embassies were set up in Britain, France, Prussia and Austria.

French forces under Napoleon Bonaparte landed in Egypt on 1 July 1798, and Selim declared war on France; peace came in June 1802. Provincial notables such as Osman Pazvantoğlu defied the sultan, and in Serbia the Janissaries returned and murdered his governor. The Janissaries had viewed the reforms as a threat from the start. The Derebeys were alarmed by the confiscation of timars to pay for the new troops, and the ulama objected to European models. In 1806 an armed confrontation at Edirne between the New Order and a coalition of Balkan magnates and Janissary garrisons ended with the imperial forces retreating to Istanbul and Anatolia.

The Janissaries rose again, obtained a fatwa against the reforms from the Sheikh ul-Islam, and placed Selim's cousin on the throne as Mustafa IV on 29 May 1807. The European embassies were dismantled and the New Order troops dispersed. Alemdar Mustafa Pasha marched on Constantinople with an army to restore Selim but arrived too late, and Selim was killed on 28 July 1808. He was buried in the Laleli Mosque. Mahmud II then took the throne. Selim was also a composer who created fourteen makams, and sixty-four of his compositions are known.
semarang: Semarang lies on the northern coast of Java, bounded by the Java Sea to the north and by Kendal, Demak and Semarang regencies to the west, east and south. Its coastline is 13.6 kilometres long, and its elevation ranges from 0.75 to 348 metres above sea level. It is the capital and largest city of Central Java province, and its population is predominantly Javanese with a significant Chinese presence.

The history of the place goes back to the 9th century, when it was known as Bergota. At the end of the 15th century the Demak Sultanate appointed an Islamic scholar, Ki Ageng Pandan Arang, to build an Islamic school in this fishing village. On 2 May 1547 Sultan Hadiwijaya of Pajang declared him the first bupati of Semarang, which created the city administratively and politically. In 1678 Sunan Amangkurat II promised control of Semarang to the Dutch East India Company as a debt payment, and on 5 October 1705 Susuhunan Pakubuwono I gave the company extensive trade rights in return for wiping out Mataram's debt, making it officially a company city.

The early Dutch settlement was a pentagonal fortress with five towers, beside a Muslim quarter called Kauman and a Chinese quarter; only the Dutch quarter counted as the city. The Great Mail Road of 1847 connected the northern coastal cities of Central and East Java, and railways followed at the end of the 19th century. The mail and railway projects brought an economic boom in the 1870s, but the Javanese kampongs reached as many as 1,000 inhabitants per hectare, and cholera, tuberculosis, dysentery, typhoid and malaria were rife. The city doctor Willem T. de Vogel and the councilman Hendrik Tillema campaigned to extend the city into the healthier hills to the south. By the 1920s the city had doubled in size.

In 1918 the Indonesian People's Hall was established by Sarekat Rakyat as a centre for political and social activity; the Dutch closed it in 1927. Japan occupied the city in 1942. After the Proclamation of Indonesian Independence reached Semarang on 17 August 1945, a local government under the Republic was set up, and the Five Days Battle between Indonesian forces and Japanese soldiers followed in October 1945.

Semarang was designated a city on 1 March 1906. It is a municipality of 16 districts, covers 373.78 square kilometres, and remains an important regional centre and port. It had a population of 1,653,524 at the 2020 census.
semey: Semey lies on the Irtysh River in north-eastern Kazakhstan, near the border with Russia, about 1,000 km north of Almaty and 700 km south-east of the Russian city of Omsk. It has a cold semi-arid climate with warm summers and very cold winters, and low rainfall throughout the year. It stands on the Turkestan-Siberia Railway, which links it with Almaty, Barnaul and Novosibirsk.

The first Russian settlement dates from 1718, when a fort was built beside the Irtysh near the ruins of an ancient Buddhist monastery with seven buildings. The fort and later the city took the name Semipalatinsk, Russian for Seven-Chambered City, from the monastery. The fort suffered frequent flooding from snowmelt, and in 1778 it was moved 18 km upstream to higher ground. A small city grew around it and served the river trade between the nomadic peoples of Central Asia and the growing Russian Empire. On 19 May 1854 it became the capital of Semipalatinsk Oblast, and the Turkestan-Siberia Railway of the early 20th century made it a major point of transit between Central Asia and Siberia.

The city was one of the main centres for publishing books by the Kazakh intelligentsia. Between 1917 and 1920 it was the capital, under the name Alash-qala, of the largely unrecognised Alash Autonomy, set up after the outbreak of the October Revolution. Red Army forces loyal to Petrograd took control in 1920. From October 1941 to July 1942 a Polish diplomatic post connected with the formation of Anders' Army stood in the city.

In 1949 the Soviet atomic bomb programme chose a site on the steppe 180 km west of the city for weapons testing. The Semipalatinsk Test Site operated until 1989, with 456 nuclear tests, of which 340 were underground and 116 atmospheric. Fallout and the uncontrolled exposure of workers led to high rates of cancer, childhood leukaemia and birth defects among residents of neighbouring villages.

In 2007 the city council voted unanimously to change the name from Semipalatinsk to Semey, because the old name had negative associations with the atomic testing. Semey became the administrative centre of the new Abai Region in 2022. It is a university town, home to Semey Medical University. The city has a museum to the poet Abai Qunanbayuli, and a museum of Fyodor Dostoevsky, who is listed among its notable residents, which opened in 1971 and is the only one of seven Dostoevsky museums outside Russia.
semiramis: The historical Shammuramat, the Akkadian form of the name, was the Assyrian wife of Shamshi-Adad V, who ruled from 824 to 811 BCE. She ruled the Neo-Assyrian Empire as regent for five years, until her son Adad-nirari III came of age. She governed at a time of political uncertainty after a destructive civil war, which may partly explain why Assyrians accepted rule by a woman. In the city of Aššur she had a stele inscribed naming her as queen of Shamshi-Adad, mother of Adad-nirari and daughter-in-law of Shalmaneser. It has been speculated that her achievements were retold over generations until she became a figure of legend.

According to Diodorus Siculus, who drew mainly on Ctesias of Cnidus, Semiramis was the daughter of the fish-goddess Derketo of Ascalon and a mortal. Doves fed her until the royal shepherd Simmas adopted her. She married Onnes, a general under King Ninus, and advised the king, and at the Siege of Bactra she led soldiers to seize a key defensive point.

Ninus fell in love with her and Onnes hanged himself. After Ninus died of an arrow wound she disguised herself as their son Ninyas, and Diodorus says she reigned 42 years, restored Babylon with a high brick wall and built palaces including Ecbatana. She attacked King Stabrobates of India with false elephants made of buffalo skins over camels, but was wounded and her army mostly destroyed.

About 80 ancient writers recorded legends of her. Herodotus ascribed to her the banks that confined the Euphrates, and her name was applied to monuments whose origins were forgotten, even the Behistun Inscription of Darius. In Armenian tradition, which portrays her negatively, she asked the handsome King Ara to marry her, and when he refused she marched against Armenia, where Ara was slain despite her orders to capture him alive. She is credited with founding Van, called Shamiramagerd.

Semiramis was generally viewed positively before the rise of Christianity. In the Middle Ages she became associated with lust, and a story from Pompeius Trogus, later spread by Orosius, claims an incestuous relationship with her son. Dante places her among the lustful in the Second Circle of Hell, while Christine de Pizan included her in The Book of the City of Ladies, and she was commonly found on the Nine Worthies list for women.

She appears in plays by Voltaire and Calderón and in an opera by Rossini, and Margaret I of Denmark and Catherine the Great were called the Semiramis of the North. In 1853 Alexander Hislop's The Two Babylons made her a figure in a claimed conspiracy, a view that scholars such as Lester Grabbe have rejected. Armenians and Assyrians still use Shamiram as a girl's name.
semitic-languages: The Semitic languages are a branch of the Afroasiatic language family. They occur in written form from a very early date: Akkadian, also known as Assyrian and Babylonian, and Eblaite texts, written in a script adapted from Sumerian cuneiform, appear from about 2600 BCE in Mesopotamia and the north-eastern Levant respectively. Egyptian, from about 3000 BCE, is a sister branch of Afroasiatic, related to Semitic but not part of it. Amorite appeared about 2100 BCE, followed during the 2nd millennium BCE by the Canaanite languages, including Hebrew and Phoenician, by Aramaic, and by Ugaritic. Where Semitic-speaking peoples originated is still debated: Mesopotamia, the Levant, Ethiopia, the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa have all been proposed.

The Semitic languages are notable for their nonconcatenative morphology. Word roots are sets of consonants, usually three, and words are formed by filling in vowels between them. In Arabic the root k-t-b, dealing with writing, gives kitāb, book, and kataba, he wrote; Hebrew uses the same root in katav, he wrote, and michtav, letter. Most Semitic scripts are abjads, which omit some or all vowels. The Geʽez script of Ethiopia and Eritrea is technically an abugida, and Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin script. The reconstructed word order of Proto-Semitic is verb–subject–object, which Classical Arabic and Biblical Hebrew keep.

Scholars have accepted the similarity of Hebrew, Arabic and Aramaic since medieval times. Guillaume Postel published a comparison of them in Latin in 1538, but did not name the group. The term Semitic was created by the Göttingen school of history, first by August Ludwig von Schlözer in 1781, from Shem, one of Noah's three sons in the Book of Genesis, and Johann Gottfried Eichhorn popularised it in 1795. Classical Syriac, an Aramaic dialect of about 200 CE, became a literary language of early Christianity. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, and Maltese descends from the extinct Siculo-Arabic of Sicily.
semmering-railway: The Semmering Railway, which starts at Gloggnitz and leads over the Semmering to Mürzzuschlag, was the first mountain railway in Europe built with standard gauge track. It was constructed between 1848 and 1854 by some 20,000 workers under the project's designer and director, Carl von Ghega. The works include 14 tunnels, among them the 1,431 m summit tunnel, 16 viaducts, several of them two-storey, and over 100 stone arch bridges and 11 small iron bridges.

Over a track length of 41 km the line overcomes an altitude difference of 460 m. On 60% of its length the gradient is 2.0–2.5%, equivalent to a rise of one metre in 40, and 16% has a curve radius of only 190 m. This was an entirely new technical dimension of railway construction, and new instruments and methods of surveying had to be developed.

A competition in 1851, the Semmering trials, decided which locomotives to buy. One stretch had gradients of 1 in 40 and curves with a minimum radius of 190 metres, and entrants had to hold a speed of 11.5 kilometres per hour with a maximum axle loading of 14 tonnes. Four entrants met the conditions but did not prove reliable in practice.

The railway itself used the Engerth design, in which the tender is articulated with the main locomotive frame so that part of the fuel and water weight rests on the driving wheels to improve adhesion, while the locomotive can still take relatively sharp curves. Sixteen Engerth locomotives were supplied between November 1853 and May 1854, and could climb a 1 in 40 gradient at 19 kilometres per hour.

Even while it was being built, the railway was seen as a form of landscape gardening, an attempt to combine technology and nature harmoniously. The travel experience it offered contributed greatly to opening the Semmering region to tourism, and numerous hotels and mansions date from that epoch. The line remains part of the Southern Railway, operated by the Austrian Federal Railways. In 1998 it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list.
semyon-dezhnev: Dezhnev was a Pomor Russian, probably born in 1605, possibly at Veliky Ustyug or the village of Pinega. According to the anthropologist Lydia T. Black he was recruited for Siberian service in 1630. He served for eight years at Tobolsk and Yeniseisk and went to Yakutia in 1639 or earlier, where he married a Yakut captive and spent three years collecting yasak, the fur tribute. In 1641 he moved north-east under Mikhail Stadukhin, and in 1643 he, Stadukhin and Yarilo Zyrian built a fort on the Kolyma River, then the easternmost Russian frontier. The Kolyma soon proved one of the richest areas of eastern Siberia.

From about 1642 Russians heard of a Pogycha River to the east, rich in sable, walrus ivory and silver ore. A first attempt to reach it in 1646 failed, and in 1647 an expedition organised by Fedot Alekseyev, agent of a Moscow merchant, was turned back by drift ice. In 1648 they tried again, in koch vessels, with between 89 and 121 people. They set out on 20 June (old style). Four of the seven vessels were lost before the strait, and Gerasim Ankudinov's koch was wrecked near it. A storm then separated the rest; Alekseyev's koch disappeared, and Dezhnev's was wrecked somewhere south of the Anadyr River.

His 25 survivors wandered for ten weeks until they reached the mouth of the Anadyr. In 1649 the twelve who were left built boats from driftwood and went upriver, where they built winter quarters and subjected the local Yukaghirs to tribute. Dezhnev found a walrus rookery at the Anadyr's mouth and accumulated over two tons of ivory. In 1664 he reached Moscow, where he sold 4.6 tons of tusks, and he died there.

Dezhnev deposited his reports at Yakutsk, but the sea route was of little commercial use, and they stayed in the local archives. In 1728 Vitus Bering entered the strait, and in 1736 Gerhardt Friedrich Müller found the reports, which he published in 1758. Some people have doubted the story since 1777, because the documents are poor and no one repeated the route until Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld in 1878. Most scholars agree that the account is basically correct. Cape Dezhnev, the easternmost cape of Eurasia, a mountain ridge in Chukotka and a bay of the Bering Sea bear his name.
sen-no-rikyu: Sen no Rikyū was born in Sakai, now in Osaka Prefecture. His father was a warehouse owner named Tanaka Yohei, who later also used the family name Sen. As a young man he studied tea under the Sakai townsman Kitamuki Dōchin, and at nineteen, through Dōchin's introduction, he began to study under Takeno Jō'ō, who is also associated with the development of the wabi aesthetic. He is believed to have received the Buddhist name Sōeki from the Rinzai Zen priest Dairin Sōtō of Nanshū-ji in Sakai. He married around the age of 21 and trained in Zen at Daitoku-ji in Kyoto. Little is known about his middle years.

In 1579, at the age of 58, Rikyū became tea master to Oda Nobunaga, and after Nobunaga's death in 1582 he served Toyotomi Hideyoshi. He entered Hideyoshi's circle of confidants and became the most influential figure in the world of chanoyu. In 1585 he needed extra credentials to enter the Imperial Palace to help at a tea gathering Hideyoshi gave for Emperor Ōgimachi, and the emperor bestowed on him the lay name and title Rikyū Koji. He also played a central role in the Grand Kitano Tea Ceremony of 1587.

In his later years he began to use very small rustic tea rooms called sō-an, 'grass hermitage'. The two-tatami room Tai-an at Myōki-an temple in Yamazaki, credited to his design, is a National Treasure. Raku ware tea bowls originated in his collaboration with a tile-maker named Raku Chōjirō. He preferred simple, local wares to the costly Chinese items then fashionable. Though he did not invent the philosophy of wabi-sabi, he is among those most responsible for popularising it and bringing it into the tea ceremony. His style became known as sōan-cha or wabi-cha.

Hideyoshi ordered Rikyū to commit ritual suicide, apparently because of crucial differences of opinion and because Rikyū was too independent. One year earlier Hideyoshi had had Rikyū's disciple Yamanoue Sōji tortured and beheaded. Hideyoshi's reason may never be known for certain. Rikyū committed seppuku at his residence in Hideyoshi's Jurakudai palace in Kyoto on 21 April 1591, at the age of seventy. Okakura Kakuzō wrote that his last act was to hold a tea ceremony and that he left a death poem. Three houses of tea, the Omotesenke, Urasenke and Mushakōjisenke, descend directly from him. His grave is at the Jukō-in sub-temple in the Daitoku-ji compound.
sena-gallica: Senigallia is a resort town and comune on Italy's Adriatic coast, in the province of Ancona in the region of Marche, about 30 kilometres north-west of Ancona. Its small port lies at the mouth of the River Misa. The town is one of the endpoints of the Massa–Senigallia Line, an important dividing line, or isogloss, in the classification of the Romance languages. The name Sena is probably a corrupted form of Senones, and Gallica, meaning Gaulish, distinguished the place from Sena, the present Siena, in Etruria.

The Gallic Senone tribe first settled the place in the 4th century BCE. In 284 BCE the Romans took over the area and the settlement and established the colony of Sena Gallica to control the region they called the Ager Gallicus. In 207 BCE, in the prelude to the Battle of the Metaurus between Romans and Carthaginians, Sena Gallica was the southernmost point of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Barca's invasion of Italy.

Alaric ravaged the town as the Roman Empire declined, and it was fortified when it became part of the Byzantine Empire. The Lombards laid it waste in the 8th century and the Saracens in the 9th. It was one of the five cities of the medieval Adriatic duchy of Pentapolis.

The diocese and bishopric were long established, and around the 13th century the town saw economic development, including the Magdalena Fair, visited by merchants from Europe and the Levant. In the 15th century the town was captured and recaptured many times in the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict. Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta of Rimini fortified it in 1450–1455, and Pope Sixtus IV later assigned the lordship to the Della Rovere family. In 1503 Cesare Borgia ordered a series of executions there as revenge for the Magione conspiracy, in which princes who had been his military allies plotted to remove him.

In 1516 Pope Leo X transferred the lordship to Lorenzo II de' Medici, and the Della Rovere took it again, until in 1624 the town was annexed to the Papal States' legation of Urbino. Giovanni Maria Mastai Ferretti, later Pope Pius IX, was born there in 1792.

In the First World War the town and its port were devastated by shelling from Austro-Hungarian naval units led by the battleship SMS Zrínyi. A strong earthquake damaged it in 1930, and it suffered again in the Second World War, so that much of the present city is modern. Its sights include the Rocca Roveresca, a castle of Gothic origins restored by Baccio Pontelli in 1492, the 17th-century Palazzo Comunale and the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie.
sendai: Sendai stretches from the Pacific Ocean to the Ōu Mountains, which form the east and west borders of Miyagi Prefecture. Its eastern part is a plain, its centre hilly and its west mountainous, and the highest point is Mount Funagata at 1,500 metres. Unusually for a large Japanese coastal city, the city core stands on a terrace 40 to 60 metres above sea level. The area was inhabited as early as 20,000 years ago, though the history of Sendai as a city begins with Date Masamune. It became a designated city in 1989 and has five wards, whose names deliberately avoid directions.

Date Masamune was unhappy with his previous stronghold at Iwadeyama, in the north of his territories and hard to reach from Edo. Sendai lay in the centre of his newly defined lands on the major road from Edo, and Tokugawa Ieyasu gave him permission to build a new castle on Aobayama after the Battle of Sekigahara. The name had been written with characters meaning a thousand generations, and Masamune changed it to characters meaning a hermit and a platform. The characters come from a Chinese poem praising a palace of the Han emperor Wen, and tradition says Masamune chose them so that the castle would prosper like a mountain inhabited by an immortal hermit.

In 1613 Masamune built a galleon to send an embassy headed by Hasekura Tsunenaga to the Pope in Rome. The embassy established relations with the Holy See, but the suppression of Christianity in Japan frustrated Masamune's plans. The first railway between Sendai and Tokyo, now the Tōhoku Main Line, opened in 1887 and put the area within a day's travel of Tokyo. Tohoku Imperial University was founded in 1907 and became the first Japanese university to admit women in 1913. After the Second World War the city was rebuilt as a transport and logistics hub for the region.

Sendai is the capital of Miyagi Prefecture and the largest city of the Tōhoku region. It is known as the City of Trees, because of the zelkova trees along Jōzenji Street and Aoba Street, and its Tanabata Festival is the largest in Japan. The ruins of Sendai Castle stand on Aobayama, and the Zuihōden is the tomb of Date Masamune. The Ōsaki Hachimangū shaden, built by Masamune in 1607, is a National Treasure. On 11 March 2011 coastal areas of the city suffered severe damage from a magnitude 9.0 offshore earthquake and the tsunami it caused.
seneca-falls-convention: In the decades before 1848 a small number of women pushed against the limits placed on them. Charles Grandison Finney allowed women to pray aloud in mixed gatherings from 1831, and from 1832 William Lloyd Garrison's anti-slavery associations encouraged women's full participation. The Grimké sisters and Abby Kelley spoke to mixed audiences against slavery, and Ernestine Rose lectured from 1836 on the enfranchisement of women. Under state statutes and common law women could not inherit property, sign contracts, serve on juries or vote, and they were paid about half of what men earned for the same work. On 7 April 1848 the New York State Assembly passed the Married Woman's Property Act.

The convention was planned on 9 July 1848 over tea at the Waterloo home of the Quaker Jane Hunt, where Lucretia Mott, Mary Ann M'Clintock, Martha Coffin Wright, Jane Hunt and Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the only non-Quaker, agreed to call a meeting while the Motts were in the area. The notice in the Seneca County Courier appeared on 11 July, giving eight days' warning. At the M'Clintock home on 16 July the women drafted ten resolutions and the Declaration of Sentiments, which Stanton adapted from the Declaration of Independence, adding the phrase "and women" to "all men … are created equal". Stanton added an eleventh resolution, on women's suffrage.

On 19 July the chapel doors were found locked, and Stanton's young nephew was lifted through a window to open them. About 40 men came although the first day had been announced for women only, and they were asked to stay silent. Stanton and Mott spoke, the declaration was read and amended, and Mott gave an evening address to a large audience. On the second day James Mott chaired the morning meeting, since a woman chairing before men and women was still thought too radical. The declaration was adopted unanimously, and 100 of about 300 present signed it, 68 women and 32 men. Many, Mott among them, urged dropping the suffrage resolution, but Frederick Douglass argued for it and it was kept.

Other conventions soon followed, including one at Rochester two weeks later, and the first of a series of annual National Women's Rights Conventions met at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1850. The historian Judith Wellman has called the Declaration of Sentiments the single most important factor in spreading news of the movement in 1848 and afterwards. By the convention of 1851 women's suffrage had become a central tenet of the American women's rights movement. Contemporaries differed over the event: Mott saw it as one step among many, while Stanton considered it the beginning of the movement.
seneca-the-younger: Seneca's father, Seneca the Elder, was a Spanish-born Roman knight who had gained fame as a writer and teacher of rhetoric in Rome, and his brother Annaeus Mela was the father of the poet Lucan. His early career as a senator seems to have been successful, and he was praised for his oratory. According to Cassius Dio, the emperor Caligula was so offended by his success in the Senate that he ordered him to commit suicide, and Seneca survived only because he was seriously ill and Caligula was told that he would soon die anyway.

From 54 to 62 Seneca advised Nero together with the praetorian prefect Sextus Afranius Burrus, and he was appointed suffect consul in 56. His satire Apocolocyntosis lampoons the deification of Claudius. Tacitus and Dio suggest that Nero's early rule, while he listened to Seneca and Burrus, was quite competent. After Burrus died in 62 Seneca's influence declined rapidly, and Tacitus reports that Nero refused his requests to retire in 62 and 64. He lived quietly on his country estates, rarely visiting Rome.

Seneca wrote mostly on ethics, with one work, Naturales Quaestiones, on the physical world. Many upper-class Romans found in Stoicism an ethical framework for political involvement. He was once regarded as eclectic, but modern scholarship sees him as a fairly orthodox Stoic, albeit a free-minded one. Among his later works are the Letters to Lucilius, which set out his philosophical thought.

His plays are tragedies, and ten are attributed to him, of which probably eight are his. Their intense emotions and grim tone seem the opposite of his Stoic beliefs, and until the 16th century he was often thought to be two people, a philosopher and a dramatist. Many scholars have held that they were written for recitation only, while others think they were meant for performance.

In 65 Seneca was caught up in the aftermath of the Pisonian conspiracy, and Nero ordered him to kill himself, though it is unlikely that he took part. He cut several veins, and his wife Pompeia Paulina tried to share his fate but was saved on Nero's order. According to Tacitus, his age and diet made him bleed slowly, and he also took poison, which was not fatal. The early Christian Church thought well of him, and Tertullian called him our Seneca. In the later Middle Ages he was read mostly through the Letters to Lucilius, and Petrarch quoted him more than any authority except Virgil. His suicide has been a popular subject in art.
senegal: Senegal lies on the western coast of Africa between latitudes 12° and 17°N. It almost completely surrounds the Gambia, which separates the southern region of Casamance from the rest of the country. The landscape consists mainly of the rolling sandy plains of the western Sahel, rising to foothills in the southeast, where the highest point, the Baunez ridge, reaches 648 metres. The Senegal River forms the northern border and gives the country its name, and the Gambia and Casamance rivers also cross it. The capital Dakar lies on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of continental Africa. The dry season runs from December to April, with hot, dry harmattan winds.

Archaeological findings indicate that Senegal was inhabited in prehistoric times and continuously occupied by various ethnic groups. Kingdoms were created between the 6th and 14th centuries, among them Takrur in the 6th century, Namandiru and the Jolof Empire in the 13th and 14th centuries, and eastern Senegal was once part of the Ghana Empire. Islam was introduced by the Toucouleur and Soninke through contact with the Almoravid dynasty, and the Serers in particular resisted it. Between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, typically after capture in warfare.

The Jolof Empire grew more powerful in the 14th century, uniting Cayor and the kingdoms of Baol, Siné, Saloum, Waalo, Futa Tooro and Bambouk. It was a voluntary confederacy rather than a state built on conquest, founded by Ndiadiane Ndiaye, and it collapsed around 1549 after the defeat and death of Lele Fouli Fak at the hands of Amari Ngone Sobel Fall.

The Portuguese landed on the coast in the mid-15th century, followed by traders from other countries, including the French. In 1677 France gained control of the island of Gorée, a minor hub of the Atlantic slave trade. From the 1850s the French expanded onto the mainland under Governor Louis Faidherbe, taking over all the kingdoms except the Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum. Senegal became independent in 1960.

Dakar is the capital and largest city, and was once the capital of all French West Africa. Senegal is a semi-presidential republic. French is the official language, ratified in 1960, but over 30 languages are spoken, and Wolof is the most widely spoken, serving as a lingua franca alongside French. The largest ethnic groups are the Wolof, Fula and Serer, and Senegalese people are predominantly Muslim. Griots, whose profession is passed down through generations, have kept West African history alive through words and music. Senegal is a member of the African Union, the United Nations and the Economic Community of West African States.
senegal-river: The Senegal River is 1086 kilometres long and drains a basin of 270,000 square kilometres. Its headwaters, the Bafing and the Semefé (Bakoye), both rise in Guinea and meet at Bafoulabé in Mali. From there the river flows west and then north through the Talari Gorges and over the Gouina Falls, past Kayes, and receives the Falémé River at Bakel. It then crosses semi-arid land, forming the border between Senegal and Mauritania, and takes in the Gorgol at Kaédi.

Below Kaédi it divides into two branches, the main river and the Doué, which rejoin a few kilometres downstream of Podor and enclose a long strip of land called the Île à Morfil. The river passes Richard Toll and Rosso and turns south around the island on which Saint-Louis stands, separated from the Atlantic by a thin strip of sand, the Langue de Barbarie.

Early Mediterranean writers knew of the river: Pliny the Elder called it, or some other river, Bambotus, and Ptolemy called it Nias. Hanno the Carthaginian visited it around 450 BCE. From about 800 CE the Trans-Saharan trade between Morocco and the Ghana Empire restored contact, and the Arab geographers al-Masudi (957), al-Bakri (1068) and al-Idrisi (1154) gave some of the earliest descriptions. Some of them believed the upper Senegal and the upper Niger formed a single river, the Western Nile, and later writers called it the Nile of Ghana. Because it reached into the gold-producing Ghana Empire and later the Mali Empire, traders called it the River of Gold, and European maps from the 14th century, among them the Hereford Mappa Mundi, drew it.

Europeans sought its mouth from 1291, when the Genoese Vivaldi brothers sailed down the coast and were not heard of again. Under Prince Henry the Navigator, Gil Eanes passed Cape Bojador in 1434. In 1445 Nuno Tristão reached the Langue de Barbarie, and Dinis Dias was the first known European since antiquity to reach the river's mouth. Between 1448 and 1455 the captain Lourenço Dias opened regular trade with the Wolof states of Waalo and Cayor, exchanging horses and Mediterranean goods for gold and slaves.

In 1972 Mali, Mauritania and Senegal founded the Organisation pour la mise en valeur du fleuve Sénégal to manage the river basin, and Guinea joined in 2005. Two large dams stand on the river: the Manantali Dam in Mali, and the Maka-Diama Dam on the Mauritania-Senegal border near the sea, which keeps salt water from moving upstream. The river's aquatic life is closely linked to that of the Gambia River basin.
sengoku-period: The Emperor was officially the ruler of Japan, but he was largely a marginalised, ceremonial and religious figure who delegated power to the shogun. From 1346 to 1358 the Ashikaga shogunate expanded the authority of the shugo, local military and police officials, and the first shugo daimyo appeared. The sixth shogun, Ashikaga Yoshinori, was assassinated in the Kakitsu Rebellion, and the shogunate gradually lost control over the daimyo.

Historians choose different starting points: the Kyōtoku incident of 1454, the Ōnin War of 1467 or the Meiō incident of 1493. The Ōnin War, between an Eastern Army under Hosokawa Katsumoto and a Western Army under Yamana Sōzen, grew from a dispute over the succession to the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa. It lasted until 1477 and devastated two thirds of Kyoto. Daimyo then returned to their provinces, where their deputies, the shugodai, sometimes seized power or declared independence. The sengoku daimyo, unlike the earlier shugo daimyo, ruled their regions on their own, without appointment by the shogun.

The period saw vassals rebel against their lords, succession disputes within noble families and the installation of figurehead lords. People of other social strata sometimes made names as warriors and became samurai. Hōjō Sōun was the first common samurai to rise to the rank of sengoku daimyo, and Uesugi Kenshin, a shugodai, replaced his lord. Peasants, craftsmen and merchants rose in uprisings called ikki. In the Kaga Rebellion in 1488, with the support of the True Pure Land sect, an ikki took control of the whole province of Kaga.

In Kyoto the Hosokawa clan made the shogun a puppet after the Meiō incident, and the Miyoshi clan later rose, until the 13th shogun, Ashikaga Yoshiteru, was killed. Elsewhere Mōri Motonari pacified the Chūgoku region, and Uesugi Kenshin fought Hōjō Ujiyasu and Takeda Shingen in the Kantō and Chūbu regions, including five battles at Kawanakajima between 1553 and 1564. When the Portuguese brought the matchlock gun to Japan in 1543, the tanegashima was soon mass-produced. Standing armies of ashigaru foot soldiers became essential, small local lords could no longer remain independent, and land passed to sengoku daimyo with vast territories.

There is no agreed end date. Candidates include Oda Nobunaga's march on Kyoto in 1568, the abolition of the Muromachi shogunate in 1573, Toyotomi Hideyoshi's law of 1587 prohibiting war, the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, the establishment of the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603 and the suppression of the Shimabara Rebellion in 1638. Modern Japan recognises Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu as the three great unifiers, for restoring central government. Hideyoshi's rise from a peasant background to samurai, sengoku daimyo and kampaku is often considered the most spectacular of the era.
senlis: Senlis stands on the river Nonette, 40 km north of Paris, between the forests of Chantilly and Ermenonville to the south and Halatte to the north. The highest point of the town, 140 metres, lies in the heart of the forest of Halatte, and the lowest on the banks of the Nonette. The area is a vast limestone plateau of the Lutetian, covered mostly in silt.

The town was known in early imperial times as Augustomagus and later as Civitas Silvanectium, the city of the Silvanectes. In the 3rd century a defensive wall seven metres high was built round it in response to Frankish incursions; about half of it still stands, and it remained in use into the 13th century. A Roman amphitheatre seating as many as 10,000 people stood about 500 m west of the walled town, and its remains are still visible. Monarchs of the early French dynasties lived at Senlis, drawn by the venison of the Chantilly forest, and built a castle on the foundations of the Roman settlement.

Senlis came into the ownership of Hugh Capet in 981. In 987 Archbishop Adalbero of Reims called an assembly and asked it to choose Hugh as king of France; he was crowned at Noyon. Under Capetian rule Senlis became a royal city and remained one until the reign of Charles X.

It reached its height in the 12th and 13th centuries as trade in wool and leather increased and vineyards were planted; a second set of ramparts, larger and higher than the Gallo-Roman ones, was built under Philip II, and King Louis VII granted a municipal charter in 1173. The Bailiwick of Senlis was created in 1265. The Hundred Years' War devastated the town, though it escaped destruction despite a siege by the Armagnacs, and in 1493 Charles VIII signed the Treaty of Senlis there with Maximilian I of Austria. In early September 1914 the Germans occupied the town and executed its mayor, Eugène Odent, with six other civilian hostages.

The cathedral, a Gothic church and national monument, was built between 1153 and 1519; its spire dates from the 13th century, and the southern portal of the 16th century is the work of Martin Chambiges. The former bishopric was abolished by the Concordat of 1801. The royal castle, whose present building dates from the 12th century under Louis VII, stands beside the priory of Saint Maurice. St Vincent Abbey was founded in 1065 by Queen Anne of Kiev. The town has museums of art and archaeology, of hunting and of the Spahis, and its old streets have often served as a film setting.
sennacherib: Sennacherib was the son and successor of Sargon II, who ruled Assyria from 722 to 705 BCE. His mother's identity is uncertain; the Assyriologist Josette Elayi considers it more plausible that she was Ra'ima, another of Sargon's wives, than Ataliya, as was once held. As crown prince he exercised royal power with his father or alone as a substitute while Sargon campaigned, oversaw domestic affairs, and managed the empire's military intelligence network.

In 705 BCE Sargon led a disastrous campaign against King Gurdi of Tabal in central Anatolia and was killed, and the Anatolians carried off his body. The Assyrians believed the gods had punished him for some major misdeed. Sennacherib, then about 35, reacted by distancing himself from his father, abandoning Sargon's new capital, Dur-Sharrukin, and moving the capital to Nineveh.

Sargon's death inspired rebellions across the empire. In Babylonia Sennacherib took the title of king of Babylon, unlike earlier rulers who had styled themselves viceroys, and did not undergo the traditional coronation ritual before the Statue of Marduk. The Chaldean chief Marduk-apla-iddina II, who had been Babylon's king until Sargon defeated him, retook the city and allied with the Elamites. Sennacherib reclaimed the south in 700 BCE and appointed his son Ashur-nadin-shumi as vassal king, but the Babylonians and Elamites captured him, and he disappeared, presumably executed.

In the Levantine War of 701 BCE the Assyrians invaded Judah, whose king Hezekiah had stopped paying tribute. Sennacherib's own account says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a caged bird, while the biblical narrative has an angel destroy the Assyrian army. An outright defeat is unlikely, since Hezekiah submitted at the end of the campaign. After a final war against Babylon, which had caused his son's death, Sennacherib destroyed the city in 689 BCE. He then devoted himself to Nineveh, which he enlarged with great walls, temples, a royal garden and the Southwest Palace, which he called the Palace without Rival.

In 684 BCE Sennacherib replaced his second son and heir Arda-Mulissu with a younger son, Esarhaddon, for unknown reasons. In 681 BCE Arda-Mulissu and his brother Nabu-shar-usur murdered him. Babylonia and the Levant welcomed his death as divine punishment, while the Assyrian heartland probably reacted with resentment and horror. Esarhaddon raised an army, seized Nineveh and took the throne. Sennacherib's image has been mainly negative since, owing to his portrayal in the Bible and the destruction of Babylon, and Lord Byron's poem of 1815 pictures the Assyrian coming down like a wolf on the fold.
sens: Sens lies on the Yonne, 120 km south-east of Paris, at the point where the Vanne empties into that river. It stands at the extreme north-west of the present region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, on the border of Île-de-France, Grand Est and Centre-Val de Loire. The hills of Paron and Saint-Martin-du-Tertre border it to the west and the forest of Othe to the east, while the Yonne valley leads north towards the Brie.

The city is said to have been one of the oppida of the Senones, one of the oldest Celtic tribes in Gaul. The Battle of the Allia, fought around 387 BCE between the Senones under Brennus and the Roman Republic, involved the same people. Julius Caesar mentions Agedincum several times, and in 53 BCE he wintered six legions at a place south of the city called the camp of Caesar. The Roman town was built in the first century BCE and walled in the third; parts of the walls remain, and the city keeps the skeleton of its Roman street plan. After the reorganisation of the empire in 375 it became the chief town of Lugdunensis Quarta.

The bishop of Sens became an archbishop as early as the mid-5th century, and in the Middle Ages the archbishops held the role of primate of Gaul and Germany. The archdiocese ruled over the dioceses of Chartres, Auxerre, Meaux, Paris, Orléans, Nevers and Troyes, summarised by the acronym CAMPONT. From 1135 the cathedral, dedicated to Saint Stephen, was rebuilt as one of the first Gothic cathedrals.

Louis IX of France held his wedding to Marguerite of Provence there in 1234. The town witnessed the trial of Peter Abelard, sheltered Pope Alexander III for a time and received Thomas Becket during part of his exile between 1162 and 1165. William of Sens was the principal architect of Canterbury Cathedral. During the Wars of Religion, in 1562, 100 of the town's Huguenot residents were killed in the Massacre of Sens.

Sens is a sub-prefecture and the second largest city of the Yonne department, with 27,106 inhabitants in 2023. Its main sights are the cathedral, the Archbishops' Palace, the churches of St Maurice and St Pierre le Rond, the House of Abraham and a museum. The Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1904.
senusret-i: Senusret I was the son of Amenemhat I and a queen named Neferitatjenen. His chief wife was his sister Neferu III, and their son Amenemhat II succeeded him. In the twenty-first year of Amenemhat I a coregency was set up, with Senusret as junior coregent. In year 30 of his father, which was year 10 of Senusret, Amenemhat I was assassinated while Senusret was leading a campaign against the Libyans. According to the Story of Sinuhe, he hurried back to the palace without telling his army. A civil war followed, and he was forced to suppress his opponents harshly; how he secured the throne is not known.

Senusret continued his father's expansion into Nubia, launching expeditions in his tenth and eighteenth years. In year 18 he conquered Lower Nubia down to the Second Cataract, where he placed a garrison and a victory stele, and Egypt's formal southern border was established there. He also sent an expedition to an oasis in the Western Desert and opened diplomatic relations with some rulers of towns in Syria and Canaan. At home he tried to centralise the political structure by supporting nomarchs loyal to him. In year 25 a low Nile flood caused a famine across Egypt, and quarrying expeditions went to the Sinai Peninsula and the Wadi Hammamat.

His long reign saw many shrines and temples built or rebuilt in Egypt and Nubia. At Heliopolis he rebuilt the temple of Re-Atum and raised two red granite obelisks for his thirty-year jubilee; one still stands, 67 feet tall, and is the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt. He remodelled the temple of Osiris at Abydos and worked at the temples of Satet on Elephantine, Min at Koptos and Montu at Armant and El-Tod. At Karnak the White Chapel marked the jubilee.

In year 43 he named Amenemhat II junior coregent. The Turin King List gives him 45 years, and he was buried in his pyramid complex at el-Lisht. The White Chapel at Karnak was later demolished and used as filling in the Third Pylon, and has been reconstructed from blocks found by Henri Chevrier in 1926.
senusret-ii: Senusret II, also called Sesostris II, was the fourth king of the 12th Dynasty of Egypt and the son of Amenemhat II. His mother is identified as Queen Senet, on the strength of her titles King's Daughter, King's Wife and King's Mother, although this is not certain. A double-dated stela at Konosso, the stela of Hapu, supports a co-regency in which Amenemhat II appointed his son co-ruler, and many Egyptologists accept co-regencies in this dynasty, though Claude Obsomer rejects them. His throne name was Khakheperre, meaning The Ka of Re comes into being.

The length of the reign is disputed. The Turin Canon is believed to give Senusret II nineteen years, but the latest attested regnal year is his eighth, and some scholars prefer a reign of nine or ten years. Others, such as Jürgen von Beckerath and Frank Yurco, keep the longer figure because of the scale of the building he undertook.

He took a great interest in the Faiyum, a region of Middle Egypt that had been inhabited for more than 8,000 years. There he built a dike at El-Lahun and a network of canals drawing water from Lake Moeris, in order to reclaim land for farming and to exploit the marshes for hunting and fishing. His successors continued the work, which matured under his grandson Amenemhat III. He moved the royal necropolis from Dahshur to El-Lahun, where he built his pyramid, and the nearby town of Senusrethotep, now Kahun, is the first known workers' quarter.

His reign was a time of peace, with no recorded military campaigns and growing trade with the Near East. The tomb paintings of the official Khnumhotep II show visiting Western Asiatic foreigners labelled Aamu, among them a leader named Abisha, the first known use of the name Hyksos.

Senusret II was succeeded by his son Senusret III, born to Khenemetneferhedjet I. Whether the two shared a co-regency is debated: the majority view favours three years, but the only evidence is a scarab bearing both names, and Murnane argued that any co-regency lasted no more than a few months.
senusret-iii: Khakaure Senusret III, also written Senwosret III or Sesostris III, was the fifth king of the late Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom. He was the son of Senusret II and Khenemetneferhedjet I. Three wives are known for certain, Itakayt, Khenemetneferhedjet II and Neferthenut, all known mainly from their burials beside his pyramid at Dahshur. His son Amenemhat III succeeded him.

His military campaigns were followed by an era of peace and prosperity that reduced the power of regional rulers and revived craftwork, trade and urban development. In Nubia he built massive river forts including Buhen, Semna, Shalfak and Toshka, and carried out at least four major campaigns, in his Years 8, 10, 16 and 19. The campaign of Year 19 was less successful: the Nile ran lower than normal, and the king's forces withdrew to avoid being trapped in hostile territory.

A stela at Semna dated to the third month of Year 16 records that he made his southern boundary at Heh, further south than his fathers, and charged his successors to hold it, calling any who abandoned it no son of his. A statue of the king was set at the border.

He cleared a navigable canal through the first cataract of the Nile, documented by rock inscriptions near Sehel Island. Late in his reign he built at Abydos, where he founded the planned town of Wah-Sut, a mortuary temple and a second tomb cut into the rock. A stela of his official Sebek-khu records the earliest known Egyptian military campaign in the Levant.
A double-dated papyrus joins his Year 19 with Year 1 of Amenemhat III, which is generally taken as proof of a coregency, though Pierre Tallet and Harco Willems doubt that it ever occurred.

His pyramid complex at Dahshur, north-east of the Red Pyramid, far surpassed earlier Twelfth Dynasty pyramids in size. Its base is 105 metres and its height 78 metres, with a granite-lined burial chamber. Six smaller pyramids for royal women stood around it. Some have suggested that he was in fact buried in his complex at Abydos, making the pyramid a cenotaph.

Senusret III was among the few Egyptian kings deified and honoured with a cult in his own lifetime. A cycle of six songs in his honour, preserved among the papyri of Illahun, compares him to the goddess Sekhmet, and his cult at south Abydos lasted roughly 300 years. Later generations worshipped him as a deity at Semna, and he is regarded as one of the sources of the legend of Sesostris.
seokguram: The grotto is said to have been built by Kim Daeseong and was originally called Seokbulsa, the Stone Buddha Temple. Construction began in 751, in the cultural peak of the kingdom of Unified Silla, and the Silla court completed it in 774, shortly after Kim's death. The tradition of carving Buddhist images and stupas into cliff walls and natural caves began in India and passed to China and then Korea, although the hard granite of the Korean Peninsula is not suited to carving cliff walls, so the grotto is an artificial structure.

Seokguram is a hermitage that forms part of the Bulguksa temple complex, about 3 kilometres from it on the mountain Tohamsan. It rests 750 metres above sea level and overlooks the East Sea. An arched entrance leads to a rectangular antechamber, a narrow corridor lined with bas-reliefs, and a main rotunda. The domed ceiling and corridor were built from more than 360 stone slabs, with no mortar, the structure being held by stone rivets, and natural ventilation was used. The rotunda is slightly irregular, its diameter measuring from 6.58 to 6.8 metres.

The seated Buddha, 3.5 metres tall on a lotus pedestal 1.34 metres high, probably represents Shakyamuni; the position of its hands symbolises enlightenment. Instead of a halo attached to the head, a granite roundel carved with lotus petals on the back wall creates the illusion of one. Around it are bodhisattvas, ten disciples, the Hindu gods Brahma and Indra, and ten further statues in niches. The Four Heavenly Kings guard the corridor, and an Eleven-faced Avalokitesvara, 2.18 metres tall, stands on the back wall. The identity of the main Buddha is still debated.

Repairs took place in 1703 and 1758, in the Joseon period, but Confucian-oriented rulers suppressed Buddhism, and the remote grotto was seriously damaged by the turn of the 20th century. Japanese works of 1913 to 1915 almost completely dismantled and reassembled the structure and encased it in concrete, which caused humidity and leaks; a second round followed in 1920 to 1923. After World War II a major restoration was ordered in the 1960s by President Park Chung Hee. Seokguram was designated a National Treasure of South Korea in 1962, and the interior can now be viewed only through a glass wall.
seongjong-of-joseon: Seongjong, whose personal name was Yi Hyeol, was the ninth monarch of Joseon. He was born the second son of Crown Prince Yi Jang and Crown Princess Su of the Cheongju Han clan, and his father died a few months after his birth. He was a grandson of King Sejo, and in 1467 he married Han Song-yi, youngest daughter of Han Myŏnghoe.

Although he had an older brother and the late King Yejong had left a biological son, Jalsan was chosen as successor and was made the adopted son of Yejong and his second wife, Queen Han. After his accession his biological father was honoured with the temple name Deokjong, and his mother became queen with the honorary name Insu.

Seongjong was only 12 when he was crowned, so his grandmother, Grand Queen Dowager Jaseong, ruled with his mother, Queen Insu, and his aunt and adoptive mother, Queen Dowager Inhye. In 1476, at the age of 19, he began to govern in his own name. After his first wife died in 1474 he promoted a concubine, Lady Yun, to queen. She was later executed for trying to poison other concubines and harm the king, which became a major reason for the tyranny of his successor, Yeonsangun.

His reign was marked by economic prosperity and growth, resting on the laws of Taejong, Sejong and Sejo. The Grand Code for State Administration, begun by his grandfather, was completed and put into effect, and he ordered revisions of it. He expanded the Office of Special Advisors (Hongmungwan), an advisory council and royal library, and strengthened the Three Offices (Samsa) as a check on the court. For the first time since Sejong the Great, Confucian scholars whose views clashed with those of the conservative officials were brought to court, and he appointed able administrators regardless of their politics. He prohibited the construction of new monasteries and the ordination of new monks.

He encouraged books on geography, social etiquette and subjects that benefited the common people. The Widow Remarriage Ban of 1477 barred the sons of remarried women from public office, strengthening an existing stigma. In 1491 a campaign led by General Heo Jong drove the Jurchens commanded by Udige north of the Amrok River.

Seongjong died in January and was buried south of Seoul, in the tomb known as Seonneung, where his third wife, Queen Jeonghyeon, was interred 35 years later. He was succeeded by his son, Crown Prince Yi Yung, known as Yeonsangun.
seonjo-of-joseon: Seonjo was born Yi Yeon on 6 December 1552 in Hanseong, today's Seoul. His father was Prince Deokheung, a son of King Jungjong. He was given the title Prince Haseong and was adopted by Queen Insun. When King Myeongjong died young without an heir, Prince Haseong was next in the line of succession, and by decision of the royal court he was crowned king in 1567.

At the start of his reign Seonjo promoted Confucianism and attempted reforms. He encouraged the Sarim scholars, who had been persecuted in four literati purges between 1498 and 1545, and appointed Yi Hwang, Yi I, Chŏng Ch'ŏl and Yu Sŏngnyong to office. He reformed the civil service examination to give more weight to politics and history, and restored the reputations of executed scholars such as Cho Kwangjo.

Officials then split into the Westerners, headed by Shim Eui-gyeom, and the Easterners, headed by Kim Hyowŏn, a two-faction system that lasted 200 years. In 1589 the rebellion of Chŏng Yŏrip led to the purge of more than 1,000 scholars affiliated with the Easterners. The factions disagreed over how to read Japan's intentions, and Seonjo did not prepare for war.

The Imjin War began on 13 April 1592, when 700 Japanese ships carrying 18,700 troops under Konishi Yukinaga landed. After the defeats at Sangju and Chungju, Seonjo left the capital for Pyongyang and then for the border city of Uiju. While he was away, people who had lost hope in the government plundered the palace and burned public buildings, including the Gyeongbokgung. At Uiju he wrote the Joseon government's first public document written solely in Hangul, probably so that commoners could understand it.

Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy defeated the Japanese fleet several times, and Ming forces arrived at Seonjo's request and retook Pyongyang. When Seonjo returned to Hanseong the palaces had been burnt, so he took over a royal family house and renamed it Deoksugung. The Japanese invaded again in 1597, and withdrew in 1598 after the death of Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

The war left a devastated land and starving people, and after it political quarrels among the factions and famine impeded his wish to rebuild the nation. The succession also became a matter of contention, because the queen gave birth to Grand Prince Yeongchang when the crown prince, Gwanghaegun, was the son of a concubine. King Seonjo died on 16 March 1608. Historians remember him for his early reforms and for the discord and poor leadership of the Imjin War.
seosan: Seosan lies at the north-western end of South Chungcheong Province. It is bounded on the east by Dangjin, Naepo New Town, Yesan-gun and Hongseong-gun, and on the west by Taean-gun and the Yellow Sea. It stands 125 km south of Seoul and 159 km north-west of Daejeon, and is a transport hub of the west coast where several expressways and national highways meet. Its census population was roughly 175,000 in 2017. The city is known for its oysters and garlic, and for dishes such as gegukji, a sweet and spicy broth made with crab meat and kimchi, and marinated blue crab in soybean sauce.

During the Three Kingdoms period the Seosan and Haemi area was under the control of Baekje. Few ruins of that time survive there, and the Yeonghyeon-ri Rock-carved Buddha Triad is an exception. Carved under Baekje, it shows a Buddha standing on a lotus leaf, flanked by two bodhisattvas, and it has been designated a National Treasure of Korea. Nearby stands Bowonsa, a small temple built during the Unified Silla period, which holds a Baekje-style pagoda and monuments added when the temple was enlarged under Goryeo, and it too is regarded as a National Treasure.

Gaesimsa was built in 1484, in the reign of King Seongjong, and is one of only a handful of wooden buildings in Korea that date from before the 17th century. It houses an Amitabha Buddha statue carved in the 14th century and a hanging mural painted in the 15th. Haemieupseong Fortress in Haemi-eup was completed in 1491 on a flat plain rather than a hill, as a military command post for the Chungcheong region and a defence against Japanese pirates on the western coast. Much of it was torn down in the early 20th century as the town grew, and it was restored from 1973.

Of the fortress only the South Gate and parts of the walls are original. Along with Yeosutgol it is regarded as a Holy Ground by Korean Catholics because of the Byeongin Persecutions of 1866, when many Catholics of the Chungcheong area were killed at the fortress. At Yeosutgol, about two hundred metres from it, Catholics were buried alive, drowned and otherwise killed in large numbers. Some remains were rediscovered in 1935, and the site now holds a memorial hall and is a major Catholic pilgrimage site.
seoul: Seoul lies in the north-west of South Korea, in mountainous and hilly terrain, with Bukhansan on its northern edge. The Han River roughly divides it into northern and southern halves, and the city proper covers 605.25 square kilometres. Four main mountains stand in the centre: Bugaksan, Inwangsan, Naksan and Namsan. The Seoul Fortress Wall, which historically bounded the city, runs over these heights.

People lived in the area 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Around 4,000 BCE they lived in huts with lowered floors called umjip, and around 1,500 BCE communities began to farm at scale and enter the Bronze Age. After the fall of Wiman Joseon (194 to 108 BCE), refugees went south to the Han River basin, bringing the culture and technology of the Chinese Warring States and speeding the region's entry into the Iron Age.

Baekje, founded in 18 BCE as one of the statelets of the Mahan confederacy, became the dominant local power by the 2nd century CE. Its capital, Wiryeseong, is believed to have lain in what is now south-eastern Seoul, though its exact site is uncertain. In July or August 553 Silla took the region from Baekje, and it became part of the new Sin Province. Later names include Bukhansan-gun under Goguryeo, Namgyeong under Goryeo and Hanseong under Joseon.

Seoul was designed as a capital in the late 14th century, and the Joseon dynasty built the Five Grand Palaces there: Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung, Deoksugung, Gyeongbokgung and Gyeonghuigung. In the early 20th century the city was occupied by the Empire of Japan. In the Korean War it changed hands four times and was left mostly in ruins, and it has since been rebuilt and rapidly urbanized.

Seoul is the capital and largest city of South Korea, with about 9.6 million residents. It is divided into 25 districts, called gu. The Constitutional Court of Korea declared in 2004 that Seoul must remain the national capital as an unwritten constitutional custom, though many ministries have moved to Sejong City. Five UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in the Seoul Capital Area, among them Changdeokgung, Jongmyo and the Royal Tombs of the Joseon dynasty.
sephardic-jews: The name Sephardic comes from Sepharad, the Hebrew word for Iberia. The earliest significant Jewish presence in the Iberian Peninsula is traced to the Roman period, in the first centuries CE. Around 300 CE the Synod of Elvira enacted decrees restricting contact between Christians and Jews, among them bans on intermarriage and communal dining. Jewish communities faced persecution under Visigothic rule and largely welcomed the Muslim conquest that began in 711. Under Islamic rule in Al-Andalus, Jews were dhimmis, protected but second-class monotheists, who practised their religion with relative autonomy in return for a special tax.

After the conquest of Toledo by Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085, the Almoravids expelled Jews from administrative posts in Granada and Seville, and by the 13th century Jewish life had largely shifted to Christian territories. Alfonso X of Castile patronised scholars of many backgrounds, including Jews, but the legal code compiled in his reign, the Siete Partidas, imposed restrictions on Jews, among them distinguishing clothing and residential segregation. In the summer of 1391 anti-Jewish riots began in Seville and spread across Castile and Aragon. Jewish quarters were looted, synagogues destroyed, thousands killed and thousands more forcibly baptised, and the Jewish communities of Valencia and Barcelona were wiped out.

On 31 March 1492 the Catholic Monarchs issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering practising Jews out of Castile and Aragon by 31 July, and King Manuel I of Portugal issued a similar edict. Over 200,000 Jews converted to Catholicism, and between 40,000 and 100,000 were expelled. Many found refuge in the Ottoman Empire, where Istanbul's Jewish population grew to around 40,000 between 1477 and 1535 and Thessaloniki's, nonexistent in 1478, to over 16,500 by 1519. Others settled in North Africa, in Italian ports such as Venice and Livorno, and in Amsterdam. Many conversos stayed in Iberia, some secretly keeping Jewish practices; they were investigated by the Spanish Inquisition and by the Portuguese Inquisition, established in 1536.

Sephardic Jews spoke variants of Spanish, Catalan or Portuguese. Ladino or Judaeo-Spanish, also called Judezmo, derives from Old Spanish and Old Portuguese, with additions from Hebrew and local languages, and was often written in Rashi script. In North Africa the variety known as Haketia took on Arabic influences. Wherever Sephardim settled they founded schools that used Spanish. They are commonly divided into Eastern Sephardim in the Ottoman lands, North African Sephardim, and Western Sephardim, descendants of conversos, who in the 17th century were prominent in Amsterdam. They reached England in the mid-17th century.
sepphoris: Sepphoris, known in Hebrew as Zippori and in Arabic as Saffuriya, lies 286 metres above sea level, 6 kilometres north-north-west of Nazareth, and overlooks the Beit Netofa Valley. Over time the city had other names. Herod Antipas called it Autocratoris, coins of about 68 CE give Eirenopolis and Neronias, and from the 2nd century it was also Diocaesarea, a name Jewish writers did not use.

Pottery shows that the site was inhabited in the Iron Age, and building can be verified from the 4th century BCE. The Hasmoneans took Galilee in 104 BCE, and Rome ruled it from 63 BCE. After Herod the Great's death in 4 BCE a rebel named Judas sacked its treasury and weapons, and the Roman governor Varus is reported by Josephus to have burnt the city and sold its people into slavery. Herod Antipas then rebuilt it as the Ornament of the Galilee.

After the Bar Kokhba Revolt of 132 to 135 Jewish refugees from Judea settled there, and Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi, the compiler of the Mishnah, moved to Sepphoris with the Sanhedrin. Before moving to Tiberias by 220 some yeshivot were also based there. The city reportedly held some 30,000 people of several faiths, and it was the seat of a Christian bishopric. It was razed after the Jewish revolt of 351 to 352 against Constantius Gallus and hit by the earthquake of 363, but was rebuilt.

Arab forces took the town in 634 and a village, Saffuriya, grew on its ruins, developing most under the Mamluks. The Crusaders built a fort and a church of Saint Anne on the hill, and called it Le Saforie or Sephoris. In 1187 the field army of the Latin kingdom marched from its well-watered camp there to be destroyed at the Battle of Hattin by Saladin.

The Mamluk sultan Baybars captured it between 1263 and 1266. It remained a village under the Ottomans. Israeli forces captured it on 16 July 1948 in Operation Dekel; all but 80 villagers fled, and the rest were later deported or resettled in nearby Arab villages. The moshav of Tzippori was founded on 20 February 1949.

The ancient site was designated Tzipori National Park in 1992. It holds a Roman theatre, two early Christian churches, a Crusader fort partly rebuilt by Daher al-Umar in the 18th century and more than sixty mosaics dating from the third to the sixth century CE.
septimania: Septimania was the western part of the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis. It extended to a line halfway between the Mediterranean and the river Garonne in the north-west, with the Rhône separating it from Provence in the east and the Pyrenees forming the southern boundary. Its name may derive from the Roman name of Béziers, Colonia Julia Septimanorum Baeterrae, which alludes to veterans of the Seventh Legion, or from the seven cities of the territory: Agde, Béziers, Elne, Lodève, Villeneuve-lès-Maguelone, Narbonne and Nîmes.

In 462 the remaining Western Roman government, controlled by the general Ricimer, granted the Visigoths the western half of Gallia Narbonensis. After the Visigoths lost Toulouse and most of Gaul to Clovis I following the Battle of Vouillé in 507, Septimania remained in Visigothic hands; an attempt to take Carcassonne was defeated by the Ostrogoths in 508. The Visigothic kings favoured Narbonne as a capital until Theudis moved the capital to Barcelona. In the Visigothic Kingdom the province was both an administrative province and an ecclesiastical province whose metropolitan was the Archbishop of Narbonne. Julian of Toledo's remark that it held a large Jewish population dates from the time of King Wamba.

Muslim forces under al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani invaded in 719 and deposed the Visigothic kingdom in 720, renaming the region Arbunah. Odo the Great, Duke of Aquitaine, defeated them at Toulouse in 721, and al-Samh died of his wounds at Narbonne. The Franks conquered Narbonne in 759, and Roussillon fell in 760. Septimania became a march of the Carolingian Empire, later called Gothia or the Gothic March. Charlemagne found it devastated and depopulated and granted land to Visigothic and other refugees in some of the earliest identifiable fiefs. In the 12th century the court of Ermengarde of Narbonne was one of the cultural centres where courtly love developed. French kings gained effective control in the early 13th century after the Albigensian Crusade.

The medieval territory corresponds roughly to the former region of Languedoc-Roussillon in southern France, together with the departments of Aude, Gard, Hérault, Lozère and Pyrénées-Orientales. Narbonne became a major centre of Jewish learning in Western Europe.
septimius-severus: Lucius Septimius Severus was born on 11 April 145 at Leptis Magna, the son of Publius Septimius Geta and Fulvia Pia, in a wealthy family of equestrian rank. His father's family was of Libyan-Punic origin and his mother's descended from the Italian Fulvii, so he is considered the first emperor born into a provincial family of non-Italian origin.

He grew up speaking Punic, and was educated in Latin and Greek, which he spoke with a slight accent. Around 162 he sought a career in Rome, where Marcus Aurelius admitted him to the senatorial order. He married Paccia Marciana about 175 and, after her death, Julia Domna in 187. They had two sons, Caracalla and Geta.

In 191 the emperor Commodus appointed Severus governor of Pannonia Superior. After the murder of Pertinax in early 193 his legion XIV Gemina acclaimed him emperor at Carnuntum on 9 April. He marched on Italy, where Didius Julianus, who had bought the throne at an auction, was condemned by the Senate and killed. Severus dismissed the Praetorian Guard that had murdered Pertinax and replaced it with veterans of his Danubian legions. He defeated the rival claimant Pescennius Niger at the Battle of Issus in 194, and Clodius Albinus, the governor of Britannia, at the Battle of Lugdunum on 19 February 197. He then had 29 senators executed for supporting Albinus.

Severus sacked the Parthian capital Ctesiphon and annexed the northern half of Mesopotamia, though he failed twice to take the fortress of Hatra. He also expanded the Limes Arabicus. In 202 he campaigned in Africa and Mauretania against the Garamantes, capturing their capital Garama and extending the Limes Tripolitanus along the southern desert frontier. He raised the number of legions from 30 to 33 and raised the soldiers' pay from 300 to 400 denarii a year. He was the first emperor to station part of the imperial army in Italy. His relations with the Senate were poor, and Cassius Dio records that executions of senators continued.

Severus travelled to Britain in 208 and strengthened Hadrian's Wall. In 209 he invaded Caledonia with an army of 50,000 men, but he died of an infectious disease in early 211 at Eboracum, now York. His sons Caracalla and Geta, advised by Julia Domna, succeeded him. They founded the Severan dynasty, the last dynasty of the Roman Empire before the Crisis of the Third Century. The Arch of Septimius Severus in Rome commemorates his victory over the Parthians.
septuagint: Biblical scholars agree that the first five books of the Hebrew Bible were translated into Koine Greek by Jews living in the Ptolemaic Kingdom, probably in or around Alexandria, and can be dated with confidence to the mid- or late 3rd century BCE. The remaining books were presumably translated in the 2nd century BCE. Few people could read Hebrew in the Second Temple period, and Koine Greek and Aramaic were the lingua francas of the Jewish community, so the translation met a need.

According to tradition, Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent seventy-two translators, six from each of the Twelve Tribes, from Jerusalem to Alexandria to translate the Torah for the Library of Alexandria. The story is told in the Letter of Aristeas to his brother Philocrates, which some scholars regard as pseudepigraphical, and was repeated by Philo, Josephus and the Babylonian Talmud.

The name derives from the Latin phrase for the version of the seventy translators, and it was not until Augustine of Hippo that the Greek translation was called Septuaginta. The Greek text was produced within Hellenistic Judaism and completed by 132 BCE, though it continued to be revised in Jewish and Christian communities through the fourth century CE.

The Septuagint is not a single unified corpus but a collection of ancient translations of the Tanakh along with other Jewish texts now called apocrypha. The canon of the Hebrew Bible was still evolving while it was written, and the books were translated by different people, in different places and for different purposes, in styles that range from literal to paraphrase. Samuel and Kings form one four-part book, Of Reigns, and Chronicles is titled Of Things Left Out. Books found in it but not in the Hebrew Bible include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, the additions to Daniel and Esther, and 1 to 4 Maccabees.

Most Jews abandoned it around the 2nd century. The earliest gentile Christians had used it out of necessity, since it was the only Greek Bible and most could not read Hebrew, and its association with a rival religion may have made it suspect. Differences between it and the contemporary Hebrew scriptures were also discovered, and Greek-speaking Jews tended to prefer other versions, such as that of Aquila. The New Testament writers freely used the Greek translation when citing the scriptures. It formed the basis of the Old Latin versions and of the Old Church Slavonic, Armenian, Georgian and Coptic versions of the Old Testament. Origen's Hexapla produced the first major Christian recension.
seqenenre-tao: Seqenenre Tao, called the Brave, ruled the last of the local kingdoms of the Theban region in the Seventeenth Dynasty, during the Second Intermediate Period. He was probably the son and successor of Senakhtenre Ahmose and Queen Tetisheri.
