The second set, in 350 BCE, brought a standardised system of land allocation and tax reforms.

Most of the measures were taken from policies tried elsewhere, such as those of Wu Qi of Chu, but his were more thorough and extreme and placed policy in the ruler's hands. He partly abolished primogeniture and doubled the tax on households with more than one adult son, to break large clans into nuclear families. He also moved the capital from Yueyang to Xianyang to reduce the influence of nobles.

The Qin nobility despised Shang Yang, and he was vulnerable after the death of Duke Xiao. The next ruler, King Huiwen, ordered the nine familial exterminations against him on grounds of fomenting rebellion. He was executed by being torn apart by chariots, and his family was killed. Sima Qian tells it differently: he fled to Wei, was expelled, raised a rebel army in his fief and died in battle. King Huiwen kept his reforms.

Han Fei credits him with the theories of fixing the standards and equality before the law, and the Book of Lord Shang is likely the work of both him and his followers. Sima Qian reports that after ten years of the ordinances the commoners of Qin were delighted, and that no one picked up lost articles on the road.
shangdu: Shangdu, meaning Upper Capital, lies in what is now Zhenglan Banner, Inner Mongolia, in the grasslands north of the Great Wall, about 350 km north of Beijing and 28 km north-west of present-day Duolun County. It was designed by the architect Liu Bingzhong, a trusted adviser to Kublai Khan and a former Buddhist monk, as a seasonal retreat that blended Mongolian steppe traditions with Chinese urban planning.

The city was first called Kaiping and was established between 1252 and 1256. In 1264 Kublai Khan renamed it Shangdu and made it the summer capital of the Yuan dynasty. It was laid out in three parts: an outer city, an inner city and a central imperial palace whose enclosure measured about 550 metres on each side, roughly 40 per cent of the later Forbidden City in Beijing. Kublai Khan held court there, received foreign envoys and conducted affairs of state. At its height the city had a population of over 100,000 and included gardens, hunting grounds, temples and administrative quarters.

Marco Polo visited around 1275 and described a marble palace whose rooms were gilded and painted with figures, set within a walled park with fountains and rivers. He also recounted a portable cane palace with lacquered dragons that could be taken apart and moved at the emperor's command. When the Yuan dynasty fell, the last Yuan emperor, Toghon Temür, is credited with a lament for his Yellow Steppe of Xanadu. The city was largely destroyed and abandoned, and though its original name, Kaiping, was briefly restored, the settlement never recovered.

In 1872 the British diplomat Steven Bushell visited the ruins and noted surviving temples, marble blocks and decorative tiles, but by the late 20th century local residents of Dolon Nor had scavenged many of these materials for building. The Chinese government has worked to preserve and study the site since 2002, and UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 2012.

In the West the name entered literature through Samuel Purchas, who in 1614 described Xandu as a pleasure palace with a vast park, drawing on Marco Polo. Samuel Taylor Coleridge, inspired by Purchas, wrote the poem Kubla Khan, begun in 1797, whose opening line has Kubla Khan decree a stately pleasure-dome in Xanadu.
shanghai: Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south and the East China Sea to the east. The Huangpu River bisects the city. The land is an alluvial plain formed by the Yangtze's deposition and by land reclamation, and most of it is flat, with an average elevation of four metres. The soil is soft, so skyscrapers have to be built on deep concrete piles to avoid sinking.

The western part of the area was inhabited 6,000 years ago. In the Spring and Autumn period it belonged to the Kingdom of Wu, which was conquered by Yue and then by Chu. The name Shanghai, on the sea, is first found in the 11th-century Song dynasty, and in 1280 the place was renamed Shanghai.

Originally a fishing village and market town, Shanghai grew to prominence in the 19th century through trade and its port. It was one of five treaty ports forced open to European trade after the First Opium War, and the Shanghai International Settlement and the French Concession were set up there. In the 1930s it was a primary commercial and financial hub of Asia. In the Second World War it fell under Japanese rule after the Battle of Shanghai, and the Communists took it during the Chinese Civil War. The reform and opening up supported by Deng Xiaoping led to extensive redevelopment by the 1990s, especially in the Pudong New Area.

Shanghai is one of the four municipalities under the direct administration of the Central People's Government and is divided into 16 districts. Its historic sites include the City God Temple, Yu Garden and the row of early 20th-century buildings along the Bund.
shangqiu: Shangqiu lies in the easternmost part of Henan province, on the North China Plain, where the land is mostly flat and the soil fertile. Its name means Hills of Shang. The city and its surroundings were an important base of the Shang dynasty. Tradition places the early rulers Shennong, Zhuanxu and Ku in this area, together with Ku's son Xie, who helped Yu the Great to control the floods and received the land of Shang as a fief.

According to tradition, Xie's thirteenth-generation descendant Tang overthrew the Xia dynasty and founded the Shang, whose first capital, Nanbo, lay south of present-day Shangqiu. When the Zhou replaced the Shang around the 11th century BCE, the Shang royal descendants were given the area, which became the State of Song, with its capital Suiyang. Song was a major power in the Spring and Autumn period, declined in the Warring States period and fell to Qi and Wei in 286 BCE. Under the Han, Suiyang was the capital of the Kingdom of Liang, and a failed siege of it brought the collapse of the main rebel army in the Rebellion of the Seven States.

A ten-month siege of Suiyang in 757, during the An Lushan rebellion, turned the war in the Tang's favour. Zhao Kuangyin was military governor of a region centred on Songzhou before he founded the Song dynasty in 960 and took its name from it. The city was the Southern Capital of the Northern Song. After the Jurchens captured Kaifeng in 1127 the court withdrew to Shangqiu because of its link with Emperor Taizu, and Gaozong was crowned there on 12 June 1127. The capital moved to Yangzhou in 1128 and to Hangzhou in 1129. The present name dates from 1545, when Shangqiu County was created.

Shangqiu is a prefecture-level city of Henan. The Longhai railway, completed in 1916, made it a regional transport centre, and the Beijing-Kowloon line crosses it there. The Suiyang old city, built in 1511 under the Ming, is one of the best preserved traditional cities in China and was listed as a historical city by the central government in 1986. The philosophers Zhuangzi and Mozi are said to have come from the area.
shanhai-pass: The Shanhai Pass, whose name means Mountain-Sea Pass, commands the narrowest choke point of the Liaoxi Corridor, a coastal plain between the foothills of the Yan Mountains and the Bohai Sea. This is the only easily traversable land route between North China and the Northeast. It lies in what is now Shanhaiguan District of Qinhuangdao in Hebei, on the east bank of the Shi River, with walls running from the mountains to the shore of Liaodong Bay. An army wishing to avoid a costly siege had to circumvent it through narrow mountain passes deep in the Yan Mountains, which made long supply lines and large invasions difficult.

Passes stood here under the Northern Qi, Sui and Tang dynasties, and by 785 a garrison had been established at Yuguan, as the Tang called the site. The area was later controlled by the Liao dynasty, and garrisons were built under the Jin and Yuan. In 1381 the Ming general Xu Da was ordered to repair the old Yongping and Jieling passes, and from this the present pass took shape. It was reinforced heavily after the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, and in the late sixteenth century the general Qi Jiguang began building a military city around it, with forts to the east, south and north.

In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng entered Beijing, ending the Ming dynasty, and tried to win over Wu Sangui, the Ming general commanding the Ningyuan garrison. Instead of submitting to Li's Shun dynasty, Wu contacted the Manchu Qing and proposed a joint effort to drive the rebels out of the capital. The Qing regent Dorgon marched to the pass, and together Wu and the Manchus defeated Li's army near it. Li abandoned Beijing, and the Qing army entered unopposed.

The pass is square, with a perimeter of about four kilometres and walls 14 metres high and 7 metres thick, surrounded on three sides by a moat. Of its four gates only the Zhendong Gate in the east wall survives. It is one of the best preserved passes of the Great Wall, and the point where the wall meets the sea is known as the Old Dragon's Head. It was listed as part of the Great Wall as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
shanxi: Shanxi lies on a plateau made up of higher ground to the east, in the Taihang Mountains, and to the west, in the Lüliang Mountains, with a series of valleys in the centre through which the Fen River runs. The name means west of the mountains, a reference to its position west of the Taihang range. The Great Wall forms most of the northern border with Inner Mongolia, and the province also borders Hebei to the east, Henan to the south and Shaanxi to the west. The highest peak is Mount Wutai, at 3,058 metres, and the total area is 156,700 square kilometres.

The state of Jin, which existed in what is now Shanxi during the Spring and Autumn period (c. 770 – c. 481 BCE), gave the province its one-character abbreviation, Jin. Jin split into three states, Han, Zhao and Wei, in 403 BCE, a date sometimes taken as the start of the Warring States period, and all of them had fallen to the state of Qin by 221 BCE. The Han dynasty ruled the region as Bingzhou. During the Sixteen Kingdoms period several regimes controlled it in turn, followed by the Northern Wei (386–534), a Xianbei kingdom with one of its early capitals at present-day Datong.

Under the Ming and Qing dynasties Shanxi merchants, also called Jin merchants, dominated China's commerce and finance, a phenomenon that lasted for centuries from the Song to the Qing. Their networks reached Russia, Japan, Korea, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and South Asia. They controlled the overland tea trade with Russia and Mongolia, monopolised trade routes across the Great Wall and handled the Qing government's tax remittances between provinces.

After the Qing collapsed, Shanxi was governed for nearly four decades by Yan Xishan and kept a high degree of de facto autonomy within the Republic of China. When Japan invaded in 1937, Shanxi was one of the first areas attacked, and Yan invited Communist forces to re-enter the province. They arrived in time to help defeat a stronger Japanese force at the Pingxing Pass, in the Battle of Pingxingguan.

Shanxi is a province of North China whose capital and largest city is Taiyuan. The population is more than 99 per cent Han Chinese, and the dominant local language, Jin Chinese, is the only major Sinitic variety in northern China that is not classified within the Mandarin group. The province holds roughly one third of China's coal reserves. It has by far the largest number of historic buildings of any Chinese province, over 28,000 ancient structures, and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Pingyao Ancient City, the Yungang Grottoes and Mount Wutai.
shaoxing: Shaoxing is a prefecture-level city on the southern shore of Hangzhou Bay in north-eastern Zhejiang province, on the south bank of the Qiantang River estuary. It borders Ningbo to the east, Taizhou to the south-east, Jinhua to the south-west and Hangzhou to the west. The city was first named Shaoxing in 1131 during the Southern Song dynasty, after the reign period of Emperor Gaozong of Song.

The city lies north of the Kuaiji Mountains, an important centre of the people of Yue in the Spring and Autumn period. Chinese legend connected the mountains with events in the life of Yu the Great, the founder of the Xia. Around the early 5th century BCE, in the time of the Yue king Goujian, his people began to establish permanent centres on the plain north of the hills. After his release from captivity in Wu, Goujian commissioned his adviser Fan Li to build a major triangular fortification in the area of the present Yuecheng District.

After the Qin conquest in 222 BCE the First Emperor visited Mount Kuaiji in the last year of his reign, 210 BCE, and sacrificed to the spirit of Yu. The stele he erected is lost, but Sima Qian saw it and preserved its text in his Records of the Grand Historian. The area's capital was known as Kuaiji until the 12th century, when it was renamed Shaoxing.

Under the Ming and Qing dynasties Shaoxing was a prefecture of eight counties. From the later Ming through the Qing it was known, sometimes with disapproval, for its network of natives in the imperial bureaucracy, who cooperated out of loyalty to their place of origin. It also supplied unofficial legal specialists, the Shaoxing masters, whose knowledge of the Qing legal code let officials trained in the Confucian Classics judge local cases. In the early 20th century the prefecture was abolished and its name applied to a new county.

Shaoxing is a prefecture-level city administering three districts, two county-level cities and one county. It is known for Shaoxing rice wine, brewed with the water of Mirror Lake, and for Yue opera, sung in the local dialect. Its sites include the Tomb of Yu the Great, the Orchid Pavilion, commemorating the calligrapher Wang Xizhi, and the Shen Garden, associated with the poet Lu You. Several places connected with the writer Lu Xun, who was born in the city, survive.
shapur-i: Shapur was a son of Ardashir I, the founder of the Sasanian Empire, and his wife Murrod, whom Shapur names as his mother in his inscriptions. A semi-historical biography of Ardashir tells that the Parthian king's daughter Zijanak tried to poison her husband and was hidden with her son for seven years, but modern historians treat this as a story meant to link the Sasanians with the Parthian nobility. Shapur took part in his father's war against the Arsacids, including the Battle of Hormozdgan on 28 April 224, in which Artabanus IV was defeated and killed. Ardashir considered him the gentlest, wisest, bravest and ablest of his children and named him his successor.

In the east Shapur annexed most of the land of the Kushans and founded the city of Nishapur. In the west he seized Nisibis and Carrhae and advanced into Syria. Gordian III's forces defeated him at the Battle of Resaena, but he then won the Battle of Misiche and forced Philip the Arab to sign a peace in 244 and pay 500,000 gold denarii, which the Romans called a most shameful treaty. Later he annihilated a Roman force of 60,000 at the Battle of Barbalissos and ravaged Syria.

Emperor Valerian recovered Antioch by 257, but he pursued the Persians to Edessa, where he and the Roman army were captured. Shapur then took Caesarea and deported many thousands of Roman subjects, who built a dyke near Shushtar and the city of Bishapur. Captives of Antioch were settled in Gundeshapur. He did not seem interested in permanently occupying Roman provinces, preferring plunder, and in the 260s Odaenathus of Palmyra and Roman forces forced his withdrawal.

Shapur was the first Iranian monarch to style himself King of Kings of Iranians and non-Iranians, a title that became regular under his son Hormizd I. He called himself Mazda-worshipping, founded many fire temples, and treated Zoroastrian priests generously. He was tolerant of Mani, who joined his court and dedicated to him the Shabuhragan, but Shapur remained a Zoroastrian. According to Shapur's inscription at Hajiabad he was still active at court in his later years. He died of illness in Bishapur and was succeeded by Hormizd I; two other sons, Bahram I and Narseh, also became kings. His victory over Valerian is shown in reliefs at Naqsh-e Rustam.
shapur-ii: Shapur II was the son of Hormizd II, who died in 309. His successor, Adur Narseh, was killed by nobles after a few months, and they blinded the second son and imprisoned the third, who later escaped to the Roman Empire. The throne was kept for Shapur, who took the title of King of Kings at birth. Sources differ on whether he was born after his father's death or was an infant, and a legend that he was crowned before birth is regarded as fiction by modern historians. The nobility and priesthood held power until 325, when he reached the age of sixteen.

At sixteen Shapur led an expedition against Arab tribes that had raided Pars, defeating the Iyad in Asoristan, crossing the Persian Gulf to al-Khatt and attacking the Banu Tamim in the Hajar Mountains. He deported several tribes and ordered a wall built near al-Hira. Historians consider the accounts of his cruelty exaggerated.

His main aim in the west was to undo the Peace of Nisibis of 298, which had given Rome provinces in Mesopotamia. In 337 he broke the peace, and he besieged Nisibis three times without taking it, while the Battle of Singara in 344 was indecisive. Nomad invasions in the east halted the war by 350. In 359 he took Amida after a siege of seventy-three days and deported its people to Khuzistan. After the Roman emperor Julian was killed in 363, his successor Jovian gave up the districts beyond the Tigris, Nisibis and Singara. Armenia remained contested: a joint Roman and Armenian army defeated Persian forces in 371, and a seven-year truce followed.

In the east he gained territory in what is now Afghanistan and Pakistan around 350, but from about 360 Bactria fell to the Kidarites. Under Shapur the collection of the Avesta was completed, heresy and apostasy were punished, and Christians were persecuted, a reaction to the Christianization of the Roman Empire under Constantine.

Shapur died in 379 and was succeeded by his brother Ardashir II, who agreed to rule until Shapur's son, Shapur III, came of age. At his death the empire was larger and stronger than when he took the throne. His death began a conflict of about 125 years between the great nobles, the wuzurgan, and the kings.
shar-kali-sharri: Shar-Kali-Sharri reigned about 2218 to 2193 BCE by the middle chronology, as ruler of Akkad, and succeeded his father Naram-Sin, who had deified himself in his lifetime. In the 1870s Assyriologists thought he was the same person as Sargon of Akkad, the first ruler, a mistake recognised in the 1910s.

His name was sometimes written with the sign marking a god, and he was later deified: two of his titles are "heroic god of Akkade" and "god of the land of Warium". It has been suggested that he was governor of Nippur before he took the crown, since texts show that he was crowned there, with his sister Tudanapšum, high priestess of Enlil at Nippur, taking part. His queen was Tuta-sar-libbis.

According to the Sumerian King List his reign lasted 25 years, matching the year names from his rule. He completed the establishment of direct Akkadian rule begun by his predecessor, with governors in cities such as Adab and Lagash who called themselves his servants. Early in his reign he made a royal progress to Sumer lasting at least six months, taking in Umma, Zabala, Isin, Girsu and Nippur, accompanied by at least five generals.

Work on the Ekur, the temple of Enlil at Nippur, begun by Naram-Sin, was completed under him and appears in seven of his year names, which name the general Puzur-Eshtar as its builder. He also built temples to Annunitum and Ilaba at Babylon and another to Ilaba at Zabala.

His year names suggest a fairly peaceful reign with the usual clashes with the nomadic MAR.TU, the Gutians and the Elamites, and economic texts point to reasonable prosperity. The Gutians were growing in influence, and at some point they made Adab their capital. A later Neo-Babylonian copy of one of his inscriptions says that he faced a widespread revolt and overcame it, though it may reflect the Great Revolt faced by Naram-Sin.

Tradition held that the Akkadian Empire began to unravel in his reign. According to the Sumerian King List and later literary compositions, after his death in about 2193 BCE the region fell into anarchy and no king could dominate for long. The king list asks: "Then who was king? Who was not the king?" and names four rulers, Igigi, Imi, Nanum and Ilulu, who together ruled only three years. Akkad then recovered a degree of order under Dudu, who reigned 21 years, and Shu-turul, who reigned 15. Puzer-Mama, a later governor of Lagash, declared himself ruler, possibly on Shar-Kali-Sharri's death, and began the second dynasty of Lagash.
sharof-rashidov: Sharof Rashidov was born on 6 November 1917, the day before the Russian Revolution, into a poor Uzbek peasant family in the village of Sovungarlik, in what is now the Jizzakh region. After the Jizzakh Pedagogical College in 1935 he taught at a secondary school. He graduated in philology from Samarkand State University in 1941, and that year he was sent to the Eastern Front as a junior lieutenant. He fought in the Battle of Moscow, received two Orders of the Red Star and was demobilised in 1943 after being severely wounded. He also wrote, and his epic Chegarachi appeared in 1937.

Rashidov sat in the Supreme Soviet of the Uzbek SSR from 1947, chaired its Presidium from 1950 to 1959, and in March 1959 became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Uzbekistan, a post he held until his death. He led the Samarkand faction and purged Tashkent-aligned politicians. In 1969 rivals from the Tashkent, Fergana and Bukhara factions tried to depose him; he prevailed, and the plotters lost their power.

He enjoyed the support of Brezhnev, who sent resources for industrialisation and shielded him from investigation, and the republic had an unusually high degree of autonomy. Critics likened him to a khan for his control, and he kept a network of informers. Uzbekistan saw rapid growth, with the Muruntau gold mine opening in 1969 and Tashkent rebuilt after the earthquake of 1966.

He promoted relatives to office: at least fourteen held important government posts. Moscow demanded ever more cotton, and the republic's government reported inflated figures for irrigated and harvested land and output. Bribes, tribute and forgery created the appearance of fulfilled quotas, and wealth from central Soviet funds passed to the republic and to the Rashidov family. The push for cotton also contributed to the shrinking of the Aral Sea. Yuri Andropov, who knew of the scheme, began to break up the cotton mafia after Brezhnev's death.

Rashidov died on 31 October 1983 while visiting the Karakalpak ASSR. Most sources indicate a heart attack, with the strain of the corruption investigation often suggested as a factor, but some accounts allege suicide. Inomjon Usmonxoʻjayev succeeded him. He was first buried in Tashkent's Lenin Square, but after the cotton scandal drew attention his remains were disinterred in 1986 and reburied in his home district. After Uzbek independence Islam Karimov rehabilitated his image, a district was named after him, and a museum in Jizzakh is dedicated to him.
sharpeville-massacre: Sharpeville was built in 1943 to replace Topville, a nearby township where overcrowding and illness were widespread, and from 1958 about 10,000 Africans were forcibly removed to it. Unemployment and crime were high, and a new police station was used to check passes, deport illegal residents and raid illegal shebeens.

Pass laws, meant to control the movement and employment of Africans, were updated in the 1950s. Everyone over sixteen had to carry a passbook containing an identity card, labour bureau authorisation, the employer's name and personal details. Under Hendrik Verwoerd the National Party government used these laws to enforce greater segregation and in 1959–1960 extended them to women. The Pan-Africanist Congress, led by its founding president Robert Sobukwe, called on people to leave their passbooks at home and offer themselves for arrest.

About 5,000 people gathered at the Sharpeville police station on 21 March 1960. The mood was at first peaceful and festive, and fewer than 20 police were in the station. The crowd later grew to about 20,000, and 130 police with four Saracen armoured personnel carriers arrived. There is no evidence that anyone in the crowd was armed with anything other than stones. Jets flew low over the crowd to scatter it, and the protesters threw stones, striking three policemen.

At 13:30 the police began shooting without a warning to disperse and fired 1,344 rounds within two minutes. The police record listed 69 killed and 180 injured, and many people were shot in the back as they fled. Police reports in 1960 claimed that young, inexperienced officers panicked. In 1998 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission found a degree of deliberation in the decision to open fire. The photographer Ian Berry, who recorded the scene, had at first thought the police were firing blanks.

Strikes, marches and riots spread across the country in the following week. On 30 March 1960 the government declared a state of emergency and detained more than 18,000 people, among them Nelson Mandela. The United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 134 on 1 April, and South Africa became increasingly isolated; the event also played a part in its departure from the Commonwealth of Nations in 1961.

The banning of the Pan-Africanist Congress and the African National Congress followed, and the killings were one of the catalysts for a shift from nonviolent resistance to armed struggle. Poqo, the military wing of the PAC, and Umkhonto we Sizwe, that of the ANC, were founded soon afterwards. Since 1994 21 March has been Human Rights Day in South Africa, and a memorial opened in 2002 as part of the Sharpeville Human Rights Precinct.
sharur-district: Sharur is one of the seven districts of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of Azerbaijan. It borders the districts of Kangarli and Sadarak, the Vayots Dzor and Ararat provinces of Armenia, and the West Azerbaijan Province of Iran. Its capital and largest city is Sharur. The area has full-flowing rivers and fertile soils that favoured early plant-growing, and its people have long been engaged in agriculture, horticulture, viticulture, cotton growing and beekeeping.

Research indicates that people settled in the area in the late glacial period. Excavations have revealed settlements and burial places of the Neolithic, the Bronze Age and the Antique period. The settlement of Oghlangaya, covering 40 hectares on the Garatepe mountain, dates to the second and first millennia BCE, and mid Bronze Age monuments have been found along the Araz River and the Arpachay. Research in 1980 to 1990 uncovered a Stone Age cave with many stone tools. The place appears as Sharuk in the epic of the Book of Dede Korkut.

When the Nakhichevan Khanate was disestablished and annexed to the Russian Empire in 1828, the Sharur area was included in the Nakhichevan Uyezd of the Armenian Oblast and later in the Erivan Governorate. In 1870 the Sharur and Daralayaz mahals were detached as a separate district, the Sharur-Daralayaz Uyezd, which had 76,551 inhabitants in the Russian census of 1897. After the brief independence of Armenia and Azerbaijan in 1918 to 1920, the Sharur area, mostly controlled by local Azerbaijanis, was assigned to the Nakhichevan ASSR within the Azerbaijan SSR.

On 8 August 1930 the Sharur Uyezd was reorganised as the Norashen raion. It was renamed Ilich, or Ilichyovsk, in honour of Vladimir Lenin from 1964 to 1991, and on 28 February 1991 the name Sharur was restored. The district's administrative centre is the city of Sharur.
shatt-al-arab: The Shatt al-Arab, Arabic for River of the Arabs, is about 200 km long. It forms where the Euphrates and Tigris meet at al-Qurnah in the Basra Governorate and flows into the Persian Gulf south of the city of al-Faw. It is about 232 m wide at Basra and 800 m at its mouth. The Karun joins it from the Iranian side at Khorramshahr and deposits large amounts of silt, so that continuous dredging is needed to keep the river navigable. In Iran it is known as the Arvand Rud, the Valiant River. In the mid-1970s its banks held 17 to 18 million date palms.

Control of the river was disputed in the age of the Ottomans and the Safavids. The Safavids gained most of present-day Iraq in the early 16th century, but lost it to the Ottomans after the Peace of Amasya in 1555. Abbas I recovered the river, and the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 permanently ceded it to the Ottomans, although it never marked the southern frontier precisely. Nader Shah restored Iranian control for a time, until the Treaty of Kerden of 1746. Treaties of Erzurum in 1823 and 1847 and a protocol of 1913 again failed to settle the boundary.

In 1937 Iran and Iraq signed a treaty that placed the border at the low-water mark on the eastern bank, except at Abadan and Khorramshahr, so that Iraq controlled almost the whole waterway; ships had to fly the Iraqi flag and take an Iraqi pilot, and Iran paid tolls. Iran abrogated the treaty in April 1969. In March 1975 the Algiers Accord fixed the border on a line close to the thalweg, the deepest channel, in exchange for an end to Iranian support for the Iraqi Kurds.

Saddam Hussein abrogated that treaty in 1980 and invaded Iran, and the waterway was the scene of much of the fighting in the Iran-Iraq War, which lasted until 1988. When Iran captured al-Faw in 1986, Iraq's shipping through the river virtually stopped.

The southern part of the river forms the border between Iraq and Iran down to its mouth. It is Iraq's only outlet to the Persian Gulf, and Basra is a major port for loading oil tankers. Kuwait's Bubiyan Island is part of its delta. By 2002 more than 14 million of the date palms had been destroyed by war, salt and pests.
shawnee: The Shawnee are a Native American people of the Northeastern Woodlands, and their language is an Algonquian language. Their precontact homeland was likely centred in southern Ohio. Some scholars propose that they descend from the Fort Ancient culture of the Ohio region, which flourished from about 1000 to 1650 CE, though others suggest that they entered the region later and occupied Fort Ancient sites. In the 17th century Europeans met them over a wide area. A Dutch map of 1614 shows a group called Sawwanew east of the Delaware River, while French accounts place them along the Ohio River.

In the early 18th century they were concentrated mainly in eastern Pennsylvania, then dispersed again across Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. Shawnee towns might have forty to one hundred bark-covered houses, similar to Iroquois longhouses, with a council house for public deliberations. They fought to keep their homelands in the French and Indian War, Pontiac's War, Lord Dunmore's War and the American Revolutionary War, in which most allied with the British. Cornstalk led a minority that favoured neutrality.

After the Revolution the Shawnee and the Miami formed a powerful alliance in the Ohio Valley. Defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 led most Shawnee bands to sign the Treaty of Greenville the next year, ceding large parts of their homeland; other groups refused and moved to Missouri. Tecumseh did not sign it, and he later organised the intertribal alliance known as Tecumseh's confederacy. After his death and the end of the War of 1812 the Shawnee signed further treaties, and the 1830 Indian Removal Act sent them west of the Mississippi River, later to Indian Territory.

Before contact the Shawnee had a patrilineal social system, unlike many other peoples whose descent was traced through the mother. The tribe had five divisions, among them the Chillicothe, the Hathawekela, the Kispoko, the Mekoche and the Pekowi, and a 1935 study found six clans or name groups, each present in all five divisions. Today Shawnee people are enrolled in three federally recognised tribes, the Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma, the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma and the Shawnee Tribe, all headquartered in Oklahoma. The Shawnee language is still spoken by fewer than 100 people, according to estimates of 2017.
shaybanids: The Shaybanids, more accurately the Abu'l-Khayrid Shibanids, were a dynasty of Uzbek origin descended in the male line from Shiban, the fifth son of Jochi and a grandson of Genghis Khan. As the lineages of Batu and Orda died out in the civil wars of the 14th century, the Shaybanids under Abu'l-Khayr Khan declared themselves the only legitimate successors to Jochi and claimed his whole ulus, including parts of Siberia and Kazakhstan. Their rivals, the Tukay-Timurid dynasty, who claimed descent from another son of Jochi, ended up in control of the Great Horde and its successor khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea.

Under Abu'l-Khayr Khan, who led the Shaybanids from 1428 to 1468, the dynasty began consolidating the Uzbek tribes, first around Tyumen and the Tura River and then down to the Syr Darya region. His grandson Muhammad Shaybani, who ruled from 1500 and gave the dynasty its name, conquered Samarkand, Herat, Balkh and Bukhara, which ended the Timurid dynasty and created the short-lived Shaybanid Empire. Shaybanid descendants ruled the Khanate of Bukhara from 1505 to 1598 and the Khanate of Khwarazm, or Khiva, from 1511 to 1695. The Shaybanids also ruled the Khanate of Sibir from 1563, whose last khan, Kuchum, was deposed by the Russians in 1598.

Muhammad Shaybani and his successors began a programme of translating Persian literature into Chagatai Turkish, although Persian remained the main language of administration. By the 17th century most Shaybanid Uzbeks had been assimilated into a Chagatai Karluk culture and had made peace with the Timurid dynasty in India by proclaiming themselves heirs and protectors of the Timurid heritage. The Kalan Mosque, built in 1121, was entirely rebuilt in the early 16th century, and in 1530 Ubaidullah Khan added the Mir Arab Madrasa opposite it. Abdullah II built the Modari Khan Madrasa in 1567 and the Abdullah II Madrasa between 1588 and 1590.
shebelle-river: The Shebelle River begins in the highlands of Ethiopia and flows south-east into Somalia towards Mogadishu, and its length is 1,820 km. Near Mogadishu it turns sharply south-west and follows the coast. Below Mogadishu the river becomes seasonal. Its flow varies with the rains: it has been described as reaching the Jubba River, and so the ocean, only in seasons of heavy rainfall, and in drier years it dwindles into wetlands and sandy plains. Its tributaries include the Erer, Galetti and Wabe rivers, and it was known historically as the Nile of Mogadishu.

The area around it is inhabited by the Arsi Oromo and by Somali people in the Somali Region of Ethiopia and in Somalia. In the lower basin, farming has largely replaced the traditional nomadic herding way of life.

In the Middle Ages the Shebelle was under the control of the Ajuran Empire, which rose to prominence in the thirteenth century and monopolised the water of the Shebelle and the Jubba. Its rulers built many limestone wells and cisterns by hydraulic engineering, and developed systems of agriculture and taxation that remained in use in parts of the Horn of Africa until the nineteenth century. The wells drew Somali and Oromo nomads with their livestock, and officials of the state mediated their disputes.

Irrigation ditches called kelliyo carried water from the Shebelle and Jubba to plantations growing sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton, supported by dikes and dams. The farms of Afgooye, Bardhere and other places grew more productive, and the crops were sold at the coastal ports of Mogadishu, Merca, Barawa and others to merchants who traded with Arabia, Persia, India, Venice, Egypt, Portugal and as far as Java and China.

The source of the river is cultivated by the Arsi Oromo. In 1989, with the help of Soviet engineers, the Melka Wakena Dam was built on its upper reaches in the Bale Mountains, producing 153 megawatts. Along the lower river, the cultivation of bananas contributes significantly to Somalia's export industry. The river has a history of destructive flash floods, among them the hidigsayley of 1965 and the kabahay of 1978.
sheberghan: Sheberghan lies at an altitude of 335 metres along the banks of the Sari Pul River, about 130 kilometres west of Mazar-i-Sharif on the Afghanistan Ring Road. It sits astride the main route between Balkh and Herat, controls the direct route north to the Amu Darya, about 90 kilometres away, and a branch route south to Sar-e Pol. For millennia it has been the focal point of power in the north-eastern corner of Bactria.

The name is a corruption of its classical Persian name, Shaporgân, meaning King Shapur's town. Two Sasanian kings bore the name Shapur and both built many cities; it is more likely that Shapur I, governor of the eastern provinces, built a roadway between a few important cities, among them Nishapur, Bishapur and Peshawar.

Sheberghan was a flourishing settlement along the Silk Road. A few kilometres north-east lies the fortified town of Yemshi-tepe, about 500 metres from the necropolis of Tillia Tepe. A joint Soviet-Afghan team excavated there from 1969 to 1979, and six royal tombs yielded a vast amount of gold and other treasure, together with coins of the early 1st century CE and none later. A team that began work in 1977, 5 kilometres north of the town, found mud-brick columns and a cross-shaped altar of a temple dating to at least 1000 BCE. The town has been proposed as the site of Xidun, one of the five divisions of the early Kushan Empire.

Marco Polo visited in the 13th century and wrote of its honey-sweet melons. The town later became the capital of an independent Uzbek khanate, which the Anglo-Russian border agreement of 1873 allotted to Afghanistan. In 1856 J. P. Ferrier described a citadel where the governor Rustem Khan lived, good gardens and excellent cultivation, and a town of 12,000 people, mostly Uzbeks. He added that its water came from the mountains of the Khanate of Sirpool and that disputes over it often threatened war.

Sheberghan is the capital of Jowzjan Province and has an estimated population of 213,411, mostly Turkmens and Uzbeks, with Tajiks, Pashtuns, Hazaras and Arabs as well. Turkmeni is the first language of many natives, though Dari and Pashto are the official languages of Afghanistan. Jowzjan University stands in the centre. Irrigated land around the city supplies fruit and vegetables to other cities, and natural gas has been worked nearby since 1967, when the Khowaja Gogerak field was opened with Soviet help and a pipeline linked Sheberghan with Keleft in the Soviet Union.
shechem: Shechem lay in a narrow valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, two of the largest mountains in Samaria. The valley was a principal highway for merchants and travellers moving between the northern and southern hills, which made the city a trade hub. Many springs made wells easy to dig, and the fertile soil supported agriculture and livestock. The site was identified as Tell Balata after a German party led by Hermann Thiersch came upon it in 1903.

The oldest settlement dates to the Chalcolithic period, around 3500 to 3000 BCE. The first substantial building belongs to the Middle Bronze Age IIA, around 1900 BCE, and the city is mentioned on the stele of Sebek-khu, a noble at the court of Senusret III. In the Middle Bronze IIC, around 1590 to 1550 BCE, it reached its largest size and power, with a Fortress Temple and cyclopean walls. In the Amarna letters of about 1350 BCE, Šakmu was the centre of a kingdom made by the Canaanite prince Labaya, who recruited Habiru mercenaries.

In the Iron Age II the city, in the northern Kingdom of Israel, had an estimated 1,200 inhabitants in the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. In the Hellenistic and Roman periods it was the main settlement of the Samaritans, whose religious centre stood on Mount Gerizim. Josephus says Sextus Vettulenus Cerialis destroyed it in the First Jewish-Roman War, and in 72 CE Vespasian built Flavia Neapolis two kilometres to the west, the origin of the name Nablus.

The Hebrew Bible mentions Shechem some sixty times. Genesis tells that Abraham built an altar at the oak of Moreh there, and that Jacob's sons Simeon and Levi killed the city's men after the abduction of their sister Dinah. Joshua assembled the Israelites there to choose whom to serve. Abimelech, son of Gideon, was made king there and later destroyed the city. After Solomon's death the northern tribes met at Shechem, and Jeroboam fortified it as the capital of the new kingdom. The kings later moved to Tirzah and then to Samaria, and Shechem lost importance.

Around 128 BCE the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim and in 107 BCE the city, which never recovered. Jacob's Well and Joseph's tomb stand nearby, and some scholars identify Shechem with the Samaritan city of Sychar in the Gospel of John.
sheikh-lotfollah-mosque: Construction began in 1011 AH (1602/1603 CE) and finished in 1028 AH (1618/1619 CE). The architect was Muhammad Reza, son of Husayn, a builder from Isfahan whose name appears on an inscription around the mihrab. The mosque was meant for the royal court alone, unlike the public Shah Mosque, so it has no minarets and is smaller. Shah Abbas had a tunnel built from the Ali Qapu Palace under the square to it, ending in a winding passage with guards, apparently to shield the women of the harem.

It was named in 1622 after Shaykh Lutfallah Maysi al-Amili, a prominent scholar and father-in-law of Shah Abbas, who came to Isfahan at the shah's orders and lived on the site but was never involved in the building. Reza Shah Pahlavi had the mosque restored in the 1920s, on the advice of Arthur Upham Pope.

The building is closer to a mausoleum in type than to a four-iwan mosque, which historians ascribe either to private worship by the shah's family or to its use as a women's sanctuary. It has a single domed chamber, 19 metres on a side, with no courtyard and no interior iwans. Because the square runs north to south and the qibla lies to the south-west, the architect joined the entrance to the chamber by an L-shaped vestibule, so the dome stands 6.5 metres off the axis of the portal iwan as seen from the square.

The visitor passes through two dim corridors before facing the mihrab in a room lit by nearly a score of windows. The dome, one of the few single-shell domes of Safavid architecture, is 13 metres across. Concentric rings of lozenge-shaped tilework shrink towards a central sunburst, often called a peacock because the light through the opening forms its tail.

The mosque is regarded as a masterpiece of Safavid architecture and is registered with Naqsh-e Jahan Square as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was added to the Iran National Heritage List on 6 January 1932. In The Road to Oxiana, Robert Byron wrote that he knew of no finer example of the Persian Islamic genius than the interior of the dome. The dome's design is said to derive from the Shah Vali Mosque in Taft, Yazd.
sheikh-mujibur-rahman: Mujib was born on 17 March 1920 in the village of Tungipara in the Faridpur district of Bengal, into a Bengali Muslim family of small landlords. His father was a law clerk in the courthouse of Gopalganj. He became a student activist, and in 1943 was elected a councillor of the Muslim League. At Islamia College in Calcutta he worked under his mentor Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy and campaigned for inclusion of the Sylhet district in Pakistan in the 1947 referendum. After partition he studied law at the University of Dhaka, from which he was expelled in 1949 for inciting employees against the university.

In 1948 Mujib founded the East Pakistan Students' League and was drawn into the Bengali language movement, which opposed making Urdu the sole national language. In 1949 he became a joint secretary of the Awami Muslim League, later the Awami League, and after Suhrawardy's death in 1963 its general secretary. He was elected to the East Bengal Legislative Assembly in 1954 and briefly served in the cabinet of A. K. Fazlul Huq. He spent many years in prison. The government of President Ayub Khan arrested him in 1967 in the Agartala Conspiracy Case, accusing him of plotting with Indian agents. Mass protests forced it to drop the charges on 22 February 1969, and he was then given the title Bangabandhu, Friend of Bengal.

In 1970 the Awami League won Pakistan's first general election, but the military government of President Yahya Khan refused to transfer power. On 7 March 1971 Mujib gave a speech that called vaguely for independence. The army arrested him late on 25 March and began a crackdown on Bengali civilians. In the early hours of 26 March the Proclamation of Bangladeshi Independence was issued in his name, and nationalists declared him head of the provisional government while he was held in West Pakistan.

Mujib returned to Bangladesh in January 1972. His government drew up a secular constitution, held the first general election and normalised relations with most countries. In 1974 he gave the first speech in Bengali to the United Nations General Assembly. The country suffered a severe famine in 1974, and the government formed a paramilitary force, the Jatiya Rakkhi Bahini, against a left-wing insurgency; it was later accused of human rights abuses. In 1975 he introduced a one-party system as the Second Revolution and became president. He was assassinated with most of his family at his Dhanmondi residence in a military coup on 15 August 1975. UNESCO has listed his speech of 7 March 1971 in its Memory of the World Register.
shen-kuo: Shen Kuo was born in Qiantang, modern Hangzhou, in 1031. His father, Shen Zhou, was a lower gentry figure serving in provincial posts, and his mother, from the Xu family of Suzhou, was well educated and gave Shen Kuo and his brother their first schooling, including the military doctrines of her elder brother Xu Dong. Lacking the prominent clan history of many northern elite families, Shen relied on his own ability. In 1063 he passed the imperial examinations, placing in the higher category of candidates. At Yangzhou he drew the notice of the fiscal intendant Zhang Chu, who recommended him for a post in the financial administration at court and whose daughter he later married.

Shen rose to be a finance minister, a state inspector, head official of the Bureau of Astronomy, Assistant Minister of Imperial Hospitality and an academic chancellor. Politically he belonged to the New Policies Group of the Reformist faction led by Chancellor Wang Anshi. With his colleague Wei Pu he planned a five-year project of daily observations to chart the paths of the Moon and planets, but political opponents blocked it. In 1075 he reported on his reforms of the calendar, which the court adopted only in part.

Chancellor Cai Que later held him responsible for a disaster and loss of life, removed him from office and placed him on probation in a fixed residence for six years. Cut off from government, Shen devoted himself to scholarship, and after he completed two geographical atlases for a state programme the court lifted the probation and pardoned him. His largest atlas had twenty-three maps of China and foreign regions at a uniform scale of 1:900,000. He spent his last years at his Dream Brook estate.

The Dream Pool Essays of 1088 contains some 507 essays across physics, mathematics, astronomy and medicine, and argues that technology does not conflict with Confucian precepts. In it Shen is the first to describe the magnetic needle compass, with experiments on suspended needles and the concept of true north through magnetic declination. He also described Bi Sheng's ceramic movable type, the drydock and the pound lock, and he offered a hypothesis of land formation from marine fossils and silt, and another of gradual climate change after finding petrified bamboo in a dry northern region. He improved the armillary sphere, the gnomon and the water clock.

As an archaeologist he held that ancient objects should be studied for how they were made and used, and he credited their manufacture to common artisans rather than to sages. Only six of his books survive, four of them significantly altered since he wrote them. Joseph Needham ranked his mind among the best scientific minds in Chinese history.
sheng-shicai: Sheng Shicai was an ethnic Han Chinese born in Kaiyuan, Manchuria, to a well-to-do peasant family. He studied in Mukden and Shanghai and then in Tokyo, where he took political economy at Waseda University and met leftist publications such as The ABC of Communism. By his own admission he became a Marxist in 1919, the year he took part in the May Fourth Movement. He then chose a military career, trained in Kwantung and the Northeastern Military Academy, served under Guo Songling and was sent to the Imperial Japanese Army Academy. In 1927 he joined the Northern Expedition. He reached Xinjiang in the winter of 1929–30 at the invitation of its governor Jin Shuren, who made him Chief of Staff of the Frontier Army.

On 12 April 1933, amid the Kumul Rebellion and fighting with the Hui commander Ma Zhongying, White Russians and provincial officials overthrew Jin, and two days later the coup leaders appointed Sheng military governor, or duban. He had the coup leaders removed, and by June 1934, with help from the Soviet Union, which he had invited to intervene, he had defeated Ma Zhongying and Zhang Peiyuan, subordinating himself to the Soviets in return.

In 1934 his government published an administrative plan promising racial equality and religious freedom, and it gave non-Han peoples a place in the provincial government for the first time. The Soviets gained a monopoly over trade and exploited the province's rare materials and oil, and Sheng joined the Soviet Communist Party in August 1938.

In 1937, in parallel with Stalin's Great Purge, Sheng carried out his own, which swept the Uyghur and Hui political elite and later struck Han Chinese sent from Moscow; an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 people died. In July 1942, with the Soviet Union at war with Germany, he approached the Nationalist government and expelled Soviet personnel, and he purged the Chinese Communists whom he had brought in to fill posts. In 1944 he tried to turn back to the Soviets, but Stalin refused to intervene, and the Nationalist government removed him. On 29 August 1944 he was named Minister of Agriculture and Forestry.

He left Xinjiang on 11 September 1944 with 135 truckloads of wealth, held the ministry until July 1945 and later advised Hu Zongnan in Xi'an. After the Chinese Civil War he went with the Kuomintang to Taiwan, where he lived in retirement and died in Taipei in 1970. He was called the King of Xinjiang during his rule.
shenyang: Shenyang lies in the central part of Liaoning province. Its western districts are on the alluvial plain of the Liao River system and its eastern part reaches into the forested hinterland of the Changbai Mountains. The name means the yang side of the Shen River, the old name of the Hun River, which runs on the southern side of the city; in Chinese naming custom a river's north bank is the sunny, or yang, side. Humans lived here as early as 8,000 years ago, and the remains of the Xinle culture, a late Neolithic society over 6,800 years old, are kept in a museum in Huanggu District.

In the 14th century the city came under the Ming dynasty, for which it was an important military stronghold. In 1625 the Jurchen leader Nurhaci captured Shenyang and moved his whole administration to it. The Manchu name was Simiyan hoton, and in 1634 the official name became Mukden, or Shengjing, meaning rising capital, from the Manchu word mukdembi, to rise. The imperial palace was built from 1626 on Nurhaci's orders, with more than 300 rooms and 20 gardens.

After the First Sino-Japanese War Japan obtained the Liaodong Peninsula by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 but had to give it up under the Triple Intervention. A secret treaty of 1896 allowed Russia to build a railway through Manchuria, and after the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 Russian forces occupied most of Manchuria, making Mukden a Russian stronghold. The Battle of Mukden of 1905 was fought south of the city, and Japanese influence grew afterwards. In 1914 the city took back the name Shenyang, though Mukden stayed in use in English and in Japan for decades.

The Mukden incident of 1931 led to the Japanese invasion and occupation of the rest of Manchuria and the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Red Army occupied the city in August 1945, and British and American reports say Soviet troops looted and terrorised its people. The Communists captured it in 1948 after the Liaoshen campaign.

Shenyang is the capital of Liaoning province, with 9,070,093 residents at the 2020 census. It has been a centre of heavy industry since the 1930s, and many factories were built in Tiexi district in the first five-year plan, 1951 to 1956. After the 1980s heavy industry declined and hundreds of thousands of workers were laid off. It is the railway hub of north-eastern China.
shenzhen: Shenzhen lies on the east bank of the Pearl River estuary on the central coast of Guangdong. It borders Hong Kong to the south, Dongguan to the north, Huizhou to the northeast and Macau to the southwest. Although it sits about a degree south of the Tropic of Cancer, it has a warm, humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon and the Siberian anticyclone, with mild winters and a rainy season that lasts until late September or early October.

The city roughly follows the administrative boundaries of the historical Bao'an County. Its name means deep ditch in the local vernacular, from words used for irrigation ditches. The earliest recorded mention of the name dates from 1410, under the Ming dynasty, but no market town was established there until the Qing dynasty.

Humans have lived in the area for some 6,700 years, with the oldest evidence from the mid-Neolithic period. Historic counties were first established there about 1,700 years ago, and the towns of Nantou and Dapeng were built over 600 years ago. After the Second Opium War the United Kingdom seized Hong Kong Island and was leased the New Territories, which fixed the modern boundary between Hong Kong and the area of Shenzhen, then a village on the border.

In 1953 the Bao'an County government moved to Shenzhen, which was closer to the Kowloon–Canton Railway and had a larger economy than Nantou. From the 1950s to the end of the 1970s the county received a large influx of refugees trying to reach Hong Kong; between 100,000 and 560,000 are said to have lived there. The place became a city by 1979. In May 1980 the Central Committee designated it the first special economic zone in China, as part of the reform and opening up promoted by Deng Xiaoping, an experiment in market capitalism within a community guided by socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then had a population of 30,000.

Shenzhen is a prefecture-level city with nine districts and one new district. Its permanent population was recorded as 17,560,000 in 2020, many of them migrants from other parts of China, so that the population is younger than that of most Chinese cities. Before the zone was established the local communities spoke Cantonese or Hakka, and the main local cuisine is Cantonese.

The city is a centre of the technology and manufacturing industries, and is home to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange and companies such as Huawei, Tencent and DJI. Its port is one of the large container ports of the world. The Shenzhen Metro, a rapid transit system, serves the city, and the city is part of the Pearl River Delta Metropolitan Region together with Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau, among others.
shephelah: The Shephelah, also written Shfela and known as the Judaean Foothills, is a transitional region of soft, rolling hills between the Judaean Mountains and the Coastal Plain. It is about 60 kilometres long from north to south. It is divided into a western Low Shephelah, rising to no more than about 200 metres above the Coastal Plain, and an eastern High Shephelah, between 250 and 450 metres above sea level.

A series of east-west valleys cuts it into districts: from north to south the valleys of Ayalon, Sorek, Elah, Guvrin, Lachish and Adorayim. The Ayalon was the primary access corridor to Jerusalem along the ascent of Horon, and passage between the east-west and north-south valleys has dictated the communication routes throughout history. The hills are of soft chalk covered with marl, unlike the hard chalk and dolomite of the Judaean Hills, and bell-shaped caves are a feature of the south, as at Beit Guvrin.

Surveys have found habitation in the Late Bronze period. In the early Iron Age the population of what is widely believed to have been a Canaanite enclave between Philistia and the Israelite and Judahite highlands declined, although a string of settlements survived on the eastern edge.

Growth resumed in the Iron Age IIA-B, beginning with the short-lived settlement at Khirbet Qeiyafa, and the incoming settlers, identified with the highland culture, expanded as Philistia declined. By the 8th century BCE it was the most densely populated region of the Kingdom of Judah, but the Assyrian invasion of 701 BCE destroyed most excavated sites and left it largely depopulated in the following century.

After Babylon destroyed Judah in 587 BCE the Edomites gradually took the region, which became the core of Idumea. It flourished in the Hellenistic period, was strongly affected by the First Jewish-Roman War of 66 to 70, and was largely depopulated of Jews after the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 136. It flourished again in the Byzantine period and saw one of the major battles of the Muslim conquest of the Levant in the 7th century. In the late Mamluk and early Ottoman periods permanent villages contracted, and ruins were reused as seasonal shelters.

The Shephelah is largely rural with many farms, and the cities of Ashdod, Ashkelon, Rehovot, Beit Shemesh and Kiryat Gat roughly surround it. The Hebrew Bible mentions it many times and assigns land in it to the tribes of Judah and Dan. Its archaeological sites include Lachish, Azekah, Gezer, Maresha and Tel Burna.
sher-shah-suri: Sher Shah was born Farid Khan in Sasaram in present-day Bihar, a Pashtun of the Sur clan. His birth year is disputed, with some accounts giving 1472 and others 1486. His grandfather Ibrahim Khan Sur migrated from the region of Roh in present-day Afghanistan and began as a horse trader, and his father Hasan Khan Sur held jagirs in Bihar. He received the title Sher Khan, from Persian for lion, after killing a tiger that leapt at the governor of Bihar.

He managed his father's jagirs for 21 years, reforming land revenue assessment and the commissions of tax collectors, until the resentment of his stepmother and step-brothers led him to resign in 1518. He went to Agra, observed the Mughal leadership of Babur and then entered the service of the governor of Bihar. When Sultan Mohammad of Bihar died in October 1528, the queen Dudu Bibi became regent and Sher Shah her deputy governor.

By 1530 Sher Shah was regent and de facto ruler of Bihar. He gained the fort of Chunar by marrying the widow of its governor, defeated the Lohani chiefs of Bihar and the Sultan of Bengal at Surajgarh in March 1534, and in 1538 took Rohtasgarh and Gauda while the Mughal emperor Humayun was engaged elsewhere. After defeating the Mughals he took Agra and Delhi. He then conquered Malwa in 1542, and in 1543 took Raisen, where the Rajputs who left the fort under a promise of safe conduct were massacred, an act considered the darkest mark on his reign.

He ordered the empire's administration and army. He divided Bengal into 47 administrative divisions, paid his soldiers fixed salaries, assigned roles through the Dagh system and promoted by merit. He abolished taxes at provincial borders, leaving only a levy on goods brought in and one on goods sold. He extended the Grand Trunk Road from Chittagong to Kabul and issued a silver coin of 178 grains called the rupee, the precursor of the modern rupee.

Sher Shah besieged Kalinjar fort for seven months, and the circumstances of his death are uncertain. In one account a bomb thrown at the fort fell back on a store of bombs, and he was found half-burned and lived two more days, ordering the assault until he heard the fort had fallen. He died on 22 May 1545. His son Jalal Khan, known as Islam Shah Suri, won the succession and ruled until 1553, after which the Sur Empire fell apart in civil war until the Mughals reconquered it. Historians debate his religious policy, and many hold that he showed tolerance toward Hindus.
sherborne: Sherborne lies on the River Yeo, on the edge of the Blackmore Vale, six miles east of Yeovil, in north-west Dorset. Its name was scir burne, meaning clear stream, after a brook running through the centre, and the Domesday Book gives it so. The A30 road from London to Penzance passes through. Much of the old town, including much of the abbey and many medieval and Georgian buildings, is built from a honey-brown local material called Sherborne Stone. The town became a borough in 1227.

In 705 the diocese of Wessex was split between Sherborne and Winchester, and King Ine founded an abbey for Saint Aldhelm, first Bishop of Sherborne, whose see covered Dorset, Somerset and Devon. The large diocese lasted until about 909, when it was divided into three sees, Sherborne keeping Dorset. In 1075 the bishop's seat moved to Old Sarum and the church became a Benedictine monastery. The abbey was damaged by fire in 1437 after tension between the town and the monastery came to a head, but much of the Norman structure stands. In 1539, after the Dissolution of the Monasteries, Sir John Horsey bought the buildings and the abbey church became the parish church.

In the 12th century Roger de Caen, Bishop of Salisbury and Chancellor of England, built a fortified palace. Sir Thomas Fairfax besieged it in 1645 in the English Civil War, and it was left in ruins. In 1594 Sir Walter Raleigh built an Elizabethan mansion in the grounds, known as Sherborne Castle.

Sherborne had 10,361 residents at the census of 2021. A school is said to have existed there since the time of King Alfred, who was educated there; it was refounded in 1550 as King Edward's Grammar School, using some of the abbey buildings, and is now Sherborne School. Its alumni include Cecil Day-Lewis, Alan Turing and John le Carré. The town holds 378 listed buildings, among them St Johns' House, an almshouse founded in 1437, and the Abbey Gatehouse, which has housed Sherborne Museum since 1966. The Pack Monday Fair, held for centuries on the Monday after 10 October, was originally an agricultural fair.
shetland: Shetland lies between Orkney, the Faroe Islands and Norway, about 80 kilometres northeast of Orkney, 170 kilometres from mainland Scotland and 220 kilometres west of Norway. The largest island, known as the Mainland, is the fifth-largest in the British Isles, and 16 of the islands are inhabited. The climate is oceanic and the coastline rugged, on islands that are virtually treeless. Almost all place names are of Norse origin. The name may derive from the Old Norse hjalt, hilt, and land.

Humans have lived in Shetland since the Mesolithic period. Because people built in stone on treeless islands from at least the early Neolithic, the islands hold over 5,000 archaeological sites. Norse settlers colonised Shetland in the late 8th and 9th centuries; the fate of the preceding population is unresolved, though there is no established archaeological evidence that settlement involved violent extermination.

From the mid-13th century Scottish monarchs sought to control the islands around their seas. This led King Haakon IV of Norway to invade Scotland; after the stalemate at the Battle of Largs he retreated to Orkney and died in December 1263. Under the 1266 Treaty of Perth the Hebrides and Mann passed to Scotland, but the Scots recognised continuing Norwegian sovereignty over Orkney and Shetland.

After 1380 Norway formed a union with Denmark and royal interest in the islands declined. Orkney in 1468 and Shetland in 1469 were pledged by Christian I as security for the unpaid dowry of his daughter Margaret on her marriage to James III of Scotland, with a right of redemption, and the islands were absorbed into Scotland in 1472. Later Danish rulers made repeated attempts to recover them. Shetland kept its own legal system until 1612.

Shetland is the northernmost region of the United Kingdom. Its administrative centre and only burgh is Lerwick, capital since 1708, when it replaced Scalloway. The Norse heritage is reflected in the Up Helly Aa fire festivals and a strong fiddle tradition, and writers have often used the Shetland dialect of Scots. Oil and gas were first landed at Sullom Voe in 1978.
shibam: Shibam stands in Wadi Hadhramaut in the desert of Ramlat al-Sab'atayn, in the central-western part of the Hadhramaut Governorate. Its main road links Sanaa and other cities of western Yemen with the far eastern territories, and another road from the village of Alajlanya links it to Mukalla, the governorate's capital on the Indian Ocean. The nearest towns are Seiyun, which has an airport, and Tarim, both to the east. The climate is hot desert, with June the hottest month. The town is officially called the Old Walled City of Shibam, from the fortified wall that surrounds it.

The first known inscription about the city dates from the 3rd century CE. According to the geographer al-Hamdani, its origins go back to the pre-Islamic period, and it became the capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut in 300 CE, after the destruction of the earlier capital, Shabwa, in the far west of the valley. Its position along ancient trade routes contributed to its prosperity. Whether the present town stands on the site of the ancient city is unclear.

One theory explains its rise of more than six metres above the surrounding plain by the accumulation of ruins, but no excavations support this, and it might be a natural outcrop of the mountain spur behind it. Two archaeological sites lie nearby: Jujah, a quarry for large squared building stones, and Gabusa, where an Assyrian-style bronze lion's head was found.

Shibam has been inhabited continuously for an estimated 1,700 years, although the present town dates to 1533, and many houses have been rebuilt numerous times in recent centuries. In the 20th century it was one of the three major cities of the Qu'aiti Sultanate, with Mukalla and Ash-Shihr. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1982.

The houses of Shibam are all built of mud brick, and about 500 of them are tower blocks of five to eleven storeys, with one or two rooms on each floor. The design was meant to protect residents from Bedouin attacks. Some towers stand over 30 metres high, which makes the town one of the oldest and best examples of urban planning on the principle of vertical construction, and it is often called the oldest skyscraper city in the world.

The walls must be maintained routinely with fresh layers of mud against rain and erosion. A tropical storm in 2008 flooded the town and brought down some buildings, and in 2015 UNESCO listed it, with Old Sanaa, as cultural heritage at risk.
shiga-prefecture: Shiga Prefecture borders Fukui Prefecture to the north, Gifu to the northeast, Mie to the southeast and Kyoto to the west. Lake Biwa, Japan's largest lake, lies at its centre and occupies one-sixth of its area. The Seta River is the only natural river that flows out of the lake, running through Kyoto to Osaka Bay. The lake divides the prefecture into four areas: Kohoku to the north, Kosei to the west, Kotō to the east and Konan to the south. Mountain ranges enclose it, among them the Hira Mountains, Mount Hiei, the Ibuki Mountains and the Suzuka Mountains. Southern Shiga is usually warm, while the north is cold with high snowfall.

Shiga was known as Ōmi Province, or Gōshū, before the prefectural system was established. Ōmi neighboured Nara and Kyoto, at the junction of western and eastern Japan. Between 667 and 672 Emperor Tenji founded a palace at Ōtsu, and in 742 Emperor Shōmu founded one at Shigaraki. In the early Heian period Saichō, born in the north of Ōtsu, founded Enryaku-ji, the centre of Tendai. Oda Nobunaga subjugated Ōmi and built Azuchi Castle on the eastern shore of Lake Biwa in 1579.

In 1600 Ishida Mitsunari, based at Sawayama Castle, made war against Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara. Afterwards Ieyasu made Ii Naomasa lord of Sawayama, and Naomasa established the Hikone Domain. Ii Naosuke, of that house, became the Tokugawa shogunate's Tairō and concluded commercial treaties with the Western powers. With the abolition of the han system eight prefectures were formed in Ōmi, and they were unified into Shiga Prefecture in September 1872. It is named after Shiga District, to which Ōtsu belonged until 1898.

Ōtsu is the capital and largest city; other major cities include Kusatsu, Nagahama and Higashiōmi. Hikone Castle is one of four national treasure castles in Japan, and Enryaku-ji is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The southern half adjoins Kyoto and forms part of Greater Kyoto. The Hikiyama festival of floats, held in ten areas including Nagahama each April, was designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1979.
shikoku: Shikoku is 225 kilometres long and between 50 and 150 kilometres wide, and lies south of Honshu and north-east of Kyushu. With its surrounding islands it covers about 18,800 square kilometres. Mountains running east and west divide it into a narrow northern zone facing the Seto Inland Sea and a larger, sparsely populated southern part facing the Pacific Ocean. Mount Ishizuchi in Ehime, at 1,982 metres, is the highest mountain. The major river is the Yoshino, which runs 196 kilometres from near Mount Ishizuchi to the sea at the city of Tokushima. Unlike Japan's other main islands, Shikoku has no active volcanoes, although a major volcanic caldera near Mount Ishizuchi was active around 14 million years ago.

The island's ancient names include Iyo-no-futana-shima, Iyo-shima and Futana-shima. Its present name, meaning four provinces, refers to the four former provinces that make it up: Awa, Tosa, Sanuki and Iyo. Shikoku has historically been quite isolated and therefore kept the original characteristics of Japan for longer, especially in vegetation and some architectural techniques. Until the Great Seto Bridge network opened in 1988, the central part of the island was isolated from the rest of Japan.

Shikoku is known for a pilgrimage of 88 temples, established by the Heian-period Buddhist priest Kūkai, a native of present-day Zentsūji in Kagawa Prefecture. According to legend Kūkai still appears to pilgrims. Pilgrims wear white jackets bearing the characters dōgyō ninin, meaning two travelling together. Because of wheat production, Sanuki udon became an important part of the diet in Kagawa Prefecture, formerly Sanuki Province, in the Edo period.

Shikoku is the smallest of Japan's four main islands and has the smallest population, about 3.4 million. It consists of four prefectures: Ehime, Kagawa, Kōchi and Tokushima. Matsuyama, the capital of Ehime Prefecture, is the largest city, and most inhabitants live in the north. Three expressways, which together form the Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project, connect the island to Honshu. Annual festivals include the Awa Odori in Tokushima, held in August at the time of the Obon festival, and the Yosakoi festival in Kōchi.
shillong: Shillong lies in the middle of the Shillong Plateau, the only major uplifted structure in the northern Indian shield, and is surrounded by hills. Three of these are revered in Khasi tradition: Lum Sohpetbneng, Lum Diengiei and Lum Shyllong. The name comes from Lei Shyllong, a powerful deity believed to live on Shillong Peak, which overlooks the city. The city is about 100 kilometres from Guwahati by road, through hills and past Umiam Lake. Its climate is subtropical highland, with cool, very rainy summers and cool, dry winters. Its biggest market is Ïewduh.

During the First Anglo-Burmese War the British wanted a road connecting Sylhet and Assam across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. David Scott, an East India Company civil servant and agent of the governor-general for the North East Frontier, overcame opposition from the Khasi chiefs, the Syiems, and in 1829 negotiated with the Syiem of Sohra for a sanatorium for the British. In early 1829 a Khasi confederation rose against British occupation, but by January 1833 its leader, Tirot Sing, had surrendered to Scott and was detained in Dacca. The British disliked the climate and facilities of Sohra, also known as Cherrapunjee, and moved to Shillong, which took its name because the new town lay below Shillong Peak.

The British designated Shillong the civil station of the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in 1864. In 1874 a separate Chief Commissionership of Assam was formed with its seat at Shillong, chosen for its convenient position between the Brahmaputra and Surma valleys and for its much cooler climate. It included Sylhet, the Naga Hills, the Lushai Hills and the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills. A proclamation of 1878 made Shillong and its suburbs a station under the Bengal Municipal Act of 1876, with the villages of Mawkhar and Laban included by agreement with Haiñ Manik Syiem of Mylliem, dated 15 November 1878. An earthquake of 12 June 1897, of moment magnitude 8.1, killed 27 people in Shillong and destroyed much of the town.

Shillong was capital of undivided Assam under British rule and for 25 years in independent India. When the state of Meghalaya was created on 21 January 1972 it became the capital of Meghalaya, and Assam moved its capital to Dispur in Guwahati. It is the headquarters of the East Khasi Hills district. The rolling hills reminded the British of Scotland, so they called it the Scotland of the East.
shilluk-people: The Shilluk, who call themselves Chollo, are a major Luo Nilotic people living on the western bank of the White Nile in the Upper Nile state of South Sudan. They speak Dhøg Cøllø, which belongs to the Luo branch of the Western Nilotic subfamily, and they are the third-largest ethnic group of South Sudan after the Dinka and the Nuer. According to one account they formed their kingdom in 1454. Its king, the reth, came from the divine lineage of the culture hero Nyikang, who is believed to affect the nation's health.

The kingdom was historically a patriarchal monarchy, and society was somewhat hierarchical, with castes of royals, nobles, commoners and enslaved people. Today the Shilluk are governed by an elected headman chosen by a council of hamlet heads. Before the Second Sudanese Civil War the Shilluk also lived on the northern bank of the Sobat River, near where it joins the Nile.

Christian missions divided them: the Episcopal Church of Sudan dates its beginning to the late 19th century, when the Church Mission Society sent missionaries, the Catholic Church ran stations at Lul, Detwoc, Tonga and Yoynyang on the western bank, and the American Inland Mission ran one at Doleib Hill. The Shilluk were a minority in the Sudan People's Liberation Movement for most of the Second Sudanese Civil War.

In the summer of 2010 the Sudan People's Liberation Army, trying to disarm the people and stop a local Shilluk rebellion, burned several villages in the Shilluk Kingdom and killed an untold number of civilians. More than 10,000 people were displaced during the rainy season and fled into the forest, often without bedding, shelter or food, and many children died from hunger and cold. Violence began again in April 2011 with a crackdown on rebel-controlled regions, and broke out again in late 2022.

Most Shilluk are settled farmers, and both sexes do agricultural work. As among most Nilotic peoples, cattle-raising is a large part of the economy, though agriculture and fishing matter more than usual. Marriage involves bride-wealth, which traditionally included about ten head of cattle, several sheep and symbolic spears, although the amount depended on the groom's means. The ceremonies include a cattle exchange, a wedding feast at the bride's home and a symbolic mock battle between the families. Most Shilluk have converted to Christianity, some follow the traditional religion or a mixture of the two, and a few have converted to Islam.
shimabara-rebellion: Shimabara had been the domain of the Christian Arima clan, which was moved out in 1614 and replaced by the anti-Christian Matsukura. The new lord, Matsukura Shigemasa, hoped to rise in the shogunate by sponsoring costly projects, among them work on Edo Castle and a planned invasion of Luzon, and built a new castle at Shimabara. He placed a heavily disproportionate tax burden on his people and persecuted Christianity strictly, policies his heir Matsukura Katsuie continued. The Amakusa Islands suffered similar treatment under the Terasawa family, and the region held many unemployed samurai, former retainers of the Arima, Konishi and other houses.

Discontented rōnin and impoverished peasants plotted in secret, and the uprising broke out on 17 December 1637 with the assassination of the magistrate Hayashi Hyōzaemon. A charismatic 16-year-old, Amakusa Shirō, emerged as leader. The rebels besieged Tomioka and Hondo castles and Shimabara Castle but were forced back by armies from neighbouring Kyushu domains. They gathered at the ruins of Hara Castle, former seat of the Arima, and used weapons and provisions plundered from the Matsukura storehouses.

The shogunate's allied army, under Itakura Shigemasa, besieged Hara Castle. The swordsman Miyamoto Musashi was present as an adviser to Hosokawa Tadatoshi. The Dutch supplied gunpowder and cannon, and the ship de Ryp bombarded the castle before withdrawing. Itakura was killed in a failed advance and replaced by Matsudaira Nobutsuna. On 3 February 1638 a surprise attack killed 2,000 warriors of the Hizen Domain, but the castle's food and ammunition then ran out. Troops of the Kuroda clan stormed the outer defences on 12 April 1638, and the rebels were routed on 15 April.

The shogunate executed an estimated 37,000 rebels and sympathizers. Amakusa Shirō's head was displayed in Nagasaki, and Hara Castle was burned and buried with the dead. Katsuie was beheaded in Edo, the only daimyō decapitated in the Edo period, and Terasawa Katataka's lands were confiscated. Portuguese traders, suspected of helping the rebels, were expelled, and national seclusion was stricter by 1639. Christianity survived only underground.

Migrants from other parts of Japan resettled the peninsula, whose towns had lost most of their men, and every inhabitant was registered with a local temple.
