The rebellion is often portrayed as Christian, but the academic consensus is that it was driven chiefly by peasant anger at misgovernment, with Christians joining later. Apart from local peasant risings, it was the last large-scale armed clash in Japan until the Boshin War.
shimane-prefecture: Shimane Prefecture lies on the Sea of Japan side of the Chūgoku region of Honshu, with the Chūgoku Mountains to the south. It borders Yamaguchi, Hiroshima and Tottori prefectures. The mountains make the interior harder to live in, and over two thirds of the population lives along the coast. Rice is grown mostly on the Izumo plain. The Shimane peninsula encloses two brackish lakes, Lake Shinji and Nakaumi, and the Oki Islands off the coast also belong to the prefecture. The largest cities are Matsue, the capital, Izumo, Hamada and Masuda.

The history of Shimane begins with mythology. The Shinto god Ōkuninushi was believed to live in Izumo, an old province, and Izumo Shrine honours him. The area was divided into the provinces of Iwami, Izumo and Oki until the abolition of the han in 1871. In the Nara period Kakinomoto no Hitomaro wrote a poem on Shimane's nature when he was sent as governor. In the Kamakura period the shogunate exiled the emperors Go-Toba and Go-Daigo to Oki, and Go-Daigo escaped and rallied supporters against the shogunate.

In the Muromachi period the Kyōgoku clan controlled Izumo and Oki. After the Ōnin War the Amago clan expanded its power from Gassantoda Castle and the Masuda clan dominated Iwami. Many battles were fought between them for the silver of the Iwami Ginzan mine, which lay between their territories. Mōri Motonari conquered Izumo, Iwami and Oki in 1566. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, which the Mōri lost, Horio Yoshiharu entered Izumo and Oki and built Matsue Castle. In 1638 Matsudaira Naomasa, a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, became ruler because the Horio had no heir, and his family ruled until the han were abolished. The Iwami mine, under direct shogunate control, was one of the nation's largest silver mines by the early 17th century.

After the abolition of the han in 1871 the old Shimane and Hamada provinces formed the area of the present prefecture. Oki became part of Tottori that year, Hamada Prefecture was merged into Shimane in 1876, and the present border was formed in 1881.

Shimane is the second-least populous prefecture of Japan. Izumo-taisha, one of the oldest Shinto shrines in Japan, stands at Izumo, and Matsue Castle dates from the Tokugawa era. The Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine, with its cultural background, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Izumo-taisha main shrine and the Kamosu Shrine main shrine are National Treasures.
shimla: Shimla stands in the south-western ranges of the Himalayas at an average altitude of 2,206 metres, along a ridge with seven spurs. It stretches nearly 9.2 kilometres from east to west and lies within the historical cultural Mahasu region. The nearest river, the Sutlej, is about 21 kilometres away. According to one theory the name comes from Shyamalaya, a blue slate house on Jakhu Hill built by a fakir. According to another it comes from Shamli or Shyamala, the Hindu goddess Kali, whose temple is said to have stood on the Jakhu hillside.

In the 18th century most of the area was dense forest, with the Jakhu Temple, a few houses and nearby villages. Bhimsen Thapa of Nepal captured it in 1806, and the British East India Company took control under the Sugauli Treaty after the Anglo-Nepalese War, with David Ochterlony storming the fort of Malaun in May 1815. The surveying Gerard brothers described Shimla on 30 August 1817 as a middling-sized village.

In 1819 Lieutenant Ross built a wood cottage, and in 1822 Charles Pratt Kennedy built the first permanent house, Kennedy Cottage. In 1830 the British acquired the surrounding land from the chiefs of Keonthal and Patiala. The settlement grew from 30 houses in 1830 to 1,141 in 1881.

Officers came for the climate, which they found like Britain's. By the late 1830s the town had theatre and art exhibitions, and businessmen, mainly from the Sood and Parsi communities, arrived to supply the growing European population. Christ Church's foundation was laid on 9 September 1844. In 1863 the Viceroy John Lawrence decided to move the summer capital there, though it meant shifting the administration twice a year from Calcutta, over 1,600 kilometres away.

The Viceregal Lodge was later built on Observatory Hill. A fire cleared the Upper Bazaar, where the native Indian population lived, and its people were moved to the Middle and Lower Bazaars so that the east end could become the centre of the European town.

Shimla is the capital of Himachal Pradesh and its largest city. After partition it briefly served as capital of East Punjab until Chandigarh was built. Buildings of the colonial era in Tudorbethan and neo-Gothic styles survive, including the Viceregal Lodge and Christ Church, along with temples such as Jakhu Temple. The Kalka-Shimla Railway, built by the British, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The city hosted the Simla Deputation of 1906 and the Shimla Agreement of 1972.
shimonoseki: Shimonoseki is the westernmost point of Honshu and of Yamaguchi Prefecture. It borders the Sea of Japan to the west and the Seto Inland Sea to the south, across the Kanmon Straits. The city is long from north to south and fan-shaped, opening towards the Seto Inland Sea, and the Asa and Ariho rivers run through it. It was formerly called Bakan. Its climate is humid subtropical, with hot summers and cool winters, and it is nicknamed the home of fugu, for the pufferfish caught and cooked locally.

Shimonoseki was part of ancient Nagato Province and has prospered since ancient times as the gateway to Honshu from the Asian continent, including Kyushu, China and the Korean Peninsula. According to the Nihon Shoki, Emperor Chuai built a palace on the site of the present city hall in the Kofun period. The name appears in Heian period documents from 869 as the site of a checkpoint controlling maritime access to the Seto Inland Sea, although by the Kamakura period the name Akamanoseki was more common.

During the Genpei War the Heike and Genji fought the Battle of Dan-no-ura near the present Kanmon Bridge. In the Muromachi period the Ōuchi clan, shugo of both Nagato and Buzen in Kyushu, controlled trade and diplomatic missions from Ming China and Joseon Korea.

In the Edo period the area belonged to Chōfu Domain, ruled by the Mōri clan. In February 1691 the German explorer Engelbert Kaempfer visited the town during his two-year stay in Japan and described it as a major port for supplying ships, with around 400 to 500 houses. The Bombardment of Shimonoseki took place in 1864, and in 1895 the Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed, by which a defeated China handed over Taiwan, Penghu and Port Arthur to Japan. Akamagaseki city was established on 1 April 1889 under the modern municipal system and renamed Shimonoseki on 1 June 1902.

Shimonoseki is the largest city in Yamaguchi Prefecture. It has long had a thriving industry in shipping, trade and finance, and it remains the economic centre of the prefecture. It is the largest harvester of pufferfish in Japan. In 2005 it absorbed the towns of Hōhoku, Kikugawa, Toyota and Toyoura, and in the same year it was designated a core city with increased local autonomy. Universities in the city include Shimonoseki City University and the National Fisheries University.
shin-saimdang: Shin Saimdang was the third of five daughters of Shin Myeong-hwa, a government official of the Pyongsan Shin clan who was a friend of the scholar Cho Kwangjo but not politically active, and Lady Yi of the Yongin Yi clan. Her father lived largely apart from the family for 16 years in Hanseong while he prepared for the civil examinations, and he never went beyond the jinsa test.

Because her mother kept living with her own parents after marriage, she had more freedom in educating her daughters. Having no brothers, Saimdang received an education that would normally have been given to a son, learning the Thousand Character Classic from her father and studying Neo-Confucianism, history and literature, which surprised her father's visitors.

Her father chose Yi Won-su as her husband, although many thought it poor judgement, since his family was poor and he had no post. Shin Myeong-hwa put first a husband who would let her continue her art, and Yi Won-su did not object. She married him on 20 August 1522, at 17, and with his consent kept spending time at her parents' home in Gangneung. The couple had eight children, five boys and three girls, and at 33 she went back to Gangneung to give birth to her third son, Yi I.

Her paintings are known for delicate beauty, with insects, flowers, butterflies, orchids, grapes, fish and landscapes among her favourite themes. About 40 works in ink and stone colours remain, although many others may exist. Little of her calligraphy survives, but the scholar Eo Suk-kwon compared her grapes and landscapes to those of the artist Ahn Gyeon. In 1868 the governor of Gangneung remarked on her calligraphy as filled with nobility, elegance, serenity and purity.

Saimdang disapproved when her husband took up with a kisaeng named Kwon, and the couple's relationship cooled; she asked him not to remarry after her death. She died suddenly in 1551, aged 46, after moving to the Pyongan region. Her son Yi I had prayed daily for her recovery at the shrine of his maternal grandfather.

After her death Yi Won-su did not marry Kwon but brought her to live with the children, causing conflict with Yi I, who ran away from home. Her respectful nickname was Eojin, Wise Mother, and she is often held up as a model of Confucian ideals. Along with Queen Munjeong, Jeong Nan-jeong and Hwang Jin-yi she is considered one of the most significant women of the period.
shina-language: Shina, also known by its exonym Gilgiti, is an Indo-Aryan language of the Dardic branch of the Indo-European family. It is spoken primarily by the Shina people of northern Pakistan, in Gilgit-Baltistan and Kohistan. A small community of speakers lives in the Gurez valley of Jammu and Kashmir and the Dras valley of Ladakh in India. Related outliers include Brokskat in Ladakh, Kundal Shahi in Azad Kashmir, Palula and Sawi in Chitral and Kunar, Ushojo in the Swat Valley and Kalkoti in Dir.

Ethnologue estimated 1,146,000 speakers in Pakistan in 2018, most of them in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan. In Ladakh, the speakers in the far north of Kargil district numbered about 32,200 in the 2011 census, and in the Kashmir Valley Shina people form the majority in Gurez. Under the influence of Urdu and English, and the religious weight of Arabic and Persian, the language keeps adding loan words.

Shina words are often distinguished by three contrasting tones: level, rising and falling. The tone is heard only on long vowels. Where the stress falls on the first mora of a long vowel the tone is falling, and where it falls on the second mora the tone is rising. The word written the means the imperative Do! with a level tone, while Thée means Will you do? and Theé means after having done. There are five vowels, each short or long, and all but one can also be nasalised. In the dialects of Dras in India the original initial and final consonant clusters have been preserved, while those spoken in Pakistan have lost them.

Shina is one of the few Dardic languages with a written tradition, yet it was unwritten until a few decades ago and remains mostly spoken. Since the first attempts to represent its phonology accurately in the 1960s, several orthographies have been proposed. Debates have centred on how to write retroflex sounds absent from Urdu and whether to mark vowel length and tone. Only in the late 2010s was the orthography standardised, and primers and dictionaries endorsed by the government of Gilgit-Baltistan have been published. The alphabet is a Perso-Arabic one, developed by writers including Professor Muhammad Amin Ziya, Shakeel Ahmad Shakeel and Razwal Kohistani. Diacritics mark the rising and falling tones.
shinano-province: Shinano Province, also called Shinshu, was an old province of Japan that is now Nagano Prefecture. It bordered Echigo, Etchu, Hida, Kai, Kozuke, Mino, Mikawa, Musashi, Suruga and Totomi Provinces, and its ancient capital stood near modern Matsumoto, which became an important city of the province. The province consisted of sixteen districts, among them Azumi, Chiisagata, Chikuma, Hanishina, Minochi, Saku, Sarashina and Takai, together with the four districts of the former Suwa Province: Ina, Kamiina, Shimoina and Suwa. The Suwa Taisha was designated the chief Shinto shrine, the ichinomiya, of the province. The aircraft carrier Shinano of the Second World War was named after it.

In 713 the road across Mino and Shinano was widened to take the growing numbers of travellers through the Kiso District. In the Sengoku period the province was often split among fiefs, and castle towns such as Komoro, Ina and Ueda developed. Shinano was one of the main centres of Takeda Shingen's power in his wars with Uesugi Kenshin and others.

After Oda Nobunaga's assassination in the Honno-ji Incident, Shinano was contested between Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Go-Hojo clan of Odawara Castle. The Tokugawa, Uesugi and Hojo each hoped to seize Shinano, the Ueno region and Kai Province, which were then ruled by the remnants of the many small clans that had served the Takeda. The three-way conflict became known as the Tensho-Jingo War.

It turned in favour of the Tokugawa, helped by the defection of Sanada Masayuki to their side, and the Hojo negotiated a truce, sending Hojo Ujinobu while the Tokugawa sent Ii Naomasa to the preliminary meetings. In October representatives of the Oda clan, Oda Nobukatsu and Oda Nobutaka, and Toyotomi mediated until the truce was concluded.

In 1871 the han system was abolished and prefectures established. The former domains, among them Komoro, Ueda, Matsushiro, Suzaka, Iiyama, Suwa/Takashima, Iida and Matsumoto, were merged into Nagano, first called Nakano Prefecture in 1870, and Chikuma prefectures. When the prefectures were merged again in 1875/76, Chikuma was split, its western part covering Hida Province going to Gifu and its eastern part in Shinano to Nagano. Since then Nagano has been essentially contiguous with Shinano.
shingon-buddhism: The word shingon is the Japanese reading of the Chinese zhenyan, which translates the Sanskrit mantra. The Zhenyan lineage was founded in China in about the 7th and 8th centuries by Indian masters such as Śubhakarasiṃha, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra. Kūkai, born into the aristocratic Saeki clan in Shikoku, converted to Buddhism in his twenties and practised as an ascetic in the mountains. In 804 he went to Chang-an, where he studied under Huiguo, a student of Amoghavajra, and brought back many texts, mandalas and ritual items. In 809 he was allowed to reside at Takaosanji, now Jingo-ji, and under Emperor Saga's patronage he began to give esoteric initiations. He established his tradition on Mount Kōya, which remains its central pilgrimage centre.

Shingon teaches that buddhahood can be attained in this very body, through practices that use the three mysteries of mudra, mantra and mandala: gestures of the body, sacred formulas of speech and meditation of the mind. At its centre stands Mahāvairocana, or Dainichi, the universal Buddha who is the basis of all phenomena. Another influential doctrine is that all beings are originally enlightened. Practice depends on initiation by ordained masters. A central meditation is Ajikan, contemplation of the letter A in a white moon disk upon a lotus, and the goma fire ritual has roots in the Vedic homa.

After Kūkai, Tō-ji rose under Kangen to be the head temple, and Mount Kōya declined before recovering in the 11th century with the support of Fujiwara nobles such as Fujiwara no Michinaga. In 1615 Tokugawa Ieyasu issued regulations that brought the school into the administrative temple system. After the Meiji Restoration the state separated Shinto from Buddhism, and many Shingon temples closed after confiscations of land. In 1941 the schools were forcibly merged, and after the war they separated again. About eighteen major schools now exist. Shingon influenced Tendai, Shugendo, Shinto and the ritual repertoire of Soto Zen, and shaped medieval Japanese aesthetics and art.
shining-path: The Shining Path, officially the Communist Party of Peru, was founded in 1969 by Abimael Guzmán, a former university philosophy professor whom his followers called Presidente Gonzalo, together with 11 others. Guzmán was heavily influenced by a trip to China and admired Mao Zedong. Its common name comes from a maxim of Mariátegui: Marxism–Leninism will open the shining path to revolution.

From 1970 to 1977 it built a student organization and regional committees in Lima and the central sierra. It first gained a foothold at San Cristóbal of Huamanga University in Ayacucho, where Guzmán taught, and between 1973 and 1975 controlled the student councils at the universities of Huancayo and La Cantuta.

By 1980 it had about 500 members. When Peru's military government allowed elections for the first time in twelve years, the Shining Path declined to take part and began a guerrilla war in the highlands of the Ayacucho Region. On 17 May 1980, on the eve of the presidential elections, it burned ballot boxes in the town of Chuschi, its first act of war. Through the 1980s it grew in territory and militants, particularly in the Andean highlands, gaining some peasant sympathy by filling a political gap left by the central government and offering what it called popular justice: public trials with swift sentences, including public executions.

The government's response was initially tepid. On 29 December 1981 it declared an emergency zone in Ayacucho, Huancavelica and Apurímac and let the military detain any suspect. The military abused this power, arresting many innocent people and subjecting some to torture and rape.

On 12 September 1992 the Special Intelligence Group captured Guzmán and several leaders in an apartment above a dance studio in Lima. The leadership vacuum was large, and the organization suffered defeats from rural self-defence organizations of campesinos, supposedly its social base. When Guzmán called for peace talks, it split between those for and those against them.

The party was designed on a concentric model, with Communist Party organs at the centre, the paramilitary wing around them and the political wing on the outside, so that the party controlled both. Its ideology moved from Marxism–Leninism–Mao Zedong thought to Marxism–Leninism–Maoism–Gonzalo thought, and some authors see a cult of personality around Guzmán.

It has been widely condemned for brutality against peasants, as in the Lucanamarca massacre, and against trade unionists, rival Marxist groups and elected officials. The Asháninka minority suffered disproportionately, with about 6,000 killed, over 10% of their 1993 population.
shinsengumi: Japan's forced opening to the West in 1854 increased internal instability, and loyalists, particularly in the Chōshū Domain, began to rebel in Kyoto in the name of sonnō jōi, 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'. In response the Tokugawa shogunate formed the Rōshigumi on 19 October 1862, a squad of 234 rōnin drawn from the sword schools of Edo, to protect the 14th shōgun, Tokugawa Iemochi, on a journey to Kyoto to meet Emperor Kōmei. The squad's leader, Kiyokawa Hachirō, who was loyal to the emperor, planned to gather other rōnin to police the city, and when this scheme came out the squad was ordered back to Edo.

Nineteen members, mainly from the Mito clan, stayed in Kyoto and formed the Mibu Rōshigumi. On 18 August 1863 Matsudaira Katamori, who had judged that the mission should become patrolling Kyoto's streets in the name of the Tokugawa bakufu, renamed it the Shinsengumi, meaning Newly Selected Corps.

Early on there was internal strife. Matsudaira Katamori ordered the killing of the erratic Serizawa Kamo, and in October 1863 Hijikata Toshizō led a group that assassinated him. On 8 July 1864, in the Ikedaya incident, thirty Shinsengumi suppressed a cell of twenty Chōshū revolutionaries, possibly preventing the burning of Kyoto; the incident led to soldiers enlisting in the squad.

In January 1868 they fought for the shogunate at the Battle of Toba–Fushimi. Reformed as the Kōyō Chinbutai, they lost the Battle of Kōshū-Katsunuma on 29 March 1868. Kondō was captured by Imperial forces and beheaded on 17 May 1868. Hijikata went on to fight at Aizu and, in December 1868, joined the Republic of Ezo in the north. He was killed by a gunshot at the Battle of Hakodate on 20 June 1869, and the last commander, Sōma Kazue, surrendered with the survivors three days later.

At its peak the Shinsengumi had about 300 members. It was the first samurai group of the Tokugawa era to admit people from non-samurai classes such as farmers and merchants, though it is a misconception that most members were of those classes: of 106 members whose origins are recorded, 87 were samurai. Its code, created by Hijikata Toshizō, had five articles, forbidding deviation from the samurai code, leaving the group, raising money privately, taking part in others' litigation and engaging in private fights. The penalty for breaking any rule was seppuku. Its first uniform was a light-blue haori with white mountain stripes. After about a year the corps appears to have adopted an all-black uniform instead.
shinto: Shinto has no single founder, no canonical text and no central authority, so beliefs and practices vary widely. One proposed broad definition is that Shinto is a belief in kami, the supernatural beings that practitioners hold to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent places. They are not regarded as omnipotent, omniscient or necessarily immortal, and the dead may become kami. Kami are worshipped at household shrines called kamidana and at public shrines called jinja, where priests known as kannushi offer food and drink. Shinto stresses ritual over doctrine, and above all purity: humans are seen as fundamentally pure, and pollution, or kegare, is a temporary condition removed by rites of purification.

Kami veneration has been traced back to the Yayoi period, from 300 BCE to 250 CE, when bronze bells, weapons and mirrors seem to have played a role in ritual. Historians debate when it is suitable to speak of Shinto as a distinct religion. Buddhism reached Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread quickly, and the two merged so closely, in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō, that kami came to be seen as part of Buddhist cosmology.

The earliest written tradition of kami worship is in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, which were commissioned by ruling elites to legitimise and consolidate their rule. They describe a universe in three parts: the Plane of High Heaven, where the kami live, the world of humans, and the Nether World. Although never of great importance to Japanese religious life, their accounts were proclaimed factual by the government in the early 20th century.

Japan has around 100,000 public shrines, about 80,000 of them affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines, which shrines formed in 1946. Festivals, called matsuri, mark the seasons of the agricultural year and give thanks to the kami, while rites of passage include a child's first visit to a shrine and weddings. Shinto was formally separated from the state during the U.S. occupation after World War II. A new constitution separated religion from the state, and the emperor declared that he was not a kami.

Numerically Shinto is the largest religion in Japan, with Buddhism second, but most people take part in both. Many Japanese say they have no religion, partly because they dislike the connotations of the Japanese word shūkyō, which suggests sect doctrine. Aspects of Shinto have been taken into new religious movements such as Tenrikyo and Oomoto.
shiraz: Shiraz is the capital of Fars province, historically known by the exonym Persia proper. It lies in a green plain at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 1,500 metres above sea level, and has been a regional trade centre for over a thousand years. The earliest reference to the city, as Tiraziš, is on Elamite clay tablets dated to 2000 BCE, and tablets from the Persepolis treasury archives mention major workshops there. The name became Old Persian Širājiš and then the modern Persian Shirāz.

The Arab Muslim army conquered Fars in expeditions between 640 and 653 and captured the area around Shiraz in 641. Because the Sasanian capital Istakhr was deeply associated with the Sasanian Empire and the Zoroastrian religion, the Arabs sought to establish a rival cultural and administrative centre in nearby Shiraz. It was founded or restored in 693 by Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, brother of the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, or by the latter's kinsman Muhammad ibn Qasim. In the 13th century it became a leading centre of the arts and letters, through its ruler's encouragement and the presence of Persian scholars and artists.

Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty, captured Shiraz in 1504. After the fall of the Safavids the city declined, and a revolt of its governor against Nader Shah ended with a siege of many months and a sack. By Nader Shah's murder in 1747 most of its historical buildings were damaged or ruined, and its population had fallen to 50,000, a quarter of that in the 16th century. Karim Khan, de facto ruler of Iran from 1760 until 1779, made Shiraz his capital.

Shiraz is the fifth-most-populous city of Iran, with 1,995,500 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It is known as the city of poets, gardens, wine, nightingales and flowers. Hafez and Saadi were born there, and their tombs lie on the north side of the present city. The Eram garden is among its old gardens, and the Arg of Karim Khan, the citadel, stands beside the Vakil Bazaar and Vakil Bath. Shiraz has historically had major Jewish and Christian communities.
shirkuh: Asad al-Dīn Shīrkūh was a Kurdish commander who served the Zengid dynasty and then the Fatimid Caliphate. He was the uncle of Saladin, and his efforts in Egypt were a key factor in establishing the Ayyubid dynasty there. His name may mean the mountain lion, and his honorific Asad ad-Din means the lion of faith. Latin writers called him Siraconus.

He came from a Kurdish village in Armenia near the city of Dvin, the son of the Kurdish chief Shadhi ibn Marwan and brother of Najm ad-Din Ayyub, ancestor of the Ayyubid dynasty. When the last Shaddadid was deposed in Dvin in 1130 the family moved to Baghdad and then to Tikrit, where Shadhi was made governor. In 1138 Shirkuh killed a man he was quarrelling with in Tikrit, and the brothers were exiled; Saladin was supposedly born the night they left. They entered Zengid service, and Shirkuh received Homs, ar-Rahba and other appanages. In 1154 the brothers negotiated the surrender of Damascus to Nur ad-Din.

In 1163 Shawar asked Nur ad-Din to intervene in Egypt in his dispute with Dirgham over the Fatimid vizierate. Nur ad-Din sent Shirkuh, with a grant of 200,000 dinars and 2,000 soldiers chosen from his regiments, in the first of three ventures into Egypt; Saladin went as his advisor. Shawar was restored and Dirgham killed, but Shawar quarrelled with Shirkuh and allied with Amalric I of Jerusalem, who besieged Shirkuh at Bilbeis in 1164. Nur ad-Din meanwhile attacked the Crusader states and almost captured the Principality of Antioch.

The Fatimid caliph al-Adid invited Shirkuh back in 1167 to help defeat the Crusaders attacking Cairo. Shawar again allied with Amalric, who besieged Shirkuh in Alexandria until he agreed to leave. A Crusader garrison stayed in Egypt, and Amalric allied with the Byzantine Empire. Shawar switched sides to Shirkuh, and after a pitched battle the Crusaders retreated. In January 1169 Shirkuh entered Cairo, was welcomed by al-Adid, and had Shawar executed.

Shirkuh accepted the office of vizier but died two months later, in March 1169, of a severe quinsy, according to Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, who says he was given to rich meats and suffered many bouts of indigestion. His nephew Saladin succeeded him as vizier and from 1174 also succeeded Nur ad-Din, uniting Egypt and Syria. Some historians hold that Shirkuh's death helped Saladin consolidate his position as undisputed head of the Ayyubid family. In 1179 Saladin gave Homs to Shirkuh's son Muhammad, whose descendants ruled it until 1263.
shiva: The name Shiva means auspicious, propitious or gracious. In the Rig Veda (c. 1700 to 1100 BCE) the word is an adjective applied to several deities, among them Rudra, a fearsome god of the roaring storm. Shiva is associated with Rudra, and the Hindu scriptures treat the two as the same figure. The Shiva of later Hinduism is, however, regarded as an amalgamation of various older Vedic and non-Vedic deities into a single god, a process linked to the Hindu synthesis of post-Vedic times. How this composite figure formed is not well documented and has attracted much speculation.

Some authors have read Mesolithic rock paintings at Bhimbetka as depictions of Shiva, but Howard Morphy holds that in context they more probably show hunting parties with animals. The Yajurveda gives both terrifying (rudra) and benign (shiva) attributes, and later texts such as the Atharvashiras Upanishad declare that all gods are Rudra.

For Shaivas, the followers of Shaivism, Shiva is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects and transforms the universe. In the Shakta tradition the Goddess is the equal and complementary partner of Shiva. Within the Trimurti he is the destroyer or transformer beside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, though ancient and medieval texts also contain many triads that do not include him.

Shiva is a god of ambiguity: fierce and benevolent, an ascetic yogi on Kailasa and a householder with his wife Parvati and their children Ganesha and Kartikeya. His attributes include the third eye, with which he burned Kama, desire, to ashes, the crescent moon in his hair, the river Ganga flowing from his matted locks and the trident. He is shown as Nataraja, Lord of Dance, and is usually worshipped in the aniconic form of the linga, which the Linga Purana presents as the manifested sign of the signless.

Shiva is revered across India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Indonesia, especially Java and Bali, where he is known as Batara Guru, a spiritual teacher blended with local spirits and heroes. His worship spread in Central Asia under the Kushan and Hephthalite empires, and wall paintings from Penjikent in Sogdia show him with a halo, a sacred thread and a tiger skin.

The Siva Sutta shows him conversing with the Buddha, and he appears as Mahakala in Vajrayana, as Maheshvara in Mahayana and as Ishana in Theravada Buddhism, in most forms ranked below Mahabrahma or Sakra. The Japuji Sahib of the Guru Granth Sahib names Shiva beside Vishnu and Brahma.
shivaji: Shivaji was born in the hill fort of Shivneri near Junnar, now in Pune district, and was named after a local deity, the goddess Shivai Devi. Scholars disagree on his date of birth. He belonged to the Bhonsle family. His father Shahaji served as a chieftain in the Maratha uplands under the Sultanate of Bijapur, hoping for rewards of jagir land, and Shahaji's campaigns against the Mughals were generally unsuccessful.

In 1647 the 16-year-old Shivaji captured Torna Fort, by stratagem or bribery, while the Bijapur court was in confusion, and used the treasure found there to build Rajgad, which served as his seat for over a decade. In 1657 Bijapur sent the veteran general Afzal Khan to arrest him. After Shivaji defeated forces sent against him, Siddi Jauhar besieged him at Panhala in 1660. Shivaji escaped by night, and at the pass of Ghod Khind the sardar Baji Prabhu Deshpande and 300 soldiers volunteered to fight to the death to hold back the pursuers.

Until 1657 Shivaji kept peaceful relations with the Mughal Empire, then raided its Deccan territory. After his defeat by Jai Singh I at Purandar he entered Mughal vassalage. In 1666 Aurangzeb summoned him to Agra, where he took offence at being made to stand among low-ranking nobles and was placed under house arrest, and he later escaped. Peace followed until 1670, when Shivaji recovered much of the territory he had surrendered.
In 1674 he was formally crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad Fort despite opposition from local Brahmins, a title that gave him a legal basis to rule and set him above other Maratha leaders.

Shivaji set up the Ashta Pradhan Mandal, a council of eight ministers who advised him on political and administrative matters. At his court Marathi replaced Persian, his royal seal was engraved in Sanskrit, and in 1677 his official Raghunath Pandit produced the Rājavyavahārakośa, a thesaurus of state usage. He employed people of all castes and religions, including Muslims and Europeans, and many commentators regard his religious policies as tolerant.

His army was small but effective, built on Maratha and Kunbi peasants. He avoided pitched battles against the heavy Mughal cavalry and used guerrilla tactics, known in Marathi as Ganimi Kawa, cutting supply lines and luring enemies into hills and jungle. Hill forts were central to his strategy: the historian Jadunath Sarkar counted some 240–280 at his death, each held by three officers of equal status so that no single traitor could hand it over.
shkoder: Shkodër extends over the Mbishkodra Plain between Lake Shkodër and the foothills of the Albanian Alps, on a hill where the lake drains into the Buna. It is bounded by the Kir to the east, the Drin to the south and the Buna to the west. Lake Shkodër, the largest lake in southern Europe, forms the frontier between Albania and Montenegro. The city has been continuously inhabited since the Early Bronze Age and has roughly 2,200 years of recorded history. Its ancient name Skodra, in Latin Scodra, is certainly pre-Roman, and the forms Scutari and Skadar later spread in Italian, English and Serbo-Croatian.

An urban settlement called Skodra was founded in the 4th century BCE by the Illyrian tribe of the Labeatae. It became the capital of the Illyrian kingdom under the Ardiaei and Labeatae. The Romans annexed and sacked it after the third Illyrian War in 168 BCE, when King Gentius was defeated. In the 3rd century CE it became the capital of Praevalitana under Diocletian's reform, and in the 4th century the Archdiocese of Scodra was founded.

In the Middle Ages the city passed among Byzantines, Serbian rulers of Zeta and the Balšić family, who surrendered it to the Republic of Venice in 1396 as a protection against the Ottomans. Mehmed II laid siege to it in 1478 and 1479; an agreement between Venice and the Ottomans ended the siege, letting the citizens leave unharmed. It then became the seat of the Ottoman Sanjak of Scutari. From 1757 to 1831 it was the centre of the pashalik of the Bushati family, and in the later 19th century the centre of a vilayet and a trading hub with over 3,500 shops.

The city was important in the Albanian national movement. After the Balkan Wars Montenegro left it to the new Albania in May 1913. Under the communist regime the Shkodër Bazaar and the port on the Buna were demolished.

Shkodër is regarded as the traditional capital of northern Albania and the centre of Roman Catholicism in Albania, with the Metropolitan Archdiocese of Shkodër-Pult. Its mosques and churches reflect its religious diversity. Rozafa Castle, linked to a legend of a woman who sacrificed herself so it could be built, and the Marubi National Museum of Photography are among its landmarks.
shkumbin: The Shkumbin is 181.4 km long and drains a basin of 2,444 square kilometres. It rises in the eastern Valamara Mountains of south-eastern Albania, between Maja e Valamarës and Gur i Topit, and runs north through Proptisht and Qukës in many deep gorges and canyons. It then flows inside a syncline between the Mokra and Shebenik mountains to the east and the Polis mountains to the west. Near Librazhd it turns about 50 km west of its source and joins the Rapun stream, crosses the Myzeqe Plain and forms a small delta in the Karavasta Lagoon, close to the Adriatic Sea.

The name comes from the Latin Scampinus, also recorded as Scampis, which replaced the Illyrian name of the river, Genusus. A Slavic origin has been rejected. The Latin name entered Proto-Albanian as a loanword, which fits the existence of a large Roman town near present-day Elbasan that gave the river its new name.

In antiquity several Illyrian peoples lived in the valley. The Parthini held the middle valley. To their west lived the Taulantii, on the coast and in the lower valley, and to their east the Dassaretii, around Lake Ohrid and in the upper valley.

The Via Egnatia followed the river and made it a strategically important corridor between east and west. The road began in two branches, a northern one from Epidamnos and a southern one from Apollonia, which converged at Ad Quintum near modern Elbasan and continued east through the Shkumbin valley. In Roman imperial times the boundary between the provinces of Illyricum and Epirus Nova ran roughly along the valley, which also formed approximately the border between the Latin and Greek-speaking areas.

The river is roughly the geographical dividing line between the Tosk and Gheg dialects of Albanian, with Gheg spoken north of it and Tosk south. The dialect split occurred after the Christianisation of the region in the 4th century CE, and the river is the historic dialectal boundary, which runs along the Jireček line.
shoghi-effendi: Shoghi Effendi was related to the Báb through his father, Mírzá Hádí Shírází, and to Baháʼu'lláh through his mother, Ḍíyáʼíyyih Khánum, the eldest daughter of ʻAbdu'l-Bahá. As his eldest grandson he had a special relationship with ʻAbdu'l-Bahá, who gave him much of his early training and taught him prayers. Private tutors taught him Arabic, Persian, French, English and literature at home. From 1907 to 1909 he attended the Jesuit College des Frères in Haifa, and he later studied in Beirut, at a Jesuit school and then at the Syrian Protestant College. From the end of 1918 he was ʻAbdu'l-Bahá's full-time secretary and translator.

In 1920 Shoghi Effendi went to Balliol College, Oxford, to study political science and economics. ʻAbdu'l-Bahá died on 28 November 1921, news that reached him as a shock, since he had not known his grandfather was ill. He returned to Haifa on 29 December 1921, and the Will and Testament of ʻAbdu'l-Bahá, read then, named him Guardian of the Baháʼí Faith. He was 24. With his Western education and dress, his style differed from that of his grandfather. He signed his letters "your true brother", stressed the institution rather than himself, and led largely by correspondence. On 24 March 1937 he married Mary Maxwell, a Canadian, entitled Rúhíyyih Khánum.

He organised the administration of the Baháʼí World Centre, which needed secretarial help for a growing correspondence, and set up a Baháʼí Bureau in Geneva to represent the community at international bodies. The number of localities with Baháʼís rose from 1,034 in 1935, when the first plan began, to 2,700 in 1953, when he launched a ten-year global crusade. The faith spread widely in parts of Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, India, Southeast Asia and the Pacific islands. He judged that the Universal House of Justice could be elected only after national spiritual assemblies existed.

Shoghi Effendi wrote in English and Persian. As authorised interpreter, he gave the meaning of the words of Baháʼu'lláh and ʻAbdu'l-Bahá, and Baháʼís regard his interpretations as authoritative. His translations include the Hidden Words in 1929, the Kitáb-i-Íqán in 1931, Gleanings in 1935, Epistle to the Son of the Wolf in 1941 and the historical text The Dawn-Breakers. His longer letters include World Order of Baháʼu'lláh, Advent of Divine Justice and Promised Day is Come.

He insisted that no Guardian should be regarded as equal to ʻAbdu'l-Bahá or as a holy person, and asked that his birthday not be marked. He died in London on 4 November 1957, and is buried at New Southgate Cemetery. After his death the Hands of the Cause led the faith until the Universal House of Justice was first elected in 1963.
shogun: Shōgun is short for sei-i taishōgun, a title meaning commander-in-chief of the expeditionary force against the barbarians. The barbarians in question were the Emishi, tribes of northern Japan who resisted the governance of the imperial court at Kyoto. In the early Heian period the title was given to commanders for the length of a campaign. Sakanoue no Tamuramaro (758–811), who brought the Emishi lands of Mutsu and Dewa under the Yamato state, is generally recognised as the first shogun, although sources also name Ōtomo no Otomaro and Tajihi no Agatamori. In this early period shoguns held no real political power, and the Fujiwara clan controlled the court.

When Minamoto no Yoritomo gained ascendancy over Japan in 1185, the title was revived to regularise his position. He established a system based at Kamakura in which the samurai gained some political powers, while the emperor and aristocracy remained the rulers in law. Emperor Go-Toba awarded him the title in 1192. The Hōjō clan, the family of Yoritomo's wife, then took power from the Kamakura shoguns. Ashikaga Takauji was awarded the title in 1338 and established the Ashikaga shogunate, which nominally lasted until 1573.

Tokugawa Ieyasu was given the title in 1603 and set up the Tokugawa shogunate at Edo, now Tokyo. Fifteen Tokugawa shoguns ruled the Edo period, which ended in 1867 when Tokugawa Yoshinobu relinquished the office to Emperor Meiji in the Meiji Restoration.

The shogun's officials were known as the bakufu, tent government, a term that recalled the shogun's role as field commander and suggested an office meant to be temporary. The shogun held civil, military, diplomatic and judicial authority and in theory served the emperor, who acted as chief priest of Shinto. No shogun tried to usurp the throne, partly because the shogun's authority was held to come from the emperor and partly because of a tradition that traced the imperial line from the age of the gods. During parts of the Kamakura and Sengoku periods the shoguns were figureheads. The shogunate lasted nearly 700 years.
shoshenq-i: Shoshenq I was the son of Nimlot A, Great Chief of the Ma, and Tentsepeh A, the daughter of another Great Chief of the Ma, and was of Meshwesh ancestry. His uncle Osorkon the Elder, also a Meshwesh, had served on the throne as regent during the preceding 21st Dynasty, so his rise was not wholly unexpected. Under Psusennes II he was chief adviser to the king and Commander-in-Chief of the army, and he held his father's title of Great Chief of the Ma, the Egyptian word for the ancient Libyans. His son Osorkon I married Psusennes II's daughter Maatkare B. His ancestors had settled in Egypt in the late New Kingdom, probably at Herakleopolis Magna, though Manetho claims he came from Bubastis.

Libyan ideas of rule allowed related leaders to hold power side by side, and Shoshenq used this to consolidate control. He ended the hereditary succession of the high priesthood of Amun and appointed men to it, most often his own sons. His eldest son, Osorkon I, was chosen as his successor; his second, Iuput A, became High Priest of Amun at Thebes, Governor of Upper Egypt and Commander of the Army; and his third, Nimlot B, became leader of the army at Herakleopolis. A quarry inscription at Gebel el-Silsila dated to his twenty-first year records stone being cut for a great pylon and festival hall at Karnak to celebrate his first campaign of victory.

Late in his reign he pursued an aggressive foreign policy. A statue base from Byblos and a fragment of a stela from Megiddo bear his name, and the Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists conquered places in Syria, Philistia, Phoenicia, the Negev and Israel, among them Megiddo, Taanach and Shechem. It is the first military action outside Egypt formally commemorated for several centuries. He is generally presumed to be the Shishak of the Hebrew Bible, who took treasure from the temple at Jerusalem in the fifth year of Rehoboam, but the Karnak list does not include Jerusalem, and scholars offer different explanations for the gap.

Shoshenq I reigned for 21 years and was succeeded by Osorkon I. His tomb has not been found. A canopic chest of unknown origin was given to the Egyptian Museum of Berlin in 1891, and Egyptologists have suggested that he was buried at Tanis, at Bubastis or at the temple of Ptah at Memphis. The dates of his reign are disputed. Kenneth Kitchen's conventional dates are 945 to 924 BCE, while an astronomical reading of the Dakhla stela by Rolf Krauss gives his first year as 943 BCE, the date now often used.
shoshone: The Shoshone, who call themselves Newe, meaning People, have four large cultural and linguistic divisions: the Eastern Shoshone of Wyoming, the Northern Shoshone of southern Idaho, the Western Shoshone of California, Nevada and northern Utah, and the Goshute of western Utah and eastern Nevada. Their name comes from Sosoni, a word for high-growing grasses, and some neighbouring tribes call them Grass House People. Early American explorers and neighbouring tribes sometimes called them the Snake Indians. Meriwether Lewis recorded them in 1805 as the Sosonees or snake Indians. They originated in the western Great Basin and spread north and east into present-day Idaho and Wyoming.

By 1500 some Eastern Shoshone had crossed the Rocky Mountains onto the Great Plains. As one of the first northern tribes to adopt horses and firearms for hunting and warfare, the Shoshone became a dominant power, and another branch moved as far south as Texas, emerging as the Comanche by 1700. After 1750 their advantage diminished, and pressure from the Blackfoot, Crow, Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho pushed the Eastern Shoshone back towards the Rocky Mountains, until the Shoshone Reservation was established on the Wind River in the 1860s.

As settlers moved west, wars occurred throughout the second half of the 19th century. The Northern Shoshone, led by Chief Pocatello, fought settlers in Idaho in the 1860s. In the Bear River Massacre of 1863, United States forces killed an estimated 250 Northwestern Shoshone at their winter encampment in present-day Franklin County, Idaho, many of them non-combatants, including children; 21 soldiers also died. It was the largest loss of life the Shoshone suffered at the hands of United States forces. The Northern and Western Shoshone, allied with the Bannock, fought in the Snake War of 1864 to 1868 and the Bannock War of 1878. The Eastern Shoshone under Chief Washakie allied with the American government and secured treaties at Fort Bridger in 1863 and 1868.

Shoshone people are divided into traditional bands based on both homeland and main food source, with names such as Salmon Eaters on the Lemhi and Snake rivers, Mountain Sheep Eaters, Jack Rabbit Eaters and Pinenut Eaters. Their language, Shoshoni, belongs to the Central Numic branch of the Uto-Aztecan family; about 1,000 people speak it, from central Nevada to central Wyoming. Reservations include Wind River in Wyoming, shared with the Northern Arapaho, Fort Hall in Idaho, and the Duck Valley and Goshute reservations. Sacagawea (1788–1812), a Lemhi Shoshone, guided the Lewis and Clark Expedition.
shota-rustaveli: Almost nothing is known about Rustaveli from contemporary sources. In the prologue of his poem the poet calls himself a certain Rustveli. This is not a surname but a territorial epithet, meaning of or holder of Rustavi, though a 10th-century manuscript fragment found in 1975 at Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai attests its use as a cognomen by a noble house of Ru(i)staveli. Georgian authors of the 15th to 18th centuries are more informative and almost unanimously name him Shota Rustaveli.

Both folk tradition and the 17th-century royal poet Archil II make him a native of Meskheti in southern Georgia, where his home village of Rustavi lay. A legend says he was educated at the academies of Gelati and Ikalto and then in Greece, meaning the Byzantine Empire. He knew Persian well enough to read its poetry without translations and may have composed Persian verse.

Rustaveli wrote The Knight in the Panther's Skin, regarded as the national epic of Georgia. He must have composed it no earlier than the 1180s and no later than the first decade of the 13th century, most probably in 1205 to 1207. The poem is set in a fictional India and Arabia, and events in those distant lands are read as an allegory of the rule of Queen Tamar and the size and glory of the Kingdom of Georgia in its Golden Age.

The poem was first printed in 1712 in Tbilisi. Two folios from the 16th century and some lines from the 14th century are kept at the Georgian National Center of Manuscripts in Tbilisi. All other known copies date from the 17th century.

A name preserved on a fresco and in a document from the former Georgian Monastery of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem identifies Shota as a sponsor of the monastery and a high treasurer, which echoes a popular legend that he served at Tamar's court and retired to the monastery in old age. The fresco, the only known contemporary portrait, was described by the Georgian pilgrim Timote Gabashvili in 1757 and rediscovered by Georgian scholars in 1960. It was defaced in 2004 and has since been restored.

The highest Georgian state prize for art and literature bears his name, as do Rustaveli Avenue in Tbilisi and many other landmarks. The Hungarian painter Mihály Zichy made the illustrations most often used in editions of the poem.
shravanabelagola: Shravanabelagola lies in the Channarayapatna taluk of Hassan district, about 51 km south-east of Hassan and 144 km from Bengaluru. Its sacred places are spread over two hills, Chandragiri and Vindhyagiri, and among the villages at their foot. The name means "white pond of the Shravana", with the pond referring to a pool in the middle of the town. A tradition holds that a pious old woman anointed the great image with milk she carried in a gullakayi, an eggplant, which gives a second derivation of the name.

Tradition says that Acharya Bhadrabahu and his pupil Chandragupta Maurya meditated here, and that Chandragupta died on Chandragiri in 298 BCE after becoming a Jain monk. Chandragiri also holds memorials to monks and lay followers who meditated there from the fifth century CE. Hundreds of inscriptions have been found at the town, from about 600 to 1830 CE, written in Kannada. They mention the Western Ganga dynasty, the Rashtrakutas, the Hoysala Empire and the Vijayanagara Empire, and B. Lewis Rice devoted the second volume of Epigraphia Carnatica to them.

On Vindhyagiri stands the monolithic statue of Gommateshwara, 17.37 metres high. A Prakrit inscription at its base praises the king who paid for it and his general Chavundaraya, who is said to have erected it for his mother. Nearby the Tyagada Brahmadeva Pillar, about 2.3 metres tall, was commissioned by Chamundaraya. Among the temples are the Chamundaraya Basadi on Chandragiri, dedicated to the 22nd Tirthankara Neminatha, and in the town the Akkana Basadi of 1181 and the Bhandari Basadi, built in 1159 under the Hoysala king Narasimha I.

The Mahamastakabhisheka, the great anointing of the statue, takes place every twelve years, with milk, sugarcane juice, saffron paste and powders of sandalwood, turmeric and vermilion. It was last held in February 2018, and past ceremonies were attended by figures such as Krishna-Rajendra Wodeyar in 1910 and Jawaharlal Nehru in 1951. The town is the seat of an old Bhattaraka Matha of the Digambara tradition. The Archaeological Survey of India lists the statue, several basadis and the inscriptions as Adarsh Smarak monuments.
shravasti: Shravasti, in Pali Savatthi, is a town in Shravasti district of Uttar Pradesh, near the Rapti river and the Nepalese border. As the capital of Kosala it stood at the junction of three major trading routes. Archaeologists call the site Saheth-Maheth: Saheth, the smaller part, holds the Jetavana monuments, and Maheth is the walled complex inside a damaged mud fort, less than 2 kilometres away. The Bhagavata Purana says a king named Shravasta of the Ikshvaku dynasty built the city, and Jain and Ajivika texts know it as Saravana, Kunalnagari and Chandrikapuri.

Buddhist sources are the fullest. According to Woodward, 871 suttas in the four Nikayas are set in Shravasti, and the texts say the Buddha spent twenty-five rainy seasons there. It was the home of King Prasenajit, the Buddha's royal patron, and of the donor Anathapindada, who offered the Jetavana grove. The Buddha is remembered for performing the great miracle and the twin miracle there. The commentator Buddhaghosa gave the city 5.7 million residents, a figure that is implausible, though it reflects a memory of a large and prosperous capital.

Jain texts name it as the birthplace of the Tirthankaras Sambhavanatha and Chandraprabha and say Mahavira spent a rainy season there. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian visited around 399 CE. By the time of Xuanzang, the capital was desolate, with over a hundred monasteries, many in ruins, and the remains of Prasenajit's palace and the stupa of Angulimala. An inscription of the Vikram year 1176 shows the site was an active Buddhist centre until the early 12th century, and it was destroyed and covered with mounds in or after the 13th century.

Alexander Cunningham identified the site in 1863 and began clearing it in 1876. Hoey excavated in 1885, and around 1908 Vogel confirmed that Sahet-Mahet was the ancient Shravasti. Marshall and Sahni followed in 1910, and Sinha excavated in 1959, finding that the walls were built and repaired between the 3rd century BCE and about the 1st century CE.

Japanese archaeologists under Yoshinori Aboshi worked there for nine seasons between 1986 and 1996, using carbon dating. They found an earthen rampart about 5.2 kilometres around enclosing 160 hectares, layers from the 8th century BCE onward, a large bathing tank and repeated flood damage. Thick layers of charcoal showed that monastic complexes were burnt down together. Today the Jetavana site is the main pilgrim destination, and monasteries from Thailand, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Tibet and China stand nearby.
shrewsbury: Shrewsbury is a market town on the River Severn, about 9 miles (14 km) east of the border between England and Wales. It is the county town of Shropshire and serves as the commercial centre for the county and parts of mid-Wales. The town lies to the west of Haughmond Hill, where some of the oldest rocks in the county are found, and stands on largely Carboniferous rock.

Traces of earlier settlement include a Neolithic place of worship found at Sutton Farm, an Iron Age double ring ditch at Meole Brace and a roadside settlement on the Roman military road linking Viroconium Cornoviorum and Caersws. A hoard of more than 9,000 Roman coins was found near the town in 2009.

Shrewsbury has Anglo-Saxon roots, and its institutions may represent a cultural continuity reaching back as far as the 8th century. William the Conqueror gave the town to Roger de Montgomery, who was created Earl of Shrewsbury. He built Shrewsbury Castle around 1074, a work that destroyed 51 properties and probably relied on forced local labour, and he founded Shrewsbury Abbey as a Benedictine monastery in 1083.

The town is described as a borough in the Domesday Book of 1086, and its earliest known charter was issued by Henry II. The Black Death reached it in the spring of 1349, and church records show twice as many vacant benefices in that year as in the previous ten years together.

In the 1470s Edward IV established the Council of Wales and the Marches with its headquarters in the town. The Abbey closed in 1540 in the Dissolution of the Monasteries. Henry VIII meant to make Shrewsbury a cathedral city, but the citizens declined, which is the origin of the term Proud Salopians. In the 16th and 17th centuries the town was at the height of its commercial importance, controlling the Welsh wool trade, which the Shrewsbury Drapers Company dominated; Draper's Hall of 1560 and Ireland's Mansion of 1575 date from this time.

During the English Civil War it was a Royalist stronghold. Charles I had a temporary base there in the autumn of 1642, and Prince Rupert made his headquarters there on 18 February 1644. By the 18th century it was a stopping point for stagecoaches between London and Holyhead.

Shrewsbury's centre has a largely undisturbed medieval street plan and over 660 listed buildings, including several timber-framed examples from the 15th and 16th centuries. The castle and the abbey both survive. The town suffered very little from air raids in the Second World War, which is why many ancient buildings remain intact. It is the birthplace of the naturalist Charles Darwin.
shropshire: Shropshire is a ceremonial county on the border with Wales, bordered by Cheshire, Staffordshire, Worcestershire and Herefordshire in England and by Powys and Wrexham in Wales. It covers 3,487 square kilometres, with Shrewsbury as its county town and Telford as its largest settlement. The south-west is upland, taking in the Stiperstones, the Clee Hills, the Long Mynd and Wenlock Edge, and the Wrekin stands isolated west of Telford. The north is a plain, an extension of the Cheshire Plain, where most of the larger towns lie. The River Severn enters from the west, flows through Shrewsbury and leaves the county south of Bridgnorth.

There is evidence of Neolithic and Bronze Age occupation, and the hillfort at Old Oswestry dates from the Iron Age. The remains of the Roman city of Viroconium Cornoviorum survive. After the Roman occupation ended in the 5th century the area lay in the eastern part of the Welsh kingdom of Powys, and in the Anglo-Saxon period it was part of Mercia. The county is first recorded in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in the annal for 1006, under the Old English name Scrobbesbyrigscīr, meaning the shire of the fortified place in the scrublands. Much Wenlock grew up around the priory founded by the abbess St Milburga, daughter of King Merewalh of the Magonsæte.

In the High Middle Ages Shropshire was part of the Welsh Marches. From 1472 to 1689 Ludlow was the seat of the Council of Wales and the Marches, which administered justice in Wales and in Herefordshire, Shropshire, Worcestershire and Gloucestershire. The border with Wales was fixed in the 16th century. In the English Civil War the county was Royalist, and Charles II fled through it after his defeat at the Battle of Worcester, hiding in an oak tree. In the 19th century Much Wenlock was the birthplace of the modern Olympic movement.

The area around Coalbrookdale in the Ironbridge Gorge is regarded as one of the birthplaces of the Industrial Revolution and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The first iron-framed building in the world was built at the Flaxmill Maltings in Shrewsbury. The Shropshire Hills form a national landscape. The county has no cities but 22 towns, among them Oswestry, Bridgnorth, Ludlow and Market Drayton. It was called Salop in the official record from 1972 until 1980, when the name Shropshire was restored. For local government it consists of two unitary authority areas, Shropshire and Telford and Wrekin.
shroud-of-turin: The shroud is a rectangular linen cloth measuring approximately 4.4 by 1.1 metres, woven in a three-to-one herringbone twill. It bears a faint, brownish image of the front and back of a naked man with his hands folded across his groin. Reddish-brown stains on the cloth correlate with the wounds in the Gospel descriptions of the crucifixion. In 1898 Secondo Pia produced the first photographs and found that the image can be discerned more clearly in a black-and-white negative.

There are no definite historical records of this particular cloth before the 14th century. It began to be exhibited in the new collegiate church of Lirey in 1354. In 1389 the bishop of Troyes, Pierre d'Arcis, denounced it as a forgery, and in 1390 Antipope Clement VII allowed its display but ordered that it be declared a painting or panel made to represent the Shroud. In 1506 Pope Julius II reversed this position and authorised its public veneration, with its own mass and office.

The House of Savoy acquired the cloth in 1453. A fire damaged it at Chambéry in 1532, and in 1578 the Savoys moved it to their new capital, Turin. In 1694 it was placed in the Chapel of the Holy Shroud, designed by Guarino Guarini, and in 1993 it was moved to the cathedral. After the death of Umberto II of Italy in 1983, ownership passed from the House of Savoy to the Catholic Church.

The first direct examination by a scientific team took place in 1969 to 1973. In 1978 the microscopist Walter McCrone concluded from tape samples that the image had been painted with dilute red ochre in a gelatin medium and the stains with vermilion, findings other researchers disputed. In 1988 laboratories at the University of Oxford, the University of Arizona and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology dated the cloth with 95 per cent confidence to between 1260 and 1390. Experts accept the result, though defenders of authenticity have argued that the samples may have been contaminated or repaired, hypotheses that have been refuted. The Catholic Church neither endorses nor rejects the shroud as a relic of Jesus.
shu-sin: Shu-Sin, also written Šu-Suen, bears a name that honours the moon god Sîn and was formerly read Gimil-Sin. He was king of Sumer and Akkad and the fourth king of the Ur III dynasty, and he succeeded Amar-Sin, who might have been his father. His reign began about 2037 BCE by the Middle Chronology. As crown prince he held the position at Der. When his father conducted a long military campaign against Huhnuri, Shu-Sin returned to hold the city of Ur.

After an open revolt of his Amorite subjects, Shu-Sin directed the building of a fortified wall between the Euphrates and the Tigris in his fourth year, meant to hold off further Amorite attacks. The year name calls it the Amurru wall, muriq-tidnim, 'holding back the Tidanum'. Another inscription records that he gave his daughter in marriage to the ruler of Šimānum. Šimānum, Habura and the surrounding districts then rebelled against the king and chased his daughter from her residence. Shu-Sin conquered Šimānum and restored his daughter there.

The year names of his reign are all known and record its events: the caulking of the boat of Enki, called the ibex of the abzu, in the second year, the destruction of Šimānum in the third, a stele for Enlil and Ninlil in the sixth, the destruction of the land of Zabszali in the seventh and the building of a temple of Szara at Umma in the ninth. Many artifacts carry inscriptions in his name.

An erotic poem addressed to Shu-Sin by a female speaker survives on a cuneiform tablet known as Istanbul 2461, in which the speaker expresses strong desires and longings for the king. He was succeeded by his son Ibbi-Sin.
shudra: Shudra is one of the four varnas of the Hindu class system in ancient India. The word appears once in the Rigveda, in the Purusha Sukta, a creation story in which the four varnas form from the body of a primeval man: the brahmin from his mouth, the kshatriya from his arms, the vaishya from his thighs and the shudra from his feet. This verse is now generally considered a later insertion, possibly a charter myth. The historian Ram Sharan Sharma suggests that it may have been meant to show a common lineage for all the varnas.

Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel Brereton find no evidence in the Rigveda for an elaborate, much-subdivided caste system and describe the varna system there as embryonic, a social ideal rather than a social reality. According to Sharma, the Shudra class arose from Indo-Aryans and non-Indo-Aryans relegated to that position through external and internal conflicts.

The legal texts list disabilities for shudras. They were barred from studying and hearing the Vedas and from performing Vedic sacrifices, although they could hear the Itihasa and Purana texts and build wells, temples and parks. The Manusmriti, according to Patrick Olivelle, allows brahmins to seize property from shudras, who own nothing, and says shudras should not accumulate wealth. The texts vary widely: the Apastamba Grhyasutra excludes shudra students from hearing the Vedas, while the Mahabharata states that all four varnas may hear them.

Traditionally shudras were peasants and artisans, and their duty was service of the other three varnas. Scholars note that this is a theoretical account found in select texts. G. C. Ghurye argues that in reality the hereditary occupations of the varnas were missing from large parts of India, and that members of all four were farmers, traders or warriors as opportunity required. Some early texts describe shudras as ministers and kings.

Evidence from medieval India is mixed. Cynthia Talbot notes that varna is rarely mentioned in the medieval records of Andhra Pradesh, and Richard Eaton finds that in the Kakatiya population of the Deccan between the 11th and 14th centuries shudras were part of the nobility and that fathers and sons often had different professions. Several poet-saints of the Bhakti movement, among them Tukaram and Namdev, were born in shudra families, and Sikh Gurus included sixty of Namdev's compositions in the Guru Granth Sahib.

Bhim Rao Ambedkar argued that the shudras were originally kshatriyas denied the initiation ritual of upanayana by the brahmins, a claim Sharma contested. In Bali, among Hindu communities, the Soedra have typically been temple priests.
shukri-al-quwatli: Shukri al-Quwatli was born in Damascus on 6 May 1891 into a Sunni Muslim mercantile family from Baghdad that had moved to Damascus in the 18th century. He studied political science and public administration at the Mekteb-i Mülkiye in Istanbul, graduating in 1913. He worked for the Ottoman civil service in Damascus, and in February 1914 he was imprisoned briefly after refusing to kiss the hand of the governor of Syria, Jamal Pasha. He joined the secret society al-Fatat, which sought independence and unity for the Arab territories of the Ottoman Empire.

In 1920 the French sentenced him to death, among 21 nationalist leaders, and he fled to Cairo. There he served as virtual ambassador of the Syrian-Palestinian Congress and helped finance the Great Syrian Revolt of 1925-1927 through funds and arms from the Hejaz. After a general amnesty in 1930 he returned to Syria and joined the National Bloc.

Quwatli became president of Syria on 17 August 1943 after refusing a French offer of support in return for a treaty of military cooperation. When French forces attacked Damascus and other cities in May 1945, British troops entered Syria at his request, reaching Damascus on 1 June, and the French campaign halted. He was elected to a second term on 18 April 1948. He opposed the partition of Palestine and ordered the Syrian army into Palestine on 15 May 1948, though he had hoped to leave the fighting to volunteers. On 30 March 1949 Husni al-Za'im overthrew him; he resigned on 7 April and went into exile in Alexandria.

He returned in 1955 and won the presidential election in a second round of voting in parliament, 91 votes to 41. Syria moved towards neutralism, and after the United States refused to supply arms it turned to the Eastern bloc. In March 1955 he and Gamal Abdel Nasser began an Egyptian-Syrian defence agreement, concluded on 20 October. In 1958 Quwatli merged Syria with Egypt as the United Arab Republic and stepped down for Nasser, who gave him the title First Arab Citizen.

Quwatli soon became disenchanted with the union and backed the secessionist coup of 28 September 1961. He left Syria after the Ba'athist coup of 1963. He died of a heart attack in Beirut on 30 June 1967, weeks after the Six-Day War, and was buried in Damascus on 1 July. Radio Damascus honoured him on the day of the funeral, and he is proclaimed a founding father of the Syrian Arab Republic.
shulgi: Shulgi, whose Sumerian name may mean Noble Youth, was the son and successor of Ur-Namma, who founded the kingdom of Ur and died in battle. His mother was Ur-Namma's wife, probably named Watartum. The circumstances of his accession can only be inferred from literary sources of uncertain reliability. One hymn, Shulgi D, may refer to a campaign he led early in his reign to avenge his father against the Gutians. He reigned for 48 years, a figure based on the reconstructed sequence of his year names.

The first two decades are poorly documented. Shulgi continued his father's projects, building at the major sanctuaries, extending the road network and building a palace, and fought a hard campaign near Der, on the route to Elam. After about the twentieth year came a turning point. A series of reforms, which scholars dispute in detail, made the kingdom more centralised and imperial in character, with an administrative apparatus that produced thousands of accounting tablets. His family helped him rule: sons held posts in the army and provinces, and daughters became priestesses or were married to officials or foreign rulers. He had at least thirty children, and several wives of differing status.

He took the title divine Shulgi no later than his twenty-first year, the second Mesopotamian ruler after Naram-Sin of Akkad to be deified in his lifetime, and from about year 26 called himself King of the four corners of the world. Royal hymns in Sumerian presented him as chosen by the gods An, Enlil and Nanna and as the perfect king. From about year 25 the army went to war nearly every year, chiefly in the western Zagros, to control trade routes, secure tribute and plunder and keep threats away. Historians do not know whether he took part in any campaign.

Shulgi died in his forty-eighth year, perhaps at 65 to 70. Offerings were made to him within days, and a text records that he ascended to heaven. The best candidate for his burial place is an underground structure of vaulted chambers beside the Ehursag palace at Ur. His son Amar-Sin succeeded him and expanded his cult, and Shulgi was listed among the gods honoured at Nippur. The kingdom prospered for about twenty years after his death, then declined and disappeared around 2000 BCE. He is considered one of the most important kings of ancient Mesopotamia, and his hymns were copied long after his reign.
shunzhi-emperor: The Shunzhi Emperor, personal name Fulin, was the ninth son of Hong Taiji and the grandson of Nurhaci, the founder of the Eight Banners system. When Hong Taiji died on 21 September 1643 without naming a successor, a committee of Manchu princes chose the five-year-old Fulin and appointed two co-regents, Dorgon and Jirgalang. His mother was the Khorchin Mongol Bumbutai, honoured as Empress Dowager Zhaosheng. Dorgon took control of the government and, by early June 1644, firm control of the military.

In June 1644 Dorgon entered Beijing, ordered his Banner troops not to loot and had all claimants to the Ming throne executed. The Shunzhi Emperor was enthroned in Beijing in November 1644. Under Dorgon the Qing subdued almost all of China and pushed the Southern Ming loyalists into the far south-west, despite unpopular measures such as the hair-cutting edict of 1645. Li Zicheng, who had taken Beijing, was killed in September 1645.

Dorgon died on 31 December 1650, and the emperor then ruled personally. He announced a purge of corruption in April 1651, issued the Six Edicts in 1652, encouraged Han Chinese to take part in government and in 1658 re-established the Hanlin Academy and the Grand Secretariat. Court factions frustrated his efforts. Ming resistance revived in the 1650s, but by 1661 his armies had defeated the last enemies, Koxinga and the Prince of Gui, both of whom died the following year. In the late 1650s he became a fervent follower of Chan Buddhism.

His favourite consort, Donggo, died in September 1660. The emperor contracted smallpox on 2 February 1661, chose his seven-year-old third son Xuanye as heir and died on 5 February at the age of twenty-two. His will named four regents, Oboi, Soni, Suksaha and Ebilun, but they and the empress dowager clearly tampered with it before it was published. It expressed regret for his Chinese-style rule and neglect of Manchu traditions. Rumours that he had retired to a monastery circulated, but the evidence suggests that his death was not staged.

Citing the will, the regents abolished the Thirteen Eunuch Bureaus, eliminated the Hanlin Academy and limited the Deliberative Council to Manchus and Mongols. Because fewer documents survive from his reign than from later ones, it is a relatively little-known period of Qing history. He was succeeded by the Kangxi Emperor.
shusha: Shusha, or Shushi in Armenian, stands at an altitude of 1.4 to 1.8 kilometres in the Karabakh mountains, and was a mountain resort in the Soviet era. Several historians derive its name from the New Persian shīsha, meaning glass or flask, and Armenian sources from the dialectal Armenian shosh or shush, meaning tree sprout or, figuratively, a high place. Its earlier name Panahabad honoured Panah Ali Khan. The town matters religiously, culturally and strategically to both Armenians and Azerbaijanis, and is often considered a cradle of Azerbaijani music and poetry. It also contains Armenian Apostolic churches, among them Ghazanchetsots Cathedral.

The origin of the city is disputed. In the 1750s Panah Ali Khan founded the Karabakh Khanate, and the city developed with the building of the fortress of Shusha, in alliance with Melik Shahnazar, the Armenian prince of Varanda. Some Armenian sources identify an earlier fortress called Shosh on the site. From the mid-18th century to 1822 Shusha was the capital of the khanate, which withstood a six-month siege by Fath-Ali Khan Afshar in 1756 or 1759. After the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813 Russia held the khanate, and the town became a cultural centre of the South Caucasus, home to many Armenian and Azerbaijani intellectuals, poets and musicians.

Clashes between Armenian and Azerbaijani inhabitants in August 1905 killed hundreds and burned more than 200 houses. In the Shusha massacre of 1920 the Armenian half of the city was destroyed by Azerbaijani forces, resulting in the death or expulsion of its Armenian population, up to 20,000 people. The Mountainous Karabakh Autonomous Region was set up within the Azerbaijan SSR in 1923, and Stepanakert soon became its capital.

In the First Nagorno-Karabakh War Azerbaijani forces shelled Stepanakert from Shusha. Armenian forces captured the town on 9 May 1992, its Azerbaijani population fled, and most of the city was destroyed. It was under the control of the unrecognised Republic of Artsakh until Azerbaijani forces took it on 8 November 2020.
shushtar: Shoushtar is an ancient fortress city about 92 kilometres from Ahvaz, the centre of Khuzestan province. Much of its past agricultural productivity derived from an irrigation system centred on the Band-e Kaisar, the first dam bridge in Iran. The whole water system consists of 13 sites, called the Shoushtar Historical Hydraulic System, which UNESCO registered as a World Heritage Site on 26 June 2009. It was then the tenth work of Iran on the list.

The Band-e Kaisar, or Caesar's dam, is an overflow dam about 500 m long over the Karun. Tradition holds that after the Sasanian Shah Shapur I defeated the Roman emperor Valerian, he ordered the captive Roman soldiers to build a large bridge and dam. The structure shows typical Roman building techniques, and its dual-purpose design influenced Iranian civil engineering and the development of Sasanian water management. The traditional account is disputable, but it is not implausible that Roman prisoners were involved. It was repaired many times in the Islamic period and fell out of use in the late 19th century.

In Elamite times the city was known as Adamdun, and in the Achaemenid era as Šurkutir. According to tradition it was founded by king Hushang after he built Susa. In the Sasanian era it was an island city on the Karun, chosen as a summer capital; the river was channelled to form a moat, and qanats connected the river to private reservoirs, supplying water for homes and irrigation and during wartime when the gates were closed. Sugar cane cultivation there dates back to 226.

Shoushtar was always among the most important textile-producing cities in Khuzestan. Al-Istakhri, writing about 933, listed brocade and tiraz, and al-Maqdisi, about 1000, listed brocade, carpets, cotton and Merv-style clothes. Its commercial importance was recognized when it was chosen in 933 to produce the Kiswah, the embroidered covering for the Kaaba.

In 1831 a cholera epidemic killed about half of the inhabitants. The Karun steamship service of 1887 made Shoushtar the farthest point upstream, and it became the main commercial centre of south-western Iran, with 28,000 residents by 1938. After the Trans-Persian Railway bypassed it in favour of Ahvaz, its commerce and population declined.

Shoushtar is the capital of Shoushtar County in Khuzestan province. Most of its people speak Shoushtari, a dialect of Persian. It has a hot semi-arid climate. The Mandaean community of the Subbi Kush neighbourhood lived there for centuries, though Mandaeans no longer lived there by the 21st century because of emigration.
siad-barre: Mohamed Siad Barre was born to pastoral parents at a time when no birth records were kept, and guesses at his birth year range from 1909 to 1921. His father was Marehan and his mother Ogaden, both of the Darod clan family. By concealing his unofficial birthplace, as many others did, he became eligible for the Italian colonial police force and military in Somalia. He rose to command the Somali National Army.

After the assassination of President Abdirashid Shermarke, Barre came to power in the coup of 21 October 1969. The Supreme Revolutionary Council renamed the country the Somali Democratic Republic and made it a one-party Marxist–Leninist state, and a personality cult styled him the Victorious Leader. Early policies included the nationalisation of banks, industry and land, public works, and a literacy campaign. In 1972 Somali became the language of instruction, replacing Italian in the south and English in the north, and in 1973 highways linked the two regions. Somalia joined the Arab League in 1974, the year Barre chaired the Organization of African Unity. A law of 1970 allowed the security service to detain critics indefinitely without trial.

In 1977 Barre launched the Ogaden War against Ethiopia, and between September 1977 and March 1978 his forces captured virtually the whole Somali region. The Soviet Union then turned against him; he expelled its advisers and moved towards the United States, which gave about US$100 million a year in aid until 1989. His popularity declined after the defeat. After a coup attempt in 1978 most of those accused were summarily executed, and survivors who escaped abroad formed the first of the groups that opposed his regime by force. In May 1986 he was badly injured in a car accident.
