His epithet Thassi suggests "the Wise", and it can also mean "the Director", "the Guide", "the Man of Counsel" and "the Zealous". He is also called Simon the Hasmonean, Simon Maccabee or Simon Maccabeus.

The Seleucid king Antiochus VI appointed him strategos, or military commander, of the coast from the Ladder of Tyre to Egypt. In that post he took Beth-zur and Joppa, garrisoned them with Jewish troops and built the fortress of Adida.

When the Seleucid general Diodotus Tryphon captured Jonathan, the people assembled at Jerusalem chose Simon as their leader. He completed the fortification of the city and secured Joppa, and at Hadid he blocked Tryphon's advance. Tryphon demanded a ransom and Jonathan's sons as hostages. Josephus and 1 Maccabees both say Simon agreed, although he knew he would be deceived, so that the people could see he had done all he could. Jonathan was killed anyway and the hostages were not returned.

Simon then sided with the Seleucid king Demetrius II and asked for freedom from taxation, which was granted. This implied recognition of Judea's political independence. A large assembly of priests, people and elders decreed that he should be leader and high priest "forever, until there should arise a faithful prophet". He became High Priest and Ethnarch, the first prince of the Hasmonean dynasty. The Roman Senate recognised the new dynasty about 139 BCE, when his delegation was in Rome.

Simon and two of his sons, Mattathias and Judah, were killed at a banquet at Dok by his son-in-law Ptolemy, the Seleucid governor at Jericho. His third son John Hyrcanus succeeded him as high priest and ruler, but at first could not capture Ptolemy, who held John's mother hostage.

The name Simon, and its Hebrew form Simeon, became the most popular male name for some three centuries in the Hasmonean Kingdom and Roman Judaea, both to honour the leader who had won independence and because it did not sound strange to Greek ears.
simone-de-beauvoir: Beauvoir was born on 9 January 1908 in Montparnasse, in Paris. Her father, Georges Bertrand de Beauvoir, was initially a lawyer but aspired to be an actor, and her mother, Françoise, was a devout Catholic and a banker's daughter. The promised dowry was lost when Françoise's father was jailed. Her parents were often absent, and she was raised chiefly by a nanny, Louise. She had a younger sister, Hélène, born on 6 June 1910. Intellectually precocious and encouraged by her father, she wrote that the contrast between her father's individualism and pagan standards and her mother's rigid conventional morality made her life an endless disputation, the main reason she became an intellectual.

After her studies Beauvoir saw teaching as a way to earn her own living. She did her practice teaching at the same secondary school as Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Claude Lévi-Strauss, and from 1929 to 1943 she taught at lycées in Marseille, Rouen and Paris until she could live on her writing. She then became a public intellectual. Her first novel, She Came to Stay, appeared in 1943, followed by The Blood of Others (1945), which tells a love story between two young students in the French Resistance during the Second World War.

With Jean-Paul Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty she co-founded Les Temps Modernes, a monthly political journal that carried communists, Catholics, Gaullists and socialists, whose first issue appeared on 1 October 1945. Sartre and Merleau-Ponty later quarrelled, and Beauvoir sided with Sartre. She remained an editor until her death and in later years held the editorial meetings in her flat.

Her first philosophical essay, Pyrrhus et Cinéas (1944), was followed by The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), in which she argues that the freedom of the self requires the freedom of others. The Second Sex (1949) turned the existentialist principle that existence precedes essence into a feminist one: One is not born, but rather becomes, woman. It articulated the distinction between biological sex and the social construction of gender, and showed how sexual difference is used to trap women in the role of the Other. The Mandarins (1954), a roman à clef about Sartre's and Beauvoir's circle after the war, won the Prix Goncourt.

Beauvoir at first denied being a feminist but later admitted it. The Second Sex opened the way for second-wave feminism, and Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Juliet Mitchell, Ann Oakley and Germaine Greer read it in translation and acknowledged their debt to her. Betty Friedan said that reading it in the early 1950s led to her own analysis of women's existence.
simone-martini: Simone Martini was born in Siena around 1284. It is thought that he was a pupil of Duccio di Buoninsegna, the leading Sienese painter of his time, although the Renaissance biographer Giorgio Vasari instead made him a pupil of Giotto di Bondone, with whom he went to Rome. His brother-in-law was the artist Lippo Memmi. Very little documentation of his life survives, and many attributions to him are debated by art historians.

Among his first documented works is the Maestà of 1315 in the Palazzo Pubblico in Siena. Lippo Memmi painted a similar Maestà for the Palazzo Comunale in San Gimignano soon afterwards, an example of the lasting influence of his models. During a stay in Naples at the request of the king he painted Saint Louis of Toulouse Crowning His Brother Robert of Anjou in 1317, now in the Museo di Capodimonte, and he painted a polyptych of Saint Catherine of Alexandria in Pisa in 1319.

He also painted the Annunciation with St. Margaret and St. Ansanus of 1333, now in the Uffizi in Florence, and frescoes in the San Martino Chapel in the lower church of the Basilica of San Francesco in Assisi. A Christ Discovered in the Temple of 1342 is in the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool.

His Sienese style contrasts with the sobriety and monumentality of Florentine art and is noted for soft, stylised, decorative features, sinuous line and courtly elegance. His art owes much to French manuscript illumination and ivory carving, examples of which reached Siena along the Via Francigena, a main pilgrimage and trade route. He greatly influenced the International Gothic style.

He likely moved to Avignon in 1334 or 1335 and died there in July 1344 in the service of the papal court. He was commissioned to paint frescoes for the porch of Avignon Cathedral, of which only faint sinopia outlines remain. According to Vasari, he painted a portrait of Laura de Noves for his friend Petrarch, who refers to it in two sonnets of the Canzoniere.
simonides-of-ceos: Few clear facts about Simonides' life have survived, and ancient sources are uncertain even about his date of birth. Modern scholars generally accept 556 to 468 BCE, though this would make him about fifty years older than his nephew Bacchylides. He was the son of Leoprepes and was born in Ioulis on Ceos, an island with a rich musical culture, where choirs were trained at a school in Carthaea, and a tradition of athletic competition that made it fertile ground for the victory ode, a genre of choral lyric he pioneered. About the age of thirty he was drawn to Athens by the court of the tyrant Hipparchus, where his rivalry with the chorus-trainer Lasus of Hermione later became a joke.

After the assassination of Hipparchus in 514 BCE Simonides withdrew to Thessaly, under the patronage of the Scopadae and Aleuadae. A tradition related by Cicero and Quintilian says that Scopas refused to pay him in full for an ode that spoke too much of Castor and Pollux, and that the poet was called out of the banquet hall just before it collapsed, which was said to have led him to devise a system of mnemonics based on places. Quintilian dismisses the story as fiction.

He returned to Athens during the Persian Wars and became a prominent international figure as the author of commemorative verses. After the defeat of the second Persian invasion he composed epitaphs for Athenians, Spartans and Corinthians, a song for Leonidas and his men, and poems on the battles of Artemisium, Salamis and Plataea. His last years were spent in Sicily as a friend of Hieron of Syracuse, and he is said to have made peace between Hieron and Theron of Acragas. Callimachus records that he was buried outside Acragas.

Simonides wrote choral lyrics, elegiac verses, dirges, paeans and dithyrambs, and an epigram credits him with 57 victories in dithyrambic competitions. He is generally credited with popularising the victory ode, an extension of the hymn, and with establishing the choral dirge as a recognised form. Only a small part of his poetry survives, in papyrus fragments and quotations, and modern scholars consider just one of the epigrams attributed to him unquestionably authentic, an inscription for the seer Megistius, which places even the Thermopylae epitaph in doubt.

His style is clear and simple, with restraint and balance, and Quintilian praised his power to excite pity. Aristophanes made him a type of the miser, and a tradition holds that he was the first poet to charge fees. Plato quotes his poem on the difficulty of being truly good, which holds that only a god can be perfect and that a man is good enough if he does nothing shameful willingly.
simplon-pass: The Simplon Pass is a high mountain pass between the Pennine Alps and the Lepontine Alps in Switzerland. It connects Brig in the canton of Valais with Domodossola in Piedmont, Italy. The pass itself and the villages on each side of it, such as Gondo, lie in Switzerland. Its lowest point, which is also the lowest point of the watershed between the basins of the Rhône and the Po in Switzerland, lies in marshland about 500 metres west of the settlement of Simplon Pass. Peaks that can be climbed from the pass include the Wasenhorn, the Hubschhorn, the Breithorn and Monte Leone.

A passage through the mountains had been used locally for several centuries, but the pass acquired international significance during the Napoleonic occupation. Between 1801 and 1805 the engineer Nicolas Céard built the Simplon Road at the direction of the emperor, so that artillery could be moved between the Rhône valley and Italy. From then on the pass could be used by road vehicles: first post carriages, replaced early in the twentieth century by post buses. The former département of Simplon, the Swiss canton of Valais, was named after the pass.

The cantonal authorities made a plan in 1950 to keep the road open all year instead of closing it between October and late April, as was usual at this altitude. It called for avalanche shelters and wider tunnels for full-size coaches. In October 1970 journalists were told that the work had been finished on 37 of the 42.5 kilometres between Brig and the Italian frontier at Gondo. The Simplon Tunnel, 20 kilometres long, opened in 1906, and the Orient Express used the Simplon route intermittently during the twentieth century on its way between Istanbul and Paris.

The road remains one of the few major Alpine passes kept open throughout the year. The Hospice du Simplon at the top is owned by the Congregation of Canons Regular at Grand-Saint-Bernard. A granite eagle about nine metres high, designed by the architect Erwin Friedrich Baumann and inaugurated in September 1944, commemorates the 11th Alpine Brigade of the Swiss Army; a memorial of 2005 marks the 200th anniversary of the Napoleon Road.
simurgh: The Persian word sīmurğ derives from Middle Persian sēnmurw, which comes from Avestan mərəγō Saēnō, the bird Saēna, originally a raptor, likely an eagle, falcon or sparrowhawk. In Persian the phrase sī murğ also means thirty birds, a play on words used by Attar of Nishapur.

The figure appears in all periods of Iranian art and literature, and in the iconography of Georgia, medieval Armenia and the Eastern Roman Empire. The Sasanians used it heavily, as a tribal emblem and in their art and propaganda. Through Persian influence it reached the Arabic-speaking world, where it was conflated with other mythical birds such as the ghoghnus and developed into the rukh, the origin of the English word roc. Representations were adopted in early Umayyad art and coinage.

In Iranian art the simurgh is a winged creature in the shape of a bird, gigantic enough to carry off an elephant or a whale. It appears as a peacock with the head of a dog and the claws of a lion, and sometimes with a human face. It is inherently benevolent, and being part mammal it suckles its young.

The simurgh was thought to purify land and water and so bestow fertility, and it mediated between earth and sky. It roosted in Gaokerena, the Hōm tree of life in the middle of the sea Vourukasha, whose all-healing seeds it scattered when it took flight. It is also linked with farr, divine glory, the mandate underlying a king's authority; it appears resting on the head or shoulder of would-be kings and clerics as a sign that Ormuzd accepts them.

In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh the simurgh raises Zal, son of Saam, who was born albino and abandoned on the mountain Alborz. She gives him three golden feathers to burn if he needs her help. When his wife Rudaba is near death in labour, Zal burns a feather and the simurgh instructs him in performing a caesarean section, so that Rostam is born. The simurgh later heals Rostam and his horse Rakhsh after Esfandiyar's arrows and tells Rostam how to make the double-headed arrow that blinds Esfandiyar. In the fifth trial of Esfandiyar, a different simurgh is killed.

In Persian Sufi poetry it is a metaphor for God. In Attar's 12th-century Conference of the Birds, a group of pilgrim birds led by the hoopoe seeks the simurgh and at last finds only a lake in which they see their own reflection, a pun on thirty birds.
sinaloa: Sinaloa is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the Federal Entities of Mexico. It covers 58,328 square kilometres and is divided into 20 municipalities. It borders Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango and Nayarit, and faces Baja California Sur across the Gulf of California. The Sierra Madre Occidental dominates the east, and many rivers flow from it to the gulf through fertile valleys and a narrow coastal plain. The most popular explanation of the name, attributed to Eustaquio Buelna, combines the Cahita words sina, the pitahaya plant, and lobola, rounded.

Sinaloa belongs to the northern limit of Mesoamerica, and the Fuerte River marks the start of Aridoamerica to the north. Before European contact it was inhabited by groups such as the Cahitas, the Tahues, the Acaxees and the Xiximes. In 1531 Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán, with a force of over 10,000 men, established a Spanish and allied Indian outpost at San Miguel de Culiacán. Over the next decade the Cahíta suffered severe depopulation from conquest and from smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans.

Starting in 1599 Jesuit missionaries spread out from a base at what is now Sinaloa de Leyva, and by 1610 Spanish influence reached the northern edge of the territory. Their movement into the east prompted the Acaxee Rebellion of 1601; the Spanish executed 48 Acaxee leaders. After independence Sinaloa was joined with Sonora as the Estado de Occidente, and in 1830 it separated to become the 20th state of the First Mexican Republic, with Culiacán as its capital. Los Mochis was founded in 1893 by American settlers led by Albert K. Owen as the Topolobampo colony, inspired by utopian socialism.

The capital and largest city is Culiacán; other large cities include Mazatlán, a tourist resort, and Los Mochis. Irrigation projects built after the revolution turned arid land into farmland and earned Sinaloa the name granary of Mexico. Banda music, popularized there in the late 19th century, is its best-known cultural tradition, and ulama, a form of the ancient Mesoamerican ballgame, is still played in a few rural communities near Mazatlán.
sinchi-roca: Sinchi Roca, written Sinchi Rocca or Cinchi Roca in Hispanicized spellings and Sinchi Ruq'a in Quechua, where the name is glossed as "valorous generous Inca", belonged to the Hurin dynasty, the first dynasty of the Kingdom of Cusco. Tradition makes him the son of two of the original Inca siblings, Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo, who may have conceived him at Huaynacancha. His wife was Mama Cura of the Sanu lineage, a daughter of Sitic-huaman, and their children included Lloque Yupanqui and a son named Sapaca. His dates are given as about 1230 to about 1260.

In one of the Inca foundation myths Sinchi Roca led his family into the valley of Cuzco. He is thought to have divided his land into territories and to have begun the first census of the Inca population. He is also said to have ordered all Inca to pierce their ears as a sign of nobility. The chronicler Pedro Cieza de León states that he built terraces and brought in large quantities of soil to improve the fertility of the valley.

Sixteenth-century Spanish writers, Cabello de Balboa among them, affirm that Sinchi Roca was the first Inca to wear the mascapaicha, later the sign of Inca sovereignty. It was a fringe of red wool, each strand passed through a small gold tube, set above the forehead beneath two or three black and white feathers of the sacred Andean mountain caracara and held by a braided headband called the llautu. The word sinchi later came to mean a warlord, while Capac, one of his father's names, became the title of a sovereign.
sindh: Sindh lies in the south-east of Pakistan and is bounded by the Arabian Sea to the south, Balochistan to the west and Punjab to the north; to the east it shares a border with the Indian states of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Its landscape is mostly alluvial plain on either side of the Indus River, with the Thar Desert in the east and the Kirthar Mountains in the west. The name Sind is a Persian derivative of the Sanskrit sindhu, meaning river, and the Greeks under Alexander the Great called the Indus Indos. The spelling Sindh replaced the older Sind in 1988.

Settled life began around Sindh and Punjab some 9,000 years ago and developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation. Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BCE, was one of the largest settlements of that civilisation, with standardised bricks, street grids and covered sewerage. It was abandoned in the 19th century BCE as the civilisation declined, and was not rediscovered until the 1920s. Around 1000 BCE the Indo-Aryan kingdom of Sindhu-Sauvira emerged and lasted until the Achaemenids captured the region in 518 BCE, after whom came the Macedonians, Mauryans, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Guptas and Sasanians.

The first Muslim naval raids came in 636 under the caliph Umar. Arab forces conquered Sindh in 712 under the Umayyad Caliphate and made it a province, which laid the foundations of the Muslim period in South Asia. The Habbari Emirate emerged in the 9th century, and between the 11th and 16th centuries the Soomra, Samma and Arghun dynasties ruled, mostly as vassals of the Delhi Sultanate. Akbar, himself born at Umerkot in Sindh, sent an army in 1591 to 1593 to take lower Sindh from the Tarkhan dynasty. Mughal rule ran from the provincial capital Thatta, while the Kalhora dynasty held upper Sindh from Khudabad. The Talpur dynasty ruled from 1783, and the East India Company later captured the province.

Sindh became a separate province in 1936. After the Lahore Resolution of 1940 it was the first province to endorse the Pakistan Movement, and it joined the Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. It was merged into West Pakistan in 1955 and restored as a province in 1970.

Karachi, on the southern coast, is the provincial capital and the largest city. Sindhi, spoken by about 60 per cent of the population at the 2023 census, is the most widely spoken language, and about 90 per cent of residents are Muslim. Sufism is an important marker of Sindhi identity for Muslims and Hindus alike, and the poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai lived here. Two World Heritage Sites lie in the province, Mohenjo-daro and the Makli Necropolis near Thatta.
sindhudurg-district: Sindhudurg is the southernmost district of Maharashtra, about 5,207 square kilometres in area. It is bordered on the north by Ratnagiri district, on the south by Goa, on the south-east by Belagavi district of Karnataka, and on the west by the Arabian Sea. To the east, across the crest of the Western Ghats, lies Kolhapur district. It is part of the Konkan, a narrow coastal plain between the Ghats and the sea, with a warm, humid climate and rains from June to October. The district has deposits of iron, bauxite and manganese, and most people speak Malvani, a distinct dialect of Konkani and Marathi, and are fluent in Marathi too.

The name Konkan is of Indian origin and great antiquity, though its derivation has never been definitively explained. Tradition places the Pandavas in the region during the 13th year of their exile. In the middle of the sixth century kings of the Maurya and Nala dynasties appear to have ruled in the Konkan, and Ratnagiri district was under the Silahars. In the 16th century Portuguese power rose on the west coast. A local sultan lost his hold on the district in 1675 with the rise of Shivaji, and the district became part of the Maratha Empire, which ruled it until 1817, when the whole Konkan passed to the British.

Shivaji built the sea fort of Sindhudurg near Malvan, whose name means Sea Fort. Work began on 25 November 1664 and was completed in three years, and the fort was designed so that enemies approaching from the Arabian Sea could not easily see it. In 1819 South Konkan became a district, later named Ratnagiri. The former state of Sawantwadi was merged with the district in 1949, and the area became part of Maharashtra in 1960. Sindhudurg district was formed on 1 May 1981 by dividing Ratnagiri district.

The district has eight talukas: Sawantwadi, Kudal, Vengurla, Malvan, Devgad, Kankavli, Vaibhavwadi and Dodamarg. Its headquarters are at Oros, and at the 2011 census it had a population of 849,651, of whom 12.59 per cent lived in towns. Rice, coconut, kokum, mango and cashew are the main crops, and Devgad is known for its Alphonso mangoes. Sindhudurg and Ratnagiri Kokum received a Geographical Indication tag in 2016. Malvani cuisine, built on coconut, rice and fish, is the local food, and the Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg forts and Tarkarli beach are among its places of interest.
singapore: Singapore lies about one degree of latitude, 137 kilometres, north of the equator, off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Its territory is a main island, also known as Pulau Ujong, over 60 satellite islands and one outlying islet, and two man-made connections, the Johor–Singapore Causeway and the Tuas Second Link, join it to Johor in Malaysia. The highest natural point is Bukit Timah Hill, at 163.63 metres. Land reclamation has raised the land area from roughly 580 km2 in the 1960s to 770 km2. The name is an anglicisation of the Malay Singapura, from the Sanskrit for 'lion city', and the island was earlier known as Temasek.

According to the Malay Annals, the Kingdom of Singapura was founded in 1299 by Sang Nila Utama, although historians debate the accounts. In the 14th century, as Temasek, Singapore was a trading port under the influence of both the Majapahit Empire and the Siamese kingdoms. Around the end of that century its ruler Parameswara was attacked, by either the Majapahit or the Siamese, and moved to Malacca, where he founded the Sultanate of Malacca. Portuguese raiders burned the settlement in 1613, and the island then faded into obscurity for two centuries, nominally part of the Johor Sultanate.

Stamford Raffles arrived on 28 January 1819, when around 150 people lived on the island, 120 of them Malays. With the help of the Temenggong of Johor, he brought Tengku Long back from exile and recognised him as Sultan Hussein, and in the Treaty of Singapore of 6 February 1819 the Sultan granted the British the right to establish a trading post. Singapore came under direct British control in 1867 as part of the Straits Settlements, was occupied by Japan in 1942, gained self-governance in 1959 and joined Malaysia in 1963. It was expelled from the federation two years later and became independent in 1965.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic based on the Westminster system. Its population was 6,110,200 in 2025, of whom 3,660,200 were citizens. The 2020 census reported 74.3% of residents of Chinese descent, 13.5% Malay and 9.0% Indian. English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil are the four official languages, and 78.7% of resident households live in public housing developed by the Housing and Development Board.
singhasari: Singhasari, also called Tumapel, was a Javanese Hindu-Buddhist kingdom in eastern Java that succeeded the Kingdom of Kediri as the dominant power there. Its name comes from Sanskrit singha, "lion", and Old Javanese sari, which could mean either "essence" or "to sleep". Most of what is told of its founding comes from the Pararaton, which mixes in mythical elements. By that account Ken Arok, an orphan, rose from servant of the regional ruler Tunggul Ametung at Tumapel to ruler of Java, killed Tunggul Ametung, and was himself later assassinated by Anusapati, Tunggul Ametung's son.

Ken Arok is considered the founder of the Rajasa dynasty, from which both the Singhasari and the later Majapahit rulers descended. Anusapati was killed by Ken Arok's son Panji Tohjaya, who reigned only a few months in 1248 before his nephews Ranga Wuni and Mahisha Champaka revolted and ruled together as Vishnuvardhana and Narasimhamurti.

Kertanegara, the fifth ruler, reigned from 1268. In 1275 he launched the Pamalayu naval expedition against the weakened remains of Srivijaya, and in 1284 he led an expedition that brought Bali into the kingdom. He also sent troops and envoys to Sunda, Pahang, Borneo and the Maluku islands, and allied himself with the king of Champa.

Kublai Khan of the Yuan dynasty sent envoys to Java demanding tribute in 1280, 1281 and 1289, and Kertanegara refused each time, scarring the face of the envoy Meng Ki. In 1292 the vassal king Jayakatwang of Daha, assisted by Arya Wiraraja of Madura, attacked from north and south while Kertanegara's forces were spread thin. His southern army sacked the capital Kutaraja and killed the king during a Tantra ceremony, ending the kingdom.

Kertanegara's son-in-law Raden Wijaya escaped, took refuge under the patronage of Arya Wiraraja, and was allowed by Jayakatwang to open a settlement in the Tarik forest, named Majapahit after its bitter maja fruits. When a Mongol fleet of about 1,000 ships reached the coast near Tuban in early 1293, Wijaya allied with it against Daha, then turned on the Mongols and forced them off Java on 31 May 1293. He took the throne as Kertajasa Jayawardhana on 12 November 1293, founding the Majapahit Empire, which took over Singhasari's territory.
singing-revolution: The Soviet Union annexed Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania around 1940, following the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, and the annexation was not widely recognised; the United States, for one, never recognised it and kept receiving Baltic diplomats in Washington. After Germany's occupation in 1941 the Soviets reconquered the three countries in 1944-45 and defeated the armed resistance of the Forest Brothers by the early 1950s. From the late 1970s Moscow tried to replace the native languages with Russian, largely without success, especially in Estonia, where gathering to sing in Estonian helped keep the language alive. In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev introduced glasnost and perestroika, which loosened limits on political freedom and made it harder for Moscow to hold the non-Russian republics.

Civic groups such as Sąjūdis in Lithuania, the Popular Front of Latvia and the Estonian Popular Front organised petitions, rallies and forums, and mass song festivals became a main form of protest. The term Singing Revolution was coined by the Estonian activist and artist Heinz Valk in an article written a week after the spontaneous mass singing of 10 and 11 June 1988 at the Tallinn Song Festival Grounds. On 23 August 1989, the fiftieth anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, about two million people joined hands in the Baltic Way, a human chain of some 600 kilometres from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius.

The three republics were the first in the Soviet Union to proclaim sovereignty, in 1988 and 1989. Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990, and Latvia's Supreme Soviet adopted a declaration on 4 May 1990 calling for the restoration of the inter-war state. In January 1991 Soviet forces attacked in Vilnius, where fourteen unarmed protesters died on 13 January defending the Television Tower and Parliament, and in Riga, where demonstrators raised barricades. Unarmed volunteers in Estonia shielded the parliament, radio and television buildings. Estonia declared its independence restored late on 20 August 1991, during the failed coup in Moscow.

After the coup failed, countries began to recognise Baltic independence, with Iceland the first to recognise Estonia, on 22 August 1991. The Soviet Union recognised the three states in September 1991, more than two months before its own dissolution. The three countries joined the EU and NATO in 2004. The movement is regarded as a leading example of nonviolent collective action of the late twentieth century, and it has been compared to the changes in East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
sinicization: Sinicization, also called sinification or sinonization, is the process by which non-Chinese societies or groups are acculturated or assimilated into Chinese culture, particularly the language, societal norms, cultural practices and ethnic identity of the Han Chinese. It touches diet, writing, industry, education, law, architecture, politics, philosophy, religion, science and technology, value systems and lifestyle. The term is also used for the adoption of Chinese norms by neighbouring East Asian societies and for policies towards minority groups within China. The adoption of the Chinese writing system in Korea, Japan and Vietnam is often cited as evidence, as writing has long unified the Sinosphere and carried Chinese culture to other Asian countries.

Peoples of southern China, collectively called the Baiyue, were sinicised over time; some in the Yangtze delta began as early as the 11th century BCE, marked by the founding of the state of Wu, and southward movement of Han Chinese, mostly as war refugees, completed the process for most of them. From the late Han dynasty to the early Jin, large numbers of Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di and Qiang settled in northern China and were sinicised to varying degrees.

Cao Cao moved Xiongnu nomads away from the frontier near Taiyuan, where they gave up nomadism and their elite were educated in Confucian literate culture. The Northern and Southern dynasties, from 386 to 589, accelerated the process, with Buddhism and Daoism spreading as well. The Tuoba Wei is described as a sinicised empire of Mongolic-Xianbei origin, and the Shatuo Turks founded three sinicised dynasties in northern China.

In the 8th and 9th centuries Tang soldiers who moved into Guizhou married native women. Under the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty, a Muslim from Bukhara, Sayyid Ajall Shams al-Din Omar, was made governor of Yunnan after the conquest of the Dali Kingdom. He founded a "Chinese style" city, Zhongjing Cheng, on the site of modern Kunming, built the province's first Confucian temple in 1274 and introduced Confucian education, rituals and marriage and funeral customs, as well as promoting Islam.

Assimilation policy in China is a type of Chinese nationalism aimed at strengthening the Chinese national identity, Zhonghua minzu. Proponents believe it develops shared values, pride in citizenship and acceptance of cultural differences. Critics argue that assimilation destroys ethnic, linguistic and cultural diversity; there are 292 non-Mandarin languages spoken by native peoples in China. The historian James A. Millward has claimed that the People's Republic of China has used the concept of sinicization to obscure Han settler colonialism. In recent times the word has sometimes been used more narrowly for specific government policies towards ethnic minorities and the promotion of ethnic unity.
sinjar: Sinjar lies about five kilometres south of the Sinjar Mountains, in the Sinjar District of the Nineveh Governorate in northern Iraq. Its name is written Şingal in Kurdish and Shingar in Syriac. In the 2nd century CE it became a Roman military base called Singara, part of the Roman limes, and it remained Roman until the Sasanians sacked it in 360. Singara was long a bone of contention between the Sasanian and Byzantine empires and several times changed hands. A 6th-century source describes its population as pagans, Christians and Jews.

Arab Muslims under the commander Iyad ibn Ghanm conquered Sinjar in the 630s and 640s, and it became part of the Diyar Rabi'a district of the Jazira province. The Hamdanid dynasty took it in 970, and the Uqaylids later built a citadel there. From the rule of the Turkmen atabeg Jikirmish in 1106/07 Sinjar entered its most prosperous period, lasting to the mid-13th century. The Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din conquered the area in 1169 and 1171, and a cadet branch of the Zengids was established under Zengi II (r. 1171–1197), whose court was noted for its high culture.

The scholar Ibn Shaddad described a double wall, two mosques, six madrasas, a shrine of Ali ibn Abi Talib and three Sufi buildings. A minaret credits Qutb ad-Din Muhammad (r. 1197–1219) with its building in 1201. Sinjar later came under Ayyubid rule and then that of Badr al-Din Lu'lu' of Mosul. The Ilkhanid Mongols destroyed its double wall and the shrine in 1262. The geographer Zakariya al-Qazwini called it little Damascus, and Ibn Battuta wrote that its inhabitants were Kurds.

After the Timurid conquest and the Ak Koyunlu and Kara Koyunlu, the Safavid dynasty took Sinjar in 1507/08 and the Ottomans in 1534. In 1833 Mir Muhammad of Rawanduz massacred as many as 10,000 Yazidi men, and an Ottoman campaign that followed reportedly destroyed three quarters of the population. Five neighbourhoods were Arabized by the Iraqi government in 1974 and 1975. In August 2014 the Islamic State took the city and killed and enslaved Yazidis, an event described as a genocide; Kurdish forces retook it in November 2015.

The town was estimated in 2013 to have 88,023 inhabitants and is predominantly Yazidi. A 2013 survey of the district recorded Kurds, Arabs, Turkmens and Assyrians, and Yazidis, Sunni Muslims and Christians. Few visible traces remain of the ancient town of Singara, and a minaret of 1201 survives from the Zengid period.
sinjar-mountains: The Sinjar Mountains form a range about 100 kilometres long, running east to west and rising above the surrounding steppe plains to 1,463 metres. The highest section, some 75 kilometres long, lies in Nineveh Governorate, and the lower western section, about 25 kilometres long, in Syria. The city of Sinjar stands just south of the range. Geologically it is a breached anticline of sedimentary strata from the Late Cretaceous to the Early Neogene, and its groundwater supports farming and stock. The Yazidis regard the mountains as sacred.

The mountains appear in records of the second and third millennia BCE under the name Saggar, which was also the name of a deity of the area, and texts from Mari and Mesopotamia describe them as a source of basalt and of nuts, especially pistachios. They were mostly a frontier between empires, held by the Roman Empire from 115 CE and from 363 on the Persian side of the Byzantine and Sasanian frontier, which brought Zoroastrianism.

Christianity was established there by the 4th century, and from the late 5th century the Arab tribe of the Banu Taghlib lived there. After the Muslim conquest of the 630s–640s the Christian inhabitants paid a poll tax. Yazidis lived there in the 11th century, and since the 12th century they have mainly inhabited the area, taking the highest peak to be where Noah's Ark came to rest.

The most prosperous period of Sinjar was the 12th and 13th centuries, under Jikirmish, a cadet branch of the Zengid dynasty and then Ayyubid rule. In the first half of the 13th century Badr ad-Din Lu'lu' of Mosul led a campaign against the Yazidis of the mountains, massacring them and desecrating the mausoleum of Sheikh Adi at Lalish.

Yazidis revolted against the Ottomans in 1850–1864, and in 1915 they sheltered Armenians and Assyrians fleeing genocide. From late 1974 Saddam Hussein's government destroyed 137 mostly Yazidi villages and resettled their people in eleven new towns north and south of the mountains, to keep them from the Kurdish rebellion of Mustafa Barzani.

In August 2014 forces of the Islamic State raided the city of Sinjar, which fell on 3 August, and an estimated 40,000 to 50,000 Yazidis fled to the mountains. Stranded without water or food, they depended on airdrops, and by 10 August Kurdish forces had rescued about 30,000 through a corridor into Syria and Iraqi Kurdistan. It has been reported that 7,000 Yazidi women were taken as slaves and more than 5,000 people were killed.
sinn-fein: The name is Irish for Ourselves or We Ourselves, frequently mistranslated as ourselves alone, from the early 20th-century slogan Sinn Féin Amháin. It asserts Irish national sovereignty and self-determination rather than political union with Great Britain under the Westminster Parliament. The party was founded on 28 November 1905 when Arthur Griffith, at the first annual Convention of the National Council, outlined a policy to establish in Ireland's capital a national legislature endowed with the moral authority of the Irish nation. Its first platform was conservative and monarchist, advocating an Anglo-Irish dual monarchy modelled on the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867. It won 27 per cent of the vote in the 1908 North Leitrim by-election, after which support and membership fell.

Its members founded the revolutionary Irish Republic and its parliament, the First Dáil, and many were active in the Irish War of Independence, when the party was associated with the Irish Republican Army. The party split before the Irish Civil War and again afterwards. Pro-Treaty deputies formed Cumann na nGaedheal in 1923, which governed the Irish Free State for nine years and merged with other groups to form Fine Gael in 1933. In 1926 Éamon de Valera, after losing a motion to let elected members take their seats if the Oath of Allegiance were removed, resigned and founded Fianna Fáil, taking most of the party's deputies with him. The remaining party was small, and for decades often without parliamentary representation.

A split in 1970, at the start of the Troubles, produced the modern party, linked in that conflict with the Provisional Irish Republican Army, and for most of it affected by broadcasting bans. Under Gerry Adams, leader from 1983, electoral politics became more important. The party dropped abstention from the Dáil in 1986, and some members formed Republican Sinn Féin in protest. In the 1990s Adams and Martin McGuinness took part in the Northern Ireland peace process leading to the Good Friday Agreement, and in 2006 the party signed the St Andrews Agreement and agreed to support the Police Service of Northern Ireland.

Sinn Féin operates under democratic centralism, and describes itself as an Irish republican and democratic socialist party. It is active in both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, and its main political goal is a united Ireland. It continues a policy of abstaining from the House of Commons at Westminster. Caoimhghín Ó Caoláin, elected to the Dáil in 1997, was the first person under the Sinn Féin name to take a seat there since 1922. Mary Lou McDonald succeeded Gerry Adams as president in 2018.
sino-british-joint-declaration: Hong Kong became a British colony in 1842 after the British defeated the Qing dynasty in the First Opium War, and in 1860 the Kowloon Peninsula and Stonecutters Island were added after the Second Opium War. In 1898 Britain obtained from the Qing a 99-year lease of the New Territories, rent-free, as a compensatory concession after France obtained a lease at Guangzhouwan. The lease's end in 1997 set the deadline. In March 1979 Governor Murray MacLehose raised the issue with Deng Xiaoping, who said that Hong Kong held a special status that would continue to be respected.

Formal negotiations began in September 1982, when Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Governor Edward Youde went to Beijing to meet Premier Zhao Ziyang and Deng. The first phase turned on sovereignty. China said it would resume sovereignty and administration in 1997, by force if necessary, and proposed a special administrative region run by local residents with existing systems kept for 50 years. Talks stalled until Britain conceded sovereignty over the entire territory, and a British attempt to extend its administration was rejected. After the Hong Kong dollar fell sharply on Black Saturday in September 1983, the British accepted in November that they would hold no authority after 1997.

A draft was initialled on 26 September 1984, and Thatcher and Zhao signed the treaty in the Great Hall of the People on 19 December 1984. Ratifications were exchanged on 27 May 1985, and both governments registered it at the United Nations on 12 June 1985. In the main text China declared it would resume sovereignty over the whole of Hong Kong on 1 July 1997, and Britain agreed to transfer it. A special administrative region would be autonomous in local affairs, and its economic, social and legal systems would remain basically unchanged.

Annex I listed 14 Chinese policies: a high degree of autonomy except in defence and diplomatic affairs, and the capitalist economy and civil liberties unchanged for 50 years, to be set out in the Basic Law. Annex II created the Joint Liaison Group, an advisory body, which ended in 2000. Annex III protected land leases, allowing extension to no later than 30 June 2047. Memoranda created a new nationality, British National (Overseas), without right of abode in the United Kingdom.

From 2014 the Chinese and Hong Kong governments stated that the Declaration had no continuing legal effect, and in 2017 China called it a historical document. The United Kingdom and the G7 maintained that it remained valid. After the national security legislation of 2020 and the election changes of 2021 the United Kingdom declared China in a state of ongoing non-compliance, and China rejected such accusations as foreign interference.
sino-french-war: French interest in northern Vietnam dated from the late 18th century. France began its colonial campaign in 1858 and formed the colony of Cochinchina in 1862. French explorers hoped the Red River would give a trade route to Yunnan, but the Black Flag Army, a private army led by Liu Yongfu, taxed its trade heavily. In 1873 Lieutenant Francis Garnier attacked northern Vietnam beyond his instructions and was killed by the Black Flags at Hanoi, and in 1882 Commandant Henri Rivière stormed the citadel of Hanoi against his orders.

Vietnam, long a tributary of China, asked for help. China armed the Black Flags and covertly opposed the French, and in 1882 Chinese regular armies occupied Lạng Sơn, Bắc Ninh and other towns. On 20 August 1883 Admiral Amédée Courbet stormed the forts at Thuận An and forced the Treaty of Huế, placing Tonkin under French protection. Talks between France and China in 1883 failed.

Negotiations broke down in mid-August 1884. On 23 August Courbet's squadron destroyed China's Fujian fleet at Fuzhou in a two-hour engagement, sinking nine Chinese ships in less than an hour. Chinese losses may have amounted to 3,000 dead, while French losses were minimal. Neither country declared war. The defeat brought patriotic fervour in China, marred by attacks on foreigners.

In Tonkin, General Brière de l'Isle beat off a Chinese invasion of the Red River Delta in the Kép Campaign of October 1884. French troops shot or bayoneted scores of wounded Chinese soldiers after Kép, and prisoners were rarely taken by either side. On 23 February 1885 General de Négrier won the Battle of Đồng Đăng. The French later withdrew in haste from Lạng Sơn, which Qing forces held by early April. In Taiwan they occupied Keelung but advanced no further in seven months. Fighting ended on 4 April 1885.

The peace treaty of June 1885 gave France control of Annam and Tonkin. The French evacuated Formosa and the Pescadores and dropped demands for an indemnity. In 1887 Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin and Cambodia were joined in French Indochina, and Laos followed after 1893. French pacification of Tonkin lasted about a decade, with Liu Yongfu's forces and Cần Vương insurgents still fighting.

In France the war ended Jules Ferry's career, and his successor Henri Brisson resigned after the Tonkin Debate of December 1885, in which Clemenceau and other opponents of expansion nearly won a withdrawal. The Chamber voted the 1886 credits by 274 votes to 270. Some Chinese commanders protested the end of the fighting, and the war strengthened the dominance of Empress Dowager Cixi over the Qing government.
sino-indian-war: China and India shared a long border with several disputed regions. At its western end lies Aksai Chin, about 38,000 square kilometres, which India considered part of Ladakh and China part of Xinjiang. At its eastern end China claimed the North-East Frontier Agency, about 90,000 square kilometres, administered by India. The two fronts lay roughly 1,000 kilometres apart. India recognised the Johnson Line in the west and the McMahon Line in the east, and China did not. The western boundary goes back to the conquest of Ladakh by Raja Gulab Singh in 1834 and the British transfer of Jammu and Kashmir in 1846. China built a road through Aksai Chin linking Tibet and Xinjiang, which was one of the triggers of the conflict.

After the Tibetan uprising of 1959, when India granted asylum to the 14th Dalai Lama, border skirmishes increased. Talks between officials in 1960, following an agreement between Nehru and Zhou Enlai, failed. In 1961 China began patrolling along the McMahon Line, and India answered with a forward policy of setting up outposts behind Chinese troops. In June 1962 India set up the Dhola Post below Thagla Ridge, and in August China began occupying positions on the ridge.

China abandoned attempts at a peaceful settlement on 20 October 1962 and launched simultaneous offensives on both fronts. In the east, Chinese forces overran Indian positions at Namka Chu and Tawang. In the west they took the Chip Chap Valley and Pangong Lake. After a lull of three weeks, they resumed the offensive on 14 November and captured Se La, Bomdila and Gurung Hill in the east, while the battle of Rezang La in the west cost both sides heavy casualties.

The fighting was mountain warfare, with large-scale combat at altitudes above 5,000 metres. It took place entirely on land, with no naval or air assets, and neither side declared war or broke off diplomatic relations. China declared a unilateral ceasefire on 20 November 1962 and announced a withdrawal to its pre-war position, the effective China–India border.

The war was a major military and political setback in India. India rapidly modernised and expanded its armed forces and strengthened its border defences, and it reassessed its policy towards China. The conflict permanently damaged relations between the two states. As the Sino-Soviet split deepened, the Soviet Union supported India with the sale of military hardware, and India turned to the Soviets for aid because the United States and the United Kingdom refused to sell it advanced weapons.
sino-soviet-split: During the Second Sino-Japanese War, Joseph Stalin ordered Mao Zedong to cooperate with Chiang Kai-shek against Japan, and after Japan's surrender the Chinese civil war resumed and the communists won by 1949. In 1950 Mao and Stalin signed the Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance. Stalin gave a loan of 300 million dollars, promised military aid should Japan attack, and handed over the Chinese Eastern Railway, Port Arthur and Dalian; in return the People's Republic recognised the independence of the Mongolian People's Republic. Unlike the satellite states of Eastern Europe, China was not controlled by the Soviet Union.

In early 1956 relations began to deteriorate after Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin in his speech On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences. His turn from confrontation with the West to peaceful coexistence posed problems of credibility and authority for Mao, who had modelled his leadership on Stalin's. Mao called the Soviet policy revisionism.

In 1958 Chinese domestic politics took on an anti-Soviet tone, and China became more sensitive about sovereignty and foreign policy, especially over Taiwan. In 1959 Khrushchev met US President Dwight Eisenhower, the Soviet Union reneged on an agreement for technical aid for China's atomic bomb project, and it sided with India in the border dispute. In 1960 Mao expected Khrushchev to hold Eisenhower to account over a shot-down U-2 spy plane, and when Khrushchev did not win an apology at the Paris summit, the Chinese held rallies demanding military confrontation. By 1961 China formally denounced Soviet communism as the work of revisionist traitors.

From then communications were written. In June 1963 the Chinese Communist Party published its proposal on the general line of the international communist movement, attacking the Soviet Union by name, and the Soviets replied with an Open Letter. Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966, and Red Guards harassed the Soviet embassy in Beijing. After the Zhenbao Island border incident of 1969 the Soviet Union reportedly considered a large-scale nuclear strike against China, and the Chinese leadership was evacuated from Beijing before both sides returned to negotiations.

Talks over border issues began in October 1969 and lasted a decade. Both sides built up forces along the frontier, with an estimated 1 million to 1.2 million Soviet troops and as many as 1.5 million Chinese. The split turned the bipolar Cold War into a tripolar one and helped make possible President Richard Nixon's visit to China in 1972. It also weakened the Western idea of monolithic communism. In the 1970s the two states competed for influence in Africa, Asia and the Middle East, though both supported North Vietnam.
sino-vietnamese-war: The Chinese Communist Party and the Viet Minh had a long history, and communist China aided the Viet Minh against France. After Stalin's death in 1953 relations between the Soviet Union and China deteriorated into the Sino-Soviet split, and Vietnam did not support China against the Soviets. China viewed the growing Soviet-Vietnamese relationship with alarm and feared encirclement. Tensions by the mid-1970s also involved Vietnam's treatment of ethnic Chinese, border conflicts and Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia.

China supported the Maoist Khmer Rouge, who came to power under Pol Pot in 1975. After numerous border clashes, Vietnam invaded Cambodia on 25 December 1978, and by 7 January 1979 its forces had entered Phnom Penh. Border skirmishes rose from 125 in 1974 to 2,175 in 1978.

On 17 February 1979 a People's Liberation Army force of about 200,000 troops with about 200 tanks entered northern Vietnam, in the army's first major combat operation since the China-India War of 1962. It advanced in two directions, the eastern commanded by Xu Shiyou towards Cao Bằng, Lạng Sơn and Quảng Ninh, and the western commanded by Yang Dezhi towards Ha Tuyen, Hoang Lien Son and Lai Châu. Chinese forces quickly captured several cities near the border.

The Soviet Union took no direct military action but supplied intelligence and equipment and airlifted Vietnamese troops from Cambodia to the north. It also deployed troops on the Sino-Soviet and Mongolian-Chinese borders, though it refused to defend its ally directly. China had to keep most of its forces along its northern frontier as a deterrent. On 6 March China declared its punitive mission accomplished and withdrew.

Casualty figures are disputed. A Vietnamese agency claimed over 44,000 Chinese casualties, which Western analysts thought greatly inflated, and leaks from Chinese military sources indicate 6,954 Chinese dead. China held 1,636 Vietnamese prisoners and Vietnam 238 Chinese, and they were exchanged in May and June 1979. Vietnam continued to occupy Cambodia until 1989, so China did not achieve one of its stated aims, though it showed that the Soviet Union could not protect its Vietnamese ally.

In Vietnam the authorities expelled about 8,000 Hoa people from Hanoi to southern New Economic Zones in spring 1979 and expelled 20,468 members from the Communist Party. Border skirmishes continued through the 1980s, including a naval battle over the Spratly Islands in 1988. Relations were normalized in November 1991, and a border pact was signed in 1999.
sinoe-county: Sinoe is one of the fifteen counties of Liberia and is divided into seventeen districts, with Greenville as its capital. Its tropical lowland forests have mid-sized hills, valleys and watercourses, and receive very high rainfall, from 3,000 to 4,100 millimetres a year in two distinct seasons. The uplands suit rice cultivation, and the low-lying areas yield yams, cocoa, plantains, vegetables, rubber, coffee and sugarcane. The county has the third-largest area of Liberia's counties and the second-lowest population density after Gbarpolu County. Its flag is a green cross on a white background with the flag of Liberia in the top left corner.

The area was long settled by indigenous peoples. In 1835 more than 300 freed African Americans from the Prospect Hill Plantation in Mississippi settled there under the auspices of a chapter of the American Colonization Society, and the colony was called Mississippi-in-Africa.

Greenville was established in 1838 with freed Black Americans of the society and named after Judge James Green, who had helped bring a group of enslaved people from the Mississippi Delta to Liberia. The town became a prominent exporter of rubber, lumber and agricultural products. It was destroyed during the First Liberian Civil War but has been rebuilt, and boats connect it to Monrovia and Harper.

Sapo National Park, a national protected area of 180,436 hectares, lies in the county, along with the proposed Sankwehn Reserve of 80,348 hectares and two community forests, Nitrian and Nimopho. The districts are Bodae, Bokon, Butaw, Dugbe River, Greenville, Jaedae, Jaedepo, Juarzon, Kpayan, Kulu Shaw Boe, Plahn Nyarn, Pynes Town, Sanquin 1, 2 and 3, Seekon and Wedjah.
sinti: The Sinti are a subgroup of the Romani people, found mostly in Germany, France, Italy and Central Europe and numbering some 200,000. Like the broader Romani people, they originated in the northern Indian subcontinent. The origin of their name is disputed. Jan Kochanowski and many Sinti themselves hold that it derives from Sindhi, the name of the people of Sindh. Ian Hancock rejects the link on linguistic grounds and notes that the earliest samples of Sinte Romani use the name Kale. Yaron Matras argued that Sinti is a term in use only from the 18th century, and Ronald Lee thought it probably comes from the German Reisende, travellers.

The Sinti reached Austria and Germany in the Late Middle Ages and divided into two groups, the Eftavagarja, the Seven Caravans, and the Estraxarja, those from Austria. They were in Germany before 1540. The Eftavagarja spread to France and Portugal, where they are called Manouches, and to the Balkans; the Estraxarja went to Italy and Central Europe. They were traditionally itinerant and lived on the outskirts of communities. Their occupations included musician, gardener, waiter, iron picker and mechanic, and some played for nobles and in concert halls across Europe.

By 1899 the German police kept a central register of Sinti, Roma and Yenish. The Nazi regime treated them as racially inferior. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 applied to them, and from that year Sinti were interned in camps called Zigeunerlager.

In December 1938 Heinrich Himmler issued the decree Combating the Gypsy Plague, which ordered that they be registered and classified by race. Many were deported, and many were murdered. At Auschwitz-Birkenau Sinti and Roma were held in a special section, the so-called gypsy camp, which was closed on 2 August 1944, when about 4,000 of them were gassed that night. That day is commemorated as Roma and Sinti Holocaust Remembrance Day. In the camps Sinti wore a black triangle, marking them as asocial, or a brown one reserved for Sinti, Roma and Yenish.

From 1926 to 1973 the Swiss charity Pro Juventute, with the support of the authorities, took children of Yenish, Manouche and Sinti families from their parents and placed them in foster homes and institutions, a project called Kinder der Landstrasse. Today only a small share of Sinti remain unsettled. They speak Sinti-Manouche, a variety of Romani with strong German influence, and music remains central to their identity; gypsy jazz is popular among them.
sintra: Sintra is a town and municipality in the Greater Lisbon region, on the Portuguese Riviera. The Sintra Mountains, a granite massif ten kilometres long, rise abruptly between a plain to the north and the Tagus estuary and wind towards the Atlantic and Cabo da Roca, the most westerly point of continental Europe. Local tradition of astral cults called them the Mountain of the Moon, Promontorium Lunae. A micro-climate, fertile soils and the nearness of the estuary drew considerable early settlement, and the mountains support a park of dense foliage with a rich botanical diversity.

The earliest traces of human occupation, at Penha Verde, date to the early Paleolithic. Neolithic remains with decorated ceramics and microlithic flint tools from the 5th millennium BCE were found beside the chapel of the Moorish Castle. In July 1109 Count Henry reconquered the Castle of Sintra. A year before, Prince Sigurd the Crusader, son of Magnus III of Norway, had tried to take it on his way to the Holy Land, but failed. The castle surrendered definitively in November 1147, after Afonso Henriques, supported by Crusaders, conquered Lisbon in October, and he founded the Church of São Pedro de Canaferrim within its walls.

The royal palace was until the end of the 17th century one of the principal residences and summer estates of the court. John I decided there to conquer Ceuta in 1415, Afonso V was born and died there, and John II was acclaimed king in the palace in 1481. Royal visits declined during the war with Spain from 1640 to 1668 and as Mafra and Queluz rose in the 18th century. After the proclamation of the Portuguese Republic in 1910, development was promoted, wine growing at Colares was regulated, and parts of the medieval village were destroyed in 1911. The early decades of the 20th century were the time of Sintra's fastest urbanisation, helped by the rail link to Lisbon.

The municipality had 385,654 inhabitants in 2021 and covers 319.23 square kilometres. The historic centre of Sintra is known for its 19th-century Romanticist architecture, estates, gardens and royal palaces, and the town is classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its landmarks include the medieval Castle of the Moors, the Romanticist Pena National Palace and the Portuguese Renaissance Sintra National Palace. The area includes the Sintra-Cascais Nature Park.
sion-switzerland: Sion is a municipality in the Rhône valley and the capital of the canton of Valais and of the district of Sion. Its German name is Sitten and its Latin name was Sedunum. Landmarks include the Basilique de Valère and the Château de Tourbillon. Several neighbouring municipalities have merged into it: Bramois in 1968, Salins in 2013 and Les Agettes in 2017. It is one of the driest and sunniest areas of Switzerland.

Sion is one of the most important prehistoric sites in Europe. The oldest trace of settlement dates from about 6200 BCE, in the late Mesolithic, and early Neolithic farmers from the Mediterranean settled there around 5800 BCE. Their descendants buried the dead in stone cists with engraved stelae and later in large dry stone communal tombs such as the Dolmen of Le Petit-Chasseur. At the end of the 1st century BCE it was the capital of the Seduni, one of four Celtic tribes of the Valais, and the Romans conquered them in the 10s BCE.

The Roman Catholic diocese of Sion is the oldest in Switzerland. In the Middle Ages the citizens gained a limited independence through privileges granted by the bishop. An agreement of 1217 was the first written charter of freedom for the city, and in 1269 the burghers had their own council. In 1339 Emperor Louis the Bavarian raised Sion to a free imperial city. From the middle of the 14th century to 1475 the city was repeatedly attacked: it was pillaged by an army from Savoy in 1352, attacked in 1384 and 1418, and attacked again during the Burgundian Wars in 1475.

After the French invasion of Switzerland on 5 March 1798 the town was divided between supporters of the revolution, who raised a liberty pole on 10 March, and conservatives. A counter-revolutionary rising in the upper Valais was crushed by French and Vaudois troops on 17 May 1798, and Sion was plundered.

Archaeologists found six aligned standing stones in the Petit-Chasseur district in July 2019, near where about thirty such stones and the dolmens were found in 1960. Three were carved, and the largest, of about two tonnes, appears to represent a male figure in geometrically decorated clothing. Most residents speak French as their first language. Sion has an airfield for civilian and military use that serves as a base for air rescue.
sipahi: The sipahi were the professional Turkish heavy cavalry of the Ottoman Empire. They were taken over from the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum and developed into a standing cavalry force at the end of the 14th century. There were two kinds. The provincial tımarlı sipahi held land grants called tımars and made up most of the Ottoman army, while the kapıkulu sipahi were salaried household troops, serving beside the Janissaries. The irregular light cavalry known as akıncı, or raiders, were not counted as sipahi. The tımar system was standardised in the second half of the 15th century and had its origin in the Byzantine pronoia.

A tımar included arable land that the state owned and that the sipahi supervised in return for collecting taxes, keeping order and serving in the army. The sipahi received no salary. Peasants had the right to farm the land and had to work the sipahi's own plot, the çift, for a number of days. Tımars were small units; a ziamet was a larger holding for officers, and a has the largest, held by the highest-ranking commanders. A sipahi was bound to join campaigns when the sultan called, bringing a number of armed retainers, the cebelu, according to his revenue. Failure to appear meant losing the tımar, while distinction in battle could enlarge it.

In war the sipahis and their retainers gathered under their regimental beys, who gathered under the sanjakbeys and then the beylerbeys. Both flanks of the classical Ottoman army consisted of tımarlı cavalry, with Janissary infantry and artillery in the centre. The cavalry were the mobile striking arm, opening with skirmishes, charging weaker or isolated units and withdrawing when faced with heavy cavalry, and drawing enemy horse away from its infantry. A sipahi carried a composite bow, a sabre, a spear and a shield. The kapıkulu cavalry had six divisions, among them the Sipahis, the Silahdars and the Ulufecis, all paid quarterly.

The kapıkulu sipahis considered themselves superior to the Janissaries, who were officially slaves recruited through the devşirme, and a Turkish proverb says that horsemen do not mutiny. From the middle of the 16th century the Janissaries gained importance, but the sipahis remained a factor in the empire's economy and politics; in the early years of Sultan Murad IV they were, with the Janissaries, the de facto rulers. In 1826 they helped Sultan Mahmud II disband the Janissaries after a revolt, and two years later he revoked their privileges too. Older sipahis kept their tımar lands for life, and younger ones joined the new army as cavalry. The French army later adopted the term Spahi for cavalry units in its colonial armies.
siraj-ud-daulah: Siraj ud-Daulah was born in 1733 to Mirza Muhammad Hashim and Amina Begum, the youngest daughter of Alivardi Khan. He was raised at the Nawab's palace with the education suited to a future Nawab and accompanied Alivardi on campaigns against the Marathas in 1746. In 1750 he revolted against his grandfather and seized Patna, but he soon surrendered and was forgiven.

Siraj succeeded his maternal grandfather in April 1756, at the age of 23. His nomination aroused the jealousy of his aunt Ghaseti Begum, Mir Jafar, Jagat Seth and his cousin Shaukat Jang, the governor of Purnia, who was killed in a clash with him. Siraj seized Ghaseti Begum's wealth and replaced Mir Jafar as paymaster of the army with Mir Madan. He resented the East India Company's growing presence in Bengal and charged it with strengthening Fort William without approval, abusing trade privileges and sheltering some of his officers.

When the Company went on strengthening Fort William despite his order to stop, he took Calcutta in June 1756, briefly renaming it Alinagar. The British captives were put in a prison cell, and in the confusion of command they were left there overnight and many died. In the parliamentary inquiry into Robert Clive, Sir William Meredith cleared Siraj of any blame for the Black Hole.

A conspiracy formed at his court, among them Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh, Yar Lutuf Khan, Omichund and Jagat Seth, and the Company signed a treaty with Mir Jafar on 4 June 1757 to put him on the throne. At Plassey on 23 June Mir Jafar advised Siraj to halt the fighting for the day, and when the soldiers turned back to camp Clive attacked and the army fell into disorder. Siraj fled to Murshidabad and then tried to escape towards Patna by boat, but was captured. Mir Jafar's son Mir Miran ordered his execution, carried out on 2 July 1757. His tomb is at Khushbagh, Murshidabad.

He has a positive reputation in India, Bangladesh and Pakistan for opposing the start of British rule, and as the independence movement grew he was counted with Tipu Sultan among those who resisted imperial aggression. The historian Sushil Chaudhary argued that his villainous image is a misrepresentation.
siret: Between 1211 and 1225 the Teutonic Knights built a fortress on a hill near Siret. The town and the castle were destroyed by the Tatars in 1241. According to some historical sources the first document naming Siret dates from 1339, and the town appears as a Russian city in Wallachia in the List of Russian Cities, Far and Near, compiled between 1370 and 1390. In the late fourteenth century it was the capital of the Principality of Moldavia.

Latin missionaries were welcomed early: a monastery was founded at Siret in 1340. Prince Lațcu, who ruled from 1365 to 1373, promised Rome the conversion of himself and his people and asked Pope Urban V to found a Latin diocese in the capital. It was erected in 1371, at first directly subject to the Holy See and from 1412 a suffragan of the Archbishopric of Lviv. It declined from 1388, when Prince Petru moved the capital to Suceava, and from about 1418 the Holy See erected a new Moldavian bishopric at Baia, which inherited its territory.

Siret lies at the north-eastern edge of Suceava County, on the right bank of the Siret River and 2 kilometres from the border with Ukraine. It is one of the main border crossings in northern Romania, and its railway changes from standard gauge to broad gauge, so that Siret is one of the few places in Romania with equipment to change the gauge of wagons. It had 6,708 inhabitants at the 2021 census, and most are Romanian Orthodox. A Jewish community, recorded by the mid-sixteenth century, made up 14 per cent of the population in 1930; in June 1941 its members were deported to Transnistria, where more than 700 died.
sirhind: Sirhind is a twin city of Fatehgarh Sahib in Punjab, India, and hosts the municipal council of Fatehgarh Sahib district. According to popular belief its name comes from Sar-i Hind, meaning the Frontier of Hind, because the Mughal emperors saw it as the gateway to Hindustan. In the 2011 census Sirhind-Fatehgarh had a population of 60,852.

The Sanskrit treatise Brihat Samhita of Varahamihira (505-587) mentions the area as Satudar Desh, and the place was later inhabited by a tribe of Sairindhas, from whom the present name is said to come. The Chinese traveller Huan Tsang, who visited India in the seventh century, describes Sirhind as the capital of the district of Shitotulo, or Shatadru, the present-day River Sutlej. In the 12th century it came under the Chauhan Rajputs of Delhi and became a military outpost of Prithvi Raj Chauhan (1168-1192). Jasrat Khokhar besieged it in 1421 but failed to take it.

Under the Mughal Empire Sirhind became a provincial capital controlling the Lahore-Delhi highway and the headquarters of the Mughal administration in Eastern Punjab. Many European travellers described its splendours, and it developed into a cultural centre known for dozens of saints, scholars, poets, historians, calligraphers and scribes. Muslims honour Shaykh Ahmad al-Farūqī al-Sirhindī (1564-1624), a Hanafi jurist and a prominent member of the Naqshbandi Sufi order, who is called Imām-e-Rabbānī. It is said that in its heyday the city had 360 mosques, as well as gardens, tombs, caravansarais and wells.

Many buildings from the Mughal period survive, including the Aam Khas Bagh, the Tomb of Mir-i-Miran, the Tomb of Ustad and Shagird and the shrine of Syed Ahmad Sirhindi at Rauza Sharif. The Jahaji Haveli is the haveli of Diwan Todar Mal. The town also has shrines, among them Gurudwara Fatehgarh Sahib, Gurdwara Jyoti Sarup and Gurdwara Shahid Ganj, as well as a Jain temple at Attewali. Sri Guru Granth Sahib World University is among its educational institutions.
sirimavo-bandaranaike: Sirimavo Bandaranaike was born Sirima Ratwatte on 17 April 1916 at Ratnapura in British Ceylon, into a Sinhalese Kandyan aristocratic family. Her father, Barnes Ratwatte, was a native headman and politician, and her mother, Rosalind Hilda Mahawalatenne Kumarihamy, was an informal Ayurvedic physician. She was educated in Anglican, English-medium schools but remained a Buddhist and spoke Sinhala as well as English.

On 2 October 1940 she married S. W. R. D. Bandaranaike, in a wedding the press called the wedding of the century. They had two daughters, Sunethra and Chandrika, and a son, Anura. As the wife of the founder of the Sri Lanka Freedom Party, she acted as hostess and informal adviser and worked on the welfare of rural women and girls. After his assassination in 1959 she was persuaded to lead the party.

The Freedom Party won the July 1960 election by a landslide, and on 21 July 1960 she was sworn in as prime minister, the first woman to hold the post anywhere. As she was not a member of Parliament, she was appointed to the Senate. In her first term she nationalised banking, foreign trade, insurance, the petroleum industry and funded parochial schools, and she took control of seven newspapers. Her government survived a plot by military officers in 1962. She followed a policy of non-alignment, attended the first four summits of the Non-Aligned Movement and chaired it in 1976–1977.

The 1965 election made her Leader of the Opposition, and the United Front won a large majority in 1970. Her second government faced an insurrection by the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna in 1971, and in May 1972 a new constitution replaced Ceylon with the Republic of Sri Lanka. It recognised the supremacy of Buddhism, made Sinhala the only official language and abolished the Senate. In 1975 she created an agency on women's issues, later the Ministry of Women and Child Affairs. She lost heavily in 1977. A 1978 constitution introduced a presidential system, and she returned as prime minister in 1994 under her daughter Chandrika Kumaratunga, who had become president.
Bandaranaike died on 10 October 2000 of a heart attack, on the day of a parliamentary election in which she had been casting her vote. Two days of national mourning were declared.

She served more than seventeen years as prime minister across three terms. Her policies of nationalisation and of Sinhala as the official language remained points of dispute, and her language policy aggravated discontent among the Tamil population. Her children also held prominent public positions, and the Bandaranaike family became one of the leading political families of the country.
sirmium: Sirmium stood on the Sava river, on the site of modern Sremska Mitrovica in Vojvodina, 55 kilometres west of Belgrade. Archaeologists have found traces of organised human life there from the fifth millennium BCE. The city was first mentioned in the 4th century BCE and was inhabited by Illyrians and Celts, among them the Amantini and the Scordisci. Its name means flowing water or wetland, from its position by the river, and the modern region of Syrmia takes its name from it.

The Roman proconsul Marcus Vinicius took Sirmium around 14 BCE, with the Scordisci as allies. It became a Roman colony in the 1st century CE, and Trajan, Marcus Aurelius and Claudius II prepared campaigns there. In 103 it became the capital of Pannonia Inferior. With the Tetrarchy of 293 it was one of the four capitals of the empire, with Trier, Mediolanum and Nicomedia, and the capital of Galerius. From 318 to 379 it was capital of the prefecture of Illyricum. It had an imperial palace, a mint, a hippodrome, theatres, baths and luxury villas, and Ammianus Marcellinus called it the glorious mother of cities.

Ten Roman emperors were born in or near the city, among them Claudius II, Aurelian, Probus, Maximian, Constantius II and Gratian, and Theodosius I became emperor there in 378. Sirmium had a Christian community by the third century, and its first known bishop, Irenaeus, was martyred in 304. From 335 it was a stronghold of the Arian movement, and four synods on the Arian controversy met there between 347 and 358. The Huns conquered the city in 441, and later the Ostrogoths and Gepids held it; the Pannonian Avars conquered and destroyed it in 582.

Remains of Sirmium lie beneath Sremska Mitrovica, and the site is protected as an archaeological Site of Exceptional Importance. Excavations have uncovered a palace at Glac, more than eighty altars from a sanctuary of Jupiter found in 1971, eight early Christian churches, and a hippodrome about 450 metres long under the town centre.
sisak: Sisak lies in central Croatia, 57 km south-east of Zagreb, where the Kupa, Sava and Odra rivers meet, and is usually considered the point where the Posavina, the Sava basin, begins. It is the administrative centre of Sisak-Moslavina County, Croatia's biggest river port and a centre of river shipping. Before Roman rule the region was Celtic and Illyrian, and the settlement was called Segestica or Segesta. Roman rule gave it the name Siscia. Roman writers describe it as a great town on an island formed by the Sava and two other rivers, the Colapis and the Odra, which a canal dug by Tiberius completed.

Siscia was strongly fortified from the first. After Tiberius captured it, in the reign of Augustus, it became one of the most important places in Pannonia, a centre of commerce and the base from which Augustus and Tiberius carried out their undertakings against the Pannonians and Illyrians. Under Septimius Severus it received fresh colonists. The town held an imperial mint that struck coins under a series of emperors between 262 and 383 CE. The Christian martyr Quirinus of Sescia, the presumed first bishop, was tortured in Diocletian's persecution and is the patron saint of Sisak. When Diocletian divided Pannonia, Siscia became capital of Pannonia Savia.

In the Middle Ages Braslav of Lower Pannonia reigned from Sisak until he was killed in the Hungarian invasion around 898, and Duke Tomislav reclaimed it soon after. In 1593 Croats, Austrians and Carniolans defeated the Ottomans there at the Battle of Sisak, led by the Croatian Ban Thomas Erdődy. Even so, the Ottomans took the town on 24 August 1593, and on 11 August 1594 they fled and set the fortress on fire as a Habsburg and Croat army approached. Until the late 19th century the Kupa divided the town into Civil Sisak, part of the Kingdom of Croatia, and Military Sisak, part of the Croatian Military Frontier.

During World War II the Ustaše government of Croatia set up the Sisak children's concentration camp for Serbian, Jewish and Romani children, where an estimated 1,160 to 1,600 children died. On 22 June 1941 the 1st Sisak Partisan Detachment, with 79 members, was formed in the Brezovica Forest, the first Partisan armed anti-fascist unit in occupied Yugoslavia.

The well-preserved 16th-century triangular fortress of the Old Town, now a museum, is the main destination for visitors. Other landmarks are the Baroque palace of Mali Kaptol, the classicist Veliki Kaptol and the brick Old Bridge over the Kupa. Croatia's largest oil refinery stands in Sisak.
sisavang-vong: Sisavang Vong was born as Prince Khao on 14 July 1885 in the Golden Palace of Luang Prabang, the eldest surviving son of King Zakarine and Queen Consort Thong-sy. His father reigned there under French colonial authority. As a child he studied at the Lycee Chasseloup-Laubat in Saigon and afterwards at the Ecole Coloniale, and then returned to Laos.

His father died on 26 March 1904, and Khao became heir apparent on 15 April 1904. He ascended the throne at the Old Royal Palace in Luang Prabang and was crowned on 4 March 1905, taking the courtesy name Sisavangvong in keeping with Lao tradition. He was the last ruler of the Lao Kingdom of Luang Prabang and the founding king of the Kingdom of Laos.

In the early years of his reign the French built the Royal Palace of Luang Prabang as his residence. He united several provinces under his authority: Houaphan in 1931, Houakhong, Xiengkhouang and Vientiane in 1942, and Champassak and Sayboury in 1946. Throughout his reign he supported the French administration in Laos.

In late 1945 he briefly ruled as king of a Japanese puppet state of Luang Prabang, but he refused to collaborate with Lao nationalists, and the Lao Issara removed him from power for his pro-French stance when they declared the nation's independence. The French regained control in April 1946 and restored him as king. It was the first time in almost 250 years that a Lao monarch ruled the whole of Laos. His reign lasted 55 years.

When he fell ill Sisavang Vong appointed his son, Crown Prince Savang Vatthana, as regent, and the son succeeded him after his death in 1959. He was cremated and buried at Vat That Luang in Luang Prabang in 1961. The funeral procession included a royal funeral carriage, a wooden hearse 12 metres high decorated with a carved seven-headed snake, and many dignitaries attended the state funeral, among them Prince Bhanubandhu Yugala, who represented Thailand. Sisavangvong University was founded in his honour but was closed in 1975, when the communist regime took control of Laos. Statues of him survive in Luang Prabang and Vientiane, showing him giving the people a constitution.
sisebut: Sisebut ruled Hispania, Gallaecia and Septimania from 612 until his death in February 621.
