The Chronicle of Fredegar reports that before becoming king he captured Cantabria from the Franks, a puzzling entry, since the region was already Visigothic under Leovigild. As king he campaigned successfully against the remnants of Byzantine power in Spania, strengthened Visigothic control over the Basques and Cantabrians, built friendly relations with the Lombards of Italy and reinforced the fleet that Leovigild had established. Nearly all the territory in the Iberian peninsula that the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian had seized was recovered, except the Algarve. He struck coins at Recopolis, as other Visigothic kings did, and his political practice recalled late Roman traditions.

Sisebut was devoted to Chalcedonian Christianity. On his accession in 612 he forced his Jewish subjects to convert, and in 616 he ordered that those who refused be punished with the lash. The historian Herwig Wolfram places these measures within a broader tradition of imperial legislation that had the approval of the Church Fathers. He also consecrated churches, among them the martyrial basilica of St Leocadia at Toledo in 618.

He was closely associated with Isidore of Seville and is presented as the author of a Latin poem on astronomy, the Carmen de Luna, dedicated to a friend identified as Isidore. The historian Chris Wickham compares him with Alfred the Great as a king with a reputation as a writer, though he adds that Sisebut was otherwise undistinguished apart from his persecution of the Jews. His son succeeded him as Reccared II.
sistan: Sistan, also written Sakastan and Sijistan, is a largely desert region of south-eastern Iran that extends across the border into south-western Afghanistan. It corresponds mostly to the Achaemenid region of Drangiana. The Helmand River runs through it and empties into Lake Hamun, which forms part of the border between the two countries. Its name derives from Sakastan, after the Saka, a Scythian people who migrated to the Iranian plateau and the Indus valley between the second century BCE and the first century CE. In the Shahnameh the region is also called Zabulistan, and it is the homeland of the hero Rostam.

In prehistoric times the Jiroft civilisation covered parts of Sistan, and the third-millennium BCE city of Shahr-e Sukhteh is its best-known site. The region fell to the Achaemenid Empire after 550 BCE, and Alexander the Great annexed it in the fourth century BCE. After passing through Seleucid, Mauryan, Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek hands, it was overrun by the Saka, and around 100 BCE Mithridates II of Parthia defeated them and made Sakastan part of the Parthian Empire. The Sasanian Empire formed the province around 240 under Shapur I, with Zrang as its capital, and governed it through princes and later through a Karenid governor.

Yazdegerd III, the last Sasanian king, fled to Sakastan in the mid-640s. The Rashidun Caliphate took it after a campaign under Rabi ibn Ziyad Harithi, when its governor Aparviz made peace in return for heavy tribute. In the 860s the Saffarid dynasty emerged in Sistan and conquered most of the Islamic East, until the Samanids checked it in 900. Mahmud of Ghazni ended Saffarid rule in 1002. Mongols sacked the region in 1222, and the Mihrabanid dynasty ruled it from 1236 as vassals of the Ilkhanate and later of Tamerlane, the Timurids and the Safavids.

Between 1747 and 1872 Persia and Afghanistan contested Sistan. A boundary mission led by General Frederick Goldsmid assigned most of it to Persia, and a second commission under Arthur Mac Mahon, in 1903 to 1905, defined the border more precisely. The Iranian part belongs to the province of Sistan and Baluchestan, and the Afghan part to Nimruz province, whose capital is Zaranj. In Zoroastrian tradition Lake Hamun keeps the seed of Zoroaster, and in the Sasanian era it was one of two pilgrimage sites for followers of that religion.
sisteron: Sisteron stands on the banks of the Durance just below the point where the Buëch and the Sasse join it, in a narrow gap between two long mountain ridges. This position has earned it the name Gateway to Provence, and although the town is small it is signed as a navigation point as far away as Grenoble. It lies 135 km from Marseille and 135 km from Grenoble, 180 km from Nice and 40 km from Forcalquier.

The site has been inhabited for about 4,000 years, and the Romans used the route through it, as a Latin inscription in the rocks near the road to Authon shows. It escaped the barbarian invasions that followed the fall of Rome but was ravaged by the Saracens. The Counts of Forcalquier first fortified it in the 11th century, and it later formed the northern boundary of the domain of the Counts of Provence. In 1483, under Louis XI, Sisteron rejoined the kingdom of France.

Around that time seven plagues killed two thirds of the population. Between 1562 and 1594 Protestants and Catholics fought over the town and its citadel, which was besieged twice, and the town walls were built in these years. The plague returned in 1630 and typhus in 1744. The town stayed Royalist during the French Revolution, and when Napoleon passed north after escaping from Elba in 1815 it ignored him and let him through. On 15 August 1944 French and American bombers tried to destroy the bridges over the Durance in unfavourable weather, and bombs that fell on the town killed about 100 people and damaged the citadel; the bridges were destroyed two days later.

The citadel and the 12th-century former cathedral of Notre Dame des Pommiers and Saint Thyrse are the main buildings. The town has three museums, including the Citadel Museum and the Baden-Powell Scout Museum. The A51 motorway now bypasses the town, and a railway line runs from Marseille to Briançon and Grenoble.
sistine-chapel: The chapel stands on the site of an older Cappella Maggiore, recorded in 1368, which by the time of its demolition was ruinous, with its walls leaning. The present building was designed by Baccio Pontelli for Pope Sixtus IV and built under the supervision of Giovannino de Dolci. Its proportions follow those of the original: the length divided by three gives the width and by two the height, and there were six windows down each side and two at each end. The chapel is about 35 metres long and 14 metres wide, and its exterior is plain, since it is entered only from rooms within the Apostolic Palace.

The first mass was held on 15 August 1483, the Feast of the Assumption, when the chapel was consecrated and dedicated to the Virgin Mary. Its main function is as the chapel of the Papal Chapel, one of the two bodies of the papal household, and a permanent choir, the Sistine Chapel Choir, sings there without instruments.

The side walls carry two paired cycles, the Life of Moses and the Life of Christ, commissioned in 1480 and painted in 1481–1482 by Domenico Ghirlandaio, Sandro Botticelli, Pietro Perugino, Cosimo Rosselli and their workshops. Above them is a gallery of popes, and below them are painted hangings. The ceiling was first painted blue and studded with gold stars.

Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to repaint the ceiling, which he did between 1508 and 1512. The first plan was for the twelve apostles, but Michelangelo obtained a free hand. He painted nine scenes from Genesis, twelve prophets and sibyls, and the Ancestors of Christ, with more than three hundred figures in all. He built his own scaffold of a platform on brackets, after the one designed by Donato Bramante proved flawed, and painted standing. Years later, finishing in 1541, he painted the Last Judgement on the altar wall for Clement VII and Paul III. Its nude figures drew accusations of obscenity, and Daniele da Volterra later covered the genitalia. In 1515 Pope Leo X commissioned Raphael to design ten tapestries for the lower walls.

The Sistine Chapel is the venue of papal conclaves. The first held there was that of 6 to 11 August 1492, which elected Alexander VI. A chimney is fitted in the roof during a conclave, and white smoke signals that a pope has been elected, while black smoke shows that no candidate has received the required two-thirds vote.

A restoration of the ceiling began on 7 November 1984, and the chapel reopened to the public on 8 April 1994. The cleaning removed layers of smoke and earlier restoration, and some critics feared that it was too severe and had taken away work Michelangelo added on dry plaster.
sistine-madonna: The Sistine Madonna, also called the Madonna di San Sisto, was commissioned in 1512 by Pope Julius II in honour of his late uncle, Pope Sixtus IV, as an altarpiece for the church of the Benedictine monastery of San Sisto in Piacenza, with which the Rovere family had a long-standing relationship. The commission required that the painting show both Saint Sixtus and Saint Barbara. It was one of the last Madonnas painted by Raphael. Giorgio Vasari called it a truly rare and extraordinary work. Tradition holds that Antonio da Correggio, on first seeing it, cried out that he too was a painter.

The oil painting on canvas measures 265 by 196 centimetres. The Madonna, holding the Christ Child and flanked by Saint Sixtus and Saint Barbara, stands on clouds before dozens of obscured putti. Two distinctive winged putti rest on their elbows beneath her. Pigment analysis shows the usual pigments of the Renaissance, among them malachite mixed with orpiment in the green drapery, natural ultramarine mixed with lead white in the Madonna's blue robe, and lead-tin yellow, vermilion and lead white in Saint Barbara's yellow sleeve.

The putti are well known in their own right and have been printed on stamps, postcards and wrapping paper. Stories grew around them: one tells that the children of Raphael's model came to watch him paint and that he added them as he saw them.

In 1754 Augustus III of Poland bought the painting for 110,000 to 120,000 francs, the highest price paid for any painting for many decades, and it went to Dresden. Johann Joachim Winckelmann praised it in his history of ancient art of 1764, and a legend of "Raphael's Dream" arose in the late 18th century. It became an icon of German Romanticism and influenced Goethe, Wagner and Nietzsche. Dostoyevsky called it a revelation of the human spirit. In 1855 it was given a room of its own in the new museum designed by Gottfried Semper.

It survived the bombing of Dresden in the war, stored in a tunnel in Saxon Switzerland. The Red Army took it to Moscow, where it was shown at the Pushkin Museum in 1946. In 1955, after the death of Joseph Stalin, the Soviets returned it to Germany. Western reports that it had been damaged in storage were denied by Soviet witnesses. It hangs in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister in Dresden, which marked its 500th anniversary in 2012.
sita: The name Sita derives from the Sanskrit word sīta, meaning furrow. According to the Ramayana, Janaka found her while ploughing as part of a yajna and adopted her. The word was a poetic term for fertility and the blessings of settled agriculture, and the Sita of the epic may have been named after an older Vedic goddess Sita, mentioned once in the Rigveda as an earth goddess who blesses the land with good crops.

Other versions of her birth exist. In the Mahabharata's Ramopkhyana and in the Paumachariya of Vimala Suri she is Janaka's biological daughter, and Fr. Camille Bulcke held that this was the authentic version of the Valmiki Ramayana and that the story of the furrow was inserted later.

In the epic, Sita chooses Rama, the prince of Ayodhya, in a svayamvara, a ceremony at which Janaka set the condition that she would marry only a prince able to string Shiva's bow, the Pinaka. Rama broke it in two. When Kaikeyi, one of King Dasharatha's queens, used two boons to make her son Bharata king and send Rama into exile for 14 years, Sita and Rama's brother Lakshmana willingly gave up the palace and went with him. In the Dandaka forest Ravana, the Rakshasa king of Lanka, abducted her and held her in the garden of Ashoka Vatika until Rama rescued her and slew Ravana.

After the war, in some versions, Rama asks her to undergo an Agni Pariksha, an ordeal of fire, to prove her chastity. In other versions an illusion, Maya Sita, created by Agni, was abducted in her place while the real Sita hid in the fire. Back in Ayodhya, when a man questioned her fidelity, Rama, to preserve the dignity of the kingdom, sent the pregnant Sita into the forest. She sheltered at Sage Valmiki's ashram and gave birth to twin sons, Kusha and Lava. Years later she reunited them with their father and returned to the womb of her mother, the earth.

In Hinduism Sita is regarded as an avatar of the goddess Lakshmi and as the goddess of beauty and devotion, and she is the chief goddess of the Ramanandi Sampradaya. Her birthday is observed every year at Sita Navami. The Sita Upanishad, attached to the Atharva Veda, identifies her with primordial nature and names her three powers: will, action and knowledge. Mithila art, which originated at her birthplace, depicts her marriage to Rama.
sitka: Sitka lies on the west side of Baranof Island and the south half of Chichagof Island, in the Alexander Archipelago of the Pacific Ocean, in the Alaska Panhandle. Its name comes from the Tlingit Sheetʼká, a contraction of Shee Atʼiká, meaning people on the edge of Shee, Shee being the Tlingit name for Baranof Island. Mount Edgecumbe, a stratovolcano of about 3,200 feet, stands on Kruzof Island about 24 km to the west. Under Russian rule the settlement was called New Archangel.

Russian explorers settled Old Sitka in 1799 and named it the Fort of Archangel Michael. Alexander Baranov, governor of Russian America, arrived under the auspices of the Russian-American Company, a trading company chartered by Emperor Paul I. In June 1802 Tlingit warriors destroyed the original settlement and killed many of the Russians, and only a few escaped. Baranov had to pay a ransom of 10,000 rubles to Captain Barber of the British ship Unicorn for the safe return of the surviving settlers.

The transfer ceremony for the Alaska Purchase took place at Sitka on 18 October 1867. The agreement to buy Alaska had been made in April of that year, and the price was 7.2 million dollars. According to the account, Russia, which had lost the Crimean War in 1856, wished to sell before British Canadians tried to conquer the territory, and Secretary of State William Seward had long wanted to buy it.

In 1880 Sitka, with 916 residents, was the largest community in Alaska, of whom 540 were Tlingit, 219 Creole and 157 White. By 1890 Juneau had overtaken it. The Alaska Native Brotherhood was founded in Sitka in 1912 to address racism against Alaska Native people, and by 1914 it had built its hall on Katlian Street, named after a Tlingit war chief of the early Russian period. Sitka was incorporated as a city in 1913.

In 1937 the United States Navy established the first seaplane base in Alaska on Japonski Island, and in 1941 construction began on Fort Ray, an army garrison to protect it. The naval station was deactivated in June 1944. The Alaska Pulp Corporation, the first Japanese investment in the United States after the Second World War, began producing pulp in 1959 from the Tongass National Forest and closed in 1993.

Sitka is a unified city-borough, formed by incorporation in 2000, and covers a total area of 4,811 square miles, much of it water. Sitka National Historical Park lies within it, and the Tongass National Forest, one of several protected areas around it, borders it. The O'Connell Bridge, built in 1972, joins the town to Japonski Island.
sitting-bull: Sitting Bull was born on land later included in Dakota Territory. He was named Ȟoká Psíče, Jumping Badger, at birth, and nicknamed Húŋkešni, Slow, an allusion to his careful and unhurried nature. At 14 he joined a raid on a Crow camp and displayed bravery by counting coup on one of the Crow. His father then conferred his own name, Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake, roughly Buffalo Bull Who Sits Down, upon him, together with an eagle feather, a warrior's horse and a shield to mark his passage into manhood.

During Red Cloud's War of 1866 to 1868, Sitting Bull led war parties against Fort Berthold, Fort Stevenson and Fort Buford. He did not agree to the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, telling the missionary Pierre Jean De Smet, "I do not propose to sell any part of my country." Custer's 1874 expedition to the Black Hills announced gold and set off a gold rush. In November 1875 President Ulysses S. Grant ordered all Sioux bands outside the Great Sioux Reservation to move onto it, and bands gathered in a large camp around Sitting Bull, estimated at more than 10,000 people.

A week before the Battle of the Little Bighorn on 25 June 1876 he performed the Sun Dance and had a vision of soldiers falling into the camp. He did not take a direct military role in the battle but acted as a spiritual leader. Afterwards thousands more soldiers were sent to the area, and in May 1877 he led his band into Canada, near Wood Mountain, where James Morrow Walsh of the North-West Mounted Police became his friend. Hunger brought him back to surrender at Fort Buford on 19 July 1881. In 1885 he toured for four months with Buffalo Bill's Wild West.

As the Ghost Dance movement reached Standing Rock, Sitting Bull allowed dancers to gather at his camp, though he did not appear to dance. Fearing he would flee with them, the agent James McLaughlin ordered his arrest. At about 5:30 a.m. on 15 December 1890, 39 police officers and four volunteers approached his house. When he refused to comply, the police used force and the camp erupted; Lieutenant Bull Head fired into Sitting Bull's chest and Red Tomahawk shot him in the head. He was buried at Fort Yates, and in 1953 his Lakota family reburied what they believed to be his remains near Mobridge, South Dakota.
sivas: Sivas lies at an elevation of 1,278 metres in the broad valley of the Kızılırmak and is the seat of Sivas Province. It has long been a communications hub for the north-south and east-west trade routes to Iraq and Iran. When railways were built it became a junction of important lines linking Ankara, Kayseri, Samsun and Erzurum. The name is a truncated form of the Byzantine Greek Sivasteia, from the Koine Greek Sebasteia, meaning that it was named in honour of an emperor with the title Sebastos, the Greek equivalent of Augustus.

Little is known of the city before the Roman period. In 64 BCE Pompey the Great, reorganising Asia Minor after the Third Mithridatic War, founded a city there called Megalopolis. Coins suggest it was renamed Sebaste in the last years of the 1st century BCE. Under Diocletian it became capital of the province of Armenia Minor. In the 4th century it was the home of the bishops Saint Blaise and Saint Peter of Sebaste, and the place of martyrdom of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste. In 536 Justinian I made it the capital of Armenia Secunda and refortified it.

Sebasteia was the first important city plundered by Turkish tribes, in 1059. They hesitated before the unwalled city, mistaking the domes of its churches for the tents of a camp, and then burned it for eight days and killed a large part of its population. After the Battle of Manzikert in 1071 it came under the Danishmend dynasty.

The Seljuk ruler Mesud I sacked it in 1143, and in 1174 Kilij Arslan II captured it, after which it periodically served as capital of the Sultanate of Rum along with Iconium. Under Seljuk rule it was a trade centre on the Silk Road, with madrasas, four of which survive.

Bayezid I acquired the city for the Ottomans. Tamerlane's forces destroyed it in 1400, and the Ottomans retook it in 1408. In 1914 about a third of its 45,000 inhabitants were Armenians. From July 1915 its Christian community was exterminated by deportations and mass executions during the genocides of Armenians and of Greek Christians. The Sivas Congress met from 4 to 11 September 1919, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's position as chair of the executive committee of the national resistance was confirmed there.

Sivas is a city of central Turkey. Its economy has traditionally rested on agriculture, with rail repair shops and the making of rugs, bricks, cement and textiles. The surrounding region grows cereals and has large deposits of iron ore, which are worked at Divriği.
sivasagar: Sivasagar lies at an average elevation of 86.6 metres above sea level in Assam. It is known for its Ahom palaces and monuments and is today an important centre of the tea and oil industries. The Assam Trunk Road, National Highway 37, runs through the district, and Sibsagar Town railway station serves the town. It has several colleges, among them Sibsagar Commerce College and Bir Lachit Borphukan College, and Sibsagar University.

Tradition holds that the original name of the place was Kalansupar, after Kalansu Gohain, who lived in a village on the site where the tank now stands. In 1733 the Ahom queen Ambika Devi had a tank of 257 acres dug at the Ahom capital Rangpur. The place came to be called Sivpur from the Siva temple, the Siva Dol, built on its bank, and over time the name became Sibsagar.

The Ahom kingdom had its capital at Rangpur from 1699 to 1788, and the Ahoms ruled Assam for six centuries until the Burmese Konbaung dynasty overthrew their kingdom in 1819 and all but wiped out the ruling class. During the reign of Gaurinath Singha, from 1780 to 1795, a battle was fought against the Moamoria rebels near the tank. The British conquered the province in 1825 and annexed it completely in 1826, dividing it into three sub-divisions for administration.

A separate civil district of Sivasagar was declared in 1984, with its district judiciary set up in 1985. In the district most people speak Assamese, and there are villages of the Buddhist Khamyang and Turung peoples as well as small populations of Tiwas, Konyak, Meitei and Nocte; many Rajasthani families live in the city.
six-day-war: After the 1956 Suez Crisis, Egypt agreed to the stationing of a United Nations Emergency Force in the Sinai to ensure that all parties kept to the 1949 Armistice Agreements. In the following years there were many minor border clashes between Israel and its Arab neighbours, particularly Syria. In November 1966 Syria signed a mutual defence agreement with Egypt. In April 1967 a border incident led to an aerial engagement in which six Syrian jets were shot down.

In mid May the Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser mobilized 100,000 troops on the border with Israel and ordered the withdrawal of the UN peacekeepers. Eight days later he announced that the Straits of Tiran, Israel's only access to the Red Sea, would be closed to Israeli vessels; Israel had stated that this would be an act of war. On 30 May Egypt signed a defence pact with Jordan, and on 4 June Israel decided to go to war.

The war began on 5 June 1967 with Operation Focus, a surprise Israeli attack in which almost all of the air force's nearly 200 operational jets struck Egyptian airfields. Nearly all of Egypt's air force was destroyed, and Israel gained air supremacy. At the same time Israeli forces advanced into the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip, and by the fourth day Israel had occupied all of the Sinai. Jordan joined the fighting on the first morning with an attack on West Jerusalem. Syria largely stayed out for four days, then shelled northern Israel, and Israeli forces occupied the Golan Heights. Egypt and Jordan agreed to a ceasefire on 8 June.

Israel now held the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. Around 280,000 to 325,000 Palestinians left the West Bank and Gaza, and over 100,000 Syrians fled the Golan Heights. Egypt closed the Suez Canal from 1967 to 1975. On 19 June 1967 the Israeli cabinet voted to return the Sinai and the Golan Heights in return for peace agreements. Israel made peace with Egypt after the Camp David Accords of 1978 and completed its withdrawal from the Sinai in 1982, and signed a treaty with Jordan in 1994.
sixteen-kingdoms: Since the Western Han dynasty (202 BCE–9 CE), non-Han peoples of the northern steppe and western highlands had been resettling in northern China. In the northwest the Qiang and Di were brought in, mostly as farmers and slaves in the Guanzhong basin. They lived among the Han and were sinicized to different degrees while keeping their tribal affiliations, but they also faced discrimination and oppression, which led to racial tension and frequent rebellions.

During the Jin civil wars, Liu Yuan, a noble of the Five Divisions and a descendant of the Southern Xiongnu chanyu, served as a general for one of the princes. Returning to Shanxi, he rebelled and declared his intent to restore the fallen Han dynasty. Historians call his regime, later renamed Zhao, the Han-Zhao. The Jin court at Luoyang fell in 311 and Chang'an in 316, ending the Western Jin dynasty, while the Jin continued in the south from Jiankang as the Eastern Jin.

Shi Le, a general of the Jie people, founded the Later Zhao in 319 and destroyed the Han-Zhao in 329, placing most of northern China under his control. From 376 to 383 the Former Qin unified northern and northwest China and Sichuan, but its campaign to conquer the south was stopped by the Eastern Jin at the Battle of Fei River. The Former Qin then splintered, and by 400 as many as nine states existed in the north. The period ended in 439, when the Northern Wei, founded by the Xianbei Tuoba clan, unified northern China.

The name comes from the 6th-century historian Cui Hong, whose Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms gathered the records of the states. He counted five Liangs, four Yans, three Qins, two Zhaos, Cheng-Han and Xia.

Rulers of these states took Han-style dynastic names, claimed the Mandate of Heaven and used era names and offices such as Grand Chancellor. Buddhism gained mainstream recognition in this period. The Later Zhao was among the earliest regimes to give it statewide backing, and in 401 Yao Xing of the Later Qin welcomed the Kuchean monk Kumārajīva to his court and sponsored his translation of Sanskrit texts into Chinese. This was the first time in the imperial era that non-Han rulers governed a large part of the Chinese heartland as emperors, and the question of how far to adopt Chinese culture continued into the Northern and Southern dynasties.
sixth-crusade: The Fifth Crusade ended in 1221 without gaining anything, and Emperor Frederick II, who had vowed to take part, never joined it. In the Agreement of San Germano of 25 July 1225 he promised Pope Honorius III to depart by 15 August 1227, to stay two years and to keep 1,000 knights in Syria. He married Isabella II, daughter of John of Brienne, by proxy in 1225, which gave him a claim to the kingdom of Jerusalem. Honorius died in 1227, and his successor Gregory IX held a long-standing dislike of Frederick. In Egypt and Syria the Ayyubids were fighting among themselves, and the sultan al-Kamil was ready to offer territory for peace and for support against his brother al-Mu'azzam.

The first crusaders sailed from Brindisi in August 1227. Crowding and heat at the port brought disease, and many returned home. Frederick sailed with the second wave in September but fell ill and turned back, and Gregory IX excommunicated him on 29 September 1227, accusing him of feigning his illness. Frederick finally sailed on 28 June 1228 with a small force, stopped five weeks in Cyprus and arrived at Acre on 7 September 1228. The Templars, Hospitallers and clergy received him warmly but refused him the kiss of peace because of his excommunication.

Frederick realised that, lacking the manpower to fight, his only hope was to negotiate for Jerusalem. Al-Kamil's position had grown stronger after the end of his civil conflicts, but he was friendly and the talks went on through envoys. The result was the Treaty of Jaffa. The patriarch Gérold of Lausanne and the masters of the military orders felt betrayed by its concessions, which they thought made the Holy City nearly impossible to protect, and the patriarch tried to prevent Frederick from entering Jerusalem by threatening his army with excommunication and the city with interdict.

Contemporaries judged the crusade differently. Frederick boasted of a great success in a letter to Henry III of England, while the patriarch's letter to all the faithful painted a darker picture of the emperor. On the Muslim side al-Kamil himself was pleased, but Arabic sources called the treaty one of the most disastrous events of Islam and blamed the sultan alone.

The treaty was to last ten years, and its expiry led Gregory IX to call a new crusade for the time beyond 1239. This became the Barons' Crusade, a disorganised affair with limited support from the emperor and the pope, which nevertheless regained more land than the Sixth Crusade had.
sixth-dynasty-of-egypt: The Sixth Dynasty, with the Third, Fourth and Fifth, forms the Old Kingdom. Many authorities consider it the last dynasty of the Old Kingdom, although the Oxford History of Ancient Egypt includes Dynasties VII and VIII. Manetho writes that its kings ruled from Memphis, since their pyramids stand at Saqqara, very close to it.

Teti is named the first king of the dynasty by Manetho. His relationship to his predecessors is unclear, but his wife Iput is thought to have been a daughter of Unas, who died without a male heir, so Teti would have come to the throne as his son-in-law. He took the Horus name Seheteptawy, meaning He who pacifies the Two Lands.

Teti exempted the temple at Abydos from taxation and was the first ruler closely associated with the cult of Hathor at Dendera. Manetho claims that a bodyguard assassinated him, but no contemporary source confirms it. If true, it might explain the brief ruler Userkare, who appears in the Turin Canon and the Abydos king-list.

Expeditions went to Wadi Maghara in the Sinai to mine turquoise and copper, and to the mines at Hatnub and Wadi Hammamat. Djedkara sent trade expeditions south to Punt and north to Byblos, and Pepi I sent expeditions to these places and as far as Ebla in modern-day Syria. Tomb inscriptions confirm a plot against Pepi I that failed, and a letter by the young Pepi II expressed his excitement that an expedition would bring back a dancing pygmy from the land of Yam, south of Nubia. Pepi II is credited with a reign of 94 years, the most notable of the dynasty.

The growing number of biographical inscriptions in non-royal tombs widened later knowledge of the period, and they also show the rising power of the nobility, which further weakened the king's absolute rule. It is believed that after the death of the long-lived Pepi II his vassals were entrenched enough to resist the authority of his many successors, which may have contributed to the rapid decline of the Old Kingdom. The ancient king lists broadly agree on the order of the dynasty's kings. Nitocris, once held by some to be the first female pharaoh, is now accepted as a mistranslation of the king Neitiqerty Siptah.
skagerrak: The Skagerrak is a strait about 240 km long and between 80 and 140 km wide. It runs between the Jutland peninsula of Denmark, the east coast of Norway and the west coast of Sweden, and connects the North Sea with the Kattegat. It deepens toward the Norwegian coast, reaching over 700 metres in the Norwegian Trench. Among its ports are Oslo, Larvik and Kristiansand in Norway, Skagen, Hirtshals and Hanstholm in Denmark, and Uddevalla, Lysekil and Strömstad in Sweden. The International Hydrographic Organization draws its western limit from Hanstholm to the Naze at Lindesnes and its south-eastern limit from Skagen to Paternosterskären.

The name most likely means the Skagen strait, after Skagen, a town near the northern cape of Denmark known as the Skaw. The second part, rak, is a Dutch word for a straight waterway, and the name was probably given by Dutch seafarers, as was that of the neighbouring Kattegat. Older names for the combined Skagerrak and Kattegat were the Norwegian Sea or the Jutland Sea, the latter appearing in the Knýtlinga saga.

Until the Eider Canal was built in 1784, the Skagerrak was the only way in and out of the Baltic Sea, and for that reason the strait has carried busy international traffic for centuries. Traffic increased after the Industrial Revolution. In 1862 a shortcut, the Thyborøn Channel at the Limfjord in Denmark, was constructed through the Jutland coast, linking the North Sea directly with the Kattegat.

The strait was strategically important to Germany in both world wars. The largest naval battle of the First World War, the Battle of Jutland, which in Germany is known as the Battle of the Skagerrak, was fought here from 31 May to 1 June 1916. In the Second World War the importance of controlling the only sea access to the Baltic was a motive for the German invasions of Denmark and Norway and for the construction of the northern parts of the Atlantic Wall. Both wars left numerous shipwrecks on the seabed.

The Skagerrak supports an intensive fishing industry and is home to about 2,000 marine species, among them the Skagerrak cod, a variety of Atlantic cod that spawns off the Norwegian coast. Cold-water coral reefs grow in it, and the Tisler Reef in Ytre Hvaler National Park in Norway is the largest known coral reef in Europe. Ytre Hvaler National Park in Norway and Kosterhavet National Park in Sweden protect parts of the strait. Oslo and Gothenburg are the only large cities in the region.
skandagupta: Skandagupta was a son of the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I. His mother may have been a junior queen or a concubine, since his inscriptions name his father but not his mother, and his Bhitari pillar inscription lists the chief queens of his ancestors but not Kumaragupta's. A. L. Basham, reading a line of that inscription as saying he was raised to Aryan status by bards' praise, suggested that she came from a Shudra background. Dasharatha Sharma and Jagannath Agrawal reject this, and Jappen Oberoi holds that she was a queen, which makes him a legitimate son.

Skandagupta came to the throne in the year 136 of the Gupta era, about 455–456 CE. The Bhitari inscription says he restored the fallen fortunes of his family by defeating enemies who had grown wealthy and powerful, then visited his widowed mother with eyes full of tears of joy. Many scholars read the enemies as the Pushyamitras, a tribe on the Narmada; others read Yudhyamitras, a generic word for enemies, and suggest a disputed succession. The Junagadh inscription says he became ruler of the earth by his own prowess, and gold coins show a woman offering him a garland or ring, perhaps the goddess Lakshmi. Records name possible rivals, including Govindagupta, Ghatotkacha-gupta and Prakashaditya.

During his time the Indo-Hephthalites, called Hunas in India, advanced from the north-west as far as the Indus. The Bhitari inscription says he joined in close conflict with them, and the Junagadh inscription of 457–458 records his success against the mlechchhas, probably the Hunas. His governor Parnadatta, appointed to Surashtra, had his son Chakrapalita repair the Sudarshana lake after its dam burst in about 456–457. A Vakataka inscription claims that Narendrasena's commands were obeyed in Malava, which suggests a raid on Gupta lands.

He issued fewer gold coins than his predecessors, with less gold, which may reflect the strain of his wars. He changed from the old dinar weight standard to the suvarna standard of about 9.2 grams, which later Gupta rulers followed, and he installed an image of Vishnu in memory of his father.

He is generally considered the last of the great Gupta emperors. He was most probably succeeded by Purugupta, who appears to have been his half-brother. Later Gupta records omit his name, which may mean only that those kings descended from Purugupta. In 1928 the poet Jaishankar Prasad wrote a play, Skandagupta, about his life.
skanderbeg: Skanderbeg, born Gjergj Kastrioti, belonged to the Kastrioti family. His father, Gjon Kastrioti, held territory between Lezhë and Prizren that included Mat, Mirditë and Dibër in north-central Albania. The origin of his mother Voisava is disputed. His birthplace is also debated, though a birth year of 1405 is now largely agreed. He was sent as a hostage to the Ottoman court at Adrianople in 1415 and again in 1423, and received military training at the Enderun School. He served the sultan Murad II for about twenty years and was appointed sanjakbey of the Sanjak of Dibra in 1440.

During the Battle of Nish in 1443 Skanderbeg deserted the Ottomans and became ruler of Krujë and nearby areas. In March 1444 he founded the League of Lezhë with local noblemen. Venice at first supported him as a buffer against the Ottomans, but a dispute over the fortress of Dagnum led to an Albanian–Venetian war in 1447–1448, in which Venice offered rewards for his assassination. In June 1450 Murad II and his son Mehmed II besieged Krujë with an army of about 100,000. Skanderbeg left a garrison of 1,500 under Vrana Konti and harassed the Ottoman supply caravans, and the garrison repelled three major assaults.

By the Treaty of Gaeta of 26 March 1451 he recognised the sovereignty of Alfonso V of Aragon over his lands in exchange for military aid, though he remained in practice an independent ruler. In 1460 he sent cavalry to help Ferdinand I of Naples against an Angevin revolt. In 1463 Pope Pius II intended him as chief commander of a crusade, but the Pope died while the armies were gathering. He fought the Ottomans alongside the Venetians until his death.

Skanderbeg died on 17 January 1468. After his death and the Ottoman conquest of his lands, many Albanians found refuge in the Kingdom of Naples, which contributed to the formation of the Arbëresh communities of southern Italy. Many in Western Europe saw him as a model of Christian resistance to the Ottomans, and he became a central figure of the Albanian National Awakening of the 19th century and is the national hero of Albania. Historians note that none of his victories permanently stopped the Ottomans from invading the western Balkans.
skardu: Skardu stands at an average elevation of nearly 2,500 metres in the Skardu Valley, at the confluence of the Indus and Shigar rivers. The valley is 10 kilometres wide and 40 kilometres long and lies about 180 kilometres off the Karakoram Highway, to which the Baltistan Highway links it. Glaciers from the Indus and Shigar valleys broadened it, and active erosion in the Karakoram has left large deposits of sediment across it. The Indus separates the Karakoram from the Ladakh Range, and Skardu is a gateway to the eight-thousanders of the Karakoram.

The name is believed to come from a Balti word meaning a lowland between two high places. The earliest mention dates to the first half of the 16th century, when Mirza Haidar described Askardu in his Tarikh-i-Rashidi as a district of Baltistan.

The valley was part of the cultural sphere of Buddhist Tibet from the mid-7th century CE, and Tibetan inscriptions across Baltistan attest tantric Buddhism. After Tibetan suzerainty dissolved, about the 9th or 10th century, the Maqpon dynasty took control and ruled Baltistan for around 700 years. Around 1500 Maqpon Bokha was crowned and founded the city of Skardu as his capital, bringing craftsmen from Kashmir and Chilas. Islam spread through scholars from Central Asia from the 14th century and became dominant by the end of the 17th.

Ali Sher Khan Anchan, who became Maqpon king in 1580, extended the kingdom from Gilgit to Ladakh. The Mughal emperor Akbar conquered Baltistan in 1586, and the Maqpon ruler pledged allegiance. In 1839 the Dogra commander Zorawar Singh seized Skardu Fort on behalf of the Dogra dynasty of Jammu, and by 1845 the region was completely subjugated. Skardu was the winter capital of the Ladakh Wazarat until 1947.

Skardu is the capital of Skardu District and the Baltistan Division, and one of the primary cultural and administrative centres of Gilgit-Baltistan. The Skardu Fort, also called Kharphocho, stands on the Khardrong hill above the town and was built by the Maqpon rulers. Roads from Skardu lead to Askole and Hushe, the main gateways to peaks including K2, the Gasherbrums and Broad Peak, and to the glaciers of Baltoro, Biafo and Trango. The main tourist season runs from April to October.
skopje: Skopje lies in the north of North Macedonia, in the centre of the Balkan peninsula and about halfway between Belgrade and Athens. The city was built in the Skopje Valley, which runs west to east along the Vardar river and is about 20 km wide. Mountain ranges to the north and south limit its expansion, so the city spreads along the Vardar and the Serava, a small river that comes from the north. Within its administrative boundaries it stretches for more than 33 km but is only 10 km wide.

The name is first attested in Ptolemy's Geography, c. 150, as Scupi, a city of Roman Dardania. The Macedonian Skopje is the local Slavic rendering of that name, Shkup is the Albanian form, and Üsküb is the Ottoman Turkish one, which Western languages adapted as Uskub or Uskup and used until 1912.

The earliest traces of settlement, from the Chalcolithic period (4th millennium BCE), come from the rocky promontory on which Skopje Fortress stands. The Roman city of Scupi was founded in the late 1st century under Domitian and abandoned in 518 after an earthquake destroyed it. It was rebuilt under Justinian I. The city later belonged to the First Bulgarian Empire, to the Byzantine Empire and to the Second Bulgarian Empire, before it passed to Serbia.

Before the Austro-Turkish war and the great fire of 1689, Skopje was one of the biggest cities of the Balkans, with a population estimated at between 30,000 and 60,000. The fire was set by the retreating Austrian forces and was followed by a long decline: the city had only 10,000 inhabitants in 1836. Growth resumed after 1850, and the population reached 32,000 in 1905. Annexed by Serbia in 1912 after the Balkan Wars, Skopje was held by Bulgaria in 1915-1918 and again in 1941-1944, and in between formed part of Yugoslavia.

The earthquake of 1963 destroyed 80 per cent of the city. Its reconstruction was directed mainly by the Polish architect Adolf Ciborowski, who had already planned the rebuilding of Warsaw after World War II. He divided Skopje into zones for particular activities: parks along the Vardar, high-rise housing and shopping centres between the main boulevards, and individual housing and industry in the suburbs. Population density was kept low to limit the effects of a future earthquake.

The 2021 census counted 526,502 inhabitants, roughly a quarter of the country's population. Ethnic Macedonians form the majority, with Albanians a significant minority. The city is the seat of the Ss. Cyril and Methodius University, the Macedonian Academy of Sciences and Arts and the National Theatre.
skradin: Skradin lies near the Krka river and at the entrance to the Krka National Park, 17 kilometres from Šibenik and 100 kilometres from Split, in Šibenik-Knin County. The park's main attraction is the series of waterfalls called Slapovi Krke, the biggest of which, Skradinski buk, is named after the town. The municipality had a population of 3,349 at the 2021 census, and the town itself 508.

In antiquity the town was known as Scardon and Scardona, a name found in Strabo, Procopius, Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy. Its ending is thought to be an Illyrian suffix, and the prevailing theory links the root of the name to a term meaning steep. After the Roman conquest Skradin became an administrative and military centre of the region and was mentioned as a municipium in 530. It was destroyed in the Migration Period in the 7th century and restored under Croatian rulers in the early Middle Ages. In the 10th century it was one of the fortified towns of Croatia, the centre of the Skradin županija.

Skradin flourished in the late 13th and early 14th centuries as the capital of the Šubić bans Paul I and Mladen II. They built the Turina fortress on the hill above the harbour, raised the settlement below it to a free city with its own statute and administration, and founded richly endowed monasteries that housed Dominicans, Franciscans and other orders.

The Ottomans conquered the town in 1522 and held it, with some interruptions, until 1684. The Ottoman-Venetian wars devastated it and it was relocated. In October 1683 uskoks from Venetian Dalmatia, mainly Morlachs from Ravni Kotari, took Skradin and other border towns whose Muslim population had fled, and the Venetians finally took it in 1684. It became the centre of a municipality in 1705, and was later occupied by Napoleon as part of the French Empire and then by Austria-Hungary. The centre of the region shifted to Šibenik, and the Diocese of Skradin was abandoned in 1828.
skype: Skype was founded in 2003 by Niklas Zennström from Sweden and Janus Friis from Denmark, and its software was created by Estonian developers. Friis and one of the Estonians, Toivo Annus, are credited with the idea of cutting the cost of voice calls by using a peer-to-peer protocol like that of Kazaa. An early alpha version was tested in the spring of 2003, and the first public beta was released on 29 August 2003. The name came from the words sky and peer-to-peer, which became Skyper. Some domain names for Skyper were already taken, so the final r was dropped.

Skype was a proprietary telecommunications application best known for videotelephony, videoconferencing and voice calls. It also offered instant messaging, file transfer and paid calls to landline and mobile telephones over traditional networks. Registered users had a unique Skype ID and could hold voice chats between pairs of users and conference calls using a proprietary audio codec. It originally ran as a hybrid of peer-to-peer and client-server systems. An early web page described it as highly secure with end-to-end encryption, but its protocol was never made public, so the claim could not be independently verified.

In September 2005 eBay agreed to acquire Skype Technologies, based in Luxembourg. In 2009 eBay sold 65 per cent of it to Silver Lake, Andreessen Horowitz and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board. Microsoft acquired it on 10 May 2011 for 8.5 billion US dollars and used it to replace its own Windows Live Messenger, which it discontinued in April 2013. In 2011 most of the development team and 44 per cent of the division's employees were in Tallinn and Tartu, in Estonia.

At the end of 2010 there were over 660 million registered users worldwide. In February 2012 there were 34 million users online at one time, and by January 2013 more than 50 million. In 2011 its free version was reported to be used increasingly by teachers and schools for global education projects and language learning. Microsoft retired Skype in favour of Microsoft Teams on 5 May 2025.
slavery: Slavery predates written records and has existed in many cultures. It is rare among hunter-gatherers, because it requires economic surpluses and a substantial population density, and became widespread only with the invention of agriculture in the Neolithic Revolution about 11,000 years ago. It was practised in almost every ancient civilisation, through debt bondage, punishment for crime, the enslavement of prisoners of war, child abandonment and the enslavement of slaves' offspring.

The English word slave came through Old French esclave from Byzantine Greek sklábos. According to a widespread view, known since the 18th century, this derives from the self-name of a Slavic tribe, because its people were often captured and enslaved; the view has been disputed since the 19th century.

Slavery is the ownership of a person as property, especially with regard to their labour, and typically involves compulsory work, with place of work and residence dictated by the holder. Many cases of enslavement followed a breach of the law, indebtedness, military defeat or the pursuit of cheaper labour; others were instituted along lines of race or sex. In chattel slavery the slave is legally the personal property of the owner and can be bought and sold like livestock. Depending on era and country, slaves sometimes had limited legal rights: a 1686 statute in the Province of New York punished those who deliberately killed slaves.

Chattel slavery was widely accepted, and in ancient Greece and the Roman Empire was considered a keystone of society. Other examples are medieval Egypt, Sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, the antebellum United States, Cuba and Haiti. In the Senegambia region between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, and in early Islamic states of the western Sahel, including Ghana, Mali, Segou and Songhai, about a third.

Economists have argued that slavery becomes desirable where land is abundant and labour scarce, and that slavery and then serfdom declined in Europe as the population grew, then returned in the Americas and Russia where large areas had few inhabitants. It was common where tasks were simple and easy to supervise, as on large plantations of sugarcane and cotton.
slavery-abolition-act-1833: Slavery had been judged to have no legal basis in England in 1772, in Lord Mansfield's judgment in the Somerset case. By 1783 a movement to end the slave trade had begun among the British public, and the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade was founded in 1787. The Slave Trade Act 1807 outlawed the slave trade within the Empire but not slavery, and the Slave Trade Felony Act 1811 made it a felony. The Anti-Slavery Society was founded in London in 1823. In the 1820s abolitionists and the Colonial Office followed a policy of gradualism, beginning with amelioration measures put in place by the Order in Council of 1824 which the colonies only partly carried out.

Two events changed the balance. The Baptist War, a slave revolt in Jamaica organised by the Baptist minister Samuel Sharpe, broke out in the Christmas holiday of 1831 and was suppressed about ten days later, and two parliamentary inquiries followed. The Reform Act 1832 swept away the rotten borough seats that the West India lobby had bought to resist abolition. In March 1833 Edward Stanley, the Colonial Secretary, introduced a bill with two innovations, apprenticeship and compensation for owners; the apprenticeship was cut from twelve years to six, and compensation rose from 15 to 20 million pounds. Members of the Commons, anxious about property rights, approved the full amount.

The act passed the Commons on 7 August 1833 and the Lords on 20 August, received royal assent on 28 August and came into force on 1 August 1834. Children under six were freed at once. Others became apprentices: field workers, the praedial class, until 1 August 1840, and the non-praedial class, including house servants, until 1 August 1838. Apprentices owed up to 45 hours of unpaid work a week in return for food, clothing, medical care and housing, and could buy their discharge.

The act excluded the territories of the East India Company, Ceylon and Saint Helena, which the Indian Slavery Act 1843 brought in. The act gave 20 million pounds to owners, not to the enslaved, financed by a loan of 15 million pounds from Nathan Mayer Rothschild and Moses Montefiore. About 42,000 people in the colonies and 3,500 in Britain received compensation. Antigua and Bermuda gave immediate freedom instead of apprenticeship.

Abolitionists opposed apprenticeship from the start. After a campaign in 1837 and 1838, and an amendment of April 1838 that banned flogging of apprentices, the colonial legislatures ended apprenticeship on 1 August 1838. Barbados acted first, on 16 May, and Jamaica was the last, in the middle of June. Around 800,000 freed slaves were attested in the claims process. The act was repealed by the Statute Law (Repeals) Act 1998, and other laws still forbid slavery.
slavonia: Slavonia lies in the Pannonian Basin, largely bordered by the Danube, Drava and Sava rivers. Its west consists of the Sava and Drava valleys and the mountains around the Požega Valley, and its east of plains, under a moderate continental climate. The name comes from the Slavs who settled there and called themselves Slověne; the land between the Sava and the Drava was Slověnьje in Proto-Slavic. Finds of the Starčevo culture near Slavonski Brod are dated to 6100–5200 BCE, and finds of the Vučedol culture near Vukovar to 3000–2500 BCE.

The Romans completed their conquest in 11 BCE and created the province of Illyricum, which was soon renamed Pannonia. After the Western Roman Empire fell, the Ostrogoths and then the Lombards held the area until the Lombards withdrew in 568, and Avars and Slavs controlled it by 582. A Slavic principality whose rulers were vassals of the Francs followed the fall of the Avar Khaganate, before Hungarian tribes overwhelmed it. Croatian influence spread north under King Tomislav, and in 1102 Croatia and Hungary entered a personal union under Coloman. From the 13th century a separate ban governed a Kingdom of Slavonia, and Croatia and Slavonia shared one ban from 1476.

The Ottomans took Đakovo in 1536 and Požega in 1537, and completed their conquest of Slavonia in 1552 with the capture of Virovitica. Požega became the chief Ottoman centre. The frontier steadied after the Battle of Sisak in 1593. During the Great Turkish War the Ottomans left the region between 1684 and 1691, and the Treaty of Karlowitz transferred it to the Habsburgs, with Osijek as the administrative centre of the restored kingdom. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 united Croatia and Slavonia, and in 1918 the region joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and then Yugoslavia. Fighting in 1991–1995 included the Battle of Vukovar in 1991.

Slavonia roughly corresponds to five Croatian counties: Brod-Posavina, Osijek-Baranja, Požega-Slavonia, Virovitica-Podravina and Vukovar-Syrmia. Its largest city is Osijek, followed by Slavonski Brod and Vinkovci. Tamburica music is characteristic of the region, and the traditional song form bećarac is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Erdut, Ilok and Kutjevo are centres of winemaking.
slavs: The oldest mention of the Slavic name is from the 6th century, when Procopius wrote Sklaboi and related forms in Byzantine Greek and his contemporary Jordanes wrote Sclaveni in Latin. It is usually derived from slovo, word, so that it meant people who speak the same language, in contrast to the Slavic word for Germans, němьcь, meaning mute people.

Roman sources of the 1st and 2nd centuries refer to early Slavic peoples as Veneti, living east of the Suebi and west of the Sarmatians between the upper Vistula and the Dnieper. The Slavs, called Antes and Sclaveni, first appear in Byzantine records in the early 6th century, emerging from the area of the Carpathian Mountains, the lower Danube and the Black Sea to invade the Danubian provinces of the Eastern Empire under Justinian I.

The westward movement of Germanic tribes in the 5th and 6th centuries, together with that of the Huns and later the Avars and Bulgars, began the great migration of the Slavs, who settled lands the Germanic tribes had left. They moved west towards the Oder and the Elbe-Saale line, south into Bohemia, Moravia, the Pannonian plain and the Balkans, and north along the upper Dnieper. By the end of the 6th century they had settled the Eastern Alps.

In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo supported the Slavs against their Avar rulers and became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first known Slav state in Central Europe. The First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 681 as an alliance of the ruling Bulgars and the numerous Slavs, and Old Church Slavonic became its official language in 864. The Principality of Serbia dates from the 8th century, and the Duchy of Bohemia and Kievan Rus' from the 9th.

From the mid-19th century a pan-Slavic movement stressed the common heritage of the Slavic peoples, especially in the Balkans, where South Slavs had long been ruled by other empires. In 1918 the Slavs established Czechoslovakia, the Second Polish Republic and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Procopius, in 545, described the Sclaveni and Antae as having once shared the name Sporoi. He wrote that they lived under a democracy, believed in one god, the maker of lightning, to whom they sacrificed, and lived in scattered housing, often changing settlement. In war they were mainly foot soldiers with shields, spears and bows and little armour.
slobodan-milosevic: Milošević was born in Požarevac, four months after the Axis invasion of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and was raised during the occupation. His ancestral roots were in Montenegro. His father, a Serbian Orthodox theologian, died by suicide in 1962, and his mother, a teacher and active member of the Communist Party, in 1972. He studied law at the University of Belgrade, where he befriended Ivan Stambolić, whose uncle Petar Stambolić had been president of the Serbian Executive Council. The connection proved crucial for his career, as the two climbed through the party hierarchy.

Milošević was elected president of the Belgrade city committee of the League of Communists in 1984. In 1987 he emerged as a force in Serbian politics by declaring support for Serbs in Kosovo, who said the provincial government, dominated by ethnic Albanians, was oppressing them; he called for reducing Kosovo's autonomy. From 1988 the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution, a series of rallies in Vojvodina and Montenegro, led to the resignation of their governments and the election of officials allied with him. His supporters call it a genuine grass-roots movement.

He became president of Serbia in 1989 and led the Socialist Party of Serbia from its foundation in 1990. Under United Nations sanctions during the Yugoslav Wars, Serbia's economy collapsed. In 1997 he became president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Counteraction against the Kosovo Liberation Army escalated into armed conflict in 1998 and NATO air strikes in 1999. After a disputed presidential election in 2000 he resigned amid demonstrations.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia indicted him in May 1999 for crimes in Kosovo, and later for Croatia and Bosnia, including genocide. Arrested in 2001 by Yugoslav authorities on suspicion of corruption, he was extradited to the tribunal, which he denounced as illegal; he refused counsel and conducted his own defence. He was found dead in his cell in The Hague on 11 March 2006, of a heart attack, before the trial concluded. Later verdicts found him part of a joint criminal enterprise that used violence to remove Croats, Bosniaks and Albanians from parts of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo. He remains a controversial figure in Serbia and the Balkans.
slovakia: Slovakia covers about 49,000 km2 and is mostly mountainous, with the Carpathian Mountains across most of the northern half. The Tatra Mountains hold 29 peaks above 2,500 metres, and Gerlachovský štít, at 2,655 metres, is the highest point in the country. The largest lowland is the Danubian Lowland in the southwest, followed by the Eastern Slovak Lowland in the southeast. Forests cover 41% of the land, nine national parks cover 6.5%, and hundreds of caves lie under the mountains, five of them on UNESCO's World Heritage list. The name means the Land of the Slavs, and the present Slovak form Slovensko is first attested in 1675.

The oldest human artefacts, stone tools dated to 270,000 BCE, come from near Nové Mesto nad Váhom, and a Neanderthal cranium of about 200,000 BCE was found near Gánovce. Slavs arrived in the 5th and 6th centuries, and parts of the territory came under the Avar Khaganate before the Principality of Nitra was annexed by the Principality of Moravia, later Great Moravia. The land passed into the Principality of Hungary, which became the Kingdom of Hungary in 1000. The Mongol invasion of 1241 and 1242 destroyed much of it, and the south was part of Ottoman provinces in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Slovak Uprising of 1848 did not achieve its aim but helped to cement a Slovak national identity. Czechoslovakia was proclaimed in 1918, with its borders set by the Treaty of Saint Germain in 1919 and the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. The first Slovak Republic, established in 1939 as a one-party clerical fascist client state under Nazi Germany, joined the Axis in 1940. Czechoslovakia became a communist state after the Soviet-backed coup of 1948, the Prague Spring was suppressed by the Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968, and the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule.

Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993 after the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia, and its constitution, ratified on 1 September 1992, took effect that day. It is a parliamentary democratic republic with a directly elected president of limited powers and a 150-seat National Council. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004, the Schengen Area in 2007 and the eurozone in 2009.

The 2021 census recorded 83.8% Slovaks and 7.8% Hungarians, the largest minority, and 55.8% of the population identified as Catholic. About 90,000 Jews lived in Slovakia before the Second World War, and most were murdered in the Holocaust; about 2,300 remain.
slovenes: In the 6th century CE Slavic people settled the region between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea in two waves: the first came from the Moravian lands around 550, and the second, from the southeast, followed the migration of the Lombards to Italy in 568. From 623 to 658 Slavic peoples between the upper Elbe River and the Karawanks mountain range united under King Samo in what is known as Samo's Tribal Union. It collapsed after his death, but a smaller principality, Carantania, remained, centred on present-day Carinthia. Facing the danger of Avar tribes, the Carantanians accepted a union with Bavaria in 745 and later recognised Frankish rule and accepted Christianity.

The last Slavic state formation in the region, the principality of Prince Kocel, lost its independence in 874. Slovene ethnic territory then shrank under pressure from Germans in the west and the arrival of Hungarians in the Pannonian plain, and it stabilised in its present form in the 15th century. The first mentions of a common Slovene identity date from the 16th century, when the Protestant preacher Primož Trubar and his followers printed the first books in Slovene and Jurij Dalmatin translated the whole Bible.

Under Maria Theresa and Emperor Joseph II, reforms included compulsory primary education in Slovene in 1774, and a national revival began. In 1848 the first Slovene political programme, United Slovenia, demanded an autonomous kingdom of all Slovene-speaking lands within the Austrian Empire. It failed, but it remained a platform for later activity, including mass rallies called tabori. The first Slovene political parties appeared in the 1890s, all loyal to Austria.

After the First World War most Slovenes joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, then the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In the territory given to Italy, about 327,000 of 1.3 million Slovenes were subjected to forced Fascist Italianization. In the Second World War Slovenia was divided among Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Hungary. After the war it formed part of socialist Yugoslavia, and in 1991 it became independent after a brief ten-day war.

Most ethnic Slovenes are Roman Catholic, with historical Protestant minorities, especially Lutherans in Prekmurje. The Freising manuscripts are the first written words in Slovene. Anton Tomaž Linhart was the first to define Slovenes as a separate branch of the Slavic people, in his work of 1791. Between 1880 and the First World War the largest numbers of Slovenes emigrated to America, and the largest group in the United States settled in Cleveland, Ohio.
slovenia: Slovenia covers 20,271 km2 and is mostly mountainous and forested. Four major European geographic regions meet there: the Alps, the Dinarides, the Pannonian Plain and the Mediterranean Sea. The highest peak, Triglav, at 2,864 metres, appears on the national coat of arms and flag. The Adriatic coastline stretches approximately 47 kilometres, the southwest has a limestone Karst Plateau of underground rivers, gorges and caves, and the landscape of the northeast is essentially flat. The name means land of the Slavs.

Evidence of habitation dates to around 250,000 years ago. A pierced cave bear bone from Divje Babe cave near Cerkno, dated to 43100 ± 700 years before present, is considered a kind of flute and possibly the oldest musical instrument discovered. Pile dwellings over 4,500 years old in the Ljubljana Marsh are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Ljubljana Marshes Wooden Wheel is the world's oldest wooden wheel. In Roman times the area was divided between Venetia et Histria and the provinces of Pannonia and Noricum, with posts at Emona (Ljubljana), Poetovio (Ptuj) and Celeia (Celje). In 394 the Battle of the Frigidus took place in the Vipava Valley, where Theodosius I defeated the usurper Eugenius.

Slavic tribes migrated to the Alpine area in the early Middle Ages. From 623 or 624 King Samo united the Alpine and Western Slavs against the Avars, and after his death around 658 the ancestors of the Slovenes formed Carantania and Carniola. Charlemagne decisively defeated the Avars in 803. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was formed in December 1918 and became known as Yugoslavia in 1929. Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, Hungary and the Independent State of Croatia partitioned Slovenia in 1941.

Slovenia was established in 1945 as one of six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and modern Slovenia emerged in June 1991, when it declared independence and became a sovereign state after the brief Ten-Day War. It is a parliamentary republic whose head of state is a president elected for five years, and legislative power rests mainly with the 90-member National Assembly. In 2007 it was the first new member state of the European Union to adopt the euro. The population is about 2.1 million, and Slovenes make up 83.1% of the inhabitants. Four sites are on UNESCO's World Heritage list, among them the Škocjan Caves and the Idrija Mercury mining site.
slupsk: Słupsk lies on the Słupia River in northern Poland, in the historical region of Pomerania, or more exactly in the part now called Central Pomerania. The town grew from a few medieval settlements on the banks of the river, at a ford on a trade route linking the territories of the present Pomeranian and West Pomeranian voivodeships. This led to the building of a grod, a West Slavic fortified settlement, on an islet in the river. It stood on an artificial hill, was protected by a palisade and had a natural moat formed by branches of the Słupia, and swamps around it gave good defence.

Records confirm that the area was part of the Polish realm under Mieszko I and in the 11th century. Słupsk received city rights in 1265. By the 14th century it was a centre of local administration and trade and an associate of the Hanseatic League. Between 1368 and 1478 it was the residence of the Dukes of Słupsk, who until 1474 were vassals of the Kingdom of Poland. Under a peace treaty Słupsk became part of Brandenburg-Prussia, and in 1815 it joined the new Prussian Province of Pomerania.

As Stolp, the town was not directly affected by fighting in the First World War. It stood close to the border of the Polish Corridor, and Polish claims to it were refused during the Treaty of Versailles negotiations. In the interwar years it was the regional centre of the eastern part of Eastern Pomerania and was known as Little Paris. During the Second World War the Nazis created a labour camp in 1941 and, in 1944, a subcamp of the Stutthof concentration camp at the railway repair works, where over 600 Jewish prisoners were held, and a forced labour camp for women and children, in which over 200 children died.

After the war the city became part of Poland. Most of the German population fled or was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement, and Poles, many of them expelled from the former eastern territories annexed by the Soviet Union, settled the city.

Słupsk is a city with powiat rights in the Pomeranian Voivodeship and the seat of Słupsk County. From 1975 to 1998 it was the capital of its own voivodeship. Its monuments include the Renaissance Ducal Castle, which houses the Museum of Middle Pomerania, and the Castle Mill, the oldest preserved industrial structure in Poland. The city is also the seat of the Pomeranian University in Słupsk.
slutsk: Slutsk was first mentioned in writing in 1116. It was at first part of the Principality of Turov and Pinsk but became the capital of a separate principality in 1160, and from the 1320s or 1330s it belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Casimir IV Jagiellon vested it with Magdeburg town rights in 1441. It was a private town of the Olelkovich and Radziwiłł families, who made it a centre of the Polish Reformed Church with a gymnasium and a strong fortress. Scottish immigrants settled there in the middle of the 17th century.
Later the town became known for kontusz belts, among the most expensive garments of the szlachta, so that such belts worn over the żupan were often called belts of Slutsk whatever their real origin.

In 1778 it became a county seat within the Nowogródek Voivodeship, and after the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 it was part of the Russian Empire. Germany occupied it in 1918, and Poland held it in 1919 and 1920. In 1920 it was the centre of a major anti-Bolshevik uprising known as the Slutsk defence action.

The first Jews are recorded in 1583, and the community was formally recognised in 1601. By 1691 Slutsk was one of the five leading communities of the Lithuanian Jewish Council. In 1750 there were 1,593 Jews, a third of the population, and three quarters of the town's merchants were Jewish. By 1897 there were 10,264 Jewish inhabitants, 77 percent of the population. The town was important for Torah study, and the Slutsk-Kletsk Yeshiva was founded there in 1883 by Rabbi Yaakov Dovid Wilovsky.

German forces occupied Slutsk on 26 June 1941. On 27 and 28 October 1941 Jews were taken to pits in the Gorovakha ravine and shot in what is known as the Slutsk affair, with 3,400 victims by German sources and 8,000 by Soviet ones. Thousands more were killed in 1942, and the town ghetto was liquidated on 8 February 1943. The Red Army recaptured the town on 30 June 1944.

Slutsk lies on the Sluch River 105 kilometres south of Minsk and is the administrative centre of Slutsk District in the Minsk Region of Belarus. Its symbol is the woven belt, to which the Museum of the History of Slutsk Belts is dedicated.
smallpox-vaccine: Smallpox in its severe form, variola major, killed up to 35 per cent of those infected in some outbreaks. Before the vaccine, immunity was induced by inoculation, or variolation, which probably occurred in Africa and China well before it reached Europe. The first clear reference is by the Chinese author Wan Quan in a work of 1549, and in China powdered smallpox scabs were blown up the noses of the healthy; the method carried a mortality of 0.5 to 2.0 per cent, against 20 to 30 per cent for the disease itself. Two reports on the Chinese practice reached the Royal Society in London in 1700.

Edward Jenner was born in Berkeley, England, and as a child was variolated and nearly died. As an apprentice he noticed that people who caught cowpox from cattle did not catch smallpox, though the idea was not taken up at the time. In 1768 Dr John Fewster had reported that variolation caused no reaction in people who had had cowpox. Jenner trained in London from 1770 to 1772 as the private pupil of John Hunter, and in 1796 demonstrated that cowpox infection conferred immunity to smallpox.

The word vaccine comes from Jenner's term variolae vaccinae, smallpox of the cow, from the Latin vacca. Jenner's friend Richard Dunning first printed vaccination in 1800, and in 1881 Louis Pasteur proposed widening both terms to cover other protective inoculations, to honour Jenner. The vaccine virus is called vaccinia, and in 1939 Allan Watt Downie showed that it was serologically distinct from cowpox. Genome sequencing later found it most closely related to horsepox, identified in the 2010s as its likely ancestor.

From 1796 to the 1880s the vaccine passed from arm to arm. It was maintained in cattle from the 1840s, and calf lymph became the leading vaccine in the 1880s. Without adequate safety methods, contaminated vaccine at times transmitted erysipelas, tetanus, septicaemia and tuberculosis, and arm-to-arm transfer risked syphilis. Second-generation vaccines, grown in membranes or cell cultures, gave greater purity, and third-generation ones used attenuated vaccinia strains.

An international search for outbreaks, backed by vaccination, began in 1967 under a World Health Organization unit headed by Donald Henderson. The last case in the Americas was in Brazil in 1971, in south-east Asia in Indonesia in 1972, on the Indian subcontinent in Bangladesh in 1975, and the last endemic case anywhere occurred in Somalia in October 1977. A commission chaired by Frank Fenner concluded in December 1979 that smallpox had been eradicated, and the WHO endorsed this in May 1980. After the attacks of 2001 many governments rebuilt vaccine stockpiles, and smallpox vaccines were later used against the mpox outbreak, for which the WHO declared an emergency on 23 July 2022.
smendes: Smendes may have been a son of Hrere, Chief of the Harem of Amun-Re and probably the wife of a high priest of Amun. If so, he was the brother of Nodjmet and the brother-in-law of the High Priests Herihor and Piankh. He married Tentamun, likely a daughter of Ramesses IX, and he is described as son-in-law of Ramesses XI. His birth name was Nesbanebdjed, meaning He of the Ram, Lord of Mendes; Smendes is the Greek form used by later writers such as Josephus and Sextus Africanus.

Smendes succeeded Ramesses XI, the last ruler of the Twentieth Dynasty, and founded the Twenty-First. He may have resided at Tanis or at Memphis, and blocks and statues at Tanis bear his names, some of them reused from earlier Ramesside kings. Tanis became the capital under Psusennes I, but the move from Pi-Ramesses may have begun with Smendes.

He ruled a divided Egypt. His nominal authority in Upper Egypt is attested by a quarry stela at Ed-Dibabiya, which tells how he, residing in Memphis, ordered repairs to the temple of Luxor after a flood threat, and by a graffito at the Temple of Monthu at Karnak. Middle and Upper Egypt were effectively under the High Priests of Amun, such as Pinedjem I, Masaharta and Menkheperre.

Manetho's Epitome assigns him twenty-six years. A date in Year 25 on the Banishment Stela, recording how Menkheperre put down a revolt at Thebes and exiled its leaders to the oases of the Western Desert, can refer only to Smendes. His throne name, Hedjkheperre Setepenre, was later adopted by five kings, among them Shoshenq I.

He appears in the Report of Wenamun, a story in which a priest of Amun sent by Herihor to Byblos for timber first calls on Smendes at Tanis and receives a ship from him. Egyptologists question its historical accuracy, and since Karl Jansen-Winkeln proposed reversing the order of Herihor and Piankh, Arno Egberts has argued that the tale is set in Smendes's fifth year. He was succeeded by Amenemnisu, who may have been his son. His tomb has not been found; a canopic jar of his is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
smithsonian: The Smithsonian Institution was founded on 10 August 1846 by act of the United States Congress, which created it for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. It is named after its founding donor, the British scientist James Smithson. It operates as a trust instrumentality and is not formally part of any of the three branches of the federal government, and the legislation called for a Board of Regents to govern it, which includes the chief justice and the vice president as ex officio members.

Earlier, in 1816, a group of Washington citizens had founded the Columbian Institute for the Promotion of Arts and Sciences, chartered by Congress in 1818, whose members included John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson and Henry Clay. Its charter expired in 1838.

The first secretary, Joseph Henry, wanted the institution to be a centre of scientific research, but it also became the depository for various Washington and United States government collections. The thousands of specimens and artefacts gathered by the United States Exploring Expedition, which circumnavigated the globe between 1838 and 1842, joined the collections, as did the finds of military and civilian surveys of the American West, including many Native American artefacts. In 1846 the regents planned weather observation, and in 1847 money was appropriated for meteorological research. From 1857 to 1866 it was a magnet for young scientists who formed the Megatherium Club.

Building the Smithsonian Institution Building, known as the Castle and designed by James Renwick Jr., began in 1849, and it opened in 1855. The Arts and Industries Building followed in 1881, built after the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876 earned enough income. The National Zoological Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, opened in 1889, and the National Museum of Natural History in June 1911. The institution was originally organised as the United States National Museum, a name that ceased to exist administratively in 1967.

Today the Smithsonian is a group of museums, libraries, research centres and a zoo, mostly in Washington, D.C., with others in Maryland, New York and Virginia, and it has affiliated museums across the United States and in Panama and Puerto Rico. Its collections are among the largest of any museum complex, and the National Museum of Natural History holds most of the items, mainly scientific specimens. Only a small fraction is on public display at any time, and the rest is kept for research. Almost all visitors are admitted without charge.

In 2020 it released about 2.8 million images and 173 years of staff-created data into the public domain under a Creative Commons Zero dedication. It publishes Smithsonian magazine, begun at the suggestion of Secretary S. Dillon Ripley, and awards such as the James Smithson Medal, established in 1965.
smolensk: Smolensk stands on the Dnieper River, 360 kilometres west-southwest of Moscow, and is the administrative centre of Smolensk Oblast. In the early medieval period it lay on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks. Rus' travellers sailed up the Western Dvina and portaged their boats to the upper Dnieper, and at Smolensk they are supposed to have mended leaks with tar, which one explanation gives for the name. Others derive it from the Smolnya River or from a Slavic tribe, the Smolyans. The Byzantine emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus described the city around 950 as a key station on the route.

The Ustyug Chronicle of the 16th century first mentions Smolensk under 863, and the Primary Chronicle names it as the centre of the Krivichi. After Oleg the Wise took Kiev in 882, it became part of Kievan Rus'. The Principality of Smolensk was founded in 1054 and by the end of the 12th century was one of the strongest in Eastern Europe, its princes often holding the Kievan throne.
