His father, Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard, was a devoutly Christian wool merchant from Jutland who was devoted to the rationalist philosophy of Christian Wolff. The figure of Socrates, whom Kierkegaard met in Plato's dialogues, later shaped his interest in irony and indirect communication.

He met Regine Olsen on 8 May 1837 and proposed to her on 8 September 1840, after passing his theological examinations. He broke off the engagement on 11 August 1841, and after she pleaded with him he ended it verbally on 11 October 1841. His journals blame his melancholy, but his precise motive remains unclear, and the broken engagement is generally considered to have had a major influence on his work.

Kierkegaard published some works under pseudonyms, each presenting a distinct viewpoint, as a way of indirect communication. Either/Or, considered his magnum opus, and Fear and Trembling, his central writing on religion, both appeared in 1843. Critics have accused him of playing with viewpoints without committing to one, though he said all his work came from a service to Christianity.

His key ideas include subjective and objective truth, the knight of faith, anxiety, faith as a passion and the three stages on life's way. He wrote, "Christianity teaches that the way is to become subjective, to become a subject." He attacked Hegelianism by parody, though he admired Hegel personally. A dispute that began with an article by Peder Ludvig Møller in December 1845 led him to ask the satirical paper The Corsair to satirise him. His journals run to over 7,000 pages.

In his last years Kierkegaard attacked the Church of Denmark in newspaper articles and in a series of self-published pamphlets, The Moment. The attack began after Hans Lassen Martensen called the dead Bishop Jacob Peter Mynster a truth-witness, which Kierkegaard strongly objected to. He later said his earlier writing had been preparation for it. He collapsed in the street, spent over a month in Frederiks Hospital, refused communion, and died on 11 November 1855. His nephew Henrik Lund protested at the funeral against burial by the official church.

His work was written in Danish and was at first read mainly in Scandinavia, but was translated into French, German and other languages around the turn of the 20th century. Georg Brandes published the first book on his life and philosophy in 1879. His fame grew greatly in the 1930s, when the existentialist movement named him a precursor, and philosophers both theistic and atheistic drew from him the notions of angst, despair and the importance of the individual.
sorghaghtani-beki: Sorghaghtani was the daughter of Jakha Gambhu, the younger brother of the Keraite leader Toghrul. Around 1203 Temüjin proposed a marriage between his eldest son Jochi and a daughter or granddaughter of Toghrul. Toghrul refused and later tried to kill Temüjin by inviting him to discuss the proposal. Temüjin escaped, the Keraites were routed in the war that followed, and Toghrul was killed, possibly by the Naimans.

Unlike his brother, Jakha usually supported Temüjin. He gave two daughters to him and one to Jochi. Genghis Khan married the elder, Ibaqa Beki, and gave the young Sorghaghtani, still a teenager, to his son Tolui. Jakha was killed by the general Jürchedei when the Keraites revolted after 1204.

Mongol women held great authority at home, since the men were often away. Sorghaghtani was illiterate but valued literacy, and each of her sons learned a different language for a different region. She was a Christian of the Church of the East and respected other faiths: she financed a madrasa in Bukhara and gave alms to both Christians and Muslims.

Tolui died in 1232, aged 41. Ögedei Khan confirmed her authority over his estates, which included parts of northern China, and reportedly consulted her on many matters. He proposed marriage to her, and then marriage to his son Güyük, but she refused, saying her four sons needed her attention. In 1236 she asked for part of Hebei as her appanage, and Ögedei, after hesitating, agreed.

After Ögedei died in 1241, his wife Töregene Khatun ruled as regent until Güyük was elected Khagan in 1246. Güyük moved against Sorghaghtani and other powerful women. She had meanwhile allied herself secretly with Batu Khan, and when Güyük died in 1248 on a march westward some speculated that she had taken direct action. She and Batu then promoted her eldest son Möngke, who was formally named Great Khan at a kurultai in the Mongol homeland. The families of Ögedei and Güyük tried and failed to overthrow him.

Sorghaghtani died in February or March 1252, a few months after Möngke's accession, and was buried in a Christian church in Gansu. Her sons Möngke, Kublai, Hülegü and Ariq Böke each held power: Kublai as Great Khan and ruler of the Yuan dynasty, Hülegü as khan of the Ilkhanate, and Ariq Böke briefly as a rival Great Khan before Kublai captured him in 1264.

In 1310 she was honoured as Empress in a ceremony that included a mass, and in 1335 she was enshrined in a church in Ganzhou, where sacrifices were ordered. The Persian historian Rashid al-Din Hamadani called her extremely intelligent and able, and the Syriac scholar Bar Hebraeus also praised her. European accounts sometimes presented Mongol princesses such as her as daughters of Prester John.
sorghum: Sorghum bicolor was domesticated from a wild ancestor more than 5,000 years ago in eastern Sudan, in the area of the Rivers Atbara and Gash. It has been found at an archaeological site near Kassala dating from 3500 to 3000 BCE, and is associated with the Neolithic Butana Group culture. Sorghum bread from graves in Predynastic Egypt, some 5,100 years ago, is displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Turin.

About 4,000 years ago the crop spread to the Indian subcontinent, and about 3,000 years ago it reached West Africa. Wetter conditions in parts of the Horn of Africa between about 2,500 and 1,000 years ago supported its expansion and contributed to complex agricultural societies such as Aksum.

Sorghum is a large stout grass, typically annual, that grows in clumps and may reach over 4 metres high. Its bushy flowerheads carry up to 3,000 seeds each. It is also called great millet, Indian millet, Guinea corn, jowar and milo. Most varieties tolerate drought and heat, and the plant can grow in soils from heavy clay to sandy ground and recover after some drought. It suppresses weeds by producing a chemical called sorgoleone, and is usually grown by small farmers without fertilizer. Its name comes from the Italian sorgo, most likely from medieval Latin surgum and perhaps from Latin syricum, grass of Syria.

The first domesticated form had tight husks that had to be removed by force. Four further races evolved through cultivation with larger, free-threshing grains: caudatum in the Sahel, durra most likely in India, guinea in West Africa and magentiferum, from which came the varieties of Southern Africa.

Sorghum remained the staple food of the medieval kingdom of Alodia and of most Sub-Saharan cultures before European colonialism. In the Middle Ages the Arab Agricultural Revolution spread it, with other crops, across the Arab world as far as Al-Andalus. The grain is eaten as porridge, couscous or flatbread, such as the Indian jōḷada roṭṭi, and has no gluten. It is brewed into drinks: malwa beer in South Africa, and in China and Taiwan kaoliang liquor, a type of baijiu.

In the 19th century sweet sorghum, called the Chinese sugar-cane, was promoted as a source of sugar for the northern United States and the West Indies. Red leaf-sheaths have dyed leather in Nigeria and wool in Algeria, and in India the panicle stalks are used as broom bristles.
soria: Soria sits on the banks of the upper Douro, at about 1,065 metres above sea level, which makes it the second highest provincial capital in Spain. Its oceanic climate has very cold winters by Spanish standards and scant rainfall. The name may come from dauria, a form of the name of the river Durius, the Douro. Older explanations, that it descended from a castle named Oria after a Greek knight called Doricus, or that the first inhabitants were Dorians or Suebi, have been abandoned for lack of evidence.

The first recorded inhabitants of the area were the Celtiberians, around the 4th century BCE. After the Arab conquest the town grew in importance because it lay near the border of the Christian lands. In 869 it was the centre of a rebellion by Suleyman ibn-Abus against the emir of Córdoba. Soria itself enters history with its repopulation between 1109 and 1114 by the Aragonese king Alfonso I the Battler, who held the territory until 1134. It received a short fuero in 1120, confirmed by Alfonso VII of León in 1143.

Because Soria lay where several kingdoms met, it was at the centre of medieval conflicts. Alfonso VIII of Castile, who was born there, rewarded its support with privileges that it kept into modern times, and Alfonso X held his court there when he received the offer of the throne of the Holy Roman Empire. It prospered in the late Middle Ages through its border location and its control of the cattle industry, but lost importance after the union of Aragon and Castile in 1479 and the decree of exile of the Jews in 1492. French troops captured it and set it on fire in 1808.

Soria is a city and municipality in Castile and León and the capital of its province. Its heritage includes extensive medieval walls, Renaissance palaces and distinctive Romanesque churches such as San Juan de Rabanera. A few kilometres to the north lie the ruins of Numantia, a Celtiberian town whose inhabitants destroyed it rather than let it fall to Scipio, and the Numantine Museum holds finds from it. Antonio Machado spent five years teaching French in a secondary school in Soria, an experience that shaped his poetry.
sorrento: Sorrento is a city and comune on the Sorrentine Peninsula, overlooking the Bay of Naples, with views of Vesuvius and the island of Capri. The Amalfi Drive, a narrow road along high cliffs above the Tyrrhenian Sea, connects it with Amalfi. In antiquity its position was protected by deep gorges, and only about 300 metres on the south-west needed walls. The line of those walls is followed by the modern town.

From the 8th century BCE the area had a community of indigenous villages that was a crossing point for Etruscan traffic, and it later fell to the Osci, whose ruins at Surrentum date from about 600 BCE. Before coming under the Roman Republic Surrentum was subject to Nuceria. Its temples included those of Athena and of the Sirens. It was known in antiquity for wine, fish and red Campanian vases. An inscription shows that Titus restored the town's clock and its decoration in the year after the earthquake of 79 CE.

Sorrento became an archbishopric around 420. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it was ruled by the Ostrogoths and then returned to the Eastern Empire. In the 9th century it became an autonomous duchy, ruled by figures elected by the people who received honorary titles from the Byzantine emperor. It fought Amalfi, the Saracens and the Lombard duchies, and with Neapolitan help resisted a siege by Benevento in 839. Guaimar IV of Salerno acquired the city in 1035, and what remained of its independence ended in 1137, when Roger II of Sicily conquered it and annexed it to the Kingdom of Sicily.

On 13 June 1558 the Ottoman navy under Dragut and Piali sacked the town and reportedly took 2,000 captives, which led to a new line of walls. In 1648 there was a revolt against Spanish domination, led by Giovanni Grillo, and in 1861 Sorrento was annexed to the new Kingdom of Italy.

Sorrento was the birthplace of the poet Torquato Tasso, author of the Gerusalemme Liberata. Visitors have included Lord Byron, Keats, Goethe, Ibsen and Nietzsche, who wrote Human, All Too Human there in 1876. The song Torna a Surriento, with words by Giambattista De Curtis and music by his brother Ernesto, is named for it. Its cathedral dates from the 14th century and has 11th-century doors from Constantinople. It is a tourist resort, known for ceramics, lacework and marquetry, and it produces limoncello.
sotho-people: The Basotho are a Sotho-Tswana people, a mixture of Bantu-speaking clans that mixed with the San who already lived in southern Africa. Their ancestors are believed to have come from north-east Africa and to have migrated south in the fifth century CE. Separation from the Batswana is assumed to have taken place by the 14th century, and by the 16th century iron-working was well established in Basotho communities.

By at least the 17th century a series of Basotho kingdoms covered the southern part of the African plateau, in what is now the Free State, parts of Gauteng and the North West. Society was highly decentralised: each kraal, or extended clan, was ruled by its own chief, and chiefdoms were united only in loose confederations.

In the 1820s refugees from the Zulu expansion under Shaka came into contact with the Basotho of the highveld. In 1823 one group, the Kololo, migrated north and in 1845 conquered Barotseland. Moshoeshoe I meanwhile unified a loose confederacy of Basotho clans and Nguni peoples, and shaped refugee groups escaping the Difaqane into a cohesive nation.

He established his capital at Butha-Buthe in 1822 and later moved it to Thaba Bosiu. To meet the advance of the Boer voortrekkers he encouraged French missionaries of the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society, who advised him on foreign affairs, helped him to buy weapons and, between 1837 and 1855, set down Sesotho orthography and printed its first books.

After losing the western lowlands to the Boers in the Free State–Basotho Wars, Moshoeshoe appealed to Queen Victoria in 1868 to make Basutoland a British protectorate, with a British administration at Maseru. Borders were drawn in 1869, leaving large numbers of Sesotho speakers in the Orange Free State. Moshoeshoe died in 1870 and was buried on the summit of Thaba Bosiu. Basutoland became independent in 1966 as the Kingdom of Lesotho.

Sesotho is the first language of about 1.5 million people in Lesotho and of almost 4 million in South Africa according to the 2011 census, where it is one of eleven official languages. Missionary printing opened the way to a written literature, including Thomas Mofolo's epic Chaka. Because of the central part missionaries played in securing Moshoeshoe's kingdom, most Basotho became Christian, often blending Christianity with older beliefs in Modimo, a supreme being approached through the ancestors. Lesotho men have long migrated to South African cities to work in the mines. Traditional dress includes the mokorotlo, a conical hat, and the Basotho blanket, worn over the shoulders or waist.
soufriere-hills: The Soufrière Hills is a complex stratovolcano of andesitic rock, with many lava domes forming its summit. Montserrat is an overseas territory of the United Kingdom. Chances Peak was the island's highest summit until the mid-1990s, but rising and falling lava domes have since eclipsed it. The Centre Hills in the middle of the island and the Silver Hills in the north are older volcanic massifs related to the subduction zone. Many Caribbean volcanoes bear the name Soufrière, French for sulphur outlet, among them La Soufrière on Saint Vincent and La Grande Soufrière on Guadeloupe. An explosive eruption formed the crater at the summit around 2460 BCE, and about 1550 CE lava erupted at Castle Peak.

There had been seismic activity in 1897-1898, 1933-1937 and 1966-1967, but the eruption that began on 18 July 1995 was the first since the turn of the 20th century. The first phreatic explosion came on 21 August 1995, and after 18 weeks of such activity an andesitic lava dome began to form. Pyroclastic flows were first observed on 27 March 1996, and on 3 April 1996 southern Montserrat, including the capital Plymouth, was permanently evacuated after earlier evacuations. A major flow on 17 September 1996 damaged the village of Long Ground. A large eruption on 25 June 1997 killed nineteen people and destroyed the airport, and by August 1997 pyroclastic flows had buried much of the south of the island, including most of Plymouth.

About 7,000 people, two thirds of the population, left Montserrat, 4,000 of them for the United Kingdom, and the destroyer HMS Liverpool took a major part in the evacuation. The British and Montserrat governments led the aid effort, including a package of 41 million pounds. Riots followed an offer of 10 million pounds, as people protested that the British Government was not doing enough, and Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne resigned after allegations that he was too pro-British. The tourist industry collapsed, though it began to recover within fifteen years.

The volcano kept erupting until 2010, and its last eruption was in 2013. An eruption began without warning at 11:27 pm on 28 July 2008, with an ash column about 12,000 metres high and flows reaching Plymouth. On 11 February 2010 a partial collapse of the lava dome sent ash clouds over Guadeloupe and Antigua. The volcano is monitored by the Montserrat Volcano Observatory, operated by the British Geological Survey.
souphanouvong: Souphanouvong was born on 13 July 1909 at the Palace Sisouvanna, Xieng Dong, Luang Prabang, a son of Prince Bounkhong, the last viceroy of Luang Prabang. Unlike his half-brothers Souvanna Phouma and Phetsarath Ratanavongsa, whose mothers were of royal birth, his mother was a commoner, Mom Kham Ouane. He attended the Lycée Albert Sarraut in Hanoi and studied civil engineering at the École nationale des ponts et chaussées in Paris. After graduating in 1937 he returned to French Indochina and worked at the public works bureau in Nha Trang, building bridges and roads in central Vietnam and Laos, until 1945.

After the Japanese surrender he sought the support of the Việt Minh for Lao independence from French rule and met their leader, Hồ Chí Minh, who greatly impressed him. He became a leader of the Lao Issara movement, serving as its provincial chairman in Thakhek, then as foreign minister of its government and commander-in-chief of its army. Wounded in defeat by the French at Thakhek on 21 March 1946, he fled to Bangkok, where he remained in exile, resigning as foreign minister in March 1949 after disputes over continued cooperation with the Việt Minh.

In August 1950 he convened the first congress of the Lao Freedom Front, the Pathet Lao, supported by North Vietnam, and was elected its president, becoming known as the Red Prince. The movement was led by Kaysone Phomvihane, however, and Souphanouvong was more of a figurehead. In 1958 he served in Souvanna Phouma's unity government and was elected to the National Assembly with the most votes of any candidate. He was arrested in July 1959, escaped in May 1960, and helped negotiate the Geneva agreement on the neutrality of Laos in 1962. He publicly professed Marxism-Leninism only in 1967.

After the communist seizure of power in 1975 Souphanouvong became the first president of the Lao People's Democratic Republic, and he was president of the Supreme People's Assembly from 1975 to 1988. In 1991 he became an adviser to the Central Committee of the party. He was married to Nguyen Thi Ky Nam, a Vietnamese woman, and they had ten children. He spoke eight languages, including Greek and Latin. He died in Vientiane on 9 January 1995 of heart disease, and the government decreed five days of mourning. He was buried in a stupa next to the Pha That Luang, and in 2012 his remains were moved to the new national cemetery in Vientiane.
sourou-migan-apithy: Sourou-Migan Apithy was born on 8 April 1913 in Porto-Novo. He descended from an Ogu royal family but was not born into privilege, and his middle name, Migan, signified family ties with the chief ministers of the old Dahomeyan kingdoms. He studied at mission schools, became an assistant teacher, and in 1933 went to Paris, where he qualified in accounting. He volunteered for the army and fought as an artillery officer in 1939 and 1940. He did not return to Dahomey until 1945, when the Catholic pastor Francis Aupiais encouraged him to enter politics.

Running as a Socialist, Apithy was elected in 1945 to represent Togo and Dahomey at the French Constituent Assembly, with 6,600 of 9,057 votes. His nomination was a strategic move by Europeans, who wished to elect a black person to appease the colonists while keeping full power. In November 1946 he won Dahomey's single seat in the French National Assembly. There he sat on commissions on overseas territories and finance, and proposed a bank covering French West Africa and Togo, which became law.

The election of 17 June 1951 brought a second seat and a new rival, the northern teacher Hubert Maga. Apithy won 53,463 of 147,350 votes, and 64 per cent of them came from the Porto-Novo area. This election is cited as the point when regionalist parties arose, and it produced three de facto zones led by Maga in the north, Apithy in the south-east and Justin Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin in the south-west. Apithy's support came mostly from the Yoruba, Maga's from the Bariba and Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin's from the Fon and Goun. He became mayor of Porto-Novo in 1956 and later president of the Territorial Assembly of Dahomey.

He was the second president of Dahomey from 25 January 1964 until 27 November 1965, when Christophe Soglo overthrew him after infighting in the government, and he fled to Paris. After a disputed election on 28 March 1970, the three leaders formed a presidential council on 7 May, with the chair rotating every two years. Apithy shared in the council's decisions, among them the expulsion of the Togolese opposition leader Noe Kutuklui in 1971, which sparked demonstrations in Cotonou.

On 26 October 1972 soldiers led by Major Mathieu Kérékou seized power, calling the triumvirate "truly a monster". Maga, Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin and Apithy spent more than nine years in prison before Kérékou freed them in 1981. Apithy then settled in Paris, where he died on 3 December 1989, a few days before Kérékou ended socialism in the country.
sousse: Sousse lies on the Sahel coast of central-eastern Tunisia, on the Gulf of Hammamet, about 140 km south of Tunis. It stands between two wadis, the Wadi Bliban to the north and the Wadi al-Halluf to the south-east. The present city has grown to include the ruins of the ancient Hadrumetum. It has long been an agricultural and commercial centre, and an olive grove covering more than 2,500 square kilometres has been one of its riches since antiquity.

Tyrians founded Hadrumetum in the 11th century BCE as a trading post on the routes to Italy and the Strait of Gibraltar, at a river mouth about 9.7 km north of old Sousse. It became part of the Carthaginian world and appears in the Punic Wars, in the third of which it gained territory and privileges by aiding Rome, and in Caesar's Civil War. It was the second city of Roman Africa after Carthage and became the capital of Byzacena under the Diocletianic Reforms. Its natives included the jurist Salvius Julianus and the emperor Clodius Albinus. Extensive Roman and Byzantine catacombs lie beneath the city.

The Vandals sacked the city in 434, and the Byzantine Empire retook it in 534 and rebuilt its fortifications and churches. It was sacked again during the Umayyad conquest in the 7th century. Under the Aghlabids a new town called Susa was established near the ruins and served as their main port, from which the invasion of Sicily was launched in 827. Medieval Susa was known for silk and flax cloth called Sūsī and for its robes. Norman Sicily briefly occupied it in the 12th century, it fell to the Ottoman Empire in the 16th, and a French and Venetian fleet bombarded it in the 18th.

Tunisia became a French protectorate in 1881, and railways built between 1896 and 1911 linked Sousse to Tunis, Kairouan, Sfax and Mahdia. Before World War I it had about 25,000 inhabitants, including around 10,000 French. It suffered 39 bombardments between December 1942 and May 1943. It became a governorate capital after independence in 1956.

The medina, with its walls, souks, kasbah and mosques, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in 1988. The Ribat, a combined watchtower and minaret of the Aghlabid period, was built with marble taken from the churches of Melite, and the Great Mosque at the entrance to the medina dates from the 9th century. The city is the capital of the Sousse Governorate and Tunisia's third-largest city after Tunis and Sfax. Tourism and the port are important to its economy.
south-africa: South Africa covers 1,221,037 square kilometres at the southern tip of Africa, with 2,798 kilometres of coastline along the South Atlantic and Indian oceans, and it encloses Lesotho. The interior is a large, almost flat plateau between 1,000 and 2,100 metres high, surrounded by the Great Escarpment, whose eastern stretch is the Drakensberg; Mafadi, at 3,450 metres, is the highest peak. The south-western plateau is the sparsely populated Great Karoo, and the well-watered Highveld holds a great proportion of the commercial farmland and the largest conurbation, Gauteng. The country has three capitals: Pretoria, Cape Town and Bloemfontein.

South Africa holds some of the oldest archaeological and human-fossil sites in the world, among them the caves of the Cradle of Humankind in Gauteng, and modern humans have inhabited Southern Africa for at least 170,000 years. The indigenous San and Khoikhoi were predominantly hunter-gatherers, and the Khoikhoi also practised pastoralism; they were largely displaced or absorbed by the Bantu expansion between 1,500 and 2,000 years ago.

The Kingdom of Mapungubwe formed in the north in the 13th century, and the Venda Kingdom in the 17th. The Dutch established the first European settlement at Table Bay in 1652, the Cape Colony. Its invasion in 1795 and the Battle of Blaauwberg in 1806 led to British occupation, and the Mfecane, a period of upheaval, led to the formation of kingdoms including the Zulu Kingdom.

The Mineral Revolution brought industrialisation and urbanisation. After the Second Boer War the Union of South Africa was created in 1910 by the amalgamation of the Cape, Natal, Transvaal and Orange River colonies, and it became a republic after the 1961 referendum. The multi-racial Cape Qualified Franchise was gradually eroded, and the vast majority of black South Africans were not enfranchised until 1994. The National Party imposed apartheid in 1948, institutionalising earlier racial segregation, and after a struggle by the African National Congress and others the repeal of discriminatory laws began in the mid-1980s.

Universal elections took place in 1994, and since then all racial groups have held political representation in a parliamentary republic of nine provinces, in which the president is both head of state and head of government. The 2022 census counted Black African South Africans at 81%, Coloured at 8.2%, White at 7.3% and Indian or Asian at 2.7%. The country has 12 official languages and has been called the rainbow nation.
south-african-border-war: Namibia was governed as German South West Africa until the First World War, when it was invaded and occupied by Allied forces under General Louis Botha. After the Armistice of 11 November 1918 the League of Nations placed it under a mandate. After the Second World War the United Nations superseded the League, and Jan Smuts, who led the South African delegation, distrusted the proposed trusteeship system because of the vague wording of Article 77 of the Charter. Mounting opposition to apartheid inspired a South West African nationalist movement in the 1950s, and in 1955 students and teachers formed the South West African Progressive Association under Uatja Kaukuetu.

Ethiopia and Liberia petitioned the International Court of Justice in November 1960, and on 21 December 1962 the court ruled that they had the right to bring the case. SWAPO formed its armed wing, the People's Liberation Army of Namibia (PLAN), in 1962 with help from the Soviet Union and sympathetic African states such as Tanzania, Ghana and Algeria.

Fighting between PLAN and the South African security forces broke out in August 1966. PLAN grew more confident in 1973: on 26 January about 50 insurgents attacked a police base at Singalamwe in the Caprivi with mortars, machine guns and a rocket launcher, and by the end of the year the insurgency had spread across Caprivi, Ovamboland, Kaokoland and Kavangoland. The Carnation Revolution in Portugal of 25 April 1974 then destabilised Angola. South Africa feared a Soviet-backed government there allied with SWAPO, and in 1975 its forces became involved in Angola as the Central Intelligence Agency armed the FNLA and the MPLA received Soviet arms through Cuba.

From 1975 to 1988 the South African Defence Force staged large conventional raids into Angola and Zambia against PLAN bases, and used counter-insurgency units such as Koevoet and 32 Battalion. In 1978 P. W. Botha succeeded Vorster as prime minister and made Cuban withdrawal from Angola a condition of Namibian independence, a policy the United States supported and SWAPO denounced. In 1987 the Angolan army launched Operation Saluting October against UNITA, and the fighting around Cuito Cuanavale caused alarm in South Africa because of its casualties.

The South African government concluded in 1988 that it had reached the political limits of further escalation, and war weariness had grown among its civilians. The 1988 Tripartite Accord and the terms of Security Council Resolution 435 provided the basis for a settlement: elections for a constitutional assembly, confinement of PLAN and the Defence Force to their bases, withdrawal of all but 1,500 South African troops, demobilisation of paramilitary forces and the return of refugees. The United Nations Transition Assistance Group was to supervise the process, and the war ended on 21 March 1990.
south-african-communist-party: The Communist Party of South Africa was founded on 12 February 1921 by the joining of the International Socialist League and other groups, under the leadership of William H. Andrews. It first came to prominence in the Rand Rebellion of 1922, a strike by white miners against mining companies that planned to employ Black workers in semi-skilled jobs at low wages.

The party supported the strike as a struggle between the working class and the capitalists but distanced itself from the racist slogans linked with it. At its 1924 congress it turned to organising Black workers, and by 1928 1,600 of its 1,750 members were Black. In 1928 the Communist International had it adopt the Native Republic thesis, which held that South Africa belonged to its Indigenous Black population, and by 1948 the party had officially abandoned that policy.
Aware that the National Party, elected in 1948, was about to ban it, the party decided by a majority to dissolve itself, and it was declared illegal in 1950 under the Suppression of Communism Act.

In 1953 a group of former members launched the South African Communist Party, which stayed aligned with the Soviet Union. Its members worked mainly within the ANC to turn its programme towards a non-racial one, and many white members formed the Congress of Democrats, which joined the Congress Alliance. The alliance adopted the Freedom Charter, to which the party contributed.

When the ANC, previously committed to non-violence, turned to force, Nelson Mandela and Walter Sisulu allied with the communists to form Umkhonto we Sizwe, which began a campaign of bombings. Joe Slovo was its Chief of Staff, and his wife Ruth First was a leading theoretician of the struggle. The ban on the party was lifted in 1990, when Mandela was released from prison.

After 1994 several communists held prominent positions on the ANC benches, and Mandela appointed Joe Slovo as Minister for Housing. After Mandela's death in 2013 the ANC confirmed that he had been a party member and served on its central committee.

The party is a member of the Tripartite Alliance with the ANC and the Congress of South African Trade Unions. The party was often an ideological opposition to the policies of Thabo Mbeki's presidency, which became most apparent when he was ousted as ANC leader in 2007 and as president in 2008; Jacob Zuma replaced him. It marked its 90th anniversary on 30 July 2011.
south-america: South America lies entirely in the Western Hemisphere and mostly in the Southern Hemisphere. It is bordered on the west by the Pacific Ocean, on the north and east by the Atlantic Ocean, and on the south by the Drake Passage, and it has an area of 17,840,000 square kilometres. The geography of the west is dominated by the Andes, the longest mountain range in the world, whose highest mountain is Aconcagua at 6,962 metres. The east contains highlands and vast lowlands where the Amazon, Orinoco and Paraná flow.

The continent holds several superlatives: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, the Amazon is the largest river by volume, and the Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on earth. Lake Titicaca is the highest commercially navigable lake. Most of the population lives near the western or eastern coasts, forming what is called a hollow continent.

South America is thought to have been first inhabited by people who crossed the Bering Land Bridge at least 15,000 years ago and moved south through North America. The Monte Verde II site in Chile, suggested to date to around 14,500 years ago, is among the oldest evidence of human presence. Ancient DNA evidence shows that the peopling was more complex than a single migration, with at least three major dispersals. Llamas and alpacas were domesticated in the Andean highlands circa 3500 BCE.

Caral-Supe on the central Peruvian coast, generally dated to around 3500 BCE, was a pre-ceramic culture whose monumental architecture created one of the first cities of the world. Chavín followed by 900 BCE according to some estimates, and its civilisation spanned 900 to 300 BCE, with artefacts found at Chavín de Huántar in Peru. Irrigation systems and widespread fishing helped establish agrarian societies by 2000 BCE.

The continent includes twelve sovereign countries, two dependent territories and one internal territory, French Guiana. Brazil covers a little less than half of its land area and holds around half of its population. Most countries are presidential republics, and Guyana and Suriname are parliamentary republics. It is the only inhabited continent without monarchies, though the Empire of Brazil existed in the 19th century.

The population is estimated at more than 434 million. Spanish and Portuguese are by far the most spoken languages, with approximately 200 million speakers each. Indigenous languages include Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní, which are recognised with Spanish as national languages.
south-arabia: South Arabia, also called Greater Yemen, is the historical region of the southern Arabian Peninsula. It is centred on what is now the Republic of Yemen, but it historically included Najran, Jazan and Asir, now in Saudi Arabia, and Dhofar, now in Oman. Its people share linguistic and ethnic affinities, traditions and culture that cross recent political boundaries. Two groups of indigenous languages belong to it, both Semitic and unrelated to each other: the extinct Old South Arabian languages and the Modern South Arabian languages.

The name Yemen is variously derived from ymnt, meaning south, and from yamn or yumn, meaning felicity or blessed, since much of the country is fertile. The Romans called the region Arabia Felix, fertile Arabia, as opposed to Arabia Deserta, and classical Latin and Greek writers sometimes called it India. Southern Arabia lay on the Indian Ocean trade routes for millennia.

About three thousand years ago several ancient states occupied South Arabia: Main, Qataban, Hadhramaut and Saba. The region was known for the great dam at Marib, the cosmopolitan incense trade and the Queen of Sheba of tradition. Some two thousand years ago the Himyarites conquered South Arabia and dominated it for several centuries.

The title of one of the kings of the second Himyarite Kingdom, Shammar Yahri'sh, includes the term Yamnat, which probably referred to the south-western and southern coastlines of the peninsula between Aden and Hadramout. The Himyarites were defeated and displaced by Persian armies of the Sasanian dynasty in 575 CE, which also arrived by sea. Half a century later, in 628 CE, the region was integrated into the first Islamic state.
south-asia: South Asia is the southern sub-region of Asia, defined in both geographical and ethnic-cultural terms. Topographically it is dominated by the Indian subcontinent and is bounded by the Indian Ocean in the south and by the Himalayas, Karakoram and Pamir Mountains in the north. Most of it rests on the Indian Plate, which drifted northeastwards from ancient Gondwana and collided with the Eurasian plate nearly 55 million years ago. The extent of the region is not clear cut: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka are commonly included, and Afghanistan often is too, though it may also be classed as part of Central Asia.

Settled life emerged in the western margins of the Indus basin 9,000 years ago and developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished from c. 3300 to 1300 BCE. By 1200 BCE an archaic form of Sanskrit had spread into India from the northwest, and by 400 BCE caste stratification had emerged within Hinduism, while Buddhism and Jainism had arisen proclaiming social orders unlinked to heredity.

Mahmud of Ghazni raided northern India seventeen times between 997 and 1030, and the Delhi Sultanate was founded in the 13th century. The Mughal Empire followed in 1526, while the Vijayanagara Empire and the Kingdom of Mewar remained under Hindu kings and local Muslim rulers held parts of the Deccan. The British East India Company gradually expanded its rule; Crown rule began in 1858. In 1947 the British Indian Empire was partitioned into the Dominion of India and the Dominion of Pakistan, amid large-scale loss of life and migration. East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh after the war of 1971.

South Asia has an area of 5.2 million square kilometres, about 10 percent of Asia, and about 2 billion people, which makes it the most populous and the most densely populated geographical region in the world. Hindus form about 68 percent of its people and Muslims about 31 percent, while Buddhists, Jains, Christians and Sikhs make up most of the rest. The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, founded in 1985 with seven members, brings together the nations of the region.
south-carolina: South Carolina borders North Carolina to the north and northeast, the Atlantic Ocean to the southeast, and Georgia to the west and south across the Savannah River. From east to west it has three natural regions: the Atlantic coastal plain, the Piedmont and, in the northwestern corner, the Blue Ridge Mountains. The coastal plain makes up two-thirds of the state, and its eastern edge is the Sea Islands, a chain of tidal and barrier islands. It has many salt marshes and estuaries, and natural ports such as Georgetown and Charleston.

There is evidence of human activity in the area from about 50,000 years ago. When Europeans arrived, around 1500, there were many separate Native American polities, among them the powerful Cofitachequi. About a dozen tribes of Siouan background lived up the rivers of the coastal plain, the Cherokee further west and the Catawba along the Catawba River. They lived in villages and relied on agriculture.

The Spanish were the first Europeans in the area. On 8 October 1526 they founded San Miguel de Gualdape near present-day Georgetown, the first European settlement in what is now the contiguous United States. It began with five hundred settlers and was abandoned eight months later by one hundred and fifty survivors. In 1540 Hernando de Soto explored the region and the main town of Cofitachequi.

The state is named for King Charles I of England, who first formed the English colony, Carolus being Latin for Charles. The Province of South Carolina was formed in 1712 and became a royal colony in 1719. More than 200 battles and skirmishes of the Revolutionary War were fought within it, and it ratified the United States Constitution on 23 May 1788, the eighth state to do so. As a slave state it was the first to vote for secession, in 1860, and it was readmitted to the Union in 1868. The civil rights movement of the mid-twentieth century helped end segregation and legal discrimination in the state.

South Carolina is composed of 46 counties. Its capital is Columbia and its most populous city is Charleston. A Gullah community lives in the state, and the Catawba Indian Nation is its one federally recognised tribe.
south-caucasus: The South Caucasus lies on the border of Eastern Europe and West Asia and takes in the southern part of the Caucasus Mountains and their lowlands, from the Main Caucasian Range to the Turkish and Armenian borders and from the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea coast of Iran. It includes the whole of the Lesser Caucasus, the Colchis Lowlands, the Kura-Aras Lowlands and the eastern Armenian Highlands. The older name Transcaucasia is a Latin form of the Russian Zakavkazye, meaning the area beyond the Caucasus, and so implies a Russian vantage point.

Lying on the edges of Iran, Russia and Turkey, the region was for centuries an arena of political, military, religious and cultural rivalry. It came under the Achaemenid, Parthian, Roman, Sasanian, Byzantine, Umayyad, Abbasid, Mongol, Ottoman, Safavid and Russian empires, among others. Its ancient kingdoms included Colchis, Urartu, Iberia, Armenia and Albania, which were incorporated into Iranian empires, and Zoroastrianism became the dominant religion. After the kingdoms converted to Christianity the region became an area of religious as well as military conflict.

In the middle of the 8th century Umayyad armies captured Derbend and most of the region became part of the caliphate. The Orthodox Christian Kingdom of Georgia later dominated most of it, before conquest by Seljuk, Mongol, Safavid, Ottoman and Qajar dynasties. Russia took most of the region from Qajar Iran in the Russo-Persian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828. By the Treaty of Gulistan Iran ceded eastern Georgia and most of present-day Azerbaijan, and by the Treaty of Turkmenchay it lost present-day Armenia and the rest of Azerbaijan. In 1844 the three present-day countries were combined in one government-general.

After the fall of the Russian Empire the region was united twice, as the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic in 1918 and as the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic from 1922 to 1936. It then remained in the Soviet Union as three separate republics, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia, each of which became an internationally recognised sovereign state in 1991. The region has a total area of about 186,100 square kilometres, and its products include oil, manganese ore, tea, citrus fruits and wine.
south-china-sea: The South China Sea is bounded in the north by South China, in the west by the Indochinese Peninsula, in the east by Taiwan and the north-western Philippines, and in the south by Borneo, eastern Sumatra and the Bangka Belitung Islands. It covers around 3,500,000 square kilometres and connects with the East China Sea through the Taiwan Strait and with the Philippine Sea through the Luzon Strait. Its average depth is 1,212 metres. Major rivers flowing into it include the Pearl, the Red and the Mekong.

The sea lies above a drowned continental shelf, and during recent ice ages, when sea level was hundreds of metres lower, Borneo was part of the Asian mainland. The basin opened around 45 million years ago, when the so-called Dangerous Ground rifted away from southern China, and extension ceased around 17 million years ago.

The sea has long been a trade route between north-east Asia, China, Southeast Asia, India and the West. Many trading-ship wrecks on its floor attest to commerce going back centuries, and nine historic ships carrying ceramics dating from the 10th to the 19th century were excavated under the Swedish engineer Sten Sjöstrand.

The names for the sea reflect its users. The Yi Zhou Shu, a chronicle of the Western Zhou dynasty, gives the first Chinese name, Nanfang Hai, the Southern Sea, and says that people from the sea sent tribute of hawksbill sea turtles to the Zhou rulers. In Southeast Asia it was once called the Champa Sea, after the maritime kingdom of Champa, which flourished there before the 16th century. Portuguese sailors in the 16th century called it the China Sea. Most of the sea came under Japanese naval control during World War II, after Japan took many surrounding territories in 1941.

The sea contains over 250 small islands, atolls, cays, shoals and reefs, most without indigenous people and many covered at high tide. They include the Spratly Islands, the Paracel Islands, Pratas Island, Macclesfield Bank and Scarborough Shoal. The largest of the Spratlys, Taiping Island, is just over 1.3 kilometres long. Several states border or claim parts of the sea, and the claims are reflected in the variety of names for it.
south-east-england: South East England is one of the nine official regions of England used for statistical purposes. It consists of nine counties: Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, East Sussex, Hampshire, the Isle of Wight, Kent, Oxfordshire, Surrey and West Sussex. Its land area is 19,072 square kilometres. Officially it does not include London, which is a separate region, although the term is used colloquially for a varying area. Until 1999 a south east statistical region also included Bedfordshire, Greater London, Essex and Hertfordshire. The highest point is Walbury Hill in Berkshire at 297 metres, and the River Thames flows through the region.

In medieval times the region included much of the Kingdom of Wessex, the precursor of the modern state of England. Winchester was the capital of England after the unification of the various states, including the kingdoms of Kent, Sussex and Mercia, and ceased to be the administrative capital some time in the 13th century as the City of London came to dominate commerce. Richard II, crowned there in 1377, was the last monarch crowned at Winchester, and Queen Mary I in 1553 the last crowned by the Bishop of Winchester.

In 1656 John Wallis of Kent introduced the symbol for infinity and the standard notation for powers of numbers, and Thomas Bayes, a statistician from Tunbridge Wells, gave his name to a theorem of probability theory. The Canterbury and Whitstable Railway, built by George Stephenson and hauled by the locomotive Invicta, began on 3 May 1830 as the world's first passenger train service. Sir Francis Pettit Smith of Kent invented the screw propeller. In the Second World War much of the Battle of Britain was fought in the region, especially in Kent, and RAF Bomber Command was based at High Wycombe.

The region has no directly elected regional government. A voluntary South East England Regional Assembly, based in Guildford, existed from 1998 until its abolition on 31 March 2009. Its eight legally chartered cities are Brighton and Hove, Canterbury, Chichester, Milton Keynes, Oxford, Portsmouth, Southampton and Winchester. Places of interest include Canterbury Cathedral, the White Cliffs of Dover, Windsor Castle, Blenheim Palace, Leeds Castle and HMS Victory at Portsmouth. The New Forest and the South Downs are national parks. The King's School, Canterbury, claims a foundation in 597, and the University of Oxford stands in the region.
south-india: South India, also called Peninsular India, is the southern part of the Deccan Peninsula. It is bound by the Bay of Bengal in the east, the Arabian Sea in the west and the Indian Ocean in the south, and its heartland is a plateau bordered by the Western and Eastern Ghats. The Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Penna, Tungabhadra and Vaigai are important non-perennial rivers. The southernmost tip of mainland India is at Kanyakumari. The word Deccan is an anglicised form of the Prakrit dakkhiṇa, from the Sanskrit dakshiṇa, meaning south. The region has a tropical climate and depends on monsoons for rainfall.

Ash mounds associated with Neolithic cultures date back to 8000 BCE, and iron technology spread through the region towards 1000 BCE, though no fully developed Bronze Age seems to have preceded it. The region lay on a trade route from Muziris to Arikamedu linking the Mediterranean to East Asia, and trade with Phoenicians, Romans, Greeks, Arabs, Syrians, Jews and Chinese began in the Sangam period, from about the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE. Dynasties that shaped the culture of its parts include the Cheras, Cholas, Pandyas, Pallavas, Satavahanas, Chalukyas, Hoysalas, Rashtrakutas and Vijayanagara.

Europeans arrived in the 15th century, entering India through Kerala, and by the middle of the 18th century the French and British were in a protracted struggle for military control. After the defeat of Tipu Sultan in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War in 1799 and the end of the Vellore Mutiny in 1806, the British consolidated their power over much of the region, except French Pondichéry. Under British rule it was divided into the Madras Presidency, Hyderabad State, Mysore and the Madras States Agency. Of the 72 delegates at the first session of the Indian National Congress in December 1885, 22 came from South India. The States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which reorganised the states on linguistic lines, weakened the proposal for a separate Dravida Nadu.

South India comprises the states of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu and the union territories of Puducherry and Lakshadweep. Most of its people speak at least one of the four major Dravidian languages: Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam. Tamil was the first language granted classical language status, in 2004, and the others followed. Hinduism is the major religion, with Shaivism and Vaishnavism among its main traditions, and the Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
south-korea: The Korean Peninsula was inhabited as early as the Lower Paleolithic. According to Korea's founding mythology, the history of Korea begins with the founding of Gojoseon in 2333 BCE by Dangun; Chinese records note Gojoseon in the early 7th century BCE. In 108 BCE the Han dynasty defeated Wiman Joseon and installed four commanderies in the north of the peninsula. The Lelang commandery remained a centre of cultural and economic exchange for four centuries, until Goguryeo conquered it in 313 CE.

From the Proto-Three Kingdoms states of Buyeo, Okjeo, Dongye and Samhan emerged the Three Kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla. Goguryeo was the largest and a highly militaristic state, with 700 years of history. Under Gwanggaeto the Great and his son Jangsu it subdued Baekje and Silla. In the Goguryeo-Sui War it is said to have defeated a force of over a million men.

The Goryeo dynasty (918 to 1392) achieved lasting unification, and the Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1897) followed it, maintaining an isolationist policy from the mid-17th century. The Korean Empire (1897 to 1910) was annexed by the Empire of Japan in 1910. After Japan's surrender in World War II, Korea was divided into a Soviet-occupied northern zone and a United States-occupied southern zone, and the Republic of Korea was established in August 1948.

The Korean War began in 1950 with a North Korean invasion and ended in 1953 with an armistice, with three million Koreans dead and both economies in ruins. No peace treaty was signed. South Korea then endured a series of dictatorships punctuated by coups, revolutions and violent uprisings, while its economy grew rapidly and it became one of the Four Asian Tigers. The June Democratic Struggle of 1987 ended authoritarian rule and led to the Sixth Republic.

Under the 1987 constitution South Korea is a unitary presidential republic with a unicameral National Assembly. It is divided into ten provinces, three special self-governing provinces and several cities with special status. Its recorded economic growth was among the fastest between the early 1960s and the late 1990s; South Koreans call this the Miracle on the Han River.

The population was roughly 51.7 million in 2022. South Korea shares its traditional culture with North Korea, though the two have developed distinct contemporary cultures since 1945. It has 16 World Heritage Sites.
south-ossetia: South Ossetia is a very mountainous region in the Caucasus. It occupies the southern slopes of the Greater Caucasus range and its foothills, which form part of the Iberia Plain, and the Likhi Range marks its western boundary. The Greater Caucasus forms its northern border with Russia, and the only main road across the range, the Transkam highway through the Roki Tunnel, was completed in 1986. The mountains shield it from cold air from the north, so it is warmer there than in the Northern Caucasus.

The Ossetians are believed to descend from the Alans, a nomadic Iranian people whose kingdom of Alania emerged in the northern Caucasus in the 8th century. Alania fell to a Mongol invasion and later to the armies of Timur, who massacred much of its population, and surviving Alans retreated into the central Caucasus and gradually migrated south into the Kingdom of Georgia. In 1306, after a three-month siege of Gori, George V of Georgia took Gori and the territory of South Ossetia from them. Georgian historians place the mass migration of Ossetians into Georgia in the 17th century, while Ossetian historians say they lived there since ancient times.

After the Russian Revolution the area became part of the Democratic Republic of Georgia. In 1918 conflict began between landless Ossetian peasants, influenced by Bolshevism, and the ethnic Georgian aristocrats who owned the land. The first Ossetian rebellion began in February 1918, and further uprisings in 1919 and 1920, covertly supported by Soviet Russia, were defeated. Ossetian sources allege that the crushing of the 1920 uprising killed 5,000 Ossetians, with more than 13,000 further deaths from hunger and epidemics.

Soviet authorities established the South Ossetian Autonomous Oblast in 1922, and it declared independence from the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic in September 1990. Georgia abolished its autonomy and sent troops, which led to the 1991–1992 South Ossetia War, with Russian involvement on the Ossetian side. Escalations in 2004 and in the Russo-Georgian War of August 2008 left Ossetian and Russian forces in full de facto control of the former oblast.

South Ossetia's status is disputed. Russia recognised it as independent after the 2008 war, while Georgia and most other states regard it as Georgian territory under Russian occupation. Its capital is Tskhinvali, and it has the official names Republic of South Ossetia and State of Alania, which the 2017 referendum gave equal standing.
south-saskatchewan-river: The South Saskatchewan River begins in southern Alberta, at the confluence of the Bow and Oldman Rivers north of Grassy Lake, and ends at the Saskatchewan River Forks in central Saskatchewan, where it joins the North Saskatchewan River to form the Saskatchewan River. Both of its source rivers draw on winter snowpack and rainfall in the Rocky Mountains near the border of British Columbia and Montana. Glacier and snowmelt from the Rocky Mountains and foothills supply nearly 90 per cent of the annual flow, most of it in July and August.

From the headwaters of the Bow River the South Saskatchewan flows for 1,392 kilometres. At its mouth it has an average discharge of 280 cubic metres per second and a watershed of 146,100 square kilometres, of which 1,800 lie in Montana. The Red Deer River is its major tributary, joining 16 kilometres east of the Alberta-Saskatchewan border.

For the first half of the 20th century the river froze over completely in winter, and its ice breaks made conditions spectacular and dangerous at Saskatoon, Medicine Hat and elsewhere; at least one bridge in Saskatoon was destroyed by ice. The Gardiner Dam, built in the 1960s, lessened the river's power by diverting a substantial part of its flow into the Qu'Appelle River, and by the 1980s many permanent sandbars had formed as the level fell. The dams created the reservoir of Lake Diefenbaker.

Sections of the riverbank are prone to slumping, and Saskatoon has dealt with a number of slope failures since its founding; the control of riverbank development was a factor in the establishment of the Meewasin Valley Authority in 1979.

Below the dam the river flows north through Saskatoon, and the Meewasin Valley Authority is responsible for conserving the river environment for about 60 kilometres near the city. Oxbows of the river formed several lakes there, among them Moon Lake and Pike Lake. Four Important Bird Areas of Canada lie along the river, two at Lake Diefenbaker. In the Saskatchewan section the valley floor is heavily wooded, with eastern cottonwood, Manitoba maple and green ash, and its birds include the piping plover and the great blue heron. The fish of the river include walleye, sauger, northern pike, goldeye and lake sturgeon.
south-sudan: South Sudan lies between latitudes 3° and 13°N and is covered in tropical forest, swamps and grassland. The Nile river system runs south to north across its centre. The White Nile, known locally as the Bahr al Jabal, passes Juba and forms the Sudd, a large swamp of seasonally flooded grassland. Habitats include plateaus, savannahs, floodplains and wetlands, and Bandingilo National Park hosts one of the largest wildlife migrations in the world.

The Nilotic peoples of the region, among them the Dinka, Anyuak, Bari, Acholi, Nuer and Shilluk, first entered South Sudan sometime before the tenth century. From the 15th to the 19th century migrations, largely from the area of Bahr el Ghazal, brought the Anyuak, Dinka, Nuer and Shilluk to their modern locations, while the Acholi and Bari settled in Equatoria. The Zande and others, who entered in the 16th century, established the region's largest state, in Equatoria. In the 18th century the Avungara sib rose to power over the rest of Azande society.

Egypt under Khedive Ismail Pasha first tried to control the region in the 1870s, setting up the province of Equatoria; its governors were Samuel Baker from 1869, Charles George Gordon from 1874 and Emin Pasha from 1878. Sudan was governed as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium from 1899 until independence in 1956. British policies favouring Christian missionaries, such as the Closed District Ordinance of 1922, together with the swamplands along the White Nile, limited the spread of Islam to the south. Colonial policy emphasised the development of the Arabised north and largely ignored the south, which lacked schools, hospitals, roads and bridges.

After Sudan's first independent elections in 1958, continued neglect of the south by the Khartoum government led to revolts and the longest civil war on the continent. Following the First Sudanese Civil War the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region was formed in 1972 and lasted until 1983, when the Second Sudanese Civil War began. It ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005, and southern autonomy was restored. More than 2 million people are said to have died in the wars and more than 4 million were displaced. South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after 98.8% voted for independence in a referendum in January 2011.

South Sudan is a landlocked country in East Africa, and its capital and largest city is Juba. Its transitional constitution, in force since 9 July 2011, sets up a presidential system with a two-house National Legislature. The population is composed mostly of Nilotic peoples, the Dinka being the largest group, followed by the Nuer and the Azande. The common languages are Juba Arabic and English. A civil war was fought from 2013 to 2018.
south-tyrol: South Tyrol, officially the Autonomous Province of Bolzano/Bozen – South Tyrol, is Italy's northernmost province, with an area of 7,398 square kilometres, and its capital and largest city is Bolzano. It is bordered by Austria to the east and north, by the Swiss canton of Graubünden to the west, and by the Italian provinces of Belluno, Trentino and Sondrio. The landscape is highly mountainous: the Dolomites, parts of which UNESCO recognized in 2009, lie within it. Its three main valleys, the Adige, the Eisack and the Puster, were formed by the Ice Age Adige glacier and its tributaries, and the Adige drains 97 per cent of the territory.

The name reflects that the province was made from the southern part of the historic County of Tyrol, a former state of the Holy Roman Empire and crown land of the Habsburgs. German and Ladin speakers call it Südtirol; the Italian name is Alto Adige.

South Tyrol as an administrative entity originated in the First World War. The Allies promised the area to Italy in the Treaty of London of 1915 as an incentive to enter the war on their side. Until 1918 it was part of the Austro-Hungarian County of Tyrol, but this almost wholly German-speaking territory was occupied by Italy at the war's end in November 1918 and annexed in 1919. The province as it exists today was created in 1926. The Italianization of South Tyrol and the settlement of Italians from the rest of the country after 1918 significantly changed local demography; most Italian place names were translated from German by Ettore Tolomei.

After the Second World War the Allies left the province in Italy on condition that its German-speaking population be granted significant self-government. The Gruber–De Gasperi Agreement of September 1946 created the autonomous region of Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol, with German and Italian as official languages. Austria judged its implementation unsatisfactory, and the South Tyrolean Question was taken up by the United Nations in 1960. Negotiations in 1961 failed, partly because of a campaign of terrorism. Italy and Austria officially ended the dispute in 1992, on the basis of an agreement of 1972.

South Tyrol has a considerable level of self-government, with exclusive legislative and executive powers, and it is cited as a model for protecting linguistic minorities. German and Italian are official languages, and Ladin is a third in some eastern municipalities. Since 1996 it has formed, with Austria's Tyrol and the Italian province of Trento, the Euroregion Tyrol–South Tyrol–Trentino, whose boundaries match the old County of Tyrol. Its economy rests on agriculture, notably apples and wine, industry and tourism. The South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano holds the mummy of Ötzi the Iceman.
south-wales: South Wales is a loosely defined region of Wales, bordered by England to the east and mid Wales to the north. It is generally taken to include the historic counties of Glamorgan and Monmouthshire and to extend west to Carmarthenshire and Pembrokeshire, though people west of Swansea may think of themselves as living in both south and west Wales. The Brecon Beacons National Park covers about a third of the region and holds Pen y Fan, the highest British mountain south of Cadair Idris.

It is the most populous and most urban part of Wales, a result of its industrial past, when small towns became cities on the money of mining, smelting and shipping. Cardiff, the capital, lies in it, together with Newport, Swansea, Merthyr Tydfil and Barry.

Between the Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 and the Laws in Wales Act 1535, crown land in Wales formed a Principality of south Wales, made up of Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire, former parts of the kingdom of Deheubarth, with a Justiciar of South Wales at Carmarthen. Other parts of the south were held by Marcher Lords. The Laws in Wales Acts 1542 created the Court of Great Sessions, whose circuits set seven southern counties apart from six in the north.

The valleys of Glamorgan and Monmouthshire were once rural, but in the early Industrial Revolution they were exploited for coal and iron. By the 1830s hundreds of tons of coal went by barge to Cardiff and Newport, and in the 1870s Newport Docks were the largest coal-exporting docks in the world. Merthyr Tydfil grew around the Dowlais Ironworks and had 60,000 people at the 1831 census, more than Cardiff, Swansea and Newport combined. The Rhondda grew from about 3,000 people in 1860 to 160,000 by 1910. Workers came from the Midlands, Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall and Italy, and many settled in English-speaking valley communities, while overcrowding brought cholera and the Welsh language declined sharply.

Mining was dangerous. In 1896 fifty-seven men and boys died in a gas explosion at Tylorstown Colliery. In October 1966 a coal tip above Aberfan, left unstable by heavy rain, slid onto the village, killing 114 children and 28 adults. The 1930s Depression closed almost half the pits of the coalfield, and by July 1985 only 31 remained. The last traditional deep mine, Tower Colliery, closed in January 2008.

Service industries, call centres and a growing film and television sector have largely replaced coal and iron, though Port Talbot Steelworks remains a large producer of steel. Welsh was historically the majority language and is now outnumbered by English, but it survives strongly in places such as the Neath and Swansea valleys. The landscape is marked by Nonconformist chapels, and several secondary schools teaching in Welsh operate across the region.
south-yemen: South Yemen's origins go back to 1874 and the creation of the British Colony of Aden and the Aden Protectorate. Before 1937 Aden had been governed as part of British India. In 1959 six protectorate states signed an accord to form the Federation of the Emirates of South Arabia, and on 18 January 1963 Aden Colony was merged with it as the Federation of South Arabia.

The first uprising against British rule came in Radfan on 14 October 1963, when about 7,000 armed tribesmen joined the National Liberation Front, which used hit-and-run tactics. In November 1967 the Federal Army came out in support of the NLF and Britain negotiated a hasty handover.

The last British troops left eleven hours before the People's Republic of Southern Yemen was born at midnight on 29–30 November 1967, ending 128 years of colonial rule, and it joined the United Nations on 14 December 1967.

The National Front, as the NLF was now called, had around 26,000 members and no experience in government, and it split into right and left wings. On 22 June 1969 the Marxist–Leninist faction under Abdel Fattah Ismail and Salim Rubai Ali overthrew President Qahtan al-Shaabi in a bloodless coup called the Corrective Move. A constitution drafted with Egyptian and East German advisers was promulgated on 30 November 1970, and the Front was replaced by the Yemeni Socialist Party, formalised in 1978.

The state received aid from the Soviet Union and East Germany, which stationed several hundred Stasi officers there, though by the mid-1980s the Soviet Union under Mikhail Gorbachev had largely distanced itself.

On 13 January 1986 fighting broke out in Aden between supporters of Ali Nasir and of the returned Ismail. It lasted more than a month, with thousands of casualties, Ali Nasir's ouster and Ismail's presumed death, and some 60,000 people fled to North Yemen. The People's Democratic Republic of Yemen united with the Yemen Arab Republic on 22 May 1990.

South Yemen was a centralised Marxist–Leninist state in which legislative authority rested with the Supreme People's Council and the official ideology was scientific socialism. Its economy moved from Aden's colonial port system to central planning, land reform and state-backed cooperatives, and major petroleum deposits were found in Shabwah Governorate in late 1986. The state set up a welfare system with health care and education, and the Family Law of 1974 banned child marriage and polygamy.
southampton: Archaeological finds suggest the area has been inhabited since the Stone Age. After the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 and the conquest of the local Britons in 70, a fortress settlement named Clausentum was established at the site of modern Bitterne Manor. It was an important trading port and defensive outpost of Winchester, defended by a wall and two ditches, and is thought to have had a bath house. Clausentum was not abandoned until around 410.

After the Norman Conquest of 1066 Southampton became the major port of transit between Winchester, then the capital of England, and Normandy. Southampton Castle was built in the 12th century, and the surviving remains of merchants' houses such as King John's House and Canute's Palace show the wealth of the town at that time. By the 13th century it was a leading port, importing French wine in exchange for English cloth and wool. French pirates raided it, which led to the building of the fortified town walls, many of which still stand.

In 1415, before Henry V left for the Battle of Agincourt, the ringleaders of the Southampton Plot, Richard, Earl of Cambridge, Henry Scrope, 3rd Baron Scrope of Masham, and Sir Thomas Grey of Heton, were accused of high treason, tried at what is now the Red Lion public house in the High Street and executed outside the Bargate. The friary was dissolved in 1538. The Pilgrim Fathers set out from the port aboard the Mayflower in 1620, though the ship was forced to return to Plymouth. In 1642, during the English Civil War, a Parliamentary garrison moved in, and the Royalists, who advanced as far as Redbridge in March 1644, were prevented from taking the town.

The town expanded greatly in the Victorian era. The Southampton Docks company was formed in 1835, the foundation stone of the docks was laid in October 1838, the first dock opened in 1842, and the railway link to London was fully opened in May 1840. It became known as The Gateway to the Empire. In 1912 the RMS Titanic sailed from Southampton; 497 men, four in five of the crew on board, were Sotonians. The city was heavily bombed in the Second World War and was a major embarkation point for D-Day. Southampton acquired city status in 1964, had a population of 248,922 at the 2021 census, and has the longest surviving stretch of medieval walls in England.
southeast-asia: Southeast Asia lies south of China, east of the Indian subcontinent and northwest of mainland Australia. It divides into Mainland Southeast Asia and Maritime Southeast Asia, covers about 4,500,000 square kilometres, and has mostly a hot, humid tropical climate shaped by monsoons. It lies near the meeting of geological plates, and Indonesia is one of the most volcanically active places in the world. Europeans long called it the East Indies, and Chinese sources called it Nanyang, the Southern Ocean.

Homo erectus lived in the region about 1,500,000 years ago. Rock art in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo, dated to 40,000 to 60,000 years ago, is currently the oldest known. Contact with the Indian subcontinent from about 400 BCE began a gradual Indianisation: traders and religious figures brought religions, architecture and political administration, and Sanskrit and Pali became the elite languages. Northern Vietnam was never fully Indianised, having been under Chinese rule from 111 BCE to 938 CE.

Islam reached the region through trade from the eighth century but spread widely only later. The Sultanate of Kedah was established in 1136, Samudera Pasai converted in 1267, and Malacca became a centre of Islamic study and maritime trade. Southeast Asia was a critical part of the world trading system before Europeans arrived, above all for spices such as pepper, cloves and nutmeg. Spain, Portugal, the Dutch, the British and the French followed, and commercial interests gradually became annexation. Several countries were briefly occupied by the Empire of Japan in the Second World War, and most of the region was decolonised afterwards.

The region has eleven countries, all members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). About 676 million people live there, and Indonesia is the most populous country. Nearly 800 native languages are spoken. Islam is the most practised faith, with about 240 million adherents, concentrated in Indonesia, Brunei, Malaysia, southern Thailand and the southern Philippines. Its culture shows the long influence of India, China, Islam and the colonial powers.
southeast-asia-treaty-organization: The Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty was signed in Manila on 8 September 1954 as part of the American effort to build anti-communist collective defence treaties, aimed in this case at keeping China in check. Secretary of State John Foster Dulles is considered the main force behind it, and Vice President Richard Nixon had advocated an Asian equivalent of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which became the model. The organization itself was set up on 19 February 1955 at a meeting in Bangkok, where its headquarters stood. Dulles had preferred to call it the Manila Pact, to avoid identifying it publicly with NATO.

It was headed by a Secretary General, an office created in 1957, with a council of representatives and committees for economics, security and information. The first Secretary General was the Thai diplomat Pote Sarasin.

Eight members joined in all: Australia, France, New Zealand, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States. Only the Philippines and Thailand were Southeast Asian states. Burma and Indonesia rejected joining, and Malaya chose not to take part formally. The Geneva Agreements of 21 July 1954 barred North Vietnam, South Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos from joining military alliances, but SEATO placed them under its protection, and Cambodia rejected this in 1956. Unlike NATO, SEATO had no joint commands with standing forces, and its response protocol to a common danger was vague.

The members held joint training but never deployed forces. SEATO could not intervene in Laos because France and the United Kingdom rejected military action, so the United States gave unilateral support to Laos after 1962. The United States and Australia cited membership as a reason for involvement in the Vietnam War, though British and French refusal kept SEATO itself out. Pakistan withdrew in 1973, after East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh, and France withdrew its financial support in 1975. After a final exercise on 20 February 1976, SEATO was dissolved on 30 June 1977.

Historians have generally regarded the pact as a failure, and the British diplomat Sir James Cable called it a fig leaf for the nakedness of American policy. Its cultural and educational programmes had lasting effects. In 1959 SEATO founded the SEATO Graduate School of Engineering in Thailand, now the Asian Institute of Technology, and a Teacher Development Center in Bangkok. It set up cholera research laboratories in Bangkok and Dacca; the Dacca laboratory became a leading cholera research centre and is now the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh.
southern-african-development-community: The origins of the organisation lie in the 1960s and 1970s, when the leaders of majority-ruled countries and national liberation movements coordinated their political, diplomatic and military struggles to end colonial and white-minority rule in southern Africa. The immediate forerunner of its political and security cooperation was the informal grouping known as the Frontline States, formed in 1980.

The forerunner of its socio-economic cooperation was the Southern African Development Coordination Conference. Nine majority-ruled southern African countries adopted the Lusaka declaration on 1 April 1980, which paved the way for the formal establishment of the conference that April. Membership of the Frontline States and of the conference sometimes differed.

The conference was transformed into the Southern African Development Community on 17 August 1992, when its founding members and the newly independent Namibia adopted the Windhoek declaration and the treaty establishing the new body. The 1992 treaty provided for both socio-economic and political and security cooperation. The Frontline States were dissolved only in 1994, after South Africa's first democratic elections, and later efforts to place political and security cooperation on a firm institutional footing under the Community failed.

On 14 August 2001 the treaty was amended, beginning an overhaul of structures, policies and procedures. Political and security cooperation was institutionalised in the Organ on Politics, Defence and Security, one of the principal bodies, subject to the oversight of the Summit of heads of state or government.

The Community's goal is to further regional socio-economic cooperation and integration, as well as political and security cooperation, among 16 countries in southern Africa. Its primary objectives are development, economic growth and poverty alleviation, though peacekeeping has become increasingly important. It has 27 legally binding protocols on subjects such as defence, the illicit drug trade, free trade and the movement of people, including the Protocol on Politics, Defence and Security Co-operation of 2001. It has six principal bodies: the Summit, the Organ on Politics, Defence and Security, the Council of Ministers, the Tribunal in Windhoek, the National Committees and the Secretariat in Gaborone. Except for the Tribunal, committees and Secretariat, decisions are taken by consensus.

The SADC Free Trade Area was established in August 2008, after the Protocol on Trade of 2000 laid its foundation. Its original members were Botswana, Lesotho, Madagascar, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Eswatini, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe. In October 2008 the Community joined the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa and the East African Community in agreeing a single free trade zone of 26 countries.
southern-bug: The Southern Bug, also called the Southern Buh, is a navigable river in Ukraine and the longest river flowing exclusively within the country, second only to the Ukrainian part of the Dnieper. It rises in the Volhynian-Podolian Upland in the west of Ukraine, about 145 kilometres from the Polish border, and flows south-east through the southern steppes into the Bug Estuary of the Black Sea basin. It is 806 kilometres long and drains 63,700 square kilometres. It should not be confused with the Western Bug, which flows in the opposite direction towards the Baltic. Towns on its banks include Khmelnytskyi, Vinnytsia, Pervomaisk, Voznesensk and Mykolaiv.

Herodotus refers to the river by its ancient Greek name, Hypanis. During the Migration Period of the 5th to the 8th centuries CE it was a major obstacle to the peoples moving through the area, and Jordanes in his Getica calls it Bogossola. Its long-standing Slavic name, Boh, may derive from an Indo-European root meaning a bend, and the French military engineer Guillaume Le Vasseur de Beauplan recorded it in the 17th century as Bog.

From the 16th to the 18th centuries most of the south of Ukraine was under Ottoman domination, and the colonists renamed the river Aq-su, the White river. Slavic place names were re-established after the conquest of the Pontic region in the 17th and 18th centuries. After the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774 the river became a border between Imperial Russia and the Ottomans.
