In 1918 the Central Council of the Ukrainian People's Republic created a district called Pobozhia, the lands of the Boh, near its source. Between 1941 and 1944 the river formed the border between German-occupied Ukraine, the Reichskommissariat Ukraine, and the Romanian-occupied Transnistria.

The river is navigable for dozens of kilometres up from its mouth, and river ports such as Mykolaiv stand on it. At Mykolaiv the Varvarivskyi Bridge, a swing bridge that lets ships built in the city pass, has a span of 134 metres, the largest of its kind in Europe, and is the southernmost bridge over the river. The main tributaries include the Inhul, 354 kilometres long, on the left bank and the Chychyklia and Kodyma on the right.
southern-dobruja: Southern Dobruja, also called the Quadrilateral (Romanian: Cadrilater) or Dobrogea Nouă, meaning New Dobruja, comprises the provinces of Dobrich and Silistra. It covers 7,412 square kilometres and has a population of about 358,000. It is historically noteworthy as a point of contention in Bulgarian-Romanian relations.

At the beginning of the modern era the region had a mixed population of Bulgarians and Turks with smaller groups of Gagauz, Crimean Tatars and Romanians. In 1910 its 282,007 inhabitants included 134,355 Bulgarians (47.6 per cent), 106,568 Turks (37.8 per cent), 12,192 Roma, 11,718 Tatars and 6,484 Romanians. It was part of the autonomous Bulgarian principality from 1878 and of the independent Bulgarian state from 1908, until Bulgaria's defeat in the Second Balkan War, when it was ceded to Romania by the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913. Bulgaria targeted it again during the war that began in 1914.

Under Romanian rule the region formed two counties, Durostor and Caliacra. In 1914 the Romanian state demanded that landowners prove their property and surrender one third of the land they claimed, or pay its value. Many of the peasants who received land were settlers, among them tens of thousands of Aromanians and Megleno-Romanians from Macedonia and Romanians from Wallachia, which led to claims that the reform had a nationalist purpose.

Bulgaria regained the region on 7 September 1940 under the Treaty of Craiova, which was accompanied by a compulsory population exchange. About 110,000 Romanians, Aromanians and Megleno-Romanians, almost 95 per cent of whom had settled there after 1913, had to leave Southern Dobruja, while 77,000 Bulgarians had to leave Northern Dobruja. Only a few hundred Romanians and Aromanians remain in the region.
southern-netherlands: The Southern Netherlands, also called the Catholic Netherlands, were the parts of the Low Countries belonging to the Holy Roman Empire that came under Habsburg rule. They covered most of modern Belgium and Luxembourg, small parts of the modern Netherlands and Germany, and until 1678 most of the present Nord-Pas-de-Calais region of France. Several small states in the region were never ruled by Spain or Austria: the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, the Imperial Abbey of Stavelot-Malmedy, the County of Bouillon, the County of Horne and the Princely Abbey of Thorn. The capital, Brussels, lay in Brabant.

The Netherlands were wealthy and led by a merchant class, and Habsburg attempts to raise taxes for their wars, together with penal laws that made heresy a capital crime, provoked a rebellion that began the Eighty Years' War. The seven northern provinces, led by Holland and Zeeland, established their independence as the United Provinces after 1581, while Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, reconquered the ten southern ones. In the early 17th century the Archduchess Isabella and her husband Archduke Albert of Austria governed from a flourishing court at Brussels, from which the painter Peter Paul Rubens emerged. Albert's death in 1621 returned the territory to formal Spanish control.

As Spanish power waned, France took a growing share. By the Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 it annexed Artois, and the treaties of Aix-la-Chapelle and Nijmegen later added Cambrai, Walloon Flanders and half of Hainaut. The Treaty of Rastatt in 1714 gave what was left to Austria, largely at British and Dutch insistence, since they feared French domination. Barrier fortresses along the border were garrisoned with Dutch troops.

Joseph II's centralizing policies provoked a rebellion in 1788, and the provinces formed the United States of Belgium in January 1790. His brother and successor Leopold II restored Austrian rule by the end of that year. After the Battle of Sprimont in 1794 French armies overran the region, which was annexed to the French Republic in 1795. Most of the population was hostile to French rule, above all because of conscription, the assignat and the Republic's anti-religious policies: in 1797 nearly 8,000 priests refused an oath and went into hiding.

Austria confirmed its loss at Campo Formio in 1797. The Congress of Vienna of 1815 gave the region to the new United Kingdom of the Netherlands, and after the Belgian Revolution of 1830 it became the independent Kingdom of Belgium.
souvanna-phouma: Souvanna Phouma was born on 7 October 1901, the son of Bounkhong, the last vice-king of Luang Prabang, and a nephew of King Sisavang Vong. He received a French education in Hanoi, Paris and Grenoble, where he gained a degree in architecture and engineering. He returned to Laos in 1931, married Aline Claire Allard, daughter of a French father and a Lao mother, and entered the Public Works Service of French Indochina.

Around the end of the war he joined the Lao Issara, or Free Laos, movement with his brother Prince Phetsarath Rattanavongsa and his half-brother Prince Souphanouvong. The movement was set up to oppose the French occupation and the provisional government at Vientiane of 1945. When the French reoccupied Laos he fled into exile in Bangkok, and he came back in 1949 as France began to concede autonomy.

In 1951 Souvanna became prime minister under the banner of the National Progressive Party and held the post until 1954. After the elections of December 1955 he returned to office on a platform of national reconciliation. In August 1956 he and the Communist Pathet Lao, headed by his half-brother Souphanouvong, agreed on broad proposals for a government of national union. In the elections of May 1958 for 21 extra assembly seats, parties aligned with the Pathet Lao won 13. Souphanouvong entered the government as Economic Minister, and Phoumi Vongvichit took the Ministry of Religion and Fine Arts.

In June 1958 the rightists forced Souvanna to resign again. King Sisavang Vatthana signed Royal Ordinance No. 282 dismissing his government and gave power provisionally to a Revolutionary Committee, and Royal Ordinance No. 283 approved a provisional government under Prince Boun Oum, who acted as front man for Phoui Sananikone. The king asked three princes to form a coalition between the rightists and the Pathet Lao, but it collapsed and the Laotian Civil War began. Souvanna was prime minister again in 1960 and from 1962 to 1975, and between May and August 1960 he was president of the National Assembly.

He led the neutralist faction throughout these years, seeking a settlement between the rightists and the Pathet Lao. After the civil war he became an adviser to the new government. He died in Vientiane on 10 January 1984. His honours included the Order of the Million Elephants and the White Parasol of Laos and the French Legion of Honour.
sovereignty: The word comes from unattested Vulgar Latin superanus, from Latin super, meaning chief or ruler, and entered English in the fourteenth century. In classical antiquity the Roman jurist Ulpian recorded that the people had transferred all their imperium and power to the emperor, and that the laws did not bind him. Medieval monarchs were not absolute, for they shared power with the feudal aristocracy and both were constrained by custom.

The concept returned in the late sixteenth century, when civil wars created a craving for stronger central authority. Jean Bodin, partly in reaction to the French wars of religion, argued in Les Six Livres de la République of 1576 that sovereignty must be absolute. Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan of 1651, reached a similar view for a different reason: people must join in a commonwealth and submit to a sovereign power that can compel them to act for the common good.

Sovereignty is generally defined as supreme, independent control and lawmaking authority over a territory, with hierarchy inside the state and autonomy abroad. The notion of state sovereignty contains four aspects: territory, population, authority and recognition. Stephen D. Krasner distinguishes domestic, interdependence, international legal and Westphalian sovereignty. De jure sovereignty is the legal right to rule a territory and de facto sovereignty the ability to do so in practice. Max Weber described it as a community's monopoly on the legitimate use of force. Internal sovereignty concerns the legitimacy of a government, which may rest on the divine right of kings or on a social contract. Sovereignty may be shared, as in a condominium.

In the Age of Enlightenment sovereignty gained legal and moral force as the main Western description of the state, and by 1800 the social contract was widely accepted as a way of establishing it, especially in the new United States and France. In federal systems, constituent states keep some powers independently, and differing interpretations of state sovereignty, tied to the expansion of slavery and fugitive slave laws, led to the American Civil War.

After the Second World War sovereign prerogatives were increasingly limited by European integration and international human-rights norms. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948, and the Genocide Convention the day before. The meaning of sovereignty has never been universally agreed.
soviet-japanese-border-conflicts: Japanese expansion in Northeast China created a common border between Japanese-occupied Manchuria and the Soviet Far East. After the Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931 and 1932, violations of the borders between Manchukuo, the Mongolian People's Republic and the Soviet Union became frequent. Many were misunderstandings arising from a poorly marked frontier, but some were deliberate acts of espionage.

The Imperial Japanese Army counted 152 border disputes between 1932 and 1934, and the Soviets blamed the Japanese for 15 border violations, 6 air intrusions and 20 episodes of "spy smuggling" in 1933 alone. Trust declined further when the Seventh Comintern Congress of July 1935 openly called the Japanese "fascist enemies".

The first armed clash, the Halhamiao incident, took place on 8 January 1935, when Mongolian cavalry met a Manchukuo patrol led by a Japanese adviser, leaving two dead. Japanese records list 108 such incidents between early 1935 and April 1939. In June 1937 Soviet gunboats landed troops on Kanchazu Island in the Amur, and Japanese artillery sank one and drove off the others, killing 37 Soviet soldiers.

The Battle of Lake Khasan, from 29 July to 11 August 1938, began when the Japanese 19th Division expelled a Soviet garrison from disputed ground. The division repulsed repeated attacks by a far larger Soviet force, and both sides suffered heavy losses. The Japanese ambassador in Moscow asked for peace on 10 August, and the Soviets reoccupied the area.

In 1939 the Battles of Khalkhin Gol, known in Japan as the Nomonhan Incident, followed. After a Japanese attack in July stalled, a Soviet counteroffensive in late August encircled the Japanese 23rd Division, and by 31 August the Soviets and Mongolians had destroyed all Japanese forces on their side of the river. A cease-fire was agreed on 15 September.

The Khalkhin Gol defeat freed Stalin from a threat in the Far East, and the Soviet invasion of Poland began on 17 September 1939. Japan and the Soviet Union signed the Soviet–Japanese Neutrality Pact on 13 April 1941. Japan kept it after Germany attacked the Soviet Union later that year, largely, it is said, because of the defeat at Khalkhin Gol, which led Japan to give up the Hokushin-ron plan of joining Germany against the Soviets and to turn to Southeast Asia instead. On 5 April 1945 the Soviet Union denounced the pact, and in August it declared war on Japan.
soviet-union: The word soviet means council in Russian. Soviets as workers' councils first appeared during the 1905 Russian Revolution and were quickly suppressed. After the February Revolution of 1917, workers' and soldiers' soviets emerged across the country and shared power with the Russian Provisional Government. The Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, demanded that all power pass to the soviets, and after the October Revolution they seized power in their name. Following the Bolshevik victory in the Russian Civil War, the Russian Socialist Federal Soviet Republic and its subordinate republics were merged into the Soviet Union in 1922.

War communism involved nationalisation of industry and forced requisition of agricultural production. After a severe economic collapse Lenin replaced it in 1921 with the New Economic Policy, which legalised free trade and private ownership of small businesses. After Lenin's death in 1924 Joseph Stalin emerged as undisputed ruler. By 1928–1929 he had abandoned the New Economic Policy for full central planning, forced collectivisation and rapid industrialisation. Collectivisation is linked to a devastating famine in the 1930s that killed millions. The Gulag was expanded, and the Great Purge of the late 1930s brought deportations, executions and the Moscow trials.

The Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with Nazi Germany in 1939, and Germany invaded in 1941. The Soviet Union suffered around 27 million casualties, the most deaths of any country in the Second World War. The Cold War followed, and Soviet forces suppressed uprisings in East Germany, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. Mikhail Gorbachev sought reform from 1985 through glasnost and perestroika. After a failed coup by hardliners in 1991, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus seceded, and on 26 December Gorbachev recognised the dissolution of the Soviet Union. All fifteen republics became independent.

The Soviet Union was a federal union of national republics, the largest being the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. The Communist Party governed under Marxism–Leninism through soviet councils, and the general secretary of the party's Central Committee was the de facto highest office. Elections were uncontested. The economy was centrally planned. Its area of 22,402,200 square kilometres made it the world's largest country, with its capital and largest city at Moscow. Culture went through stages: relative freedom of artistic experiment in the first decade, then under Stalin the imposed style of socialist realism, with other trends severely repressed and many writers imprisoned or killed.
soweto-uprising: The Afrikaans Medium Decree of 1974 required black schools to use Afrikaans and English in equal measure as languages of instruction. From 1 January 1975 Afrikaans was to be used for mathematics, arithmetic and social studies from standard five, English for general science and practical subjects, and indigenous languages only for religious instruction, music and physical culture.

Black South Africans associated Afrikaans with apartheid, and Desmond Tutu, then bishop of Lesotho, called it the language of the oppressor. Punt Janson, the Deputy Minister of Bantu Education, said he had not consulted the people affected and would not do so. On 30 April 1976 children at Orlando West Junior School went on strike, and the refusal spread to other Soweto schools.

Students such as Teboho Tsietsi Mashinini of Morris Isaacson High School proposed a meeting on 13 June 1976. An Action Committee, later the Soweto Students' Representative Council, organised a peaceful demonstration for 16 June with support from the Black Consciousness Movement. Thousands of students marched towards Orlando Stadium, finding police barricades on their intended route, and carried placards against Afrikaans, one of them saying that if the students must learn Afrikaans, Vorster must learn Zulu.

Police used tear gas, batons, dogs and live ammunition. Among the first to be shot dead were 15-year-old Hastings Ndlovu and 12-year-old Hector Pieterson. The photographer Sam Nzima photographed the dying Pieterson as he was carried away by Mbuyisa Makhubo, with his sister Antoinette beside him, and the picture became the symbol of the uprising. Crowds targeted bottle stores, beer halls and offices of the state, and Melville Edelstein, a welfare officer and sociologist, was killed by a mob. On the next day, 17 June, 1,500 armed police were deployed in Soweto.

Unrest spread to townships across the country. The Cillie Commission, set up to investigate, estimated 575 deaths from violence up to 28 February 1977, of whom 496 were black Africans, 75 coloured, 2 white and 2 Indian. About 400 white students of the University of the Witwatersrand marched in Johannesburg in protest, and the UN Security Council passed Resolution 392 condemning the apartheid government.

The African National Congress distributed leaflets calling for Mandela to be freed and Vorster to be hanged. The Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum opened in Soweto in 2002. 16 June is a public holiday in South Africa, Youth Day, and elsewhere is known as the Day of the African Child.
soyo: Soyo, originally spelled Sonho and pronounced Sonyo, was a province of the Kingdom of Kongo that stretched south from the mouth of the Congo River to the River Loze and inland about 100 kilometres. It was already an administrative unit, ruled by a governor with the title mwene Soyo, when the Portuguese arrived in 1482. Its ruler, baptised Manuel and said to be an uncle of the king, was the first Kongo lord to be baptised, in 1491. The king then allowed Soyo to expand over sub-provinces such as Pambala, Kimi, Tubii and Lovata.

Soyo's port of Mpinda near the river mouth became important in the sixteenth century. A community of Portuguese settled there and traded in slaves, ivory and copper. A Kongo royal inquest of 1548 found that as many as 4,000 slaves a year passed through Mpinda on the way to São Tomé and then Brazil.

In the sixteenth century Soyo was usually ruled by a member of Kongo's royal family appointed by the king for a limited term. In the early 1590s Miguel was named a count when King Álvaro II introduced European titles, but tension with the crown left him a more or less independent ruler. Later kings placed their own candidates in Soyo again. In 1641 Daniel da Silva replaced Paulo and was opposed by King Garcia II, who attacked in 1641, 1643, 1645 and 1656 without success, partly because his armies could not take the fortified wooded area of Nfinda Ngula near the capital. Soyo's rulers then took the title Prince, and later Grand Prince.

In 1670 the Portuguese governor, taking advantage of a Kongo civil war, invaded Soyo. After an early victory his forces were routed at the Battle of Kitombo on 18 October 1670, a day still kept as a holiday. The city then had about 30,000 residents. In the 1680s Count Antonio II Baretto da Silva fought Kakongo and Ngoyo north of the river, and after 1708 Soyo took no part in the elections of Kongo's rulers.

Soyo, formerly called Santo António do Zaire, is a city in the province of Zaire in Angola, at the mouth of the Congo River. The city had 200,920 inhabitants at the 2014 census, and the municipality 221,555 at the 2024 census. It has an airport and a sea port and lies close to offshore oil extraction, which gives it a large place in Angola's oil industry.
sozh-river: The Sozh rises in the Smolensky District of Smolensk Oblast in Russia and is mostly snow-fed. It flows south through the Pochinkovsky and Khislavichsky Districts, then along the border between Khislavichsky and Shumyachsky Districts in Russia and the Mogilev Region of Belarus, before joining the Dnieper on its left bank. Its length is 648 kilometres, of which 493 lie within Belarus, and its catchment covers 42,140 square kilometres. The river freezes between November and early January, and the ice thaws from late March or April.

Its main tributaries are the Vikhra and Pronia on the right and the Ostyor, Besed, Iput and Uts on the left. It is one of six tributaries longer than 500 kilometres that join the Dnieper. The name comes from Old East Slavic Съжь; Vadim Zhuchkevich derived it from an Old Russian word for burned parts of a forest prepared for ploughing.

Several centuries ago the East Slavic Radimichi lived in the Sozh basin and founded the town of Gomel. They farmed, reared cattle, fished and gathered honey, and the river carried their trade towards the north-west and south-east of Europe. Gomel is first reported in 1142 under Kievan Rus. It came under Lithuanian control in 1537, then Polish rule under the Truce of Andrusovo, and passed to Russia in 1772. Embankments built along the river there are credited to the Rumyantsevs and the Paskeviches, statesmen and commanders of the Russian Empire.

Vetka, on the river north-east of Gomel, was gutted by Russian forces in 1735 and 1764, and its people were resettled in eastern Russia. It was known for icon painting and wood carving and was annexed by the Russian Empire in 1852. Excavations have found a Palaeolithic boat in the river's soils, now in the Museum of Ancient Belarusian Culture, and the remains of temples dated to the 3rd and 4th centuries at the mounds of Tushemlia and Haradok, which have been inferred to be Baltic. Remains of woolly mammoth have been found along the river as well. Russian myths set the turbulent Sozh against the quiet Dnieper.

The Sozh is navigable from Krychaw, with locks in its upper reaches, and timber is floated along it. Gomel, the second largest city in Belarus, stands on it, as do Krychaw, Cherykaw, Slawharad and Vietka. The mouth of the river is 150 metres broad and swampy. Phosphorite lies along its banks between Mstislavl and Krichev.
space-race: The Space Race grew out of the ballistic missile arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union after the Second World War. Launching satellites and people required large missiles such as Wernher von Braun's A-4, known as the V-2, developed by Nazi Germany. After the war both powers took custody of German rocket assets. The United States recruited von Braun and most of his team in Operation Paperclip, and they later developed the Redstone rocket at Huntsville, Alabama. On 29 July 1955 the United States announced that it intended to launch small Earth circling satellites for the International Geophysical Year, and five days later the Soviet Union said it would also launch one in the near future.

The Soviet launch of Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957 caused what the Western public called the Sputnik crisis. The United States launched Explorer 1 on 31 January 1958, and its instruments helped prove the existence of the Van Allen radiation belt. The Soviet Luna 2 impacted the Moon on 14 September 1959, and Luna 3 sent back pictures of its far side the next month. Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight in Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961 led President John F. Kennedy, on 25 May 1961, to ask Congress to commit to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the end of the decade.

Both countries built super heavy-lift rockets. The United States developed the Saturn V, and Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in July 1969 with Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin. The Soviet N1 rocket did not succeed and was cancelled, and the Soviet Union turned to the Salyut space stations and to robotic landings on Venus and Mars. The United States landed five more Apollo crews on the Moon.

Détente followed. In May 1972 Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev agreed to the Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, and in July 1975 a US astronaut crew and a Soviet cosmonaut crew met in Earth orbit. Many observers consider this the final act of the race, though competition was only gradually replaced by cooperation. In 1993 the United States and Russia agreed on the Shuttle–Mir and International Space Station programmes.

Historians disagree on who won. Many see the Apollo landings as a decisive American victory, but Asif A. Siddiqi stresses that the Soviet Union's early and sustained robotic exploration of the Moon and planets shows a broader rivalry than one event. Walter A. McDougall describes space exploration as a demonstration of each superpower's political and technological systems.
spain: Spain covers most of the Iberian Peninsula and has an area of 505,992 square kilometres, making it Europe's fourth largest country. It also includes the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, the Canary Islands in the Atlantic and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa, so that it is a transcontinental country. Mount Teide on Tenerife, at 3,715 metres, is the highest peak in Spain. The Pyrenees form the border with France and Andorra, and the border with Portugal, at 1,214 kilometres, is the longest uninterrupted border within the European Union.

Archaeological research at Atapuerca shows that the Iberian Peninsula was populated by hominids very early, and Neanderthal populations survived in parts of Iberia until around 40,000 years ago. The paintings in the Altamira cave of Cantabria were created from 35,600 to 13,500 BCE. Before the Roman conquest the major cultures were the Iberians along the Mediterranean coast, the Celts in the interior and north-west, the Lusitanians in the west and the Tartessians in the southwest, while Phoenicians, Carthaginians and Greeks established trading settlements. The Roman conquest created the province of Hispania. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the Visigoths established a kingdom centred on Toledo.

In the early 8th century the Umayyad Caliphate conquered most of the peninsula, with Al-Andalus centred on Córdoba. The northern Christian kingdoms launched the so-called Reconquista, which culminated with the fall of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada.

The union of the Crown of Castile and the Crown of Aragon in 1479 under the Catholic Monarchs is often seen as the de facto unification of Spain as a nation state. During the Age of Discovery Spain led the exploration and conquest of the New World, completed the first circumnavigation of the globe and established one of the largest empires in history. The 19th century brought the Peninsular War of 1808 to 1814 and the loss of most American colonies, and the Spanish Civil War of 1936 to 1939 was followed by the Francoist dictatorship until 1975.

Spain had a population of 49,570,725 in 2026, with Madrid as the capital and largest city. A national referendum on 6 December 1978 approved the new constitution with 88% of voters, and Spain transitioned from a one-party personalist dictatorship to a multiparty parliamentary democracy of seventeen autonomous communities and two autonomous cities. It is a parliamentary monarchy with King Felipe VI as head of state. Spain joined the European Economic Community in 1986 and took part in the launch of the euro in 1999.
spandau: Spandau is the westernmost of the twelve boroughs of Berlin, at the confluence of the Havel and the Spree, and extends along the western bank of the Havel. It has the smallest population of the boroughs but the fourth largest land area, 91.91 square kilometres. Outside Berlin it borders the districts of Oberhavel and Havelland and the city of Potsdam.

The history of Spandau begins in the 7th or 8th century, when the Slavic Heveller settled the area and later built a fortress. King Henry I conquered it in 928, but it returned to Slavic rule after the rebellion of 983. In 1156 the Ascanian Albrecht the Bear took possession of the region. Spandau was first mentioned as Spandowe in 1197 in a deed of Otto II, Margrave of Brandenburg, forty years before the Cölln part of medieval Berlin, and it received city rights in 1232. Joachim II of Brandenburg completed the citadel, begun under Ascanian rule, between 1559 and 1594.

In 1634, during the Thirty Years' War, Spandau was surrendered to the Swedes, and in 1689 a commune of French Huguenots and Waldensians was established. French troops under Napoleon took the city after the Battle of Jena and Auerstedt in 1806, and Prussian and Russian troops besieged the citadel the following year. The revolutionary Gottfried Kinkel was held in the town prison from 1849 until Carl Schurz freed him on the night of 6 November 1850. Before the First World War the arsenal made Spandau a centre of the German arms industry, and in 1920 it was incorporated into Greater Berlin.

After World War II Spandau lay in the British sector of West Berlin. Spandau Prison, rebuilt in 1876, held the Nazi war criminals given custodial sentences at the Nuremberg Trials. After the death of its last inmate, Rudolf Hess, in 1987, the Allied powers demolished it completely, and a shopping mall later replaced it. In the south of the district, Gatow airfield served the Royal Air Force during the occupation and the Berlin Airlift, and since 1995 has housed the Gatow Museum of Military History.

The Renaissance citadel, the town hall of 1913 and the Catholic church of St Marien am Behnitz, built in 1848, are among its landmarks. A subcamp of the Sachsenhausen concentration camp, mainly for Polish and Hungarian women, operated there during World War II.
spanish-american-war: The nineteenth century was a period of decline for the Spanish Empire, which had lost most of its American colonies in the early wars of independence. Cuba supplied Spain with prestige and trade and served as a training ground for its army. The first serious bid for Cuban independence, the Ten Years' War, began in 1868 and was subdued in 1878. In early 1895 José Martí launched a new invasion and revolt. Spanish authorities suppressed it harshly, and under Governor-General Valeriano Weyler they adopted a policy of reconcentration.

American newspapers, notably Joseph Pulitzer's New York World and William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal, denounced Spain, and historians debate how far they swayed opinion. In January 1898 President William McKinley sent the cruiser USS Maine to Havana to protect American citizens, and on 15 February 1898 it was sunk by an explosion in the harbour.

The Teller Amendment of 19 April 1898 promised that the United States did not intend to annex Cuba. On 21 April the United States began a blockade of Cuba, and the two countries declared war. In the Pacific, a US squadron destroyed the Spanish fleet at Manila Bay on 1 May 1898. The first US forces landed in Cuba on 10 June, fought at El Caney and San Juan Hill on 1 July, and captured Santiago de Cuba on 17 July. Guam surrendered without resistance on 20 June, and US troops landed on Puerto Rico on 25 July. An armistice was signed on 13 August. Disease killed far more soldiers than combat did.

The Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 December 1898, ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States, which paid Spain 20 million dollars for the Philippines. Cuba was to become independent in 1902, though in practice it became a US protectorate.

The war made the United States a major power with island possessions across the globe and provoked a debate over imperialism. President McKinley and the supporters of expansion prevailed over opponents led by William Jennings Bryan, and Mark Twain wrote The War Prayer in protest. In the Philippines the revolution against Spain led to the Philippine–American War. In Spain the defeat was a shock to national life and prompted the reassessment of the Generation of '98.
spanish-american-wars-of-independence: Political independence was not the foreordained outcome of the turmoil in Spanish America, and there was little interest in it at first. In the 18th century the Bourbon Reforms increased the Crown's control and changed the language used of the overseas lands from kingdoms to colonies, and the appointment of peninsulars, born in Spain, to royal offices thwarted creole elites. Enlightenment ideas and the examples of the Atlantic Revolutions also spread through the empire.

The trigger was in Europe. In 1808 Napoleon Bonaparte forced the Spanish royal family to abdicate and installed his brother Joseph as king. The Spanish world almost uniformly rejected this, but there was no clear answer to the lack of a king. Juntas formed in Spain, and in 1809 short-lived juntas in Chuquisaca, La Paz and Quito opposed the Supreme Central Junta of Seville. Most Spanish Americans who supported the new governments saw them as a way to keep their autonomy.

Juntas appeared across Spanish America in 1810 when the Central Junta fell to the French, among them the Junta Suprema de Caracas of 19 April 1810. Royal officials split between liberals who supported the Cortes of Cádiz and conservatives. Those who favoured outright independence, calling themselves Patriots, used the juntas to promote their cause, and a war between Patriots and Royalists spread across the continent.

With the restoration of Ferdinand VII in 1814, Spain turned its main effort to South America, and by 1815 a stalemate had set in. In northern South America Simón Bolívar, Francisco de Paula Santander and José Antonio Páez fought in the Orinoco basin and on the Caribbean coast. On 1 January 1820 Rafael Riego led a rebellion in Spain that forced Ferdinand to restore the Constitution of 1812, which let Rioplatense, Chilean and Colombian revolutionaries converge against the Viceroy of Peru. In New Spain Agustín de Iturbide began the process that led to Mexican independence. The Spanish fortifications at Veracruz, Callao and Chiloé held out until 1825–1826.

The new national boundaries largely followed the colonial provinces. The republics abandoned the Inquisition and noble titles, but slavery was not immediately abolished, and total abolition came in most countries only in the 1850s. Creoles and mestizos replaced Spanish-born officials in most offices, and creoles stayed at the top of the social order. The wars weakened the economies and political institutions and hindered economic development for most of the nineteenth century. Gran Colombia and the Federal Republic of Central America collapsed after a decade or two. Cuba and Puerto Rico remained under Spanish rule until the war of 1898.
spanish-armada: England and Spain had been allies for many decades after Henry VII of England formed a strategic relationship with Ferdinand II of Spain against the threat of France. The French Wars of Religion were the ultimate cause of the break between Philip II of Spain and Elizabeth I. The fleet's purpose was to reinstate Catholicism in England, end English support for the Dutch Republic and stop attacks by English and Dutch privateers on Spanish interests in the Americas.

The fleet was commanded by Alonso de Guzmán, Duke of Medina Sidonia, an aristocrat appointed by Philip. When it left Lisbon it numbered 141 ships, with 10,138 sailors and 19,315 soldiers. Its orders were to sail up the English Channel, join the army of Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, in Flanders and escort an invasion force to England. The English fleet, based at Plymouth, was faster and more manoeuvrable than the larger Spanish galleons, and it kept beyond grappling range and bombarded the Spanish from a distance.

The armada anchored off Calais on 7 August. Parma's army, reduced by disease to 16,000, was not ready, and the barges meant to carry it would have had to cross waters dominated by the Dutch navy. That night English fire ships forced the Spanish to scatter. The armada suffered further losses at the Battle of Gravelines and was in danger of running aground on the Dutch coast when the wind changed and let it escape into the North Sea. Pursued by the English, the ships returned by way of Scotland and Ireland, and up to 24 were wrecked on the way.

In Spain the news brought shock, and the nation went into mourning. Philip is claimed to have said that he sent the armada against men, not God's winds and waves. In England the victory was marked with pamphlets, medals and celebrations, and it fed national pride for years. A medal bore the inscription meaning God blew, and they are scattered. England's own counter-armada of 1589 failed, and Spain sent three further armadas in 1596, 1597 and 1601, which also failed.

The English use of naval guns from windward, rather than ramming and boarding, has been seen as a revolution in naval tactics. Historians have long debated the causes. Early writers stressed God's favour, and later scholars have examined the comparative power of English and Spanish guns, the part of Francis Drake and Charles Howard, and the weather.
spanish-civil-war: Spain had known instability since the overthrow of Queen Isabella II in 1868. The short-lived First Republic of 1873 was overthrown in 1874 and the monarchy restored under Alfonso XII; in 1923 a coup brought Miguel Primo de Rivera to power, and he resigned in January 1930. The Second Republic that followed had broad support, but according to one historian plans for a counter-revolution were already discussed on the day it was proclaimed, and by March 1934 the conspirators had won the agreement of Benito Mussolini to aid a future coup. After the Popular Front won the election of 1936, officers began to plan a rising, with General Emilio Mola as the chief planner.

The coup began in Spanish Morocco on 18 July 1936 and in Spain proper a day later. It was meant to be swift but succeeded only in part: the rebels failed to take any major city except Seville, which gave a landing point for Franco's African troops, and the conservative Catholic areas of Old Castile, León and Galicia fell quickly, leaving Spain divided. Francisco Franco became the supreme leader of the Nationalists on 1 October 1936. In the Republican zone the arming of workers' movements led to a social revolution, especially in Aragon and Catalonia.

Italy sent about 50,000 men and Germany its Condor Legion to the Nationalists, while the Soviet Union and Mexico supported the Republic and tens of thousands of foreign volunteers joined the International Brigades. The United Kingdom, France and the United States followed non-intervention.

The Nationalists captured most of the northern coast in 1937 and took Málaga on 8 February. Republicans took Teruel in January 1938 and lost it again by 22 February, and the Aragon Offensive reached the Mediterranean by 14 April, cutting the Republican zone in two. Franco's troops conquered Catalonia in the first two months of 1939, taking Barcelona on 26 January. On 5 March Colonel Segismundo Casado led a coup against the Republican government to seek peace, which Franco refused. Franco entered Madrid and declared victory on 1 April 1939.

Hundreds of thousands of Republican supporters fled Spain, mostly to camps in southern France, and many who stayed were persecuted. Both sides committed atrocities: the historian Paul Preston estimates at least 130,000 executed by the Nationalists, while between 38,000 and 70,000 civilians were killed in Republican territory. The total death toll remains disputed, with estimates from 250,000 to 1 million. The Nationalists ruled Spain until Franco's death in November 1975. The war was seen variously as a class struggle, a religious struggle, or a struggle between democracy and dictatorship, and it inspired worldwide passion; George Orwell's Homage to Catalonia, published in 1938, recounts his experience of it.
spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire: The Aztec Empire, also called the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, was formed in 1428 and under Moctezuma II had established dominance over central Mexico through conquest and alliances. It ruled hegemonically through local rulers, and its power rested on the perception of unchallengeable military supremacy, a system the Spanish sources show to have been vulnerable to a loss of prestige. The Spanish had settled permanently in the Caribbean from 1493, and in 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba led an expedition to the Yucatán coast.

A third expedition followed the voyage of Juan de Grijalva in 1518. The Cuban governor Diego Velázquez named his brother-in-law Hernán Cortés to command it, but in an agreement of 23 October 1518 limited it to exploration and trade. Cortés invested much of his own fortune and, using the legal knowledge he probably gained as a notary, presented Velázquez as a tyrant acting against the Crown. His men then named him military leader and chief magistrate of the expedition.

Cortés left Cuba on 10 February 1519 and landed on the Gulf coast on 21 April. Among the women given to the Spanish by the Potoncan leaders on 24 March was one known as Doña Marina or La Malinche, who spoke Nahuatl, Mayan and later Spanish and became one of their main translators. He then made alliances with Aztec tributaries and with political rivals of the Mexica, particularly the Tlaxcaltecs and the Tetzcocans, a former partner in the Triple Alliance.

After eight months of battles and negotiations, Cortés arrived in Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519, and his men and allies took up residence there. Cortés claimed that he took Moctezuma captive, but modern scholars are sceptical and think the Spanish writings show that Moctezuma was captured only later. In 1520 the first wave of smallpox killed between 5 and 8 million people. The campaign ended on 13 August 1521, when a coalition of Spanish forces under Cortés and Tlaxcalan warriors led by Chichimecatecuhtli captured the emperor Cuauhtémoc and the capital.

The fall of Tenochtitlan marks the establishment of New Spain within the Spanish Empire, with its capital at Mexico City, built on the ruins of the Aztec capital. The Aztec polities came under Spanish rule while largely keeping their internal structures of ruling elites and tribute-paying commoners, and their landholding and other economic arrangements.

Accounts of the conquest come from the Spanish conquerors, notably Cortés's letters to Charles V and Bernal Díaz del Castillo's True History of the Conquest of New Spain, and from Nahuatl speakers whose recollections the friars Bernardino de Sahagún and Diego Durán recorded. All of them contain biases and exaggerations.
spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire: When the Spanish reached the borders of the Inca Empire in 1528 it stretched from the Ancomayo, now the Patía River in southern Colombia, to the Maule River in what became Chile, and from the Pacific to the edge of the Amazonian forests. It had grown from about 400,000 square kilometres in 1448 to 1,800,000 in 1528, and scholars estimate its population at 12 to 16 million.

Many regions kept distinct cultures and were reluctant to belong to the imperial project, and travel on foot or by boat made the empire hard to govern. Some scholars, such as Jared Diamond, think the empire may already have passed its peak. Huayna Capac, who ruled it, died after smallpox introduced by Europeans reached the empire, and a civil war broke out between his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa.

Francisco Pizarro and his brothers were drawn by rumours of a rich kingdom, and in 1529 he obtained permission from the Spanish Monarchy to conquer the land they called Peru. In 1532 he found it very different from five years earlier, since disease had devastated it. Atahualpa, who commanded at least 30,000 well-trained soldiers from the north, had escaped the troops of Huáscar, who held Cuzco and the south. Pizarro's 168 soldiers, with his brothers and Indigenous auxiliaries, captured Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532. Peoples oppressed by the Inca, among them the Huancas, Chankas, Cañaris and Chachapoyas, joined the Spanish.

In 1533 Diego de Almagro arrived and Atahualpa was executed after ordering Huáscar's death. Pizarro subdued Cuzco and installed the seventeen-year-old Manco Inca as emperor. In 1535 Pizarro founded Lima, and Almagro left for present-day Chile. Historians are unsure that a united empire would have defeated the Spanish, given the mortality from disease and the conquistadors' horses, dogs, metal armour, swords, cannon and firearms.

In 1536 Manco Inca rebelled after Gonzalo Pizarro took his wife, besieged Cuzco and killed Juan Pizarro, while the Inca general Quizo Yupanqui attacked Lima. In 1537 Almagro seized Cuzco, and Manco fled to Vilcabamba, capital of the Neo-Inca State. Hernando Pizarro executed Almagro in 1538, Francisco Pizarro was murdered by Almagro's supporters in 1541, and Manco was murdered by them in 1544.

In 1572 the viceroy Francisco Toledo declared war on the Neo-Inca State; Vilcabamba was sacked, and Túpac Amaru, the last Inca emperor, was captured and executed in Cuzco. The conquest led to campaigns into present-day Chile and Colombia and expeditions into the Amazon Basin, and the region became the Viceroyalty of Peru.
spanish-empire: The marriage of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile created a personal union of their crowns that most scholars view as the foundation of the Spanish monarchy. Each kingdom kept its own administration, and the two ruled jointly as the Catholic Monarchs, a title given them by Pope Alexander VI after the conquest of the Emirate of Granada was completed in 1492. Earlier expansion had begun with the conquest of the Canary Islands, finished by Castilian armies between 1478 and 1496; by 1504 more than 90 percent of the native Canarians had been killed or enslaved. Columbus arrived in the Caribbean in 1492, and Santo Domingo was founded in 1496.

Their grandson Charles inherited the Castilian possessions in the Americas, the Aragonese lands in the Mediterranean and lands in the Low Countries and Germany, beginning the rule of the Spanish Habsburgs. His son Philip II oversaw the colonisation of the Philippines from 1565 and annexed Portugal and its overseas empire in 1580. Silver from Zacatecas, Guanajuato and Potosí financed military campaigns, and Genoese bankers lent to the crown. Most conquests in the Americas were carried out by small groups of adventurers working under the encomienda system.

By the mid-17th century the empire strained Spain's economic, administrative and military resources. After the childless Charles II died in 1700, the Treaties of Utrecht of 1713 made Philip V of the House of Bourbon king and ceded Spain's possessions in the Netherlands and Italy to others and Gibraltar and Menorca to Britain. The Bourbons centralised power and reformed colonial rule. In 1808 Napoleon took the Spanish crown under his control, and the resulting Peninsular War led to about twenty new independent states in Spanish America. By the mid-1820s Spain had lost Mexico, Central America and South America, and after the Spanish–American War it lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam in 1898.

Spain's trade system aimed to keep wealth within the empire, but smuggling was widespread, and much of the silver paid for foreign soldiers and for goods made in northern Europe. The empire left a lasting linguistic, religious, political and architectural legacy in the Western Hemisphere. Spanish spread from Castile across Spanish America and became the language of the successor republics, while many indigenous languages were lost as populations were decimated by war and disease.
spanish-golden-age: The Golden Age, or Siglo de Oro, is conventionally dated from 1492, a year that saw the conquest of Granada, the first voyage of Christopher Columbus, the establishment of the Inquisition and the publication of Antonio de Nebrija's Grammar of the Castilian Language. It followed the union of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, which brought stability after years of conflict. Its political phase is often regarded as ending in 1659 with the Treaty of the Pyrenees, although in cultural terms it is understood to continue until Calderón's death in 1681. The most significant patron was Philip II, whose palace of El Escorial attracted architects and painters, among them El Greco.

In literature, close ties with Renaissance Italy brought the influence of Petrarch, Boccaccio and Sannazaro. Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605 and the second in 1615; it is called the first novel published in Europe. Lope de Vega shaped the commercial drama known as comedia, Garcilaso de la Vega brought Italian verse into Spanish, San Juan de la Cruz and Teresa of Ávila brought mystical literature to its summit, and Quevedo and Góngora dominated Baroque poetry.

In painting, El Greco, Greek by birth, settled in Toledo after studying in Italy from 1568 to 1577. Diego Velázquez, born in Seville in 1599, became court painter to Philip IV and painted the Surrender of Breda in 1635. Zurbarán's austere religious works reflected the Counter-Reformation, and Murillo developed a polished style. Architecture ran from the Palace of Charles V at Granada, begun in 1527, to the sober Herrerian style of El Escorial. In music Tomás Luis de Victoria and Francisco Guerrero wrote mainly church music.

Don Quixote gave Cervantes a stature in the Spanish-speaking world comparable to that of Shakespeare in English, and it was an international success in its own time, read as satire, social commentary and a forerunner of self-referential literature. The Baroque poets Quevedo and Góngora influenced later writers and the Spanish language itself, and Guerrero's music remained popular for hundreds of years, especially in the cathedrals of Latin America.
spanish-inquisition: During a stay in Seville in 1477 and 1478 Queen Isabella I became convinced that Andalusian conversos were secretly practising Judaism. A report by Pedro González de Mendoza, Archbishop of Seville, and the Dominican Tomás de Torquemada, confessor to the monarchs, supported this. Pope Sixtus IV granted the bull Exigit sincerae devotionis affectus in 1478, allowing the monarchs to appoint three bishops or priests as inquisitors, and the first inquisitors, Miguel de Morillo and Juan de San Martín, were named in 1480. Because the crown chose them, the tribunal replaced the Medieval Inquisition, which had been under papal control, and became an instrument of state power.

Its attention spread from conversos from Judaism to Moriscos, converts from Islam, after the decrees of 1492 and 1502 forced Jews and Muslims to convert, leave or face death. It also pursued Alumbrados, people labelled Lutheran, and those accused of witchcraft, blasphemy, bigamy and Freemasonry, and it worked in Southern Italy and the Americas as well as in Spain.

The crown appointed the Inquisitor General, whose authority reached across the whole empire, and he presided over the Council of the Supreme and General Inquisition, created in 1483. Below it sat local tribunals, at first itinerant and later fixed, such as those at Seville and Córdoba in 1482 and Toledo in 1485. Each had two inquisitors, theological assessors, a bailiff and a prosecutor, and in 1608 Philip III required inquisitors to have a legal background.

Torquemada set out the procedure in a 28-article code in 1484 that stayed largely unchanged for over three centuries. On arriving in a city an inquisitor read an Edict of Grace, which allowed people thirty to forty days to confess and denounce others without harsh penalties. After about 1500 the Edicts of Faith dropped the grace period. Accusers' names were kept from the accused, who was assigned a defence counsel. Sentences ranged from acquittal, which was rare, to penance, exile, flogging, service as a galley oarsman or handing over to the civil authorities for execution. The sentence was announced at an auto de fe, which grew into an elaborate public ceremony. The last public auto took place in 1691.

Historians estimate that about 150,000 people were prosecuted and that 3,000 to 5,000 were executed, mostly early in its history. Property confiscation was an important aspect of many punishments, and contemporaries said that the rich were burnt for their money. Blood purity statutes, first enacted in Toledo in 1449, barred conversos from offices and were used by many bodies. The Inquisition also issued Indexes of prohibited books, the first in 1551. Its activity declined during the Enlightenment, and how severe it really was remains a subject of dispute among historians.
spanish-language: Spanish evolved from the Vulgar Latin that the Romans brought to the Iberian Peninsula during the Second Punic War, beginning in 210 BCE. Several pre-Roman languages had been spoken there, including Proto-Basque, Iberian, Lusitanian, Celtiberian and Gallaecian. The first documents to show traces of what is regarded as the precursor of modern Spanish date from the 9th century, and the first systematic written use of the language happened in Toledo in the 13th century.

The language takes its alternative name, castellano, from the Kingdom of Castile. The Spanish Constitution of 1978 uses castellano for the official language of the whole of Spain. The Royal Spanish Academy, founded in 1713, called the language castellano from 1713 to 1923 and now prefers español, though it regards both terms as synonymous and equally valid.

Spanish is a fusional Romance language of the Ibero-Romance group, written in the Latin script with the addition of the letter ñ. It has five vowel phonemes and between 17 and 19 consonant phonemes, depending on the dialect. Nouns and adjectives have two genders and two numbers, and there are about fifty conjugated forms per verb. About 75% of the modern vocabulary is Latin in origin.

Other influences on the vocabulary came from neighbouring Romance languages such as Mozarabic, Catalan, Portuguese and Occitan, and from Andalusi Arabic, with about 8% of the vocabulary having Arabic roots. Words from Quechua, Nahuatl and other indigenous languages of the Americas were also absorbed, and French, English and German loanwords arrived in the 18th to 20th centuries. For written Portuguese and Spanish, Ethnologue gives a lexical similarity of 89%.

Spanish colonialism in the early modern period carried the language overseas, most notably to the Americas. It is now the world's second-most spoken native language, with an estimated 519 million native speakers in 2025 and about 636 million speakers in total. Mexico has the largest population of native speakers, with about 130 million.

Spanish is an official language of the United Nations and the European Union. The Association of Spanish Language Academies, created in Mexico in 1951, unites the academies of 23 countries. In the United States, Spanish is the second most spoken language, and over 50 million people were estimated to speak it in 2015.
spanish-town: The Spanish founded Villa de la Vega in 1534 as the capital of their colony. It was later also called Santiago de la Vega or St. Jago de la Vega. The Taino had lived in the area for roughly a thousand years before, but this was the first European settlement on the south of the island.

When the English conquered Jamaica in 1655 they renamed it Spanish Town in honour of its Spanish origin. The town was badly damaged in the conquest, so Port Royal served as an unofficial capital at first. After an earthquake devastated Port Royal in 1692, Spanish Town had been rebuilt and again functioned as the capital. Kingston, founded after the earthquake, became a rival, and in 1836 Governor Lionel Smith observed that the capital was in ruins, with no commercial, manufacturing or agricultural concern in operation. After the Morant Bay Rebellion of 1865, Sir John Peter Grant ordered the seat of the colony moved to Kingston, a larger port, and this was done in 1872. The town then lost much of its economic and cultural vitality.

Spanish Town stands on the west bank of the Rio Cobre, 21 kilometres from Kingston. Its street names recall its colonial past, including Red Church and White Church streets and Nugent and Manchester streets, named for the governors George Nugent and William Montagu, 5th Duke of Manchester. Regency buildings in the centre include the Rodney Memorial and the facade of the Old King's House, the governor's residence until 1872. The Old Iron Bridge over the Rio Cobre, designed by Thomas Wilson and made by Walker and Company of Rotherham, was erected in 1801 at a cost of £4,000.
sparta: In classical antiquity the state was known as Lacedaemon, while Sparta referred to its capital, a cluster of villages in the valley of the Eurotas River in Laconia, in the south-eastern Peloponnese. Mount Taygetus to the west and Mount Parnon to the east bounded the valley, and these natural defences protected the city from invasion. Between the 8th and 7th centuries BCE the Spartans went through lawlessness and civil strife, attested by Herodotus and Thucydides, and then carried out reforms that they later attributed to a semi-mythical lawgiver, Lycurgus.

In the 6th century BCE Sparta founded the Peloponnesian League and established its hegemony over most of the Peloponnese. In 480 BCE King Leonidas led a small force against the army of Xerxes at the Battle of Thermopylae, and Sparta led the Greek alliance at the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE. It then led the Peloponnesian League against Athens in the Peloponnesian War of 431 to 404 BCE and won it after Lysander's victory at the Battle of Aegospotami. Epaminondas defeated it at Leuctra in 371 BCE; Messenia was freed from Spartan rule, and the loss of the enslaved labour it provided sent Sparta into terminal decline as a military power.

In the early second century BCE Sparta was forced into the Achaean League. Under Roman rule it became a free city and a tourist attraction for the Roman elite, who came to observe its customs. Alaric I sacked it in 396 CE, and in the Middle Ages much of the population moved to nearby Mystras. The modern town was re-founded in 1834 by decree of King Otto of Greece.

Sparta was an oligarchy ruled by two hereditary kings of the Agiad and Eurypontid families. Spartiates were full citizens, perioikoi were free non-citizens who held trade and manufacture, which Spartiates were barred by law from practising, and helots, the largest class, farmed the land and were owned by the state and treated harshly. Boys entered the training system known as the agoge at seven, and at 20 a citizen joined one of the dining messes called syssitia. Spartan women of the citizen class had more status than women elsewhere in Greece. Thucydides remarked that the city had no splendid temples and resembled a group of villages.

Admiration of Sparta, called Laconophilia, was widespread even in rival Athens, and many philosophers described it as an ideal state. The French classicist François Ollier warned in 1933 that all surviving accounts were written by non-Spartans, who often idealised it, a distortion now called the Spartan Mirage.
spartacist-uprising: On 10 November 1918, after the collapse of the German Empire, a Council of the People's Deputies under Friedrich Ebert of the Majority Social Democratic Party (MSPD) and Hugo Haase of the more left-wing Independent Social Democratic Party (USPD) formed a provisional government. In the secret Ebert-Groener Pact the army command promised its loyalty, and Ebert promised prompt action against leftist uprisings. The MSPD sought elections to a constituent assembly, while the USPD and part of the working class wanted a council republic. Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht founded the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) on 1 January 1919. The dismissal of Berlin's police chief Emil Eichhorn on 4 January was the immediate trigger.

A protest on 5 January drew 100,000 people, and armed demonstrators occupied the printing plants of the newspaper Vorwärts and the Berliner Tageblatt. That evening about 70 leaders voted to form a revolutionary committee to overthrow the government. Up to 500,000 people answered its call for a general strike on 7 January, but the committee could not agree on how to proceed and the crowds went home. Negotiations with Ebert failed over the occupied buildings and Eichhorn's reinstatement.

Ebert gave Gustav Noske command of the troops around Berlin, and Freikorps units formed from former frontline soldiers were mustered. On 11 January the Vorwärts building was taken with flame throwers, machine guns, mortars and artillery. Many insurgents surrendered, and seven men who came to negotiate were taken to the Dragoon Barracks and shot. An investigative committee of the Prussian parliament put the death toll at 156.

On the evening of 15 January Luxemburg and Liebknecht were arrested in Wilmersdorf and taken to the Eden Hotel, where Captain Waldemar Pabst had them interrogated and beaten. Luxemburg was shot in the temple and thrown into the Landwehr Canal; Liebknecht was shot in the Tiergarten as a supposed fugitive. At the trial in May 1919 Otto Runge received two years in prison and Kurt Vogel 28 months, and Pabst was not charged. Elections to the National Assembly were held on 19 January, and it finalised the Weimar Constitution. The MSPD received 37.9 per cent, and its part in the suppression weighed on it throughout the Weimar Republic.
spartacus: No contemporary sources for Spartacus exist. The accounts of Plutarch and Appian were written more than a century after his death, by people who were not involved, and they contradict one another. Plutarch calls him a Thracian of nomadic stock, possibly of the Maedi tribe, who lived in what is now south-western Bulgaria. Appian says he had once served as a soldier with the Romans, but had since been a prisoner and was sold as a gladiator.

Plutarch adds that his wife, a prophetess of the Maedi, was enslaved with him. One modern author estimates that he was about 30 when the revolt began. He was trained as a murmillo at the gladiatorial school of Lentulus Batiatus near Capua.

In 73 BCE about 70 slaves plotted to escape the school. They seized kitchen utensils, fought their way out, took wagons of gladiatorial weapons and defeated the soldiers sent after them. They retired to Mount Vesuvius and chose Spartacus and two Gallic slaves, Crixus and Oenomaus, as leaders. The Roman legions were busy with a revolt in Hispania and the Third Mithridatic War, and Rome first sent a militia under the praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber. Spartacus's men climbed down the mountain on ropes of vines and attacked the camp from behind. Slaves, herdsmen and shepherds then flocked to the rebels, swelling their numbers to some 70,000.

In 72 BCE the Senate sent two consular legions, which beat a group of 30,000 rebels under Crixus and were then defeated by Spartacus. The Senate then gave command of eight legions to Marcus Licinius Crassus. According to Plutarch, Spartacus bargained with Cilician pirates to carry some 2,000 men to Sicily, but they betrayed him. Crassus fortified the isthmus at Rhegium, and the rebels broke through and marched towards Brundusium.

In the final battle in 71 BCE, which one account places in the High Sele Valley in Lucania, the rebels were routed and most were killed. Plutarch, Appian and Florus claim that Spartacus died in it, though Appian adds that his body was never found. Six thousand captured survivors were crucified along the Appian Way from Rome to Capua. The ancient historians disagree about his aims: Plutarch says he wanted to escape over the Alps and send his men home, while Appian and Florus say he intended to march on Rome. None of his actions suggests that he aimed to abolish slavery.
In later centuries he became a symbol of resistance. Voltaire called the Third Servile War the only just war in history, and Karl Marx admired him. The German Spartacus League took his name.
spear-thrower: The user holds the spear-thrower in one hand and rests the butt of a dart in its cup, or hooks it on its spur. The dart is much longer than the thrower. An overhand throwing motion, driven by the upper arm and wrist, lets the thrower act as a low-mass extension of the arm, so the force acts on the dart over a longer distance and gives it higher speed. Darts are typically 1.2 to 2.7 m long. Experiments with replicas of Basketmaker spear-throwers found exit velocities of 72 to 108 km/h, and the device is most accurate at 20 m or less.

Designs added thong loops for the fingers, flexible shafts and small stone weights of 60 to 80 grams strapped to the middle, often called bannerstones. Scholars disagree on their purpose: for greater force, for stability, for a quieter swing, or as spindle weights for making string. The woomera, usually made of mulga wood and about 60 cm long, also served to mix ochre, to fend off spears and as a fire-making saw.

Wooden spears are at least 400,000 years old, as the Clacton Spear and the Schöningen spears show. Most stratified European finds of spear-throwers come from the Magdalenian, when elaborate pieces in the form of animals are common; one in the British Museum is carved with a mammoth. During the Ice Age the device gave hunters the power to pierce the thick skin of megafauna. In Europe the bow and arrow supplemented it in the Epi-Paleolithic, since a bow stores the elastic energy in the weapon and not in the projectile. By the Iron Age a strap called the amentum was the standard way of throwing lighter javelins.

In the Americas it may have crossed the Bering Land Bridge with the first settlers and was widespread at European contact. It appears in the art of the Basketmaker, Maya and Moche, and Spearthrower Owl, a ruler from Teotihuacan, is a figure in Maya stelae. The Aztecs opened battles with atlatl darts and then fought hand to hand with the macuahuitl. John Whittaker suggests that the device was a social equalizer, since it needs skill more than muscle, so that women and children could join the hunt.

The spear-thrower survives in Australia, where some Aboriginal people use the woomera for hunting, and among Yup'ik hunters near the mouth of the Yukon River, who call it the nuqaq and use it for seal hunting. The World Atlatl Association was formed in 1987 to promote it as a sport, and throws of almost 260 m have been recorded.
special-administrative-regions-of-china: The provision for special administrative regions entered the Constitution of China in 1982, in anticipation of talks with the United Kingdom over the sovereignty of Hong Kong. Article 31 says that the state may establish special administrative regions when necessary, and that the systems to be instituted in them are to be prescribed by law enacted by the National People's Congress. The principle of one country, two systems was proposed by Deng Xiaoping.

Hong Kong and Macau were transferred to China in 1997 and 1999 under the Sino-British and Sino-Portuguese Joint Declarations, signed in 1984 and 1987. These are binding treaties registered with the United Nations and provide that the regions shall enjoy a high degree of autonomy. The model was also envisioned for an eventual unification with Taiwan: a proposal of 1981, known as Ye's nine points, and Deng Xiaoping's six points of 1983 both offered Taiwan the status of a special administrative region.

A special administrative region is one of four types of province-level division directly affiliated with the Central People's Government. It has the highest degree of autonomy, though the National People's Congress and its Standing Committee remain able to enforce laws for it. Each of the two regions has a codified constitution called the Basic Law, a capitalist economy, its own courts of final appeal and its own multi-party legislature.

The central government is responsible for diplomatic and military affairs. Hong Kong and Macau keep their own legal systems, police forces, customs territories, immigration policies, left-hand traffic, official languages and educational systems. The Hong Kong dollar and the Macanese pataca are their currencies, and the Macanese pataca is pegged to the Hong Kong dollar. They belong to organisations such as the WTO and APEC and send their own teams to events such as the Olympic Games as Hong Kong, China and Macau, China. The People's Liberation Army is garrisoned in both.

The term has had other uses. Between 1912 and 1949, special administrative regions were areas designated by the Beiyang government, most of which the Nationalist government converted into provinces in 1928. The Wolong Special Administrative Region in Sichuan, founded in 1983 with the approval of the State Council, is a nature reserve and not a region under Article 31.
special-region-of-yogyakarta: The Special Region of Yogyakarta lies in southern Java. On the landward side it is surrounded by Central Java Province to the west, north and east, and it has a long coastline on the Indian Ocean to the south. With a land area of 3,170.363 square kilometres, it is the second-smallest province-level unit of Indonesia after Jakarta. Mount Merapi stands immediately north of the city of Yogyakarta and Sleman Regency. It has erupted regularly since 1548 and is the most active volcano in Indonesia. The region also has nine geo-heritage sites, among them pillow lava at Berbah, dunes at Parangtritis Beach and a prehistoric volcano at Nglanggeran.

The Yogyakarta Sultanate was established in 1755 and survived Dutch rule and the 1942 invasion of the Dutch East Indies by Japan in 1942. In August 1945 Sukarno proclaimed Indonesian independence, and by September Sultan Hamengkubuwono IX and Duke Sri Paku Alam VIII had written to him acknowledging the Sultanate as part of the Republic. The Sunanate of Surakarta did the same, and both Javanese kingdoms were given special status. Surakarta lost its status in 1946 after a leftist anti-royalist uprising and was absorbed into Central Java.

During the Indonesian National Revolution (1945–1949) the city of Yogyakarta served as the capital of Indonesia from January 1946 to December 1948, after Jakarta fell to the Dutch. When the Dutch also invaded Yogyakarta, the capital was moved to Bukittinggi in West Sumatra on 19 December 1948. In return for its support, Yogyakarta received its special status in full in 1950, which made it the only region in Indonesia headed by a monarchy. A 6.3-magnitude earthquake struck on 27 May 2006, killing 5,782 people and leaving 600,000 homeless; Bantul Regency suffered most.

The region is co-ruled by the Yogyakarta Sultanate and the Principality of Pakualaman, and it is the only officially recognised diarchy within the government of Indonesia. Under the laws on its status, the governor and vice governor are chosen from the descendants of the ruling family, and until 1988 the reigning Sultan held the post of head of the region automatically. The region has four regencies and one city, and Javanese is its official language alongside Indonesian.

The city is known as a centre of classical Javanese art and culture, such as batik, music and shadow puppetry, and the Sultan's palace, the Kraton, lies at its core. It has more than one hundred institutions of higher education and is the home of Gadjah Mada University, the first state university established in Indonesia.
speicherstadt: From 1815 the independent city of Hamburg belonged to the German Confederation but not to the German Customs Union. After the Austro-Prussian War it was obliged to join the North German Federation, but Article 34 of the North German constitution kept Hamburg and the other Hanseatic cities as free ports outside the customs border until they applied for inclusion. Article 34 was carried into the imperial constitution of 1871. Hamburg came under great pressure from Berlin after 1879, when the Customs Union greatly increased its external tariff. In 1881 an agreement was signed under which Hamburg joined the Customs Union with all its territory except a permanent free port district, for which Article 34 still applied.

In 1883 the demolition of the Kehrwieder and Wandrahm area began to clear space, and more than 20,000 people had to be relocated. The Freihafen-Lagerhaus-Gesellschaft, the predecessor of the Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG, managed the construction, which was completed before the start of World War I, and it was also responsible for the later operation.

The Speicherstadt, meaning City of Warehouses, is the largest warehouse district in the world whose buildings stand on timber-pile foundations, in this case oak logs. It was built from 1883 to 1927 in the port of Hamburg as a free zone in which goods could be transferred without paying customs. It is 1.5 kilometres long and interlaced by loading canals, called Fleets in Low German. The warehouses were built with different support structures, but Franz Andreas Meyer gave them a Neo-Gothic red-brick outer layer with small towers, alcoves and glazed terracotta ornaments. They are multi-storey buildings with entrances from both water and land, and one of the oldest, Kaispeicher B, houses the International Maritime Museum.

About half of the buildings were destroyed in the bombing of Operation Gomorrah in World War II, and a conservative rebuilding was finished in 1967. The Hanseatic Trade Center occupies the sites of the completely destroyed structures. The district was listed as a protected heritage site of Hamburg in 1991 and has been part of the HafenCity quarter since 2008. On 5 July 2015 the Speicherstadt and the Kontorhaus District were made a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as an exceptional example of Neo-Gothic and modernist architecture and for its testimony to the development of international maritime trade. It is a major tourist attraction, with museums such as the German Customs Museum and Miniatur Wunderland, while some buildings keep their original use as warehouses.
spessart: The Spessart is a Mittelgebirge, a range of low wooded mountains in the German states of Bavaria and Hesse, bordered by the Vogelsberg, the Rhön and the Odenwald. Its extent can also be described by its rivers: the Main to the south and west, the Kinzig to the north and the Sinn to the north-east. It covers about 2,440 square kilometres, of which 1,710 lie in Bavaria, and its highest point is the Geiersberg at 586 metres.

The name derives from Spechtshardt, from the German Specht, woodpecker, and Hardt, an old word for hilly forest. Its lowest strata are gneiss and mica schist about 1,200 million years old, and most of the Hochspessart is capped by red sandstone up to 400 metres thick, the stone used for many public buildings including Mainz Cathedral.

People have lived in the region since at least the Bronze Age, and hill forts attributed to Celts of the La Tène culture were built there between 500 and 100 BCE. The Roman frontier, the Limes, met the Main at Großkrotzenburg and followed the river south to Miltenberg, so the Spessart proper lay outside the empire, and the Romans kept the northern Vorspessart as an uninhabited buffer zone. The Burgundians came in the late 3rd century and the Allemanni ousted them in the 5th, before the Franks absorbed the Allemanni.

Under the Franks the forests were used for hunting, and in Charlemagne's reign they were a royal hunting preserve. The uplands were settled only after abbeys were founded, among them the Benedictine abbey of Neustadt am Main around 770, which Charlemagne endowed with woodland.

In 974 Emperor Otto II gave much of the former royal preserve to the collegiate church of Aschaffenburg, and in 982 Otto I, Duke of Swabia and Bavaria, left his territories in the area to Mainz. Between the 12th and 15th centuries the Prince-Electors and Archbishops of Mainz and other nobles built hunting lodges and moated castles such as Mespelbrunn, and in the 14th century Mainz set up local officers to supervise hunting, forestry, fishing and the rafting of logs.

About 85 percent of the Hochspessart is covered by forest, mainly oak and beech. The Bavarian Spessart Nature Park, set up in 1961 as the first in Bavaria, covers 171,000 hectares and has the largest continuous mixed forest in Germany; the Hessian park followed in 1962 and covers 72,900 hectares. No cities or large towns lie inside the parks. The Nordspessart has more evergreens because its original tree cover was largely gone by the 15th century, owing to the fuel needs of local glass foundries. Beavers, hunted to extinction in the region, have been re-established since the 1980s.
spetses: Spetses is one of the Saronic Islands. Its municipality has an area of 27 square kilometres and includes the uninhabited islands of Spetsopoula, Falkonera and Velopoula. The town of Spetses is the only large settlement. The name comes from the Greek spétses, spices or herbs, which derives from the Italian and Venetian spezie; the ancient name Pityussa means abounding in pine trees. No private cars are allowed in the town, and visitors come by ferry and hydrofoil from Piraeus.

The island was first occupied in the Mesolithic period, about 8000 BCE, when an isthmus joined it to the mainland of Argolis. The first Hellenic settlement found there, at Saint Marina, dates to the 3rd millennium BCE, and late Mycenaean settlements are known as well. Strabo and Pausanias call the island Pitiousa. A raid by the Goths on the Eastern Roman Empire sent refugees to Spetses, who resettled it around the Old Port. The Venetians, who had ruled the island since 1220, named it Spezia in the 15th century because it lay on a spice trade route.

In the 18th century many Arvanites took refuge there from Ottoman persecution and built the old village at Kastelli. During the Orlov Revolt, a rising in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774, the island's merchant fleet fought the Ottomans, and in 1770 the Turks destroyed its only village. New settlers from the opposite coast of the Peloponnese reoccupied it in 1774, after the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca. Sailing under the Russian flag, they rebuilt a powerful merchant fleet, which prospered especially during the trade embargoes of the Napoleonic Wars.

In the Greek War of Independence Spetses was the first island to raise the flag of revolution, on 3 April 1821 by the old calendar. Its fleet took part in raids on the Turkish coast, in the sieges of Nafplion and Monemvasia and in the naval battles of Samos in 1824 and Kafireas in 1825. It was the home of Laskarina Bouboulina. On 8 September 1822 the combined fleets of Spetses, Hydra and Psara faced an Ottoman fleet trying to supply Nafplion, which fell to the Greeks about two and a half months later.

The island declined as a maritime centre in the 19th century. In 1899 the shipping heir Sotirios Anargyros, a wealthy tobacco merchant returned from the United States, began to transform it, planting pines and building the Poseidonion Hotel, which became a favourite holiday place of wealthy Athenians. The Armáta Festival each September commemorates the battle of 1822. The island served as the basis for the island of Phraxos in John Fowles's novel The Magus of 1965.
spice-trade: Spices such as cinnamon, cassia, cardamom, ginger, pepper, nutmeg, star anise, clove and turmeric were known in antiquity and traded across Asia, northeast Africa and Europe. Peoples of the Indian Ocean and Island Southeast Asia traded spices, obsidian, seashells and gemstones as early as the 10th millennium BCE. The ancient Egyptians traded with the Land of Punt in the 3rd millennium BCE. The first true maritime network in the Indian Ocean was built by Austronesian sailors from Maritime Southeast Asia, who opened routes to South India and Sri Lanka from around 1500 BCE to 600 BCE, carrying cloves and nutmeg from the Maluku Islands.
