Stavropol was founded on 22 October 1777, after the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774, as a military encampment, and was granted city status in 1785. Prince Grigory Potemkin, who founded it as one of ten fortresses built between Azov and Mozdok at the request of Catherine the Great, played a leading role. Don Cossacks settled in and around Stavropol to defend the empire's borders, and in 1809 Alexander I invited several Armenian families to settle by the fortress in order to encourage trade.

Its strategic position aided the Russian conquest of the Caucasus, and by the early 19th century it was a busy trade centre. An Episcopal see of the Russian Orthodox Church was established there in 1843, and in 1847 the city became the seat of Stavropol Governorate. During the Russian Civil War it changed hands several times and was captured by the Red Army from General Denikin's Volunteer Army on 29 February 1920. It was renamed Voroshilovsk in 1935, and the original name was restored in 1943. Germans occupied it from August 1942 to January 1943. Natural gas began to be extracted near the city in 1946.

Stavropol is home to North-Caucasus Federal University, Stavropol State Agrarian University and Stavropol State Medical University. Its economy focuses on automobiles, furniture, and construction equipment and materials. Mikhail Gorbachev, born in Stavropol Krai, worked in the city for several years as head of the krai's administration, and the poets Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Lermontov, then in political disfavour, stayed there.
steam-turbine: The first device that may be classed as a reaction steam turbine was little more than a toy, the aeolipile described in the 1st century by Hero of Alexandria in Roman Egypt. Steam turbines were also described by the Italian Giovanni Branca in 1629 and by John Wilkins in England in 1648. The devices described by Taqi al-Din and Wilkins are now known as steam jacks. In 1672 Ferdinand Verbiest designed a small toy car driven by an impulse turbine, and in 1775 James Watt designed a reaction turbine used at the Soho Manufactory. The modern form was invented by Sir Charles Parsons in 1884.

A steam turbine extracts thermal energy from pressurised steam and turns it into mechanical work at a rotating shaft. Its efficiency comes largely from expanding the steam in several stages. In an impulse turbine, fixed nozzles turn the steam into high-speed jets that strike the rotor blades. In a reaction turbine, associated with Parsons, the rotor blades themselves form convergent nozzles, and the pressure falls across both stator and rotor.

Turbines are made in sizes from units of under a kilowatt that drive pumps and compressors to machines of 1,500 MW. Their blades work at high temperatures and stresses, so creep is a major design problem, met with superalloys and ceramic coatings. A large turbine is warmed slowly, with a turning gear rotating it to prevent uneven expansion, and a governor controls its speed.

Large steam turbines driving electric generators made central-station electricity generation practical, because large reciprocating steam engines had become bulky and ran slowly. Such turbogenerators are the core of thermal power stations fuelled by fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, geothermal heat or solar energy.

In ships a turbine is smaller, lighter and less prone to vibration than a reciprocating engine, but it works efficiently only at thousands of revolutions per minute, while propellers work best below 300. Early vessels such as Turbinia, built in 1894, drove the propeller shafts directly. Reduction gears became available around 1911, and the battleship USS New Mexico, launched in 1917, introduced turbo-electric drive. The first steam turbine railway locomotive was built in 1908 for a firm in Milan.
stefan-decanski: Stefan Uroš III was the son of King Stefan Uroš II Milutin and his first wife Jelena, a Serbian noblewoman. While still a youth he was sent as a hostage to the court of Nogai Khan of the Golden Horde, to keep the peace between the Serbs and the Tatars, and stayed there until about 1297. By 1309 Milutin had made him governor of Zeta. In 1314 he quarrelled with his father, who sent him to Constantinople to be blinded; he was never totally blinded and was probably not blinded at all. At the court of Andronikos II Palaiologos he wrote to Danilo, Bishop of Hum, asking him to intercede, and in 1320 he was allowed to return to Serbia with the appanage of Budimlje.

Milutin died on 29 October 1321 without formal instructions about the succession. His son Stefan Konstantin was crowned in Zeta, while Dečanski and his cousin Stefan Vladislav II also claimed the throne. Dečanski revealed that his eyesight was intact and claimed a miracle, and the people rallied to him. On 6 January 1322 Archbishop Nicodemus crowned him king and his son Stefan Dušan young king. Konstantin was defeated and killed in Zeta. Vladislav, supported by Hungarians, Bulgarians and Bosnians, was defeated in battle in late 1324 and fled to Hungary. A dispute over Ragusan merchants who had backed Vladislav led Dečanski to seize their property in 1324, and he returned it by the end of that year.

In 1326 Serbia lost Hum to Bosnia. Dečanski generally kept an alliance with Andronikos II and stayed out of the Byzantine civil war. Tsar Michael Asen III of Bulgaria, whose divorce from Dečanski's sister Anna was followed by his marriage to a Byzantine princess, planned a joint invasion of Serbia in 1330 with Andronikos III Palaiologos. At the Battle of Velbazhd Dečanski defeated and killed Michael, with help from Dušan, and Andronikos withdrew. Serbia's border moved south into Byzantine Macedonia.

Some courtiers, discontented with his policies, conspired to put Dušan in his place. In 1331 Dušan came from Skadar to Nerodimlje and Dečanski fled to Petrič, which Dušan took on 21 August 1331 after a siege. Dečanski was imprisoned in Zvečan Fortress and died there on 11 November 1331. Epic poetry shows him as a noble character, and the Serbian Orthodox Church canonised him. His remains are venerated at Visoki Dečani, where a supplicatory canon is chanted every Thursday and an Akathist daily.
stefan-dragutin: Stefan Dragutin was the eldest son of King Stefan Uroš I of Serbia and Helen of Anjou. The place and date of his birth are unknown, but a remark by the monk Domentijan in 1264 led the historian Miodrag Purković to place it around 1244. He married Catherine of Hungary, granddaughter of Béla IV of Hungary, most probably as part of the peace that followed Uroš's failed raid on the Hungarian province of Mačva in 1268.

By 1271 he held the title of "younger king", marking his right to succeed his father. His Hungarian in-laws expected Uroš to cede lands to him, but Uroš, who had spent years strengthening his central government, was reluctant to divide his kingdom. In 1276 Dragutin rose against him with Hungarian and Cuman troops sent by his brother-in-law Ladislaus IV of Hungary, and routed his father near Gacko. Uroš abdicated and entered the Sopoćani Monastery.

Dragutin gave large territories, including Zeta and Trebinje, to his mother in appanage. In early 1282 he fell from his horse and broke his leg, and a council at Deževo saw him abdicate in favour of his brother Milutin. Accounts differ on whether this was meant to be permanent: Dragutin later said he ceded power only until he recovered, while Archbishop Danilo II wrote that he saw the injury as God's punishment for his acts against his father. Serbia was in effect divided, and Dragutin kept the north along the Hungarian border, including the silver mine at Rudnik, and lands on the river Lim.

In the second half of 1284 Ladislaus IV granted him the banates of Mačva, Usora and Soli, which he held as a Hungarian vassal. Because Mačva was also called Sirmia ulterior, his contemporaries often styled him King of Srem. He was the first Serbian monarch to rule Belgrade.

With Milutin's help he took the Banate of Braničevo from the warlords Darman and Kudelin in 1291 or 1292. From the 1290s he acted as an independent ruler. His quarrel with Milutin became open war in 1301, and ended in 1312 after Milutin's mercenaries inflicted a decisive defeat on him; Dragutin acknowledged his brother as lawful king but kept his Serbian lands.

Before his death Dragutin became a monk and took the name Teoctist. According to Archbishop Danilo II, he said as he lay dying that he could not be venerated as a saint. He died on 12 March 1316 and was buried in the Đurđevi Stupovi Monastery, which his great-grandfather Stephen Nemanja had built and of which he is regarded as the second founder. His son Stefan Vladislav II succeeded him in the northern domains. He is venerated in the list of Serbian saints on 12 November or 30 October, by Old Style and New Style dates.
stefan-dusan: Stefan Dušan was the eldest son of King Stefan Dečanski and Theodora Smilets, daughter of the Bulgarian emperor Smilets. In 1314 his father quarrelled with his own father, King Stefan Milutin, and was exiled; the family lived in Constantinople until his recall in 1320. There Dušan became acquainted with Byzantine culture and learned Greek. After a civil war Dečanski was crowned on 6 January 1322, and Dušan was crowned young king and later given Zeta, which marked him as the intended heir.

In his youth Dušan fought in two battles, defeating Bosnian forces in 1329 during the War of Hum and the Bulgarian emperor Michael III Shishman at Velbužd in 1330. He became king of Serbia on 8 September 1331 after the struggle with his father, and sealed an alliance with Bulgaria by marrying Helen, sister of Ivan Alexander.

On 16 April 1346 Dušan convoked an assembly at Skopje, attended by the Serbian archbishop, the Archbishop of Ochrid, the Bulgarian patriarch and clerics of Mount Athos. It raised the Serbian archbishopric to a patriarchate, and the first patriarch, Joanikije II, crowned Dušan Emperor and autocrat of the Serbs and Romans, a title soon enlarged to include the Greeks, Bulgarians and Albanians. He had his son Uroš crowned king of the Serbs and Greeks. Dušan gave Byzantine court titles to his nobles, such as despotes, sebastocrator and caesar, and was the first Serbian monarch to write most of his letters in Greek.

In 1347 he conquered Epirus, Aetolia and Acarnania, placing his half-brother Simeon Uroš over them, and in 1348 Thessaly, under the governor Preljub. He then sought Constantinople, for which he needed a fleet, and negotiated with Venice, which politely declined a military alliance. In 1349 he introduced Dušan's Code.

In 1354 the Hungarians occupied part of northern Serbia. Dušan repelled the invasion, and peace with Louis I of Hungary followed in May 1355. He had intended to capture Constantinople and lead a crusading army against the Turks, but died suddenly on 20 December 1355 and was buried in his foundation near Prizren. His remains were later moved to the Church of Saint Mark in Belgrade. His empire, spanning a large territory, slowly crumbled under his son Stefan Uroš V as regional aristocrats drew away from central rule.

Stefan Dušan is remembered as the most powerful Serbian ruler of the Middle Ages and remains a folk hero to Serbs. The aim of restoring his empire stayed an ideal for Serbs under Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian rule.
stefan-lazarevic: Stefan Lazarević, also called Stefan the Tall, was born about 1377 in Kruševac, the son of Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović and Milica, a member of a collateral branch of the Nemanjić dynasty. After his father was killed at the Battle of Kosovo on 15 June 1389, he became prince, and his mother ruled for him until he came of age in 1393. His state was surrounded by powerful neighbours: Bayezid I, Vuk Branković, who had married Stefan's sister Mara, the Bosnian king Tvrtko I and, to the north, King Sigismund of Hungary.

As an Ottoman vassal Stefan led troops in several campaigns, including the Ottoman attack on Bosnia in 1398. In 1402 he and his brother Vuk went from Bursa to Constantinople, where in August John VII Palaiologos gave him the Byzantine title of despot, ranking just below the emperor. His rival Đurađ Branković, backed by Süleyman, was defeated at the Battle of Tripolje in November. Stefan then allied himself with Sigismund, who gave him possessions including Belgrade and the Golubac Fortress. In 1408 Sigismund founded the Order of the Dragon, and Stefan is the first knight named in its charter. His brother Vuk rebelled in 1409 with Ottoman help, and Stefan later allied with Musa Çelebi in the Ottoman civil war.

At home he broke the resistance of the Serbian nobles. His Code of Mines of 1412 included rules for Novo Brdo, then the largest mine in the Balkans, and silver mining became the economic base of the despotate. He also inherited Zeta and fought Venice. Stefan married Helena Gattilusio on 12 September 1405; the marriage appears to have produced no children, and Anthony Luttrell thought she may never have come to Serbia.

Stefan was himself a writer, and his best-known work, A Homage to Love, has Renaissance themes. He sheltered scholars and refugees from neighbouring lands taken by the Ottomans, and the Resava School of arts was formed in his reign. He introduced knightly tournaments, modern battle tactics and firearms to Serbia and continued the Morava school of architecture. Having no children, he named his nephew Đurađ Branković as heir in 1426, and he died on 19 July 1427. The Serbian Orthodox Church canonised him on 1 August 1927, and his relics are kept at Koporin Monastery.
stefan-milutin: Milutin was the youngest son of King Stefan Uroš I and Queen Helen, a member of the Nemanjić dynasty. He became king unexpectedly in 1282, when his brother Stefan Dragutin abdicated, at about the age of 29. He is credited with strongly resisting the efforts of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos to impose Roman Catholicism on the Balkans after the Union of Lyons in 1274. The Serbian Orthodox Church later proclaimed him a saint, and he is known as the Holy King.

Immediately after his accession Milutin took northern Macedonia, including Skoplje, which became his capital. The next year he advanced with Dragutin as far as Kavala. After some fifteen years without change, peace came in 1299, when Milutin kept the conquered lands as the dowry of Simonis, daughter of Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos. In 1291 he and Dragutin defeated the Bulgarian lords Darman and Kudelin, and Milutin later devastated Vidin when its prince Shishman attacked Serbia.

After 1299 Milutin fought his brother Dragutin, whose capital was Belgrade, in a war that lasted with sporadic cease-fires until Dragutin's death in 1316. By 1309 he had named his son Stefan Dečanski governor of Zeta, making him heir in place of Dragutin's son. To gain an edge he sought papal support and even offered to convert the Serbs to Roman Catholicism. Dečanski rebelled in 1314 and was exiled to Constantinople, but returned in the spring of 1321 and was pardoned. After 1316 Milutin took most of Dragutin's lands, including Belgrade, but Charles I of Hungary regained Belgrade in 1319.

Serbian economic power grew rapidly under Milutin, mostly through mining. He founded Novo Brdo, the richest silver mine in the Balkans, and the mines at Trepča and Janjevo were also important. He struck imitations of Venetian coins, which Venice banned, and Dante's Divine Comedy mentions him among the counterfeiters. At the end of his life Serbia was second in strength in Southeast Europe after Hungary, and many ceremonies were taken over from the Byzantine court.

Milutin founded a hospital in Constantinople and built many churches and monasteries, among them Our Lady of Ljeviš at Prizren, Banjska and Gračanica. He died on 29 October 1321, and a short civil war followed before Stefan Dečanski took the throne.
stefan-nemanja: Stefan Nemanja was born about 1113 or 1114 in Ribnica in Zeta, near present-day Podgorica, the youngest son of Zavida, a prince of Zachlumia who had been sent to Ribnica after a conflict with his brothers. Because western Zeta was under Roman Catholic jurisdiction, Nemanja was baptised in the Latin rite, although much of his later life was spent balancing Western and Eastern Christianity. In 1165 the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Comnenus removed the Grand Župan Desa and gave the land to the administration of Zavida's sons, who belonged to the pro-Byzantine party. The eldest, Tihomir, became Grand Župan, and Nemanja received the areas around Ibar, Toplica and Dubočica.

Tihomir imprisoned Nemanja in a cave near the fortress of Ras. Nemanja escaped, took Kotor and overthrew his brother, and Manuel sent a force against him in 1168. Nemanja then turned towards Venice and Hungary, but in 1172 Manuel advanced and Nemanja surrendered at Niš, barefoot, with a rope round his neck and his sword in his hands. He was confirmed as Grand Župan, led through Constantinople in the emperor's triumph, and sent auxiliary troops to Byzantine campaigns, among them the defeat at Myriokephalon in 1176. Around 1176 he also convened an assembly against the Bogumil heresy, whose leader had his tongue cut out; the sect's members suffered confiscation, expulsion and the burning of their books.

The fall of Andronikos I in 1182 freed him from vassalage. In 1183 he joined Béla III of Hungary in an offensive against Byzantium, took Skadar and besieged Dubrovnik, and in 1189 he met Frederick Barbarossa at Niš, his new capital, though the emperor would promise nothing. Isaac II Angelos defeated him at the South Morava in 1191, and a peace of 1193 arranged for his middle son Stefan to marry the emperor's niece Eudokia and to succeed him.

In 1196, at an assembly at Ras, Nemanja abdicated in favour of Stefan, leaving his eldest son Vukan in charge of Zeta and other lands. He became a monk named Simeon and went to Mount Athos, where his youngest son Sava was already a monk. With permission from the Byzantine emperor they rebuilt Hilandar, and he issued the Charter of Hilandar. He died there on 13 February 1199 and was buried at Hilandar.

In 1207 Sava brought the remains to Studenica, Nemanja's own foundation, and made peace between his brothers. Myrrh was reported to flow from the grave, and the Serbian Orthodox Church canonised him as Saint Simeon the Myrrh-streaming. His cult helped to consolidate Serbian national identity.
stefan-stambolov: Stefan Nikolov Stambolov was born in Veliko Tarnovo, the son of a man who had taken part in the Velchova Zavera plot against Turkish rule in 1835. He began his education in his home town and studied at the seminary in Odessa from 1870 to 1872. He joined the Bulgarian Revolutionary Central Committee, and after the death of its founder Vassil Levski he was chosen as his successor. He led the unsuccessful uprising at Stara Zagora in 1875 and the Turnovo revolutionary committee in the April Uprising of 1876, and after the Treaty of Berlin he was a leader of the Kresna-Razlog uprising of 1878-1879.

Stambolov took part in the first Bulgarian parliament, the Founding Assembly of 1879, and after 1880 became vice-chairman and later chairman of the National Assembly. In 1885 he helped bring about the union of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia. On 20 August 1886 officers aligned with Russia overthrew Prince Alexander. Stambolov led a counter-coup on 28 August that removed the provisional government and became regent, and Russian hostility barred Alexander's return; he abdicated on 8 September. At 32 Stambolov was at once a minister, president and regent for an absent monarch.

He found a successor in Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, proclaimed Knyaz of autonomous Bulgaria on 7 July 1887 and crowned on 14 August 1887. Stambolov had first supported Carol I of Romania, but Russian opposition forced Carol to refuse. Stambolov then served as prime minister for seven years, from 1887 to 1894, and strengthened the country's diplomacy, economy and state power. Critics called his methods dictatorial. In 1891 members of the Supreme Macedonian-Adrianople Committee tried to kill him and instead killed the finance minister Hristo Belchev. He later clashed with Ferdinand, whom he blocked from seizing extra authority, and by 1894 he resigned, which Ferdinand gladly accepted.

In July 1895 four men ambushed Stambolov in the centre of Sofia on his way to a club near his home. They beat him badly, and he died of his injuries a few days later. The plot came from the Supreme Macedonian-Adrianople Committee, which blamed his support for the Ottoman Empire and his repression of the Committee. He is considered one of the Founders of Modern Bulgaria and was sometimes called the Bulgarian Bismarck. He appeared on the Bulgarian 20 lev banknote, and Stambolov Crag on Livingston Island in Antarctica is named after him.
stefan-the-first-crowned: Stefan Nemanjić was the second-eldest son of Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja and Anastasija. His elder brother Vukan ruled Zeta and neighbouring provinces, and his younger brother Rastko, later Saint Sava, ruled Hum. In 1190 the Byzantine emperor Isaac II Angelos launched a punitive expedition against the Serbs, and Nemanja was defeated in the battle of South Morava. Isaac II wanted to win back Niš and the road to Belgrade and to make allies of the Serbs, and he called for peace. Stefan's marriage to Eudokia Angelina, a niece of Isaac II, was confirmed, and Stefan received the title of sebastokrator.

In 1196, at a state assembly near the Church of Saints Peter and Paul, Nemanja abdicated in favour of Stefan, who became grand zoupan, while Vukan kept Zeta and nearby lands. Nemanja became a monk named Simeon and went to Mount Athos, where he and Sava rebuilt the Hilandar monastery. Around 1200 Stefan expelled Eudokia, who took refuge with Vukan. Vukan then allied with King Emeric of Hungary against him, and a civil war broke out. Stefan lost and fled in 1202 to Kaloyan of Bulgaria.

The Fourth Crusade turned on Constantinople in 1204, and Stefan used the upheaval to return to Ras with Kaloyan's help. The brothers stopped fighting in 1205. Stefan remarried in 1207 or 1208, taking Anna Dandolo, a granddaughter of the Venetian doge Enrico Dandolo. In 1208 he married his daughter Komnena to Dhimitër Progoni, prince of Albania, and by 1216 he controlled Zeta. He sheltered Strez, a noble exiled by Tsar Boril, and refused to hand him back. In 1217 he declared independence from Byzantium and took the title Crowned King and Autocrat of all Serbian and coastal lands. Many Serbian clergy opposed the coronation, and the Serbian church became autocephalous under Sava in 1219.

Stefan built many fortresses, among them Maglič. At the end of his life he took monastic vows under the name Symeon and died soon after, on 24 September 1228. He was canonised, as his father was. His sons Stefan Radoslav, Stefan Vladislav I and Stefan Uroš I later ruled as kings, and his son Sava II became an archbishop. Local tradition at the Reževići Monastery says he built its Church of the Dormition.
stefan-uros-i: Stefan Uroš was the youngest son of Stefan the First-Crowned and Anna, a granddaughter of Enrico Dandolo, Doge of Venice. He had two older half-brothers, Stefan Radoslav and Stefan Vladislav, who both reigned before him. Scholars have argued that strong and unpopular Bulgarian influence caused the opposition that led to Vladislav's deposition. The rebellious nobility chose Uroš as their candidate, and from 1242 to the spring of 1243 a war for the throne ended with Vladislav forced to give up the crown. Vladislav's wife, Beloslava, led the main resistance. Uroš treated his brother courteously and gave him the administration of Zeta.

Uroš took the throne at about 25, and the land had been looted by the Tatars and torn by internal conflicts. He pushed south into Macedonia and came into conflict with Hungary on the Danube. He subordinated both the Orthodox and the Catholic churches to the interests of the state and helped settle a dispute between the archbishoprics of Bar and Dubrovnik in favour of Bar. He protected writers and encouraged a new and fuller biography of his grandfather Nemanja, on whom he modelled himself, and he lived modestly at a court where everyone worked.

He was the first to exploit Serbia's mines, which became a main source of its medieval wealth. They were developed by Saxons, who lived by their own laws in settlements near the mines and could keep Catholicism and build their churches, at Novo Brdo, Brskovo and Rudnik. Trade with Dubrovnik and Kotor grew, and Serbian coins were minted on the Venetian model.

He fought Ragusa in 1252–1253, ending the war with a charter of 22 May 1254, and again in the later 1260s, when a treaty of 1268 fixed the tribute Dubrovnik paid the Serbian crown each year. In 1268 he invaded Hungarian lands in Mačva, was captured and had to buy his release. The peace married his son Stefan Dragutin to Catherine, daughter of the future King Stephen V of Hungary. Uroš also allied with Charles of Anjou against Emperor Michael Palaiologos.

Uroš refused his eldest son an appanage and appears to have considered making his younger son, the future Stefan Milutin, his heir. In 1276 Dragutin demanded the throne, and when his father refused he rebelled with Hungarian help and defeated him. Uroš abdicated and retired to a monastery in Hum, where he died soon afterwards. His remains were later moved to his foundation at Sopoćani.

His reign laid the foundations for the expansion of the Serbian medieval state, which became an empire in the middle of the 14th century. He is known as Uroš the Great and is counted among the most important rulers in Serbian history.
stefan-uros-v: Stefan Uros V was the only son of Stefan Dusan and Helena of Bulgaria, the sister of Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria. He was crowned king, the second highest title, as heir and co-ruler in 1346, after Dusan was crowned emperor. By the time he became sole ruler and emperor in 1355 he was no longer a minor, but he remained heavily dependent on his mother and on various members of the court. In historiography and folk tradition he is known as Uros the Weak, and he is recognised as a saint by the Serbian Orthodox Church.

In the spring of 1356 Nikephoros Orsini landed on the coast of Thessaly and overran it, then drove the despot Simeon Uros, the emperor's paternal uncle, from Aetolia and Acarnania. Simeon retreated to Epirus and western Macedonia, seized Kostur and proclaimed himself tsar, hoping to share the throne or replace Uros. The state council at Skoplje rejected his claims, and with the magnates' endorsement Uros became more active and issued a number of charters. Simeon was defeated in 1358 when he attacked the Skadar region, and in 1359 he retook Epirus and Thessaly and ruled there as emperor of Serbs and Greeks.

In the following years the empire fragmented into principalities, some of which did not even nominally acknowledge Uros. His mother Helena ruled autonomously from Serres in alliance with Jovan Ugljesa, and the Dejanovic and Balsic families and Nikola Altomanovic acted in the same way. By 1365 the most powerful nobleman was Ugljesa's brother Vukasin Mrnjavcevic, who became co-ruler with the title of king. By 1369 Vukasin had named his eldest son Prince Marko as heir, as Uros was childless.

Uros died childless in December 1371, after the Turks had destroyed much of the Serbian nobility in the Battle of Maritsa earlier that year. The cause of his death is unknown. He was canonised 211 years after his death, and his body is kept in the Jazak monastery on Fruska Gora.

Marko inherited his father's title, but real power in northern Serbia lay with Lazar Hrebeljanovic, who took no imperial or royal title. Serbian folklore and epic poems describe Uros as a just ruler of pleasant appearance but weak character, a view many historians share, although some argue that the decline began much later in his reign than is supposed. It was long held that Vukasin murdered him, but Vukasin was proven to have died before the emperor.
stefan-zeromski: Stefan Żeromski was born on 14 October 1864 at Strawczyn, near Kielce. His parents died young and left him impoverished. He studied at the Kielce Municipal High School, worked as a private tutor in 1888, and in 1890 took a job in Nałęczów, a spa town that attracted many intellectuals, artists and writers. There he met Oktawia Rodkiewicz, a widow whom he married on 2 September 1892; the novelist Bolesław Prus, who had admired her and opposed the marriage, was one of the witnesses. The couple moved to Switzerland, where from 1892 to 1896 he worked as a librarian at the Polish National Museum in Rapperswil, and Prus, though no admirer of his writing, helped them as far as he could.

Żeromski belonged to the Young Poland movement at the turn of the twentieth century and was called the conscience of Polish literature. He also wrote under the pen names Maurycy Zych, Józef Katerla and Stefan Iksmoreż. His early works include the short story Twilight of 1892 and Doctor Peter of 1895. The Labors of Sisyphus, of 1898, deals with Tsarist efforts to russify the Russian-occupied part of Poland, and Homeless People followed in 1899. Ashes appeared in 1904, The Faithful River in 1912, Struggles with Satan in volumes from 1916 to 1919 and The Spring to Come in 1924. His Journals were published after his death, from 1953 to 1956.

In 1913 Żeromski began a new family with the painter Anna Zawadzka, whom he had met in 1908; they had a daughter, Monika. In 1924 President Stanisław Wojciechowski gave him a three-room apartment on the second floor of the Royal Castle in Warsaw, and that year he was shortlisted for the Nobel Prize in Literature, for which he was nominated four times. He died in Warsaw on 20 November 1925. Several of his novels have been filmed, among them Ashes by Andrzej Wajda and The Spring to Come by Filip Bajon, and in 2018 he was posthumously awarded the Order of the White Eagle.
stelvio-pass: The Stelvio Pass, in Italian Passo dello Stelvio and in German Stilfser Joch, lies at 2,757 metres in the Ortler Alps of northern Italy, on the border with Switzerland. It runs between Stilfs, in Italian Stelvio, in South Tyrol and Bormio in the province of Sondrio, and connects the Valtellina with the Vinschgau valley and the town of Meran. It is the highest paved mountain pass in the Eastern Alps. The Umbrail Pass joins its western ramp to Santa Maria Val Müstair. The nearby Three Languages Peak is named because the Italian, German and Romansh language areas meet there.

The Austrian Empire built the original road in 1820-25 to link its former possession of Lombardy with Austria, a climb of 1,871 metres. Carlo Donegani was the engineer and project manager, and was knighted in 1840 as Carl Donegani von Stilfserberg. The route has changed very little since. The southern side is 22 kilometres long with 34 hairpin turns and six tunnels near Bormio, and the northern side is 28 kilometres long with 48 mostly tight hairpin bends, numbered with stones.

Before the end of the First World War the pass formed the border between the Austro-Hungarian Empire and the Italian Kingdom. Switzerland had an outpost and a hotel on the Three Languages Peak, and fierce battles were fought in ice and snow around it. The three states agreed not to fire over Swiss territory, which jutted out between Austria to the north and Italy to the south, so that they fired down the pass instead. After the war and the expansion of Italy the pass lost its strategic importance.

The pass is open to traffic from May to November and is important to cycling and motorcycling. The Giro d'Italia first crossed it in 1953, when Fausto Coppi beat Hugo Koblet, and when it is the highest point of a race it is named the Cima Coppi. On one day each year, the Stelvio Bike Day, roads to the pass are closed to all but bicycles. Stelvio National Park, established in 1935 and the largest in the Italian Alps, covers the Ortles-Cevedale massif, and its wildlife includes deer, chamois, ibex and wolves. A summer skiing area lies beside the pass road.
sten-sture-the-elder: Sten Sture was born around 1440, the son of Gustav Anundsson of the Sture family and Birgitta Stensdotter Bielke, half-sister of the future King Charles VIII. His father, castellan of Kalmar Castle, died when Sten was four. The 15th century in Sweden was marked by struggles between unionists, who wanted Sweden united with Denmark and Norway under Danish kings, and separatists, who wanted an independent Swedish kingdom. Through his ties to King Charles he joined the separatists young, and he fought at Haraker in 1464, defeated Erik Karlsson Vasa's rising at Uppbo in 1470 and beat back Christian I's forces at Öresten.

Charles VIII named Sture heir to his personal domains and left him in charge of the crown lands, including Stockholm and its castle. After the king's death on 15 May 1470, Sture was elected Lord Protector and Regent at the meeting at Arboga on 1 May 1471. At the Battle of Brunkeberg on 10 October 1471 his army routed Christian I's Danish and unionist forces, and he became a national saviour.

For about a quarter of a century he made the regency almost an office in itself. He relied on the peasantry, the mining interests of Bergslagen and the lower nobility against the high nobility and clergy. In 1483 the high nobility confirmed King Hans of Denmark as king at Kalmar, but Sture kept power. In 1477 he supported Archbishop Jakob Ulvsson in founding Uppsala University, and in 1487 he forced the Tott family to cede Öland and Borgholm to Sweden. From 1495 to 1497 he repelled a Russian invasion of Finland, but he fell out with most of the nobility, including Svante Nilsson, and the Privy Council deposed him on 8 March 1497.

Peasant forces supporting him were defeated at Rotebro by Hans, who invaded in July 1497. Sture surrendered in Stockholm on 6 October, was reconciled with Hans and received the highest authority below the king. When Sweden rebelled in 1501 he took office as regent again. In May 1502 the garrison in Stockholm, led by Queen Christina, capitulated after a long siege.

On his way back from escorting the queen to Halmstad, he fell ill and died on 14 December 1503. His only child, Birgitta, was born outside marriage and became a nun at Vadstena Abbey. The male line of the Sture family died out with him, and his nephew Erik Johansson Vasa inherited his domains. Svante Nilsson succeeded him as regent.
stendal: Stendal lies west of the Elbe valley, about 125 km west of Berlin, 170 km east of Hanover and 55 km north of Magdeburg. It is the capital of the Stendal District and the unofficial capital of the Altmark region. A deed attributed to Emperor Henry II in 1022 that seemed to mention the place is a 12th-century forgery, and the town was in fact founded and granted Magdeburg rights by the first Brandenburg margrave, Albert the Bear, about 1160.

St Mary's Church is first mentioned in 1283, and the town received walls about 1300, joined the Hanseatic League in 1358 and bought the right to mint coins from the Brandenburg margraves in 1369. A Latin school is documented from 1338. In 1502 the Elector Joachim I Nestor married Princess Elizabeth of Denmark at Stendal. The citizens turned Protestant in 1539, and Waldensian, Palatine and Swiss refugees settled in the town in the 1680s and 1690s. After the Napoleonic Wars the Altmark passed to the Prussian Province of Saxony, and Stendal had been a Prussian garrison town since the 17th century.

In World War II the town had a Luftwaffe airfield and was hit by ten air raids, and more than 300 civilians died when the Röxe district was devastated. On 4 May 1945 General Maximilian von Edelsheim signed the capitulation of the German 12th Army at the town hall. The town was in East Germany from 1949 to 1990, and the Soviet barracks remained until 1994. Construction of a nuclear power plant north of the town, begun in 1974, was abandoned after reunification.

Stendal is officially a Hanseatic city, and preserves several well-preserved medieval churches, the Tangemünde Gate, dating from 1220, and the Uenglinger Gate of the 15th century. St Mary's Church, with two towers 84 metres high, was inaugurated in 1447, and a statue of Roland stands by the 14th-century town hall. The art historian Johann Joachim Winckelmann was born here in 1717, and the writer Stendhal, who lived near the town in 1807–08, is generally believed to have taken his pen name in tribute to him.
stepan-razin: Razin's father, Timofey Razya, is said to have come from a suburb of Voronezh, and the identity of his mother is debated. He first appears in the sources in 1652 and, after six years without a trace, reappeared as the leader of a band that levied tribute from vessels on the Volga. His elder brother Ivan was executed in 1665 for deserting the war with the Poles. Wars with Poland and the Russo-Swedish War had raised taxes and conscription, serfdom had been fixed by the Law Code of 1649, and many peasants fled south to join the Cossacks.

In 1667 Razin led a small group of Cossacks from the Don down the Volga to the Caspian, aiming to set up a base at Yaitsk, which he took in July 1667 by posing as a pilgrim. In 1668 he defeated the voivode Yakov Bezobrazov and raided Persia for about eighteen months. He failed to take Derbent, and Persians killed roughly 400 of his Cossacks at Rasht, but he pillaged Farahabad and in July 1669 destroyed a Persian fleet off Suina. In August 1669 he accepted a pardon from Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich at Astrakhan.

In 1670 he rebelled openly, capturing Cherkassk and Tsaritsyn and sailing down the Volga with almost 7,000 men. At Astrakhan the local musketeers, the streltsy, let him in, and he killed those who opposed him and set up a Cossack republic. He moved up the Volga, taking Saratov and Samara, but Simbirsk held out, and on 1 and 4 October his army was beaten there by Yuri Baryatinsky. His envoys had stirred up areas as far as Nizhny Novgorod, Tambov and Penza, but the Don Cossacks turned against him after the Patriarch anathematized him.

In 1671 Razin and his brother Frol were captured at Kagalnik by Cossack elders and handed to the tsar's officials in Moscow. Razin was quartered on the scaffold on Red Square on 16 June 1671. The historian Paul Avrich notes that the repression of the revolt was far more brutal than the insurgents' own atrocities. Razin had revolted against the traitor boyars rather than the tsar, and the revolt ended in greater government control and some loss of Cossack autonomy.

He became a figure of folklore and song. A poem by Dmitry Sadovnikov of 1883, set to music, tells of him throwing a captured Persian princess into the Volga; modern historians doubt the episode, which two Dutch travellers report in different forms.
stepan-shaumian: Stepan Shaumian was born on 1 October 1878 in Tiflis to a family of Armenian cloth merchants, descended from the Shaumian line of meliks of Meghri. He became involved in revolutionary politics as a student, entered the Riga Polytechnic Institute and in 1899 formed Armenia's first Marxist group in the village of Jalaloghli, today Stepanavan. Expelled from the institute in March 1902, arrested and exiled to Transcaucasia, he co-founded the Union of Armenian Social Democrats in Tiflis. He studied philosophy in Berlin, met Lenin, Julius Martov and Georgi Plekhanov, and sided with the Bolsheviks. By 1907 he headed the Bolshevik movement in Baku, where Joseph Stalin was also active and the two clashed.

Shaumian led a general strike in Baku in 1914 and was imprisoned until the February Revolution of 1917. After the October Revolution he became Commissar Extraordinary for the Caucasus and chairman of the Baku Council of People's Commissars, heading a government of Bolsheviks, Left Socialist-Revolutionaries, Mensheviks and Dashnaks. At the end of March 1918 the disarming of Azerbaijani soldiers led to fighting in which the commune, supported by Dashnak forces, attacked the Muslim quarters. Estimates of the Azerbaijanis and other Muslims killed range from 3,000 to 12,000. In September 1918 an Ottoman-led Army of Islam retook Baku and killed an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 Armenians.

Shaumian was ordered from Moscow to refuse British help, though he understood what refusing it might cost the Armenians. On 26 July 1918 the Bolsheviks were outvoted 259 to 236 in the Baku Soviet, and he left the city, saying he and his comrades were forced to leave. A new government, the Central Caspian Dictatorship, was formed as British forces under General Lionel Dunsterville arrived.

On 31 July the commissars sailed for Astrakhan, but their ships were captured on 16 August and they were jailed in Baku. When Baku fell in mid-September they escaped or were released and sailed to Krasnovodsk, where anti-Bolshevik forces arrested them. They were executed on the night of 20 September 1918 in the Turkmen desert. The British role is disputed: Captain Reginald Teague-Jones later claimed he left before the decision was made. The Soviet government made Shaumian a hero, and Khankendi was renamed Stepanakert and Jalaloghli Stepanavan. In January 2009 Azerbaijan demolished the 26 Commissars Memorial in Baku, which caused an outcry in Armenia.
stephen-bathory: Stephen Báthory was born on 27 September 1533 at Somlyó, in a noble Hungarian family. Around 1549–1550 he visited Italy and probably attended lectures at the University of Padua. He then joined the army of Ferdinand I and fought the Turks, and some time after 1553 he was captured by them. When Ferdinand refused to pay his ransom he joined John II Sigismund Zápolya in the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom as a commander and diplomat. After Zápolya's death in 1571 the Transylvanian estates elected him voivode of Transylvania. By 1573 he had defeated Gáspár Bekes, who was supported by the Habsburgs, in the civil war that followed.

The throne of Poland-Lithuania fell vacant in 1572 with the death of Sigismund II Augustus. After Henry III of France left it, an election in 1575 produced two claimants, and a faction around Chancellor Jan Zamoyski secured the election of Báthory, who married Anna Jagiellon and was crowned on 1 May 1576. He first had to win recognition. Lithuania accepted him after he agreed to its conditions, and Danzig, which had supported the Habsburg candidate, was defeated in the field on 17 April 1577 and then agreed to recognise him and pay compensation of 200,000 zlotys.

With Zamoyski he reorganised the courts through the Crown Tribunal of 1578 and the Lithuanian Tribunal of 1581, and he raised infantry from the peasantry. He founded the Academy of Vilnius from a Jesuit college and protected Polish Jews while promoting Catholicism. Against Ivan the Terrible in the Livonian War he took Polotsk in 1579 and Velikiye Luki in 1580, and in 1581 he besieged Pskov. The Truce of Jam Zapolski of 15 January 1582 gave the Commonwealth Polotsk, Veliz and most of Livonia.

In 1584 Báthory allowed Zamoyski to execute Samuel Zborowski for treason and murder, a conflict between the king and the nobility that remained controversial. He was planning another war against Russia when he died on 12 December 1586. He left no legitimate children. He remained interested in Hungarian affairs, never learned Polish, and sponsored works about his own deeds, so that he became a recurring figure in Polish literature.
stephen-count-of-blois: Stephen Henry was the son of Theobald III, count of Blois, and Gersent of Le Mans. He is first mentioned approaching William the Conqueror to ask for the hand of his daughter Adela of Normandy, and he received it. Theobald gave him the administration of Blois and Chartres in 1074, and in 1089, on his father's death, he became count of both. The couple married around 1090 at Chartres, and they had a large family.

Stephen was one of the leaders of the First Crusade, commanding one of its major armies and often writing enthusiastic letters to his wife about its progress. He was present at the Siege of Nicaea, where he wrote that the defenders surrendered out of fear of the siege towers. Either before or at the start of the Siege of Antioch in October 1097 he was chosen as leader of the army, a role that seems not to have gone much beyond presiding over the assemblies of the leaders and handling provisioning and housekeeping for the armies.

On 2 June 1098, the day before Antioch was captured, Stephen withdrew from the siege, leaving his comrades in a difficult position as a superior Turkish army under Kerbogha approached. On the way back to the West he met the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who was marching with an army to help the crusaders, and persuaded him that the expedition was futile. Alexios turned back, which added to the crusaders' suspicion that the Byzantines were not to be trusted and to later conflicts with Byzantium.

Stephen came home with his vows unfulfilled and was in disgrace. Adela pleaded with him to make a second pilgrimage, and he joined the crusade of 1101 with others who had also returned prematurely. He took part in the disastrous campaign in Anatolia to free Bohemond from prison, then sailed from Constantinople to St Simeon and on to Jerusalem, finally fulfilling his vows.

In 1102, already on his way home, King Baldwin of Jerusalem persuaded him to fight the Fatimids at the Second Battle of Ramla. Stephen was taken prisoner and executed, probably at Ascalon on 19 May. His children included William, Count of Sully, Theobald II, Count of Champagne, Stephen, later King of England, and Henry, Bishop of Winchester. His daughter Matilda and her husband Richard d'Avranches, Earl of Chester, drowned in the White Ship disaster on 25 November 1120.
stephen-i-of-hungary: Stephen was the only son of Grand Prince Géza and his wife Sarolt, who was descended from a prominent family of gyulas. He was given the pagan name Vajk at birth. His birth year is uncertain: later chronicles give 967, 969 and 975, and the late 11th-century and early 12th-century hagiographies, which call him still an adolescent in 997, support 975. His Lesser Legend places his birth at Esztergom. Both his parents were baptised, but Stephen was the first of the family to become a devout Christian. He married Gisela of Bavaria, a member of the Ottonian dynasty.

Géza died in 997, and an assembly at Esztergom declared Stephen grand prince. Succession by a son contradicted the older principle of seniority, under which his relative Koppány, Duke of Somogy, had the stronger claim. Koppány announced his claim, supported mostly by pagans, and Stephen defeated him with the help of foreign knights such as Vecelin, Hont and Pázmány and of native lords. Part of Koppány's quartered body was displayed at Gyulafehérvár, the seat of Gyula the Younger. Stephen was crowned with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II, on 25 December 1000 or 1 January 1001.

In wars against semi-independent chieftains, including the Black Hungarians and Gyula the Younger, he united the Carpathian Basin. He founded an archbishopric at Esztergom, a bishopric at Kalocsa and other sees, and three Benedictine monasteries, so that the Church in Hungary developed independently of the archbishops of the Holy Roman Empire. His local administration rested on counties organised around fortresses and run by royal officials. Hungary became a route for pilgrims and merchants, and Stephen set up hostels for pilgrims in Constantinople, Jerusalem, Ravenna and Rome.

Relations with Emperor Henry II, Stephen's brother-in-law, were friendly. Under Conrad II they worsened, and in 1030 Conrad's invading army had to withdraw from Hungary; in 1031 Conrad ceded the lands between the rivers Lajta and Fischa.

Stephen's son Emeric died in a hunting accident in 1031, and Stephen survived all his children. According to the Annals of Altaich he named his sister's son, the Venetian Peter Orseolo, as heir, and his cousin Vazul, who had the strongest claim, was blinded. Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was buried in his basilica at Székesfehérvár. Civil wars followed for decades.

King Ladislaus I initiated his canonisation, and he was canonised in 1083 with Emeric and Bishop Gerard of Csanád. His right hand, the Holy Dexter, became an object of veneration. A work of moral instruction attributed to him, the Admonitions, argues that kingship is bound to the Catholic faith. His feast day, 20 August, is a public holiday in Hungary, State Foundation Day.
stephen-king-of-england: Stephen was born in Blois in France, the fourth son of Stephen-Henry, Count of Blois and Chartres, who was killed at the battle of Ramlah while on crusade when Stephen was at most ten years old. His mother, Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders, was known for her piety and strong personality and shaped his upbringing. Placed in the court of his uncle Henry I of England, he rose in prominence and was granted extensive lands. By his marriage to Matilda of Boulogne in 1125 he gained estates in Kent and Boulogne.

In 1120 Stephen planned to sail on the White Ship from Barfleur but left it at the last moment. The ship sank with the heir to the throne, William Adelin, and nearly all its passengers, which left the succession open to challenge.

When Henry I died in 1135, Stephen crossed the Channel and took the throne with the help of his brother Henry, Bishop of Winchester, arguing that keeping order took priority over his earlier oaths to support the Empress Matilda. In 1138 Robert, Earl of Gloucester, renounced his fealty and declared for Matilda, while Geoffrey of Anjou invaded Normandy and David I of Scotland invaded northern England. Stephen created many new earldoms for loyal supporters, many of them for his advisor Waleran de Beaumont and his family.

Matilda and Robert landed in England on 30 September 1139 with 140 knights. At the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141 Stephen fought on foot, and after his sword broke he used a borrowed battle axe, but he was overwhelmed and taken prisoner. He was freed only after his wife and William of Ypres captured Robert at the Rout of Winchester. By 1147 England had suffered extensively, and the chronicle of the time recorded nothing but disturbance and wickedness and robbery. The royal coinage fragmented, and unauthorised castles multiplied.

Late in his reign Stephen sought to have his son Eustace crowned, but Pope Eugene III refused. In 1153 Henry, the Empress's son, invaded England. The armies met at Wallingford, but neither side's barons wished to fight another pitched battle, and the sudden death of Eustace hastened peace. By the Treaty of Winchester Stephen recognised Henry as his heir, passing over his second son William. He died on 25 October 1154, and Henry II succeeded him. Modern historians have debated whether his personality, external events or weaknesses in the Norman state caused the long civil war.
stephen-the-great: Stephen was the son of Bogdan, himself a son of Alexander the Good, Prince of Moldavia, and of Maria Oltea. His birth date is unknown, and historians estimate it between 1433 and 1440. The death of Alexander the Good in 1432 began a succession crisis of more than two decades. Bogdan seized the throne in 1449 with the support of John Hunyadi, and Stephen was styled voivode in his charters as his heir and co-ruler. In 1450 father and son repulsed a Polish invasion. Peter III Aaron murdered Bogdan in October 1451, and Stephen fled to Hungary. He won the throne in 1457 at the Battle of Orbic with the support of his cousin Vlad the Impaler.

Stephen captured the Danube port of Chilia in January 1465 and ordered the Church of the Assumption at Putna in 1466 to commemorate it. After repulsing Matthias Corvinus of Hungary at the Battle of Baia, he stopped paying tribute to the Ottoman sultan in 1473. He then invaded Wallachia to replace Radu the Fair, an Ottoman-installed vassal, with his own protégé, Basarab III Laiotă, and took Bucharest. Each prince he put on the throne was soon forced to pay homage to the sultan. In 1475 he defeated a large Ottoman army at the Battle of Vaslui, and Pope Sixtus IV called him Athleta Christi, Champion of Christ, though promised support never came.

The following year Mehmed II routed Stephen at the Battle of Valea Albă but withdrew from Moldavia for lack of provisions, a failed siege of Neamț and an outbreak of plague. The Ottomans and their Crimean Tatar allies took Chilia and Cetatea Albă in 1484, and Stephen's efforts to recover them failed. From 1486 he again paid a yearly tribute to the Ottomans. He played Poland, Hungary and the Ottomans against each other, and defeated the Polish army of John I Albert at the Battle of the Cosmin Forest in 1497. In 1502 he and his Crimean Tatar allies destroyed the remnants of the Golden Horde at the Battle of Samara River. He acknowledged the loss of his ports to the Ottomans in 1503.

Stephen died on 2 July 1504 after a reign of more than 47 years, during his last years sharing government with his son Bogdan III. He restored old fortresses and built new ones, and from 1487 more than a dozen stone churches were built at his initiative, among them Voroneț in 1488 and Tazlău in 1496 to 1497. They mixed Byzantine and Gothic elements with local tradition and helped form a Moldavian style of architecture. The Romanian Orthodox Church canonised him in 1992, and he is regarded as a national hero in Romania and Moldova.
stephen-tomasevic: Stephen Tomašević was born about 1438 into the Kotromanić dynasty, a son of the Bosnian prince Thomas by a commoner, Vojača. Thomas became king in 1443 and converted from the Bosnian Church to Roman Catholicism about 1445. In 1459 he arranged his son's marriage to Helen, eldest daughter of the late Lazar Branković, Despot of Serbia, who took the name Maria. It was meant to unite Bosnia and the Serbian Despotate against the Ottomans.

Stephen took the Serbian throne at Smederevo on 21 March 1459, but his Catholicism made him unpopular. When Sultan Mehmed II attacked, he surrendered the fortress on 20 June 1459 and fled to Bosnia. Matthias Corvinus of Hungary accused him of selling it for gold, an allegation the sources do not support.

Stephen succeeded his father on 10 July 1461. He made peace with the powerful nobleman Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, and on 17 November 1461 a papal legate crowned him in Jajce with a crown sent from Rome, the last coronation in Bosnia. He corresponded with Pope Pius II, but Western rulers refused help.

By spring 1462 it was known that Mehmed meant to conquer Bosnia. Kosača's quarrel with his son Vladislav Hercegović broke out again, and Vladislav sought help from Mehmed. In June 1462, relying on Matthias, Stephen refused the customary tribute. In the spring of 1463 Mehmed marched into Bosnia with an army of 150,000 men. Bobovac fell within days, and Stephen was pursued to Ključ, where he surrendered on a written promise that no harm would come to him.

Mehmed's mullah, Ali al-Bistami, ruled that the sultan was not bound by a promise made without his knowledge. Stephen was beheaded on 25 May 1463 in a field near Jajce, with his uncle Radivoj, his cousin and two noblemen. His fall ended the Kingdom of Bosnia, which submitted within weeks. His half-siblings were taken to Constantinople and converted to Islam, and his stepmother, Queen Catherine, campaigned unsuccessfully from the Papal States for the kingdom's restoration.
stepwell: A stepwell has two parts: a vertical shaft from which water is drawn, and the inclined passages, chambers and steps that give access to it. The galleries and chambers around the shaft were often carved profusely and became cool, quiet retreats in the hot summers. Some stepwells have several storeys, and water could be raised to the first or second floor by a Persian wheel pulled by a bull.

The names vary by region. In Hindi-speaking areas they include baoli, baori and bavadi, in Gujarati and Marwari vav or vavri, and in Kannada kalyani or pushkarani. A related form, the stepped pond, usually stands beside a temple, is open to the sun and is rectangular, whereas a stepwell is dark, more linear and more isolated.

A stepwell may have first appeared in periods of drought to secure access to water. Dholavira has tanks with flights of steps, and the great bath at Mohenjo-daro has steps on opposite sides. Ashoka's Pillar Edict No 7 says that wells were dug and flights of steps built every eight kos along roads, and that this was an old practice of former kings.

One of the earliest bath-like ponds reached by steps lies in the Uperkot caves at Junagadh, dated to the 4th century, and the stepwells at Dhank in Rajkot district are dated to 550-625 CE. The Mata Bhavani stepwell in Gujarat, built in the 11th century, is among the earliest surviving examples and has elaborately ornamented columns, brackets and beams.

Stepwells gave water in a land where fresh water is abundant only in the monsoon. Because they were built without mortar, groundwater filtered through the stone, and at depth the water was less exposed to sun and heat. Most surviving stepwells served for bathing, washing, farming and watering animals, and as places for social gatherings and religious ceremonies. Women, who collected the water, prayed at them and offered gifts to the goddess of the well. Stepwells were also thought to spread disease, since the water attracted insects and animals.

The Mughal emperors encouraged the building of stepwells, while British authorities in the Raj found their hygiene poor and installed pipes and pumps. Babur's garden at Agra, the Aram Bagh, is said to have drawn on stepwells for its reflecting pool. The Stepwell Atlas, begun in 2016, mapped over 2,800 stepwells in India, and some have been restored to their original purpose as water shortages have grown.
stesichorus: Ancient tradition has Stesichorus born at Metauros, modern Gioia Tauro in Calabria, around 630 BCE and dying at Katane, modern Catania, in Sicily around 555 BCE. Some say he came from Himera, which they explain by a later move there from Metauros. He was thought to have been exiled from Pallantium in Arcadia. The Suda says his name was originally Tisias and that he was called Stesichorus because he first established a chorus of singers to the cithara. Its claim that Hesiod was his father is called fantasy by modern writers. Aristotle mentions two public speeches by him, one warning the people of Himera against Phalaris and another warning the people of Locri against presumption.

According to the Suda his works, in the Doric dialect, filled 26 books, each probably a long narrative poem. Titles recorded include Helen, Sack of Troy, Nostoi, Geryoneis, Cerberus, Cycnus, Eriphyle, Europa, Oresteia and Boar-hunters. The Geryoneis, on Heracles' theft of Geryon's cattle, ran to about 1500 lines. Papyri show that he composed in units of three stanzas, strophe, antistrophe and epode, a form later used by Bacchylides and Pindar. His best-known poem is the Palinode, written, according to ancient accounts, after he was blinded for abusing Helen. It absolves her of blame for the Trojan War: in one version she never sailed to Troy, and in another only her image reached Troy while she went to Egypt.

Quintilian wrote that he sustained the weight of epic poetry on his lyre and might have rivalled Homer had he shown restraint, but that he was redundant and diffuse. Many modern scholars hold that his narratives were composed for solo performance with the lyre rather than for choirs.

Stesichorus ranked among the nine lyric poets esteemed by the scholars of Alexandria, yet few fragments survive. David Campbell wrote that time has dealt more harshly with him than with any other major lyric poet. Discoveries on Egyptian papyrus, notably the disputed Lille Stesichorus, confirm his role as a link between Homer's epic narrative and the lyric narrative of Pindar. He influenced the representation of myth in sixth-century art and the development of Athenian drama.
stethoscope: The word comes from the Ancient Greek stêthos, breast, and skopéō, to look. Laennec's wooden tube was similar to the common ear trumpet, a historical form of hearing aid. He called his device the stethoscope, meaning chest scope, and called its use mediate auscultation, because it was listening with a tool intermediate between the body and the physician's ear. Today auscultation means all such listening, mediate or not.

The first flexible stethoscope of any sort may have been a binaural instrument with articulated joints, not very clearly described in 1829. When Golding Bird published his description in 1840 he noted an earlier design that he thought of little use, which he called the snake ear trumpet.

An acoustic stethoscope carries sound from the chest piece through air-filled hollow tubes to the listener's ears. The chest piece usually has two sides, a diaphragm, a plastic disc, and a bell, a hollow cup. The bell transmits low-frequency sounds and the diaphragm higher ones. An electronic stethoscope amplifies body sounds and can record them or transmit them wirelessly. A fetal stethoscope, shaped like a listening trumpet and also known as a Pinard horn after the French obstetrician Adolphe Pinard, is placed against a pregnant woman's abdomen. The stethophone, described by Somerville Scott Alison at the Royal Society in 1858, had two separate bells for comparing sounds from two places.

Cammann also wrote a major treatise on diagnosis by auscultation, which the binaural stethoscope made possible. The medical historian Jacalyn Duffin has argued that the invention helped to redefine disease from a bundle of symptoms to a problem of an anatomical system, even where no symptoms are visible, because before it there were no non-lethal instruments for exploring internal anatomy.

In the early 1960s David Littmann, a Harvard Medical School professor, produced a lighter stethoscope with better acoustics. In 1999 Richard Deslauriers patented the first external noise-reducing stethoscope, the DRG Puretone. The stethoscope has also become a symbol of healthcare professionals.
steve-biko: Bantu Stephen Biko was born on 18 December 1946 at his grandmother's house in Tarkastad, Cape Province. His family settled in Ginsberg township at King William's Town, where Xhosa, Afrikaans and English were all spoken. His father, a former police officer who worked as a clerk, died in 1950, and the family depended on his mother's wages as a cook. Advised that law was too closely tied to political activism, Biko entered the University of Natal Medical School in 1966 and was soon elected to the Students' Representative Council.

Biko joined the National Union of South African Students but grew frustrated that white liberals dominated it and, in his view, failed to understand the black experience. He became a leading figure in founding the South African Students' Organisation, launched in July 1969, and was elected its first president. Influenced by Frantz Fanon, Malcolm X and the Black Power movement, the organisation adopted Black Consciousness as its ideology.

Biko rejected the government's division of the population into whites and non-whites, which he saw as defining people by an absence. He described blackness as a mental attitude rather than a matter of pigmentation and applied the word to Africans, Coloureds and Indians. He urged black people to free themselves of any sense of inferiority, popularised the slogan "black is beautiful", and hoped for a non-racial South Africa with one person, one vote.

The government came to regard Biko as a subversive threat and banned him in 1973. On 17 August 1977 he broke the order by driving to Cape Town with his friend Peter Jones. On 18 August they were stopped at a police roadblock near Grahamstown and arrested. Biko was beaten to death by state security officers and died on 12 September 1977. More than 20,000 people attended his funeral.

Biko is regarded as the father of Black Consciousness and as the first icon of the anti-apartheid movement. Nelson Mandela called him "the spark that lit a veld fire across South Africa". Peter Gabriel's song "Biko" was a hit in 1980 and was banned in South Africa, and Donald Woods's 1978 biography of him was the basis of the film Cry Freedom. His political legacy remains a matter of contention.
steyr: Celts settled the area from about 600 BCE, and their kingdom of Noricum became part of the Roman Empire in 15 BCE. The Roman Iron Road led from the Erzberg mine along the Enns River to the camp of Lauriacum on the Danube. Slavic settlers who moved in during the 6th century were defeated by Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria, who granted the land to Kremsmünster Abbey in 777.

A fortress above the Steyr River, built by the Traungau counts during the Hungarian invasions, is first mentioned as Styraburg in a deed of 980. From 1055 the castle and the adjacent March of Styria were ruled by the Otakar dynasty, who controlled the iron mining at the Erzberg and made Steyr a centre of courtly culture and Middle High German poetry.

In 1180 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised Margrave Ottokar IV to Duke of Styria, but the line died out in 1192 and under the Georgenberg Pact of 1186 his lands passed to the Babenberg dukes of Austria. Steyr then lost its importance as a residence but remained a centre of ironworking, producing mainly knives and arms.

After the Habsburg king Rudolf I won the Battle on the Marchfeld in 1278, his son King Albert I confirmed the town privileges and market rights in 1287, and the citizens profited from a preferred place in the iron trade of the Holy Roman Empire, above all with Venice. In the 13th and 14th centuries Steyr was a centre of the Waldensian movement, and the Reformation spread quickly there from about 1525.

The iron trade declined during the Thirty Years' War and the Peasants' War of 1626. A fire in 1727 destroyed the medieval Styraburg, which the Baroque Lamberg Castle replaced. The Armistice of Steyr was signed there on 25 December 1800.

Steyr is a statutory city in Upper Austria, where the Steyr and Enns rivers meet beneath Lamberg Castle. The firm of Leopold Werndl, founded in 1830, became a stock company in 1864 and later the Steyr-Werke, which merged with Austro-Daimler and Puch in 1934. The town was heavily bombed in February 1944. Its historic centre around the Stadtplatz was restored after the war, and the Gothic Bummerlhaus is among its best-known buildings.
stilicho: Stilicho was the son of a Vandal cavalry officer and a provincial Roman woman. There is little to suggest that he saw himself as anything but a Roman, and he was probably a Nicene Christian like his patron Theodosius I. The main sources are the panegyrics of the poet Claudian, whom he patronised and who portrays him in a positive light, and, for the years after 404, Zosimus, who drew on one historian hostile to Stilicho and one supportive.

He rose through the army under Theodosius, who sent him in 383 to the court of the Persian king Shapur III at Ctesiphon to negotiate over the partition of Armenia. He then married Serena, the niece of Theodosius, and was promoted to senior commands. After the Battle of the Frigidus Theodosius appointed him guardian of his son Honorius, shortly before the emperor's death in 395.

Honorius became emperor in the West and his brother Arcadius in the East. Stilicho became the de facto commander-in-chief of the western armies and tied himself to the throne by giving Honorius his daughter Maria in marriage in 398 and, after her death, Thermantia in 408. In 395 he led the army into the Balkans against the Goths of Alaric but obeyed an order from Arcadius to send back the eastern troops. He defeated Alaric's forces in Macedonia in 397 and put down the revolt of Gildo in Africa.

In 402 he broke Alaric's siege of Mediolanum, where Honorius was living, and defeated him at the Battle of Pollentia on Easter Sunday, the last victory marked by a triumphal march in Rome. In 406 he surprised and captured the force of Radagaisus at Florentia, executed Radagaisus and enrolled 12,000 of his warriors, selling the rest into slavery.

To defend Italy Stilicho had weakened the Rhine frontier, and on 31 December 406 a coalition of Vandals, Alans and Suevi crossed it and devastated Gaul. His reputation never recovered. He failed to put down the rebellion of Constantine III in Britain. After rumours that he intended to place his son on the throne, the army at Ticinum mutinied on 13 August 408 and killed senior officers. Stilicho retired to Ravenna, did not resist arrest and was executed on 22 August 408. His son Eucherius was killed soon after.

In the disturbances the families of barbarian federates in Italy were massacred, and perhaps 30,000 of these soldiers joined Alaric, who stood before Rome by September 408 and sacked it in August 410. Many historians hold that the removal of Stilicho was the main catalyst of that event.
stip: Štip lies in the eastern part of North Macedonia, where the Lakavica, Ovče Pole and Kočani valleys meet. Two rivers pass through it: the Bregalnica, the second longest in the country, and the Otinja, which divides the city centre. The Isar hill, crowned by an early medieval fortress, dominates the town, which is commonly described as the town under the Isar. The name developed from the ancient Astibos to the Byzantine Stipeon and the modern Štip. The ancient writer Polyaenus records that the Paeonian kings bathed ritually in the river Astibo as a coronation rite.

The capital of the Paeonian royal house was probably in the area of Astibos. In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE the Paeonians lived west of the Axius basin, and two tribes lived along the Astibo: the Derrones, named after their god of healing Darron, and the Laeaeans, who minted heavy coins. The Persian invasion of 480 BCE under Xerxes I weakened them, and they were absorbed into the Macedonian realm before 360 BCE.

A settlement called Estipeon is first mentioned under the emperor Tiberius as an important place in the Roman province of Macedonia and a stop on the road from Stobi to Pautalia. In the 6th century Slavs raided the Balkans and destroyed the Byzantine settlement, and the Slavic tribe of the Sagudates settled the area permanently.

Štip belonged to the Bulgarian Empire until the Byzantine victory at Kleidion in 1014, and it was Byzantine again until Bulgaria was re-established in 1185. From the mid-13th century it changed hands several times. By 1284 the Serbian king Stefan Milutin had conquered the region, and in 1334 a charter of Stefan Dušan gave the Church of the Holy Archangel, built by the protosebastos Hrelja, to the Hilandar monastery. It was annexed in 1385 by the Ottoman Empire and made it the seat of a sanjak; it was held by Austria only in 1689–1690.

In 1912 Bulgaria occupied it in the First Balkan War, but in 1913 all of Vardar Macedonia was annexed by the Kingdom of Serbia, and from 1929 to 1941 Štip belonged to the Vardar Banovina of Yugoslavia.

Štip is the centre of the textile and fashion industry of North Macedonia and has the Goce Delčev University. Its three 14th-century churches date from the time of medieval Serbia: St Michael under the Isar, built in 1332, St John the Baptist, built in 1350, and the Ascension church, built in 1369, which keeps 14th-century frescoes. The Bezisten, a stone Ottoman indoor bazaar, is now an art gallery. The ruins of the ancient city of Bargala lie nearby.
stirling: Stirling lies on the River Forth, 42 km north-east of Glasgow and 60 km north-west of Edinburgh. It stands where the flatter Lowlands meet the slopes of the Highlands along the Highland Boundary Fault, and for this reason it is called the Gateway to the Highlands. To the west and east stretches the Carse of Stirling, one of the flattest and most productive expanses of farmland in Scotland. Control of the lowest crossing point of the Forth brought military advantage in times of unrest and tolls in peacetime. Stirling remained the river's lowest reliable crossing until the Alloa Swing Bridge was built in 1885.

Stirling's oldest catalogued artefact is a stone cist found in 1879, whose bones were radiocarbon dated to between 2152 and 2021 BCE. Prehistoric carvings of cup and ring marks near King's Park date to about 3000 BCE, and Iron Age forts stand on Gillies Hill. David I created Stirling a royal burgh between 1124 and 1127. The name appears as Strivelin in early sources; scholars once thought it Brittonic, but a survey of 2017 derives it from Gaelic srib-linn, a pool in the river. A 9th-century legend says a wolf's howl woke a sentry when Danish invaders attacked, and the wolf became a symbol of the town.

On 29 July 1567 the infant James VI was anointed King of Scots in the Church of the Holy Rude, and he grew up in Stirling, educated by George Buchanan. James III and his queen, Margaret of Denmark, are buried at Cambuskenneth Abbey; the king died at the Battle of Sauchieburn. The Battle of Stirling was fought in the town on 12 September 1648. The earl of Mar failed to take the castle in 1715, and in January 1746 the army of Bonnie Prince Charlie took the town but not the castle, blowing up the church of St Ninians, where it had stored munitions. Only the tower survives.

Stirling is visually dominated by Stirling Castle, once a principal royal stronghold of the Kingdom of Scotland. It was granted city status in 2002 and is the administrative centre of the Stirling council area. The old town below the castle keeps its cobbled streets and buildings such as Mar's Wark and Argyll's Lodging. The University of Stirling opened in 1967. The custom of Walking the Marches, which inspects the town's boundaries each year, is thought to have begun in the 12th century.
stirrup: The stirrup came late in history, since horses were domesticated in about 4000 BCE and the earliest saddle-like equipment, fringed cloths or pads, was used by Assyrian cavalry around 700 BCE. The earliest hard foot support was a toe loop holding the big toe, used in India late in the 2nd century BCE and possibly as early as 500 BCE. Buddhist carvings at Sanchi, Mathura and the Bhaja caves show horsemen with toes slipped under girths, and the archaeologist John Marshall called the Sanchi relief the earliest example of stirrups by some five centuries.

The solid saddle tree allowed the true stirrup to develop, since without it the rider's weight creates pressure points that make the horse's back sore. Some credit the Sarmatians with the first stirrups.

The earliest extant pair of stirrups was found in the tomb of the Northern Yan noble Feng Sufu, who died in 415, made of mulberry wood gilded with bronze and iron plates. Stirrups are mentioned in Chinese texts by the end of the 4th century, and their appearance coincided with the rise of heavily armoured cavalry, which dominated Chinese warfare until the early Tang dynasty. In Japan the earliest stirrups come from 5th-century tombs.

In Europe, stirrups were adopted more widely by the 8th century, but they were rare in western graves: of 704 eighth-century male burials excavated in Germany by 1967, only 13 had them. In Denmark in the 920s to 980s, under the Jelling kings, many leading men were buried with stirrups, bits and spurs. Accounts of the Empire of Mali also mention stirrups and saddles in its cavalry.

The stirrup has been called one of the most significant inventions in the history of warfare before gunpowder, the third step in equipment after the chariot and the saddle. A rider supported by stirrups was less likely to fall and could deliver a blow with the weight and momentum of horse and rider. Some scholars credit it with the birth of feudalism. Others argue that it gives little advantage in shock warfare and mainly lets a rider lean further to either side, so that it was not the reason for the shift from infantry to cavalry. In the Ottoman and Mughal empires the stirrup became a symbol of the ruler's presence.
stjepan-radic: Stjepan Radić was born in Desno Trebarjevo, near Sisak, in the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia within Austria-Hungary, the ninth of eleven children. Expelled from his gymnasium in Zagreb, he finished school in Karlovac. In 1888 he visited Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer in Đakovo to ask for help with a journey to the Russian Empire, and stayed six weeks at the Monastery of the Caves in Kiev.

He enrolled in law at the University of Zagreb in September 1891. In 1893 he called the Ban of Croatia, Károly Khuen-Héderváry, a "Magyar hussar" and served four months in prison. After students burned the Hungarian tricolour on 16 October 1895, during Emperor Franz Joseph's visit to Zagreb, he was imprisoned again, expelled and barred from every university in the Monarchy. He graduated in 1899 from the École libre des sciences politiques in Paris.

After the First World War Radić opposed merging Croatia with the Kingdom of Serbia without guarantees of Croatian autonomy. On 24 November 1918 he urged delegates not to "rush like geese into fog", and he was the only member of the National Council's central committee to vote against sending a delegation to Belgrade. A resolution he wrote on 8 March 1919 refused to recognise the new kingdom, and he was arrested and held until February 1920.

His party won 50 of 419 seats in the elections of November 1920 and stayed out of parliament, becoming the Croatian Republican Peasant Party. The Vidovdan Constitution passed on 28 June 1921 without it. In March 1923 the party won 70 seats. In 1923 Radić travelled to England, France, Austria and the Soviet Union. After the elections of 1925 his party, renamed the Croatian Peasant Party, struck a power-sharing agreement with the People's Radical Party and recognised the monarchy and the constitution on 27 March 1925. Radić became Minister for Education, resigned in 1926 and in 1927 formed a coalition with Svetozar Pribićević.

On 20 June 1928, in the Assembly, Puniša Račić of the People's Radical Party, a deputy from Montenegro, drew a pistol and shot several opposition deputies, among them Radić, who received a serious stomach wound. He died several weeks later, on 8 August 1928, aged 57. Račić was sentenced to 60 years in prison, reduced at once to 20, and spent most of the term under house arrest in a villa. In January 1929 King Aleksandar abolished the constitution, dissolved parliament and declared a royal dictatorship.

Radić is buried in the Mirogoj Cemetery in Zagreb. His death made him a martyr and an icon for the peasantry and for Croatian patriots, and his image was used by later parties of both left and right. Croatia has awarded the Order of Stjepan Radić since 1995.
stockholm: Stockholm lies on Sweden's east coast at the 59th parallel north, where the freshwater Lake Mälaren flows out into the Baltic Sea. The central parts of the city consist of fourteen islands that continue into the Stockholm archipelago. More than 30% of the city area is waterways and another 30% parks and green spaces. Its position, at the eastern end of the Central Swedish lowland and near the Bergslagen region, reflects the early orientation of Swedish trade toward the Baltic.

The area was settled from the Stone Age, in the 6th millennium BCE. Norse sagas name the location as Agnafit, and Birka, near Stockholm, was one of Sweden's major trade centres in the Viking Age. Numerous runestones were carved in the area because of its importance as a trading hub.

The earliest written mention of the name Stockholm dates from 1252, by which time the mines of Bergslagen had made it an important site in the iron trade.
