Stock means log in Swedish, though it may also connect to an old German word meaning fortification, and holm means islet, probably the islet of Helgeandsholmen. According to Erik's Chronicle the city was founded by Birger Jarl to protect Sweden from sea invasions by Karelians, after the pillage of Sigtuna on Lake Mälaren in the summer of 1187.

The Old Town, Gamla Stan, was built on the central island next to Helgeandsholmen from the mid-13th century onward. The city rose to prominence through the Baltic trade of the Hanseatic League, developing strong economic and cultural links with Lübeck, Hamburg, Gdańsk, Visby, Tallinn and Riga. Research and higher education in the sciences began in the 18th century. Karolinska Institutet was formalised in 1811 and KTH Royal Institute of Technology was founded in 1827. The city hosted the 1912 Summer Olympics, and the Stockholm Metro opened in 1950.

Stockholm is the capital and most populous city of Sweden. Its municipality had 984,748 inhabitants in 2022, with about 1.6 million in the urban area. It is the seat of the government and the Riksdag, and Stockholm Palace is the official residence of the Swedish monarch. The Vasa Museum is the most visited museum in Scandinavia. The Stockholm region has three World Heritage Sites: Drottningholm Palace, Skogskyrkogården and Birka. The Nobel Prize ceremonies and banquet are held in the city each year.
stockholm-bloodbath: The Bloodbath grew from a conflict between pro-unionists, who favoured the Kalmar Union then dominated by Denmark, and anti-unionists, who supported Swedish independence. Sten Sture the Younger headed the anti-unionists and Archbishop Gustav Trolle the pro-unionists. Christian II intervened to help Trolle, who was besieged at Stäket, but was defeated at Vedila and again at Brännkyrka in 1518. In 1520 he returned with a large army of French, German and Scottish mercenaries.

Sture was mortally wounded at the Battle of Bogesund on 19 January 1520. The Riksdag agreed to do homage to Christian on condition of a full amnesty and rule by Swedish law, but his widow, Lady Kristina, continued to resist in Stockholm and was not defeated at Uppsala until Good Friday, 6 April. After a siege of several months Christian offered terms in which he swore that past acts against him would be forgotten, and the city opened its gates.

On 4 November 1520 Archbishop Trolle anointed Christian in Storkyrkan Cathedral, and Christian took the usual oath to rule through native-born Swedes only. A banquet followed for three days. On the evening of 7 November he summoned Swedish leaders to a private conference at the palace, and at dusk on 8 November Danish soldiers entered the great hall and imprisoned noble guests, all of whom were on Trolle's proscription list.

On 9 November a council headed by Trolle sentenced the proscribed to death as heretics, the main charge being that they had united in a pact to depose Trolle a few years before. At noon the bishops of Skara and Strängnäs were beheaded in the great square, followed by fourteen noblemen, three burgomasters, fourteen town councillors and about twenty common citizens of Stockholm. The executions continued the next day, and the chief executioner, Jörgen Homuth, gave the number of dead as 82. Lady Kristina and many other noblewomen were taken as prisoners to Denmark.

Christian justified the killings in a proclamation as necessary to avoid a papal interdict, but in apologising to the Pope for the beheading of the bishops he blamed his troops for unauthorised acts of vengeance. Gustav Vasa, whose father Erik Johansson was among the victims, travelled to Dalarna to raise a new revolt, and the population rallied to him. They defeated Christian's forces in the Swedish War of Liberation.

The massacre became the catalyst that permanently separated Sweden from Denmark, and in Sweden Christian became known as Kristian Tyrann, Christian the Tyrant. Memory of it fed hostility between the two countries that lasted nearly three hundred years.
stoicism: The name derives from the Stoa Poikile, or painted porch, a colonnade decorated with mythic and historical battle scenes on the north side of the Agora in Athens, where Zeno of Citium and his followers gathered near the end of the fourth century BCE. Unlike the Epicureans, Zeno chose to teach in a public space. The philosophy was at first called Zenonism, a name soon dropped, probably because the Stoics did not consider their founders perfectly wise and wished to avoid a cult of personality.

Zeno's ideas developed from those of the Cynics, brought to him by Crates of Thebes, whose founding father, Antisthenes, had been a disciple of Socrates. Zeno also studied under the Megarians. His most influential successor was Chrysippus, who followed Cleanthes as head of the school and moulded what is now called Stoicism. It became the foremost popular philosophy among the educated elite of the Hellenistic world and the Roman Empire.

Stoic philosophy is traditionally divided into logic, physics and ethics. Logic, which included language, grammar, rhetoric and epistemology, was held necessary for understanding ethics. Its smallest unit was the assertible, a proposition that is either true or false. Chrysippus listed five basic argument forms, called indemonstrables, to which all other arguments reduce, and the Stoics studied paradoxes such as the Liar and the Sorites, or Heap. Along with Aristotle's term logic, their propositional logic was one of the two great systems of logic in the classical world.

In physics the universe is a material reasoning substance, logos, with an active part, a primordial fire or intelligent aether, and a passive part, matter. Each human possesses a portion of this divine logos. In ethics the Stoics taught that virtue is the only good and is enough for eudaimonia, a well-lived life, pursued through the four cardinal virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice. Health, wealth and pleasure are neither good nor bad in themselves. For Chrysippus the passions, such as distress, fear, pleasure and lust, are errors of judgement that the wise person avoids.

Stoic logic was discussed alongside Aristotle's for around five hundred years. In late antiquity the school declined, its logical writings did not survive, and only elements reached the Middle Ages through Boethius and later commentators. Knowledge of Stoic logic as a system was lost until the 20th century, when logicians such as Jan Łukasiewicz and Benson Mates reappraised it. Early Christian writers used concepts such as logos, virtue and conscience, and in the late 16th century Justus Lipsius sought in Neostoicism to join Stoicism and Christianity. Albert Ellis and Aaron T. Beck drew on Stoic ideas in cognitive psychotherapy.
stolac: Stolac is a town in Herzegovina, in the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It stands on the tourist route that links the mountainous hinterland of Bosnia with the coast and Dubrovnik, along the road from Sarajevo through Mostar, Stolac, Ljubinje and Trebinje. Its natural setting, climate and hunting grounds attracted settlers from prehistory, and Illyrians, Romans and Slavs all left remains. It is described as one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world.

The area has been settled for at least 15,000 years, according to markings in Badanj Cave that experts have dated to between 12,000 and 16,000 BCE. The mainstream view holds that Daorson is 2,500 years old, though some geological studies place the ruins beneath the site at 7,000 years. Three kilometres west of the town lies the Radimlja necropolis of stećak tombstones, dating from the 15th and 16th centuries. They are carved with epitaphs, portraits of the dead, and motifs such as grapevines, hunting scenes and wild animals, and five of them are thought to mark the graves of members of the Hrabren Miloradović Vlach family.

The historic core of Stolac has nine historical layers, from prehistory through the Illyrian-Roman period, the Middle Ages, the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian periods and the first and second Yugoslavia. The town belonged to four empires, the Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian, and to three kingdoms, and its people held to Christianity, Islam and Judaism. During the Yugoslav Wars a number of monuments were demolished by Croat extremists as part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, including the town's four mosques, which dated from the 16th to 18th centuries, and the Orthodox Church of the Holy Assumption of Christ.

In 2003 the Commission to Preserve National Monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina designated Stolac Old Town a National Monument, allowing only research, conservation and restoration. A dispute followed over a series of crosses, the Way of the Cross, built within the old town from the war years onward, which the Commission and the Federation Ministry for Spatial Planning objected to. After the Dayton peace treaty the territory of the 1991 municipality was divided between Stolac and the new municipality of Berkovići in Republika Srpska, where most of the Bosnian Serbs from Stolac now live. A road of 36 kilometres linking Stolac with Neum was completed in 2022.
ston: Ston lies at the south of the isthmus of the Pelješac peninsula, in Dubrovnik-Neretva County. Its position at the gates of the peninsula, surrounded by three seas and protected by four hills, with fresh water and salt water and fertile plains, made it an important political, cultural and ecclesiastical centre. It was first an Illyrian settlement, until the Romans established a colony there in 167 BCE.

In the 6th century a diocese of Sarsenterum was set up for the Zachlumia area, and Ston was spared when the Avars destroyed Sarsenterum. After the arrival of the South Slavs in the 7th century the area formed the principality of Zachlumia, whose rulers acknowledged Byzantine supremacy. The diocese of Ston is first mentioned in 877. In 1120 it became a suffragan of the Archdiocese of Ragusa.

About 1219 Saint Sava of Serbia founded a monastery at Ston as the seat of the Eparchy of Hum. The old town was demolished by an earthquake in 1252, and the Republic of Ragusa later built a new town on the present site. Zachlumia passed in turn to Hungary, the Šubić family, and in 1325 to the medieval Bosnian state.

Ragusa bought Pelješac with Ston from the rulers of Serbia and Bosnia in 1333, in return for the tribute of Ston, and in that year began the planned building of Ston and Little Ston with walls between them to defend the peninsula. The saltworks gave the Republic 15,900 ducats a year. The walls, among the longest in Europe, were shaped over four centuries as weapons developed.

Between 1461 and 1464 the Florentine architect Michelozzo directed work on the Great Wall, which is 1,200 metres long. About half a kilometre fell in the earthquake of 1667. In the 19th century the walls of Little Ston were pulled down to suppress malaria, and stones from the complex were quarried for new buildings.

The 2021 census counted 2,491 people in the municipality, with 500 in the town itself. Restoration of the fortifications resumed after 1945, and the walls were damaged again in the Croatian War of Independence and the earthquake of 1996. Reconstruction of the Great Wall was completed in 2009, and part of the wall is open to visitors. The church of St Michael on the hill is the only one of the early Christian churches of old Ston that still stands.
stone-of-scone: The Stone of Scone is an oblong block of red sandstone, measuring 66 by 43 by 27 centimetres and weighing about 152 kilograms. A cross is roughly incised on one surface, and an iron ring at each end helps with transport. Geologists have found that it is a lower Old Red Sandstone quarried near Scone. Its first recorded use was at the coronation of Alexander III of Scotland in 1249, and it was kept at Scone Abbey, near Perth.

Legends place its origin elsewhere. One story has Fergus, son of Erc, the first King of the Scots, bring it from Ireland to Argyll, and some versions identify it with the Lia Fáil of Tara. Other traditions identify it with the Stone of Jacob, taken from Bethel and carried to Ireland by the prophet Jeremiah.

In 1296, during the First Scottish War of Independence, Edward I of England took the stone to Westminster Abbey as spoils of war. It was fitted into a wooden chair, the Coronation Chair, on which most later English and British sovereigns have been crowned. Edward sought the status of Lord Paramount of Scotland, with the right to oversee its king.

The Treaty of Northampton of 1328 provided for the stone's return, but rioting crowds prevented its removal from the abbey. When James VI of Scotland became James I of England he was crowned on it. Some have doubted that Edward took the real stone, and the Westminster Stone theory holds that the monks of Scone hid it in the River Tay or on Dunsinane Hill and tricked the English with a substitute.

On 11 June 1914 suffragettes of the Women's Social and Political Union placed a bomb beside the chair; it broke the stone in half, though this was not discovered until 1950. During the Second World War the chair went to Gloucester Cathedral and the stone was hidden in a vault beneath the abbey. On Christmas Day 1950 four Scottish students removed it, and it broke in two. It was left at Arbroath Abbey on 11 April 1951 and returned to Westminster.

On 3 July 1996 the British Government announced the stone's return. It reached Edinburgh Castle on 15 November 1996, and a handover ceremony took place on 30 November, St Andrew's Day. Since March 2024 it has been on permanent display in Perth Museum.
storming-of-the-bastille: France faced a major economic crisis in the late 1780s, caused partly by the cost of intervening in the American Revolution and made worse by regressive taxes and poor harvests. On 17 June 1789 the Third Estate reconstituted itself as the National Assembly. On 11 July Louis XVI dismissed and banished the finance minister Jacques Necker, who had been sympathetic to it. News reached Paris on 12 July, and Parisians presumed a coup was starting, the more so as royal troops, about half of them foreign regiments, were concentrated round Versailles and Paris. Camille Desmoulins rallied a crowd at the Palais-Royal, and crowds plundered places where food and arms might be kept.

On 13 July the electors of Paris agreed to raise a militia of 48,000 men, which the Marquis de Lafayette took over as the National Guard. The people seized weapons at the Hôtel des Invalides but found no powder. The commandant had moved 250 barrels of gunpowder to the Bastille, a medieval fortress that held only seven prisoners and was already scheduled to be replaced by an open public space. Its garrison of 82 veteran soldiers had been reinforced by 32 Swiss grenadiers, under the governor Bernard-René de Launay.

On 14 July a crowd of probably fewer than a thousand gathered outside and demanded the arms and powder. Negotiations dragged on, and at about 1:30 pm the crowd surged into the outer courtyard. Shooting began, apparently spontaneously, and mutinous French Guards with two cannons joined the attackers after 3:00 pm. Royal troops on the Champ de Mars did not intervene. De Launay surrendered at 5:30 pm. He was dragged towards the Hôtel de Ville and killed on the way, as were several of his garrison.

On 15 July Louis XVI backed down, sent the royal troops back to their frontier garrisons and announced that he would recall Necker. Nobles began to leave France, among them the Count of Artois, and the news set off the Great Fear in the countryside between 20 July and 5 August. The contractor Pierre-François Palloy demolished the Bastille within five months. In 1790 Lafayette sent its key to George Washington, and it is displayed at Mount Vernon.

Historians such as Ian Davidson argue that the king's surrender to the Third Estate has a better claim than the storming to be the founding event of the Revolution, but the fall of the Bastille was the first major intervention of ordinary Parisians. The fortress served the revolutionaries as a symbol of royal tyranny, and 14 July is France's national holiday.
storting: The parliament in its present form was first constituted at Eidsvoll in 1814, but its origins reach back to the allting of the 9th century, a type of thing, or common assembly of free men in Germanic societies, which met at a thingstead under lawspeakers. Such assemblies were gradually formalised and gained the backing and authority of the Crown. As oral laws were codified and Norway unified in the 10th century, lagtings, or law things, became superior regional assemblies.

In the mid-13th century the regional assemblies, the Frostating, Gulating, Eidsivating and Borgarting, were amalgamated and the law set down under King Magnus the Lawmender. This jurisdiction remained significant until Frederick III proclaimed absolute monarchy in 1660, ratified by the King Act of 1665, which became the constitution of the Union of Denmark and Norway until 1814.

The Storting has always been de facto unicameral, but until a constitutional amendment of 2009 it was de jure bicameral. After an election it elected a quarter of its members to form the Lagting, a revising chamber, and the other three quarters made up the Odelsting. The Lagting's composition came to follow the Odelsting's so closely that passing a bill in it was mostly a formality. Parliamentarianism was established in 1884. The Storting building in Oslo has been in use since 5 March 1866.

On 27 June 1940, during the German occupation, the presidium signed an appeal to King Haakon VII asking him to abdicate. In September 1940 the representatives voted 92 to 53 in favour of the results of negotiations between the presidium and the German occupation authority, but directives from Adolf Hitler obstructed the agreement. The number of seats has varied, from 114 in 1882 to 150 in 1921 and 169 since 2005.

The Storting is elected every four years by party-list proportional representation, a system adopted in 1919 in place of single-member districts. It always serves its full term, as the constitution does not allow snap elections. A bill goes through a standing committee and up to three readings, then to the King in Council for royal assent. Articles 77-79 of the constitution let the king withhold assent, a right no Norwegian monarch has used since the union with Sweden ended in 1905.

The assembly is led by a president and five vice presidents, who form the presidium. Parliament appoints the Office of the Auditor General and the Parliamentary Ombudsman, as well as the five members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee that awards the Nobel Peace Prize.
strabo: Strabo was born around 64 BCE into an affluent family of Amaseia in Pontus whose members had been involved in politics since the reign of Mithridates V. His paternal grandfather served Mithridates VI in the Mithridatic Wars and, as the war drew to a close, turned several Pontic fortresses over to the Romans. Strabo studied rhetoric at Nysa under Aristodemus and came to admire Homer. About the age of 21 he moved to Rome in 44 BCE and stayed until at least 31 BCE, studying philosophy under the Peripatetic Xenarchus and the Stoic Athenodorus Cananites, and grammar under Tyrannion of Amisus, a respected authority on geography.

Strabo's life was marked by travel, made easier by the relative peace of the reign of Augustus. He went to Egypt and Kush, west to the coast of Tuscany and south to Ethiopia, besides Asia Minor and Rome. Around 25 BCE he sailed up the Nile as far as Philae. His first major work, the Historical Sketches, written in Rome around 20 BCE to cover the history of the known world from the Roman conquest of Greece, is almost entirely lost.

The date of the Geography is uncertain. Its finished version belongs to the reign of Tiberius, and its latest datable passage mentions the recent death of Juba II of Mauretania in 23 CE. Strabo is thought to have stopped writing that year or the next and to have died about 24 CE.

The Geography is an encyclopaedic account of the political, economic, social, cultural and geographical character of almost all of Europe and the Mediterranean, from Britain and Ireland to Central Asia and North Africa. Strabo cited the astronomers Eratosthenes and Hipparchus but held that a descriptive approach was more practical for statesmen, who cared more for the character of countries than for numbers. It is the only surviving work to describe both Greek and Roman peoples and countries under Augustus.

The Geography was rarely used by contemporary writers, but copies survived in the Byzantine Empire. The first printed edition appeared in Venice in 1516, and Isaac Casaubon produced the first critical edition in 1587.
strait-of-gibraltar: The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea and separates Europe from Africa. At its narrowest point the two continents are 7.7 nautical miles (14.3 km) apart, and ferries cross in as little as 35 minutes. The depth ranges between 300 and 900 metres.

Water flows through the strait in both directions. Surface water of lower salinity moves eastwards into the Mediterranean, while a smaller flow of deeper, saltier water moves westwards into the Atlantic. The Camarinal Sill, the shallowest point at the western end, limits the mixing of the two. Around 5.97 million years ago the connection between the two seas was progressively closed, causing the Messinian salinity crisis, and about 5.33 million years ago the Zanclean flood reopened it.

Evidence of Neanderthal habitation in the area dates back 125,000 years. The short distance between the shores made the strait a quick crossing point for Carthaginians campaigning against Rome, Romans travelling between Hispania and Mauritania, Vandals moving into North Africa in the 5th century, Moors and Berbers from the 8th to the 11th centuries, and Spain and Portugal in the 16th century.

The name comes from the Rock of Gibraltar, from the Arabic Jabal Ṭāriq, Tariq's Mount, named after Tariq ibn Ziyad. In antiquity the flanking mountains were the Pillars of Hercules, and the Romans called the passage Fretum Gaditanum. After the last Muslim government north of the strait was overthrown by a Spanish force in 1492, the strait came to separate two distinct cultures that had shared much since the 8th century: Christian-European culture and the Spanish language to the north, Muslim-Arabic culture and the Arabic language to the south.

Gibraltar was ceded to Britain in the Peace of Utrecht. In the Second World War German U-boats used the currents to slip into the Mediterranean, and between September 1941 and May 1944 Germany sent 62 of them through.

The strait lies in the territorial waters of Morocco, Spain and the British overseas territory of Gibraltar. Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, vessels and aircraft pass through it under the regime of transit passage. It remains an important shipping route, and ferries run between Spain and Morocco. Spain and Morocco have discussed an undersea rail tunnel since the 1980s. The strait is also an Important Bird Area, used by hundreds of thousands of seabirds each year, and a pod of about 36 orcas lives there.
strait-of-malacca: The strait is a narrow stretch of water about 900 km long and from 65 to 250 km wide, running between the Malay Peninsula to the northeast and the Indonesian island of Sumatra to the southwest. It connects the Andaman Sea, part of the Indian Ocean, with the South China Sea. At the Phillip Channel, close to southern Singapore, it narrows to only 2.8 km. According to historical lore, the name comes from the city of Malacca, whose founder Parameswara, a Sumatran prince, named it after a tree under which he had rested.

Early traders from Arabia, Africa, India and Persia reached Kedah on the Malay Peninsula before travelling on to Guangzhou. They sailed on the monsoon winds between June and November and returned between December and May, and goods were carried overland to eastern ports such as Langkasuka and Kelantan. Kedah and Funan were prominent ports in the 6th century, before shipping began to use the strait itself.

In the 7th century the maritime empire of Srivijaya, based in Palembang in Sumatra, rose to power and gained effective control of two choke points of maritime Southeast Asia, the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait. Through conquests and raids on rival ports on both sides it kept its economic and military domination for about 700 years, profiting from the spice trade, the tributary trade system with China and trade with Indian and Arab merchants. The strait later remained central under the Malacca Sultanate of the 15th century, the Johor Sultanate, the British Straits Settlements and the city-state of Singapore.

Since the 17th century the strait has been the main shipping channel between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, and it is part of the Maritime Silk Road. The Sunda Strait to the east is shallower and narrower, so ships larger than the Malaccamax, the largest vessel that can pass the Malacca strait, use other routes. Piracy has been a problem, especially in the 2000s; regional navies stepped up patrols in July 2004, and Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand cooperate in joint naval patrols.
straits-settlements: The first settlement was Penang, taken in 1786 as the Prince of Wales Island; a strip of the mainland later became Province Wellesley, now Seberang Perai. Singapore became a British trading post in 1819, after Stamford Raffles involved the East India Company in a dynastic struggle for the throne of Johor.

The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 divided the Malay Archipelago into a British zone in the north and a Dutch zone in the south: the Dutch colony of Malacca passed to Britain in exchange for Bencoolen on Sumatra, and the Dutch conceded any rights to Singapore. The Dindings, comprising Pangkor Island and Lumut, were added by the Pangkor Treaty of 1874 and returned to Perak in February 1935.

Under the East India Company the capital was moved from George Town in Penang to Singapore in 1832. The scattered settlements were costly to administer once the Company lost its monopoly of the China trade in 1833, and they served as penal settlements for Indian civilian and military prisoners, earning the title Botany Bays of India. Convicts rose in minor uprisings in Singapore and Penang in 1852 and 1853. In 1857 the European population petitioned Parliament for direct rule, but the Indian Rebellion overtook the idea. The settlements came under the British Raj in 1858.

On 1 April 1867 they were transferred to the Colonial Office and became a Crown colony, answerable to London rather than Calcutta. Letters patent of 4 February 1867 gave a constitution in which the governor ruled with an Executive Council of officials and a Legislative Council of official and nominated members. The governor was also High Commissioner for the Federated Malay States and for British North Borneo, Brunei and Sarawak. The Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Christmas Island were added in 1886, and Labuan in 1907. The population was 306,775 in 1871 and 572,249 in 1901, growing mainly through Chinese and Indian immigration.

Japanese forces landed in Kelantan on 8 December 1941. Penang fell on 16 December, Malacca on 15 January 1942 and Singapore on 15 February, and the occupation lasted until August 1945. The colony was dissolved on 1 April 1946: Singapore became a separate Crown colony and later an independent republic, Penang and Malacca joined the Malayan Union, and Labuan was attached to North Borneo. Most of the former territories now form part of Malaysia, from which Singapore separated in 1965.
stralsund: In the Middle Ages the area formed part of the Principality of Rügen, a Danish vassal principality ruled by a local West Slavic dynasty. In the course of German settlement many settlers and merchants came to the Strale settlement, and Prince Wizlaw I of Rügen granted Lübeck law to the town in 1234. The town's success challenged Lübeck, which burned Stralsund down in 1249; it was rebuilt with a wall with 11 gates and 30 watchtowers. It joined the Hanseatic League in 1293, and in the 14th century 300 ships flew its flag in the Baltic. In 1325 the principality became part of the Duchy of Pomerania, though Stralsund kept considerable independence.

In 1628, during the Thirty Years' War, Imperial forces under Albrecht von Wallenstein besieged the city after the council refused the Capitulation of Franzburg. Stralsund resisted with Danish and Swedish support. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 made it part of Swedish Pomerania. It was lost to Brandenburg in 1678 and returned to Sweden in 1679. In the Great Northern War Charles XII led the defence of the city for a year in 1715, and Swedish control lasted until Napoleon's army occupied it in 1807. The Congress of Vienna gave it to Prussia in 1815. Allied bombing in 1944 killed some 800 people and destroyed about 8,000 dwellings, and the Red Army occupied the city on 28 April 1945.

Stralsund is a port city in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Strelasund opposite the island of Rügen, to which the Strelasund Crossing connects it. In 2002 its old town and that of Wismar were listed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites as the Historic Centres of Stralsund and Wismar, for their Brick Gothic buildings and their importance in the Hanseatic period and under Sweden. They include the Gothic city hall, St Nicholas' Church, built in 1270–1360, and St Mary's Church, built in 1383–1473, whose octagonal tower is 104 metres high.
strandzha: Strandzha is a mountain massif of about 10,000 square kilometres in the south-east of the Balkans, between the plains of Thrace to the west, the lowlands near Burgas to the north and the Black Sea to the east. Its highest peak, Mahya Dağı, rises to 1,031 metres in Turkey; the highest point on Bulgarian territory is Golyamo Gradishte at 710 metres.

The Veleka and the border river Rezovska are its main rivers. The climate is shaped by the Black Sea, humid continental in the mountains and humid subtropical on the coast. Its plant communities developed before the Bosporus separated Europe from Asia, and since ice never reached the massif in the Pleistocene, plants of the Tertiary period survive there.

In antiquity Strandzha was inhabited by the Thracians, and it holds a large concentration of ruins of Thracian sanctuaries, sacrificial altars and dolmens. The Preobrazhenie Uprising of 1903 against Ottoman rule was crushed by Ottoman troops. After the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 the south-eastern part of the massif became part of Turkey and the northern part part of Bulgaria. Thracian Bulgarians were expelled in 1913, and Muslims from Bulgaria were settled in the Turkish part. In the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, Greeks were expelled to Greece and Muslims from Greece settled there, as did Muslim immigrants from former Yugoslavia.

Strandzha Nature Park, created in 1995 in the Bulgarian part, covers 1,161 square kilometres, the largest protected area in Bulgaria, and the İğneada Floodplain Forests National Park was established in 2007 on the Turkish side. The Bulgarian villages, among them Malko Tarnovo and Brashlyan, are known for their architecture and for rituals such as nestinarstvo, barefoot dancing on live embers, which preserve pagan elements. The Turkish part is known for charcoal burning, goat farming and cheesemaking.
strategos: Strategos, plural strategoi, is a compound of the Greek stratos, army, and agos, leader. In Classical Athens the office existed already in the 6th century BCE but took its best known form with the reforms of Cleisthenes in 501 BCE, which set up a board of ten strategoi elected annually, one from each tribe, in place of the polemarchos as senior commander.

At the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE they decided strategy by majority vote, according to Herodotus. In the early 5th century many combined military and political roles, among them Themistocles, Cimon and Pericles, though their power came from personal charisma. Athenians watched them closely: Pericles was removed from office and fined in 430 BCE, and six of the eight strategoi at Arginusae in 406 BCE were removed and condemned to death.

Philip II of Macedon was elected strategos autokrator, with full powers, of the Hellenic League, and his son Alexander the Great succeeded him in the post. In the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues the annually elected strategos was both chief of civil government and supreme military commander; Aratus of Sicyon and Philopoemen of Megalopolis were repeatedly re-elected in the Achaean League. In Ptolemaic Egypt the strategoi at first commanded Greek military colonists but by the time of Ptolemy II Philadelphus were heads of provincial administration, and Ptolemy V Epiphanes created the office of epistrategos to oversee them.

In the Byzantine Empire the strategos at first rendered the Latin magister militum. With the theme system of the 7th century the strategoi combined military command with civil government of a theme, and in the 8th century they often rebelled against the emperor. The themes were split up and the strategoi multiplied, from 18 around 842 to almost 90 in the Escorial Taktikon of about 971 to 975. By the 13th century the word meant simply a general.

Greek historians used strategos for the Roman praetor, and the Acts of the Apostles uses it for the magistrates of Philippi. In the Kingdom of Sicily the strategus was a local governor commanding the militia. In the modern Hellenic Army stratigós is the highest officer rank, and most other Greek general ranks derive from the word.
straubing: The area around Straubing has been continuously settled since the Neolithic. The Romans conquered it in 16 to 14 BCE and held it for about 400 years. They called it Sorviodurum, and it was an important military support base. The Roman treasure excavated in 1950 is shown in the Gäubodenmuseum. After the Roman Empire fell, the Bavarii settled mostly around St. Peter's Church, between the Allachbach and the Danube, and named the settlement after their leader Strupinga, from which Straubing evolved.

Duke Ludwig I of Bavaria founded a new town beside the old one in 1218, and it is still the centre of Straubing. When Bavaria was divided among the sons of the Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV, Straubing became the capital of the Duchy of Bavaria-Straubing under Duke Wilhelm I. Duke Albert I began the ducal castle in 1356, and the Gothic city tower was begun in 1316. The duchy later passed to Ernest, Duke of Bavaria-Munich, who ordered the murder of Agnes Bernauer in Straubing. Her grave cannot be found, but Ernest built a chapel in the graveyard of St. Peter's. The Swedish army besieged and took the city in 1633, during the Thirty Years' War.

Straubing is an independent city in Lower Bavaria and the seat of the district of Straubing-Bogen. It was one of five ducal residences of medieval Bavaria, with Landshut, Munich, Ingolstadt and Burghausen, and its old town has many Gothic buildings. They include the Gothic Basilica of St. Jacob, whose present church was begun in 1393 to plans by Hans von Burghausen, and the Romanesque Church of St. Peter of the 12th century. The Carmelite monastery was the only one to survive the dissolution of 1802. Each August the town holds the Gäubodenvolksfest, the second largest fair in Bavaria.
strength-through-joy: Strength Through Joy, in German Kraft durch Freude or KdF, was announced by Robert Ley on 27 November 1933 as part of the German Labour Front. Its aim was to give Germans access to leisure once reserved for the privileged, such as cruises and car ownership. The government feared that rising wages would slow rearmament, and so chose to raise living standards in other ways and win support for Nazism, paying for the programme with deductions from workers' wages. It hoped to bridge class divisions and build a Volksgemeinschaft, or people's community, with a population fit for work and military service.

KdF had departments for sports, adult education, leisure time, folklore and homeland, and travel, hiking and holidays. The last, headed by Bodo Lafferentz, was the largest and most profitable. A further department, Beauty of Labour, improved workplaces through toilets, washing rooms, better air and less noise, and by 1938 had improved the conditions of 34,000 workplaces, largely through unpaid overtime. The Leisure Time Office offered discounted theatre and concert tickets, with film buses and mobile stages in rural areas.

Official statistics gave 2.3 million KdF holidaymakers in 1934 and 10.3 million in 1938, and by 1939 it was the world's largest tourism operator. Cruises were its best-known offering. Six large ships, among them the Wilhelm Gustloff, were built for KdF and six more chartered, with trips to Norway, Spain, Portugal and Italy. Most cruise passengers came from the middle class rather than the working class. The government planted spies on the ships to watch the passengers' behaviour. Some KdF travellers complained of poor conditions and regimented schedules, while many on domestic trips were enthusiastic, especially those who had never travelled before.

After the outbreak of war in 1939 most programmes were suspended, and projects such as the Prora holiday resort were never completed. By then KdF had sold more than 45 million package tours and excursions, including over 700,000 sea voyages. It turned to troop entertainment, staging over 300,000 performances by the end of 1941, including for SS guards in concentration camps. Its car, the KdF-Wagen, was meant to sell for 1,000 Reichsmarks or less through a stamp-savings scheme. No private buyer received one before the war ended, and the factory at Fallersleben turned to military vehicles. The car later became the Volkswagen Beetle.
strzelce-opolskie: Strzelce Opolskie, in Silesian Wielge Strzelce and in German Groß Strehlitz, is a town in the Opole Voivodeship of southern Poland and the capital of Strzelce County. The name is Polish in origin and comes from the old Polish word strzelec, meaning hunter or archer. The town lies on the major rail line joining Gliwice and Opole, and on National Road 94. A branch line to Kędzierzyn Koźle closed in 1999.

The settlement is mentioned in documents of the 13th century, when it formed part of the Piast-ruled Kingdom of Poland, and it probably received town rights in that century. Local dukes of the Piast dynasty built a castle in the town. It was annexed by Prussia in the 18th century and from 1871 until 1945 formed part of Germany. The German census of 1890 counted 5,112 inhabitants, 500 of them Poles, or 9.8 per cent. When a local branch of the Polish Sokół movement was founded in 1904, the German authorities at first refused to register it and threatened expulsion from the town, and two of its founders lost their jobs at the sewerage company. Twelve workers resigned in solidarity.

In the Upper Silesia plebiscite of 1921, 85.7 per cent of the votes in Groß Strehlitz favoured remaining in Germany, while the neighbouring places of Nowa Wieś, Mokre Łany and Adamowice voted 69.7, 59.9 and 59.2 per cent to join Poland. A secret Sicherheitsdienst report of 1934 named the town one of the main centres of the Polish movement in western Upper Silesia, and Polish activists were persecuted intensively from 1937. In April and May 1939 German militants attacked Polish actors and the Polish bank's theatre hall, and in August and September the Germans arrested prominent local Poles.

During World War II the Germans ran a detention centre for forced labour, a subcamp of the Stalag VIII-B/344 prisoner-of-war camp at the lime quarry and a forced labour camp for Jews. Many prisoners died of exhaustion or starvation, among them Poles arrested for rescuing Jews. In 1945 the town again became part of Poland.

The town had 17,900 inhabitants in 2019. It is one of the biggest centres of the German minority in Poland. Its football club is Piast Strzelce Opolskie, with men's and women's sections. The linguist and Albanologist Gustav Meyer, born in 1850, and the politician Erich Mende, born in 1916, were natives of the town.
stuart-restoration: Richard Cromwell, Lord Protector from 1658 to 1659, ceded power to the Rump Parliament, and for a year government was dominated by the army leaders Charles Fleetwood and John Lambert. On 20 October 1659 George Monck, governor of Scotland under the Cromwells, marched south to oppose them. Lambert's army melted away and Monck reached London unopposed. The Presbyterian members excluded in Pride's Purge of 1648 were recalled, and on 24 December the Long Parliament was restored.

On 4 April 1660 Charles issued the Declaration of Breda, setting out his promises on recovering the crown. Monck organised the Convention Parliament, which first met on 25 April and on 8 May proclaimed that Charles II had been lawful king since the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1649. Charles left The Hague on 23 May, landed at Dover on 25 May and entered London on 29 May, his thirtieth birthday, a date kept afterwards as the holiday of Oak Apple Day. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1661.

The Indemnity and Oblivion Act, law from 29 August 1660, pardoned past treason but excluded those involved in the trial and execution of Charles I. In October 1660 ten men were hanged, drawn and quartered in London, among them Thomas Harrison and the preacher Hugh Peters; three more followed on 19 April 1662, and a further 19 were imprisoned for life. In January 1661 the corpses of Oliver Cromwell, Henry Ireton and John Bradshaw were exhumed and hanged in chains at Tyburn.

The Cavalier Parliament, overwhelmingly royalist, met on 8 May 1661 and sat until 24 January 1679. The leading minister of the first years was Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon, and the Church of England was restored as the national church, backed by the Clarendon Code and the Act of Uniformity 1662. In Scotland the Rescissory Act 1661 annulled all legislation back to 1633; in Ireland the union of the Commonwealth years was treated as void, and James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, returned as Lord Lieutenant in 1662.

The colonies followed at different speeds. Barbados declared for the king in July 1660, Rhode Island in October 1660 and Massachusetts last, in August 1661; New Haven, which sheltered three regicides, was merged into Connecticut in 1662. The period is commonly taken to end with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, when William of Orange landed on 5 November and James II fled to France, and with the Bill of Rights 1689.
studenica-monastery: Studenica Monastery lies 39 kilometres south-west of Kraljevo in central Serbia. It is dedicated to the Presentation of the Holy Virgin and is described as the mother church of all Serbian temples. Serbia's state authorities declared it a Monument of Culture of Exceptional Importance in 1979, and UNESCO placed it on the World Heritage list in 1986, describing it as the largest and richest of Serbia's Orthodox monasteries. Its two principal monuments, the Church of the Virgin and the Church of the King, are both built of white marble.

The monastery was built over a long period. The first stage of works was complete by the spring of 1196, when Stefan Nemanja abdicated and took monastic vows there. When he later left for Hilandar, his son and successor Stefan took over the care of Studenica. Nemanja died at Hilandar in 1199, and his third son Rastko, Saint Sava, moved his relics to Studenica after reconciling with his brothers Stefan and Vukan. Under Sava's guardianship Studenica became the political, cultural and spiritual centre of medieval Serbia.

The Nemanjić dynasty continued to care for it. King Radoslav added a narthex to the church in 1235, and King Milutin built the church of Saints Joachim and Anna, known as the King's Church, in 1314. After the fall of the last of the medieval Serbian states in 1459 the Turks often assaulted the monastery. The Church of the Virgin was repainted in 1569, and in the early 17th century an earthquake and a fire destroyed historical documents and a significant part of its artistic heritage.

The Church of the Virgin is a domed single-nave basilica faced with slabs of white marble. Externally it reconciles the Romanesque and Byzantine styles, and the blending of the two produced the style known as the Raška School. Four portals carry the sculpture, above all the west portal, whose tympanum bears an inscription in Serbian lettering; the masons probably came from the Adriatic region, perhaps from Kotor. Its frescoes date from the first decade of the 13th century, the Crucifixion on a blue background from 1209. Stefan Nemanja and Stefan Radoslav of Serbia are buried at Studenica.
stuttgart: Stuttgart lies on the Neckar in a fertile valley known as the Stuttgarter Kessel, the Stuttgart Cauldron, about an hour from the Swabian Jura and the Black Forest. The city spreads across hills, some covered in vineyards, valleys and parks, and it is the only city in Germany where wine grapes are grown within the urban area. Its name comes from the Old High German Stuotgarten, a stud farm, since Duke Liudolf of Swabia founded the place in 950 to breed warhorses.

The area has been farmed since the seventh millennium BCE. The Romans took it in 83 and built a large fort, the Cannstatt Castrum, about 90 CE, to protect the vineyards and the road from Mainz to Augsburg. Stuttgart was long overshadowed by nearby Bad Cannstatt but received a charter in 1320. The House of Württemberg made it the capital of their county, duchy and kingdom from the 15th century until 1918, and Eberhard I became the first Duke of Württemberg in 1495. Württemberg has been predominantly Protestant since 1534. The Kingdom of Württemberg lasted from 1805 to 1918, and King Wilhelm I and Queen Catherine introduced the first Cannstatter Volksfest in 1818 to ease the famine that followed the Year Without Summer.

King Wilhelm II abdicated on 30 November 1918, and in 1920 the German national government briefly sat in Stuttgart after fleeing Berlin during the Kapp Putsch. Allied air raids in the Second World War struck the city and its car production. French forces captured it on 21 April 1945 and stayed until 8 July, a presence that led to what became known as the Stuttgart Crisis. Stuttgart then served as capital of Württemberg-Baden until 1952.

Stuttgart is the capital and largest city of Baden-Württemberg, with about 630,000 inhabitants. It is known as the cradle of the automobile, since Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach industrialised the automobile there in 1887, and Mercedes-Benz and Porsche have their headquarters there. The State Theatre, the State Gallery and the Stuttgart Ballet are among its cultural institutions, and the Schlossplatz is its main square. The first Waldorf School was founded in the city in 1919.
styria: Styria, in German Steiermark, is geographically diverse. The northern and north-western parts, known as Upper Styria, are mountainous and include parts of the Northern Limestone Alps and the Central Eastern Alps, with valleys formed by the Mur, Mürz, Enns and Salza rivers. The central and southern parts include the Graz Basin, hill country, vineyards and thermal-spring regions. Its extensive forests earned it the name Green Heart of Austria, and it is also called the Green March and, for its long heritage of manufacturing and engineering, the Iron Margraviate. The March took its name from Steyr, the seat of the Otakar dynasty, in what is now Upper Austria.

Celtic tribes inhabited the area. After the Roman conquest the east of what is now Styria belonged to Pannonia and the west to Noricum. Visigoths, Huns, Ostrogoths, Rugii and Lombards conquered or crossed it, Slavs under Avar domination settled the valleys around 600, and Bavarians under Frankish domination expanded southward and eastward and absorbed the Slavic population. Under the Otakar dynasty Styria became a margraviate in 1056 and in 1180 was separated from the Duchy of Carinthia to become a duchy of its own. Under the Georgenberg Pact the Austrian Duke Leopold V also became Duke of Styria in 1192.

After the Babenberg dynasty ended, Styria came briefly under Hungary and later Bohemia, losing vast parts of its territory, including the former capital Steyr and Pitten. The Habsburgs reunified Austria in 1282 and Pitten returned to Styria until Austria finally annexed it in the 16th century. Styria formed the central part of Inner Austria with Carinthia and Carniola. Ottoman raids from the 15th to the 17th century caused severe devastation and depopulation. Archduke John of Austria, the so-called Styrian Prince, advanced its economy between 1809 and 1859.

After the First World War the duchy was partitioned broadly along ethnic lines, the south, including Maribor, Celje and Ptuj, passing to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and later Yugoslavia. This region, traditionally called Lower Styria, now belongs to Slovenia.

Styria is a state of Austria in the south-east, bordering Slovenia to the south. Its capital and largest city is Graz. It is one of Austria's major industrial and research regions, with mining, iron and steel in Upper Styria and wine, fruit growing and spas in the south and east.
su-nuraxi: Su Nuraxi is a Nuragic archaeological site at Barumini in Sardinia, Italy. The complex has a central tower, to which four corner towers were added in the Late Bronze Age. The four towers were joined by a curtain wall with an upper balcony, which no longer stands, and all communicated with an inner courtyard served by a well. In the Iron Age the whole complex was surrounded by a further curtain wall with seven lobes. The nuraghe and the village were strategically connected to other nuraghes, such as the polylobate nuraghe beneath the fifteenth-century Palazzo Zapata in Barumini.

A village was built around the nuraghe in the Late Bronze Age to house the surrounding population, and it was inhabited from the thirteenth to the sixth century BCE. Its huts stood on a circular plan, with large boulders covered by dry stone walls and conical roofs of wood and branches. Their number varied from forty to two hundred over the phases of life in the village, so the population ranged from about 100 to 1,000.

The largest and most complex huts appear to have been reserved for meetings of local leaders, and the one used for the inhabitants' meetings held symbols of the deities worshipped. Other rooms were workshops, kitchens and centres for processing crops. In the 9th and 8th centuries BCE a sewerage system, a paved square and streets were built.

The buildings were destroyed in the 6th century BCE, then restored by Carthage and later occupied by the Romans before being abandoned. The excavations confirmed that the complex remained a vibrant centre until the first century BCE, in the Roman period.

Giovanni Lilliu, a local expert, directed the full excavation between 1950 and 1957, which allowed archaeologists to follow the stages in which the towers and the village were built. It brought to light tools, weapons, pottery and ornaments. The original purpose of the nuraghe is still debated. Lilliu confirmed the traditional reading of it as a fortress.

Other archaeologists think the oldest part had a religious purpose, or served as a refuge, a civil building or even a meeting place or the residence of the village chief, with the towers added later, perhaps for military use and storage. Further finds from the nearby site at Casa Zapata are displayed in its museum.
suakin: Suakin was probably the Limen Evangelis of Ptolemy, a port on a circular island at the end of a long inlet. Al-Hamdani first mentioned it by name in the 10th century and said it was already an ancient town. It was then a small Beja settlement that grew after the port of Badi to its south was abandoned. Venetian merchants were living there by the 14th century. The Mamluk sultan Baybars was angered by one ruler, Ala al-Din al-Asba'ani, who seized the goods of merchants who died at sea nearby, and in 1264 a Mamluk force attacked and drove him out. Ibn Battuta records that in 1332 Suakin had a Muslim sultan, al-Sharif Zaid ibn-Abi Numayy ibn-'Ajlan, the son of a Meccan sharif.

After Mamluk power declined in the late 14th century the Hedareb tribe took the port as their capital, and Suakin became the most important port on the north-east African Red Sea coast. The Portuguese besieged it in 1513 and captured it briefly in 1541. After the Ottoman conquest of Egypt in 1517, Özdemir Pasha occupied Suakin in the early 1550s, and the province of Habesh was established in 1555 with its pasha residing there. The Ottomans restored the Shafi'i and Hanafi mosques and strengthened the fort. Trade nevertheless drifted away as the sea route around Africa opened, and by the early 19th century Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found two-thirds of the houses in ruins.

The Khedive Isma'il received Suakin from the Ottomans in 1865 and built houses, mills, mosques, hospitals and a church for immigrant Copts. British forces were at Suakin in 1883-1885, and Lord Kitchener made it his headquarters. After the defeat of the Mahdist State the British chose to develop the new Port Sudan, about 50 kilometres north, and by 1922 the last of them had left.

The old city was built of coral taken from the sea bed, in houses up to four storeys high with white plaster, large casement windows and doors of Java teak. Because the walls had no protective covering they decayed quickly, and the old city is now in ruins. In 2018 Turkey was granted a 99-year lease over Suakin island to restore the Ottoman port. The 2008 census counted 82,150 people in Suakin.
sub-saharan-africa: Sub-Saharan Africa is the part of the continent south of the Sahara, including the Sahel and Madagascar. It is a non-standardised region: the United Nations definition also takes in countries that lie only partly south of the desert, and the number of countries counted varies with the organisation. Since about 3900 BCE the harsh climate of the Sahara has separated the region from the north, forming an effective barrier interrupted only by the Nile in Sudan, where navigation was blocked by the Sudd and the river's cataracts. Critics have called the term a racist construction that separates Africa, and point to the historical and cultural links and the trade between North, West and East Africa.

Early hominids adopted bipedal locomotion between 10 million and 5 million years ago, when Africa was drying and the savanna spread into forested areas. The Bantu expansion began in West Central Africa, possibly around Cameroon, about 2500 BCE, reached East and Central Africa by 1000 BCE and Southern Africa in the early centuries CE. Evidence of iron-smelting in the Central African Republic and Cameroon may date back to 3,000 to 2,500 BCE, and extensive walled settlements at Zilum in Chad have been dated to the first millennium BCE. Trade and improved agriculture supported early societies such as Sao, Kanem, Bornu, Shilluk, Baguirmi and Wadai.

Nubia, in present-day northern Sudan and southern Egypt, was called Aethiopia by the Greeks and was a major source of gold for the ancient world. It is considered sub-Saharan Africa's oldest urban civilisation, and its people built numerous pyramids. In the south, Bantu-speaking iron-using farmers and herders were present south of the Limpopo by the 4th or 5th century, displacing and absorbing the earlier Khoisan speakers. The earliest ironworks in KwaZulu-Natal are believed to date from around 1050, and the medieval kingdom of Monomotapa, c. 1250–1629, lay between the Zambezi and Limpopo, with its old capital at Great Zimbabwe.

The region had about 1.1 billion inhabitants in 2019 and contains over 1,500 languages. Its principal religions are Christianity, Islam and traditional African religions, and religious syncretism is common. Its rock art is among the oldest and most varied in the world, and the Blombos Cave in South Africa holds the oldest known rock art, dated to 77,000 years ago.
subhas-chandra-bose: Subhas Chandra Bose was born on 23 January 1897 in Cuttack, then part of the Bengal Presidency, the ninth child and sixth son of Prabhabati and Janakinath Bose. His father was a successful lawyer, loyal to the government of British India. Sent to England to take the Indian Civil Service examination, Bose passed the first examination with distinction but declined the final one, citing nationalism as the higher calling. Back in India in July 1921, he met Mahatma Gandhi the same afternoon. They differed on means, since Gandhi held non-violence non-negotiable, and Gandhi sent him to C. R. Das, who launched him into nationalist politics.

Bose worked within the Indian National Congress for nearly 20 years while trying to change its course. In the mid-1930s he travelled in Europe, meeting politicians including Benito Mussolini. In 1938 he became Congress president, standing for unqualified Swaraj, including force against the British, and Gandhi opposed him. He was re-elected in 1939 over Gandhi's preferred candidate Pattabhi Sitaramayya, but the Congress Working Committee turned against him and he resigned.

In January 1941 he escaped from British surveillance in Calcutta and reached Germany through Afghanistan and the Soviet Union. There he founded the Free India Centre in Berlin and created the Indian Legion from Indian prisoners of war. In February 1943 he boarded the submarine U-180, and off Madagascar was transferred to the Japanese I-29. With Japanese support he took over the Indian National Army, and a Provisional Government of Free India was declared on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The Japanese thought him militarily unskilled.

Bose died on 18 August 1945 from third-degree burns after his aeroplane crashed in Japanese-ruled Taiwan. Many of his supporters, especially in Bengal, refused to believe the fact or the circumstances, and conspiracy theories appeared within hours. The British charged 300 INA officers with treason, but backed down in the face of opposition from the Congress.

He is a hero to many Indians, and the title Netaji, Respected Leader, was first applied to him in Germany in early 1942. His legacy is also contested. He preferred a synthesis of socialism and fascism, believed India needed a strong central government with dictatorial powers for some years, and in 1939 refused to support a Congress motion offering Jewish refugees refuge in India.
sublime-porte: The name goes back to an old practice in which a ruler announced his decisions and judgements at the gate of his palace. The Byzantine Empire followed this custom, and the Ottoman sultans adopted it from the time of Orhan I. The palace of the sultan, or the gate leading to it, therefore came to be called the High Gate. The name referred first to a palace in Bursa. After the Ottomans conquered Constantinople, the gate now known as the Imperial Gate, which led to the outermost courtyard of the Topkapı Palace, became known as the High Gate or Sublime Porte.

When Sultan Suleiman sealed an alliance with King Francis I of France in 1536, the French diplomats walked through the monumental gate, then called Bâb-ı Âlî, to reach the Vizierate of Constantinople, the seat of the sultan's government. French was the language of diplomacy, and its translation, Sublime Porte, was soon adopted in most other European languages, English among them. It was used not only for the gate but as a metonymy for the Ottoman Empire.

In the 18th century a large Italian-styled office building was built just west of the Topkapı Palace area, on the other side of Alemdar Caddesi. It became the location of the Grand Vizier and many ministries, and from then on this building and the gate leading to its courtyards bore the name Sublime Porte. Colloquially it was also called the Gate of the Pasha. The building was rebuilt after a fire in 1839 and badly damaged by another fire in 1911.

The building housed the office of the Grand Vizier, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of the Interior and the Supreme Council of Judicial Ordinances. Western states used the term in diplomacy because their envoys were received at the porte, the Turkish word for which means gate.

After the Young Turk Revolution and the start of the Second Constitutional Era in 1908, the reformed Imperial Government replaced the functions of the classical Divan-ı Hümayun. In this period the word porte came to refer to the Foreign Ministry, the Grand Vizier's office came to resemble that of a prime minister, and viziers became members of his cabinet as government ministers. The buildings now house the office of the Istanbul governor.
submarine: The word submarine means underwater, and as a noun it is a contraction of submarine boat. A report published in 1562 tells that two Greeks submerged and surfaced several times in the river Tagus near Toledo in the presence of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, with the flame they carried still alight. In 1578 the English mathematician William Bourne recorded one of the first plans for an underwater navigation vehicle.

Submarines could not enter routine naval service until suitable engines were developed, and the period from 1863 to 1904 was pivotal. The French Plongeur, launched in 1863, was the first submarine not relying on human power, using compressed air. Narcís Monturiol's Ictíneo II, launched in Barcelona in 1864, was the first air-independent, combustion-powered submarine.

The submarine became feasible as a weapon with Robert Whitehead's torpedo of 1866, the first practical self-propelled torpedo. Early submarines used gasoline engines, which gave way to kerosene and then diesel engines, and diesel-electric propulsion became the norm. Submarines were first used widely in the First World War. Before and during the Second World War their primary role was attacking surface ships, and they were particularly effective in sinking Allied transatlantic shipping in both wars and in disrupting Japanese supply routes in the Pacific. They also laid mines, landed and recovered covert agents and special forces, and rescued aircrew during air attacks on islands.

Submarines worked in polar waters early. In 1930 USS O-12 operated under ice near Spitsbergen, and USS Nautilus used an inertial navigation system to reach the North Pole on 3 August 1958. Late in the Second World War, when faster and longer submerged operation became possible, hulls again took the teardrop shape that reduces drag and noise. Civilian uses developed alongside the military ones, including marine science, salvage and exploration. The first tourist submarine entered service in 1964, and by 1997 there were 45 tourist submarines operating.
subotica: Subotica lies in the Pannonian Basin at an altitude of 109 metres, about 10 kilometres from the border with Hungary, and is the northernmost city in Serbia. Lake Palić is near it. Its earliest recorded name is Zabotka or Zabatka, from 1391, which gave the Hungarian name Szabadka. One explanation derives it from a Slavic word for a place with a Saturday market fair, while another links it to a word for free, referring to the colonists settled after the Battle of Zenta.

Subotica probably first became a settlement of note when people from nearby villages destroyed in the Tatar invasions of 1241–42 poured into it. In 1391 it was a tiny town in the Kingdom of Hungary. After Mohács in 1526 the Hungarian population mostly fled north. The Ottomans ruled the city from 1542 to 1686, and by the end little remained of the old town. They encouraged settlers from the Balkans, mostly Orthodox Serbs, and in 1687 about 5,000 Catholic Bunjevci settled in Bačka. In 1743 Subotica gained a civil charter as a market town and was called Sent-Maria.

In 1779 Maria Theresa made it a Free Royal Town and it was renamed Maria-Theresiopolis. Its population doubled twice in the 19th century as Hungarians and Jews settled there alongside the Bunjevci. After 1867 the railway came in 1869, an electric power plant in 1896, and the city acquired its fin de siècle architecture. In 1918 it became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Hungarian troops entered on 11 April 1941. Of about 6,000 Jews who had lived there before the war, many were deported, mostly to Auschwitz, and a ghetto was set up in April 1944.

Subotica is the administrative centre of the North Bačka District in the autonomous province of Vojvodina, Serbia, with 88,752 people in the city proper in 2022. It is known for buildings in the Hungarian Secession style, a variant of Art Nouveau. The Synagogue of 1902 and the City Hall of 1908–1910 were both built by Marcell Komor and Dezső Jakab, and the Raichle Palace of 1904 by Ferenc J. Raichle. The Synagogue is the second largest synagogue building in Europe.
subutai: Historians believe Subutai was born in 1175, probably just west of the upper Onon River in what is now Mongolia. An older account makes him a member of the reindeer people and an outsider to steppe horsemanship, but recent scholarship, including Stephen Pow and Jingjing Liao, discounts it. His family had been associated with the family of Temujin, the future Genghis Khan, for generations. His father, Jarchigudai, is said to have supplied food to Temujin and his followers at Lake Baljuna, and his elder brother Jelme was a general and close companion of Temujin.

In 1217 Genghis Khan sent Subutai against the Merkits and the Cuman-Kipchak confederation in what is now central Kazakhstan. Between 1220 and 1223 he and Jebe led about 20,000 men round the Caspian Sea and through the Caucasus. They defeated the Georgian army by luring its knights away from the infantry with a feigned retreat, and at the Kalka River in 1223 his 20,000 men routed a Russian army of 80,000. In 1226 he struck the Tanguts of Xi Xia from the west across mountains and deserts while Genghis invaded by the northern route. After Genghis died in 1227, Ögedei sent him to retrieve a failing campaign against the Jin dynasty.

Under the overall command of Prince Batu, Subutai directed the invasion of Rus' from 1236 to 1240. In 1241 and 1242 he was the actual commander in the field of the attack on central Europe, leading the central column against the Kingdom of Hungary. He routinely coordinated armies operating hundreds of kilometres apart, and his methods relied on feints, encirclement and rapid cavalry charges.

After the kurultai that elected Güyük as khagan, Subutai was placed in charge of a campaign against the Song dynasty in 1246 and 1247, at the age of 71. He returned to Mongolia in 1248 and spent the rest of his life at his home near the Tuul River, dying there at the age of 72. His descendants Uriyangkhadai and Aju served the Great Khans as commanders for the next three decades.

The historian Paul Buell wrote that no Mongol general played a greater role in establishing and maintaining the early Mongol Empire. Western military writers largely ignored his methods until the 20th century. Russian analysis of the Mongol campaigns fed into the deep battle doctrine of the Soviet Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, and the American theorist John Boyd cited the campaigns of Genghis Khan and Subutai as examples of maneuver warfare.
suceava: Suceava is the seat of Suceava County, in the historical regions of Bukovina and Western Moldavia. It stands in a moderately hilly area in the south-western part of the county and covers both hills, the highest being Zamca Hill, and the meadows of the Suceava river valley. Its position at the crossroads of several trade routes linking Central Europe with Eastern Europe made it a commercial town, and it is a transport hub with Ukraine to the north and Transylvania to the west. The name was explained by the chroniclers Grigore Ureche and Dimitrie Cantemir as coming from the Hungarian Szűcsvár, meaning furriers' castle, although there is no historical or vernacular evidence for this.

The area was inhabited from the Paleolithic period, and traces of a Dacian oppidum of the 2nd century survive. Suceava and the rest of Bukovina were not conquered by the Roman legions and remained among the lands of the free Dacian tribes. Ptolemy places the Celtic-speaking Anartes and Taurisci and the Germanic Bastarnae in the region. After the fall of Rome the population was invaded in turn by Goths, Gepids, Huns, Slavs, Magyars, Pechenegs and Cumans.

From 1388 to 1564 Suceava was the capital of the Principality of Moldavia, and in the Middle Ages it operated under Magdeburg law. Petru Mușat built the Princely House in wood in the late 14th century, and after 1400 Alexander I of Moldavia rebuilt it and added a stone wall and stone buildings. A fire in the second half of the 15th century burned the wooden house. The Seat Fortress and the Șcheia Fortress belonged to the principality's system of fortification.

From 1775 to 1918 Suceava was under the Habsburg monarchy, later the Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary. The Austrian census of 1880 recorded 10,104 inhabitants, of whom 5,862 were Bukovina Germans and 2,652 Romanians. In the interwar period it grew within the enlarged Kingdom of Romania.

Suceava had a population of 84,308 at the 2021 census, having grown from just over 10,000 in the late 1940s to over 100,000 in the early 1990s. The reconstructed Seat Fortress stands on the eastern edge of the city. The Saint John the New Monastery, whose Church of Saint George was built between 1514 and 1522 and served as the metropolitan cathedral of Moldavia until 1677, is one of the Churches of Moldavia inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. An equestrian statue of Stephen the Great, made in 1977, is the tallest in Romania. The Ștefan cel Mare University of Suceava was established in 1990.
sucre: Sucre lies in south-central Bolivia at about 2,790 m above sea level, in the inter-Andean valleys of the Eastern Cordillera, at the foot of the Sica Sica and Churuquella hills. The area marks the boundary between the Amazon basin and the basin of the River Plate, and its climate is mild and dry for the altitude. The city has been known as Charcas, La Plata, Chuquisaca and Sucre, and its white-painted colonial houses earned it the nickname La Ciudad Blanca, the White City.

Before the Spanish arrived the site was an Inca town called Chuquisaca, the provincial capital of the wamani of Charca, which Topa Inka Yupanqui had taken from the Aymara kingdom that held the area. The name possibly comes from Quechua words meaning a heap of silver. In 1538 Hernando Pizarro travelled there with the Emperor Paullu Inca and met Consara, the principal lord of the Charcas, who told him of the silver, gold, copper and tin deposits of the region.

The Spanish city was founded on 30 November 1538 by Pedro Anzures, Marqués de Campo Redondo, as Ciudad de la Plata de la Nueva Toledo. In 1559 Philip II set up the Audiencia of Charcas there, with authority over what is now Paraguay, south-eastern Peru, northern Chile, Argentina and much of Bolivia. It belonged to the Viceroyalty of Peru until 1776, then to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. An archbishopric was founded in 1609 and the university of St Francis Xavier in 1624.

On 25 May 1809 the bell of the Basilica of San Francisco was rung to begin the Bolivian independence movement. La Plata was proclaimed provisional capital of Upper Peru in July 1826, and on 12 July 1839 President José Miguel de Velasco named it capital of Bolivia and renamed it for Antonio José de Sucre. After the decline of Potosí's silver industry the seat of government moved to La Paz in 1898.

Sucre is the constitutional capital of Bolivia and the capital of the Chuquisaca Department; the Supreme Court sits there, while La Paz is the seat of government. Its colonial and republican centre, laid out on a grid, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Landmarks include the House of Freedom, built in 1621, where the declaration of independence is kept, and the Metropolitan Cathedral, built between 1559 and 1712. Sucre remains the seat of the Roman Catholic Church in Bolivia.
sudak: Sudak lies on the south-east coast of the Crimea, 57 km west of Feodosia and 104 km east of Simferopol. The date and circumstances of its foundation are uncertain. Its first written mention is in the Ravenna Cosmography of the 7th century, and local tradition later placed its foundation in 212 CE, while archaeology supports a foundation in Roman times. It was probably founded by the Alans: its Greek name, Sougdaia, is related to a word meaning pure or holy, or derives from Ossetian.

Under loose Byzantine influence Sougdaia was became the seat of a bishopric, first attested at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. The 8th to 11th centuries are obscure, with signs of decline and probably Khazar suzerainty until the early 11th century. The 11th to 14th centuries were a time of prosperity. The city was a terminus of Black Sea trade on the Silk Road in the 12th and 13th centuries, and the Arab traveller Ibn Battuta compared its harbour with that of Alexandria. Byzantium regained it by the mid-11th century, and it then fell under Cuman control until the 13th century.

The Seljuk Turks besieged the city in about 1222, and the Mongols raided it in 1223 and 1238; in about 1249 it came under the Golden Horde, though it kept considerable autonomy. Its population was then given as 8,300, among them Greeks, Alans, Mongols, Armenians, Latins and Jews.

Venetian and Genoese commercial colonies raised its prosperity in the late 13th century, but Genoese Tana and Kaffa eclipsed it in the early 14th. On 19 July 1365 the Genoese from Kaffa seized it, refortified it and built the citadel still visible today. Gedik Ahmed Pasha took it after a long siege in 1475, and it lost much of its military and commercial importance. Russian troops occupied it in 1771, and it passed to the Russian Empire in 1783; by the census of 1805 it had only 33 inhabitants.

Sudak is a resort best known for its Genoese fortress, the best preserved on the northern shore of the Black Sea. A Russian school of viticulture opened there in 1804. The Orthodox see of Sougdaia, raised to an archbishopric in the 10th century and a metropolitan see between 1275 and 1282, gave its old name Surozh to a diocese of the Russian Orthodox Church, and a Latin Catholic diocese of Soldaia was established under Genoese rule in 1390.
sudan: The modern state of Sudan covers 1,886,068 km2, the third-largest country in Africa by area, with an 853 km coast on the Red Sea. The terrain is generally flat plains broken by mountain ranges, and the highest point is the Deriba Caldera, at 3,042 metres, in the Marrah Mountains. The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum to form the Nile, which flows north through Egypt.

The north and centre are extremely dry, with the Nubian and Bayuda deserts, while the south has grasslands and tropical savanna. The name comes from the Arabic bilad as-sudan, the Land of the Blacks, which was historically applied to the Sahel from Senegal to Northeast Africa; before that the area was known as Nubia.

The oldest evidence is the camp remains at Affad 23, some 50,000 years old, and the war of Jebel Sahaba, around 11500 BCE, is described as the earliest known war in the world. The Kingdom of Kerma flourished from about 2500 to 1500 BCE and in its last phase became a populous empire rivalling Egypt. Egyptian rulers of the New Kingdom then held the region, beginning when Thutmose I occupied Kush and destroyed Kerma. The Kingdom of Kush lasted from about 785 BCE to 350 CE, and after its fall the Nubians formed the Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

Arab nomads settled most of Sudan between the 14th and 15th centuries. From the 16th to the 19th centuries the Funj sultanate dominated the centre and east, while Darfur ruled the west and the Ottomans the east. Egypt conquered the whole country in the 19th century. After the Mahdist Uprising was defeated by a joint Egyptian-British force, Egypt agreed in 1899 under British pressure to share sovereignty with the United Kingdom, and Sudan was in effect governed as a British possession. It became independent on 1 January 1956.

Sudan has known repeated civil war. The first, from 1955 to 1972, was followed by a second between government forces and southern rebels, which led to the independence of South Sudan in 2011. Sharia law applied from 1983 until 2020, when Sudan became a secular state.
suddhodana: The name Śuddhodana means "he who grows pure rice". His father was Sihahanu and his mother Kaccanā, and his earliest predecessor was named as King Maha Sammatha, or the first king of the Kalpa. His chief consort was Maha Maya, with whom he had Siddhartha Gautama, later called Shakyamuni, the Sage of the Shakyas. When Maya died shortly after the birth, her sister Mahapajapati Gotami was raised to chief consort. They had a second son, Nanda, and a daughter, Sundari Nanda, who both later became Buddhist monastics. At the age of 16 Siddhartha married his cousin Yasodharā, niece of Maha Maya and Mahapajapati.

Śuddhodana led the Shakya, who lived in an oligarchic republic with its capital at Kapilavastu. Later accounts of the Buddha's life often call him a king, but modern scholars dispute this and most recent scholarship rejects it. Many hold that the Shakya republic was ruled by a council of the warrior and ministerial class that chose its leader, the rājā, who did not rule autocratically, since questions were debated in the council and decided by consensus.

By the time of Siddhartha's birth the republic had become a vassal of the Kingdom of Kosala, and the rājā took office with the approval of Kosala's king. The earliest Buddhist texts do not describe the family as royal. Later texts may have misread the Pali word rājā, which can mean king, prince, ruler or governor.

According to legend, Śuddhodana tried hard to keep Siddhartha from becoming a śramaṇa, forbidding him to leave the palace and surrounding him with sensual pleasures. At 29 Siddhartha left home after his first journey outside, an episode known as the Great Renunciation.

Śuddhodana grieved at his son's departure and long sought him. Seven years later, when word of his enlightenment arrived, he sent nine emissaries to invite him back, but they joined the sangha after hearing him preach. He then sent Siddhartha's friend Kaludayi, who also became a monk but kept his word and invited the Buddha home. The Buddha returned and preached the dharma to his father. Four years later, hearing that his father was near death, he came again to the palace and preached to him, and Śuddhodana is said to have reached arhatship on his deathbed.
sudeten-germans: Ethnic Germans moved into the Kingdom of Bohemia from the 11th century, mostly into the border region later called the Sudetenland after the Sudeten Mountains. In the late 12th and 13th centuries the Přemyslid rulers promoted settlement by Germans from Bavaria, Franconia, Upper Saxony and Austria, part of the eastern settlement movement known as Ostsiedlung. The name Sudeten Germans came into use only in the early 20th century, after the fall of Austria-Hungary, and the Nazi regime used it so heavily that many Germans now prefer the older term German Bohemians.

Most Sudeten Germans were Roman Catholics, a legacy of Habsburg rule. Czechs and Germans mixed in many places, but from the second half of the 19th century each built separate cultural, educational, political and economic institutions.
