It is not a single text but a composition of which versions differ in content, order, names and the lengths of reigns. The best preserved is the Weld-Blundell Prism, from the Old Babylonian period.

Each entry names a city, its kings and their reigns, and records how the city was defeated and kingship taken elsewhere. The Weld-Blundell version opens with eight kings of five cities who reigned 241,200 years in all before the flood swept over the land; this section is missing from some copies. After the flood kingship went to Kish, whose 23 kings are credited with reigns of 1,500 to 300 years. Only Etana, who ascended to heaven, and Enmebaragesi, who made Elam submit, are given any deed.

The list runs through Uruk, Ur and other cities to Sargon of Akkad, named as cup-bearer to Ur-zababa of Kish. After Shar-kali-sharri it asks, Then who was king? Who was not king?, a sign of the chaos at the end of the Akkadian Empire. Gutian kings, the Third Dynasty of Ur and the Isin dynasty of 14 kings follow. Kug-Bau, a tavern keeper, is thought to be the only queen listed.

The first fragment was published in 1906 by Hermann Volrath Hilprecht and the second in 1911 by Jean-Vincent Scheil. During much of the 20th century many scholars treated it as an important source for Early Dynastic Mesopotamia, but recent research holds that it should be used with great caution, if at all, for that period. Only seven pre-Sargonic rulers in it, among them Enmebaragesi, Gilgamesh and Lugal-zage-si, are attested in contemporary inscriptions, and several kings it presents in sequence ruled at the same time. From the Akkadian rulers onward, and especially for Ur III and Isin, it is far more reliable. It influenced later compositions such as the Curse of Akkad, the Assyrian King List and the Babyloniaca of Berossus.
sumerian-language: Sumerian was the language of ancient Sumer, and it is the oldest attested language, dating back to at least 3100 BCE, perhaps earlier. It is a language isolate, unrelated to any other known language, and was spoken exclusively in ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Akkadian, a Semitic language, gradually replaced it as the main spoken language around 2000 BCE, though the exact date is debated. Sumerian continued as a sacred, ceremonial, literary and scientific language in Akkadian-speaking states such as Assyria and Babylonia until the 1st century CE. The history of written Sumerian is divided into periods from the proto-literate period, c. 3100–3000 BCE, through Neo-Sumerian, in which the Ur III period falls, to Old Babylonian Sumerian and later.

The scripts used for Sumerian began as pictographic proto-writing in Mesopotamia around 3300 BCE. By about 2800 BCE some tablets used syllabic elements that clearly indicated Sumerian, and around 2600 BCE cuneiform symbols were developed, made by pressing a wedge-shaped stylus into wet clay. Sumerian is an agglutinative, ergative language with a subject–object–verb word order. Its standard variety was called Emegir, and a sociolect called Emesal appears in some literary texts as the speech of female characters and in cult songs. Attempts to link Sumerian to other languages, including Indo-European, Dravidian and Turkic, have failed, and such proposals enjoy virtually no support among modern linguists.

The cuneiform script was adopted by many regional languages, including Akkadian, Elamite, Hittite, Hurrian and Aramaic, and it inspired the Old Persian alphabet. Sumerian influenced Akkadian greatly, and was influenced by it in turn. After it fell into obscurity, it was rediscovered in the 19th century when Assyriologists began deciphering the inscriptions and excavated tablets. The key came from the Behistun inscription, written in Old Persian, Elamite and Akkadian. In 1838 Henry Rawlinson, building on the 1802 work of Georg Friedrich Grotefend, deciphered the Old Persian section, and when he recovered the rest of the text in 1843 he and others gradually translated the Elamite and Akkadian sections.
sumu-la-el: Sumu-la-El, also written Sumulael or Sumu-la-ilu, was a king of the First Dynasty of Babylon. About 36 of his year names are known. He was a contemporary of Sîn-kāšid of Uruk and of Sūmu-El and Nur-Adad of Larsa. In his time Babylon contested control of the surrounding region with the city-state of Isin.

He subjugated and conquered nearby cities such as Kish, and he is known to have conquered Sippar. During the first half of his reign Marad was an independent kingdom that also controlled Dilbat. His daughter Šallurtum married Sîn-kāšid, the king of Uruk, and economic ties of his reign reached as far north as Tilmen Hoyuk.

Sumu-la-El built a string of fortresses around his territory. His year names record the city wall of Dilbat, the great city wall of Babylon, the walls of Kutha, Anzagar-urgi, Sippar and Habuz, a temple of Adad and a temple of Zababa, the Emeteursag. Other year names mark the destruction of Kish, the defeat of the army of Kazallu, the driving out of Iahzir-el from Kazallu, and the year Sumu-la-El entered Borsippa.

The Old Babylonian levels at the city of Babylon lie below the water table and have not been excavated, so what is known of him comes from other sites, such as Sippar and Marad, which Babylon controlled. A text from Sippar in the time of the later ruler Apil-Sîn records a case in which families kept houses that Sumu-la-El had given them. One of the witnesses was Ayyalatum, a daughter of Sumu-la-El.
sumuabum: Sumu-abum, also written Sūmû-abum, Su-abu or Sūmabum, was an Amorite and is counted as the first king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, also called the Amorite Dynasty. His reign is dated c. 1894–1881 BCE in the middle chronology. It fell in the period after the collapse of the Ur III Empire, when the city-states of Isin and Larsa were the major powers of the region. Babylon was then a minor administrative centre in southern Mesopotamia.

Sumu-abum freed a small area of land that had been ruled by the fellow Amorite city-state of Kazallu, and Babylon lay within it. Neither he nor the three Amorite kings who followed him claims the title King of Babylon, which suggests that the town was still of little importance at the time.

About fourteen year names of Sumu-abum are known. They record the building of the great city wall of Babylon, the temple of Ninisina, the temple Emah of Nanna and the wall of Dilbat, a city 25 kilometres south of Babylon that he controlled. In his third year he claimed to have conquered Elip, a major city of the Manana Dynasty, and another year name says he destroyed or seized Kazallu.

By his tenth year he had gained control of Kish, 12 kilometres east of Babylon, which the Manana dynasty had held for some time. Kish was briefly lost to Larsa and recovered in his thirteenth year. It was no longer a powerful city but kept an outsized symbolic importance, and one year name says that he gave it a city wall reaching heaven. He is also known to have become king of Kisurra, although an alternative view holds that the Sumu-abum who controlled Kisurra was a ruler of the 6th Dynasty of Uruk, before Sîn-kāšid.

The Old Babylonian levels at Babylon lie below the water table and have not been excavated, so what is known of him comes from other sites: Kazallu, Dilbat, Sippar and Kisurra. He should not be confused with Isi-sümü-abum of the same period, who ruled a city not yet identified. A tablet from Sippar, BM 80328, lists rulers of Babylon and names fourteen unknown rulers before Sūmû-abum.
sumy: Sumy was founded in the 1650s by the Cossack Herasym Kondratyev, who came from Stavyshche in the Bila Tserkva Regiment, on the banks of the Psel in the historical region of Sloboda Ukraine. In 1656–1658 a fort and town were built on the site under the Muscovite voivode K. Arsenyev, and from 1658 Sumy was the centre of the Sumy Cossack Regiment. A fortified craftsmen's town added in the 1670s made it the biggest fortress in Sloboda Ukraine. Muscovite troops gathered here for the Crimean campaigns of 1687 and 1689, and from December 1708 to January 1709 the city was the headquarters of Tsar Peter the Great during the Great Northern War.

After the Cossack community was abolished in 1765, the regiment became Sumy Province of the new Sloboda Ukraine Governorate, and the city became its centre. Sumy then stagnated until the 1860s. Paul's Sugar-Refining Factory, founded in 1869 by I. Kharytonenko, and the Sumy Engineering Workshops of 1896, which made equipment for sugar refineries, began its growth into an industrial and trading centre, and the railway station opened in January 1877. During the Russian Revolution of 1905 Sumy was among the areas that set up an independent peasant republic.

Germany occupied Sumy from 10 October 1941 to 2 September 1943, and the city was heavily damaged. In February 1942 about 1,000 Jews were murdered in two large operations, and the Germans ran a prison, a forced labour battalion for Jews and the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 308 there. In 1944 about 30,000 Polish soldiers were stationed in Sumy and trained before rejoining the war.

Sumy is the administrative centre of Sumy Oblast in north-eastern Ukraine, and its census population was 292,139 in 2001. Its oldest building is the Resurrection Church of 1702. The neoclassical cathedral of the Saviour's Transfiguration, of the 18th century, received its 56-metre bell tower in the 1880s. The Sumy Regional Art Museum and the Museum of Local Lore opened in 1920, and the Chekhov Museum occupies the Lintvarev country estate of the 18th and 19th centuries.
sun-quan: Sun Quan, courtesy name Zhongmou, was born in 182, the second son of Sun Jian, then a low-ranking Han official, and his wife Lady Wu. After Sun Jian's death in 191 the family moved between cities on the lower Yangtze while his elder brother Sun Ce built a warlord regime in the Jiangdong region. When Sun Ce was fatally wounded by assassins in 200, he entrusted the 18-year-old Sun Quan to his faithful officers, among them Zhou Yu, Zhang Zhao, Zhang Hong and Cheng Pu. Some followers thought him too young, and Li Shu, the Administrator of Lujiang, went over to Cao Cao, but Sun Quan defeated him and regained Lujiang.

That winter of 208 Cao Cao came south with an army of about 220,000 men, estimated against Sun's 30,000. Zhang Zhao urged surrender, while Zhou Yu and Lu Su argued that Cao Cao would not tolerate him even if he submitted. Sun Quan chose to fight, allied with Liu Bei, and defeated Cao Cao at the Battle of Red Cliffs. He then took the northern half of Jing Province and Liu Bei the southern half, and the alliance was sealed by the marriage of Sun Quan's younger sister to Liu Bei. In 211 he moved his headquarters to Moling, which he renamed Jianye the next year.

The alliance broke in 219, when Guan Yu besieged Fancheng and Sun Quan attacked him from the rear; Guan Yu was captured and executed, and Jing Province came under Sun's control. After Cao Pi ended the Han dynasty in 220, Sun Quan accepted the title King of Wu, but refused to send his son Sun Deng as a hostage to Luoyang and in November 222 declared himself independent by changing his era name. He formally became emperor in May 229. His early administration was known for its efficiency, and he delegated trust to officers such as Lu Xun and Zhuge Jin.

After the crown prince Sun Deng died in 241, two factions formed around his sons Sun He and Sun Ba. In 250 Sun Quan forced Sun Ba to commit suicide and deposed Sun He, naming his youngest son Sun Liang crown prince, and officials who objected were executed. He died in May 252, aged 70 by East Asian reckoning, and was succeeded by Sun Liang. He had the longest reign among the founders of the Three Kingdoms, and is known posthumously as Emperor Da of Wu.
sun-tzu: Sun Tzu means Master Sun and is an honorific. His birth name is said to have been Sun Wu. The earliest account of his life is a short biography in the Shiji, the Records of the Grand Historian, written around 97 BCE by Sima Qian. It says he was born in Qi, in present-day Shandong, near the end of the Spring and Autumn period. The scholar Victor Mair considers the biography essentially fictional.

According to the Shiji, King Helü of Wu heard of Sun Wu's Art of War, summoned him and asked him to show how he trained soldiers, using the king's harem of 180 concubines. Sun Tzu appointed the two concubines the king favoured most as commanders and gave orders, which they ignored, laughing. Over the king's protests he had the two commanders executed, after which the rest obeyed at once, and the king made Sun Wu a general. He is said to have led Wu to victory over the much larger state of Chu at the Battle of Boju in 506 BCE.

Beginning in the 12th century scholars began to doubt that he existed. Ye Shi noticed that the Zuo Zhuan, which describes the Battle of Boju in far more detail and was written centuries before the Shiji, never mentions Sun Tzu, and the name Sun Wu appears in no text earlier than the Shiji.

The Art of War is a Classical Chinese text in 13 chapters, each devoted to a different set of skills related to warfare, strategy and tactics. It also advocates diplomacy and the cultivation of relations with other states. The earliest parts probably date from at least a century after Sun Tzu, and since the 12th century most scholars have placed the text at the beginning of the Warring States period. Bamboo slips found at Yinque Shan in Shandong in 1972 hold about a third of the chapters of the modern text, with closely matching wording.

The earliest known commentary was written by the warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century CE. Emperor Shenzong of Song formalized the Seven Military Classics in 1080, and the Art of War led that anthology for almost 1,500 years. Lionel Giles completed the first annotated English translation in 1910.
sun-yat-sen: Sun Yat-sen was born on 12 November 1866 in the village of Cuiheng, Xiangshan County, in Guangdong, to Sun Dacheng and Madame Yang. His father owned little land and worked as a tailor in Macau and as a journeyman and porter. At 13 he went to live in Hawaii with his elder brother Sun Mei, who paid for his schooling at the ʻIolani School, where he studied English, mathematics, science and Christianity. His brother, alarmed at his interest in Christianity, sent him back to China in 1883. He graduated from the Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese in 1892.

In 1894 Sun wrote a petition on modernising China and travelled to Tianjin to present it to the viceroy Li Hongzhang, who did not receive him. He turned to revolution and founded the Revive China Society in Hawaii. Its First Guangzhou Uprising of 26 October 1895 failed after the plan leaked. In London in 1896 he was detained for 12 days at the Chinese Legation, which planned to smuggle him to China, and was freed through the efforts of James Cantlie, the press and the Foreign Office. Further uprisings also failed, and he raised money among overseas Chinese. His Three Principles of the People were nationalism, democracy and welfare.

After the 1911 revolution representatives meeting in Nanjing elected him provisional president on 29 December 1911. When the Qing emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, Sun stepped down and Yuan Shikai became provisional president. The Kuomintang was formed on 25 August 1912, and its leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated on 20 March 1913, almost certainly on Yuan's secret order. Sun's Second Revolution failed in July 1913 and he fled to Japan. In 1921 he began a military government in Guangzhou, and he later cooperated with the Chinese Communist Party.

In January 1925 an operation at Peking Union Medical College Hospital found extensive cancer of the liver. Sun died on 12 March 1925, aged 58, and an autopsy gave the primary cancer as that of the gall bladder. After his death the Nationalist government split into rival factions led by Chiang Kai-shek, Wang Jingwei and the Western Hills Group. The Republic of China calls Sun the Father of the Nation, while the People's Republic of China honours him as the Forerunner of the Revolution, and his home county of Xiangshan was renamed Zhongshan in his honour.
sunda-strait: The strait takes its name from the Sunda Kingdom, which ruled the western part of Java, an area covering present-day West Java, Jakarta, Banten and some of western Central Java, from 669 to around 1579. The name also alludes to the Sundanese people of West Java and Banten.

The strait runs roughly south-west to north-east and is essentially triangular, with two large bays on its northern side. It is very broad and deep at its south-western end, but narrows to a minimum width of 24 km between Cape Tua on Sumatra and Cape Pujat on Java and becomes much shallower, with a minimum depth of only 20 m. Shallows, very strong tidal currents and sandbanks make it notoriously difficult to navigate, and most modern large ships use the Strait of Malacca instead.

For centuries the strait was an important shipping route, above all while the Dutch East India Company used it as the gateway to the Spice Islands of Indonesia, from 1602 to 1799. It is dotted with islands, many volcanic, among them Sangiang, Sebesi, Sebuku, Panaitan and Krakatau.

The 1883 eruption of Krakatau killed tens of thousands of people with tsunamis and pyroclastic flows, and of 3,000 people on nearby Sebesi not one survived. Some land was never resettled and became Ujung Kulon National Park.

The eruption changed the strait's topography, depositing as much as 18 to 21 cubic kilometres of ignimbrite over an area of 1.1 million square kilometres. Anak Krakatau emerged from the shattered remains in 1927.

On 1 March 1942 the Battle of Sunda Strait took place, when the Allied cruisers HMAS Perth and USS Houston met a Japanese landing force near Bantam, and both were sunk. A bridge across the strait has been proposed since the 1960s, and an agreement was signed in April 2012 for a road and rail bridge, but the plan was shelved in November 2014.
sundial: The earliest sundials known from the archaeological record are shadow clocks of about 1500 BCE, from ancient Egyptian and Babylonian astronomy. By 240 BCE Eratosthenes had estimated the circumference of the world using an obelisk and a water well, and a few centuries later Ptolemy had charted the latitude of cities using the angle of the Sun. The people of Kush made sundials through geometry. The Roman writer Vitruvius lists the dials and shadow clocks known in his time in De architectura, and the Tower of the Winds in Athens had both a sundial and a water clock.

A sundial tells the time of day from the apparent position of the Sun. In its narrowest sense it consists of a flat plate, the dial, and a gnomon, which casts a shadow onto the dial. As the Sun appears to move, the shadow aligns with different hour-lines marked on the dial. For accuracy throughout the year the edge of the gnomon that tells the time, called the style, must be parallel to the axis of the Earth's rotation, and its angle from the horizontal equals the latitude. Dials differ in the surface that receives the shadow: equatorial, horizontal, vertical, polar and spherical dials are the main types, and a movable gnomon is used in analemmatic dials.

A canonical sundial indicated the canonical hours of liturgical acts, and religious orders used them from the 7th to the 14th centuries. In 1570 the Italian astronomer Giovanni Padovani published a treatise on sundials, with instructions for making and laying out vertical and horizontal dials, and sundials have been in common use since the 16th century. Portable dials included the shepherd's dial, the ring dial and the card dial; the Venerable Bede gave a table for estimating the time from the length of one's shadow. A sundial does not match clock time without corrections for time zone and for the equation of time, which can reach a quarter of an hour. Sundials often carried mottoes reminding the viewer of the passing of time.
sundiata-keita: Sundiata is known chiefly through the Epic of Sundiata, a semi-historical poem handed down orally by Maninka griots. According to it, he was the son of Naré Maghann Konaté and Sogolon Condé, and he was crippled from childhood until he rose and walked. His half-brother Dankaran Touman and Dankaran's mother, Sassouma Bereté, resented him, and after his father's death Sogolon took her children into exile. They were eventually given asylum in Mema, where its king gave Sundiata a senior position.

When King Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso conquered the Mandinka, messengers found Sundiata in Mema and persuaded him to return. The epic says the king of Mema gave him an army, and that on the plain of Siby he and his allies, among them Tiramakhan Traore, formed a pact of brotherhood. Written accounts by Ibn Battuta and Ibn Khaldun, who travelled to Mali in the following century, give independent evidence that he existed.

At the Battle of Kirina, about 1235, Sundiata and his allies defeated Soumaoro, and he became the first emperor of Mali and the first Mandinka king to take the title Mansa. He set his capital at Niani, near the present border of Mali with Guinea. His generals extended his power: Tiramakhan Traore is credited with conquests in Senegambia, including Kaabu, and with defeating the king of Jolof, while Sundiata himself is credited with Diafunu and Kita.

Mansa Sundiata was not an absolute monarch. The empire was reportedly run like a federation, with each clan holding a chief representative at court, and the Great Gbara Assembly checked the Mansa's power and chose his successor. The Manden Charter and the Kouroukan Fouga, unwritten and altered in retelling, are traced to his reign. Under him Mali began to control trade routes and gold fields, and he is reported to have introduced cotton and weaving.

The generally accepted year of his death is c. 1255. The cause is uncertain: the version now generally accepted is drowning in the Sankarani River, where a shrine bearing his name remains, while Maurice Delafosse reported an arrow during a ceremony and others an assassination. Mandinka tradition forbids disclosing the burial ground of great kings. His sons Mansa Wali Keita, Mansa Ouati Keita and Mansa Khalifa Keita succeeded him, and Mansa Musa was his great-nephew. Scholars disagree on whether he was Muslim: the original epic does not say so, and later Muslim griots added Islamic ancestry to it.
suniti-devi: Suniti Devi was born on 30 September 1864, a daughter of Keshub Chandra Sen of Calcutta and Jagonmohini Sen. She was fourteen when she married. For two years afterwards she stayed in her father's house, since her husband left for London for higher studies immediately after the wedding. She had four sons and three daughters. Two of her sons, Rajendra Narayan and Jitendra Narayan, later became Maharajas of Cooch Behar. Her daughters Sudhira and Pratibha married the brothers Alan and Miles Mander of Wightwick Manor in England, and Sukriti married Jyotsna Nath Ghoshal, a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.

In 1887, when she attended the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria with her husband, she was made a Companion of the Order of the Crown of India, the first Indian woman to receive the honour. She was also present at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

The girls' school that her husband set up in her name in 1881, later called Suniti Academy, was her idea. She gave it annual grants, exempted the pupils from tuition fees and rewarded those who did well. She arranged for palace cars to carry the girls between home and school and, to avoid controversy, ordered the car windows to be curtained. With her sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, she financed the foundation of the Maharani Girls' High School in Darjeeling in 1908. She was President of the State Council and in 1932 the first President of the All Bengal Women's Union.

She was also an author. Bengal Dacoits and Tigers, a collection of short stories, was published in Calcutta in 1916. The Beautiful Mogul Princesses, published in London in 1918, tells the lives of Mumtaz Mahal, Zebunissa, Nur Jahan and another princess. The Autobiography of an Indian Princess appeared in London in 1921, and her last book, The Life of Princess Yashodara: Wife and Disciple of the Lord Buddha, in 1929. She died suddenly at Ranchi on 10 November 1932. In Cooch Behar the school, Sunity Road and a tank known as the Sunity Tank or Bairagi Dighi are named after her.
sunjong-of-korea: Sunjong, whose personal name was Yi Cheok, was the second son of Emperor Gojong and Empress Myeongseong. In 1876, when he was two, he was proclaimed Crown Prince of Joseon. In 1882 he married a woman of the Yeoheung Min clan, later Empress Sunmyeonghyo, who died on 5 November 1904 after trying to protect her mother-in-law at the assassination of Empress Myeongseong by the Japanese military on 8 October 1895. When his father proclaimed Korea an empire in 1897, Sunjong became Crown Prince of Imperial Korea, and in 1898 he was appointed Field Marshal of the Imperial Korean Army. On 11 December 1906 he married Yun Jeung-sun of the Haepyeong Yun clan, later Empress Sunjeong.

On 19 July 1907 Gojong was deposed under Japanese coercion and Sunjong became emperor, crowned at Don-doek-jeon. His younger half-brother, Prince Imperial Yeong, was named heir. His rule was limited by increasing Japanese intervention, and he was at once forced to accept the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1907, which let the Japanese government supervise Korean administration and appoint Japanese ministers. The Korean army was dismissed on the pretext of a lack of public finance regulations. In 1909 the Japan–Korea Protocol effectively removed Korea's judicial power.

Itō Hirobumi, the Japanese Resident-General, was assassinated by Ahn Jung-geun at Harbin, which was followed by annexation. Pro-Japanese politicians such as Song Byung-jun and Lee Wan-yong helped to arrange the Japan–Korea Annexation Treaty of 29 August 1910, by which Japan abolished the Korean Empire, ending 519 years of the Joseon dynasty. Historians have characterised Sunjong as a powerless puppet of the Japanese.

After the treaty Sunjong and Empress Sunjeong lived virtually imprisoned in Changdeokgung Palace. He was demoted from emperor to king, and Japan allowed him the title King Yi of Changdeok Palace, which could be inherited. He died in April 1926 at Changdeokgung without children and was buried with his two wives at the imperial tomb of Yureung in Namyangju. His state funeral on 10 June 1926 was a catalyst for the June 10th Movement against Japanese rule.
supermarine-spitfire: In 1931 the Air Ministry issued specification F7/30, calling for a modern fighter capable of 250 mph to replace the Gloster Gauntlet biplane. R. J. Mitchell, chief designer at Supermarine Aviation Works, a subsidiary of Vickers-Armstrong from 1928, answered with the Type 224, which first flew in February 1934; the Gloster Gladiator biplane was accepted instead, and Mitchell went on to the design that became the Spitfire.

The public first saw the Spitfire at the RAF Hendon air display on 27 June 1936. Numerous problems delayed production, and the first production aircraft, K9787, left the Woolston, Southampton, line only in mid-1938. Mitchell continued to refine the design until his death from cancer in 1937, after which Joseph Smith became chief designer and oversaw its development.

In 1934 Mitchell's team chose a semi-elliptical wing to meet two conflicting needs: it had to be thin to limit drag, yet thick enough to house the retractable undercarriage, armament and ammunition. The original airframe was designed around a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine of 1,030 hp, and it was strong enough to take more powerful Merlins and, in later marks, Griffon engines of up to 2,340 hp. Because the Merlin had a carburettor, Spitfires could not nose straight down into a dive as the Bf 109E could, and RAF pilots learned to half-roll before diving after an opponent.

The first Mk I entered service with 19 Squadron at RAF Duxford on 4 August 1938. In the Battle of Britain the Hurricane flew more sorties, but the Spitfire captured the public's imagination, helped by the Spitfire Fund run by Lord Beaverbrook, the Minister of Aircraft Production. Its squadrons had a lower attrition rate and higher victory-to-loss ratio, and the usual tactic was to use Spitfires against the escorting Bf 109s while Hurricanes attacked the bombers. Afterwards it became the principal aircraft of RAF Fighter Command and served in the European, Mediterranean, Pacific and South-East Asian theatres.

It flew as interceptor, photo-reconnaissance aircraft, fighter-bomber and trainer into the 1950s, and the Seafire adaptation served the Fleet Air Arm from 1942 until the mid-1950s. On 26 September 1940 bombing destroyed the Woolston and Itchen factories, killing 92 people, and production was dispersed to small sites around Southampton. The Spitfire became a symbol of British resistance, and about 240 are preserved.
suppiluliuma-i: Šuppiluliuma's origins are unclear. Seal impressions naming him as the son of Tudḫaliya III led most scholars to take him as that king's son, though his first wife Ḫenti is called the daughter of a great king, which has led some to think he was also Tudḫaliya's son-in-law and possibly adopted son. Before he became king he served as adviser and chief military commander. According to the Deeds of Šuppiluliuma, written by his son Muršili II, he helped recover Hittite lands from the Kaška in the north, defeated King Karanni of Azzi-Ḫayaša, and fought the Arzawa confederacy in the west, retaking the city of Tuwanuwa.

Tudḫaliya III's heir, Tudḫaliya the Younger, had sworn oaths of loyalty from Šuppiluliuma and other nobles. He was murdered with some of his brothers by Šuppiluliuma's supporters, and Šuppiluliuma became king. An oracle later named the murder as a cause of the plague that afflicted the Hittite kingdom.

Šuppiluliuma set out to recover Kizzuwatna and Tegarama, which had come under the influence of Mittani. An early attack failed, so he allied with a rival Mittanian royal, Artatama II, and married a Babylonian princess. In the so-called One-Year War he overran Mittani's vassal Išuwa and plundered the capital Waššukanni, then crossed the Euphrates and took Aleppo, Mukiš, Qatna and other Syrian kingdoms. Niqmaddu II of Ugarit accepted his suzerainty, and Kadesh fell after its king Šutatarra gave battle.

In the Six-Year War, fought largely by his son Telipinu, he besieged and captured Carchemish and made his son Piyaššili its vassal king. Telipinu ruled Aleppo, and the two princes served as viceroys in Syria. When Šattiwaza, son of Tušratta, fled Mittani, Šuppiluliuma gave him a daughter in marriage and sent him with a Hittite army to take what remained of his father's kingdom, which became in effect a dependency, later of Assyria as well.

Late in his reign an Egyptian queen, usually identified as Ankhesenamun, asked him for one of his sons as husband and king. He sent Zannanza, who was killed on the way. Šuppiluliuma blamed the Egyptians, attacked Egyptian territory and took captives. Muršili II recorded that these prisoners brought a plague to the Hittite kingdom. The plague lasted at least two decades and is often considered the cause of the deaths of Šuppiluliuma and his eldest son Arnuwanda II. Muršili II blamed the kingdom's misfortune on his father's cruelty, counting the murder of Tudḫaliya the Younger and the attacks on Egypt among its causes.
suppiluliuma-ii: Šuppiluliuma II was a younger son of the Hittite great king Tudḫaliya IV and succeeded his elder brother Arnuwanda III. He made his court and subjects swear oaths of allegiance, advertising his loyalty to his dead brother and his own legitimacy, since Arnuwanda left no heirs. The surviving texts hint at disloyalty and possible challenges from members of the extended royal family. Abroad, an official was sent to rebuke Ibiranu, the vassal king of Ugarit, for failing to show him respect, and Talmi-Teššub of Carchemish was bound by a new treaty and left in charge of Syria.

Two inscriptions in Hieroglyphic Luwian, one at Nişantepe in the Upper City of Hattusa and one in Chamber 2 beside the East Pond, record his wars. They tell of conquests in Wiyanawanda, Tamina, Maša, Lukka and Ikuna in south-western Anatolia, and of the defeat, sack and annexation of Tarḫuntašša, a hostile regime in a city that had once served briefly as the empire's capital. Letters mention urgent grain shipments from Merneptah of Egypt, which suggests a famine in the late 13th century BCE.

A fleet under his command defeated either the Cypriots or a group of Sea Peoples who had settled on Alašiya, the first naval battle recorded in history. Records from Ugarit show that the Hittite king asked it for help against a threat from the west.

He was probably the ruler who abandoned Hattusa. Some scholars hold that he vanished, others that he was killed in the sack of the city. The violent end of Hattusa as the capital is now doubted, and it is suspected that he moved his court elsewhere, perhaps to the south-west. Neither he nor any later ruler returned, and the Hittite Empire disappeared as such. The causes are unclear and may have combined droughts and earthquakes with internal and external strife. Hattusa's remains were burned, and its site was reoccupied by a Phrygian fortress about 500 years later.

He is generally considered the last great king of Hatti, though Zsolt Simon has proposed from a Luwian inscription on a silver bowl that he had a successor, possibly his son Tudḫaliya V. Kuzi-Teššub of Carchemish later took the title of Great King as a descendant of Šuppiluliuma I.
supreme-leader-of-iran: The office rests on the concept of vilayat-e faqih, the Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist, set out by Ruhollah Khomeini in his book Islamic Government. He argued that government must follow the sharia and that a leading Islamic jurist must provide political guardianship, a task that fell to jurists in the absence of the twelfth Imam. Before the revolution, observant Shia Muslims chose their own leading jurist to follow, known as a marja'.

In March 1979, shortly after Khomeini returned from exile and the monarchy was overthrown, a referendum asked 'Islamic Republic, yes or no?', and 98 per cent of those voting said yes. The constitution of 1906 was declared invalid, and a new constitution was ratified by referendum in the first week of December 1979. It combines theocratic and democratic elements, and it created the office. The Deputy Supreme Leader's role was incorporated into the leader's authority in 1985, when Grand Ayatollah Hussein-Ali Montazeri held it.

The constitution calls the holder the Leader, the leader of the Islamic Revolution or the leadership of the Islamic jurist; Supreme Leader is a style of respect. The holder is the head of state, takes precedence over the president, who is head of government, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and supervises the legislative, judicial and executive branches. The judiciary, state radio and television and bodies such as the Guardian Council and the Expediency Discernment Council are subject to the office, and the holder serves for life.

The Assembly of Experts, elected by voters to eight-year terms from candidates approved by the Guardian Council, is charged under Article 111 with choosing, supervising and dismissing the leader. If the office falls vacant, an interim council of the president, the head of the judiciary and one jurist of the Guardian Council temporarily takes over its duties.

The original constitution required the leader to be a marja'-e taqlid, the highest-ranking cleric in Usuli Twelver Shia law. Shortly before Khomeini's death in 1989 he fell out with his intended successor Montazeri, who had disapproved of the mass executions of political prisoners in 1988. Khomeini chose Ali Khamenei, a lower-ranking cleric, and the constitution was amended so that Islamic scholarship was enough.
sur-empire: The Sur dynasty was of Afghan origin and ruled from Sasaram in what is now Bihar. Its founder, Sher Khan, campaigned against the Bengal Sultanate, whose ruler asked Humayun for help. Humayun marched in 1537, besieged Chunar for over six months and in September 1538 occupied Gauda, which the Afghans had stripped of its treasury. Humayun made peace, and when he crossed the Karmanasa River Sher Khan attacked at the Battle of Chausa, where the Mughals lost over 7,000 dead. At Kannauj Humayun's larger army was defeated and he fled to Sindh. On 17 May 1540 Sher Khan was crowned Sher Shah, with the epithet Sultan Adil, "Just King".

Sher Shah captured Delhi, took Lahore in November 1540 and held Multan from 1541, but did not extend his rule beyond the Indus. He put down a revolt in Bengal in March 1541, divided it into 47 smaller units, and ordered Rohtas Fort built to check the Gakhars of the Punjab. In 1542 he took Gwalior and Malwa.

He took Raisen in 1543 after a six-month siege, and a force of his then destroyed the retreating Puran Mall's men, an act the sources present as justice for Muslim families wronged at Chanderi. At Sammel in 1543 he defeated Maldeo Rathore of Marwar, after forged letters made Maldeo suspect his own commanders, though his army suffered thousands of casualties.

Sher Shah was mortally wounded when a cannon burst during the siege of Kalinjar Fort and died on 22 May 1545. His second son Jalal Khan succeeded as Islam Shah and fought rebellious amirs, among them the Niazis under Haibat Khan, who took refuge among the Gakhars.

Civil war followed after his reign. The last stage of the Mughal reconquest was the siege of Mankot, where Sikandar Shah Suri surrendered to Bairam Khan on 25 July 1557 after six months, and entered the service of Akbar.

The empire was divided into iqtas, some under military governors such as Haibat Khan in the Punjab. Iqtas were divided into sarkars and these into parganas, each with a shiqdar for order and a munsif for revenue and civil justice. Village panchayats were left to govern themselves. Sher Shah's silver rupee of 178 grains became the precursor of the modern rupee. He rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road with caravanserais, mosques, wells and shade trees, set up a postal service of relay riders and abolished internal customs duties. His criminal law was harsh and made officials answerable for crimes in their districts. Historians differ on his religious policy toward Hindus.
surat: Surat stands on the banks of the Tapti River, known popularly as the Tapi, close to its confluence with the Arabian Sea. The city lies 284 km south of Gandhinagar, the state capital, 265 km south of Ahmedabad and 289 km north of Mumbai. The Gujarati, Hindi and Urdu word surat means countenance. After dams were built on the Tapi its water flow decreased and the original port facilities closed, so the nearest port is now in the Magadalla and Hazira area of the metropolitan region.

The traditional account holds that Surat was built up around 1500 by a wealthy Hindu merchant named Gopi, who asked the king of Gujarat to approve the name Suryapur, city of the sun. The Muslim king is said to have altered it to Surat, after the word surah, the name for the chapters of the Qur'an. Both names appear in sources before 1500, so the town and its name are older than Gopi's time. Before the 1500s the nearby town of Rander was the main commercial centre; it declined because of Portuguese raids, and some of its merchants probably moved to Surat.

Under the Mughal Empire Surat was the most prosperous port of the realm. Despite its wealth it looked like a typical trader's town of mud-and-bamboo tenements and crooked streets, with a few mansions and warehouses along the riverfront and the establishments of Turkish, Armenian, English, French and Dutch traders. England established its first Indian trading factory there in 1612. Shivaji looted the city twice, the first sacking coming in 1664, and his raids scared trade away. Under the British Raj Surat declined, remaining important for textile products but less important as a port.

Surat is the commercial and economic centre of South Gujarat and the administrative capital of the Surat district. The 2011 census gave it a population of 4,467,797. Its diamond trade began in the late 1950s, when the first diamond workshops of Gujarat appeared in Surat and Navsari, and its textile industry is long established. Surat railway station was built in 1860.
surat-thani: Surat Thani is a city in southern Thailand, 651 kilometres south of Bangkok, and the capital of Surat Thani Province. It lies near the mouth of the Tapi River. It is the regional commercial centre, with a seaport dealing in the main products of the province, rubber and coconuts. The city has a tropical monsoon climate with only two seasons, wet and dry. A short dry season lasts from January to April and the wet season from May to December, with the heaviest rains in October and November.

The city was previously known as Bandon, meaning village on higher ground. King Vajiravudh, Rama VI, gave it its present name, meaning city of good people, in 1915. It was given because of the intense devotion of the local people to Buddhism, and it was taken from the Indian city of Surat in Gujarat, on the Indian river Tapi, with which the king was impressed.

On 21 December 1930 Surat Thani became a sanitary district, and on 7 December 1935 it was upgraded to a town with a municipal area of 2.67 square kilometres. The municipality was enlarged to 6.95 square kilometres in 1958 and to 68.97 square kilometres in 1994, and on 4 May 2007 the town was made a city.

The city is mainly known to travellers as the jumping-off point to Ko Samui, Ko Tao and Ko Pha Ngan, and ferries run from the mainland to the islands. The Southern Line of the State Railway of Thailand links the province with Bangkok, with its main station at Phunphin, about 15 kilometres from the city, and Route 401 connects the city to Nakhon Si Thammarat. It has 132,040 inhabitants.

Local festivals include Chak Phra, which celebrates the Buddha's symbolic return to earth at the end of Buddhist Lent with a parade, floats and long-boat races, and a vegetarian festival held every October. Higher education includes the Surat Thani campus of the Prince of Songkla University and Surat Thani Rajabhat University.
surena: Surena, or Suren, was a Parthian spahbed, a general or commander, and the leader of the House of Suren. The name is the Greek and Latin form of Sūrēn, which comes from the Avestan sūra, meaning strong or exalted, and Suren remains a common name in Iran and Armenia.

Plutarch, writing about 125 years after the events in his Life of Crassus, called him an extremely distinguished man who ranked next after the king in wealth, birth and honour, and the foremost Parthian of his time in courage and ability. He wrote that Surena's army included many slaves, though the meaning of the words for slaves there is disputed, and he described his painted face and his hair parted in the fashion of the Medes, which belied his manly skill.

In 54 BCE Surena commanded troops of Orodes II at the battle for the city of Seleucia, a contest over the Arsacid succession after Mithridates IV had deposed Orodes, and he was instrumental in restoring Orodes to the throne. He was one of the most powerful men in the Parthian Empire, and he travelled with what one scholar, Gazerani, calls an unmistakably courtly retinue.

In 53 BCE the Romans advanced on the western Parthian vassal territories, and Orodes II sent his cavalry under Surena to meet them. The armies met at Carrhae, at Harrân in present-day Turkey. The superior equipment of the Parthians and their tactic of luring the Romans into the middle of the desert let them defeat the numerically larger force of Marcus Licinius Crassus.

Plutarch speaks of 20,000 Roman dead and 10,000 prisoners. The victory echoed among the peoples of the East but brought the Arsacid dynasty no territory and no decisive shift in the balance of power. Surena was then executed by Orodes II, most likely because the king saw his power and influence as a threat.

The Battle of Carrhae is commonly seen as one of the earliest and most important battles between the Roman and Parthian empires and one of the most crushing defeats in Roman history. Surena died in 53 or 52 BCE. His place in the historical tradition has been described as curiously parallel to that of Rustam in the Shahnameh. The last work of the 17th-century French dramatist Pierre Corneille, a tragedy titled Suréna, is roughly based on his story.
surendranagar-district: Surendranagar district lies in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat. It takes its name from its headquarters, which began as Wadhwan Camp, where the British political agent for Wadhwan lived. After the agent left in 1946 the town was renamed after Surendrasinhji Jorawarsinhji (1922 to 1983), then ruler of Wadhwan, though it is still called the Camp locally. When the princely states were merged the district was known as Jhalavad, the land of the Jhala Rajputs, who held many of them. A legend says the name comes from Jhalavun, a Gujarati word meaning to hold, after the mother of Harpaldev's children who held them while fending off a wild elephant.

A Harappan site found at Rangpur in 1931, the first in Gujarat, shows that the Indus Valley civilisation reached Saurashtra, and Late Stone Age tools were found at Sejakpur in 1957-58. The early history is unclear, but the district was probably ruled in turn by the Mauryas, Indo-Greeks, Western Satraps, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Chaulukyas, then the Delhi Sultanate. In 1407 the governors of Gujarat declared independence and the district became part of the Gujarat Sultanate. After 1573 it was part of the Mughal Gujarat Subah, though real control lay with many local rulers and landlords.

In the British period the district held several states. Dhrangadhra, Wadhwan and Limbdi were ruled by Jhala Rajputs, who claimed descent from Harpaldev, a son of Kesar Makwana. Bajana was founded by Malik Haider Khan, a Jat leader driven out of Sindh, and Dasada was ruled by the Multani Maliks. Dhandhalapur passed from the Babarias to the Khadvads in 1790.

The district had a population of 1,756,268 at the 2011 census, and Gujarati was spoken by 98.77 per cent of people. Its salt pans, especially around Kharaghoda, supply a large part of India's salt, and it is a centre of cotton ginning. The Surendranagar Cotton Oil and Oilseeds Association, founded in 1964, was the first cotton futures exchange in India. The Gangavo kund at Dedadara dates to the 11th century, and a legend tells of Ranakdevi, who died by sati on the banks of the Bhogavo near Wadhwan.
suriname: Suriname lies on the Guiana Shield on the northern coast of South America, bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the north, French Guiana to the east, Brazil to the south and Guyana to the west. It is the smallest sovereign country in South America. The northern lowland coast has been cultivated, and most of the people live there. The south is tropical rainforest and sparsely inhabited savanna, covering about 80% of the land. The name may come from an Indigenous people called the Surinen, who lived there at the time of European contact. British settlers wrote it Surinam, which long remained the standard English spelling until the official change to Suriname in January 1978.

Indigenous settlement dates back to about 3,000 BCE. The Lokono were a nomadic coastal people who lived by hunting, foraging and fishing, and the Carib, using superior sailing ships, conquered them. British settlers founded the first European colony at Marshall's Creek on the Suriname River in 1630. Jews, expelled from Spain and Portugal, began to settle from the early 17th century and were granted freedom of religion in 1665. In 1667, in the negotiations leading to the Treaty of Breda, the Dutch kept the plantation colony they had gained from the English, and the English kept New Amsterdam, which they renamed New York.

Under Dutch rule Suriname was a lucrative plantation colony, mostly of sugar, driven by African slave labour. About 300,000 enslaved Africans were taken there from the mid-1600s to the early 1800s. After slavery was abolished in 1863, indentured servants were recruited mostly from British India and the Dutch East Indies. Suriname became a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954 and independent on 25 November 1975.

Suriname is a representative democratic republic under the Constitution of 1987. Paramaribo is the capital and largest city, home to nearly half the population. Dutch is the official language, and Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is widely used. No ethnic group forms a majority. The population includes descendants of indentured workers from India, Java and China and of enslaved Africans, among them the Maroons, whose ancestors escaped to the interior. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve, established in 1998, became a World Heritage Site in 2000.
suriname-river: The Suriname River is 480 kilometres long. It rises in the Guiana Highlands on the border between the Wilhelmina Mountains and the Eilerts de Haan Mountains, where it is known as the Gran Rio, and the Upper Suriname begins at the confluence of the Gran Rio and the Pikin Rio near the village of Goddo. The Brokopondo Reservoir, held back by the Afobaka Dam, divides the river into two sections. The lower river passes Berg en Dal, Jodensavanne, Carolina and Domburg before reaching Paramaribo on its left bank. It is joined by the Commewijne at Nieuw-Amsterdam and enters the Atlantic at the sandspit of Braamspunt.

The name Suriname may derive from an indigenous people called the Surinen, who lived in the area at the time of European contact. Early sources spell the river's name in many ways. Lawrence Kemys wrote of a river called Shurinama, and a Dutch fleet in 1598 mentioned the river Surinamo. A Dutch notary in 1617 wrote Surrenant for the river where a Dutch trading post had existed three years earlier, and in 1634 David Pietersz. de Vries wrote of travelling up the Sername river until he met the English colony there.

A Spanish manuscript of 1640 called the river Soronama. In 1653 instructions to a British fleet sailing to meet Lord Willoughby in Barbados used the spelling Surinam, which remained standard in English, and a royal charter of 1663 spoke of the region as called Serrinam also Surrinam.

The Suriname is the country's most important river for trade. Vessels carrying bauxite, aluminium oxide and aluminium leave by it, and nearly all vessels carrying materials vital to the country enter at Braamspunt to unload at the harbours of Paramaribo, Smalkalden and Paranam. During the Second World War the German cargo ship Goslar was scuttled in the river to keep it from Allied hands, and its wreck remains visible. The Jules Wijdenbosch Bridge at Paramaribo opened in 2000 and gives access to the eastern part of the country.
surrender-of-japan: By 1945 Japan had suffered nearly two years of defeats in the South West Pacific, India, the Marianas and the Philippines. After the loss of Saipan in July 1944 General Hideki Tōjō was replaced as prime minister by General Kuniaki Koiso, and after the loss of the Philippines Koiso was replaced by Admiral Kantarō Suzuki. The Allies took Iwo Jima and Okinawa in the first half of 1945, and Okinawa was to be a staging area for the invasion of the Home Islands.

Policy was made by the Supreme Council for the Direction of the War, the so-called Big Six. In the summer Japan's leaders privately asked the Soviet Union, then neutral, to mediate, while the Soviets prepared to attack in Manchuria in fulfilment of promises made at the Tehran and Yalta Conferences. On 26 July the United States, the United Kingdom and China issued the Potsdam Declaration, calling for unconditional surrender.

On 6 August 1945 the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Late on 8 August the Soviet Union declared war, in violation of the Soviet–Japanese Neutrality Pact, and invaded Manchuria soon after midnight. A second atomic bomb fell on Nagasaki on 9 August. The Big Six and the cabinet remained split, and Emperor Hirohito then ordered the council to accept the Potsdam terms. After several more days of negotiations, including a failed coup attempt by army hardliners between 12 and 15 August, he announced the surrender in a recorded radio address on 15 August.

The Emperor gave the public the new and cruel bomb as his reason and told the military that the Soviet entry into the war threatened the empire's foundation. The occupation began on 28 August under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, and the formal ceremony took place on 2 September aboard the battleship USS Missouri, where Japanese officials signed the Instrument of Surrender.

Allied countries marked V-J Day. Isolated Japanese soldiers refused to surrender for months and years afterwards, some into the 1970s. The Soviet Union continued fighting until early September and took the Kuril Islands, but its plan to occupy Hokkaido was frustrated by President Truman's opposition. The state of war formally ended when the Treaty of San Francisco came into force on 28 April 1952, and Japan and the Soviet Union ended theirs with a joint declaration in 1956. The part played by the atomic bombings in the surrender, and the ethics of the two attacks, remain debated.
suryavarman-ii: Suryavarman II, whose name begins with a Sanskrit root meaning sun, grew up on a provincial estate at a time of weakening central control in the empire. An inscription names his father as Ksitindraditya and his mother as Narendralakshmi. As a young prince he contended that he had a legitimate claim to the throne. He appears to have dealt with a rival claimant from the line of Harshavarman III, probably Nripatindravarman, and then to have turned on the elderly king Dharanindravarman I, his great uncle; scholars disagree about which of the two an inscription describes him killing.
In 1114 he sent a mission to the Chola emperor Kulothunga Chola I in south India. He was enthroned in 1113, with the Brahmin sage Divakarapandita officiating, and formally crowned in 1119.

During his decades in power the king reunited the empire, and vassals paid him tribute. His large military operations against the Chams and Dai Viet were largely unsuccessful. Vietnamese and Cham sources record three major attacks in Nghe An and Quang Binh provinces. In 1128 he is said to have led 20,000 soldiers against Dai Viet and been defeated, and the next year sent a fleet of more than 700 vessels against its coast.

In 1145 he appears to have invaded Champa, sacked its capital Vijaya and placed a new king, Harideva, on the throne, but Cham forces under Jaya Harivarman I recaptured the capital and killed Harideva. In 1116 he resumed formal relations with China, and in 1128 the emperor conferred high dignities on him as a great vassal of the empire.

He presided over the building of Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu and Shiva, whose five central towers evoke the peaks of Mount Meru. Other temples of his reign include Banteay Samre, Thommanon, Chau Say Tevoda and Beng Mealea. He made Vishnu, rather than Shiva, the focus of court religion, which was unusual among Khmer kings; scholars debate whether this explains why Angkor Wat faces west.

Inscriptions suggest that Suryavarman II died around 1150, possibly during a campaign against Champa, after his troops had been defeated by Vietnamese forces under Tô Hiến Thành. His cousin Dharanindravarman II succeeded him, and a period of weak rule and feuding began. He was given the posthumous name Paramavishnuloka, and Angkor Wat appears to have been completed only after his death. He is the first Khmer king depicted in art, seated on a dais in a bas-relief in the south gallery of Angkor Wat.
susa: Susa lay in the lower Zagros Mountains, about 250 km east of the Tigris, between the Karkheh and Dez rivers. Its name is of Elamite origin and appears in many languages, as Šušan in Elamite, Soûsa in Greek, Shushan in Hebrew and Šuš in New Persian. It appears in the earliest Sumerian records, among the places obedient to Inanna in Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta. Aeschylus set his play The Persians there, and the Book of Esther is set in Shushan.

Calibrated carbon-14 dates place the foundation of a settlement as early as 4200 BCE. Its inhabitants soon built a monumental platform, and a thousand or more graves near its base held ceramic vessels of great artistry. During the Uruk period Susa fell within the Uruk cultural sphere, though Daniel T. Potts argues that it adopted Uruk's writing selectively. From about 3100 BCE tablets appear and Susa became the centre of Elam. Sargon the Great took Susiana into the Akkadian Empire in about 2330 BCE. Around 1175 BCE Shutruk-Nahhunte plundered the stele bearing the Code of Hammurabi and took it to Susa, where archaeologists found it in 1901.

Cyrus the Great captured Susa in 540 or 539 BCE, bringing it under Persian control for the first time. After Alexander the Great invaded, the satrap of Susa surrendered, and in 324 BCE Alexander held a mass wedding of Persians and Macedonians there. Under the Seleucids it was called Seleucia on the Eulaeus. Trajan briefly captured it in 116 CE. Ardashir I conquered and destroyed it in 224 CE but rebuilt it. An Arab army under Abu Musa al-Ash'ari besieged it after taking Tustar in 642.

The ancient centre is unoccupied, and the population lives in the adjacent town of Shush, in Khuzestan province. The first French excavations were made in 1885 and 1886 by Marcel-Auguste and Jane Dieulafoy, who found glazed bricks and column bases from the palace of the Achaemenid kings. A tomb presumed to be that of the prophet Daniel stands in the area. Susa was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2015.
susan-b-anthony: Susan Anthony was born on 15 February 1820 in Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children of Daniel Anthony and Lucy Read Anthony, in a Quaker family committed to social equality. She added the middle initial B. in her youth, after her father's sister Susan, who had married a man named Brownell, though she never used that name herself. She collected anti-slavery petitions at the age of 17, and in 1856 she became the New York state agent for the American Anti-Slavery Society.

In 1851 she met Elizabeth Cady Stanton, who became her lifelong friend and co-worker. In 1863 they organised the Women's Loyal National League. It collected nearly 400,000 signatures for the abolition of slavery in the largest petition drive in the nation's history up to that time, with Anthony as chief organiser of some 2,000 petition collectors. After the war they began the weekly newspaper The Revolution in 1868, and in May 1869 they formed the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1890 their organisation merged with a rival to form the National American Woman Suffrage Association, with Anthony as its key force.

In 1872 she was arrested in Rochester, New York, for voting, and she was convicted in a widely publicised trial; she refused to pay the fine, and the authorities took no further action. In 1878 she and Stanton arranged for Congress to be presented with the amendment later called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment. She travelled extensively, giving as many as 75 to 100 speeches a year, and helped found the International Council of Women, which met in Washington in 1888.

Anthony died at the age of 86 at her home in Rochester on 13 March 1906. At a birthday celebration in Washington a few days earlier she had spoken of her fellow workers and said that with such women, failure is impossible, a phrase that became a watchword of the women's movement. The amendment was ratified as the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. Her home in Rochester is a National Historic Landmark, and in 1979 she became the first female citizen to be shown on a United States coin.
sushruta: Suśruta, whose name means well heard in Sanskrit, was an ancient Indian physician and surgeon. He was born in Kanyakubja and later moved to Varanasi, where he wrote the Compendium of Suśruta. The printed editions of the work open each chapter with the phrase as Lord Dhanvantari declared, framing it as Dhanvantari's discourse, but the earliest manuscripts omit this and present it as the work of Divodāsa, king of Varanasi.

Scholars now generally accept that several ancient authors contributed to the text, and that several of them used the name Suśruta, which makes misattribution possible. Rao suggested in 1985 that an original layer by an elder Sushruta was later reworked by another Sushruta and by Nāgārjuna, and that the Uttara-tantra was added as a supplement. Modern scholarship places the composition in the first millennium BCE. The surviving text is a composite that may have begun in the last centuries BCE, and it was probably known to Dṛḍhabala, a contributor to the Charaka Samhita in the fourth or fifth century CE.

The Suśrutasaṃhitā has 186 chapters and addresses general medicine, including diet, surgery, nosology, anatomy, developmental biology, therapeutics, toxicology and paediatrics. It is considered a foundational text of Ayurveda. Its chapters on surgery are historically important, but they have wrongly led some to believe that surgery is its main subject. G. D. Singhal called Suśruta the father of plastic surgery on account of its detailed accounts.

The text describes how students were taught. They studied for six years before hands-on training, then practised incisions on vegetables, dead animals or soft or rotting wood, and observed real procedures before operating themselves. Sushruta laid down rules for cleanliness: instruments of iron or copper were to be kept sharp and clean, and the operating room and wards fumigated with the smoke of guggulu, vacha, white mustard, rock salt and neem leaves.

The work describes the reconstruction of a nose with skin from the forehead or cheek, often for criminals punished by amputation. This method was historically known as the Indian method. According to reports in The Gentleman's Magazine of October 1794, Indians still practised Sushruta's surgical methods in the late 18th century.
susquehanna-river: The river forms from two main branches. The North Branch, regarded as the main branch, rises at the outlet of Otsego Lake in Cooperstown, New York, and the West Branch rises in western Pennsylvania and joins it near Northumberland. The river drains 71,000 square kilometres, including nearly half of Pennsylvania, and cuts through a succession of water gaps in the Appalachians. It enters the northern end of the Chesapeake Bay at Havre de Grace, Maryland, and provides half of the bay's freshwater inflow. The bay itself lies in the flooded valley of the Susquehanna.

At European contact the lower valley was held by the Susquehannock, first described by John Smith, who explored the upper Chesapeake in 1608. They traded furs with Virginia, New Sweden and New Netherland, fought Maryland until a treaty in 1652, and were attacked by the Haudenosaunee. By the 1670s disease and war had sharply cut their numbers, and a remnant settled on the Conestoga River in the late 1680s. The Haudenosaunee then claimed the valley by conquest and let displaced Lenape, Shawnee, Conoy, Nanticoke and Mahican groups settle at Shamokin and in the Wyoming Valley. In December 1763 the Scots-Irish vigilantes known as the Paxton Boys massacred the remaining Conestoga.

William Penn negotiated with the Haudenosaunee to open land along the Susquehanna, and in the first half of the 18th century thousands of German and Scots-Irish immigrants settled the lower valley. Lancaster County was founded in 1729. In July 1778 Loyalist soldiers and Seneca warriors under Major John Butler destroyed most of the Patriot militia at the Battle of Wyoming, and in 1779 Brigadier General James Clinton and Major General John Sullivan led a campaign down the river and up the Chemung, destroying 40 Seneca and Cayuga villages and winter food stores.

In the early 19th century canals beside the river carried anthracite coal to Atlantic ports, and Harrisburg replaced Lancaster as the state capital in 1812. Railways made the canals unprofitable by the 1850s. Before the Port Deposit Bridge opened in 1818 the river could be crossed only by ferry, so it formed a barrier between the northern and southern states.

The river is about 715 kilometres long and is the longest river on the East Coast of the United States. About 200 bridges cross it, among them the Rockville Bridge at Harrisburg, built in 1902, which is the longest stone masonry arch bridge in the world. The river was designated an American Heritage River in 1997. Floods from Hurricane Agnes in 1972 were among the worst in its recorded history.
sutan-sjahrir: Sutan Sjahrir was born on 5 March 1909 in Padang Panjang, West Sumatra, into a Minangkabau family. His father, Muhammad Rasyad Maharajo Sutan, was chief public prosecutor at the Landraad in Medan, where the family lived, and had six wives. Sjahrir was a half-brother of Rohana Kudus, an advocate of women's education and a journalist. He attended the Europeesche Lagere School and the MULO in Medan and then the Algemene Middelbare School in Bandung, where he directed and acted with a student theatre group and helped found a People's University against illiteracy.

In 1929 he went to the Netherlands on a scholarship and studied at the University of Amsterdam and then law at Leiden University, where he came to value socialist principles. He became briefly secretary of the Perhimpoenan Indonesia, from which he and Mohammad Hatta were expelled in 1931 as communist influence grew.

Sjahrir went ahead to the Dutch East Indies in 1931 to help set up the Indonesian National Party and wrote for its newspaper, Daulat Rajat. The Dutch imprisoned him and Hatta at Cipinang in March 1934 and convicted them in November for nationalist activities. They were exiled to Boven-Digoel in 1935, a year later to Banda and shortly before the Japanese conquest of 1941 to Sukabumi.

Under the Japanese occupation Sjahrir, who was ill with tuberculosis, took little public part. He, Sukarno and Hatta agreed that he would go underground and organise resistance while the other two cooperated with the occupiers. His pamphlet Our Struggle (Perdjoeangan Kita) of 1945 appeared amid the violence of the early Bersiap period and called for understanding of other ethnic groups, against racist outbursts.

Sukarno appointed Sjahrir prime minister in November 1945, at 36 the youngest world leader. He served until June 1947. His non-cooperation with the Japanese made him one of the few Republican leaders acceptable to the Dutch government, and in 1946 he played a crucial role in negotiating the Linggadjati Agreement, which some political adversaries opposed.

He founded the Indonesian Socialist Party in 1948 to oppose the Indonesian Communist Party. It was small but influential in the early years because of its leaders' education, and it did poorly in the 1955 elections. Sukarno banned it in August 1960 for supporting a rebellion in Sumatra and opposing his policies. In 1962 Sjahrir was jailed on alleged conspiracy charges and never tried. He had a stroke in 1965, lost his speech and was sent to Zürich, where he died on 9 April 1966. That day he was named a National Hero of Indonesia. The former Dutch prime minister Professor Schermerhorn called him a noble political warrior.
sutherland: Sutherland is a historic county, registration county and lieutenancy area, stretching from the Atlantic in the west to the Pentland Firth and the North Sea in the east. It is Scotland's fifth-largest county by area but has a smaller population than a medium-sized Lowland town. The west and north coasts have very high sea cliffs and deep sea lochs, and Cape Wrath is the most north-westerly point in Scotland. Ben More Assynt, at 998 metres, is the tallest peak in the county, and in the west isolated sandstone peaks such as Foinaven, Arkle and Suilven rise from Lewisian gneiss.

Much of the area belonged to the Pictish kingdom of Cat, which also included Caithness. In the 9th century it was conquered by Sigurd Eysteinsson, Jarl of Orkney, and the Scottish crown claimed overlordship from Norway in 1098. The Diocese of Caithness was established in the 12th century, and its seat moved to Dornoch Cathedral, begun in 1224. About then an earldom of Sutherland was made from the southern part of the earldom of Orkney and Caithness. A shire called Sutherland was created in 1633, with Dornoch as head burgh, and the county ceased to be used for local government in 1975.

The Sutherland Estate, about two thirds of the county, saw the largest clearances in the Highlands, mostly in 1812, 1814 and 1819-20. In the last of these, 1,068 families, an estimated 5,400 people, were evicted. They were offered resettlement on the coast with work in fishing, but many moved to farms in Caithness or emigrated to Canada, the United States or Australia.

The clearances concentrated Gaelic speakers in the new fishing villages and so prolonged the language there. East Sutherland Gaelic, spoken around Golspie, Brora and Embo, was the last Gaelic dialect commonly spoken on the east coast of Scotland, and its last known native speaker died in 2020.

The population peaked at 25,793 in 1851 and fell to 12,803 by the 2011 census. Four of Scotland's National Scenic Areas lie wholly or partly in the county. The pre-1975 boundaries are still used for land registration. A flag adopted in 2018 shows an overlapping saltire and Nordic cross, for Scottish and Norwegian heritage.
sutlej-river: The Sutlej is a major river of Asia, flowing through China, India and Pakistan, and is the longest of the five major rivers of the Punjab. It is also known as Satadru and is the easternmost tributary of the Indus. It rises on the Tibetan plateau at the lakes of Manasarovar and Rakshastal, on the southern slope of Mount Kailash, about 4,570 metres above sea level, and is fed by snow and glaciers. Under the Tibetan name Langqên Zangbo, meaning Elephant River, it flows west-northwest for about 260 kilometres to the Shipki La pass and enters India in Himachal Pradesh.

It then turns south-west, passes through the Bhakra gorge and the Anandpur Dun, and leaves the hills near Ropar to enter the plains of the Punjab. It meets the Beas near Harike, enters Pakistan, and joins the Chenab to form the Panjnad, which flows into the Indus.

The Sanskrit name was Shutudri, and it was also called Zaradros. In the Mahabharata the sage Vasishtha leapt into it, and it is said to have divided into a hundred streams, so that it became the river of a hundred courses. The upper valley was known as the Garuda Valley to the Zhangzhung, the ancient civilisation of western Tibet, who built a palace called Kyunglung there; they were eventually conquered by the Tibetan Empire.

The river was the main means of transport for the kings of the region, and in the early 18th century it carried deodar timber to Bilaspur, Hamirpur and other places along its banks. It also formed the eastern boundary of the Sikh Empire under Maharajah Ranjit Singh.

Before the 11th century the Sutlej did not join the Indus but flowed into the Hakra or Ghaggar River by one or more old channels. Geological evidence suggests that before about 1700 BCE, and perhaps much earlier, it was an important tributary of the Ghaggar-Hakra, thought by some to be the Sarasvati. Authors put its redirection at various dates, from before 8000 BCE to 2000 BCE.

If the diversion was recent, it may have caused the Ghaggar-Hakra to dry up and Harappan settlements along it to be abandoned, though the Sutlej may have been captured by the Indus thousands of years earlier.

The Sutlej is an antecedent river, one that existed before the Himalayas and cut its way down as they rose. Its waters are allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty and are mostly diverted into irrigation canals such as the Sirhind Canal and the Rajasthan canal. The Bhakra Dam, with 1,325 MW of generating capacity, supplies irrigation to Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana, and further hydroelectric works stand upstream, including the Nathpa Jhakri and Karcham Wangtoo plants.
sutri: Sutri, in Latin Sutrium, lies in the province of Viterbo, about 50 kilometres from Rome and about 30 kilometres south of Viterbo. It stands on a narrow tuff hill surrounded by ravines, with a narrow neck on the west alone connecting it with the surrounding country. In antiquity it commanded the road into Etruria, the later Via Cassia, and Livy describes it as one of the keys of Etruria, the nearby town of Nepi being the other.

Sutrium came into the hands of Rome after the fall of Veii, and a Latin colony was founded there. It was lost again in 386 BCE, but was recovered and recolonised around 383 BCE. The Etruscans besieged it in 311-310 BCE without taking it, and in 209 BCE it joined Nepi and ten other Latin colonies in refusing further help to Rome in the Second Punic War. It received a colony of veterans under the triumvirs and was a place of some importance under the empire. It was later occupied by the Lombards.

In 728 the Lombard king Liutprand and Pope Gregory II reached an agreement there by which Sutri and some hill towns in Latium were given to the papacy, as a gift to the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. It was the first extension of papal territory beyond the Duchy of Rome. A hoard of jewellery of this period, the Sutri Treasure, was found near the town in the 19th century and is in the British Museum.

The Synod of Sutri was convened at the request of Emperor Henry III to resolve three rival claims to the papacy, and ended in favour of Pope Clement II; Gregory VI abdicated at Sutri on 20 December 1046. In 1433 the condottiero Niccolò Fortebraccio set fire to Sutri, and from then on it declined in favour of Ronciglione.

The modern comune has a few more than 5,000 inhabitants. Its remains draw tourists: a Roman amphitheatre cut in the tuff, of elliptical plan and about 49 by 40 metres, an Etruscan necropolis with dozens of rock-cut tombs, and ancient walls of rectangular tuff blocks. The cathedral is Romanesque in origin but largely modern, keeping a belltower of 1207 and a crypt of the Lombard period. The church of the Madonna del Parto was developed from an Etruscan tomb and, according to some scholars, was a Mithraeum.
sutton-hoo: Sutton Hoo lies on the bank of the tidal estuary of the River Deben, opposite the town of Woodbridge, which stands 11 kilometres from the North Sea and below the lowest convenient fording place. The estuary formed a way into East Anglia after the end of Roman rule in Britain. The name derives from Old English, meaning the southern farmstead on a hill shaped like a heel spur.

The land was farmed in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, when timber roundhouses stood there, and again in the Iron Age and Romano-British period, when it was divided into small enclosures. After the Romans withdrew, Angles and Saxons settled in the south-east of Britain, and East Anglia is regarded by many scholars as a region where this settlement was early and dense.

Two Anglo-Saxon cemeteries of the 6th to 7th centuries stand there. They appear as about twenty earth mounds, the tops of which have been flattened by farming. The earliest burials are probably cremations, such as those under Mounds 3 and 4, which held ashes of a man and a horse and of a man, a woman and a horse, with imported objects from the eastern Mediterranean.

Mound 2 held a chamber burial covered by a small ship. Other graves are those of people who died violently, some by hanging and decapitation, thought to have been executed from the 8th and 9th centuries onwards near a gallows that may have stood on Mound 5.

4 metres wide, whose timber had decayed but left its form in the sand. In the chamber lay a crested and masked helmet comparable to those of Vendel and Valsgärde in eastern Sweden, a sword with a gold and garnet pommel, a shield, spears, a gold buckle with a hollow chamber, shoulder-clasps, drinking horns from aurochs, a lyre, silver from the Eastern Roman Empire and textiles.
Scholars believe that Rædwald, the first king of the East Angles, is the most likely person buried in the ship. The finds have prompted comparison with the world of the poem Beowulf.

Edith Pretty, owner of the land, had Basil Brown, a self-taught Suffolk excavator, dig from June 1938, and national scholars took over when the importance of Mound 1 became clear. Further excavations were led by Rupert Bruce-Mitford of the British Museum from 1965 to 1971 and by Martin Carver from 1983 to 1992. The principal finds are in the British Museum, which received the treasure as a gift from Pretty. The site is in the care of the National Trust, whose visitor centre holds replicas and a reconstruction of the burial chamber.
suva: Suva lies around a harbour on a hilly peninsula in the south-east corner of Viti Levu, between Laucala Bay and Suva Harbour, in Rewa Province. The mountains to the north and west catch the south-east trade winds, so conditions are moist all year. The city has a tropical rainforest climate and averages about 3,000 millimetres of rain a year, with no true dry season. Fiji's second governor, Sir Arthur Gordon, is said to have remarked that he had never seen it rain anywhere as it rains in Suva. Although the city is almost surrounded by sea, its coast is lined with mangroves, and a significant part of the centre, including the Parliament buildings, stands on reclaimed mangrove swamp.

In 1868, when Suva was still a small village, the Bauan chieftain Seru Epenisa Cakobau granted 5,000 square kilometres of land to the Australian-based Polynesia Company in exchange for its promise to pay off debts owed to the United States. More than a tenth of that land, 575 square kilometres, was near Suva. The company meant to develop cotton farming, but the land and climate proved unsuitable. Control of the Fiji Islands was ceded to the United Kingdom in 1874.

The colonial authorities moved the capital to Suva from Levuka, on Ovalau, because Levuka's position between a steep mountain and the sea made expansion impractical. Colonel F. E. Pratt of the Royal Engineers, appointed Surveyor-General in 1875, designed the new capital, assisted by W. Stephens and Colonel R. W. Stewart. Suva became a municipality in 1910 under the Municipal Constitution Ordinance of 1909, and its area stayed at one square mile until 1952, when it annexed the Muanikau and Samabula wards. In October of that year it was designated a city, Fiji's first. Later it took in Tamavua and the Cunningham area.

Among its colonial-period landmarks are the Suva City Carnegie Library, built in 1909, and Government House, built in 1882, destroyed by a lightning fire in 1921 and rebuilt in 1928. The government building complex stands on a drained creek bed, with foundations of reinforced concrete pilings driven in from 1935, and was completed in 1939. The Fiji Museum was founded in 1904 and moved to Thurston Gardens in 1954.

Suva is the capital and most populous settlement of Fiji, with 93,874 people at the 2017 census and a metropolitan population of 268,423. Indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians form the bulk of its population, alongside Rotumans, Lauans, Europeans, part-Europeans and Chinese. English is the most widely spoken language, with Fijian, Fiji Hindi and others also used.
