It is the site of the main campus of the University of the South Pacific, and Kings Wharf handles much of Fiji's international shipping. Suva hosted the Pacific Games in 1963, 1979 and 2003.
suwalki: The name derives from the Lithuanian su- (near) and valka (creek, marsh), meaning a place near a small river or swampy area. The Czarna Hańcza river flows through the town, which lies about 30 km from the south-western border of Lithuania, beside the Via Baltica road that links Warsaw with Kaunas, Riga, Tallinn and Helsinki. The Suwałki Landscape Park and Wigry National Park lie nearby. It has among the coldest climates of the larger Polish towns, and is often called the Polish pole of cold.

Yotvingian and Prussian tribes lived in the area from the early Middle Ages. After the Teutonic Order arrived in Yotvingia their lands were conquered and stayed largely depopulated for centuries. In 1667 John II Casimir, Grand Duke of Lithuania and King of Poland, granted the land around the future town to the Camaldolese monks, who built a monastery and church at Wigry. The village is first mentioned in 1688, and two years later it had just two houses.

Growth was fast. By 1700 the village was split into Lesser and Greater Suwałki, on the trade route from Grodno and Merkinė to Königsberg. In 1710 Augustus II the Strong granted it the right to hold fairs and markets, and in 1715 the order's grand master, Ildefons, gave it town rights, dividing it into 300 lots. Augustus II approved the rights on 2 May 1720 and a coat of arms showing Saint Roch and Saint Romuald. After the Partitions of Poland the area passed to Prussia in 1795, and the Wigry monastery was dissolved in 1796. Suwałki then had 1,184 inhabitants, a large part of them Jewish.

After the Congress of Vienna Suwałki belonged to Congress Poland under the Russian Empire, and in 1816 the government of the new Augustów Voivodeship was gradually moved there. It later became capital of the Augustów and then the Suwałki Gubernia. By 1857 it had 11,273 inhabitants, making it the fourth most populous town of Congress Poland. In the Second World War it was annexed to East Prussia as Sudauen. Almost all of its Jewish community of about 7,000 was deported and murdered, and the Germans ran the Stalag I-F camp for Soviet prisoners of war at Krzywólka. The Red Army took the town on 23 October 1944, and most of its historic buildings had survived.

Suwałki is the capital of Suwałki County and had a population of 69,206 in 2021. Its sights include the Saint Alexander Co-Cathedral, Neoclassical Kościuszko street and a cemetery complex holding Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, Jewish and Muslim graves. The poet Maria Konopnicka, author of Rota, is among its notable people, and a museum stands in her childhood home.
suwayda: The city was founded by the Nabataeans as Suada. In the Hellenistic period and under the Roman Empire it was known as Dionysias Soada, after Dionysus, the patron of wine, in a wine-producing region. The name Dionysias replaced the Nabataean one in 149 CE, as Nabataean influence declined and Hellenization accelerated in Coele-Syria. Dionysias belonged to the Roman province of Arabia Petraea and received the rights of a civitas under Commodus, between 180 and 185. Dionysus was worshipped in the same Nabataean temple that had been dedicated to Dushara. In the Byzantine period, under the influence of the Ghassanids, it was a diocese with a suffragan bishop from Bosra, and after the early Muslim conquests it became a titular see.

In 1516 the Ottoman Empire took the area from the Mamluk Sultanate. An Ottoman tax register of 1596 lists the place as Majdal Sawda, with five households and five bachelors, all Muslim. In the late 17th or early 18th century Druze from Mount Lebanon and other parts of Syria migrated in large numbers to the Jabal Hauran, which came to be called Jabal al-Druze, the Druze Mountain. They settled the deserted but defensible ancient villages there, and Suwayda was among the villages settled before 1812. By at least 1860 it was the main Druze settlement of the region. In the 19th century the French statesman and antiquarian William Waddington identified Dionysias as Suwayda.

Suwayda is the capital of the Suwayda Governorate, one of Syria's fourteen governorates, on the border with Jordan. The 2004 census gave it 73,641 inhabitants. It is a Druze-majority city with small Christian, mostly Greek Orthodox, and Sunni Muslim Bedouin minorities. The Bedouin live mainly on its northern and eastern outskirts.

The old part of the city holds ancient remains. Eight decorated columns of the Temple of Dionysus-Dushara still stand, and the Basilica of Saint Sergius dates from the fifth century. An arch of a ruined church, known locally as the Gallows, bears grape motifs. Old Roman houses are still lived in, and a 7th-century mosque from the time of the Rashidun Caliphate is also recorded. Much of the old city awaits excavation, including a Roman aqueduct and a larger Roman theatre.
suwon: Suwon lies in the north of the Gyeonggi plain, in a basin-like terrain among low hills. Gwanggyosan, at 582 metres, is its highest point, and the Yellow Sea coast is not far to the west. The name means water source, and almost all of the names the area has borne since antiquity share that meaning. The present name was given in 1310. The streams that rise on the hills flow south to the Yellow Sea at Asan Bay, and the city has eleven small reservoirs, one of which, Irwang Reservoir, has been designated a world heritage site for irrigation. Four districts make up the city: Jangan, Gwonseon, Paldal and Yeongtong.

Artefacts from the Bronze Age to the early Iron Age have been found in the area. In the Three Kingdoms period it was a territory of the statelet Mosuguk, part of the Mahan confederacy. It came under the influence of Goguryeo in the late 5th century, became part of Unified Silla and then fell to Goryeo after a campaign led by King Taejo. Under Joseon it was made an administrative centre of Gyeonggi Province in 1395. Until the late 18th century Suwon was administered from the foot of Hwasan. In 1796 King Jeongjo moved it to its present site at the foot of Paldalsan and commanded the building of Hwaseong Fortress to protect the new town.

Suwon became a city on 15 August 1949. In the Korean War, on 27 June 1950, United States planes there were attacked by North Korean fighters in the Battle of Suwon Airfield, the first aerial combat of the war. The city fell to the North on 4 July 1950 and changed hands four times in all. An eyewitness account by a US intelligence officer places a massacre of about 1,800 people at Suwon in late June 1950. The provincial headquarters of Gyeonggi began moving there from Seoul in 1964.

Hwaseong Fortress is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Four main gates pierce its walls, and Haenggung Palace stands in the centre. The city once lay entirely within the walls but has long since grown far beyond them. Suwon is traditionally known as the City of Filial Piety. It has about 1.2 million inhabitants and is home to Sungkyunkwan University and Ajou University, and the research and development centre of Samsung Electronics. Three expressways, the national railway and three lines of the Seoul Metropolitan Subway serve it.
suyab: Suyab, also called Ordukent, lay in the Chu river valley some 50 kilometres east of Bishkek and 8 kilometres west-south-west of Tokmok, in present-day Kyrgyzstan. A settlement of Sogdian merchants grew up there along the Silk Road in the 5th or 6th century. Its name comes from the Suyab River, an Iranian name meaning toward the water. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who passed in 629, described a walled city where merchants from many nations gathered, with a cold, windy climate and millet and grapes grown in the soil.

Under Tong Yabghu Qaghan, Suyab was the principal capital of the Western Turkic Khaganate, which also had a summer capital at Navekat. The Sogdians provided economic prosperity and the Göktürks military security. After the khaganate fell, Suyab was absorbed into the Tang dynasty and served as a military outpost between 648 and 719. A Chinese fortress was built in 679 by Wang Fangyi, and Buddhism flourished. According to some accounts the poet Li Bai was born there. The Old Book of Tang says the city had twelve gates on four sides, curved to hide its inhabitants.

Suyab was one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi until 719, when it passed to Suluk of the Türgesh, whom the Tang court named Loyal and Obedient Qaghan. After Suluk was murdered in 738, Tang forces retook it, and it was strategically important in the wars against the Tibetan Empire. The traveller Du Huan found a working Buddhist monastery among its ruins in 751. In 766 it fell to a Karluk ruler allied with the nascent Uyghur Khaganate, and little is recorded after the Chinese left the Four Garrisons in 787. The Hudud al-Alam, completed in 983, lists it as a city of 20,000 inhabitants. It is believed to have been supplanted by Balasagun in the early 11th century and abandoned soon after.

In the 19th century the ruins at Ak-Beshim were wrongly identified with Balasagun, the capital of the Kara-Khitans, and Vasily Bartold supported this after visiting in 1893–1894. Excavations began in 1938, and in the 1950s it was shown that the site had been abandoned in the 11th century, while Balasagun flourished until the 14th. The site covers some 30 hectares and holds Chinese fortifications, Nestorian Christian churches, Zoroastrian ossuaries and Turkic balbals, with many Buddha statues and stelae. There was a 7th-century Nestorian church and cemetery, and probably a 10th-century monastery with frescoes and inscriptions in Sogdian and Uyghur scripts. The ruins were inscribed in 2014 as part of the Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor World Heritage Site.
suzdal: Suzdal lies on the Kamenka, a tributary of the Nerl, 26 kilometres north of the city of Vladimir. Its name is thought to rest on an Old Russian verb meaning to make from clay, and more likely derives from the nickname of a person, perhaps a potter or bricklayer, from which the settlement was named. The region was already populated by Finnic and East Slavic tribes in the 9th and 10th centuries, and Suzdal arose on the site of a settlement of the Meryans. By 1096 it was fortified.

At the turn of the 12th century Grand Prince Vladimir Monomakh arrived with a wave of settlers and about 1102 began a stone cathedral. He made his son Yury Dolgoruky prince of Suzdal, and by Monomakh's death in 1125 the Rostov-Suzdal principality was virtually independent, with Suzdal as capital. Yury promoted the founding of new towns, among them Moscow. In 1157 the capital moved to Vladimir, and Suzdal became part of the Grand Principality of Vladimir. Following the Mongol conquest it became in 1238 the capital of the Principality of Suzdal. The Nativity Cathedral withstood the Mongol siege, though its interior was looted.

In 1341 Suzdal united with Nizhny Novgorod, and in 1350 Konstantin of Suzdal moved his capital to Nizhny Novgorod. Grand Prince Vasily I of Moscow annexed the principality in 1392. In 1445 Tatars sacked the town and set fire to the cathedral, whose upper part collapsed; it was rebuilt in 1528–1530. As political importance faded, Suzdal regained prominence as a religious centre, with building funded by Vasily III and Tsar Ivan IV, and it was the seat of a diocese until the 19th century. In the late 17th and 18th centuries wealthy merchants funded 30 churches. In 1864 local merchants failed to persuade the government to bring the Trans-Siberian Railway through the town, and it went through Vladimir, 35 kilometres away.

Suzdal avoided the industrialisation of the Soviet period, and its buildings from the 13th to the 19th century remain. It has 305 monuments and listed buildings, among them 30 churches, 14 bell towers and five monasteries and convents, and has had federally protected status since 1967. In 1992 the Saviour Monastery of St Euthymius and the Kremlin with the Nativity of the Virgin Cathedral were entered on the UNESCO World Heritage List together with other white monuments of the region. The monastery, founded in 1352, became a prison in 1766 on the orders of Catherine the Great. Suzdal is the smallest of the towns of Russia's Golden Ring, and tourism is its main industry.
suzhou: Suzhou lies in southeastern Jiangsu Province on the Lake Tai Plain, a fertile alluvial basin bordered by Lake Tai to the southwest and the Yangtze River to the north. The terrain is low and flat, crossed by many rivers and lakes, and rivers, lakes and mudflats make up 36.6 percent of the city's land area. The Yangtze River and the Grand Canal cross its northern area. It has been called the Water Capital and the Venice of the East, a comparison the Travels of Marco Polo makes in the 13th century. Along with Hangzhou it is praised in Chinese poetry as paradise on earth.

Suzhou is one of the oldest towns in the Yangtze Basin. In the Spring and Autumn period local Baiyue tribes called the Gou Wu lived in villages on the edges of the hills above the wetlands around Lake Tai. During the Zhou dynasty a settlement known as Gusu, after nearby Mount Gusu, became the capital of the state of Wu. In 514 BCE King Helü of Wu established a new capital nearby, Helü City, which grew into the modern city. It was later known as Wuxian, Wu County, and Wujun, Wu Commandery, and under the Qin as Kuaiji after its greatly enlarged commandery.

The city grew quickly by the Eastern Han dynasty, mostly through emigration from northern China. From the 10th century it was an important economic, cultural and commercial centre, and until Shanghai overtook it in about 1850 it was the largest non-capital city in the world. Silk production has a long history there. From the Song and Yuan dynasties it was one of the centres of silk weaving and dyeing, by the 13th century it was the centre of the profitable silk trade, and in the Ming dynasty its silk was praised as the clothing of the world. Painters and writers of the Ming dynasty came from the city, among them Tang Yin, Wen Zhengming, founder of the Wu School, and the writer Feng Menglong.

Suzhou is a prefecture-level city divided into six urban districts and four county-level cities. Its Classical Gardens, over 60 in number, were added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1997 and 2000. Other landmarks include Tiger Hill, the Yunyan Pagoda built in 961, which leans and is nicknamed the Leaning Tower of China, and the Baodai Bridge, first built in 806, with 53 arches. Kunqu opera originated in the Suzhou region, as did the ballad-singing tradition pingtan. In 1994 China and Singapore signed an agreement to develop the Suzhou Industrial Park, which began on 12 May of that year.
svans: The Svans call themselves Mushwan, a name that probably lies behind the Misimian of the classical authors. In their own language they are the shwanær, and in Georgian they are the svanebi. They are usually identified with the Soanes mentioned by the Greek geographer Strabo, who placed them more or less in the area that Svans still occupy, the region of Svaneti in north-western Georgia.

The Svans were Christianized between the 4th and 6th centuries and are Georgian Orthodox Christians today, although some remnants of pre-Christian belief survive. Saint George, a patron saint of Georgia known locally as Jgëræg, is the most respected saint among them. The medieval painter Tevdore, active in the 11th and 12th centuries, is among the Svans remembered for religious murals and frescoes.

In the Russian Empire and the early Soviet Union, Mingrelians and Svans had their own census grouping. The pre-1930 Soviet census counted the Svans as a separate ethnic group alongside other subgroups of Georgians, and in the 1930s they were classified under the broader category of Georgian.
The Svans speak Svan, an unwritten Kartvelian language, and most are also bilingual in Georgian, the other Kartvelian language of the region. Before the 19th century many Svans knew only Svan.

The Svans have kept many old traditions, including blood revenge, though the custom has declined as law enforcement has taken hold. Their families are small, and the husband is the head of the family. Older women in the family are strongly respected.
svantevit: Svetovit was the chief god of the Slavic tribe of the Rani, and later of all the Polabian Slavs. His name is written in Latin sources as Suantouitus, Suantevit and in other forms, and is reconstructed in Old Polabian as *Svątevit. The first part comes from the Proto-Slavic adjective *svętъ, which scholars have read either as "strong, mighty" or as "holy, sacred", and the whole name has been translated as "Strong Lord" or "Holy Lord". Many scholars of Slavic mythology regard him as a Polabian form of Perun.

The chronicler Helmold told a story, the Corvey legend, that the Rani became Christian in the ninth century and then worshipped Saint Vitus as a god. Most scholars reject it, since there is no evidence of Christianity reaching Rügen before 1168, and they think the legend was invented in the twelfth century to support Corvey's claims to Rügen. Claims that Svetovit was worshipped in Serbia and Croatia, through the feast of Vidovdan, are likewise not accepted: those names refer to Saint Vitus.

The god's main temple stood at Cape Arkona on Rügen. Medieval chroniclers describe a statue with four heads that held a horn and a sword. A white horse, a saddle, a bit, a flag and eagles were dedicated to him. Priests held that the god rode the horse at night to fight his enemies, and the horse was also used for divination: if it stepped over rows of spears with its right foot first, a planned attack was thought lucky, and if with its left, it was called off.

A large festival took place once a year, after the harvest. The priest checked the liquor in the horn held by the statue: a shortfall foretold a failed harvest and the people were told to make provisions. A large honey cake was also part of the rite. The Slavs gave one coin a year to the god, a third of captured enemy armour was dedicated to him, and merchants trading on Rügen were taxed in his honour. Neighbouring kings, among them a Danish king named Swen, were also said to have sent gifts.

The cult ended in June 1168, when the Danes under King Valdemar I and Bishop Absalon captured Arkona. According to the chronicle, Valdemar had the statue dragged with a rope round its neck before the whole army, burned it, destroyed the temple and looted its treasure. The name Światowid, read as a god seeing the four directions, was an invention of nineteenth-century Polish Romantics and is regarded as incorrect.
svatopluk-i-of-moravia: Svatopluk was a nephew of Rastislav, the second known ruler of Great Moravia, according to the Annals of Fulda, and was most probably born around 840. Sources disagree about his father, giving Svetimir, Bogislav or Morot. In the early 860s he and his uncle asked the Byzantine emperor Michael III for missionaries, and Cyril and Methodius arrived in 863. By 869 he ruled his own realm within Great Moravia, generally accepted to be the Duchy of Nitra. When Bavarian troops under Carloman invaded that year, he negotiated secretly with Carloman and then betrayed Rastislav, whom he handed over to the Franks. Carloman let him keep his principality but imprisoned him in early 871 on charges of disloyalty.

The Moravians chose Slavomír as ruler, but Carloman released Svatopluk and sent him against the rebels. On reaching the fortress he turned on the Bavarians, killing many, and became undisputed ruler. The Peace of Forchheim of 874 obliged him to pay annual tribute to Louis the German. Great Moravia expanded in the 870s: the Life of Methodius mentions the capture of a powerful pagan prince on the Vistula, and the region of Nitra was conquered. Historians debate how lasting these annexations were.

In 880 he and his people were taken under the protection of the Holy See, and in 885 Pope Stephen V addressed him as king. In 890 King Arnulf of East Francia ceded the duchy of the Bohemians to him, according to Regino of Prüm.

Svatopluk professed the Latin rite, and after Methodius died in 885 Bishop Wiching of Nitra persuaded the pope to prohibit the Slavonic liturgy. Svatopluk gave Wiching a free hand against Methodius's disciples. Some were imprisoned and expelled and others, among them Naum, were sold as slaves. The exiles found refuge in the First Bulgarian Empire.

Arnulf invaded Moravia in 892 but failed to defeat Svatopluk, and the Annals of Fulda record his death in 894 as most unlucky without giving the circumstances. Simon of Kéza says he fell in battle near Környe. His sons Mojmir II and Svatopluk II quarrelled, and Arnulf encouraged their disagreements. The Czechs withdrew in 895, and the state collapsed in the first decade of the 10th century under Hungarian invasion. Slovak writers have presented him as a Slovak king since the 18th century.
sveinn-bjornsson: Sveinn Björnsson was born in Copenhagen on 27 February 1881, the son of Björn Jónsson, an editor and later a minister, and Elísabet Sveinsdóttir. He graduated from the Latin School in Reykjavík in 1900 and took a law degree at the University of Copenhagen in 1907. That year he was licensed to practise before the upper courts. He served as public prosecutor in Reykjavík in 1907 to 1920 and again in 1924 to 1926. He was also a freemason, a founder of the Edda lodge in Reykjavík and Grandmaster of the Icelandic Order of Freemasons.

Sveinn sat on the Reykjavík City Council from 1912 to 1920 and chaired it in 1918 to 1920. He was elected to the Althing for Reykjavík in 1914-15 and in 1919 to 1920. After Iceland's independence from Denmark in 1918 he served as its minister to Denmark in 1920 to 1924 and again in 1926 to 1940.

He also helped found several Icelandic institutions. He was a founder of the shipping company Eimskipafélag Íslands in 1914 and its chairman in 1914 to 1920 and 1924 to 1926. He founded the insurance company Brunabótafélag Íslands in 1916 and helped found the Icelandic Maritime Insurance Company in 1918. In 1924 he was a founder and the first chairman of the Icelandic Red Cross.

Iceland had been a sovereign state since 1918, but Denmark conducted its foreign affairs until the Second World War. The German occupation of Denmark in April 1940 left King Christian X, who lived in Denmark, unable to carry out his constitutional functions for Iceland. Sveinn was elected Regent of Iceland three times between 1941 and 1943 and took over all the king's prerogatives in Icelandic affairs. In July 1941 United States troops occupied Iceland on the invitation of his government.

The Althing elected him the first president of the republic when it was inaugurated in 1944, for a first term of a single year, and the people re-elected him without opposition in 1945 and 1949. Iceland became a member of NATO on 30 March 1949, amid domestic controversy and riots, and signed a defence agreement with the United States on 5 May 1951. Sveinn had been in poor health since 1949 and died in Reykjavík on 25 January 1952, more than a year before his third term was due to expire.
sven-hedin: Sven Hedin was born in Stockholm, the son of Ludwig Hedin, the city's chief architect. At fifteen he saw the triumphal return of the Arctic explorer Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld from his first navigation of the Northern Sea Route, and from then on he wanted to be an explorer. After leaving school in 1885 he went to Baku as private tutor to Erhard Sandgren, and there began learning Persian, Russian and Tatar. He later learned Turkish, Kyrgyz, Mongolian, Tibetan and some Chinese.

He studied under the geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in Berlin from 1889. In 1890 he went to Tehran as interpreter and vice-consul with a Swedish legation to the Shah, climbed Mount Damavand and then travelled the Silk Road to Kashgar. In July 1892 he received his doctorate at Halle with a short dissertation on Damavand.

His first expedition, from 1893 to 1897, took him through the Pamir Mountains, the Tarim Basin and the Taklamakan Desert to northern Tibet. He covered 26,000 kilometres, about 3,600 of them through previously uncharted areas. On the second, from 1899 to 1902, he found the dried lake bed of Lop Nur. Near it he found the walled city of Loulan, with a stupa and nineteen wooden dwellings, and several hundred documents in Kharosthi script, which indicate that Loulan was abandoned around 330 CE when the lake dried out.

From 1905 to 1908 he explored western Tibet and the Transhimalaya, was the first European to reach the Kailash region, and located the sources of the Indus and Brahmaputra. From 1927 to 1935 he led an international Sino-Swedish Expedition to Mongolia, the Gobi and Xinjiang, which he called a peripatetic university in which Swedish, German and Chinese scientists worked almost independently.

Hedin recorded his routes with the detail of a topographical map, adding altitude and position measurements and panoramic drawings. He drew the first precise maps of the Pamir Mountains, the Taklamakan Desert, Tibet and the Silk Road, and was the first European known to recognise the Himalayas as a continuous range.

He was a monarchist who from 1905 opposed Sweden's move toward democracy and urged an alliance with the German Empire. His conservative, pro-German views turned into sympathy for the Third Reich, which brought controversy late in life. He was not an entirely uncritical supporter: in 1937 he refused to publish a book in Germany without passages critical of the Nazis, and he interceded for interned Norwegians, securing the release of one.
sveriges-riksbank: Before the Riksbank, Sweden was served by the Stockholms Banco, founded by Johan Palmstruch in 1656. Although the bank was private, the king chose its management. It collapsed because it issued too many notes without the necessary collateral, and Palmstruch, held responsible for its losses, was condemned to death but later received clemency.

On 17 September 1668 his privilege to operate a bank was transferred to the Riksens Ständers Bank, the Bank of the Estates of the Realm. Because of the failure of the Stockholms Banco it was placed under the direct control of the Riksdag of the Estates, to keep the king from interfering. It took the name Sveriges Riksbank when a new Riksdag was instituted in 1866.

Having learned from the Stockholms Banco, the Riksbank was not permitted to issue bank-notes, although in 1701 permission was given to issue credit-notes. When counterfeit notes appeared in the middle of the 18th century, it founded its own paper-mill, Tumba Bruk, near Stockholm. The first commercial banks were also allowed to issue notes, on condition of a deposit at the Riksbank. Through the 19th century the Riksbank was dominant as a credit institution and note issuer, and opened its first branch office in 1824.

Its position as a central bank dates from 1897, when the first Riksbank Act gave it the exclusive right to issue bank-notes, after repeated demands that private banks stop issuing them. The currency was backed by gold until 1931, when a temporary law freed the bank from the duty to exchange notes for gold; the law was renewed yearly until the constitution of 1975 made the bank a stand-alone organisation.

In November 1992 the fixed exchange rate of the krona collapsed, and in January 1993 the bank adopted a floating exchange rate and an inflation target, with help from the Bank of Canada. On 2 July 2009 it became the first central bank to set a negative interest rate, in response to the 2008 financial crisis.

The Riksbank is regarded as the world's oldest surviving central bank. After its third centenary in 1968 it instituted the annual Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, awarded with the Nobel Prizes in Stockholm on 10 December. Its motto is Hinc robur et securitas, Latin for strength and security from this. In the 2000s it closed all its branches in Sweden and put the handling of coins and notes in private hands, and by 2023 it had completed a technical pilot of an e-krona without deciding whether to issue one.
sverre-of-norway: According to Sverris saga, Sverre was born to Gunnhild and her husband Unås, a comb maker from the Faroes. The family moved there when he was five, and he was raised in the household of Unås's brother Roe, bishop of the Faroes, and ordained a priest. In 1175 his mother told him that his father was King Sigurd Munn, and the next year he went to Norway.

Historians have questioned this paternity. Some think the claim false, as did many of Sverre's contemporaries, but most hold that the question cannot be answered; he consistently refused an ordeal by fire to prove it. In January 1177 the Birkebeiners, a rebel party, were crushed at the Battle of Re, and Sverre agreed to lead their remnant, which numbered no more than seventy men according to the saga.

Sverre was proclaimed king at Øretinget in June 1177. For years his band was almost constantly on the move against King Magnus Erlingsson and his father Erling Skakke. Erling was killed at the Battle of Kalvskinnet on 19 June 1179, and Sverre secured Trøndelag. He built a large fleet, taking Bergen in 1183, and had the huge ship Mariasuda built. At the Battle of Fimreite in the Sognefjord on 15 June 1184 Magnus drowned and his party, the Heklungs, was broken, leaving Sverre sole king.

His tactics were mobile: he fought in smaller groups instead of a shield wall and often directed his men from horseback. Further risings followed, among them the Kuvlungs, whose leader Jon Kuvlung was killed at Bergen in 1188, and the Øyskjeggene, beaten at Florvåg on 3 April 1194.

A more serious breach came with the Church. Archbishop Eirik Ivarsson fled to Denmark in 1190, and Pope Celestine III's letter of 15 June 1194 backed the archbishop, who then excommunicated Sverre. In 1198 Innocent III placed Norway under interdict. A papal letter annulling the excommunication that Sverre produced in 1197 is held by most historians to have been forged. In 1196 the church-supported Baglers rose against him in a war that outlasted him.

Sverre died on 9 March 1202. Many consider him one of the most important rulers in Norwegian history. Sverris saga, written in part under his sponsorship, is the main source for his life and is probably biased; papal and episcopal letters offer an alternative on church affairs, and the two mostly agree on the hard facts. A speech against the bishops written by someone close to him argued that his excommunication was unjust and defended his right to appoint bishops.
svetitskhoveli-cathedral: According to Georgian hagiography, a Georgian Jew from Mtskheta named Elias was in Jerusalem when Jesus was crucified, bought Jesus' robe from a Roman soldier and brought it home. His sister Sidonia died on touching it and was buried with it. A cedar grew from her grave, and Saint Nino had seven columns made from it for the church. The seventh rose into the air until she prayed through the night, and a healing liquid was said to flow from it. In Georgian sveti means pillar and tskhoveli means life-giving, hence the name.

The first church was built in the fourth century in the reign of Mirian III of Kartli (Iberia), at the confluence of the Mtkvari and Aragvi rivers. Georgia officially adopted Christianity as its state religion in 337. King Vakhtang Gorgasali later built a basilica in the late fifth century, whose base was found in the restoration of 1970–71, along with the remains of an even older wooden church.

The present building was constructed between 1010 and 1029 by the architect Arsukidze, at the invitation of Catholicos Melchizedek I, in the reign of King Giorgi I. It follows the cross-dome plan that became the principal Georgian style after the unification of Georgia under Bagrat III. A legend, for which there is no documentary evidence, says that the architect's right hand was cut off out of jealousy; a relief of a hand holding a square and an inscription on the east facade name him.

The cathedral was damaged by Arabs, Persians, Timurids and during Russian and Soviet rule, and by earthquakes. It was rebuilt at the end of the fourteenth century after Tamerlane destroyed it, the present dome dates from the fifteenth century, and renovations followed in the mid-seventeenth century. King Erekle II had the defensive wall built in 1787. In the early 1830s, before a planned visit by Emperor Nicholas I, Russian authorities demolished the galleries and whitewashed the frescoes, though the tsar never came.

Svetitskhoveli was the site of the coronation of Georgian kings and their burial place. Ten are known to have been buried there, though only six tombs have been found, among them those of Vakhtang Gorgasali, Erekle II and George XII, the last king of Georgia. A small chapel built into the south side is a symbolic copy of the Chapel of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, marking the church as the second most sacred place after Jerusalem because of Christ's robe. Some frescoes survive after restoration, including a thirteenth-century Beast of the Apocalypse. A UNESCO report of 2010 found structural issues threatening the cathedral's stability.
sviatopolk-i-of-kiev: Sviatopolk's mother was a Greek nun captured by Sviatoslav I in Bulgaria and married to his heir Yaropolk I. After Vladimir had Yaropolk murdered in 980, he married the widow, who bore a child, so Sviatopolk may have been the eldest of Vladimir's sons, although his parentage has been questioned. At the age of eight he was put in charge of Turov, and he was later married to a daughter of Bolesław I the Brave of Poland. She came to Turov with Reinbern, the Bishop of Kolberg. Encouraged by his wife and Reinbern, Sviatopolk prepared for war on Vladimir, probably counting on his father-in-law, but Vladimir learnt of it and imprisoned him, his wife and Reinbern, who died in prison.

According to the Primary Chronicle, Sviatopolk was freed shortly before Vladimir's death in 1015, and his retinue hid the death from him. Once he knew, he seized power in Kiev almost at once, distributed gifts to win over the unsympathetic citizens and rid himself of three of Vladimir's sons, Boris, Gleb and Sviatoslav. Boris, who led his father's guards and army and had the citizens' support, was stabbed in his tent by the boyars of Vyshgorod. His killing earned Sviatopolk the nickname the Accursed.

Yaroslav, Prince of Novgorod, went to war with the support of the citizens of Novgorod and the Varangians and defeated Sviatopolk in 1016 near Lubech, and he fled to Poland. In 1018 he returned, defeated Yaroslav with his father-in-law's help and took Kiev. Bolesław stayed in Rus for several months and seized some Cherven towns on his way home. Yaroslav, again persuaded by citizens of Novgorod, attacked once more. Sviatopolk fled to the steppes and came back with a Pecheneg army, but was defeated on the Alta River and died on the way to Poland in July 1019.

Historians dispute how far Sviatopolk was responsible for the murders. It has been argued that Boris succeeded Vladimir in Kiev while Sviatopolk was still in prison, and a Norse saga puts the blame for a brother's murder on Yaroslav. Thietmar of Merseburg, the only contemporary chronicler, may have had his information from Sviatopolk himself and can be read in different ways. He says Bolesław supported his son-in-law against Yaroslav in 1017, which makes it unlikely that Sviatopolk was at the Polish court from 1015, as is often supposed by those who hold him guilty. The Svyatopolk-Mirsky family traces its descent from him, and Peter the Great recognised the claim.
sviatopolk-ii-of-kiev: Sviatopolk was the son of Iziaslav Iaroslavich by a concubine. While his brother Iaropolk lived, he was not regarded as a possible claimant to the throne of Kiev. In 1069 he was sent to Polotsk, a city his father had briefly taken from its ruler Vseslav, and for ten years, 1078–88, he ruled Novgorod. When his brother died he succeeded him in Turov, which stayed in the possession of his descendants until the 17th century.

When Vsevolod Iaroslavich died in 1093, the other princes acknowledged Sviatopolk as the senior son of a grand prince and let him take the throne of Kiev. He was not a popular prince, and his reign was marked by constant rivalry with his cousin Vladimir Monomakh, although he took part in the princely congresses that Monomakh organised. He is sometimes charged with encouraging wars among the Rurikid princes: with his cousin David of Volhynia and his son-in-law Bolesław III Wrymouth he took part in capturing and blinding a Galician prince.

Against the Kipchaks he was less fortunate. He was defeated in 1093 at the Battle of the Stugna River and again later that year, after which the Kipchaks destroyed Torchesk, an Oghuz Turk settlement. In 1096, while trying to force Oleg I of Chernigov into an agreement among the princes, he left his lands undefended. His father-in-law Tugorkhan raided Pereyaslavl, and the Cuman khan Boniak raided as far as Kiev and sacked three monasteries, among them the Kiev Monastery of the Caves. Tugorkhan was killed in the raid, and Sviatopolk had him buried in Kiev. In 1111 he and Vladimir Monomakh led an army that defeated a Cuman army at the Battle of the Salnytsia River.

Sviatopolk's Christian name was Michael, and he encouraged the embellishment of St Michael's Abbey in Kiev, known since as the Golden-Roofed. The history now called the Primary Chronicle was compiled by the monk Nestor during his reign. He married three times, the last time in 1104 to Barbara Komnena. His daughter Zbyslava married Bolesław III of Poland in 1102 and Predslava married Prince Álmos of Hungary in 1104. His son Iaroslav, Prince of Volynia and Turov, died in 1123, and because of his early death Iaroslav's descendants lost any claim to the Kievan throne and kept Turov and Pinsk.
sviatoslav-i-of-kiev: Sviatoslav was the son of Igor of Kiev, who was killed by the Drevlians about 945. His mother Olga ruled as regent until he reached maturity, around 963. Almost nothing is known of his youth, which he spent reigning in Novgorod, and he was tutored by a Varangian named Asmud. He had little patience for administration and lived with his druzhina in near-constant warfare. According to the Primary Chronicle he carried no wagons or kettles on campaign and slept on a horse-blanket with his saddle under his head. His mother converted to Orthodox Christianity in 957, but he remained a pagan, and the Primary Chronicle says he feared his warriors would mock him if he converted.

Shortly after he took power, Sviatoslav began campaigning in the Volga valley and the Pontic steppe. He rallied the East Slavic vassals of the Khazars, forced the Vyatichs to pay tribute to Kiev rather than the Khazars, and attacked Volga Bulgaria. He destroyed the Khazar city of Sarkel around 965 and later the capital Atil, though the order of events is disputed. He did not occupy the Khazar heartland, and Khazar successor statelets lingered, but the destruction of Khazar power opened the north-south steppe and Black Sea trade routes to Kievan Rus'.

In 967 or 968 the Byzantine emperor Nikephoros Phokas paid him 15,000 pounds of gold to attack Bulgaria. He defeated the Bulgarian ruler Boris II and occupied northern Bulgaria, but he refused to hand the conquests to the Byzantines and decided to move his seat to Pereyaslavets on the Danube. In 969 he divided his lands among his sons Yaropolk, Oleg and Vladimir and invaded Bulgaria again, capturing Philippopolis and massacring its inhabitants.

The new emperor John Tzimiskes sent Bardas Skleros, who defeated the coalition at the Battle of Arcadiopolis, and then marched on the Balkans himself. Sviatoslav was besieged at Dorostolon for sixty-five days and agreed to leave the Balkans in return for food and safe passage.

On the way home, in early 972, Sviatoslav was ambushed and killed by Pechenegs near the Dnieper rapids at Khortytsia, after, according to the chronicle, he ignored the warning of Sveneld. The Primary Chronicle says the Pecheneg khan made his skull into a chalice. His conquests were not consolidated, and his sons fought one another: Oleg was killed in 976 and Yaropolk in 978, and Vladimir became sole ruler of Kievan Rus'. The campaign in Bulgaria weakened the First Bulgarian Empire, leaving it open to attack by Basil the Bulgar-Slayer four decades later.
sviatoslav-ii-of-kiev: Sviatoslav II Iaroslavich was born in 1027, the fourth son of Yaroslav the Wise, Grand Prince of Kiev, and Ingegerd of Sweden. A list of the princes of Chernigov, the Lyubetskiy sinodik, gives his baptismal name as Nicholas. The historian Martin Dimnik thinks his father most probably appointed him to rule Vladimir in Volhynia about 1040. When Yaroslav died on 20 February 1054 he had divided the main towns among his five surviving sons: Iziaslav received Kiev and Sviatoslav received Chernigov. The three elder brothers, Iziaslav, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod of Pereyaslav, then governed Kievan Rus' together as a triumvirate.

In 1059 the brothers freed their uncle Sudislav, whom their father had imprisoned about 1035, and in 1060 they marched against the Oghuz Turks, who fled without a fight. After Vseslav of Polotsk plundered Novgorod, they defeated him on the Nemiga River on 3 March 1066 and then captured him treacherously at Orsha.

In 1068 the Cumans routed the three brothers on the Alta River. Sviatoslav withdrew to Chernigov and then defeated the Cumans with a smaller force at Snovsk on 1 November, which raised his standing. Meanwhile the townspeople of Kiev expelled Iziaslav, who returned with Polish help. Sviatoslav gave shelter at Chernigov to Anthony, founder of the Monastery of the Caves, whom Iziaslav wished to punish.

The triumvirate was restored, and on 3 May 1072 the brothers took part in moving the relics of Boris and Gleb at Vyshhorod. Soon afterwards, on 22 March 1073, Sviatoslav and Vsevolod expelled Iziaslav from Kiev. The Primary Chronicle blames Sviatoslav, who it says desired more power. Of modern historians, Franklin and Shepard write of straightforward greed, while Martin suggests that, being gravely ill, he wished to secure his sons' right to Kiev.

As grand prince Sviatoslav supported the compilation of two miscellanies of theological works, completed in 1073 and 1076; the first calls him a new Ptolemy. Feodosy, head of the Monastery of the Caves, first criticized him for usurping the throne but was reconciled with him before his death in 1074.

In 1076 Sviatoslav sent reinforcements to Poland to help his son-in-law Bolesław II against the Bohemians. He died on 27 December 1076, of the cutting of a sore according to the chronicle, and was buried in the Holy Savior Cathedral at Chernigov. Within a year Iziaslav was restored, and Sviatoslav's sons lost most of his domains.
swabia: Swabia's borders have never been clearly defined. In the Middle Ages the name covered all the lands of the Frankish stem duchy of Alamannia, from the Vosges Mountains in the west to the Lech river in the east, including Alsace, the later Margraviate of Baden, German-speaking Switzerland, Vorarlberg and Liechtenstein. The modern region is narrower. It roughly coincides with the Swabian Circle of the Holy Roman Empire, established in 1512, and is thought of as the former state of Württemberg together with Bavarian Swabia.

The area was part of the La Tène culture and, in Roman times, of the province of Raetia. By the mid-3rd century groups of the Suebi formed the core of the Alamanni, who pressed towards the Roman Limes. The Alemanni were ruled by independent kings in the 4th and 5th centuries and fell under Frankish domination in the 6th. From the 12th century Suebia was used consistently for the territory of the Duchy of Swabia.

Swabia was one of the original stem duchies of East Francia. Its abbeys of St. Gallen and Reichenau made it an important centre of Old High German literature. Burchard II won control of the duchy at the Battle of Winterthur in 919, and under Burchard III in the 960s it was incorporated into the Holy Roman Empire under Otto I. The Hohenstaufen dynasty arose here. After the execution of Conradin, the last Hohenstaufen, on 29 October 1268, the duchy was not reappointed, and it broke up into many smaller units. Rudolf I of Habsburg declared most former Hohenstaufen cities Free Imperial Cities and the stronger abbeys Imperial Abbeys.

Cities and lesser rulers formed the Swabian League of Cities in 1331 and a new Swabian League in 1488. The latter expelled the Duke of Württemberg in 1519 and was disbanded in 1534 after the Reformation divided the region: most free cities and the Duke of Württemberg turned Protestant, while ecclesiastical territories and Habsburg lands stayed Catholic. After the reorganisation of 1803 only the Kingdom of Württemberg, the Grand Duchy of Baden and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen remained sovereign, and much of eastern Swabia passed to Bavaria.

The Swabian administrative region of Bavaria and the Württemberg part of Baden-Württemberg make up the modern Swabia. Swabians speak Swabian German, traditionally heard in the upper Neckar basin, along the upper Danube and in an area centred on the Swabian Alps. It is closely related to the other Alemannic dialects of Baden, Alsace and German-speaking Switzerland. Many Swabian surnames end in -le, -er or -lin, such as Schäuble and Gmelin.
swabia-bavaria: Swabia is one of the seven administrative regions of Bavaria, in the south-west of the state, with Augsburg as its administrative capital. It consists of ten districts and 340 municipalities, four of them cities. It is divided for planning into three regions: the Allgäu, Augsburg and Donau-Iller, and the last also includes two districts and a city of Baden-Württemberg. With the district of Lindau it has access to Lake Constance.

The region is the eastern part of the former Duchy of Swabia, which was once ruled by the dukes of the Hohenstaufen dynasty. After the execution of the Swabian duke Conradin in Naples in 1268, his uncle, the Bavarian duke Louis, inherited some of Conradin's possessions in Swabia. In 1803, through the German Mediatisation, Bavaria acquired the further East Swabian territories, which it merged with Palatinate-Neuburg.

After the founding of the Kingdom of Bavaria the state was reorganised in 1808 into fifteen districts, created in the fashion of French departments and named after their main rivers. Territorial changes later reduced them to eight, and the Swabian lands with Palatinate-Neuburg formed the Oberdonaukreis, the Upper Danube District. In 1837 King Ludwig I renamed all the districts after historical territories and tribes of the area, and the Oberdonaukreis became Swabia. During the Nazi period the area was separated from the rest of Bavaria as the Gau Swabia, and it was reincorporated after the war. France detached the town of Lindau from Bavaria in 1945, and it was reunited with the district in 1955. In 1972 Neuburg an der Donau returned to Upper Bavaria.

The main sights include Augsburg and several other old cities, among them Donauwörth, Nördlingen, Memmingen, Mindelheim, Kaufbeuren and Kempten. Ottobeuren Abbey stands in the region, and the Danube runs through the north. The Allgäu Alps lie in the south, with the Hochfrottspitze and Hochvogel, and the royal castles of Hohenschwangau and Neuschwanstein stand near Füssen.
swabian-jura: The Swabian Jura, in German the Schwäbische Alb, lies in Baden-Württemberg and runs from south-west to north-east, 40 to 70 km wide. It is bounded by the Danube in the south-east and the upper Neckar in the north-west, and rises in the south-west towards the Black Forest. Its highest point is the Lemberg, at 1,015 metres. The profile is that of a high plateau that falls slowly to the south-east, with a steep forested escarpment, the Albtrauf, rising about 400 metres on the north-western side.

The rock is mostly limestone that formed the seabed in the Jurassic period. Rain seeps through cracks into a karst landscape of caves and underground rivers, so the plateau has hardly any surface water, and the Danube nearly disappears near Immendingen. The soil is thin and not very fertile. Fossils are found throughout, notably around Holzmaden, and the Nördlinger Ries is a meteorite crater 15 million years old.

Caves of the region, among them Vogelherd, Hohlenstein-Stadel, Geißenklösterle and Hohle Fels, have yielded some of the oldest known human artifacts: figures of a mammoth, a horse's head, a water bird and a lion man, all more than 30,000 years old. Flutes made from the bones of swans and griffon vultures about 35,000 years old are the oldest known musical instruments, and a flute carved from mammoth tusk dates from around 37,000 years ago. More than 3,000 engraved signs on about 260 Aurignacian artifacts, dated to roughly 40,000 to 34,000 years ago, show structured patterns that may point to a conventional system of graphic signs.

The region, south of the limes, was part of the Roman Empire from around the first to the third century. A Roman road ran along the Neckar and over the plateau, and the limes cuts across it at Aalen, named after a Roman cavalry post, the ala. In the Middle Ages castles stood along the escarpment, among them Hohenzollern, Teck and Hohenstaufen, and towns such as Reutlingen lay in the foreland.

Life on the plateau was long hard, because water was short and the soil poor. Many villages fetched water on long journeys until a modern water supply was built in the late 1880s. Sheep farming gave rise to a textile industry, from which machine building, the motor industry and electronics later grew, and the region has changed from one of the poorest in Germany to one of the richest within about 150 years.

People speak a distinct Swabian German dialect, and the Swabian-Alemannic carnival, called Fasnet, is an important tradition, notably at Rottweil. The whole area is a UNESCO global geopark covering 6,688 square kilometres, with a biosphere reserve at its centre.
swabian-war: Since the late 13th century the members of the Swiss Confederacy had gradually taken over territories that once belonged to the Habsburgs, and they held imperial immediacy, answering to the emperor alone. When the Habsburgs took the imperial throne in 1438 the Swiss could no longer count on imperial support against them. Frederick III founded the Swabian League in 1488, and the Swiss refused to join an alliance that served Habsburg interests.

At the Imperial Diet at Worms in 1495 Maximilian I and the princes proclaimed an eternal public peace, a standing army and a common penny, a head tax. The Swiss refused all of them, and Maximilian later used this as a pretext to place the Confederacy under an imperial ban. Quarrels between Swiss and Swabian mercenaries added to the hostility.

Open war began over the Val Müstair and the Umbrail Pass in the Grisons, which linked Habsburg Tyrol with Milan. On 20 January 1499 Habsburg troops occupied the valley and plundered the convent at Müstair. The Three Leagues of the Grisons, allied with the Swiss since 1497 and 1498, drove them back, and each side called on its allies. Fighting spread along the Rhine to Lake Constance and the Sundgau. The Swiss won at Hard on 20 February, at Bruderholz on 22 March, at Schwaderloh on 11 April, where the Swabians lost more than 1,000 men, and at Frastanz on 20 April.

Maximilian took command himself and declared an imperial war, without success. On 22 May 1499 the Three Leagues routed the Austrian army at Calven. Pressure from unpaid mercenaries and from peasant soldiers wishing to bring in the harvest forced a decision, and on 22 July an army of about 16,000 attacked Dornach. In the Battle of Dornach the Swabians lost their general Heinrich von Fürstenberg early, with about 3,000 dead against about 500 Swiss, and again lost all their artillery. The Swabian League, war-weary and distrustful of the king's leadership, refused to raise another army.

Milan, whose ruler Ludovico il Moro wanted Swiss and Habsburg help against France, mediated between the sides. The Peace of Basel of 22 September 1499 treated the war as one between two equal members of the empire and called Maximilian only duke of Habsburg. The Swiss remained exempt from the jurisdiction of the imperial court and gained high justice over the Thurgau; the war caused almost no territorial change.

Basel and Schaffhausen joined the Confederacy in 1501. Freed from the Rhine front, the Swiss took mercenary contracts with Milan and became deeply involved in the Italian Wars. The Habsburgs gave up their old territorial claims in the Erbeinung of 1511, and the Treaty of Westphalia of 1648 recognized the Confederacy's full exemption from the empire.
swami-vivekananda: Vivekananda was born as Narendranath Datta on 12 January 1863 in Calcutta, in an aristocratic Bengali Kayastha family. His father, Vishwanath Datta, was an attorney at the Calcutta High Court, and his mother, Bhubaneswari Devi, was devout. In 1879 he was the only student to receive first-division marks in the Presidency College entrance examination. He read widely in Western philosophy and in Hindu scriptures, corresponded with Herbert Spencer, and completed a Bachelor of Arts in 1884. He first met Ramakrishna probably in November 1881, and after his father died in 1884 Ramakrishna became his primary spiritual focus. On Christmas Eve 1886, at Antpur, he and eight other disciples took formal monastic vows.

In 1888 Narendra left the monastery as a wandering monk, with a water pot, a staff and two books, the Bhagavad Gita and The Imitation of Christ. For five years he travelled on foot and by railway, living on alms and meeting people of every religion and station. On the suggestion of Raja Ajit Singh of Khetri he took the name Vivekananda. He left Bombay for Chicago on 31 May 1893. At the Parliament of the World's Religions, opened on 11 September 1893, he began his short speech with the words Sisters and brothers of America and received a two-minute standing ovation. He then lectured across the United States and founded the Vedanta Societies of New York and San Francisco.

Vivekananda synthesised classical yoga and Advaita Vedanta. Influenced by Ramakrishna, he saw Vedanta as the basis for serving human beings as manifestations of the divine. He taught that each soul is potentially divine and that all religions are different paths to the same goal. Most of his published works, among them Raja Yoga, were based on lectures. He founded the Ramakrishna Math as a monastic order and the Ramakrishna Mission for social service and education. He died on 4 July 1902 at Belur Math after meditating. His birthday, 12 January, is observed in India as National Youth Day.
swansea: Swansea, in Welsh Abertawe, is a port and coastal city on Swansea Bay in south-west Wales, the second largest city in the country. It is part of the historic county of Glamorgan, and its principal area covers the Gower Peninsula, the first area in the United Kingdom to be designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. The Welsh name means the mouth or estuary of the Tawe and was first recorded in 1150 as Aper Tyui. The English name first appears as Sweynesse in the town's first royal charter, and the most prevalent theory derives it from swine sea, because of the porpoises in the bay.

Finds at Long Hole Cave on the Gower Peninsula have been interpreted as those of the first modern humans in Britain, and the oldest ceremonial burial in Western Europe was discovered at Paviland in 1823 and dated to 22,000 BCE. The land that would become Swansea lay in the Cantref Eginog, noted for its valuable land and highly contested by the early Welsh kingdoms. In the Viking Age the mouth of the Tawe became a focus for trade, and a trade post may have been founded between the 9th and 11th centuries.

From the early 1700s to the late 1800s Swansea was the world's leading copper-smelting area, earning the nickname Copperopolis. Smelters along the Tawe received ores from Cornwall and Devon and from North and South America, Africa and Australia. The industry peaked in the 1880s, when 60 percent of the copper ores imported to Britain were smelted in the Lower Swansea Valley, and it then declined severely. Heavy industry declined through the 20th century, and the Lower Swansea Valley Scheme reclaimed much of the derelict land.

Swansea Castle, the Tabernacle Chapel at Morriston, built in 1872, and the Guildhall, opened in 1934 and designed by Percy Thomas, are Grade I listed buildings. The ruins of the castle visible today date from the late 13th and early 14th centuries. The National Eisteddfod has been held in the city seven times, the first in 1863. The poet Dylan Thomas was born in Swansea and lived at 5 Cwmdonkin Drive for 23 years; he described it as an ugly lovely town. Local produce includes cockles and laverbread from the Loughor estuary.
swapo: German South West Africa was established in 1884. After the First World War the League of Nations gave the territory to the United Kingdom as a mandate under South African administration. When the National Party won the 1948 election in South Africa and introduced apartheid legislation, the laws were applied in South West Africa as well, which was treated as a de facto fifth province.

SWAPO was founded on 19 April 1960 as the successor of the Ovamboland People's Organization. Its leaders renamed it to show that it represented all Namibians, but its base lay among the Ovambo people of northern Namibia, who made up nearly half the population.

By 1962 SWAPO had emerged as the dominant nationalist organisation, and it absorbed other groups, among them the South West Africa National Union and, in 1976, the Namibia African People's Democratic Organisation. It used guerrilla tactics against the South African Defence Force. The first major clash took place on 26 August 1966, when a South African Police unit supported by the South African Air Force exchanged fire with SWAPO forces; the date is generally regarded as the start of what became known in South Africa as the Border War. The contract workers' strike of 1971-72 demanded an end to the contract labour system and independence, and an underlying aim was independence under SWAPO leadership.

In 1973 the United Nations General Assembly recognised SWAPO as the sole legitimate representative of the Namibian people, and the Norwegian government began giving it aid directly in 1974. After Angola became independent on 11 November 1975, its government, the MPLA, offered SWAPO bases there in March 1976. Before independence its ideology was socialist and Marxist–Leninist.

When Namibia became independent in 1990, SWAPO became the dominant political party, after winning the inaugural election of 1989. Its leader Sam Nujoma was declared the first President. The movement's original name, drawn from the territory's old name, was too deeply rooted in the independence struggle to change, so that today only the acronym is used. SWAPO and much of the government and administration have continued to be dominated by the Ovambo.
swazi-language: Swazi, also written Swati and called siSwati by its speakers, is spoken by the Swati people in Eswatini, formerly Swaziland, and in South Africa. The number of first and second language speakers is estimated at around 4.7 million. In English, Zulu, Ndebele or Xhosa it may be called Swazi, while siSwati is the official term among native speakers. It is most closely related to the other Tekela languages, such as Phuthi and Northern Transvaal (Sumayela) Ndebele, and is also very close to the Zunda languages: Zulu, Southern Ndebele, Northern Ndebele and Xhosa.

The language is taught in Eswatini and in some schools in Mpumalanga, particularly in the former KaNgwane areas. The Swati of Eswatini divides into four dialects matching the country's four administrative regions: Hhohho, Lubombo, Manzini and Shiselweni. The standard, prestige variety is spoken mainly in the north, centre and southwest. In the far south, around Nhlangano and Hlatikhulu, the speech is strongly influenced by Zulu. The Mpumalanga variety is considered closer to the standard but differs in intonation.

Swazi has clicks that do not distinguish places of articulation, and distinguishes five or six manners of articulation and phonation. It has three surface tones, high, mid and low, none of them marked in the standard orthography. Traditionally only high and mid are taken to exist underlyingly, but Bradshaw (2003) argues that all three do. The orthography uses the five vowels a, e, i, o and u and many consonant digraphs, such as dl, hl, ts and tj.

A noun (libito) consists of a prefix (sicalo) and a stem (umsuka). The prefixes sort nouns into classes, numbered to ease comparison with other Bantu languages. A Swazi person is liSwati in the singular and emaSwati in the plural. In the finger-counting etiquette, the word for six, sitsupha, means thumb, and the word for seven, sikhombisa, reflects an action.
sweden: Sweden lies on the eastern part of the Scandinavian Peninsula, west of the Baltic Sea and Gulf of Bothnia, and covers 450,295 square kilometres, making it the largest Nordic country. The Scandinavian mountain chain separates it from Norway, and Kebnekaise, at 2,096.8 metres, is the highest point. About 15% of the country lies north of the Arctic Circle, and around 65% of the land is forested. The north, Norrland, takes up almost 60% of the territory and is sparsely populated, while the highest density is in the Mälaren valley and around Stockholm. Vänern is the third largest lake in Europe.

Sweden's prehistory begins around 12,000 BCE, with reindeer-hunting camps of the Bromme culture in Scania. The Roman historian Tacitus first described the Swedes, as the Suiones, in his Germania of 98 CE, noting ships with a prow at each end. The runic script was in use among the south Scandinavian elite by at least the second century CE.

In the sixth century the Byzantine historian Jordanes named two tribes in Scandza now taken to be Swedes, the Suetidi and Suehans, who supplied black fox skins to the Roman world. The inhabitants emerged as the Geats and Swedes, part of the sea-faring Norsemen, and a unified Swedish state was established during the late 10th century.

In 1397 Sweden joined Norway and Denmark in the Kalmar Union, which it left in 1523. When Sweden entered the Thirty Years' War on the Protestant side its territories expanded, forming the Swedish Empire, which controlled much of the Baltic Sea and remained one of the great powers of Europe until the early 18th century. Most conquered territories outside the peninsula were lost in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the eastern half of Sweden, present-day Finland, passed to Imperial Russia in 1809. In 1814 Sweden forced Norway into a personal union by military means, the last war in which it was directly involved; the union lasted until 1905.

Sweden is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy, with a 349-member unicameral Riksdag. Under the 1974 Instrument of Government the king has no formal political power. The country is divided into 21 counties and 290 municipalities, and its Nordic welfare system provides universal health care. Its population is about 10.6 million, and five minority groups are officially recognised: Jews, Romani, Sámi, Sweden Finns and Tornedalians. Sweden joined the European Union in 1995 and NATO in 2024.
swedish-academy: The statutes of the Swedish Academy were drawn up by King Gustav III himself. Its motto is Talent and Taste (Snille och smak), and its stated primary purpose is to work on the purity, strength and sublimity of the Swedish language. The king assigned it the task of compiling a dictionary, set annual competitions in oratory and poetry on given themes and ordered a medal struck every year.

It is said that Gustav III first intended twenty members, half the number of the French Academy, but chose eighteen because the Swedish expression De Aderton, The Eighteen, had such a fine solemn ring. After his death in 1792 the Academy's standing deteriorated. In 1794 the member Gustav Mauritz Armfelt was excluded after a sentence for treason, and in 1795 the Academy was suspended for two years on political grounds. Armfelt was reinstated in 1805 and excluded again in 1811.

Members are elected by secret ballot, and the result must be submitted to the Academy's Patron, the King of Sweden, for approval. The members include writers, linguists, literary scholars, historians and a jurist. Writers were at first a minority, but during the twentieth century they grew to more than half of The Eighteen. Membership was held for life, and the Academy could not accept a resignation, though it could exclude a member. In 1989 Kerstin Ekman and Lars Gyllensten stopped taking part in its work after it declined to condemn the death decree issued against Salman Rushdie, and the number of active members fell.

The Academy has met in the building now known as the Stockholm Stock Exchange Building since its founding. Its ballroom was then the largest room in Stockholm that could be heated in winter, and Gustav asked to borrow it. The Academy gained permanent use of the upper floor only in 1914.

The Academy carries out its mission through reference works. Svenska Akademiens ordlista is a one-volume spelling dictionary. Svenska Akademiens Ordbok, edited on principles similar to those of the Oxford English Dictionary, runs to 39 volumes, the first published in 1893 and the last in 2023. A four-volume grammar, Svenska Akademiens grammatik, is aimed at researchers, linguists and students. Since 1901 the Academy has chosen the winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature, a task it accepted after some initial hesitation. Modernisation followed, including the election of its first female member, Selma Lagerlöf.
swedish-empire: The Great Power Era is usually dated from 1611, when Gustavus Adolphus came to the throne. Sweden's rise rested on a rapidly expanding metals economy: by the early seventeenth century it was northern Europe's leading exporter of iron and copper, which made up nearly 63 per cent of its exports in 1637 and more than 80 per cent in 1685. The Crown worked the Stora Kopparberg copper mine at Falun, then the largest in Europe, to help finance the king's political and military ambitions.

Sweden entered the Thirty Years' War and conquered about half of the member states of the Holy Roman Empire, though its defeat at the Battle of Nördlingen in 1634 damaged confidence in it among the German states it controlled. When France intervened on the same side, fortunes shifted again. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 gave Sweden territories in northern Germany, among them Swedish Pomerania. Sweden also founded New Sweden on the Delaware River in 1638.

After Gustavus Adolphus died in 1632, high nobles such as the Oxenstierna family ruled as regents for long periods. The empire reached its height in the Northern War of 1655 to 1660. By the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658 Denmark-Norway ceded Blekinge, Bornholm, Bohuslän, Scania, Trøndelag and Halland, though under the Treaty of Copenhagen of 1660 Sweden gave back Trøndelag and Bornholm. The Peace of Oliva of 1660 confirmed Sweden's possession of Livonia, and the Treaty of Cardis in 1661 gave it Ingria, Estonia and Kexholm. The empire then covered 1,100,000 square kilometres, with about 2,500,000 people.

The Scanian War, which began in 1675 after a defeat at Fehrbellin, exposed its weakness, and Swedish Pomerania was taken by its enemies. At the Riksdag of 1680 Charles XI recovered alienated crown lands, and Sweden became an absolute monarchy. His son Charles XII won at Narva and forced the Treaty of Altranstädt in 1706, but was defeated at Poltava in 1709. He was killed at Fredriksten on 30 November 1718.

The Treaty of Nystad in 1721 ended the Great Northern War and with it Sweden's time as a great power, though it remained a regional power until the nineteenth century. Finland was ceded to Russia in 1809, and Sweden's last continental territory, Swedish Pomerania, passed to Denmark after the Napoleonic Wars in exchange for Norway. The empire is also remembered as the leading power of continental Protestantism for about ninety years.
sweet-potato: The sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) originated in the warm tropical regions of South America, in what is now Ecuador, and was domesticated in either Central or South America. In Central America domesticated sweet potatoes were present at least 5,000 years ago, and local peoples most likely spread them to the Caribbean and South America by 2500 BCE. The oldest radiocarbon-dated remains known, from caves in the Chilca Canyon in Peru, are about 8080 BCE old. Ceramics modelled after sweet potatoes are often found in the Moche culture.

Before Europeans reached the Americas, the sweet potato was grown in Polynesia and has been radiocarbon-dated in the Cook Islands to 1210-1400 CE. A common hypothesis is that Polynesians who had travelled to South America and back brought a cutting to central Polynesia. Genetic similarities with indigenous Americans such as the Zenú, and the likeness of the Polynesian word kumala, as in Māori kūmara, to Quechua k'umara, point the same way, and the present scholarly consensus favours pre-Columbian contact.

The plant is a herbaceous perennial vine whose stems crawl on the ground and root at the nodes. Its large, starchy, sweet-tasting tuberous roots are eaten as a root vegetable, and the young shoots and leaves as greens. It belongs to the morning glory family and is only distantly related to the potato, and the darker sweet potatoes called yams in parts of North America are even more distant from true yams. The plant does not tolerate frost and grows best at an average temperature of 24 °C. It is propagated by cuttings or by shoots called slips, and the roots mature in two to nine months.

The first Europeans to taste sweet potatoes were members of Christopher Columbus's expedition in 1492. The name that stayed was the Taíno batata, which the Spanish combined with the Quechua word for potato, papa, to make patata for the common potato. In some tropical areas the roots are a staple food, usually cooked, though the American colonists of the Southeast ate them raw. In northeastern Uganda sun-dried slices, amukeke, are a staple, and in West Africa the leaves and vine tips are widely eaten as a vegetable. In South America the juice of red sweet potatoes mixed with lime juice dyes cloth in shades from pink to black.
sweyn-forkbeard: Sweyn was a son of Harald Bluetooth and an unknown mother. Harald had converted to Christianity in the mid-960s and extended Danish royal authority. In 986 or 987 Sweyn revolted against him with the support of sections of the nobility and seized the Danish throne. Harald was defeated and wounded in battle, driven into exile and soon died of his wounds. The historian Timothy Bolton describes a brief civil war that ended in a scandalous regicide and left a deep scar on Danish memory.

Sweyn extended Danish control east of the Øresund into Skane, and the main centres of power shifted from Jutland to Roskilde and Lund. Secure at home, he became the first Scandinavian king known to have led Viking raids. England, wealthy and militarily weak under Æthelred the Unready, was the main target, and the tribute Sweyn extracted extended his power in Scandinavia.

In 994 Sweyn and Olaf Tryggvason invaded England, attacked London without success and raided the south-east until the English paid a tribute of 16,000 pounds. King Æthelred persuaded Olaf to return to Norway to challenge Sweyn's overlordship, and many Norwegian magnates recognised Olaf as king. In 999 or 1000 Sweyn defeated him at the naval Battle of Svold and appointed the sons of Hakon Sigurdsson as jarls. He returned to England in 1003, sacked Exeter, Thetford and Norwich, until a severe famine forced him back to Denmark in 1005.

In August 1013 he came back with his son Cnut, intent on conquest, landing at Gainsborough. The magnates of the East Midlands and the North submitted, and after Bath the whole nation, London included, accepted him as king. Æthelred spent Christmas on the Isle of Wight and fled to Richard, Duke of Normandy. Historians disagree whether Sweyn was a sincere Christian; he continued the Christianisation begun by his father, with churches built at Roskilde and Lund.

Sweyn died at Gainsborough on 3 February 1014 and was buried at York; according to Thietmar a woman had the body exhumed and sent to Denmark. Most historians say he lay at Roskilde, but an empty grave found at the Holy Trinity church in Lund has been proposed as his. After his death the Danish fleet chose Cnut as king, but the English recalled Æthelred, who drove Cnut out. Medieval English hagiography made Sweyn a villain killed by Edmund the Martyr, while modern historians describe a great warrior and a remarkably successful king.
sweyn-ii-of-denmark: Sweyn was born in England, the son of Ulf Thorgilsson and Estrid Svendsdatter, daughter of King Sweyn I Forkbeard and sister of Kings Harald II and Canute the Great. He grew up a military leader and served for a time under King Anund Jacob of Sweden. In 1040 he pillaged the Elbe-Weser area but was caught by the Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, who released him shortly afterwards.

His cousin, the Danish king Harthacnut, made him a jarl and sent him on a campaign against Norway, where King Magnus I of Norway defeated them. When Harthacnut died in 1042, Magnus claimed the Danish throne and made Sweyn jarl of Jutland. In 1043 Sweyn fought for Magnus at the Battle of Lyrskov Heath, near Hedeby, and the Danish nobles then crowned him king at Viborg. Magnus defeated him several times and he fled to Sweden before establishing a foothold in Scania.

The war lasted until 1045, when Magnus's uncle Harald Hardrada returned to Norway and joined forces with Sweyn. Magnus shared his throne with Harald, and on his death in 1047 declared that Harald should take Norway and Sweyn Denmark. Harald nevertheless attacked Sweyn and fought a long war, sacking Hedeby and Aarhus in 1050.

Sweyn narrowly lost his life at the naval Battle of Niså off Halland in 1062, where the sagas credit the Norwegian victory largely to the earl Haakon Ivarsson. In 1064 Harald gave up his claim to Denmark in return for Sweyn's recognition as king of Norway. He took the name Estridsson after his mother to stress his link to the royal house, and he minted his own coins.

Sweyn courted the popes and, fearing that Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg would fill the Danish churches with Germans, brought Anglo-Danes from England. Around 1060 Denmark was divided into eight dioceses, set up by gifts of land, and after Adalbert's death in 1072 he dealt directly with the Holy See. In 1069 he sent a force against William the Conqueror in England with Edgar Atheling but took a payment to desert Edgar after capturing York, and another attempt in 1074 or 1075 failed.

Sweyn died on 28 April 1076 at the royal estate of Søderup, and was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. Danish chronicles wrongly date his death to 1074. He is often called Denmark's last Viking king and its first medieval one. Adam of Bremen, who visited him around 1070, recorded that Scania alone had 300 churches. Five of his sons, Harald Hen, Canute the Saint, Olaf Hunger, Eric Evergood and Niels, became kings of Denmark, and he fathered at least twenty children, of whom only one was born in wedlock.
swidnica: The name was first recorded as Svidnica in 1070, when the place belonged to Piast-ruled Poland. It became a town in 1250, although no founding document survives. By 1290 it had city walls and six gates, and guilds of bakers, weavers, potters, shoemakers, furriers and tailors. It was known for its beer: in the late 15th century almost three hundred houses had the right to brew, and so-called Świdnica Cellars serving its beer stood in Wrocław, Kraków, Toruń, Prague and Pisa. The Franciscans settled in 1287 and the Dominicans in 1291.

From 1291 to 1392 Świdnica was the capital of the Duchy of Świdnica and Jawor. The last Piast duke, Bolko II of Świdnica, died in 1368, his widow held the duchy until 1392, and it then passed to the Kingdom of Bohemia under Wenceslaus IV. By the end of the 14th century the town had about 6,000 inhabitants. It resisted a Hussite attack in 1429. In 1526 it came under the Habsburg monarchy, and it suffered badly in the Thirty Years' War from sieges, fires and epidemics. Prussia took it in the First Silesian War (1740–42) and made it a fortress, which it remained until 1866. After 1945 the town became part of Poland, and the German population still there was expelled.

Jews are recorded in Świdnica from the second half of the 13th century and received privileges from Duke Henry Probus in 1285. In the mid-14th century it was one of the main centres of Jewish settlement in Silesia, with rabbis such as Israel Isserlein. In 1453, after the inquisitor John of Capistrano accused the community of desecrating the Host, seventeen Jews were burned and the rest expelled. A new community was founded in 1859 and consecrated a synagogue in 1877; the Nazi era destroyed it.

Świdnica stands on the Bystrzyca River in Lower Silesia. It has been the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese since 2004. The Gothic Cathedral of St Stanislaus and St Wenceslaus, from the 14th century, has the highest tower in Silesia at 103 metres. The Evangelical Church of Peace was built in 1656–57. The 16th-century town hall combines Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque elements and houses a museum.
swindon: Swindon lies in north-eastern Wiltshire, 84 miles (135 km) west of London and 36 miles (57 km) east of Bristol, on the M4 corridor. The Cotswolds lie just to the north and the North Wessex Downs just to the south. The ancient Ridgeway, described as Britain's oldest road, runs a few miles to the south, with Avebury, the largest megalithic stone circle in the world, and the Uffington White Horse nearby. The town stands at the junction of two Roman roads, and it developed into a transport hub over the centuries.

The Anglo-Saxon settlement stood in a defensible position on a limestone hill. The Domesday Book of 1086 records it as Suindune, believed to derive from the Old English words for swine and hill, or possibly from Sweyn's hill, Sweyn being a Scandinavian name.

The town remained small until the Great Western Railway chose it for the repair and maintenance of locomotives. Isambard Kingdom Brunel's Swindon Works was built for this purpose, and the company built a small railway village to house its workers. The station opened in 1842 as Swindon Junction, and until 1895 every train stopped for at least ten minutes to change locomotives, so that the station had the first recorded railway refreshment rooms. The railway also provided a medical fund clinic and hospital for its workers, and a health centre of 1892 with clinics, baths and swimming pools.

During the Second World War new industries arrived: Vickers-Armstrong made aircraft at Stratton and Plessey produced electrical components at Cheney Manor. By 1960 Plessey was the largest employer in the town, with a mostly female workforce. A local council, the Borough of Thamesdown, was created in 1974; it was renamed the Borough of Swindon in 1997 and became a unitary authority on 1 April 1997.
