At the 2021 census the built-up area had a population of 224,942, the largest settlement in Wiltshire. The Grade II listed Railway Village survives, and the former works house the STEAM Museum of the Great Western Railway and the Swindon Designer Outlet. Other sites include Lydiard House, a Palladian house, and the Richard Jefferies Museum, dedicated to the nature writer. Swindon Town football club won the 1969 League Cup final against Arsenal.
switzerland: Switzerland covers 41,291 square kilometres between the Alps, the Swiss Plateau and the Jura Mountains. The Alps make up about 60% of the area, while most of the population lives on the plateau, where cities such as Zurich, Geneva, Basel and Bern stand. Glaciers cover 1,063 square kilometres, and the headwaters of the Rhine, Inn, Ticino and Rhône rise there; the springs of the Rhône and the Rhine are only about 22 kilometres apart, although one river reaches the Mediterranean Sea and the other the North Sea. The country has more than 1500 lakes, among them Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Maggiore.

The oldest traces of hominids in Switzerland date to about 150,000 years ago, and the oldest known farming settlements, at Gächlingen, to around 5300 BCE. The La Tène culture developed from around 450 BCE, and the Helvetii, one of its most prominent tribes, held the Swiss Plateau.

In 58 BCE they left it, under the influence of the aristocrat Orgetorix, and were defeated by Julius Caesar at the Battle of Bibracte, after which Caesar forced them back to their lands. In 15 BCE Tiberius and his brother Drusus conquered the Alps for the Roman Empire. Towns such as Aventicum and Augusta Raurica reached a considerable size in the first and second centuries CE.

The Old Swiss Confederacy arose in the Late Middle Ages as a defensive and commercial alliance, and the Federal Charter of 1291 is regarded as its founding document. Its independence from the Holy Roman Empire was formally recognised in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Revolutionary France invaded in 1798 and imposed the centralist Helvetic Republic, which Napoleon abolished in 1803, reinstating a confederation. After 1830 liberal and conservative movements came into conflict, and the constitution of 1848 created the present federal system.

Switzerland is a federal republic of 26 cantons, with Bern as the federal city. The Federal Assembly has two houses, the Council of States with 46 members and the National Council with 200, and the executive is the seven-member Federal Council. Citizens may challenge laws passed by parliament through optional referendums. The country has four principal linguistic regions, German, French, Italian and Romansh, and about 9 million people. It has followed a policy of armed neutrality since the 16th century, joined the United Nations in 2002 and hosts many international institutions.
syagrius: Syagrius was the son of Aegidius, the Roman military commander (magister militum) of Gaul under the emperor Majorian, who reigned from 457 to 461. When Majorian was murdered, Aegidius refused to recognise the new emperor Libius Severus and held on in northern Gaul, while the south was ruled by the Visigothic and Burgundian kingdoms, both allies of the emperor. Gregory of Tours says Aegidius had held Soissons before his son, though the nature of that holding is unclear. Aegidius was associated with Frankish troops and with King Childeric, who many scholars think led a Roman-aligned force against the Visigoths at Orleans in 463.

Gregory of Tours mentions Syagrius only twice. After noting that Aegidius died and left a son, he turns to battles in the Loire region in which Syagrius does not appear; he may still have been young. How power was divided in northern Gaul after Aegidius is unclear. Frankish kings ruled other former Roman districts, such as Ragnachar at Cambrai, and a Roman named Arbogast is known at Trier. Scholars generally assume that Syagrius kept some Roman authority, independent of leaders such as Childeric, for significantly longer than his father had, although no clear evidence shows it. Modern historians call his domain the Kingdom of Soissons.

Gregory records that five years into his reign Clovis I marched on Soissons with his relative Ragnachar, and that Syagrius came out to fight without hesitation. He lost and fled to Alaric II, king of the Visigoths at Toulouse. Intimidated by the Franks, the Visigoths imprisoned him and handed him over, and he was secretly executed. The victory is generally understood as a major step in Clovis's takeover of most of Gaul.

Historians have mistrusted the title rex Romanorum that Gregory gave him, as far back as Edward Gibbon; Steven Fanning argues that rex is used neutrally or favourably elsewhere. His family seems to have prospered under the Franks: a Count Syagrius went on a mission to the Byzantine Empire in 585, and the last known Syagrius was an abbot of Nantua mentioned in 757.
sybaris: Sybaris lay on the coast of the Gulf of Taranto, in modern Calabria, between the rivers Crathis and Sybaris, now the Crati and Coscile. The plain around it is the widest in Calabria and was noted for its fertility, the source of the city's wealth. It lay close to sea level and flooded periodically, so that the site now lies about 6 metres below the surface and below the groundwater. A flood in 2013 filled the excavated area with silt, and pumps are still needed to keep it dry.

Sybaris was founded around 720 BCE by Achaean settlers from Helice, accompanied by Troezenians whom the more numerous Achaeans eventually expelled. It grew rich on its farmland and by admitting foreigners to its citizenship, and may have had 300,000 inhabitants, though others give 100,000. It ruled four tribes and 25 cities, and founded colonies on the Tyrrhenian coast, among them Poseidonia, around 600 BCE. It began to mint coins around 530 BCE. Ancient writers told of the luxury of citizens such as Smindyrides, who, according to Herodotus, surpassed all other men in refined luxury.

In 510/509 BCE, according to Diodorus Siculus, a popular leader named Telys exiled the 500 richest citizens, who took refuge at Kroton. Pythagoras persuaded the Krotoniates to protect them, and their army under Milo defeated the Sybarites and razed the city. Walter Burkert doubts this account. Sybaris was not wholly destroyed, but became a dependent ally of Kroton, and its people left the site again between 476 and 452/451 BCE. The Sybarites refounded it in 452/451 BCE and were driven out in 446/445 BCE. Athenian colonists then came and in 444/443 BCE founded Thurii. The Sybarites quarrelled with the other settlers, and most were killed. Thurii was destroyed in 193 BCE and the Romans built Copia on the same grid.

Sediment from the Crati, more than 6 metres deep, buried the ruins, and the site was located only through a large core-drilling project. Because of the depth and the groundwater, only the Stombi quarter and small test pits in the Parco del Cavallo have been dug, the latter yielding decorated architectural elements from an unidentified temple. The ruins lie southeast of Sibari in the Province of Cosenza. The sanctuary of Athena on the Timpone della Motta near Francavilla Marittima, taken over by the Sybarites as their acropolis, is another source of evidence.
sydney: Sydney is a coastal basin, with the Tasman Sea to the east, the Blue Mountains to the west, the Hawkesbury River to the north and the Woronora Plateau to the south. The urban area surrounds Sydney Harbour and extends about 60 kilometres from the Pacific Ocean to the escarpment of the Blue Mountains. The Cumberland Plain, relatively flat, lies to the south and west of the harbour, and the Hornsby Plateau, cut by steep valleys, lies to the north. The flat southern areas were developed first, and the northern reaches became more heavily populated only after the Sydney Harbour Bridge was built. About seventy surf beaches lie along the coast.

The first people in the area were Aboriginal Australians. Flaked pebbles in Western Sydney's gravel might indicate human presence 45,000 to 50,000 years ago, and radiocarbon dating shows human activity from around 30,000 years ago. Before the British arrived there were 4,000 to 8,000 Aboriginal people in the region, living by fishing, hunting and gathering plants and shellfish. Greater Sydney covers the traditional lands of 28 known clans, among them the Gadigal, whose territory along the southern shore of Port Jackson includes the site of the first British settlement.

In 1788 Captain Arthur Phillip, the first governor of New South Wales, named the cove Sydney Cove after Home Secretary Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney; its Aboriginal name was Warrane. The population was under 1,000 in 1788 and almost tripled in ten years to 2,953 with convict transportation. The first five governors had near autocratic power. Governor Macquarie set ambitious standards for building, and the convict Francis Greenway, pardoned in 1818, designed the Hyde Park Barracks in 1819. Sydney was declared a city in 1842, when an elected municipal council was set up. New South Wales achieved responsible government in 1856, and in 1901, with the federation of the Australian colonies, Sydney became the capital of the state.

Greater Sydney consists of 658 suburbs spread across 33 local government areas, and the 2021 census recorded a population of 5,231,150. The Australian Museum, opened in 1827, remains Australia's oldest natural history museum, and the Museum of Sydney stands on the site of the first Government House. The Sydney Opera House is World Heritage listed. Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park holds around 1,500 pieces of Aboriginal rock art, the largest cluster of Indigenous sites in Australia.
sydney-nova-scotia: Sydney lies on the east bank of the Sydney River where it flows into the South Arm of Sydney Harbour, on the east coast of Cape Breton Island. Its elevation ranges from sea level to 66 metres. The central business district stands on a peninsula between the Sydney River and Muggah Creek, and neighbourhoods include Whitney Pier beside the former steel plant, Ashby and Hardwood Hill. The former city completely encircles the Membertou First Nation. Together with Sydney Mines, North Sydney, New Waterford and Glace Bay it forms the region traditionally called Industrial Cape Breton.

During the American Revolution, John Paul Jones sailed in command of Alfred on 1 November 1776 to free American prisoners working in the coal mines of eastern Cape Breton. Winter weather prevented that, but the voyage captured the Mellish, a ship carrying winter clothing for John Burgoyne's troops. The town was named after Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney, the Home Secretary, who appointed Joseph Frederick Wallet DesBarres lieutenant-governor of the new colony of Cape Breton Island.

The settlers who landed in November 1784 were mostly English citizens and disbanded soldiers, joined by Loyalists from New York. DesBarres arrived on 7 January 1785 and held his first executive council on 21 February. The colony was merged with Nova Scotia in 1820 so that the coal fields around the harbour could be developed; the coal leases passed to the General Mining Association in 1826.

Sydney was incorporated as a town in 1885, and early in the 20th century it became home to one of the world's largest steel plants, owned by the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation. It became a city in 1904. In the Second World War the harbour was a staging base for supply convoys bound for Europe; of the 35 merchant ships of Convoy SC 7, 20 were sunk.

The steel and coal industries declined after the war. After the plant's owners announced its closure in October 1967, about 20,000 people marched in the Parade of Concern on 19 November 1967, and the province took the plant over in 1968. Both industries closed by the end of 2001. The city was dissolved on 1 August 1995 and amalgamated into the Cape Breton Regional Municipality. The site of the plant is now Open Hearth Park, completed in 2013 after the cleanup of the Sydney Tar Ponds.
sylhet: Sylhet lies on the banks of the Surma River in north-eastern Bangladesh, in Sylhet Division. It has a tropical monsoon climate, with a rainy season from April to October; nearly 80 percent of the average annual rainfall of 4,200 millimetres falls between May and September. The surrounding region is geologically complex, and limestone deposits suggest that the whole area lay under the ocean in the Oligo-Miocene. Three major earthquakes of at least magnitude 7.5 have struck the city in the last 150 years, the most recent in 1918. The name is an anglicisation of Śilhôṭ, thought to derive from the Sanskrit Śrīhaṭṭa, which takes its name from Śrīhaṭṭanātha, the tutelary deity of the Nātha dynasty.

The region has been inhabited since ancient times. In 1303 Shamsuddin Firoz Shah, Sultan of Lakhnauti, conquered Sylhet by defeating the Hindu ruler Gour Govinda, and it became part of the Bengal Sultanate. In the 16th century the Baro-Bhuiyan zamindars, among them the Sardars of the Pathan Confederacy, controlled it. It later became a sarkar, or district, of the Mughal Empire, and after 1612 it was the Mughals' most significant imperial outpost in Bengal east of Dhaka, a position it kept throughout the 17th century.

British rule began in the 18th century under the East India Company. Sylhet became a key source of lascars for the British Empire, in part because of its ancient seafaring tradition. Robert Lindsay, District Collector from 1778 to 1790, described the town as merely a small market, with houses on hills hidden behind forests. The municipal board was established in 1867, and in 1874 the town became part of Colonial Assam.

An earthquake on 12 June 1897 demolished almost the whole town, and a modern new town on a European model was built on the wreckage. From the beginning of the 20th century the tea industry increased its importance. In 1947, following a referendum and the partition of British India, Sylhet became part of East Pakistan. In 1995 Bangladesh declared it the sixth divisional headquarters of the country.

The 2022 census counted 532,839 people in the city. Most are Muslims, with a Hindu minority of about 9 percent, and Sylheti is spoken by the vast majority. The Shah Jalal Dargah, an Islamic shrine, draws thousands of pilgrims a year. The hinterland holds the country's largest tea plantations and natural gas fields, and the city's economy is closely linked with the Bangladeshi diaspora, especially the British Bangladeshi community, whose remittances have driven growth in construction. Shahjalal University of Science and Technology and Sylhet Agricultural University are the public universities.
sylvanus-olympio: Sylvanus Olympio was born on 6 September 1902 at Kpandu, in the German protectorate of Togoland. He came from an important family of mixed Brazilian and other African descent: his grandfather was the Brazilian trader Francisco Olympio Sylvio, and his uncle Octaviano Olympio, based at Lomé, became one of the richest people in the colony. He studied economics at the London School of Economics under Harold Laski. He worked for Unilever in Nigeria and the Gold Coast, headed its operations in Togoland by 1929 and by 1938 was general manager of the United Africa Company throughout Africa.

During World War II the colony came under the Vichy France government, which treated the Olympio family with suspicion because of its ties to the British. Olympio was arrested in 1942 and held under surveillance at Djougou in French Dahomey. The imprisonment changed his view of the French, and he pushed for independence once the war ended.

Togo was a trust territory, and in 1947 Olympio sent the first petition for the resolution of grievances to the United Nations Trusteeship Council. At home he founded the Comité de l'unité togolaise, the main party opposing French control. It boycotted most elections of the 1950s because of heavy French involvement, and French authorities arrested Olympio in 1954 and suspended his right to vote and stand. His petitions led to the elections of 1958, in which his party won every elected position in the national council and he became prime minister. He defeated Nicolas Grunitzky in the presidential vote with more than 90 per cent to become the first president of Togo.

In foreign policy he drew Togo towards Britain, the United States and other Western countries, and visited President John F. Kennedy in 1962. Relations with Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana were tense, as the two quarrelled over the western part of the former German colony. Domestically he restrained spending and kept the army to about 250 soldiers. After an attempt on his life in 1961, in which Grunitzky's party and the Juvento movement were accused, the opposition was outlawed, and Togo became largely a one-party state.

Shortly after midnight on 13 January 1963, members of the military broke into the house of Olympio and his wife. Before dawn his body was found by the United States ambassador, Leon B. Poullada, near the door of the American embassy. Étienne Eyadéma later claimed to have fired the shot. Nicolas Grunitzky was installed as president, and Eyadéma took power in 1967.
symon-petliura: Symon Vasyliovych Petliura was born on 22 May 1879 in a suburb of Poltava, then in the Russian Empire, to a family of Cossack background. His father had owned a transportation business, and his mother was the daughter of an Orthodox hieromonk. He planned to become a priest, but he took part in strikes demanding Ukrainian subjects in school and was expelled from his seminary, in part because his students' choir had sung a cantata by Mykola Lysenko that Russian censorship had banned.

He turned to journalism. In Lviv he worked beside Ivan Franko and Volodymyr Hnatiuk on the Literaturno-Naukovyi Vistnyk, and after 1905 he edited Ukrainian periodicals in Saint Petersburg and Kyiv, among them Slovo in 1907–09. He is said to have published over 15,000 articles under an estimated 120 pen names.

In May 1917 Petliura was elected head of the Ukrainian General Military Committee, and when the Central Rada was proclaimed on 28 June 1917 he became its first Secretary for Military Affairs. After disagreements with Volodymyr Vynnychenko he led the Haydamaky Kish, which helped defend Kyiv against the Bolshevik Red Guard in early 1918. The government of Pavlo Skoropadskyi, which took power in April 1918, imprisoned him for four months.

With war between Ukraine and Soviet Russia in January 1919 and Vynnychenko's emigration, Petliura became the leading figure in the Directorate. His army lost Kyiv that winter, and through the year he fought the Bolsheviks, the White forces of Anton Denikin and Romanian-Polish troops. In April 1920 he signed an alliance with Poland in Warsaw, accepting a border on the River Zbruch and Poland's right to Galicia in return for military aid. The joint attack on Kyiv began on 7 May 1920, but Ukraine remained under Soviet control.

Petliura directed the government-in-exile from Tarnów, then left Poland in late 1923 and reached Paris in October 1924, where he founded the newspaper Tryzub in 1925. On 25 May 1926 Sholem Schwarzbard shot him on Rue Racine, and he died the same day. Schwarzbard said he had acted to avenge the victims of pogroms.

Petliura's role in the pogroms of 1918–1921 remains disputed. Of 1,236 recorded attacks on Jews in Ukraine, 493 were carried out by soldiers of the Ukrainian People's Republic under his command. Many in Ukraine and its diaspora regard him as a national hero, and monuments to him stand in Kyiv and Poltava.
syncretism: The English word is first attested in 1618. It comes from Modern Latin syncretismus, drawing on the Greek synkretismós, supposedly meaning a Cretan federation. This etymology goes back to Plutarch's essay Fraternal Love of the 1st century, which describes the Cretans reconciling their differences and joining in alliance when faced with external dangers. A more likely derivation is from sun- (with) and kerannumi (to mix).

Religious syncretism blends two or more belief systems into a new one, or brings beliefs from unrelated traditions into an existing one. It usually follows contact between cultures, or conquest, when the conquerors do not entirely remove the old beliefs or, especially, practices. In religion it denotes a more integrated merging than eclecticism, which selects elements from different traditions without forming a new, cohesive system.

Attitudes to the term differ. Adherents of exclusivist or revealed religions often reject the label, seeing the addition of an incompatible belief as a corruption of the original faith. Non-exclusivist systems may feel free to take in other traditions. Véronique Altglas argues that the term presupposes that the traditions combined were once pure, whereas in her view all religions are syncretic to some degree.

The Kushite kings of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt, from 721 to 664 BCE, identified their god Dedun with the Egyptian Osiris. In the Hellenistic period rulers identified local deities with Greek gods to strengthen the cohesion of their kingdoms, though the Jews rejected this, regarding the identification of Yahweh with Zeus as the worst blasphemy. The Roman Empire equated its own deities with Greek ones, forming a single Greco-Roman pantheon, and then with the local deities of its provinces.

In the 16th century the Mughal emperor Akbar proposed the Din-i Ilahi, or Divine Faith, which drew mainly on Islam and Hinduism and also on Christianity, Jainism and Zoroastrianism. It had no scriptures or priesthood and fewer than 20 disciples, all chosen by Akbar. Syncretism tends to ease coexistence between different cultures, which recommended it to rulers of multi-ethnic realms, while rejecting it in the name of orthodoxy can build a sense of uncompromised unity in a group.
synesius: Synesius was born of wealthy parents at Balagrae, now Bayda in Libya, near Cyrene, between 370 and 375. In 393, still a youth, he went with his brother Euoptius to Alexandria, where he became an enthusiastic Neoplatonist and a disciple of Hypatia. Between 395 and 399 he spent some time in Athens. In 398 Cyrene and the whole Pentapolis chose him as an envoy to the imperial court at Constantinople, where he was to obtain tax remissions for his country when the aurum coronarium was delivered.

In Constantinople Synesius gained the patronage of the praetorian prefect Aurelianus, and he addressed to the emperor Arcadius a speech, De regno, advising the ruler to give first priority to a war on corruption and on the infiltration of barbarians into the Roman army. His three years there were wearisome. Aurelianus obtained the remission for Cyrene and the Pentapolis and an exemption from curial obligations for him, but then fell into disgrace, and Synesius lost everything until Aurelianus returned to power. In 402 he left the city during an earthquake. He married in Alexandria and returned to Cyrene in 405, where his main concern was organising the defence of the Pentapolis against yearly attacks by neighbouring tribes.

In 410, though his Christianity had until then been by no means pronounced, he was popularly chosen bishop of Ptolemais. After long hesitation on personal and doctrinal grounds he accepted, and Theophilus consecrated him at Alexandria. He was allowed to keep his wife and stipulated freedom to dissent on the soul's creation, a literal resurrection and the final destruction of the world. His tenure was troubled by the deaths of his three sons in 411 and 413, by Libyan invasions that destroyed Cyrenaica and led him to exile, and by conflict with the governor Andronicus, whom he excommunicated for interfering with the Church's right of asylum.

His writings include the 159 surviving letters, nine hymns of a contemplative, Neoplatonic character, a treatise on dreams, two homilies and the Catastasis, a description of the end of Roman Cyrenaica. Aegyptus sive de providentia is an allegory in which the good Osiris and the evil Typhon stand for Aurelianus and the Goth Gainas. A letter to Hypatia contains the earliest known reference to a hydrometer, and he also wrote an essay on making an astrolabe. Several traditional Christian hymns, among them Lord Jesus, Think On Me, are based on his writings.
syngman-rhee: Syngman Rhee was born Rhee Syngryong on 26 March 1875 in Daegyeong, a village in Pyeongsan County, Hwanghae Province. He was the only surviving son of a rural family of modest means, and his family traced its lineage to King Taejong of Joseon. He attended a local Methodist school, where he converted to Christianity. After the First Sino-Japanese War of 1895 he joined anti-Japanese circles and the Independence Club, and he organised protests against corruption and the influence of Japan and the Russian Empire. He was imprisoned in 1899 and released in 1904.

In November 1904 he moved to the United States, where he met President Theodore Roosevelt in 1905 and unsuccessfully asked for help in preserving Korea's independence. He took a bachelor's degree at George Washington University in 1907, a master's at Harvard in 1908 and a doctorate at Princeton in 1910. He returned to Korea in 1910, was implicated in the 105-Man Incident in 1912 and fled to the United States.

After the surrender of Japan in 1945, Rhee returned to Korea in October on a passport provided by the US military government. He was elected the first president of the Republic of Korea by the National Assembly on 20 July 1948. His government curtailed political dissent. Kim Ku was assassinated on 26 June 1949, and the suppression of the Jeju uprising killed many; South Korea's Truth Commission reported 14,373 victims, 86 per cent at the hands of the security forces. By early 1950 about 30,000 alleged communists were in jail, and when North Korea attacked on 25 June 1950 retreating forces executed prisoners.

Rhee refused to sign the armistice that ended the Korean War, wishing to reunify the peninsula by force. In 1952 he had opposition politicians arrested and passed an amendment for direct election, then won 74 per cent of the vote. In 1956 he had the constitution amended to remove the term limit. In March 1960 he won a fourth term after his main opponent died before the election. The vice-presidential result was rejected as rigged, protests spread, and police shot demonstrators in Masan. The student-led April Revolution forced him to resign on 26 April.

Rhee left for Hawaii on 29 May 1960 and died of a stroke in Honolulu on 19 July 1965. A week later his body was returned to Seoul and buried in the Seoul National Cemetery. He claimed he had gone for medical treatment and had never been in exile. His former Seoul residence, Ihwajang, is now a presidential memorial museum. His successors in the Second Republic lasted a year before a military coup in 1961.
syphax: Syphax was king of the Masaesyli tribe of western Numidia, in present-day Algeria, during the last quarter of the 3rd century BCE. His story is told in Livy's Ab Urbe Condita. His territory extended from present-day Constantine to the Moulouya, and in some periods his influence reached from the Moulouya to the Strait of Gibraltar.

When war broke out again between Carthage and Rome in 218 BCE, Syphax was at first sympathetic to the Romans. In 213 BCE he made an alliance with them, and they sent Quintus Statorius as a military adviser to train his troops. He then attacked the Massylians of eastern Numidia, ruled by King Gala, who were allied to Carthage. When Gala died in 206 BCE and his sons Masinissa and Oezalces quarrelled over the inheritance, Syphax conquered considerable parts of the eastern kingdom.

After Publius Cornelius Scipio won the Battle of Ilipa in 206 BCE, he sent his friend Gaius Laelius to ratify the treaty with Syphax. Syphax refused to ratify any treaty except with Scipio himself, so Scipio sailed to Numidia with two quinqueremes. He reached the harbour at the same moment as Hasdrubal Gisco, who had fled from Spain. Syphax invited both men to dinner, and both were taken in by Scipio's charm. Masinissa meanwhile concluded that Rome was winning and changed sides, and the Carthaginians found a new ally in Syphax. Hasdrubal Gisco sealed the alliance by offering his daughter Sophonisba in marriage, although she had been betrothed to Masinissa until 206 BCE.

The combined forces of Syphax and Gisco at first made Scipio abandon the siege of Utica. In the Battle of the Great Plains in 203 BCE, however, Scipio overcame them. While he concentrated on Carthage, Laelius and Masinissa followed Syphax to Cirta.

During the pursuit, Syphax's army threatened to desert as Laelius and Masinissa approached its line. He rode alone towards the Roman cavalry in an attempt to rally his men, but his badly wounded horse threw him, and Roman soldiers seized him and took him to Masinissa. His troops withdrew to the capital, which fell, and Masinissa claimed his kingdom. Syphax was handed to Scipio and taken back to Rome as a prisoner. He died at Tibur, modern Tivoli.

Sophonisba then married Masinissa. Scipio, suspicious of her, demanded that she be taken to Rome to appear in his triumph. To spare her that humiliation, Masinissa sent her poison, and she killed herself.
syr-darya: The Syr Darya rises in the Tian Shan mountains, where its two headstreams, the Naryn and the Kara Darya, come together in the Fergana Valley, and flows west and north-west through Uzbekistan, the Sughd province of Tajikistan and southern Kazakhstan to the northern remnants of the Aral Sea. With the Amu Darya it is one of the two main rivers of the Aral Sea basin. It drains an area of over 800,000 square kilometres, though no more than 160,000 contribute significant flow, and its annual flow is about half that of the Amu Darya.

Along its course the river irrigates the most productive agricultural regions in Central Asia, and canals of central importance in this arid region were built and maintained by local governments through history. Many fell into disuse in the 17th and early 18th century, and the Khanate of Kokand rebuilt many in the 19th.

The earliest recorded name is the Greek Jaxartes, which echoes the Old Persian Yakhsha Arta, perhaps meaning true pearl and referring to the colour of its glacial water. Until the Arab conquest the river's Turkic name was Yinçü ögüz, the pearl river. The present name Syr does not appear before the 16th century; in Tajik it means secret.

Alexander the Great reached the Jaxartes in 329 BCE, after travelling through Bactria and Sogdia without opposition. In October of that year the Macedonians fought the Battle of Jaxartes against the Saka and killed some 1,200 combatants, including the nomads' leader. Alexander placed a garrison in the City of Cyrus and renamed it Alexandria Eschate, Alexandria the furthest; since at least the Muslim conquest of Central Asia the city has been called Khujand. Revolt then spread through Sogdia and brought two years of warfare. In the mid-19th century, during the Russian conquest of Turkestan, the Russian Empire introduced steam navigation on the river.

Soviet irrigation projects around the Syr Darya and the Amu Darya diverted their water to farmland, so that in some periods none reached the Aral Sea, once the world's fourth-largest lake. The Aral Sea virtually disappeared in the post-Soviet era.
syria: The modern state of Syria covers 185,180 km2 in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Levant. Its land runs from the Mediterranean coastal plains to the mountains of the west, where Mount Hermon, at 2,814 metres, is the highest point, and much of the centre and east is arid plateau and desert. The valleys of the Euphrates, Orontes and Khabur rivers support agriculture and settlement. Commercial petroleum was first discovered in the northeast in 1956.

The name Syria is borrowed from Ancient Greek, which took it from Luwian sura/i-, attested in the 8th century BCE, and mainstream scholarship relates it to Assyria. From the Seleucid Empire the Greeks applied it to the Levant without distinguishing the Assyrians of Mesopotamia from the Arameans of the Levant. Under the Roman Empire the larger Syria was divided into provinces such as Judaea, renamed Palaestina in 135 CE, and Phoenice, established in 194.

The Natufian culture became sedentary around the 11th millennium BCE, and the site of Tell Qaramel has round stone towers dated to 10650 BCE. The earliest recorded indigenous civilization was the Kingdom of Ebla, near present-day Idlib, which appears to have been founded around 3500 BCE and grew rich through trade with Sumer, Assyria and Akkad and contact with Egypt.

One of its early texts, the Treaty between Ebla and Abarsal of about 2300 BCE, is a trading agreement. Ebla was weakened by a long war with Mari, and in the first half of the 23rd century BCE the conquests of Sargon of Akkad and Naram-Sin ended its domination of Syria.

The modern state emerged from a French Mandate. It gained de jure independence in 1945 as a founding member of the United Nations, and French troops withdrew in April 1946. Coups and coup attempts followed between 1949 and 1971, and a union with Egypt lasted from 1958 to 1961. The Ba'ath Party took power in 1963. Hafez al-Assad came to power in 1970 and was succeeded on his death in 2000 by his son Bashar. A civil war began in 2011, and the Assad government fell in December 2024.
syria-palaestina: Judaea had been under direct Roman rule since the deposition of Herod Archelaus in 6 CE, and its capital had shifted from Jerusalem to Caesarea Maritima. In the 1st and 2nd centuries it became the centre of a series of unsuccessful Jewish rebellions against Rome. The First Jewish-Roman War of 66-73 ended with the destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple, and the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132-136 devastated the countryside of Judea, with many people killed, displaced or sold into slavery. The renamed province included Judea, Samaria, Galilee, Idumaea and Philistia, kept Caesarea Maritima as its capital and stayed distinct from Syria, whose capital was Antioch.

The new name was introduced after the revolt, and the exact date and motives are uncertain. Coins of Hadrian before the revolt still say Judaea, and a military diploma of 139 already uses the new name. Most scholars see a deliberate attempt to suppress Jewish ties to the land, and the historian Werner Eck argues that Judaea alone lost its ethnic name as a punishment, unlike rebellious provinces such as Germania, Pannonia and Britannia. David Jacobson suggests a practical reason, since the province had grown larger than Judea.

The name Syria Palaestina was already used in the Greco-Roman world, and Herodotus speaks of that part of Syria called Palestine. Jerusalem was rebuilt as the colony of Aelia Capitolina, and Jews were forbidden to settle there or nearby.

The province was governed by a consular rank governor, higher than the legate of Judaea had been, and a second legion was stationed at Legio. Around 300 Diocletian added much of Arabia Petraea, including the Negev and Sinai, and moved Legio X Fretensis from Aelia Capitolina to Aila.

The fourth century brought an economic upswing as the empire became Christian and pilgrimage to the Holy Land grew. According to the historian Moshe David Herr, the Jewish share of the population fell after the revolt from about two thirds to three fifths or less, and by the end of the 4th century to about one third. Christians formed a majority by the fifth century. The province was split into smaller ones in the 4th and 5th centuries, among them Palaestina Prima, Palaestina Secunda and Palaestina Salutaris, within the Diocese of the East.
syriac-christians: Syriac emerged in Edessa in Upper Mesopotamia during the first centuries CE and is related to the Aramaic of Jesus, a Galilean dialect, which added to its prestige for Christians. Along with Greek and Latin it became one of the three most important languages of early Christianity. The area where Syriac or Aramaic was spoken lay between the Roman and Sasanian empires and stretched from around Antioch to Seleucia-Ctesiphon. The ruins of the Dura-Europos church, from the first half of the 3rd century, are firm evidence of organised Christian communities there, but almost everything earlier is obscure. The fourth century is marked by the writings of Ephrem the Syrian, the Demonstrations of Aphrahat and the anonymous Book of Steps.

Two councils of the 5th century divided Syriac Christianity into two parties. The Church of the East, established in the Sasanian Empire at the Council of Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410, declared its Catholicos independent in 424 and ignored the condemnation of Nestorius at Ephesus in 431. The Council of Chalcedon of 451 was rejected by the churches that became the Syriac Orthodox Church, whose opponents called them Monophysites or Jacobites after Jacob Baradaeus, although they teach Miaphysitism. The Church of the East spread Christianity to India, China, Tibet and Mongolia, and the West Syriac churches also carried their faith east.

The two traditions use different liturgies. East Syriac churches use the Liturgy of Addai and Mari, and West Syriac churches use the Liturgy of Saint James. A schism in 1552 in the Church of the East produced a patriarchate that later gave rise to the Assyrian Church of the East, while at the end of the 18th century most followers of the earlier line joined Rome as the Chaldean Catholic Church. In 1783 the Syriac Orthodox patriarch Ignatius Michael III Jarweh declared himself a Catholic and became head of the Syriac Catholic Church.

In India the Saint Thomas Christians, called Syrian Christians, were originally East Syriac in rite. Those who in 1653 broke with the Catholic Church under Portuguese influence chose union with the Syriac Orthodox Church and later split into groups such as the Malabar Independent Syrian Church in 1772. In the 19th and 20th centuries persecution, especially after the Assyrian genocide, drove many Syriac Christians from the Middle East and created a large diaspora.
syrian-wars: The wars were fought between the Seleucid Empire and the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, successor states to Alexander the Great's empire, over Coele-Syria, now south-western Syria and the Beqaa Valley. The corridor linked Asia to Egypt, threatened the Nile Delta, lay within the natural continuation of Seleucid Syria and yielded substantial agricultural and commercial revenue. After the Wars of the Diadochi Ptolemy I Soter took the region in 301 BCE, exploiting events around the Battle of Ipsus, although the victors there had assigned it to Seleucus I Nicator. Seleucus, who had been helped by Ptolemy, did not try to reclaim it, and war began once both were dead.

In the First Syrian War (274–271 BCE) Antiochus I took Ptolemaic areas in coastal Syria and southern Anatolia, and Ptolemy II reconquered them by 271 BCE. The Second (260–253 BCE) saw Antiochus II, backed by Antigonus II Gonatas of Macedon, regain Miletus and Ephesus, and ended around 253 BCE with his marriage to Ptolemy's daughter Berenice Syra. The Third, or Laodicean, War (246–241 BCE) followed a succession dispute at the Seleucid court. Ptolemy III occupied Antioch and even reached Babylon, and in 241 BCE he gained Seleucia Pieria, the port of Antioch, when the Ptolemaic kingdom was at its height.

In the Fourth War (219–217 BCE) Antiochus III retook Seleucia Pieria and cities in Phoenicia, but Ptolemy IV Philopator defeated him at Raphia in summer 217 BCE, using at least thirty thousand native Egyptians as phalangites, which later fed the Egyptian Revolt. In the Fifth (202–195 BCE) Antiochus defeated the Ptolemies at Panium and completed the conquest of Coele-Syria in 198 BCE, and in 195 BCE Ptolemy V made peace and agreed to marry Antiochus's daughter Cleopatra I. In the Sixth (170–168 BCE) Antiochus IV Epiphanes defeated the Ptolemaic army in the Sinai, took Pelusium and besieged Alexandria.

In 168 BCE, at Eleusis near Alexandria, the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas gave Antiochus IV an ultimatum from the Senate to leave Egypt and Cyprus. According to Polybius he drew a circle in the sand round the king and told him to decide before stepping out of it. Antiochus obeyed, which ended the Sixth War. The conflicts drained the resources and manpower of both kingdoms and led to their eventual conquest by Rome and Parthia. In 145 BCE Ptolemy VI intervened in the Seleucid civil war and won the Battle of the Oenoparus, but died of his wounds, and Demetrius II drove the Ptolemaic force out of Coele-Syria.
syriza: Its roots lie in the Space for Dialogue for the Unity and Common Action of the Left, formed in 2001 by Greek left-wing organisations with different histories but common ground on issues such as the Kosovo War, privatisations and social rights. Out of it came the Coalition of the Radical Left in January 2004, made up of Synaspismos, the Renewing Communist Ecological Left, the Internationalist Workers Left and other groups. In the legislative election of 2004 it won 241,539 votes, 3.3 per cent, and six seats, all held by members of Synaspismos, the largest partner, which caused tension within the coalition. In 2008 Alexis Tsipras became president of Synaspismos.

In the election of 6 May 2012 the party polled over 16 per cent and became the second largest in parliament. For the election of 17 June it registered as a single party, because its coalition status would have disqualified it from the 50 bonus seats given to the largest party. It took just under 27 per cent against New Democracy's 29.8 and became the main opposition with 71 seats. A congress in July 2013 decided in principle to dissolve the member parties into a unitary party, and in the European election of 2014 it came first with 26.5 per cent. Its Thessaloniki Programme of 13 September 2014 set out its central demands.

In the election of 25 January 2015 Syriza won 36.3 per cent and 149 of 300 seats. Tsipras formed a coalition with the Independent Greeks and became prime minister, with Yanis Varoufakis as finance minister. After the government accepted the third memorandum with Greece's creditors, 25 members of parliament, led by Panagiotis Lafazanis and including the Left Platform, left to form Popular Unity. Tsipras resigned on 20 August 2015 and won the election of 20 September with 145 seats, renewing the coalition. The party lost the election of 2019 to New Democracy and went into opposition.

Synaspismos, a democratic socialist party, was the main constituent of the original coalition. The party was founded to unite left-wing and radical left groups and draws on democratic socialism, Marxism, market socialism and Trotskyism, with social democrats, Maoists and Marxist-Leninists among its members. It is a member of the Party of the European Left. From 2004 until September 2020 it was represented by three flags, red for socialism, green for ecology and purple for feminism, and afterwards by a star made of the Greek letters Σ and Υ. Among its factions were the Left Platform and the Group of 53, also called Umbrella, founded in mid-2014.
syros: Syros, also known as Siros or Syra, lies in the Aegean Sea 78 nautical miles, or 144 km, southeast of Athens. The island covers 83.6 km2 and had 21,124 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Its largest towns are Ermoupoli, Ano Syros and Vari, and Ermoupoli is the capital of the island, the Cyclades and the South Aegean. Ano Syros, built by the Venetians at the beginning of the 13th century on the hill of San Giorgio, keeps a medieval atmosphere and is dominated by the Catholic cathedral of Saint George, built in the 13th century.

Settlement on Syros goes back at least 5,000 years, to the Early Bronze Age of the Cycladic civilisation, when the hill-top settlement of Kastri began. Dated to 2800-2300 BCE, Kastri was one of the earliest settlements in Greece protected by stone walls with rounded bastions. In the Odyssey, Syros is the country of the swineherd Eumaeus, and the island was the home of the philosopher Pherecydes. After the Fourth Crusade in 1204 the Venetians under Marco Sanudo conquered it, and it stayed in the Duchy of the Archipelago until 1566, though after 1540 only by tribute to the Ottoman sultan. The corsair Barbarossa took possession in 1522, but negotiations gave the Cyclades privileges such as religious freedom and lower taxes.

Syros stayed neutral at the start of the Greek Revolution in 1821 and became a shelter for refugees from Asia Minor, Chios, Psara and elsewhere, who built Ermoupoli. The island joined the First Hellenic Republic in 1827 and the Greek Kingdom in 1834. Between 1822 and 1865 Ermoupoli was rebuilt in a neoclassical style, with a city hall designed by Ernst Ziller. Neorion was the first shipyard of Greece, and until 1860 Syros was the most important commercial harbour in the country; decline followed as steam replaced sail and Piraeus took the leading place.

Ermoupoli has a high density of neoclassical architecture, and the quarter of Vaporia is where sea captains traditionally lived. Catholics are now about 47 percent of the population, with the Greek Orthodox as the majority, and intermarriage between the churches is very common. The church of the Koimisis houses a work by El Greco, and Catholics and Orthodox on the island share the Orthodox date of Easter. Syros is a separate regional unit of the South Aegean, and its only municipality is Syros-Ermoupoli.
systema-naturae: Carl Linnaeus published the first edition of Systema Naturae in 1735 during his stay in the Netherlands. As was customary for scientific literature of the time, it was written in Latin. The binomial system of naming was partly developed by the Bauhin brothers, Gaspard and Johann, but Linnaeus was the first to use it consistently throughout a book. He had already applied two-part names to plants in Species Plantarum in 1753, and in the tenth edition of 1758 he introduced them for animals.

Linnaeus kept publishing new and larger editions because the work was popular and specimens were sent to him from around the world. It grew from 11 very large pages in 1735 to 2,400 pages in the twelfth edition of 1766 to 1768, the last under his authorship.

The work divides nature into the animal, plant and mineral kingdoms, using five levels: kingdom, class, order, genus and species. Linnaeus saw species and genera as given by God and the three higher levels as constructs meant to be easy to remember. In the tenth edition animals fall into six classes: Mammalia, Aves, Amphibia, Pisces, Insecta and Vermes. Whales, classed as fishes in the first edition, were moved among the mammals in 1758. Linnaeus was one of the first scientists to place humans among the primates, under the name Anthropomorpha.

He divided Homo sapiens into four varieties corresponding to the four known continents and four temperaments. The tenth edition added behavioural and cultural traits to these descriptions, which the Linnean Society recognises as having cemented colonial stereotypes and provided one of the foundations of scientific racism. His plant classes, the Sexual System, grouped species by the number of stamens. It was convenient, but in his view artificial. The work lists only about 10,000 species, about 6,000 of them plants and 4,236 animals.

After Linnaeus's health declined in the early 1770s, Johan Andreas Murray issued the plant section separately in 1774 as the Systema Vegetabilium, confusingly labelled the thirteenth edition. A thirteenth edition of the whole work appeared in parts between 1788 and 1793 under Johann Friedrich Gmelin, which zoologists have commonly treated as the last of the series.

The tenth edition is regarded as the starting point of zoological nomenclature, with one exception in zoology, Carl Clerck's monograph on Swedish spiders of 1757, whose names take priority. By the end of the 18th century Linnaeus's system had effectively become the standard for biological classification. Only in the animal kingdom is his higher taxonomy still recognisable, and his classification of minerals has long since fallen out of use. The old question whether something is animal, vegetable or mineral still echoes his three kingdoms.
szczecin: Szczecin lies on the Oder, south of the Szczecin Lagoon and the Bay of Pomerania, near the Baltic Sea and the German border. It is situated along the southwestern shore of Dąbie Lake, on both sides of the Oder and on several large islands between the river's two branches, and is surrounded by forests and heaths. The name, Stettin in German, is of Proto-Slavic origin, and Maria Malec lists eleven theories about it, among them an Old Slavic word for a hill peak and the personal name Szczota.

The recorded history of Szczecin began in the 8th century, when Vikings and West Slavs settled in Pomerania. The West Slavs erected a stronghold on the site of the later castle. Mieszko I of Poland took control of Pomerania in the Early Middle Ages and it became part of Poland in the 10th century, but Mieszko II Lambert effectively lost control and had to accept German suzerainty. The city was later the capital of the Duchy of Pomerania, ruled by the House of Griffin, which was at various times under the suzerainty of Poland, the Duchy of Saxony, the Holy Roman Empire and Denmark.

From the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 Stettin was the capital of Swedish Pomerania, and it was turned into a major Swedish fortress. After the downfall of the Swedish Empire under Charles XII it passed to Prussia in 1720. In October 1806 the Prussian commander Friedrich von Romberg surrendered the city to the French under General Lasalle, who had only 800 men against Romberg's 5,300; Romberg was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1809. The city grew from 6,081 inhabitants in 1720 to 224,119 in 1905.

After the Second World War the city became part of Poland again under the Potsdam Agreement, which resulted in a nearly complete exchange of population. In 1980 the first agreement between protesters and the communist regime was signed in Szczecin, paving the way for the creation of Solidarity.

Szczecin is the capital and largest city of the West Pomeranian Voivodeship and the seventh-largest city in Poland, and a major seaport. Its architecture reflects the late 19th century and early 20th, historicist Gründerzeit and Art Nouveau, with social realism prevalent in areas rebuilt after the Allied bombing. Its landmarks include the Szczecin Cathedral, the Ducal Castle and the National Museum.
szeged: Szeged lies near the southern border of Hungary on both banks of the Tisza River, just south of the mouth of the Maros, almost in the centre of the Carpathian Basin. The name may be a shortened form of Partiscum, a Roman colony of the 2nd century, or it may come from the Hungarian szeg, 'corner', for the bend of the Tisza.

The name Szeged first appears in 1183, in a document of King Béla III. The Mongol invasion destroyed the town, but its people returned from the swamps and rebuilt it. In the 14th century, under Louis the Great, it became the most important town of southern Hungary, and King Sigismund of Luxembourg had a wall built. It became a free royal town in 1498.

The Ottoman army pillaged Szeged on 28 September 1526 and occupied it in 1543, when it became a sanjak centre. It was taken from Ottoman rule on 23 October 1686 and regained free royal status in 1715. Charles III gave it the coat of arms still in use in 1719, and Piarist monks opened a grammar school in 1721. Witch trials were frequent between 1728 and 1744. In July 1849 the town was the last seat of the revolutionary government of the Hungarian Revolution.

The flood of 1879 swept away the town: only 265 of 5,723 houses remained and 165 people died. Emperor Franz Joseph promised that Szeged would be more beautiful than before, and a new city with palaces and wide streets rose from the ruins. The University of Kolozsvár moved to Szeged in 1921 after Hungary lost Transylvania. In the Second World War 6,000 inhabitants were killed, and the ghetto holding the Jews of the city and nearby villages was liquidated in June 1944.

Szeged is the largest city and regional centre of the Southern Great Plain and the seat of Csongrád-Csanád county. The University of Szeged was established in 1581. The city is known for paprika, for the Pick Szeged salami factory, which began as Mark Pick's shop in 1869, and for its fish soup, halászlé.
szekelys: Their origin has been much debated, and it is now generally accepted that they descend from Hungarians. The Székelys themselves historically claimed descent from Attila's Huns. The thirteenth-century chronicler Simon of Kéza wrote that they were remnants of the Huns who joined the returning Hungarians on the border of Ruthenia and conquered Pannonia together with them, and the Chronicon Pictum tells a similar story. After the theory of Hunnic descent lost scholarly currency in the 20th century, two ideas emerged: that they were Magyars moved from the west of Hungary in the 12th century to guard the frontiers, or that they had Turkic ancestry, Avar, Kabar or Esegel-Bulgar.

Research indicates that the Székelys spoke Hungarian. Place names in their settlement area point to a Hungarian mother tongue, and their dialect has no more Bulgaro-Turkish loanwords from before the Hungarian conquest than standard Hungarian does. A newer model sees them as descendants of people who fled the feudal state and the landlord system, mostly in the 11th and 12th centuries, and settled in border regions and hard-to-reach places, until Hungarian kings brought them back into the kingdom from the beginning of the 12th century.

The Székely territories were led by the Count of the Székelys (Latin Comes Siculorum), at first a royal appointee from the non-Székely Hungarian nobility who was in effect a margrave. From the 15th century the voivodes of Transylvania held the office themselves. The Székelys were treated as a distinct group, the natio Siculica, and from 1438 formed with the nobility and the Saxons the Union of Three Nations, which ruled Transylvania. During the Long Turkish War they allied with Prince Michael the Brave of Wallachia against Andrew Báthory, the newly appointed Prince of Transylvania.

In 1920, by the Treaty of Trianon, Transylvania, including the Székely Land, became part of Romania. In 1952, under communist rule, the counties of Mureș, Odorhei, Ciuc and Trei Scaune were designated the Magyar Autonomous Region. It was renamed the Mureș-Magyar Autonomous Region in 1960 and divided in 1968 into the non-autonomous counties of Harghita and Mureș.

The Székelys identify themselves as Hungarians but keep a somewhat distinct identity. Today's Székely Land corresponds roughly to the Romanian counties of Harghita, Covasna and central and eastern Mureș. Their symbols are the Sun and the Moon, which also appear in the coat of arms of Transylvania. Balázs Orbán described the Székely Land and its customs between 1859 and 1868, and the writer Áron Tamási set novels in its village culture. The execution of three Székelys at Târgu Mureș by the Austrian authorities on 10 March 1854 is remembered on Székely Freedom Day.
szekesfehervar: Grand Prince Géza of the Árpád dynasty founded the town in 972 on four moorland islands between the Gaja stream and the Sárvíz, and had a small stone castle built. It was first mentioned in a document of the Bishopric of Veszprém in 1009 as Alba Civitas. Stephen I granted it town rights, surrounded it with a plank wall and founded a school and a monastery, and the Romanesque basilica was built between 1003 and 1038. The town then had about 3,500 inhabitants. Forty-three kings were crowned here, the last in 1526, and fifteen were buried here, the last in 1540.

In the 12th century the town prospered and became an important station on the pilgrim route to the Holy Land. King András II issued the Golden Bull here in 1222; it set out the rights of nobles and the duties of the king, formed the basis of the Constitution of Hungary until 1848, and is often compared to England's Magna Carta. During the Mongol invasion of 1241–1242 the invaders could not approach the castle because flooding from melting snow made the surrounding marshes impassable. After the death of King Matthias in 1490, Emperor Maximilian I invaded Hungary, captured Székesfehérvár and sacked it; Hungarian troops liberated it the next year.

The Ottomans took the city in 1543 after a long siege, in which the commander György Varkoch and most of the defenders were locked out by wealthy citizens fearing Ottoman anger. Apart from a short period in 1601, the city stayed under Ottoman administration for 145 years, until 1688. The Ottomans renamed it Beograd, built mosques and made it a sanjak centre in the Budin Province, and most of the Hungarian population fled. In 1702 the great cathedral where kings were crowned was blown up, and coronations were afterwards held in Pozsony. Maria Theresa made the city an episcopal seat in 1777.

Székesfehérvár is the centre of Fejér County and the regional capital of Central Transdanubia, at a junction of seven railway lines between Lake Balaton and Lake Velence. Its centre preserves Baroque buildings, including the cathedral, the episcopal palace and the city hall, and the excavated ruins of the Romanesque basilica and the mausoleum of Stephen I can be visited. In 1944 the city's Jewish population was confined to a ghetto and deported to Auschwitz.
szlachta: The origins of the szlachta are obscure, and its members themselves called it perennial. Two theories were popular among its members and early historians: descent from the ancient Iranian Sarmatians, and descent from Japheth, a son of Noah, while the peasantry were said to descend from Ham. The szlachta secured increasing power from the reign of Casimir III the Great, who ruled from 1333 to 1370, until the end of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in the late 18th century. In 1413 the Lithuanian and Ruthenian nobilities formally joined the Polish nobility, and at the Union of Horodło forty-seven families of Catholic Lithuanian lords and boyars were adopted by Polish noble families.

The szlachta made up about 8 to 10 per cent of Polish-Lithuanian society, against about 1 per cent in Italy and France and under 1 per cent in England. Their land was held in allodium, not as a fief, and they stood as equals before the king, which Adam Zamoyski argues set them apart from the feudal nobility of Western Europe. Their rights included voting for kings, freedom from arbitrary arrest and from corporal punishment, and a monopoly on landownership. The lower chamber of parliament, the Sejm, was composed of deputies elected at local sejmiks.

The extinction of the male lines of the Piasts and then the Jagiellons let the nobles choose kings from the dynasties' female descendants, and each king on election granted privileges in his Pacta conventa, the basis of the Golden Liberty. By wealth the nobility divided into magnates, middle nobility and petty nobility, yet few legal distinctions separated them. In the 17th and 18th centuries the prevailing ideology was Sarmatism, which shaped dress, such as the żupan and kontusz, and made the sabre nearly obligatory.

Ennoblement was rare: about 800 lawful grants are estimated between the 14th century and the mid-18th century, and from 1641 only the Sejm could make them. During the three Partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795 most nobles began to lose their legal privileges and social status, and their legal status then depended on Russia, Prussia or the Habsburg monarchy until 1918. The estate was officially abolished in 1921 by the March Constitution.
